TL;DR AT THE BOTTOM
________________
Eeeeh... if you put aside all the broken promises, bugs and missing features HEX is a good game...
ONLY if you swipe that credit card or grind gold for hours so you can play one draft/get cards that are actually good.
(btw the starter packs are a huge ripoff, you're esentially paying 10 dollars for two rares; rest of the pack is bulk)
If you don't pay, you are basically restricted to few hours of campaign (it's pretty fun but almost impossible to beat with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ starter cards you get) or the Frost Ring Arena, which is the most mind-numbing videogame "feature" I have ever seen. It basically consists of you playing 15 battles against the same 20-25 enemies in a slightly different order each time you play.
If you want to do something that's actually fun in HEX without paying, here's what you have to do:
1. Grind gold for tens of hours in the mind-numbing Frost Ring Arena untill your eyes bleed or you pass out
2. Buy some boosters, open them, sell the cards to other people for platinum so you have the 100 platinum you need for an entry fee OR try to find someone who is willing to buy your gold for platinum (100 gold for 1 platinum so you'll need 10 000 gold)
3. Now when you have 100 platinum, you need 3 boosters (60 000 gold, if you have a REALLY GOOD deck you can earn around 7 500 gold in 30 minutes, but as a new player you're looking at roughly 5 000 gold for every hour spent grinding AT BEST)
4. Now play draft! Yay! But before you do, make sure you can stay glued to your PC for the next 2 or so hours because you can't leave mid-draft like in Hearthstone. You have to play until you win/lose or quit.
5. Sell all the cards (you keep the cards you draft) to other players so you can hopefully earn most of your entry fee back; if you didn't do well go back to step 1, otherwise go back to step 3.
TL;DR
If you're playing or have ever played + spent money on MTG or MTGO and have decided to stop for some reason, HEX is a good card game, BUT it is NOT a good videogame. If you're coming from purely digital card game like Hearthstone, wait a few years until HEX becomes playable without paying. By making a digital card game, HEX is competing with Hearthstone and not MTG like they intended years ago. Charging 7 dollars for a draft is a good idea when the competition is charging 14 dollars; however it's not a good idea when the competition is charging 2 dollars. The developers should take advantage of the digital platform and not force people to spend 2 hours playing draft.

If you are the fan of Heroes series and you can sleep without having all of it's releases - get it on sale (or maybe you can get it with the Heroes VII Deluxe? :)). Current Review:
Wild Warfare is one of those Early Access titles that came out too early. The content is too bare to really call it a game. Thankfully it is free to play, otherwise I would've just dismissed this game and called it a waste of money. Instead, I see it as a waste of time. There is very little content in this game, and it's in very early alpha. I find it a poor choice to release a public access to such a tile that has yet to offer anything really meaningful.

Xsyon Xsyon Xsyon...
What can I say to persuade you to play this game. Lets be up front... Xsyon isnt for everyone. This isn't a mainstream game. It's a niche game. A free world, open ended sandbox. Not sandbox themed. You get what you put into the game. There is alot of ambiguity, and alot of hiden mechanics that even the veteran players don't know. The learning curve is steep. If you have ever played any large space-based mmo's before their tutorial systems, you know what a daunting learning curve that is. This is no short-termed end-game. Here is what my personal opinion of the game is:
Pros:
Open ended, there is no end.
In depth crafting system.
Sandbox, full customization of tribal areas.
Very helpful player base, not alot of drama.
PvE or PvP Server option.
A VERY willing Developer who listens extremely close to their player base.
Big ambitions for future expansions.
Cons:
Currently a low player population
Steep learning curve
Hard to solo in the game
Slower development
While there are alot of reviews on the billing of the game, I am not fixated on subscriptions. It costs money to make a video game. Time = money. But to be a part of the metamorphasis of this game has beeen awesome. I have enjoyed this game solo and as a large tribe (guild). It is tough going solo unless you are near a larger tribe or willing to travel. That is what I ENJOYED as one of the challenges. The transparancy of development is a refreshing change and I truly feel the maturity level of the existing players is a welcome change. For those that are looking for the "next best thing", do your research. There are alot of apocalyptic games out there, this I would truly categorize as a survival game against the elements more than zombies, rogue bandits or space pirates. Watch your video clips, check out the wiki. I reccomend you overlook this game if you do not want to commit to a long-term game. If you want to be challenged, explore, and enjoy that liberating walk in the wilderness, then this game is definetly worth a try.
There is alot of fixation on billing. Dropping cash on any steam game is a gamble. If you put that money on an impulse you will always have it, yet it just takes up space on your hard drive. Do you actually play those 200 games? I have put my focus on the actual game play. I see it as an investment, and as a player in this game I make damn sure that my investments into the development get heard. It's ultimately up to you.
Frankly, I enjoy a polite, helpful global chat over epeen sword swinging egos boxing back and forth over who has the most testosterone. Steep learning curve? So what! That to me is part of the challenge. Experiment, ask questions, discover the game for yourself. You want this on a siver platter? Not going to happen. Solo play? Been there done that. I found spending time on the road to trade took too much of my time, but it was my choice to live in a place over 45 minutes real time walk from the nearest tribe to trade with.
Again, this game is not for the elite players. This is a casual game, a challenging game, and one worth getting into if you enjoy something outside of the mainstream survival genre. I look forward to seeing you ingame.

Yeah, this is the good stuff, this is a Very Me game. I wasn't a big fan of Big Robot's previous release,
- as much as the visual style and some of the sneaky-sneaky ingredients (and, yeah, the title) agreed with me, the constant tension of open-world survival is not really something I enjoy.
The Signal From Tölva (that's Alt-0246 for the diacritic; you're welcome) is a different beast. This is a very calm, quiet game. Yes, there are robot laser battles, and plenty of them, but they're sort of more punctuation than message. For me at least, the primary draw here is exploration and mystery. And rocks. This game has fantastic rocks. Seriously. I took a lot of screenshots because of the rocks.
Most of your time is just wandering the hills and canyons of this lonely alien planet, looking for signals and data recorders to scan as you work to find out what's so special about Tölva. The environment is dotted with wrecked machinery, strange rock formations and ancient ruins, any of which could hide answers, and as you find these snippets of data they're logged for you to read. So, you know, data logs, like in all those other games. Not a new thing, but
's are really nicely done; it knows not to tip its hand in lumps of exposition that nobody would ever actually write (hi, Bioshock-style audio diaries), and there's some genuinely interesting sci-fi involved. There are some other things you'll find which it's best I don't talk about.
I did say exploration is the primary draw here and yet I don't really want to talk more about it because, well, it's exploration. You probably already know whether wandering around sometimes-eerie alien worlds looking for mysterious artifacts is the sort of thing that interests you, yeah? So next, less mysterious topic then. In order to explore, you'll have to expand your reach - or at least, it would be increasingly impractical not to - which means capturing bunkers from enemy factions. And even if you're not heading to a bunker to capture, you'll periodically encounter enemy scouts and patrols in the wilderness.
Which brings us to those laser battles. First, like the rocks, these are Good Lasers. I like them very much. The guns feel great to use, consequently. Well okay no,
of the guns feel great: I didn't like the close-range sustained-beam weapons probably for much the same reason I didn't like Quake's lightning gun - they're not weak in mechanical terms, but they feel kind of weightless. Oh, and you can trade one weapon for a device that allows you to command allies to follow you, which can be very effective - they're no smarter than your enemies and "go there" is as much control as you get over them, but more firepower is more firepower.
Combat itself is kind of simple, and I was expecting not to like it. Usually a combination of instant or high-speed weapons, and no formal "cover system", just ends up feeling cheap (in both senses of the word), as you move out from behind cover and lose half your health from a hail of undodgeable fire. But actually I didn't feel that way here, and I think it's mostly down to the short-duration shield ability that absorbs some damage but needs time to recharge. It means that you can protect yourself as you emerge from cover, and between your shield, your damage-delayed slow self-repair for health, your need to reload and your occasional-use area-effect ability (can be healing, damage, distraction, something else), combat is
relatively simple (this isn't a game of fancy unlockable abilities) but there's enough different timing resources to balance in fights to make them quite a fun challenge.
Plus, you're not superman. The plot has you starring not as a unique entity in the world, but as someone offworld who's merely taking control of robots on the surface. Which means you have the same equipment and the same stats as all your allies and enemies. You can easily get overwhelmed if you pick a bad fight, and battles often have a real sense of
as you hide behind a rock on a sliver of health, waiting for your enemy's shield to tick down and hoping they don't round the corner before your rifle reloads. But it also means that if you do die...that's fine! Your robot died, not you - you just grab another robot from a location you've captured. Sometimes you can sprint back and finish the fight with your new chassis; other times, reinforcements might have arrived and it's best to rethink things. So there's no "game over", no need to reload, which is nice; you lost a battle and the world kept going, as it does. (This also gives a lore explanation for fast travel)
Really, all throughout, the game's just full of all these tiny things that I really love.
I love the proximity indicator for pickups and objects to scan. I feel like so many developers would have turned this game into a "check every single nook in every single cliff face" grindfest for secrets and loot, but Tölva doesn't do that: if there's anything to find, in a pretty sizeable radius, you get a little non-directional "getting warmer" meter until you zero in on it, which means if you don't see that, you can keep moving. On a similar note, while there are icons on the map denoting areas with collectibles in them, these are just relatively higher concentrations of the game's "credits" pickup. So you can gather them up if you enjoy ticking off map icons, but if you don't, and you don't want to check out the crashed wreckage at the site, well, move on, no stress. Tölva respects your time, basically - it
for some of the (what I consider unhealthy) collector-impulses that games have trained into players over the years, without
to them, exactly. It lets you be an explorer, not a cleaner.
I love that Because Sci-Fi, robots have coloured lights on them, which means that night-time isn't utter drudgery. Instead, I look forward to the sun going down. Sure, I may stumble into rocks during fights a bit more than usual, and obviously the joy of looking at the landscape takes a back seat temporarily, but it's lovely to be able to see the lights of a patrol crossing a hill in the distance, and high-contrast laser skirmishes have their own kind of immediacy that's quite different from the day, even if nothing much changes functionally.
I love that there's a button to turn the HUD off - I made heavy use of this for screenshots, and I wish more games would do it.
Oh, and there's a lorebook in PDF form, which is a great read for a backdrop of the game's universe. Not vital by any means, but if you're the kind of person who is interested in wandering around this strangely evocative alien world scanning data fragments in the first place, probably better-than-even odds that reading it is up your alley.
I've heard people say Tölva is a simple game, and I guess in a sense that's true, but I don't really think I'd use that word. I'm sure there's a degree to which the design
due to Big Robot knowing their limits and not wanting to bite off more than they can chew, but the game never really feels simple in the sense of only having few elements; rather, it feels
. All the empty design spaces another (bigger) developer might have filled in with jetpacks or special powers or loads of detail clutter aren't just nothing, they're important. The Signal From Tölva is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be, and, unlike this review, which is far longer than I meant it to be, does no more and no less than it needs to to achieve that.  I thought it was quietly marvellous.

The game had some enjoyable moments.  I didn't do all the item hunts but I did play all the missions.  Most of the combat was enjoyable and the game didn't overstay its welcome (or, less charitably, decided not to innovate on its iterations and opted for a smaller scope to accomodate).
But for the times where there was a difficulty spike or I messed up a mission?  Well, it's time for another lengthy walk.  And there's no autowalk hotkey (I had to script one to prevent me from pulling my hair out).  Oh and if you want to use the cool gun that makes allied NPCs follow up?  Then when you respawn you often have to decide between spawning nearby and not being able to use that ability (which takes up one of your two weapon slots), or spawning futher away and having to walk more.  A third option would be to swap out that weapon slot to a weapon, but to do that you would have to respawn further away, reconfigure loadout, and then fast-travel/respawn to the closer checkpoint (and then walk back to your destination).
Loved the visual touches, the alternate vision, the flashlight complete with high-beams, etc.  The last tier of weapons was overpowered and the last mission(s) were anti-climactic.  Taking down "tanks" (spiders) was rare, but pretty boring (time their weapon recharge rate with your shields, chip at their bullet spongyness, sometimes have to waste time blowing up a drone and then get back to work).
The narrative logs you find are nicely written and amusing, but got pretty repetitive.  Completing all the missions gives you about half of them, but I had no desire to hunt the rest because I assumed they would all say the same thing.  One of the two endings is very vague/unclear unless you've found a significant number of optional logs and/or read a lorebook.
I don't understand why weapons had tiers.  Basically there were four kinds of guns, one had three sights, one had two sights and two had no sights.  Instead of just giving you 7 options to equip, the same 7 options were repeated over and over with increasing stats (and different apperances).  You can also upgrade your shields and your AoE/special.  You get access to these upgrades by completing missions which make the items available to buy and then finding stuff/killing baddies to get cash to buy the items.  This system felt very "games these days need RPG elements" instead of adding to the game.  And the last tier of weapons was OP (which I suppose is good for people who want the extra help on the last missions, but as I mentioned before, it made them pretty anticlimatic for me) and not even fun OP with cool powers, just higher numbers on the same basic weapons.
But again... I finished it.  I enjoyed myself many times playing it.  That has to speak for something.  I am not upset about it being "short" (11 hours isn't really that short, and I do enjoy actually short games like Limbo and Inside).  But I just can't recommend it.
Anyone who plays this game for anything other than the knife has no soul and/or life. 10/10 would uninstall again.

3/4 of the way (seems like) through, this is one of the most "evocative" games I've ever played, ie it gloriously evokes the situation it sets out to depict. In this case, its the feeling of clanking around a specific sci fi landscape - one that looks like the wreckage 50 years after something off a Chris Foss book cover - as a specific type of adventurer, sussing out how a lonely eerie alien place works, with nice, light emergent bits dealing with the 3 warring robot factions (the shooty part of the game). I suspect low replayability (we'll see), since there are only so many ways to deal with the factions, but I'm 100% glad I've visited Tolva. Soon I'll find out if it sticks the story landing, but it would have to be mindboggingly bad for it to change my buy recommendation. If you're looking for replayability, you might be disappointed at $20, but as an experience, I found it 100% worth my time and money.

You Must Build A Boat offers several hours of frantic matching action that'd appeal to veterans and newcomers alike.
-charming retro graphics and soundtrack
-you not only get tiles to match but also one-use tiles for items,weapons and spells: there's also monsters to hire that provide permanent bonuses
-good quest system to clear the various levels
-a lot of upgrades for your tiles and items
-once you unlock certain NPCs you'll be able to tune some aspects of your dungeon run (higher difficulty and rewards,easier runs with no golds etc)
-smooth progression
-good sense of humour through the whole game
-new game plus mode,you go back to the beginning and must start over, but you'll get an higher difficulty for higher rewards
-some quests might be a bit frustrating, especially if you're trailing behind upgrade-wise
-despite the new game plus mode the game stays the same so the replay value is limited
-ingame monster/dungeon encyclopedia feels cramped and awkward to navigate
I'm not a veteran of the match 3 genre, in fact I generally am pretty bad at it and get frustrated pretty easily.
But You Must Build A Boat manages to give you a smooth enough progression and-eventually-enough control on how hard you want your run to be that I found myself enjoying it immensely.
Even when I got stuck it wasn't for long since a lucky streak or my upgrades eventually carried me over to the next quest: the pervasive sense of humour also helps to lighten the mood (e.g. why am I looting weird things from chests? why is the ship propelled by jumping up and down?).

Bought the game during the limited 500-copy test release they did in March, played around 25 hours total off-Steam.
The game has you take control of individual robots in faction war on a mysterious planet, covered in concrete ruins, derelict structures of unknown origins, and numerous destroyed spaceships.
For most time, you spend your time capturing bunkers/checkpoints, completing missions (which gets you access to better gear and progresses story), or looking for mysterious artefacts if you want to know more about what is actually going on.
The game is pretty. Really pretty. The art direction captures the game's "haunted wilderness" vibe perfectly, and it is nice to stare at the scenery or the night sky when you are not busy shooting anything. Sky and atmospheric lighting in general are particularly well made, making for numerous screenshot-worthy occasions during sunsets and sunrises.
Audio is good and noticeably paid attention to - weapon sounds are fairly satisfying, and the various robots make a variety of electronic noises. Audio depends on environment, such as hearing echoes within closed-space bunkers. Music-wise you are mostly left to listen to the environment, but conditionally one or other small track kicks in - sometimes ambient, sometimes mysteriously unsettling.
The game takes between 8 and 15 hours to beat, depending on how much you want to unlock \ whether you care for lore \ whether you want achievements. On the matter of achievements, unfortunately, these are largely of "do the thing a number of times" category. A few motivate you to investigate remarkable objects, and a few are blatantly grindy (such as one for staying inside a maze for an hour - the game autopauses and you thus you can't have it run in the background).
On downsides, the game is fairly resource-intensive. On my setup (a laptop with i7-5700HQ / 16GB RAM / GTX 970m) the game largely denies to run above ~45fps no matter what is done to it. It does not commonly drop below ~35fps either, so it's playable (enough to do 3 playthroughs by now), but still a bit of a shame.
One thing that I'd really like to see would be online multiplayer. Not "coop campaign" kind of multiplayer (things would feel less mysterious with additional player(s) jumping around you as you try to scan an artefact), but "custom match" kind of multiplayer - the game has a solid foundation for small-scale checkpoint based wars (see Running With Rifles), and yet there are only a few occasions through the entire campaign where you can get a big juicy gunfight. That said, however, I do not expect this to come, as if that was not actively considered in span of development, it may be very hard/expensive to do at this point.
Overall, The Signal From Tölva is a good game. Could have been better in some aspects, but regardless worth playing, in my opinion.

Very solid physics puzzler.
Maybe the most light hearted bridgebuilder in the genre.
There's three main types of constructing missions :
1) build a basic bi+ch bridge,
2) build a defensive bridge which the orcs will try to wreck with catapults,
and, the most fun:
3) build a cun+y deathtrap that collapses juuust right so that all the enemies' skulls get smashed!
The game doesn't lack depth because you can achieve these goals with all kinds of bridge types.
And after that you might want to perfect the design through shaving a few inches of wood off here and there to get a shiny gold medal in this age of achievement.
(By now it should be clear that if you don't like building stuff you should like, go, bro. )
BCM could certainly have a few more bells and whistles.
The game's medieval theme is as spartan as it gets but it works- going for a light hearted tone was a smart idea.
Sound effects are barely passable, although the main tune is nice.
Graphics aren't totally ugly but should work on a 10 year old graphics card.
Interface & controls are okay.
Most of the physics' particularities have to be discovered yourself, but that's also part of the fun.
All this doesn't take away much from the joy of engineering and tinkering:
The main process of building wood, rope & stone over medieval valley gorges works satisfactory and fluently.
The guild of poly-architects awards 3,5 sturdy crennelations out of 5,  for this edutaining time sink - quite nice.
(For hardcore bridgebuilders with wet digital mortar in their hair, BCM would score a bit lower. Theres not too much innovation going on here.)

I'd like to preface this by saying that some stuff I may go into may seem spoilery about how the game is played, but that being said the first three paragraphs and conclusion can count as my reccomendation. Also warning, essay.
I'm not quite sure what to say. This game blew me away. My friend recommended it to me and from what he told me I was expecting a linear story-based walking sim. As someone who like FPS Multiplayer games and Interesting Puzzlers it didn't seem like it was gonna be the game for me. But since I loved The Beginners Guide, I thought why not.
I'm so happy I gave the game a shot.
Firstly, I'd like to say that if you are the type of person that likes to get playtime for your money, whether that's £1=1h or £1=100h, this may seem like a hard sell. It's £15/$20 for 2-3 hours of gameplay, and not much replayability, apart from maybe going back for the achievements. But I'd like to say don't think of this as a game, think of this more as an interactive movie, in a sense. The game for the most part is extremely linear, there are a few bit and pieces of lore that you can miss, but apart from that if you follow the little white balls you'll never get lost. While this may seem like a downside about a game where you're supposed to be "Exploring" a house, but the sequence in which you explore it room to room aids you in understanding the timeline of this family your being introduced to.
Ok, to kick of the spoilery bit of the review, this talk about the bad stuff. First off, the FOV is locked at 70(or something close to that it felt) which coupled with how slow the walking feels going down the first long stretch of road at the start, really put me off at the start. Eventually when going throughout the house, and reliving all the stories, the walking seems to decrease in annoyance. The FOV being locked is because the animations are all made for that FOV, so editing it would lead to some graphical problems, and eventually I stopped noticing.
The next thing that irked me a little was the swing sequence, where you control the character swinging back and forth very fast on a tree swing. As immersive as the part is, it started to make me feel extremely nauseous. Especially since you have to play the sequence twice for the achievement.
The last thing i'd like to point out (and in hindsight most important review wise, whoops) is the lack of tutorialisation. Now, don't get me wrong here, the last thing I want is a walking sim holding my hand through all the "hard parts" where it can't tell me where to go as to not break immersion, and one of my favourite games of last year was The Witness because of how pure of a game it was. In short, Wild Warfare aims to be Team Fortress 2 with furry animals.  That lofty goal is however still aways off.  What you'll find at this early stage in development is some fairly crude stuff.  Notwithstanding, I've had fun with what I've played.
As with every Early Access game, however, what you're paying for is potential (paying if you buy the DLC, that is).  Right now I have to ask myself whether the devs aren't perhaps wasting a lot of effort with this game.  After all, we already have Team Fortress 2.  Why do a clone?  I would suppose the simplest answer to this question being -- why not do a clone?  If one thing is successful, does that presuppose that someone else shouldn't try to do the same thing and try to beat the original at its own game?  I mean, that's the core of virtually all business, isn't it?  All businesses try to do something better which others are already doing.
Since this is Early Access, prepare for some rough patches, including:
- few players
- few maps
- maps are overly simplistic, crude and small
- general lack of detail (and personality) with regards to character models
- low resolution textures
- gun models take up far too much visual space, blocking your view
- only three playable classes
- and they are horribly unbalanced
- stock music which doesn't fit the theme or the action
Right now, during Winter Sale 2014, the DLC pack is €0,41.  I've decided to buy a few and hand them out to friends to try and get the community going.  If the developers buck the Early Access trend and actually make this into a game worth playing, i.e. a product that rivals Team Fortress 2 for its polish and accessibility (while embracing the competitive edge lacking in TF2's model), then we'll be on to a winner.
In my opinion, there is a market for a competitive FPS starring cutesy animals wielding big guns (provided the guns don't block half the screen).  Now let's hope Hyper Hippo Prods. don't screw up their particular stab at that market.

so my thoughts on xsyon - I'd rank it a solid 7 outta 10 in its current state - it is playable and enjoyable - the graphics are solid for a early access indie game - for a sandbox game the grinding is not bad - compared to similar titles its down right pleasent - the game revolves on a end of the world scenario where people try to survive alone or in tribes while rebuilding - terraforming and building structures finding scrap metals plastics and other goods in rubbish piles or cutting down trees and getting rocks - fishing hunting or farming for food - all in all a pretty standard sandbox
so why should you buy it? The community while small (semi average for a sandbox indie) it is a polite and dedicated group - the 15dollars a month keeps most angry children and trolls from really being a threat to your gaming exp and to me thats worth it after having been trolled in dozens of games (didn't work but still is a waste of my limited time) with them randomly attacking me or blowing something up for no reason and taking hours and hours to repair (far more hours then it would take for me to earn the 15 dollars) so as such the monthly fee keeping the game going me not having to buy 25-40$ a month/week in cash shops to keep up with people and no paid expansion packs or DLC means I am exactly the same as everyone else in the game complete and total fairness - yeah skill based put into the game and be stronger not paid to win - the xsyon style I do enjoy the tribal indian post apocalypse blend, the several choices of buildings tools weapons and armor was very nice as I'm able to really create either a scavenger society of metal and tires or a pioneer camp of logs or even a grass and twig town allowing for large customization of my settlement
so now time for the pro and cons
- great sandbox building set with structures being as big or as small as you need with several varities of buildings fences and
- lots of choices for clothing weapons and tool styles each needing different resources
- limited grinding for resources or construction - moderate to average on skills high level skills actually making you work for them instead of being given to you.
- good blends of skill selection - starting kits tailored to your choices at start up - select axe as your weapon you get a axe select pick you get a pick ect ect - no starting short sword and shield generic kit
- solid community willing to talk and help
cons
-the games a bit confusing out of the gate - and needs a new tutorial / upgraded wiki majorly but after a week its not bad
- limited decorations for inside a house - outside a house plenty of choices but not allot of furniture rugs ect
- no current taming system - its in the works and I will remove this once its in
- combat is a bit hit and miss atm - you can kill most small animals (squirels hampsters bunnys) but they tend to run from you and the actual click to hit system is a bit sensative meaning you have to hit a small animal running through the grass
and its a bit difficult at times - they are supposed to be increaseing the hit detection area on small animals to remedy this and will be removed when added
- no ranged combat - only melee weapons sorry
- limited pvp - as the core game everyone uses is main job atm pvp feels a bit left out and the pvp server has very few people spaced far out on it.
the pro/con - this is the section that could go either way for you - some like these options some don't - and some I just have mixed feelings toward
-few to no trolls - might not be a big deal to you but I have a job / family / and life away from computer so knowing I won't have to log in and deal with some angry child blowing up half my town cause his parents told him he couldn't go out with friends is major bonus for me
- low player base - this is a game of hundreds to thousands not hundreds of thousands it is ment to be a small market game catering to the people who enjoy this kind of game not to the masses - to me this is big as finding a unique game mmo not just a mini run your own server game is a big pro for me as I feel like I know those around me at same time people get a bit quiet at times which can be a turn off for others
- many features have not been implamented - the current game is solid but allot of those I would really like features are coming but not yet in the game - while I can't wait for them to get in game I also can't wait. . . . seriously I want them now lols
so would I buy this game again? Yes - Will I play this game hard core for years? probably off and on yes like any sandbox this is a game you will keep coming back to once you have had your fill and keep enjoying it

I went through the campaign with a fireball ship originally, but then thought it would be funny to do it again with a warp-drive ramming ship. Come to find out, I was right. ... And the building field. it starts at 14x14, but can be expanded to 18x18 with some specialty parts. That's pretty big and all, but its still restricting. Aside from that, this game is actually pretty fun once you get used to the odd "space friction" and "springboard borders". If you like designing weaponized ships, this game is worth the buy.

Calling this game "Far Cry with robots" is a dissatisfying reduction of gameplay elements that doesn't begin to encompass the entirey of the game.
Well, that's what I'd like to write. In actuality, this game really is pretty much Far Cry with robots (I wish to emphasize this is not a criticism!), wrapped up in some interesting writing and existential postulating. But not too much existentialism. Just the right amount. Reading the snooped data from the hidden (from normal view) floating red polygons was the largest part of the fun in the game for me, because I live for that kind of gameplay experience. If you enjoyed the scanning mechanics of the Metroid Prime series, you're going to enjoy this game.
I found the mystery a little bit impenetrable without the context provided by the Lore Book, which can be read in the steam browser by clicking "Manual" on the game's library page or by opening the PDF found in the game's main folder. I caution players however to not open this book until after they have played some or all of the game, because most of it can be reasonably deducted or inducted by simply playing the game and reading snooped data. It's not precisely spoilers, but it does remove a lot of the interesting mysteries.
Actual gameplay itself is fairly straightforward (aside from the almost-entirely-optional "mazes"). If you're at all familiar with the Far Cry series, you'll find the game comfortably familiar, aside from the fact that there are no usable vehicles and hoofing it is a bit slow at times. Fast travel is acomplished by the amusing conceit of just taking over a new drone at the desired location. Weapons are a limited assortment of styles (Close Assault Rifles, short ranged continuous damage beams, long ranged high power rifles, scoped sniper variants of the previous, an always-equipped pistol, and the Phreaker gun that recruits allied robots to your party) with general upgrades and an assortment of sighting and optics choices. Shields can be activated and deactivated at any time, but drain power steadily when active. Managing shields is critical for surviving on Normal difficulty and above. Babying a squad of robots to your destination can be occasionally frustrating because of their poor survivability and the long cooldown of the group heal ability. At the end of the game I found myself running around without a squad because I was tired of sheparding them along. It got pretty hairy sometimes, but I managed. There's some gentle gating with needing progressively more interesting hazard protection, but it's not obstructive. The hazard areas themselves apply heavy visual effects that I found in succession charming, then distracting (but never boring). Fortunately, long ranged combat in hazard zones is extremely rare, so it was never a real burden.
As of this edit to my review there is a guide to the locations of the red Data Snooper collectables, but I can't actually recommend against searching them out like I did. Find as many as you can, but don't worry if you've missed a few by the end of the game.
Final Judgement: If you like exploring on foot, reading diary entries, and some light (but not undifficult) combat, you're going to like this game. If you liked the functional gameplay elements of the Far Cry series, you're going to like this game. If you liked scanning and reading the tidbits about the world around you in the Metroid Prime series, you're going to like this game.
Is it worth $20? Yes, but if you're not absolutely sure you like all of those things I just listed, wait for a sale.

Since you might end up with a slow ship that can't evade torpedos, it's literally impossible without raw RNG. The quality system for parts is very shallow and in some cases makes a part worse by causing the energy consumption to make it unusable, such as legendary fire rate. Enemy AI is terrible and often gets stuck on asteroids. Mostly-damaged enemies with working rockets can infinitely avoid you if your engines are damaged and make winning almost impossible.
On the good side a lot of the modules are very interest and unique and there's a few ways to build ships that I was figuring out, although getting enough missiles or carriers to do this was another matter entirely.
All the pieces are here for a great game, but they don't come together. If you like the idea but want better execution, go play Avorion.

I went from 10 dead and 2 crippled enemies in a wave mission to 12 brand new enemies and my ship still 2/3rds dead. What the heck? Condensed Warhammer 40k fun, razor sharp design. They took Dawn of War 1 and compressed out all the tedious squabbling for various flags and spamming massive amounts of units. You have four squads of the Emperor's finest. Every squad has a major strength you can control and customize with talent points as you gain levels (strong in melee, good at ranged damage, ranged harassment and camouflage, explosive, stunning melee jumps). When you work together, they become an unstoppable powerhouse capable of facing many times their number of xenos and heretics. This is good, because you will be faced with many times your number of xenos and heretics. Use them incorrectly, and all their weaknesses become exposed and your battle brothers will pay for your mistakes. You can't use all the squads you will have at once- which combinations will be the strongest?
Add to this the next element of what makes Warhammer40k fun- a giant pile of items, wargear, guns, weapons, armor, terminator armor. Grenades, flashbangs, health kits, mines. Each one has a noticeable effect on your total force's feel. Slain enemies drop green, blue and purple loot stolen from your chapter- when you take it back, it can make you even stronger, but you will have to make choices again. A lasgun can melt armored vehicles and extreme range- but is very slow for picking of swarms of infantry. A heavy bolter can mow down and suppress infantry, but is weak against armor. A missile launcher can rain down fury, but could be inaccurate when you need it most. Should your leader or your tactical squad take that terminator armor you just found? The synergy between squad composition, talents, items, and gear is amazing- there are dozens of ways to play and still win.
Test all the above in an engaging campaign storyline to save your sector from multiple initial threats- which span into a sector-wide conflict. You will track the campaign over the course of days- masterful performance lets you accomplish more missions per day, slowing the enemy and accelerating your progress. The more risk, aggression and mastery you can take on and still win, the faster your progress. But there is always more to do. Where should you stem the tide next? Which of the branching paths should you follow next? You always feel like you can do better.
The graphics are beautiful, the voices are true to Warhammer, the sound effects immerse you in battle, and even the music fits nicely into the world. They really polished everything about this game. It's fun to feel your squads grow into their full strength and realize more and more capabilities and synergies between them. You always feel like you can do even better. And as a very nice touch, at the end of the Campaign, you can save your squads and carry them directly into the sequel, Chaos Rising, with all their skills and even some of their gear intact. I usually see this game scoring in the high 90s and it deserves it. If you like nearly any sort of RTS, tactical combat, or anything about the Warhammer 40k universe at all, Dawn of War 2 is very highly recommended. Even moreso during excellent Steam Sales. It's hard to get this much fun for only a few bucks.

'Cupid' is a wonderfully constructed game that puts a twisted, out-of-the-box spin on the mythology of the Roman God of Love, Cupid. This is one of those stories best enjoyed going in blind. I would go so far as to suggest not reading Steam's extended discription, if you haven't already.
First off, if you do not enjoy horror/psychological games or visual novels, this game is not your game. It is long with lots of reading and it touches on several sensitive subjects, such as mental illness, suicide/death/murder,
, and sexuality.
If you don't mind any of that, I 100% recommend this game!
+ FREE! Though I would've been more than willing to pay
+ 6 plus hours of content (all endings and bonuses)
+ Fantastic CG & Sprite artwork (so many sprites for so many emotions, I love it!)
+ Several Bonuses incl. add-ons to the story, process & hurdles of developement, & an extra scene for laughs
+ Variety of music - always fit the mood, never got annoying/repetitive
+ Beautifully crafted story, characters, & gameplay
+ Unique player perspective and influence, compared to typical VNs
+ Did not romanticize the senstive subject mentioned above, which I appriciated
+ 67 Steam achievements - witty commentary and encouranges you to unlock everything
- Some CGs did not unlock through their appropriate playthroughs, had to speed through the game once more to obtain them.
- The Mature Content toggle didn't seem to do much - merely edited words/wording for less cursewords and sexual description of a scene, and less blood in the CGs. The differences were so small, however, I don't think it'd be of any benefit to those who don't enjoy the descriptions, curse words, and blood.
To wrap it up: Yes, I definitely enjoyed and recommend this game. It's free, so give it a shot.
I, personally, will be playing this developer's other game and am looking forward to more content from them.

The free Rusty Lake mobile games are basically room-escape games that establish atmosphere in the Rusty Lake world.  Rusty Lake Hotel is a creepy, short, can't-look-away room-escape game that is a must-play, for cheap.  This one, Rusty Lake: Roots, tells the story of the whole family in tiny little vignettes that are basically room-escape puzzles unfolded into one specific scene each.  As with Hotel, what happens to each family member is far more creepy than endearing, and it all comes together to keep you clicking along.
I was able to finish the game without hints in about 4-5 hours or so without getting stuck, but after the "final" big puzzle (no real spoilers ahead), the game uses two different mechanisms to extend the play time. One is satisfying (I zipped right through it) but the other is a clunky cheap shot.  However, I considered it worth the persistence it required only because I liked the final imagery tying this game to the previous one(s).
You can play this game without playing the others because the point of this world seems to be the feel rather than the plot.  And even though the game is at present still assembled like a mobile game, like Rusty Lake Hotel (it runs in a flash window and you may have trouble with your save file if you don't manage to allow Flash to use local storage), I consider it also a must-play if you like point-and-click puzzlers.

Fun  game.
The ship building is by far the strongest part of the game.  If you aren't into that aspect, pass on this game.  There are many components including many weapons, shields, armor, engines and more exotic things (hacking, grappling hooks, etc).  The only real complaint with this part of the game is some components are very poorly explained.  I still don't understand the point of energy chains, for example, even though I finished the game.  The only caveat with ship building is you have to earn the parts through exploration mode (it did look like you could maybe turn that off but I never tried it).  So you may not be able to build your perfect ship and it will take time for you to real use your creativity to make interesting ships.
The rest of the game is fun enough but could really use some more polish.  Exploration mode is what I spent most of my time with.  This is a campaign where you have to explore, meet civilations, do missions, buy parts and try and defeat the Von Neuman (the AI bad guys).  It is fun enough but could have been great with some more time.  The missions only have a handful of objectives so you will repeat these many times.  You even get mostly the same missions in enemy controlled regions (with basically two mission type exceptions).  After 10-15 missions you will feel like you've seen everything and just want to get more parts for your ship and get to the end.  Another problem is it is not clear how to stop the enemy expansion.  Early on you get some missions that will slow them down.  Later these mostly go away and for every sector you take from them you lose 1 or more in return.  Even the sectors you take don't seem to change hands and you don't seem to be able to stop the attacks from happening (they are marked on the map).  This definitely needed more explanation / feedback, if nothing else.
The other modes are mainly for testing your ship and goofing around.  Skirmish, wave battles, etc.  The exception is evolution mode.  The AI fights itself (without you viewing if you ever want it to complete) and the ships slowly evolve.  Very neat concept but it is too slow and has other problems.  It will sometimes build illegal ships and it seems to only hold 32 ship designs.  Those can get filled fast and you end up losing the more advanced AI designs.  Again maybe there are ways to get around these problems but it is not obvious.  The speed is the worst though.  Small ship designs can resolve in a decent amount of time, large ship designs not at all.  I gave up on that after letting it sit for many hours and only getting through 1 or 2 rounds.
In summary, worth your time if you like ship building and can put up with some rough edges and some underwhelming aspects that should have been better.  Probably best to get this when it's on sale.  Would really love to see a sequel with a campaign more along the lines of Star Control 2 or Star Flight.

-> Summmary
Their are fun aspects to HEX but because of the major gameplay system is tied to a simplistic resource system, the game becomes aggravating quickly.  Its a shame that (resources) system can't be adjust in the PvE parts to become far more interesting, instead of its simplistic nature.
Since this is a F2P game, I will look at it again only when it adds big or critical features, one of its major mechanics is just frustrating me too much right now.
--> PvE Content...
PvE content is spread out like an adventure on a big map, you go from point to point battling other AI opponents with your deck.  You are able to customize your deck, with equipment for the cards and with other cards in your library.  The story is written and their is no voice acting and it is very linear.  The battles can have some unique effects, but nothing really stands out as interesting.  There is no branching story options nor and any majorl RPG elements (besides Champions Skills).
An example is the Gnome Quest.  So your job is to bring back gnomes totaling 60, taking as many trips between 2 sections of the adventure zone with multiple battles.  The gnome cards get put inside your deck and are generally useless.  So the player has to grind many, many battles or hope that he can draw the card he needs without drawing the useless gnomes.  Makes me feel as if I am banging my head against the wall multple times, relying on luck.
Another example  Most of the difficult battles at the end end up being luck if you win.
There are other duels where you have to draw specific cards to win, which makes repeating the same battles many times.  That is horrible gameplay design theory or feature.
--> PvP Content...
There are drafts, game formats that you can buy into to play against other people.  You can also play in custom matches too.  All of the paying drafts have prizes too, in terms of ingame currency and Booster Packs (16 cards per booster pack).  There is no other game type formats besides 1vs1, would've really liked to see other multiplayer PvP formats.
There are free, one time PvP booster draft every weekend.
--> The Reource system...
Seems like nearly a direct copy of Magic the Gathering.  It is really basic with 5 differemt colors to seperate out the purpose of the 5 different colored non resource cards.
To summerize, boring and a direct copy of MGTO.
--> Crafting?
Nothing
--> A Wheel of Fortune, Kismet's Slot Machine
You get to use a slot machine to upgrade the chest you get from booster pack with better rewards (Eqiupment, cards, sleeves, mercanaries, etc) or get rewards for just rolling the slot machine.  The currency to roll is Gold, which can be earned by playing Arena or Adventure Zone.  Cool feature
-> Community features promised besides Auction House (See Kickstarter)
They would rather impliment new card sets, get monrey, because they apprently need more that what the backers gave them to finish what they promised,
-->Auction House
It works great to sell single copies of items/cards, but selling equipment or many commons on it when the player has many copies shows the Auction house needs some serious rework.
--> The parts that work well...
It is good that the player can buy and sell PvE/PvP, cards and equipment in the auction house system.  It has a good filtering system for the buyers.  The game board is layed out well with as many stops in the gameplay flow as the player wants.  The wheel of Kismet is good too.
--> That Frustrating gameplay mechanic...
In most DTCG the resource system is simplistic. A example of a simplistic system is hearhstone and Ininity Wars,  An example of an expanded resouce system in Faeria, also on steam.
Resouces are mixed into the deck, for HEX.  The recommendation for each deck in HEX to have for resource cards is 40%.  You start the turn taking 7 cards from the top of your deck.  Subsequent turns you draw 1 card per turn form the deck, you draw cards from there are a percentage of games that the player will lose because he does not get enough with his starting digital hand of cards or draws too many resources the beginning, including his cards he drew at the beginning of the games (@ 40% resources)
When you have played a lot of games and you still have the resource system do this to the player a quater of the time or more (at 40% resources) it gets to be a frustrating experience playing the game.  I cannot recommend spending money on this game to other people for this reason, though it is worth a try, as it is F2P.
I really wish the resource system was not simplistic (not including charges), that is my one major gripe for HEX.  It could have been so much deeper and interesting.  Its the one thing that stopping me from recommending this game, because it gives players a loss or win based upon random luck 1/4 of the time versus playing the game well.
While having 40% resources in a deck, still getting resources floods and starvation some of the time (recent dungeon lost 3 lives to resource disfunction with same opponent, sarcasitcally great gameplay).  I cannot keep my review at recommend this is getting frustrating to be losing by just bad luck, instead of not playing well.  Heathstone, Faeria and other DTCGs have a less disfunctional resource system.
-->  Last Thoughts...
Recommend try Faeria/Deulyst, both do more in its gameplay resource mechanics versus HEX just a direct copy of the resource system from Magic the Gathering.  For me it just doesn't have enough depth in its basic gameplay systems (including resources) for me to spend money on it.  I will continually give it a try though as it is a F2P game, every so often.

The beating heart of the game is still decidedly old fashioned, and a lick of paint and a few extra pixels here and there can't do anything to change that fact.
If you're a fan of the series then you'll likely lap up this portable version, and look past the little quirks and nuances that new players might find annoying.
If you've yet to play a Might and Magic game though, it's likely this one will leave you cold. The strategy RPG has moved on a good way since the game first came out, and it's starting to creak and groan under the strain.
The games sees you leading a hero through a map. There are areas to explore, loot to find, resources to nab, and strongholds to capture.
Start a fight and the view switches from the map to a grid-based battlefield. Here you'll pit your soldiers against an enemy army in a turn-based battle to the death.
Everything is controlled with taps, and the UI works reasonably well. It can be a little fiddly getting to grips with how everything works, and the two-finger-swipe scroll command feels a little cumbersome.
But there's a meaty, in-depth tactical RPG underneath all the retro stylings.
It can feel a little bland if you're not paying attention, but if you want to sink your teeth into settlement micro-management, resource gathering, and army-building, there's an awful lot here to grab your attention.
It's unlikely that Heroes of Might and Magic III HD will snag itself a new audience. It's a bit too fiddly, a bit too clunky, and a bit too cruel to appeal to your average mobile player.
But if you're a fan of the series this is a neatly realised, reasonably well polished port that should scratch an itch or two.

Note: I edited this review as I realized that a joking tactic just didn't work.
BossConstructor is a birds-eye view ship-to-ship combat game, utilizing pretty decent physics, a proper weight system that affects center-of-gravity and ship performance, and a variety of components for the ships themselves.
At the center of the game is the ship-building. While initially limited in your available materials, you can salvage modules from opposing ships, obtain them for completing objectives in levels, or buying them from a gambler station or a module trader. Your first ship is almost certainly going to be rather slap-dash. But as you progress through the game, you discover more modules, and more variants to them all.
This is the point where some people just stop playing, as they don't like the RNG aspect. However, that aspect doesn't play too much of a role in the game. Your success and failure both depend on your ship and how you built it, and how you use your ship. I'm not saying it's purely the player's fault, as I myself have been sidelined by a torpedo numerous times, or been rammed to oblivion. Just that maximizing strengths and minimizing weaknesses is key.
Rambling about gameplay aside, the game's performance on devices is mixed. On the older HP Notebook Pro that I mostly played this game on, it would run quite well, with occasional freezes that required a force quit via Task Manager. The computer itself had problems running pretty much anything though, including the Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, so it was to be expected. On my Macbook Pro, it runs like a dream. On both it was smooth, with lag only appearing on the old HP when hundreds of ore, modules, enemy ships, and projectiles were flooding the screen.
Overall it's an enjoyable game to just play for a while, and experimenting in ship construction in the hangar is fun, as is testing those creations out in the skirmish mode. Whether you wanted to be a stealth ship that seeds the area with mines or a factory that produces suicidal drones equipped with torpedoes, a jack-of-all-trades or a nimble speedster or a hulking tank, you can most certainly be that in this game, provided you spend some time discovering those modules you want for them.
I recommend this game despite it's faults.

I bought this game over a month ago and have not regretted making the purchase.  Please note that although my playtime record on steam is low (0.7 hours at the time of writing), it does not give a true reflection as I prefer to use the main Xsyon client - as do many other players.
There are a couple of issues that I have noticed that have crept up on the forums.
1) Subscription. Yes this game is a subscription based model. I know a lot feel its silly to charge a sub for this game. But actually having written in the official forums about possibilities of being free to play, the developer has actually tried testing out different pay models (including changing the sub fee). It was found that free to play created a destructive element in the game, in that it brought players who were not good for the game. Some of the players resorted to exploits, botted and even caused a lot of tension/drama in global chat by being rude/abusive (hence the reason why the majority talk in tribe chat and not global).
The Cash shop idea. Wouldn't be good, Basically you are asking the developer to concentrate on making things for the cash shop rather than developing things for the game or patching bugs etc.
2) It's Alpha. Well the developer has already commented on this. Basically it's on PRELUDE. So no, it not Alpha or Beta but the next step beyond that. I'm not paying to test a game. I am paying to play a game that is playable and published. Fact is that a majority of MMO's are never truly "finished" on release, hence why there are patches and expansions.
3) Player numbers and community. Steam stats do not reflect true numbers. Majority of players still use the Xsyon client via the website as it was the default thing to do pre - steam. It's also a fact that a majority only speak in tribe chat. In the past a lot of drama was caused in global chat which became really problematic and had to be sorted out by GMs in game.
The community overall is very mature and helpful. There are many vets who are happy to answer questions. Do understand though that timezone may affect peak hours for this game. I believe the majority of players are in the US/Canada timezones.
Now onto the game
The game tries to be as realistic as possible i.e. meaning you wont be able to kill bears until you have honed and got your skills really high. I believe people have high expectations from the get go and get disappointed because they cannot do the things they want to from the off. Sorry folks but this game is slower paced and longer longevity type gameplaying. Meaning be prepared to put in some hard work before expecting to be able to tackle some of the high end stuff.
1) Crafting and resource gathering. Lot's to craft with many more crafting skills planned for the future.  You will need to either trade or gather resources to be able to craft. Be prepared to spend a lot of time gathering resources so you can grind your craft. Crafting and gathering also have a bonus in that each craft skill has a primary and secondary attributes. The more you use the skill, the more likely that the associated attribues with the skill will raise. For example, doing logging will increase your strength and agility. Making you a better fighter.
2) Hunting and combat. Yes you can hunt stuff but you have to start off small i.e rats and chickens. You also need to locate them first before being able to kill them. After you kill critters, you can improve your hunting skills by skinning, gutting, decapitating etc. Don't expect to move up quickly as it will take a while to climb up the hunting ladder. There are also zombies called Revenants. Do not mistake these for players. If they kill you, they take your gear and use it. So for every critter that kills a player, they "grow" and increase in strength.
3) Thirst and Hunger. Yes you have to manage these. You can fish, forage or farm for food to eat. For thirst you can drink from rivers or fill and carry a waterpouch with you. There is a balance though as overindulging will give you penalties. Become hungry or thirsty and you don't regenerate health and energy. You can die from prolonged thirst and hunger just like in real life.
4) Health, Energy and Encumbrance. All of these can be improved as you keep grinding the associated skills. For instance grinding on a skill that increases your strength will help improve the amount you can carry and therefore your encumbrance levels.
Health is self explanatory. When it reaches zero, your dead.
Energy is basically like stamina. When you perform actions, it uses stamina. For example you can only sprint when you have more than 50% Energy. Once it reaches 50% or less, then you can no longer sprint, just light jog. When you run out of energy you have to rest or stop your action.
Encumbrance levels is your carrying capacity. Basically if you are carrying a lot if items, it will be harder to run and uses more energy doing so. One of the ways to make this less of a problem is by using a cart to transport goods.
Death has no real penalties at present.
5) Tribes. I was lucky to find a nice tribe. Personally I think it's helpful to get into a tribe early on. You can solo but expect to work a lot more. Tribes give you an advantage in that they can give you tools and food so you do not have to worry about it and can concentrate on your skills. Also having someone to give you advice or answer your questions is nice to have. Also large scale building projects is very demanding and much more easier to complete within a tribe and fun too!
Like I said I'm still having fun but it's not a game for everyone. The game requires patience and work before you see any progress  - just like in real life. People who have high expectations of being uber in the least amount of time and effort need not apply!
I wish people would try the game and give it a chance before turning a blind eye to it. You never know, you might enjoy yourself.

Numerous minor issues prevent me from recommending this title.
The upgrade vendors for sword/staff/shield show what the upgrade will do... sorta.  Current stats are not displayed prior to committing to an upgrade purchase, and then only briefly.
Forcing me to click numerous times to "get" the upgrade I just purchased, or to break my loot out of a crate, is mindless busy work, and the exact opposite of fun.  (the swipe right to open a reward chest is... tolerable)
The screen shake when selling loot is unnecessary and awful.
The artifact that makes matches possible at the start of a run feels like a punishment, not a benefit.  More often than not, it leaves the board thin of matches.  On a related note, the Matterhorn activation is incredibly jarring; the damage hose is nice, I guess, but it disrupts whatever I was trying to do on the grid.
Being a tenth of a second off on your timing invalidates whether a match is applied.  The monsters don't have to approach formally and present a Document of Formal Request to Fisticuffs, they just start swinging... why do I?
The RNG _does_ feel super capricious.  Just beat a monster, and can see a chest behind him?  LOL, we're gonna throw keys in the right spots to wreck all your easy matches!!!  Hope you weren't planning on gaining ground anytime soon!!!  LOLOLOLOL  Two monsters in a row?  Nah, we're all out of swords and staffs... try back next week.
The area progression curve is a right angle.  In spite of all the issues above, I made steady progress until Pagoda... then I slammed into a brick wall titled "grind for upgrades, nub."

Signal from Tölva is an open world FPS where you take the role of some faceless remote operator hijacking bunch of drones in order to investigate mysterious signals on the planet Tölva. The core loop consists fo walking around, shooting enemy robots, scavenging resources, conquering bases and spawn beacons and scanning for signals, which then reap rewards in the form of new equipment in the next base, as well gradual increase in rank, which represents a simple leveling system.
Different signals reap different rewards and you can see them beforehand, which help if you're looking for that particular piece of gear. You can also get a robot-hacking -weapon, with which you can hijack 1-4 (depending on your lev... rank) friendly robots to help you. The command scheme is limited to one command: go here. When near enemies the robots start to fight on their own.
The game has pretty solid shooter mechanics, and the combat feels good most of the time. Weapons break down four different types: rapid fire laser, particle beam thingy, sniper laser and robot hacker thingy, plus a weak-powered sidearm. In addition you have shields, which need toggle and consume energy, plus a few varying AOE weapons such as damage at AOE, heal at AOE, make enemies flee at AOE and an AOE stealthy thingy. All equipment have a few variants, but the stats display is somewhat lacking, e.g. displaying just DPS instead of rate of fire and damage per shot is kind of uninformative. Unless you grind the enemy robots you will never have enough money for everything, so it's unlikely to have a try at every possible weapon or variant, which is why I just went for the highest DPS rapid lasers and robot hijack weapon. The AOE options do offer a few interesting playstyle variants.
The game's narrative consists of robot-voiced non-sense narrated dialogs with your "Broker", ultimately your only ally in the job, as well as bunch of text pieces you get from scanning the story items and a few other random data items.
The backdrop and narrative is very interesting and well-written, and together with the game's visuals they paint a beautiful narrative landscape, and a world to explore. The first few hours are full of excitement and curiosity as the world reveals itself slowly. Also epic fights in the night middle of night are a beautiful sigh to behold, with all different colored beams painting a gorgeous picture of destruction. Very 80s, very nice.
For a 20€ buy, it's certainly not a bad game, offering easily over 10 hours of gameplay, however after the first few hours, the action starts to wear down a bit. The open world is great, but running around gets tired really quickly, and there's no auto run. Granted, auto hotkey or programmable keyboard macros are easy enough, but for this kind of game, it should've been a no-brainer to implement.
Aside from a few issues such as getting stuck on couple points and a texture clipping issue on high fov, I didn't experience many bugs, and none of them significant. Game also ran flawlessly with GTX 1080 supersampled to 4k resolution (I have 1440p screen).
I did enjoy my time with the game, though I am glad it ended when it did, since after a point, not too far in the game, it stopped being exotic, new and interesting, and started being a pretty mediocre shooter. There doesnt seem to be much overall choice in whatever you do. Sure, you're free to get whatever signal you want next, but in the end you go through everything, and repeat the same things all over again. Some parts of the environment are gated away by environmental hazards which require you to scan specific signals in order to obtain the equipment to scan them.
Overall, the game lacks any in-depth mechanics whatsoever and feels overly simplistic. For an indie game, the lack of experimental gameplay is very disappointing. I was hoping to at least encounter more different enemies, some kind of more advanced tactical mechanics, or have greater customization in regards to your abilities (like customizable robot parts for various purposes), more different types of weapons, with much more info on them, maybe some crazy procedural stuff etc. Instead, now I have mediocre open world shooter that's beautiful to look at, with interesting and well-written background story. In the end I felt... unimpressed.
I like the effort, but I can't fully recommend the game. While the environment, visuals and background story are excellent, the game design falls short, and core gameplay feels sadly lacking. At least check several gameplay vids before buy.

The premise is simple.  You must build a boat.  It's a tile matching RPG/Dungeon crawler where you play as a guy who must build a boat and by matching tiles you attack, get items, and get resources to progress your quest.  You can, effectively, never lose this game as after every attempt you get a "You win!" text because you will progress, albeit sometimes slowly, towards the end goal.
It was a fun romp, I must say.  I paid $3 for the game and it took me 7 hours to complete it, partially because I'm bad at puzzle games and match style games so that didn't help, so I'd say I got my moneys worth.  It has that "One more run" feel until the final area where bad luck and RNG come into play much more so then the usual amount.
My only major complaints for this game would be sometimes the game didn't react to my mouse clicks properly and I've missed many matches because of it, which would then cascade into me losing the level.  If I could change one thing it'd be the ability to store a match I made inbetween running from critter to critter because you need to clear useless tiles on the board during your brief respites but far to often would I match tiles when approaching an enemy expecting it to go through only to have the game decide that despite me being stationary I wasn't yet "active" to attack thus wasting time and possibly losing the round.
Overall though, it's a fairly enjoyable puzzle match type game that serves well as an IOS game and as a short time waster.  I'm not sure if I'd say it's great for $5 but I have no complaints at $3.

To clear things up, this is NOT a stealth game. It is not about sneaking around guards. It is about setting up electric devices in a building to set off other devices to create a Rube Goldberg effect to eventually activate the doors you need to open in order to proceed.
Which would be fine, but people looking for Mark of the Ninja or a typical stealth heist game need to be warned.
My problem was the gameplay being too tedious and the rules being too inconsistent to form any kind of puzzle solving strategy. And even if the rules did work like they should, it's too simplistic to be enjoyable.
Each electric device is connected to another, such as a lightswitch to a light or a palm scanner to a locked door. You can change the connection between 2 devices by re-drawing the conencting line, for example changing it so a lightswitch is connected to a locked door so that flicking the switch now unlocks the door.
The problem is the game VERY quickly is reduced to the exact same procedure: guards walk to the nearest lightswitch and flick it when the lights go out, so you connect devices to turn off a light to get a guard to trigger another device, by either the lightswitch or a motion detector he walks through on the way to the switch.
They try to change it up by introducing new twists such as different color devices and only devices of the same color can be connected, but it just makes it more tedious instead of more interesting. There's no creative puzzle solving because when there are only 2 or 3 devices o the same color, it's immediately apparent which device you'll need to use to trigger which, it's just a headache to map out the order you have to do things in order to reach it. Would have been a lot more fun if they got rid of the different color nonsense and just left you with an open sandbox building with tons of creative ways to use any devices you wanted, even giving you bonus points for setting up longer "combo" chain reactions. Anything would have been better than the "make the guard fumble for the switch" mechanic the whole game is based on.
What finally killed it is the rules just seem to stop working periodically. It's established in an early level that connecting a security camera to a device will activate that device whenever you step in view of the camera. Except on a later level you  connect a camera to a trap door and nothing happens. Or you connect 2 motion detectors to doors, open the doors, but suddenly the 3rd motion detector will not open a door you've connected it to. I stared at the connection for 5 minutes trying to figure out why it didn't work and couldn't see any reason it wouldn't.
I could have looked up a guide to solve the issue but at that point I had lost any interest to bother. For a better, simpler, FREE version of the same game, I recommend downloading Trilby: The Art of Theft (made by none other than Yahtzee of Zero Punctuation fame!).

This game is one of the best indie games I have ever played. This game is really cheap and offers a LOT for its small price. This game has the gameplay of the original Halo Combat Evolved and the environments of Minecraft to make a creative shooter experience that has never been done so well. I started playing this game 3 years ago on Xbox 360 and I've just moved to PC and I have 10+ hours in counting in just a month. Unlike other indie shooters it has a focus on skill while most are like generic Call of Duty minecraft reskins. Starting off you will be given a choice to create a character which isn't really the best I have to admit but there is enough to "pimp" your character. Then you have the  simple and bland offline or multiplayer. Unfortunately this game is really just a multiplayer game because all that is offered to you without Wifi connection is zombies and the PC version does not support split screen as the Xbox 360 version does.  Moving on you have standard deathmatch, TDM, CTF, Infection, Zombies, and Yolo Mode(Murdergames for Xbox 360 veterans). While both deathmatch variants are pretty simple in objective, Murder the Flag(CTF) is the classic team flag capture game mode. The funny thing is when you "murder"(capture) a flag, you can hear moans that is kinda creepy though...Moving on, zombies is a bit different than your average game. In Murder Miners, zombies are fast and attack you in packs so you BETTER run! And even worse they can even break blocks. Be sure to play this mode with a buddy or you'll be dying fast! The only problem is that the zombies are a bit dull. They all have the same objective and just continuously come at you. But there is also INFECTION! You can be the zombie and compete against player ones too. This is probably the most popular mode for the game by far(I advise you always use a shotgun btw). Being a zombie brings a new play style. You can tongue grab your victims and can level up! Then Yolo mode is really just a 1 life only game mode that can be fun and tactical. Aside from its game modes you can customize your match and lobby as you wish with many options and moddifications. Yes there are vehicles in this game, but only two. There is a hover bike which is really used for fast transportation but also a attack hovercraft known as the Murdership which fires meteors but very slow. And finally-the game has map creation. You can make your very own maps for FREE! Its not easy though, and the map creation honestly isn't much after placing blocks. You can change the skybox, make blocks undestructible(the game has destructible enviorments!) and some other stuff too. Then you can play it and have your dream battle! Even better you can upload it to steam workshop to share your map with others or get maps from the community. You can have intimate 1v1 matches or have all out 30 player warfare! The biggest concern for this game is the lack of lobbies played on PC which honestly has a lower player count than the Xbox 360. But the developers of this game is working on a sequel and it looks great with better graphics and new mechanics(see it on youtube). It still a work in progress but soon we the players will play this new great sequel! The developers of this game are bringing back something I haven't seen in many games these days-ambition.
