Out of all the games I've gotten on Steam so far, this is the first one I've felt like writing a review for, mainly because I see a lot of potential in this one and hope for it to succeed. So keep in mind this is my first review and it
for an Early Access game.
This game is a sandbox through and through, focusing obviously on the construction of a customized ship and then allowing you to test it out within various game modes from a full campaign of sorts where you establish yourself with different factions that each have their focus on research types, a survival mode, random missions and more to come I am sure. Sure, there is no story, save a generic themed enemy that apparently is a threat for some reason, but let's admit that isn't what people play sandbox games for.
There is already plenty of modules for making the ship function the way you like to play. Want a gunship? Make it happen. Want a ship that has more versatility in tools and tech? Do it. However, at the current point in the game, it feels like there is very limited uses for many of the different techs already available, and in time I hope to see more reasons and uses for it all.
Graphically speaking, it's nothing impressive, but there's plenty of particle effects to keep things flashy enough to keep my attention. I still get the inner satisfaction when I destroy enemy ships to say the least, and the effects of the weapons and other modules feels appropriate for what they are/do. The music does its job at setting the feel for the missions and stuff, but tends to get a little repetitive after awhile and I have begun muting the music to play my own during my long sit down sessions with this game (three in total so far).
(Things I believe will probably get better as development continues)
Overall this is a very entertaining experience for me, as I keep spending time trying to tweak my ships to be more streamlined, or trying to upgrade my modules. For an Early Access title, this one is one of few I have felt is worth the asking price, though I happened to find it on sale and became my replacement for another game since I can't play (and have chosen not to) Galactic Civilizations 3. With the level of customization, replayability due to a variety of game types, and the fact that the developer seems to be actively engaged with the playing community and offering frequent updates, I suggest you take a look at this game if it happens to be your cup of tea. Being still in development, it has plenty of potential to become a gem in my library.

After completing Dark Fall: The Journal, I was very eager to try out Lights Out. This game did not disappoint. I was a little bit suprised at the science fiction tone that the game took near the end, but it did not spoil the overrall experience.
I really don't want to spoil the story. Suffice it to say, you begin in 1912, then travel to 2004, 2090 B.C., and finally 2040 A.D. to solve a mystery surrounding the lighthouse on Fetch Rock.
I love the look of this game. My favorite parts of the game is when you are first discovering the lighthouse in 1912. The attention to historical detail is wonderful, and I enjoyed learning about the responsiblities and the characters themselves. It is also, in my opinion the creepiest part of the game. Exploring the lighthouse proves to be a dark and somewhat claustrophobic experience. You hear the ghostly voices of the men who have disappeared. There is great use of ambient sound, slight hints of a musical score, and sound effects. With this game, the scares come with the general creepiness and uneasy feeling of being alone and yet not alone in a lighthouse at night.
The puzzles can be somewhat tricky. Imagine if Myst were a horror/ghost story. The interface is the same as Myst which may annoy some, since you have to be at the right angle to be able to see/find key objects or solve puzzles. The puzzles will require taking notes, since there is not an in-game journal. Also, you will be reading a lot! It is very apparent what to take note of, especially if you have played Dark Fall 1.
This game has been said to be weaker than Dark Fall 1. I don't think that is very fair. The location is different and the story has more of a science fiction feel, due to the time travel. However, I do not think that this game should be called worse. It is different, and it is a fun play. I know I will definitely be playing this in the future...it'll be a lot easier since I saved all my notes!

If you enjoy puzzles and stealth games, you will probably enjoy Gunpoint.
The Good:
Using the rewire tool was fun.  I can't think of any other game with a similar mechanic.
I enjoyed the plot and futuristic noir setting.  The plot does branch, even though the levels do not, and your decisions do effect the plot and ending.  Be aware that reading is required, so if you have an aversion to that, this is not a game for you.
The graphics and sound settings PC gamers expect, and configurable key bindings, are provided.
The Bad:
Gunpoint is a
name for the game.  It has caused some customers confusion and disappointment.  It should have been named Rewire, or something similar, since it is impossible to complete the game without using the rewire tool, but it is quite possible (and recommended) to complete the game without using the gun.
The gun only has 6 bullets, and must be repurchased to replenish it, none of which is explained.  You are punished (via lower pay, lower ratings, and higher difficulty) for using it.  If you try to use it to threaten, but not shoot, guards, you will usually just get killed.  The game would have been better off without it.  People looking for a mindless shooting experience would be very unhappy with the puzzle-heavy content of the rest of the game.
The game is short, but I do not fault it for that.  The plot came to an end when it felt like it should have.  Using filler to bloat the length, as some recent games have done, would make it less satisfying to me.
I think the game is overpriced.  $2 to $5 would be fair for the 2 to 5 hours playtime most people are getting out of it.
The gimmicky blogpost as a real web page in the ending upset my anti-malware software, and is another feature the game would be better off without.  A real private eye with any sense would not publicize anything about their cases anyway.
The Ugly:
The graphics do not scale, and were clearly designed for extremely low resolution, making it very hard to see at high resolution (e.g. 1080p).

Beautiful and unique graphics, and incredible concept and atmosphere - but I'm afraid the frustrating gameplay overwhelmed them all for me. The mechanic of "forgetting" means you spend a lot of time spinning in circles, which is not great for motion sickness. This is particularly problematic for the level where you need to jump across turning cogs, whilst spinning around to make new cogs appear. This leads to many frustrating deaths, and it made me so sick I had to quit the game several times. I'm just not sure "atmospheric psychedelic mind-bender" and "frustrating platformer" are two categories that go well together?
It's also often not clear what you need to do - to the point that it can become annoying. I like surrealism and not being spoonfed, but some puzzles I completed without even knowing why or how. I'm not sure if there's meant to be a story or message we are supposed to follow, but the voice over phrases came across as nonsensical and therefore pretentious rather than genuinely deep.
I really wanted to like this, but I feel like it's a bit of a wasted opportunity. I know I've been predominantly negative, but I liked this enough to want to keep an eye out for what the developers create in the future. I really hope they build on the graphics and the atmosphere they've created here and move in a slightly different direction for their next game - hopefully more towards atmospheric exploration than face-palming platformer.

Before I get to the meat and bones of my review, let me first address one thing: this game came out in 2001, and as I write this review it is 2017. This means that Gothic is SIXTEEN YEARS OLD. If you are going to try and play a game this old on a modern OS, then you had better expect to have to do some workarounds, extra downloads, whatever. The fault is NOT with the game anymore than it is with Windows. It's just a case of the game getting old while operating systems continue to advance. Heck, I even had to get a workaround for Fallout 3 several years ago, and the game wasn't all that old then.
Anyway...
I'm coming from the world of Bethesda. I'm an old Morrowind veteran, and I've toiled around in Oblvion and Skyrim (though I've never finished Skyrim for reasons I won't get into here). So, when I first saw a video of Gothic a few weeks ago, I just knew I had to have it.
I hate to compare apples to oranges here. Morrowind is what it is, and so is Gothic. While I see some similarities between the two, they go about their objectives in very different ways.
Getting dropped into the world you soon realize just how cutthroat it is. As soon as you get dropped into the pond at the beginning, you get punched in the face by some random dude for no apparent reason. Then you meet Diego, who eventually takes you under his wing. If anything, getting into the story in Gothic is much quicker than it was in MW. For one thing, there is no character creation. You are what you are... A level 0 PC with NOTHING. This is the first RPG I've ever played where you start not at level one, but at ZERO.
I admit, I was first put off by the combat system. I found the controls tricky, and some times frustrating. But after getting used to them I've come to realize that with a lot of practice, you can actually get away with things at an early level that other RPG's might not let you do. And that summarizes the beauty of Gothic. You chose your own path, your own way of dealing with things. Even though the story itself is fairly linear, and even predictable, you're not always locked into a particular way of doing things.
One of my favorite things is the way that NPC's react to some of your actions. In Morrowind, you could go into the middle of a town with your sword drawn and no one would say anything... at least not until you tried to chop up some unfortunate passerby. You won't get away with that in this game. Keep your weapon drawn, you'll get one or two warning. After that, all bets are off.
Same thing with entering someone's hut or house. You'd better be prepared to defend yourself if you outstay your welcome. Especially in the Old Camp.
Overall the game is difficult. I would dare even say it was more difficult to learn than Morrowind was. But for some reason I can't quite put my finger on, it seems to be more enjoyable than MW, at least some some respects.
I also like that there is a clear indication of progression with the Chapters. When you reach a certain point, you get a loading screen with a new chapter number on it. It's weird, but nice to see that.
I was at odds with the levelling system for awhile. I still am, truth be told. Levelling up your strength and dex makes a certain sense. And I can deal with the fact that I have to find people to train my character. But there are a couple of skills that seem useless, or more of an after thought. Like Acrobatics. Yeah, I can do forward flips now, and I do go a little bit further, but so far it hasn't proven to be worth the wasted Skill Points.
Lock picking is also hit or miss, and levelling up only seems to decrease the chances of breaking a lock pick, but I can deal with it.
Gothic is not a perfect game. There are some glaring flaws in the formula and the way that it's executed. But I can look past most of it simply because the world feels more alive to me than it did in MW. The NPCs do things that make sense. And the fact that you have to learn different strategies for fighting the wildlife, makes the whole levelling up thing more worthwhile.
You have to work for it in this game. But in the end, it's worth it. I haven't yet completed Gothic, but I'm already starting to look forward to playing Gothic II. I just wish I'd found this game sooner.
I give it 3.5 out of 5 stars. Highly recommended, especially if you like a challenge and immersion.

The Signal from Tölva, a mysterious name inspired by the icelandic word for 'number prophet', which transcribes to 'computer.
The game starts by a cinematic intro of your faction 'Broker' uploading you into one of the planets faction 'The Surveyors' Robot, blending you in with them as they are friendly/neutral with you.
You get three guns, a powerful pistol, a mid-long range assault rifle and a strong sniper rifle.
You are introduced to a small tutorial that gives you all the information you need to get going with your journey.
Once you get the hang of the controls and the abilities of your robot (you have an activable plasma shield and various spells/abilities at your disposal) you are sent to explore the area and investigate about the signal on this planet called Tölva.
The graphics are astounding, the atmosphere is STALKER-ish and the music has an eerie feeling of deja-heard from Silent Hill.
You will be fighting against two factions, the Zealots and the Bandits.
The Bandits fight for territory and will constantly assault your bunkers while the Zealots are more interested in the ancient relics and ruins which they will protect tooth and bone.
The Surveyors, your faction, will help you out by capturing, assaulting or exploring with you.
It is appreciable that the ressource system is unlike the other modern AAA games, you collect orbs/cubes that give you a currency called 'Ressources' which you will use to upgrade your characters weapons, abilities, armors and hazard shields.
There is a day and night cycle and each has an unique and aesthetic look to it, nights are dark and gritty, reminding you a lot of Kholat, while days are shiny and blinding akin to Far Cry.
There are many subtleties to the gameplay elements presented to you but i will leave the mystery for you to solve, for a low price tag of 19.99$ the game is very well worth a buy.

It plays a lot like FTL but focuses more on exploration so it's pretty chill. It feels like a mix of No Man's Sky and FTL minus the combat.
I can see why people would get frustrated at this game. Discovering new tech, lifeforms, and planets is satisfying, but In the end it's technically RNG. The strategy is all about priorities. It requires good inventory management. You have to balance the collection of rare resources to build new tech, space in your ship, and vital resources like fuel and oxygen. You have to judge when it's best to invesigate and land on planets and do random events vs. just moving on, ignoring everything except vital resources and then racing towards the end until you have to slow down because of bad luck, then possibly adding or replacing tech because you get a new ship or discover something worth taking time to craft. It creates a nice cadence.
The story is pretty good. Each time you get to a new solar system there's a random event. Sometimes it's choices you can make, but other times it's just story elements about what you as the character are going through being in such desolate isolation for months, even years depending on how long you take, and how your sanity begins to degrade. You start hallucinating, stuff like that.
If you have a really good run, the game is beatable in as little as 2 hours start to finish, but it would be incredibly rare to finish in a single run the first time around. I've only beaten it once so am not sure if there are multiple endings, but the one I got was satisfying.
It has a fair amount of replayability as well. For $10 I think it was worth it.

Original Review (Thumbs Down)
=======================
PROS
1) Friendly community
2) Not as P2W as Hearthstone as you can farm gold to buy stuff so much faster. I absolutely love this.
3) Players who prefer the PVE aspects of TCGs would find a lot of things to do here (+make your blood boil too, read cons).
CONS
1) Game is laggy as hell. Why the hell is there a delay and rubberbanding of cards when I'm playing VS AI????? Hearthstone could do it smoothly and I'm playing with over 300ping against other LIVE players.
2) Campaign makes my blood boil. As a new player coming into TCG, my first choice would be to try the campaign out. So why exactly are the AI card draws fixed? The 2nd boss you'll face called Savage Lord plays a 6/4 + 5/3 card on turn 2 EVERY SINGLE TIME. The only way I managed to beat him was by pure RNG luck draw. This is a really great way to turn away new players like myself who are scared away by MTG and Hearthstone but want to try a new TCG. It would be so much better (and fair) if the AI's draw is random.
3) Auction house constantly freezes and takes a long time to load.
Every CON that I've stated above can be fixed and I will change my review once I see it. I really want to like this game  and I've bought the starter pack and spent another 5EUR to support the dev team please don't let me down guys.

In theory this game could have been great. I really liked the different milieus and the genre shifts. There were moments when I was genuinely spooked although I knew there would be no jumpscares and no possibility of dying. The gameplay mechanics were however so frustrating that I can't recommend this game, even though I personally enjoyed it because of the story.
Cons:
- the disorienting and dizzying task of trying to find every possible viewpoint to find the one exact view with an essential item or secret, with the added bonus of some locations (caves, rocks, vents) being impossible to navigate without going in circles FOREVER.
- accidentally doing a one-way teleport and having to take the long way back
- accidentally going through the same lengthy conversations with no option to skip them
- said conversations and ghost soundbites being much too repetitive
- the ghost hunting elements of the game being sort of... light and decorative, with none of the hands-on feel of the first Dark Fall game
- getting stuck because of the aforementioned navigational difficulties and not even being able to consult a walkthrough because this is the Director's Cut of the game and some of the puzzles and hidden locations have been changed.
That said, the game isn't impossible to finish with some good guesswork. If you're a fan of this developer's games and tricky point-and-click mysteries, you could give it a go. I kind of wish I'd listened to other reviewers and skipped this one in favour of Dark Fall: Lost Souls, but on the other hand this game does dish out more of Jonathan Boakes's worldbuilding which I do enjoy.

This is not a bad title, it is just very under-implemented right now. What does that mean?
It means that the premise is pretty solid: cartoony animals duke it out shooter style, with each animal being it's own class and filling certain niches on the team. There's even a big mech already, so that's good. And the guns looks more or elss like Nerf guns, which is the kind of hi-tech blocky look I can get behind. :)
The down side is, there are only three classes... and each class has exactly 1 weapon. Slow heavy badger(?) with a chaingun, middle-speed average-sized raccoon with a 3-round-burst rifle, and a rabbit with a wrench (he is called the engineer, but cannot build or repair things that I know of). So, the makings of some good class warfare here, but there are not yet enough thigns to differeniant them.
Potential, though. Lots of that! You can already imagine in your mind what future classes they might add, and it's not as if there is a lack of inspiration for extra gear. There is a crate system, which as far as I can tell, is cosmetic-only items and I don't believe you can buy them: crates drop from players, and keys are given as you rank up (I could be mistaken, but that's where it seems to be right now, which is good).
So hey, this is a free-to-play early access game. That means you won't pay anything but your trime to give this a download and shoot some stuff up. I think that this game is worth following, as it has the potential to shape up into something really fun and relatively unique in the world of shooters. :)

December 2017: Changed review to Negative as Crytozoic actually let players lose their accounts on the Gameforge servers when it closed down and didn't bother to create a backup account for their players. The P2W is also another major problem. I've lost my old account as well. They have a new update but it's the same game. The blatant copying of MTG's format even after so many years is destroying the game. You would think that there would be some major change after closing the Game Forge servers, but no. There is absolutely no change.
Note: Hex is done by Cryptozoic Entertainment.

1. Interesting Storyline/World
Basically divided into a centuries long battle between light and dark, with the Ardent as the light and the Underworld as the dark. A long time ago, a meteorite crashed onto the planet creating magical shards and everyone called it Hex. The meteorite also brought along some undead called the Necrotic. The Necrotic was attacked by the Human, Elves, Coyotyl
2. Hero Powers / Charges
There is a way to play even if your hand is full of mana-producing gems called Charges. Once you get enough charges, you can use a hero power to change the gameplay. There are usually a couple to choose from.
3. Interesting Races
8 in total
Ardent - Human, Elf, Orc, Coyotle (coyotes)
Underworld - Necrotic, Dwarf, Shinhare (bunnies), Vennen (spiders)
The standard Tolkien fare of Human, Elf, Orc, Dwarf and Undead have been used and re-used so many times that it's a given cliche. It is pretty interesting to see the Coyotyl which are based on Native American tribalism, Shinhare based on Japanese Imperial rule and Vennen based on an insect Hive.
4. Classes
3 main classes :
a. Cleric : Pray, Shard Attuned, <Racial Talent>
b. Warrior : Battle, Shard Attuned, <Racial Talent>
c. Mage : Replenish Spell Power, Learn Spell Soothsaying, <Racial Talent>
I expect Warlock, Rogue and Ranger classes to appear in the future.
December 2017: There is a Ranger class.
All races have access to the same classes. What I like about the variety is that while the basic skills are the same, the racial talent will vary depending on what race you picked. There are also Race-Class Combos which pair up with the Racial Talent ensuring that different heroes can change how a deck is played. I am expecting more classes in the future which will probably follow the standard World of Warcraft model.
5. Campaign
The campaign is pretty impressive. This is the one thing that I would recommend to people. There is a narrative and a proper game with a leveling up system. It's a pity for the ridiculous exchange rates.
6. Abilities that will be a Hassle in a Physical Card Game
a. 2 random troop cards in your deck get +1/+1, next troop in your deck gets +1/+1
To be totally fair with physical cards, you would need a 3rd party to randomly search through all the troop cards and do the above by placing markers on the card. If you do it yourself or get your opponent to do it, there might be cases of cheating or information given away.
b. Summon a Random Creature
You can't do that with physical cards. You would need a list, a proxy card and list of random creatures to randomise with.
c. Socketing
You would have have to prepare a marker in the card to show it's additional unique ability.
1. Pay To Win
This is really hardcore pay to win. You can't even grind to catchup. The 200 Platinum required for a pack is ridiculous. That averages out to $5 per booster pack minimum. It usually costs more.
2. Ridiculous Grinding / Exchange Rate

This is a delightful Sci-fi walker with punchy combat and an intriguing mystery
Let me break that down, Sci-fi of course is the setting that sees you take over chasses of the Surveyor Faction. Your interest is the eponymous Signal emanating from Tulva. The only problem is that there are many many many other signals that you must sift through to find the mysterious one
The walker aspect defines the majority of the gameplay, you're walking to areas of interest, through 'mazes' and around regions to pick up resources. I call it a walker vs. explorer because the entire map is revealed with big points of interest already labeled. This is not a bad thing at all but don't expect never ending worlds.
The combat is short, brutal, and really fun. You have a sidearm and 2 weapon slots. You can fill those weapon slots with better variants or tools that allow you to form a squad of other Surveyor robots. The guns sound amazing!!!! They have all earned spots in my list of iconic weapon sounds (Titanfall's Hemlock, CoD M1, and E11 Blaster to name a few) they sound great and feel powerful. Enemies are smart, will seek cover, and attack in groups, you have to be careful.
The mystery is intriguing and though I haven't beaten the game yet, I am excited to find out what it is. Writing is well done and the mood is very well set.
Finally is my descriptor as Delightful. That is they only word I can think to describe, nothing feels like a chore or drags on, the landscape is beautiful with an amazing sense of scale, and many times I've had a big grin plastered across my face for intriguing things that come up, and when the mystery is done, you still have great long range combat to enjoy.
I'd love to see this setting and systems expanded upon

I don’t normally write reviews on games, but I felt like I should for such a remarkable VN.
CUPID is a deep, psychological horror Visual Novel that tells a story you won’t forget for a long time. It’s something you won’t be able to put stop once you start because it constantly leaves you wanting to know more. And for free no less!

A thrilling, powerful yet dreadful business love is, when its whole content and capability is considered. It gives birth to all kind of miracles like affection, sympathy, passion, anger and even redemption. Yet I'm not penning this review to inform you about the package love may drop on any sane person to portray a new psyche. I just wished to take a moment and celebrate the creator of this visual novel for her in-depth and through understanding of the concept, with all its bliss and dread all the same. It is not love letters, bright sunshine and butterflies all the time. It grows, it consumes, it hurts... and that lecherous winged Roman god, Cupid would keep smiling all the same.
In 1600s France, we are invited to follow Rosa, a beautiful yet troubled young orphan, led by the sound of her mother in her head. She'll soon discover the whole content there to be for love, gain a family, lose a friend and decide the fate of the one she loves/hates the most. Any more specific storyline description would present complete spoilers, thus, I'll avoid telling you more of the story. It should suffice to warn you that this game is most assuredly +18, dealing with both explicit and gruesome topics like abuse, self-mutilation, mental instability, suggested incest and detailed sexual narrative once or twice. If you feel like you might be offended or this might simply not be your cup of tea, pick something else.
is an astonishing visual novel in both its thematic choice and narrative, which surprises me even more that it’s a freeware. The concept is slightly influenced by Roman mythology, with a darker approach to the subject compared to Renaissance idealism. There is a certain elegance in its narrative display, a hint of literary education and eloquence, and a philosophical undertone for the concept of love and human nature itself. There are sharp twists in the story masterfully presented that will keep you on your toes: from light-hearted to shocking, from fleetingly beautiful to despicably banal without a warning. All characters involved are presented with genuine depth and they harbor many facets of the human soul. They are anything but one dimensional or stereotypical. All five different endings of the visual novel rely on another concept that might born out of love; most gruesome, some heartbreaking... all bitter as the end of any love.
Display is more than appealing, with lots of beautiful CGs, elegant character designs and fitting artwork. The soundtrack brought together from a wide selection - from classic to romantic baroque, from Mediterranean to dark wave - is another proof that labor was put into this work. The game bears many choice option which may alter the ending and takes 7-8 hours if you are to go for all ending.
Take one evening, and let your heart whimper under the brilliant narrative. Take the crushing role of Rosa's mother - the voice within her head - to either lead her into wild retribution or mending compassion. You'll be astonished by the end.

Rememoried is a decent enough game with some smart ideas that shoots itself in the foot with shoddy gameplay, which is always frustrating to witness.
The main gameplay mechanic is the ability to ‘rememory’ objects (mainly platforms) by looking away, meaning the world changes when it is not observed. That’s a good idea, but it doesn’t make a good game alone. Despite being compared to and tagged as a walking simulator, Rememoried is actually a confused puzzle platformer, where you spend half your time stuck on levels whose solution doesn’t make a lick of sense (BECAUSE SURREALISM!) and the other half on drawn out, poorly-designed platforming levels where the camera, the jumping mechanics and the hypercontrasted graphics all conspire to make you fall to your death for the umpteenth time in a row.
But maybe the point of the game is the story!…except there is none. And i don’t mean « the story is confusing or barely hinted at ». I mean there are approximately two lines of trite « spoken word » per level (all of which i’ve heard about as many times as i restarted the levels, i.e. way too much), and they aren’t exactly mindblowing (« Logic is a dogma. » HOW PROFOUND.). Admittedly, the game is definitely surrealist in its lack of a defined narrative and its interest with dreams and how they shape memories, but here’s the thing: this kind of contemplation simply doesn’t fit in a game burdened with sloppy gameplay. There is nothing dreamlike or surrealist about the mechanics of the game and to me, that’s why it fails completely.
I truly wish Rememoried were an actual walking simulator, because it has a great soundtrack, a beautiful aesthetic and some truly captivating moments that made me feel like i was experiencing something different and unique to the game. But those are few and far between and I can only recommend this game as an interesting but failed experiment.
As an aside, the description states that failing a level brings the player back to previous levels. As someone who has failed every level it was possible to fail, I can say pretty confidently that this is not the case anymore. Don’t get me wrong, THANK GOD FOR THAT, but it’s something you might want to take into account.

The Signal From Tolva is an open-world game about surveying an alien planet littered with abandoned and derelict technology. Along the way you fight other factions trying to seize and understand the planet too.

As you achieve these goals you unlock new weapons, armour, abilities and most importantly a tool which lets you add friendly robots to your squad, letting you take on bigger objectives and make strategic movements.
The game is very very pretty, and has a lot of atmosphere (as well as collectibles and codex entries if that's your thing). Factions can clash with each other, dropships crash into the ground from space to reinforce positions as you attack, and the planet holds a bunch of secrets. I'm really enjoying it so far.

So this is the second game I've played from Big Robot, the first being 'Sir, You are Being Hunted'.
Signal from Tolva doesn't feel entirely different from SYABH, in that you are roving an alien countryside shooting/being shot at by robots. SFT gets rid of all of the stealth, roguelike, horror, procedurally generated, and survival aspects in exchanges them for actual combat, a light upgrade systems, territory control objectives, a pretty big world, and some basic squad capabilities.
Gameplay consists mostly of running from objective to objective, capturing bunkers, activating spawn beacons, and collecting resources. You unlock more equipment by finding and scanning signals, the same process by which you slowly rank up and earn the right to actually wear various guns/gizmos. Despite the actually quite large number of guns you unlock, none of the first ~12 I unlocked felt that different. Essentially you had assault rifle, sniper, and the 'Recruit-a-Robopal' gun (which technically counts as a weapon, and occupies one of your two weapon slots).
All in all the game feels solid, if not barren. The dynamic encounters are nifty, even from the small number I encountered, and the landscapes and 'buildings' are often interesting. However the game simply feels like it could be more. There really aren't a ton of decisions to make, or play styles to choose from. You capture various points around the map, and gain control of regions, but there are no obvious reasons to ever backtrack since enemies never try to recapture your bases. The only benefits you gain from capturing a region seem to be that you will then spawn patrols which will occasionally help you out (not that you really need it).
The robots companions are cool, and it was certainly fun sending a bunch of robo-rookies to their death/glory, but the fact that they are all identical, never communicate, and are robots made them feel ultimately pretty soulless, so I didn't really care when mine died, or didn't die, since I didn't actually need them to succeed anyway. It was a fun addition to the gameplay that up until that point (and after my robopals had all died) consisted almost exclusively of 'Shoot them in the face from very far away until they all die'.
The game is fun, and light, and I think it best plays as a sort of dyanmic sandbox in which you and some robotic goons can mess around and shoot some dudes. For that, i do recommend this game, because its pretty dope when you look at it though that lense.
That being said, if you're looking for a deep tactical game, challenging FPS, or an openworld custimization/progression based 'conquer the bases and expand your territory' (eg shadow of morder, farcry, etc) look elsewhere.
I'm looking forward to the next step Big Robot takes with its games, since this is a huge leap forward from SYABH, and shows a lot of promise.

A interesting RTS but sadly I can't recommend due to a few too many bugs and issues that hurt my experience with the game.
==Bugs/Issues==
1. Units getting easily stuck - Many times I have had units get stuck in the map. For some reason having a massive army moving all at once ended up pushing some of my infantry off the walkable path and into a rock, getting them stuck forever.
2. Path Finding - I found the A.I path finding for both your units and enemy seem very weak/stupid. Many times I have ordered my units to go a certain route only to have them do the opposite. You will need to baby sit your units a lot. Another good example is the air transport...many times I order them to land on a large flat land only to have them fly somewhere else.....like into the middle of a enemy AA defense system...
3. A.I - Many times I found my units get attacked only to stand there and take it or would follow the enemy unit to the other side of the map. This bothered me a lot since many RTS has a basic system where if a enemy attacks them or near them they will engage and if the enemy unit flees then your units retreat to their last position.
4. UI - I found the general UI works but sadly the map and the information given to you is broken. I found many times I would get a warning about units under attack only to find nothing and other times find my forces are truly under attack but will not get any warnings about it. Overall a okay RTS but nothing too amazing.

Dawn of War 2 is a great game.
(for simplicities sake I will include small references to the expansion Chaos rising here)
If you played the original series and loved it, DoW2 is a bit of a departure from the old format but is none the less very enjoyable
Overall -
New mechanics, taken from Company of Heroes, such as a retreat function
More defined rock/paper/scissors
No more base building. In multiplayer you now have one Building from which everything is produced which you can level up through technologies advances
New race - Tyranids (Space dinosaurs)
-races available - Space Marines (super soldiers in space), Orks (they are Orks in space), Eldar (Elves in space) [chaos rising] Chaos Space Marines (Evil Super soldiers in space)
Campagin - quick overview
The campaign (in which you can only play space marines) is now a squadbased/rpg esque series of missions with different characters that you can level up/give different gear to and, in chaos rising, you can corrupt them, turning them to the ruinous powers. The campaign is fun. Missions are often 10-20 minute affairs with varying objectives. The units that you control are powerful and you will smile as 10 Space marines chew through a good 5 tyranids. The campaign is Co-op as well which is fun to play with a friend. Max level for you characters is 20 and chaos rising pushes it up to 30 and adds a couple characters.
Multiplayer - quick overview
In multiplayer, mostly you will be playing matchmaking (though im not sure how much of a community there is so you might be searching for quite a while but if you get it with friends it is still fun) with the sole objective being point control. Resources are gained through capturing requisition points much like in the original DoW. Power is now generated by holding power points and building power generators on it. The four races are all unique and fun each having their own strategies. You can level up all the different races with cosmetic details as you gain experience for games.
Last stand - quick overview
Last stand is where you pick one character, which you can level up to level 20, from one of the 4(5) races (you have access to all of them no DLC unlike in retibution). Then you and 2 other people have to withstand 20 waves of enemies. A simple wave survival game mode but very fun when you get to higher waves and you have to fight 50 space marines with armour shredding plasma guns.

Alright, upon completion of SunAge's campaign, And having spent as long as I have upon the game itself, I believe I'm capable enough to write up my thoughts on the game as a whole, however I will get one thing out of the way first.
I liked the game. It was fun, it was intriguing to see where the storyline went. Not the best, but 6/10. Now I'll go into detail.
Campaign: The campaign follows through a strict 25 mission storyline detailing the whole reason you're playing it. You start off with the federals who act like a tutorial, the rakk-zun, the middling segment where you feel powerful and capable of doing anything, and then the sentinels, where the game kicks up into a higher gear. I will point out you are forced to go through this style, as playing with the sentinels and rakk-zun first would mess up the whole storyline.
Factions: The federals are us, fleshy weak human people, armed with by the book technologies and following strict rules. They play more as anti infantry and have solid defenses, but can be considered as an allround race. Their unique end game unit/capability is the ability to enact WW3 and nuke everything into oblivion with tons of silos. In reality their artillery is turned into a laser pointer for the people back home to realise where to launch the nukes.
The Rakk-zun are mutants, heavily mutated in the barren wasteland we technically call home but in reality is the worlds greatest dumpster fire ever invented. They give off an almost tribal feeling, with their own religion, beliefs and rituals. The Rakk-zun focus on maneuverability and ever encroaching walls of units and metal. Sound confusing? Well they are. They have potent anti infantry vehicles that can turn into flamethrowers, potent rocket buggies that turn into maneuverable anti air, mutants that become immortal but die of a heart attack, and walls of metal which can either explode or turn into artillery. Their special unit/ability is The Spawn, which I didn't get to play around with at all, however I believe it's quite powerful, seeing as how it summons endless waves of god forsaken sea serpents with which to bite your enemy into submission, or y'know, burn him to a crisp and then bite him. They also have the ability to convert all resources into blue fairy dust, which I'll explain later. On and their defense is rubbish, flamethower turrets and a beyblade frisby anti air system. woot.
Finally, the sentinels, who are Artificial Intelligent robots with mysterious designs, a vaguely futuristic feeling and an inherent feeling of them getting the short end of the stick. They play mostly defensively, with impressively strong defenses and semi useful units, ranging from two legged mechs that will die quite quickly to anything except laser damage, but fires lasers itself and also a minigun if you get the upgrade, to a walking gorilla mech that shoots lasers out of its eyes and has a frankly useless alternate attack. They feel really off, with their early units getting most of the attention while at most a couple measely upgrades being given out to later units, which I barely used anyway.
Combat: Combat in this game is fun, but confusing. You can't select all your units at once and charge at the enemy, because it's more squad based than that. You select a squad and tell him to move somewhere, and then select another squad and repeat. You can select multiple squads with shift clicking, but none of their abilities can be activated unless you specifically click only them, presumably due to jealousy.
The pathfinding in this game is frankly horrific, and I've played through the whole damn game with it. Aerial units will take a long way around to a target, fly around a bit and settle down like a dog getting comfy, positioning my units felt like dragging cement bricks around and selecting their formation was also horrificly bad. I'd often waste a couple minutes trying to get my squad into a certain formation but being off by one or two in either direction, so too much like a line formation, and far too close to a column formation, combine that with the pathfinding and I nearly gave up on the damn game.
Targetting an enemy structure is also off putting, as I'd tell my units to attack a target, and they'd switch out of their alternate fire, and probably die in the next three nano seconds. Why can't they just target what I point out and upon issuing a move order, they then switch out of the alternate fire if need be? It doesn't make sense otherwise. Oh, and speaking of targetting, the range system got me so confused at times. In some cases I'm firing halfway up the map with artillery, and yet I'm having trouble shooting something practically half a building away? What?? It felt like the developers just stuck a circle as the range, but forgot that due to a semi isometric view, we can actually see further. Oh and it's the same shooting down, which never makes sense.
Bugs and issues: I didn't find all too many bugs with the game itself, it was quite a solid game, even if it had some inconsistencies within in-engine cutscenes. However one bug I did encounter is during the mission Assimilation, upon trying to enter a transporter during a cutscene, the main hero won't actually enter the transporter, and will force you to restart a very long and very painfully drawn out mission.
Speaking of issues, there's something wrong with the difficulty in the campaign, as in it's just plain not working right. The final mission of the federals started off painful and actually caused me my ONLY mission failure in the entire game due to difficulty. Every other time was due to me being stupid and letting the hero die but that's besides the point. The final mission of the Rakk-zun is a piece of cake. It's not a threat, it's not challenging, it's just long and tedious. The same can be said for a number of other missions where the AI doesn't even do anything.
The final mission of the whole game has a federal base built up like it's prepared for a fierce war, and yet they're having trouble with a frankly pathetic rakk-zun outpost that lost all ability to build upon losing the slave workers they had. I never got attacked in that mission by any force of a dangerous size or composition at all, and that's just wrong. It's the same for other missions too, I didn't have any threatening attacks. The hardest mission I had in this entire game was two missions before the end, because mutants are apparently really good at killing robots. And I will point out they didn't even go for the optional objective, or at least tried and failed so poorly that they gave up. Speaking of;
Difficulty: What on earth happened? I've mostly stated what I want to above but good grief. Some missions kicked my♥♥♥♥♥until I stuck it through, others got so boring I completed them without even touching my keyboard (final rakk-zun mission). I will point out right now I played it on MEDIUM difficulty, however I still expect the ai to function during all the missions, as well as feeling at least some kind of threat, even if it's because of the AI building up a steamrolling military.
Overall: SunAge: Battle for Elysium is a pretty unique base building rts with a fairly engaging storyline, interesting unit variations and abilities with an added spice of unique factions to boot. It has its short comings, and flops in a couple areas, but it kept me entertained until the end of the campaign, which says something about both the game, and my patience.
Would I like to see another game like this, such as a sequel or a similar use of the mechanics: I would love to see an updated version of the mechanics with far less bugs and pathfinding issues, since it's uniqueness kept bringing me back, and it's why I bought the damn thing after the sale ended for it. Maybe another game, since a sequel after that. frankly boring ending wouldn't exactly work. Good job, keep up the brilliant work, and I hope the next game (if any) outshines this one and its pathing

Summary: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II is set in the grim, war-ravaged world of Games Workshop’s Warhammer 40,000 universe – a dark, futuristic, science-fiction setting where armies of technologically advanced warriors, fighting machines and hordes of implacable aliens wage constant war. Dawn of War II ushers in a new chapter in the RTS series, as ancient races – including the dauntless Space Marines and savage Orks - clash across ruined worlds on a mission to claim the galaxy and preserve their own existence. Powered by the re-vamped Essence Engine 2.0, the next evolution of Relic’s proprietary game engine made famous in the award winning Company of Heroes, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II delivers fast-paced RTS action with ferocious melee and ranged combat in fully destructible environments. The game immerses players in an in-depth non-linear single-player campaign and a fully-co-operative multiplayer mode
Dawn of War II is an excellent game in its own right. However, it is easy to understand how fans of the first game feel slightly wronged after having played it. It is very different compared to the first game, perhaps too much so for it to be called a direct sequel. But if you only look at it as a game it is still quite a great one.
The visuals are very nice and the gameplay is fluid and fun. Dawn of War keeps setting the standard for visceral combat in the RTS genre. Dawn of War II is an easy recommendation for me to make it is one of the best PC games in recent times.

I made a tiny map that consists of a house, fence , tree and garage, in 4 hours. making walls should be easier, and hills are impossible: you have to click block by block

First off, I just want to give a big shoutout to the people involved in the making of this game, it's quite amazing for such a small team, the graphics, the sound, the units, it all feels professional and like a high quality indie game. However there are a lot of small bugs.
A bit of a detailed explanation of the specificities of the game compared to other RTS I know:
+All units have 2 modes that can be switched without cooldowns (for example heavy infantry can switch between rocket launchers or mortars) it can also switch between anti-air to support heals and so on, however the alternate mode must be researched first in the research lab
+There are 4 ressource types, 1 is the base ressource widespread all around the map, easy to find, the 2 next are more rare but still common and each associated with a different type of units, vehicles or air units, with some subtleties depending on each faction, and the last one called Iberium rods, is very rare and allows to research powerful endgame techs and units.
+The game sports a unique system of power line via a complex network of electric towers required to have buildings work.
But theres also a big lack of polish on the core mechanics that make a good RTS good.
-First of all pathfinding, oh my goodness .. regardless how good your micro is, you will encounter units doing the opposite of what you ask, that's the way it is in this game, deal with it... either going the opposite direction, attacking other targets, ignoring orders and quite frequently.
-Selection tool, Basically the selection dynamically creates groups of 25 units max of the same type and move them automatically in formation, so while it may sound like a neat feature to sort units into groups quickly, in practice, combined with the poor pathfinding, it makes selecting the right units without moving the others quite a nightmare forcing you to use the alternate selection mode (basically the regular selection method but you must hold MAJ and lose accesss to custom formation when holding right click). The selection tool has I think unecessary innovations or perhaps just poorly implemented ones that it add unecessary micro for no real benefit.
-Units collision, another aspect of pathfinding here that is problematic, there is some degree of unit collision which tries to prevent several units from clipping into each other but here it is set way too high and prevents from positioning units where you want to and creates more unnecessary micro management plus a sense of not being in control of your units.
(Particularly so in this mission where you need to avoid areas of lethal gaseous clouds but your infantry just keeps happily jumping into it).
-Putting infantry in an air transport, again, this seems very specific, but it happens a lot in the campain and seems highly bugged, sometimes happening instantly teleporting all units at once into the vehicle, sometimes taking forever because some units is stuck somewhere, sometimes seeming to be done but all units pop out of the transport when it takes off, etc... in short, it's clunky, as is the way air transport land by the way, sometimes they circle around 3 times while getting hit before deciding to land, sometimes they land directly but no where you want, sometimes they take off just when you select several of them because of the automatic formation thing, etc...
So overall its a original game  with a lot of hidden depth, and neat 2D art that I think looks stunning. I just hope there will be some sort of quality of life patch because there is definitely a game with a lot of potential spoiled by minor issues here, good intensions and good ideas but also perhapsa lack of polish on the core mechanics like simply moving units around is often either overly complicated or a bit bugged.
As for the multiplayer unfortunately there is nobody left to play with online anymore.
However the solo campain is fulfilling on its own, it's long and varied enough and does a good job at teaching the game various mechanics, I just wish the story was maybe a tad bit more original like the gameplay is, but it does the job.
It's a mixed bag, I personally enjoyed it quite a bit (and I only made 1 of the 3 campains!) but be aware of the issues I mentioned before you set on buying it.

I paid a little under $5 for the bundle which included both Rusty Lake games. I regret buying and playing both of them.
This game in particular has the superior story, is longer, and... more puzzles. I don't say better or worse puzzles because while it does have some more challenging ones (in a good way) than Hotel did, it also has some that are harder (in a bad way) than Hotel.
There are intriguing puzzles that caused me to really think and learn throughout the game, but there were also janky kinds of jigsaw-puzzle areas that wouldn't function properly when you tried to "snap" the pieces in place, making it all the more furstrating trying to even solve them. There were also of course, the same kinds of puzzles that were in Hotel where you figure out the solutions either by accident, clicking things randomly and using your items on every possible item until something happens. It's a very mixed bag of super creative puzzles and god-forsakenly awful puzzles that make you want to look up guides sooner than ask for hints.
What about the story? I purchased the bundle initially because I really thought the story was interesting. And throughout, it really is. It's gorey, creepy, with minimal jump-scares, and throughout the whole thing you can feel how it's only going to get worse for the characters. But by the end...? It's kind of a let down. Some have said "It's referencing the Cube Escape games!" but I personally believe any and all spin-off stories should still be able to hold their own in their self-contained worlds. This game sort of did, but it doesn't explain motivations of most of the characters, and leaves you with a very redundant, poorly executed conclusion of: (SPOILERS BELOW)
It's all some kind of reincarnation time loop! Not very interesting, not very appealing, and because the game doesn't explain how time is repeating this way, or why, it's just kind of. Blah. We don't even get to really know the character that is the cause of this time loop, either. Or how the supposed master-mind is pulling it off/why. It's not satisfying at all.
I believe anything with effort put into it is worth some amount of money, but I do wish I had not bought these games. You can get the exact same experience just watching someone play it live, and so unless you can get it for 1 dollar, I'd say take a pass. Even if you love puzzles, the horrible excuses for puzzles, and broken controls for a good amount of them, aren't worth the head-ache. And the longer the game goes on, the more non-sensical the "puzzles" get.

Let's go over the good and the bad.
1. This game is NOT an open-space game. You have to play missions and skirmishes to unlock parts, which allow you to build bigger and better ships that use those parts so you can acquire even more parts in said missions.
2. There are really only two levels of difficulty. REALLY bloody bleeding edge hard, and super stupid easy where you have to actually try to lose in order to lose. For example, the types of enemies you face will either be teeny ships that pose zero threat to you, or really big ships that can blast you with all kinds of firepower. And inside those, there are only two types of AI. The first type is simple 'shoot at player and try to kill them" AI, and the second is the impossibly hard to fight "RAM PLAYER WITH EVERYTHING WE'VE GOT AND DON'T STOP RAMMING UNTIL ONE OF US IS DEAD". When you find a big ship utilizing ramming behavior, you pretty much always lose.
3. The ship building on this game is really really fun. However, the point of a mission is to take your ship, and blast through it, complete all the goals, and not die while leaving the warp gate. If parts of your ship get blasted off, you can recover all of them. But if they do get blasted off, you cannot re-attach them until you've completed the mission. The problem is, this makes some kinds of ship builds not very interesting. I'd love to make a 'ramming' ship, but you can't because you'll be lucky to kill two other ships before you no longer have a battering ram to ram with. Meanwhile, ramming is super effective VS you.
Okay, that was a mixture of the good and bad. This game is really unintuitive and not very fun at first, but if you can get past the clunky controls you'll have to mess around with, the awkward camera (It's being worked on as of this review), the hit and miss AI (Also being worked on), and other quirks of the game, you'll find a really solid gem of a game. I do not believe the game is currently worth $15, but if you can get it on sale for $5, it's very worth it!
I hope to see the developer continue to update and make this game great!

A thrilling, powerful yet dreadful business love is, when its whole content and capability is considered. It gives birth to all kind of miracles like affection, sympathy, passion, anger and even redemption. Yet I'm not penning this review to inform you about the package love may drop on any sane person to portray a new psyche. I just wished to take a moment and celebrate the creator of this visual novel for her in-depth and through understanding of the concept, with all its bliss and dread all the same. It is not love letters, bright sunshine and butterflies all the time. It grows, it consumes, it hurts... and that lecherous winged Roman god, Cupid would keep smiling all the same.
In 1600s France, we are invited to follow Rosa, a beautiful yet troubled young orphan, led by the sound of her mother in her head. She'll soon discover the whole content there to be for love, gain a family, lose a friend and decide the fate of the one she loves/hates the most. Any more specific storyline description would present complete spoilers, thus, I'll avoid telling you more of the story. It should suffice to warn you that this game is most assuredly +18, dealing with both explicit and gruesome topics like abuse, self-mutilation, mental instability, suggested incest and detailed sexual narrative once or twice. If you feel like you might be offended or this might simply not be your cup of tea, pick something else.
is an astonishing visual novel in both its thematic choice and narrative, which surprises me even more that it’s a freeware. The concept is slightly influenced by Roman mythology, with a darker approach to the subject compared to Renaissance idealism. There is a certain elegance in its narrative display, a hint of literary education and eloquence, and a philosophical undertone for the concept of love and human nature itself. There are sharp twists in the story masterfully presented that will keep you on your toes: from light-hearted to shocking, from fleetingly beautiful to despicably banal without a warning. All characters involved are presented with genuine depth and they harbor many facets of the human soul. They are anything but one dimensional or stereotypical. All five different endings of the visual novel rely on another concept that might born out of love; most gruesome, some heartbreaking... all bitter as the end of any love.
Display is more than appealing, with lots of beautiful CGs, elegant character designs and fitting artwork. The soundtrack brought together from a wide selection - from classic to romantic baroque, from Mediterranean to dark wave - is another proof that labor was put into this work. The game bears many choice option which may alter the ending and takes 7-8 hours if you are to go for all ending.
Take one evening, and let your heart whimper under the brilliant narrative. Take the crushing role of Rosa's mother - the voice within her head - to either lead her into wild retribution or mending compassion. You'll be astonished by the end.

It's a pay-to-win game but there is a free campaign that makes up for the major negative. There are 2 kinds of currency in the game, Gold and Platinum. Platinum is the cash shop currency while Gold is the in-game currency which you can earn from completing quests. The best exchange rate I saw was $150 for 9000 Platinum (40 Platinum per $1), each booster pack costs 200 Platinum. You can basically get 45 packs for $150.
Gameplay-wise, this is basically a pure rip-off of Magic the Gathering. Instead of lands, you play shards.
Conclusion, after playing the game, I would recommend the campaign but not the multiplayer as that would be a money drain. The campaign is honestly very good but you only need to complete it with 1 race as it's the same trail with all the others. You just want to create new champions to get the rare cards.
December 2017: Changed review to Negative as Crytozoic actually let players lose their accounts on the Gameforge servers when it closed down and didn't bother to create a backup account for their players. The P2W is also another major problem. I've lost my old account as well. They have a new update but it's the same game. The blatant copying of MTG's format even after so many years is destroying the game. You would think that there would be some major change after closing the Game Forge servers, but no. There is absolutely no change.
Note: Hex is done by Cryptozoic Entertainment.

1. Interesting Storyline/World
Basically divided into a centuries long battle between light and dark, with the Ardent as the light and the Underworld as the dark. A long time ago, a meteorite crashed onto the planet creating magical shards and everyone called it Hex. The meteorite also brought along some undead called the Necrotic. The Necrotic was attacked by the Human, Elves, Coyotyl
2. Hero Powers / Charges
There is a way to play even if your hand is full of mana-producing gems called Charges. Once you get enough charges, you can use a hero power to change the gameplay. There are usually a couple to choose from.
3. Interesting Races
8 in total
Ardent - Human, Elf, Orc, Coyotle (coyotes)
Underworld - Necrotic, Dwarf, Shinhare (bunnies), Vennen (spiders)
The standard Tolkien fare of Human, Elf, Orc, Dwarf and Undead have been used and re-used so many times that it's a given cliche. It is pretty interesting to see the Coyotyl which are based on Native American tribalism, Shinhare based on Japanese Imperial rule and Vennen based on an insect Hive.
4. Classes
3 main classes :
a. Cleric : Pray, Shard Attuned, <Racial Talent>
b. Warrior : Battle, Shard Attuned, <Racial Talent>
c. Mage : Replenish Spell Power, Learn Spell Soothsaying, <Racial Talent>
I expect Warlock, Rogue and Ranger classes to appear in the future.
December 2017: There is a Ranger class.
All races have access to the same classes. What I like about the variety is that while the basic skills are the same, the racial talent will vary depending on what race you picked. There are also Race-Class Combos which pair up with the Racial Talent ensuring that different heroes can change how a deck is played. I am expecting more classes in the future which will probably follow the standard World of Warcraft model.
5. Campaign
The campaign is pretty impressive. This is the one thing that I would recommend to people. There is a narrative and a proper game with a leveling up system. It's a pity for the ridiculous exchange rates.
6. Abilities that will be a Hassle in a Physical Card Game
a. 2 random troop cards in your deck get +1/+1, next troop in your deck gets +1/+1
To be totally fair with physical cards, you would need a 3rd party to randomly search through all the troop cards and do the above by placing markers on the card. If you do it yourself or get your opponent to do it, there might be cases of cheating or information given away.
b. Summon a Random Creature
You can't do that with physical cards. You would need a list, a proxy card and list of random creatures to randomise with.
c. Socketing
You would have have to prepare a marker in the card to show it's additional unique ability.
1. Pay To Win
This is really hardcore pay to win. You can't even grind to catchup. The 200 Platinum required for a pack is ridiculous. That averages out to $5 per booster pack minimum. It usually costs more.
2. Ridiculous Grinding / Exchange Rate
You need approximately 20,000 gold to trade for 1 booster pack. You earn 200 gold per battle in the campaign. You need 100 battles just to bid for the 1 booster pack.
3. Random Number Generator
Can one complain about how similar the mulligan rule is to Magic the Gathering and how it forces you to mulligan your whole hand? It would have been better if you could keep some cards and mulligan the rest, similar to Hearthstone.
4. Auction House
The search filters are extremely bad. You will see multiple copies of the same card for many pages and you are unable to skip ahead. The load times between page refreshes are also extremely long. This ensures that players only get to see cards that start with the letter A.
5. No Heroes Directly Affecting the Field
Sure, there are charges for hero abilities but the hero can't do anything without charges. E.g. Attack a Minion directly
6. Auto Full-Healing of Troops
Still a major problem. This makes +1 HP way too valuable as all you need to do is survive the engagement.
7. No Targetting of Blockers
You can't choose who to attack, only the blockers get to choose.
8. Mana-Screwed
Too many or too few. You die either way.
9. Magic the Gathering Ripoff
It was interesting at first but you can see all the copying that Hex did. The developers are just lazy to create a new game. They created a new name for the ability but it's still a blatant ripoff. You can see some of ripoff abilities that they have in Hex vs MTG.
Steadfast = Vigilance
Speed = Haste
Trauma = Summoning Sickness
Shards = Lands
Constant = Enchantment
Quick Action = Instant
Basic Action = Sorcery
Flying = Flying
1. Gem Socketing
Interesting to note but there is a slight negative in the idea that you have to get a specific gem to socket it rather than choosing a variation of the card. I think Hearthstone has the same idea.
1. Gender Discrepancy
This is sure to create controversy and attract attention to the game. Make the females have a different variation of racial talents from their male counterparts and let the players decide which is stronger.
2. Auction House
Advanced search parameters to remove cards that have a certain keyword from the search. E.g. "-Abominate", no Abominate cards will appear.

If you would have asked me a while ago, I would have recommended Wild Warfare without hesitation. But things have changed quite a bit recently.
Let's start off with a history lesson. Wild Warfare started off as a game called Mech Mice Academy (MMA). It was an interesting little FPS built off of a modded engine. As the game developed, more people started playing. But then something happened. The game went on kickstarter and transitioned into Wild Warfare. It launched on Steam Greenlight and then eventually released on steam. However, some of the MMA players didn't like the transition to Wild Warfare and left.
The player base has been very erratic over the past few months. Shortly after the game launched on Steam, there were 105 people playing this game at once. Since then, it has decreased. 105 was the most ever Steam players at one time Wild Warfare has ever seen, which is very sad, since this game had and still possibly has so much potential. The community is so small now that the developers have recently removed the server selection option to keep all the players together on the same servers. Sometimes this makes it very difficult to be on the same game as your friends.
There is no matchmaking whatsoever, which is a pro and a con at the same time. The pro: Since the community is so small, it helps keep the servers filled up. The con: You could be a level 1 playing on a server with 3 level 50s. There is a HUGE gap in the skill of players right now. Most players are either a complete noob or extremely skilled.
I was informed recently that the developers are putting this game off to the side and we will recieve few, if any, updates unless more people start playing. Realistically, I doubt that this is going to happen. The player base has been dwindling at about the same rate it is growing, sometimes going up and sometimes going down. Sadly, the general trend of the player base is down. However, putting this game to the side is just going to kill it. Only the games that recieve regular patches keep a consistent player base. If the game isn't dead now, it's gonna be soon.
The direction Wild Warfare has gone is very sad, since it could have been real good. Maybe even the best. But as much as I like this game and continue to play it, I simply can't recommend it to new players. Not in its current state.

Gothic is a unique little RPG and a game I highly recommend. This is a very mature work and one of the best visual novels I have read/played. As one can tell from the title, the story is about love. Not the love that's in sappy Hollywood romantic comedies, but true love, with all its hideous beauty and glorious ugliness. It questions such romantic concepts as True Love, and argues whether love even exists at all or whether it's just a nicer word for desire. Does love truly last forever, or is it best to just enjoy the memories of love and be content with the happiness you had? And (depending on the ending you get) it makes you wonder whether the expression "Love Conquers All" may in fact be the most horrific curse that can befall anyone.
The best concept of the work though may be the novel approach of who the player gets to be. In this instance you are Mother, who can arguably be called the main antagonist of the story. What is most intriguing in this visual novel is that you don't make the choices for the damaged main character; instead you try to cajole/threaten/convince her into performing various actions. Your manner of persuasion, depending on the situation, may or may not convince her. So unlike other visual novels where you have to think about the consequences of your actions, here you have to make your choices based on how best to persuade the MC to do what you want.
The art is excellent, with a great character designs and excellent sets. The music is also fantastic, with some period pieces from classical composers as well as original music that is both haunting and pleasant to listen to.
CUPID is an overall excellent product. It's very well made on almost all fronts and the fact that it is free is absolutely flooring considering the quality. There's really no reason not to play this game if you're a fan of visual novels.

So, disregard my playtime. You have to go through an extremely convoluted process to even get this game running - and I'm talking two hours worth of setting options and downloading fan patches. You basically have to download a whole fan launcher, and it doesn't add onto my playtime.
So, you may ask, is all of the headache of getting this game to run on a modern machine worth it?
...Yes. I think so. The game has a lot of bugs, though none really gamebreaking, and there's a lot of places where you can tell the game is unfinished... but the game is just
. The world is convincing, the black humor is pretty funny at times, and the RPG elements are fun to experiment with. You can steal from townsfolk, start fights, find random NPC's out in the wilderness, and so on.
One thing a lot of people don't like about the game from what I've read is the combat. It's a little clunky, but I like it - this game is hard. I'm not completely sure about the influence that this game had on the Open World RPG genre, but it really does play uniquely compared to others. If you can stomach the controls, the graphics, and the nightmare of getting it to work on W8/10, this game is worth it.

tl;dr: Whether you're a F2P player or a paying customer, if you like trading card games, Hex is absolutely worth your time.
Edit: 2016-12-06 Update
I've been playing Hex for almost three years now. Hex is without a doubt the best digital trading card game, as long as you're willing to invest a bit of your time or money (or better, both).
Business Model - Something that can be confusing for new players is the way Hex merges a very fair F2P model for the PVE campaign with a very standard P2P model for PVP. You can play as much of the campaign as you want, completely free of charge, and you will never feel pressured to put money into the game. The campaign throws free cards at you left and right, as well as a currency called Gold. Gold can be used to buy PvP cards from the auction house, but you can also just straight up trade it with other players for Platinum (the paid currency). In this way, it is possible for a completely free player to compete and win huge prizes without ever spending a dime. In fact, the winner of the top prize at the 2016 $100k Hex Invitational was one such player.
That said, the amount of grinding required to cobble together a serious constructed PvP deck is significant, and I wouldn't recommend doing so to most people. If you want to PvP in Hex, expect to spend money (though it's still much, much cheaper to get into than Magic). There are $10-$15 starter decks available in the in-game store that provide a reasonable entry point for constructed play.
On the PvP side, Hex offers a free to enter ladder for Constructed, with generous prizes (including packs, gold, sleeves, and exclusive alternate art cards) for ranking up. On the Limited side, there are gauntlet-style (play until you win 5 or lose 3) sealed queues, and a draft gauntlet where you draft cards in a pod of 8 players, then play gauntlet matches until you play 3 or lose 2. These gauntlet tournaments contribute towards your Limited ladder ranking. At the end of each 2-month season, there is a tournament for the top 64 on each ladder with a $5000 cash prize pool.
Now that the ugly money talk is out of the way, let's look at some of the pros and cons:
The Good:
- The Hex community is, bar-none, the best community for any online game I've ever played. Everyone is extremely friendly, helpful, and generous. New players frequently find themselves showered with free common and uncommon cards to help jumpstart their collections. In my opinion, the best place to hang out with the Hex community is on
. There are tons of great streamers, and you usually can't go wrong by just picking whoever has the most viewers at the moment. Watching streams is a great way to learn about the game, and both streamers and other viewers are generally thrilled to answer a new player's questions.
- Hex's gameplay is deep, complex, and rewarding. If you've played Magic: The Gathering, Hex will be instantly familiar, but Hex goes beyond Magic with mechanics that could only be accomplished in a digital game. Cards that create other cards, cards that can be modified by socketing them with gems, permanent modifiers that follow a card even if it goes into your crypt or back into your deck, and effects that happen in secretly without your opponent's knowledge are just the tip of the iceberg. If you're coming from a background with Hearthstone or other simpler CCGs, or if you have no TCG background whatsoever, buckle up, because you're in for a wild ride.
- Hex has the best, most polished interface for any digital TCG, and it's still improving with every patch.
- Card design and balance has been mostly fantastic.
- The PVE campaign is a lot of fun, and the merger of RPG and TCG mechanics works very well.
- As a digital game, Hex is capable of innovations like biasing the shuffler to get rid of the worst 15% of possible resource distributions in your opening hand, leading to smoother and less frustrating gameplay.
- The Hex development team are fantastic. They're honest, transparent, and generally very responsive about problems that crop up. When they implemented the above change to the shuffler, they released the source code of the new shuffler so that players could inspect it for bugs or unfair behavior.
- Hex support is prompt and generous to a fault. If you run into a bug (because let's face it, this is a digital game -- bugs happen) in a PvP tournament that even
have cost you the match, you will usually get your tournament entry refunded in full, in addition to whatever prizes you win from the tournament.
- The pace of development has picked up massively in 2016. Set 5 came out a mere 4 months after Set 4, and the second chapter of the campaign only 3 months after that. Things are looking bright for the future of the game.
The Bad:
- Hex currently has a somewhat limited selection of formats (no 2v2 multiplayer, no cube drafting, no house rules etc.), and being a digital game, you can't easily make up your own without the developer's support. However, the developers
The Ugly:
-  The fifth set, Herofall, has been great for the Constructed meta, but rather lackluster in Limited due to a narrow band of viable archetypes. The previous 4 sets have all been fantastic in Limited though, so this is probably just a momentary stumble, and will change when Set 6 comes out (probably around Feb 2017).
