First Impressions (40 minutes gameplay) here:
TL:DR - A great game but be cautious in your expectations. Watch some videos and make sure this is the right game for you.
Signal from Tolva is a funny beast, you can see its heritage borne of Big Robot’s ‘Sir, You Are Being Hunted’ but this is definitely not a survival sneak-a-thon, which is super refreshing given how saturated that market is these days. So what is it? Well I’d say it’s a first person mystery, exploration and combat game. Don’t go into this expecting a scripted FPS, the focus is very much on exploring the world, discovering and uncovering information and then taking on rival factions for resources and upgrades or in random encounters.
The world is handcrafted, again a welcome break from procedural worlds that just feel hollow or repetitious (looking at you NMS). It looks great, as long as you don’t get too close to the textures, with expansive views of the alien world sometimes making you stop for a minute and just soak it all in, there are some amazing vistas. Of course there are some telltale signs this is a small team though, and sometimes you desperately yearn for more interaction with the world, more things to see (and shoot) and they’re just not there, it sort of makes you a little sad and a little hopeful that Big Robot sees success here so their next title can continue to build something lavish.
Audibly the game weaves from a subtle soundtrack, to sharp static and cracks as you navigate menus and weapons, I’m sure there is a message there about nature and technology. The combat audio is fantastic, you can hear a battle occurring over a hill, echoing across the plains, it really gets the blood pumping and the trigger finger itchy. And while reviewing the game I once had some air drones drop in right on top of me, their alert noise made me literally jump in my chair!
Gameplay, you’re going to see what I’d say was a semi-linear progression from the West to the East of the map. I say semi because you only face three hard points as you cross the map that require a certain upgrade to progress, the path and pace are left totally up the to player. Along the way, you gather information to expand the story and unlock upgrades, collect Datum to buy those upgrades and secure beacons and bases to apply upgrades and respawn at. There are also additional sub-missions scattered around the map with additional story and instant upgrades but I’ll not go into that as it’s all part of the exploration and discovery. This all means playtime could be hard to judge, rush it and you’re looking at 2-3 hours, take your time and do a fair amount of exploring then 5-6 hours (which I say was your average gamer), 100% probably 2-3 hours more. Not bad for a $20 game but a warning to those who are approaching this solely as a linear shooting experience.
While there is a wide variety of weapons and upgrades to unlock, I did find that once I’d set myself up according to my play style there was little need to tweak and change for different situations. Mainly limiting later game changes to more powerful versions of the weapons I had to take on the tougher enemies. Still it’s nice that there is that ability there.
Overall I loved the feel of the game and enjoyed my playthrough. I had a few instances of “I wish there was more” while travelling between points on the maps but I tempered that feeling in the knowledge that what is there, works well. A special shout out to the droid AI, it runs across the map regardless and as a result there are some emergent scenes that occur with or without your input, they’re pretty awesome to stumble on as two factions battle away or you get assistance from allied droids mid battle.
I’d recommend this if the above whets your whistle, if you’re not sure, I’d suggest watching my video or others to get a better idea of the gameplay. The first 40 minutes represents a good proportion of the total game, albeit without the obvious increase in difficulty of enemy encounters and changes in aesthetics.

The voice acting though... In the english version the voice acting is atrocious. It sounds like they hired a random person of the street to do the voice of the Nameless Hero. Many of the characters sound extremely weird and it almost ruins the immersion.

Despite many of the bugs and the voice acting the game is still loads of fun.
Overall, Gothic is a good experience. I rate it 8/10. Some of the bugs and compatibility issues make it a pain to get running, but once you get passed all that you have an amazing RPG experience way ahead of its time.

I saw SunAge the first time way back before it was even released and I already knew I would like it. However this game isn't without its flaws.
Pros
-----
- Beautiful old skool grafics, a throw back to the 90's RTS genre. Most critic reviews I've read all say that the GFX are outdated, even ancient. Anyone that says this is, I'm sorry, but they're idiots. RTS just don't really translate that well in 3D. Believe me, it used to be my favorite genre yet there are only about 3 maybe 4 3D RTS games that I like. I don't need a rotating camera to enjoy a game.
- Sound Design. Sound it something most people think that it isn't really important, yet most of the units in SunAge have diffirent sounds for their weapons and moving.  The ambient sounds are also a nice addition.
- Campaign. Like I said RTS used to be my favorite genre, meaning I've played a whole lot of them. Among them the C&C games. And I think I can count all the campaigns from every game that I finished on one hand. Most of them or either too hard or too boring to actually finish. Yet SunAge, kept me interested enough to see the ending. Didn't encounter any mission that I found tedious or unfair.
Cons
-----
- Pathfinding. Units will act weird from time to time, just small things that you jut notice. Like sometimes units won't be able to walk onto a certain surface but they will cross it. Other times they'll fail to go to the EXACT spot you want them to go to. The  there are those moments when one unit of a group just decides that instead of standing in formation he has to go all the way around past and through the enemy base just to stand at the base of a cliff.
- Skirmish. The game has a skirmish mode against an AI opponent. However this doesn't hold up, the AI is easily defeated and doesn't seem to do that much anyway. Instead it'll build units and attack defences, but at the first sign of danger the units will run away. Only to return as soon as they don't see their attackers anymore.
- Some random bugs. Sometimes I'll encounter a game breaking bug, nothing that crashes the game, just one that prevents me from progressing, usually a reload fixes this. But not always.
Complaints
------------
Even though I really like this game it has several issues that most RTS games have, but this the 21st century after all.
- Airplanes cannot be repaired, even though the game says that you can, you can't. A all too common RTS oversight that I just plain hate.
- Not having the ability to choose your Skirmish posistion. Again a common RTS occurence, for some reason most RTS games will not give you the option to choose your starting location. Which is very annoying because when I play skirmish I want my opponent as far away from as possible. Yet sometimes they'll just spawn right next to you
My final verdict is, if you liked 90's RTS games, you love this hands down. It could benefit from a good clean-up, but then again which game wouldn't.

I remember playing the original Out There on my Android phone a couple of years ago, and when I saw this game come to Steam I was tempted to buy it again because it works well as a phone game, but isn't quite the pick up and put down fun I enjoy when I'm on the go.
Actually, this game is a little too deep for its original platform, but also almost little too simple for its own good.
Out There: Ω Edition is about being stranded and not dying. You navigate 'Systems' which are typically a type of star (Yellow Dwarf, Supernova, Red Dwarf, and more), collecting precious resources to upgrade, fuel, and maintain your ship and yourself. Every jump to a new system begins with an event, whether it's a random encounter that gives you a choice, a random encounter that is just commentary, or a random encounter that will betray you and chance ending your journey.
It is a bit of an unusual game. Consider this a kind of Choose Your Own Adventure with a hard roguelike twist. Every jump can be a disaster that is totally out of your control, and you will probably hate your character intensely before you've finished your first four or five games. He's just awful. Sometimes he will do something that will not only damage your ship or cost you resources, but could even end your game, and there's usually nothing you can do but read the text describing what happened and why it's ended your journey.
And that, friends, is half the game right there; random nonsensical, painfully awful circumstances. This game will punish you, even when you're doing well, and if you're not doing well it will only punish you. Every jump can feel like walking into a pitch black room with no sense of what's in there, what will bite you, or where a hole in the floor awaits to trip you and break your leg. Out There: Ω Edition isn't about winning, it's about eating♥♥♥♥♥♥and asking for seconds.
This is also where the game really shines.
Out there space is cruel, but if you are patient, careful, and the odds rolled favorably, you can go on, even if by a thread. You learn the value of every resource you get and it is always possible that your abundant oxygen reserves or buckets of fuel will run out in three jumps and end you. There are tactics I've used on my phone version, like finding a fuel beacon and using it as a 'tether' to keep me going as I scour all nearby systems for anything to help me along the way, but such tactics will not be enough.
This game depends heavily upon chance, and you will take quite a lot of those on the way. Halfway through the game you will even have a mandatory encounter that will cheat you,
but you can recover, and even win. I've done it on my mobile version, I will do it here.
The music and presentation are great here, but the textures on the planets are awful. Obvious seams, and blur are problems that were evidently not dealt with before moving this game to PC. Certain other issues just feel lazy, like the way the tutorial stage instructs you to 'Tap' an icon rather than 'Click'. This smacks of being a lazy port, and for the price that's a pretty bad deal. There can also be some rather laggy load times, and the narration in the intro wasn't matching up to the subtitles. There were some sound effect issues, specifically a loss of quality from the original mobile version of this game.
My number one gripe has to be the ugly font. Seriously, it's an eyesore. I work in print and writing, certain fonts are actually easier on the eyes sheerly because of their 'weight' and kerning, and some fonts are infamous for being difficult, even causing eye fatigue to the reader. The font used in this game is awful, sharing some of the very dubious qualities that make Comic Sans a tough one on the eyes. The balance of the font, kerning, etc are worth addressing because of the sheer amount of reading involved with playing this game. I can appreciate wanting to go with something original, but the font here is atrocious. If it is at all possible I hope someone will write up a guide on how to change it. A clear serif font would be welcome, but even a crisp sans-serif would be an improvement.
I truly enjoy this game, and while I have a difficult time with some of the lazier aspects of the port from mobile, and the font, I still enjoy both the feel and the style of this very unusual, often brutal game.
A difficult game to recommend, definitely a work in progress and not worth the full asking price. If you go into it with an idea of how it plays and accept that the odds are against you it can really be a fun adventure despite its shortcomings.
If you thought 10000000 was light on content, this offers much more replayability. Absolutely worth the money if you like match-3 games with a twist!

A definite improvement over the simple concept 10000000 gave us. Rather than set a goal over the whole experience, the game makes it a bit more about the journey.
Pros:
+ Shows some real evolution of the original concept with more tiles and new special attacks
+ New zones keep the enviornment interesting and the journey long
+ Heavy upgrade to the presentation of the game as everything feels nicer to execute
+ Better soundtrack than 10000000, even if it also gets a little repetitive. Has much more fitting music for the art style.
+ Earning your keep very much pushed in this game as you must do well to progress and unlock new crew members
+ Keeps an adventure feel to it rather than dangling a goal over you like in 10000000
+ Only tweaking the formula to avoid any unneccessary confusion, adding more, but not too much, for veterans.
+ Much more varied color pallet.
+ Enemies now have weaknesses and immunities.
Cons:
- Some goals still seem arbitrary.
- While nice, the new library for looking at item effects, enemy types, and weaknesses is, in the end, pointless considering you're at the mercy of the tiles.
- Still a bit more luck based than skill based.
- Not too much has changed visually.
- The way upgrading is handled stinks of a game that had microtransactions but were seemingly removed for the Steam version.
- Upgrading still feels way too slow considering the cost, now adding a minigame as if still meant for a touch device.
7/10.

You can be carrying as much fuel and iron as your ship can carry and still get screwed because you hit 10 systems in a row that don't any fuel. It's really irritating to have been playing for over an hour and have your game suddenly end this way.  It doesn't matter how well you prepare or what ship you are flying. Also, your success or failure largely depends on deciphering the alien language in order to get new tech. This is also a random process where you simply guess at the meanings of words until you get lucky enough to figure some out.
The second reason I don't like it is that is that on the rare occasions when things are going well, it's repetitive and boring. Fly to new system, probe for fuel, land on garden planet to refill oxygen and communicate with aliens, fly to next system, and repeat....  Throw in the occasional ship change and drilling for minerals and that's the whole game.  It gets old fast.....
If you want a better version of this type of game, try The Curious Expedition.

I highly recommend this game. Be warned, however, that this is a very narrative-driven game with very little to offer in terms of challenging gameplay. Most of the game falls into the emerging genre of “walking simulators”, though the game does future a number of interludes with more interesting, if still not particularly challenging, gameplay-scenarios. Additionally this is a rather short game. Your first playthrough should take somewhere between two and three hours. The game does give you the option of replaying sections or indeed the entirety of the game, but there is very little incentive to do other than a few achievements and, of course, the excellent story. Speaking of the story, it is very linear. If none of this bothers you, you are in for a treat.

The less you know about the events of the story the better, so i will not go into specifics here. If you want a quick rundown of the basic premise i recommend that you simply read the description on the store page. All i will say is that the game delivers a story that manages to be deeply emotional, without ever feeling like it’s cheating by using cheap tricks. It deals with very dark subject matter in a mature way and in the end its message remains optimistic. The most memorable parts by far are the aforementioned interludes, in which the gameplay works in conjunction with the generally well-acted voice-over to tell stories that manage to be highly metaphorical without coming off as pretentious.

Performance-wise i experienced no problems though this is not necessarily indicative of how the game will perform on other systems. There have been reports of people running into issues on min-spec systems, but the developers have been addressing these through patches.

In conclusion: If you are a fan of short narrative-driven games, then you owe yourself to play this game. Its unique use of interesting gameplay-mechanics in telling an emotional story makes it stand out from the rest of the games in the genre.

Just very quickly for now:
- great 2D space shooter with emphasis on building your own ship (boss) module by module
- caring developer with lightning fast response (next day patch)
- frequent patches bringing lots of new and improved stuff

- grid based ship editor (simpler but less flexible)

- ship size is currently rather limited, both by ship editor and by performance I reckon, but impressive beats of doom can be had
- broken modules remain broken until the end of battle, forcing the player to adapt to new ship behavior and build their ship to survive these brutal scenarios - this rewards good engineering!
I love it already and I have high hopes it's gonna get much better as it has potential to be as unique as Reassembly or SPAZ with its own mix of space shooting/engineering goodness.

I gave this game a fair chance, and it started off good: the isometric graphics are obviously glorious, the story is simple but engaging enough, voice acting is okay, I even liked the the half-baked comic cutscenes where the main character looks like a different person in every panel.
But the game itself is almost unplayable: the first thing I noticed is the strange unit selection scheme. Drawing a rectangle across the screen should select all units inside the rectangle, right? No, that is for putting units into squads, but only units of the same type, except for commander units. It doesn't add anything to the gameplay, it just makes things more complicated.
Then I noticed the units horrible pathfinding. If there is any obstacle between them and their destination, or a tight corridor, they'll go somewhere completely different, or take a step back, or refuse to move at all. This is especially awful if you take into account that in this game, bases are tightly built clusters of buildings, literally touching each other, or they don't have power. My units also ignored attack commands regularly and didn't pursue enemies. Sometimes they stop just ahead of their target and take fire until they are dispatched.
I had reasonably high hopes for this game, but it's a complete disappointment. The most amazing thing is that even though it came out in 2008, there are still patches coming out for it. The devs apparently care about their game, so why haven't they fixed these glaring issues yet, or given up entirely?
TLDR: Don't buy this!

This game is a blast to play!  The singleplayer is fine, but the meat and potatoes of this game is when you're facing a human opponent either online or locally.  The online can use a bit of work because some matches can be pretty laggy.  However, when you do get in to a match and everything works, it really works.  Still, the netcode needs improvement and I hope the fixes for that come sooner rather than later.
There's a lot of hidden depth to the gameplay as well.  You have to decide when it's right to let yourself die in order to respawn in front of your opponent before they make it to the next screen.  When is it the right time to make a break for it to get to the next screen?  When you decide to let yourself die in order to respawn as a barrier for your opponent, is there is even enough time for you to respawn in front of them?  Should I hold on to my sword, or should throw it and make a run for it hoping it distracts the opponent? These are some of the thoughts that will constantly be running through your head while playing this game and it's made all the more intense when facing off against a human opponent.
I also really dig the old-school Atari 2600-esque look of the game.  The use of colours makes the levels look really nice and I just like the simplicity of it.  The super colourful neon blood is also prety great!
The soundtrack to the game is also fantastic!  Each of the 4 levels in the game has a unique song that plays in the background and it makes the one on one battle so much more enjoyable.
I definitely recommend this game to anyone who wants a lot of local and online (when it's properly working 100% of the time) MP fun!

2 Hours. After finishing Gunpoint, my Steam Library read '2 hours' of gametime. Sounds like a turnoff, right? Well, Gunpoint is crafted in a way that makes 2 hours seem reasonable. After all, Rome wasn't built in a day, but Portal was certainly beaten in an afternoon.
(If you want a short review, I've written a shorter version at the bottom.)
I didn't bring up Portal for only one comparison: I like to think that Gunpoint is like a 2D version of Portal (if that didn't happen to exist already). Yes, there's no psychotic AI lecturing you throughout the story, there's no lasers or energy balls and it's certainly a lot more serious than Portal. However, your main utility lets you get from one place to another quickly, you don't really have a weapon on you, the starring feature of the game is used in a variety of ways, there's some very interesting puzzles that make full use of your surroundings, the game can be beaten in a single day and the humour will make you smile multiple times (personally, I think it beats Portal).
So, enough of the similarites to the puzzle game with myths concerning baked goods, what makes Gunpoint unique? Hypertrousers and the Crosslink. The former lets you leap great heights and survive them (your enemies can't); the latter  lets you rewire electronic devices to others, such as light switches to electric sockets or security cameras to doors. These two features make up the main gameplay and are VERY satisfying. Timing a pounce onto a guard and knocking him out of a glass window never got boring for me and screwing around with the Crosslink led to entertaining solutions to problems (like knocking out a guard by opening a door quickly in his face). Combine this with upgrades like larger jumps and new gadgets such as silently breaking glass or rewiring GUNS and it all works together very nicely. Every puzzle gives you a way to try again, you'll never find yourself trapped in a room from screwing up: every puzzle in Gunpoint has a solution.
The plot typically follows a noir detective setting, in modern times. You play as a freelance spy, taking on jobs in search of pay who gets caught up in a murder mystery involving rival companies, friends and people all with different motives. Each character feels different from each other in personality, which is quite the acheivement for a game where the characters are only pixelated faces and text. As these characters give you instructions, there are points where you're given 2 sides to a point, and you have to choose which one to side with. The last one is a real morality question; it WILL make you think. Conversations take place on your phone, and you have multiple responses you can make to what you're told. These can range from serious, shady quotes, to questions about your mission, to humour that physically made me laugh out loud, something Portal couldn't achieve. Speaking of humour, it's all very well-written but keeps the serious tone throughout, something I can applaud. Some of the achivements account for this humour too, such as getting one for the previous action of knocking a guard out with a door, hitting yourself with a door, and my personal favourite: punching a guard in the face over 50 times until you get an achievement begging you to stop.
As for presentation, I love it all. It takes on a retro style of pixelated characters and backgrounds but still keeps them very detailed, from graffiti on the street walls in the distance to the apartment windows in the background being on or off. THAT is good detail. Fitting the noir style, the music is mainly jazz with techno mixed in at some areas to fit your hacking abilities. It's very smooth and relaxing but also fits the mood of the mission you're on. It's simple, but effective. And great to listen to as you punch a guard in the face over 50 times until you get an achievement beggin you to stop.
CONCLUSION/SHORT REVIEW
I love Gunpoint. I love its originality, I love the humour, I love the music and the campaign length personally doesn't bother me. It's short enough to avoid being stale but long enough to make you satisifed. If you like noir settings and fun, clever puzzle games, pick this up. If you want something new, pick this up. I bought this on sale and personally wouldn't have minded paying the full price, though that's just me. If it's too short for you, there's multiple story decisions to make which affect your outcome, as well as Steam workshop maps to try out.
(If  you want to see how I did, click the link to see the games' final surprise. Don't worry, there's no spoilers for the plot.
As a final statement, let me just say this. Thank you Fabian Van Dommelen and John Roberts, your attention to detail and skill is brilliant. Thank you Ryan Ike, John Robert Matz and Francisco Cerda, 'Security, Circuitry and You' is going to be travelling through my ears for the next few months. And thank you, Tom Francis. You made a hell of a game.

When I first started playing Dawn of War 2 I was honestly expecting a re-make of the first game series, but I was pleasantly surprised to find a game that could stand up on its own two feet.
People who were familiar with the first game will remember the slightly bombastic cutscenes with in-game models and overly familiar RTS game play, and on these points DOW 2 innovates. Unlike most RTS games you're not expected to manage buildings, which is appealing. The visuals and voices also al feel well-scripted and satisfyingly re-create the chaos we've come to expect from the battlefield.
However, if you're not a fan of Space Marines you'll probably be disappointed to discover the single player campaign is somewhat frustratingly geared only to this particular race. Furthermore, DOW1 actually attempted to characterise the protagonist through its cutscenes (Including a last minute plot twist that I found truly touching!) and this is where DOW 2 falls down a bit. Nobody has any real emotion aside from heroic anger or angry heroics, the Marines all talk with an irritatingly fake batman voice and the mute protagonist fails to strike any sympathy with me as a player. This is what comes of Games Workshop trying to characterise a race who are all literally clones of one another.
So you'll find the meat of this game (The other 3 races!) in the multiplayer and custom game mode, and this makes for staisfying, if somewhat repetitive, fun. However you should prepare to be screwed around by EA-level connection issues as the game insists you connect to windows live even if you want to play offline, which earlier games managed to do without and adds absolutely nothing to the gameplay. I cannot fathom why anybody felt it needed this feature.
Even though the game is competant in single player and multiplayer scenarios, it just can't marry the two together as seamlessly as Dark Crusade did. So yes it's a good game, but it's just not as rich with variety as Dark Crusade was. I don't see why it would have been impossible to have a DC-style campaign mode with four playable races, or even a multiplayer campaign of the same nature where multiple players fight their campaigns across a planet. So in the end it's not a terrible game, it just feels like it took away features from earlier games that worked, added features nobody wanted, and somehow makes the already characterless Space Marines feel even blander.

It's a solid exploration/puzzle game that goes for a dreamlike feel and nails it really well with the Forgetting mechanic, doing a great job of mimicking how things in dreams can change and move just because you look away from them for a moment. Likewise, both the soundtrack and visuals help immerse you in the dream-world, though I will say that the random glitchy camera effects were a bit off-putting.
A few of the more platformey levels are rough around the edges, as you'll often need to Forget the area around you multiple times until the platforms end up in locations you can actually jump to, but the more puzzle-oriented levels are where the game really shines, with a number of puzzles making very clever use of the Forgetting mechanics.
If there was a story, it was so far into existential 2deep4u territory that it completely flew over my head. The dialogue seemed to be talking about varying aspects of existence and reality but there was no real cohesion to it (funnily fitting as that's how dialogue can often be in dreams).

I'm not going to argue too much about value vs. price, it is a bit on the short side, but this in itself isn't a problem. It is however a problem for this particular game from a narrative perspective. The game is quite clever gameplay wise, but it isn't used to the full extent.
For a tragedy to work, you must actually feel something for the characters as if you know them yourself. When a real-life tragedy occurs and many people die in an accident or attack far away from your own country, it is actually really, really hard to feel too much about it unless you yourself or someone you know has ties to the place in question or it is a country which is culturally close to yours. I will obviously acknowledge that the thing that transpired is tragic and horrible - regardless of where it is, but at the end of the day, there's a finite amount of mental capacity you can actually expend on caring about it.
For a tragic game to work, the storywriters actually have to overcome these boundaries of telling a story that manages to shatter this wall from a place that does not exist, What Remains of Edith Finch does not with two exceptions. It spends too little time fleshing out the characters
. A bit more time with each character would be nice, else it just becomes a
If you want to listen to a story that does more with only one voice (there's technically two voices in that game, but the first one is used for like.. 15 seconds) and without interactive cutscenes, try Gone Home instead to contrast the experiences.
Oh, and the character could've walked faster.
I'd give this game a 5/10 if I had to pick a score.

Absolutely incredible. The art direction and "level" (house) design are amazingly well done, the soundtrack brings you right into each character's story, and the voice acting is excellent (with a clever and immersive take on subtitles).

The story is revealed in pieces, covering members of Edith's extended family, and each piece is told in a unique and creative way that will make you feel feelings, good and bad.
At $20 and with a playtime of about 2 hours, it might seem a little steep, but it's well worth the cost. There's not much in terms of puzzles to solve but if you like an immersive and intriguing story, and you enjoy games such as Dear Esther, Everybody's Gone to the Rapture, Gone Home, Firewatch or The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, this game combines some of the best elements of all of those and is not one to be skipped.

Step 1: Right-click on My Computer and choose Properties. Then click on the Advanced tab and then Settings under Performance.

advanced system settings

disable data execution prevention
Step 3: Here is where it can be a bit tricky. By default, DEP should be set to the first radio button and therefore only protect essential Windows programs and services. If the second radio button is selected, it will turn on DEP for ALL processes, not just Windows processes.
If you’re having issues with a program, go ahead and try to select the first radio button, restart your computer and see if that fixes the issue. disable DEP
However, DEP is now turned on for every other program in Windows and you might end up having the same problem with other programs. In that case, you have to manually each program to the exception list.

Bossconstuctor is a unique game, catering to a relatively specific niche in games that hasn't really been touched by very many developers until recently. (2 flash games, and 6 other games share similar characteristics, as far as I know.) That niche being the ability to create a ship of your design, lego-style, using a (currently) small cache of parts.
From the start, there is a level of polish which is sufficient to make this game simply look better than anything people might tout as "crap, weak, waste of money" which I can assure you it's not. Currently, you are able to design and build a ship or fleet of ships with which to shower your rain of destruction.
There is a story mode which has, in recent patches, reflected the difficulty settings much better, where the harder modes not only include more larger enemies, but makes them a bit smarter too. It takes anywhere from 1-4 hours to complete an exploration, and now there is a save feature in case you can't do it in one sitting!
A unique aspect to this game is the evolution pool. This is where you can sit back and watch the computer fight itself, learn from itself, and make its ships better. There could be some improvement here, as with any random generation environment, it takes time to see real results.
Eventually, I'd like to see mirko add something of a large open ecosystem you can journey through rather than small world points you have to jump to, thus combining two aspects of the game. However, the game is still early access, and as such has plenty of time to improve! :D
TL,DR:
Design your own spaceship, fly it around, kill things, take their parts, and attach them to yourself. Also watch the computer kill itself. Also missions. And a storyline. More stuff pls!

It's a fighting game, but not really: there are no "super" moves, power bars, or frame timings; just run, jump, and stab. It's easy to pick up and play, and within a few minutes you'll feel like you're accomplishing the most amazing series of maneuvers. There's no need to log 300 hrs of practice to get "good" here.
I love the simplicity of it: movement, 5 "stances" (overhead, high, mid, low, crouch), a jump button, and an action button. That's it. Using combinations of those controls, you have access to a surprising variety of moves that help you push past a constantly respawning opponent, only to celebrate your victory by jumping into Níðhöggr's waiting maw.
The one downside, though, is the price. $15 is crazy. $10 would've been MUCH better. I hope they continue to develop levels/content for this to help justify the price.
There's a damn good reason this won so many IGF awards, and I'm glad it finally made it to a full release version. Thanks to the option to hold tournaments of up to 8 players, I can see this being an awesome party game, but hopefully they can flesh out the online multiplayer, as well as add more content, to keep people playing even after the party's over.

Ah yes, Dawn of War II. Some acclaim it to be the infamous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child which never excisted and cursed the entire lineage. Others acclaim it to be the praised child BORN FOR GLORY.
The reason for this is simple ; Dawn of War II took some unorthodox turns in comparison to it's older counter-parts. The campaign is where this is blindingly obvious.
Unlike previous installments, you are not set out to clear missions in the format of having buildings and producing units from thoose or choosing units from requisite points. Instead, you are left to play with 5 arguably good* Characters and your commander being a silent protagonist. *I'll get back to this point.
These characters are simply hero squads and control with supplements of initiates who can be replenished at requisite points - And they affect the overall health of the squad. In additon to this ; you gain experience and rating based on your merits during the mission. How many % of the enemies did you kill? How fast? Did anyone die?
The Experience allow you to level up and spend skillpoints in respective skill groups for squads - that specialize them towards certain ends. Perhaps more mobility, perhaps more offensive - or maybe even deployment tactics. There are options.
Beyond this ; you can get wargear from enemies. Simply, gear that is equippable for certain squads - or perhaps all. This ranges from Guns/Armors that play out differently and have different strengths ; to that of ability enabling things - say, a smoke greanade or a deployable stationary turret.
These elements allow for a very addicting and fun replay-value that makes you come back for more. "Maybe i could have beaten that time? Maybe i could have gotten 5 seals? I should try again".
The overarching story is not the strong selling point of this game - Albeit the story of the characters as they progress and how they are portrayed plays a MAJOR role in this game. You grow attached to your squads and learn to like or dislike each respective hero unit based on what you think of them. Some think of them as inhumane. But is not a space marine just that? More then a human? Others think of them as the embodiment of Authoritarian military incarnate.
The amount of content you are looking at varies ; the Single player campaign is very replayable, you can play it co-op, the pool of items is very diverse so you can end up being surprised even when having played it 100+ hours and beyond that. If you account for multi-player as well, it's great value.
But, there are flaws to this game. Mainly ; i'd say balance is a issue. Certain abilities in both Chaos rising (the expansion to this game) and Just DoW 2 - are just over the top and not properly tuned. In DoW 2 it's the terminator armor - albeit you unlock it very late ; your characters become nigh unstoppable when having aquired them. This was probably intentional to reward the player for their persistance - But it's still a noticeable power-spike.
In Chaos Rising, it's generally the ability tree for certain heroes that just goes WAAAY out of proportion in aspects of dealing damage. An example of this would be the cluster mines ability of Cyrus (a "Scout" hero) - Where he can use energy to throw a cluster of mines at stuff, that can kill MOST things in but one blast. Which is incredibly imbalanced.
There is also a issue with the highest difficulty, which is called Primarch. This difficulty, both in DoW 2 and Chaos Rising (both equally guilty here) serve to shoe-horn you into very specific builds and usage of certain characters ; as you can only use 4 at one time. Which has several gameplay mechanics to it in Chaos Rising - Not so much in DoW 2. But mainly Chaos Rising.
You are simply left with NEEDING to go certain squads and certain builds to be able to even COMPLETE certain missions (There is a EXTREMELY noticeable part of this in Chaos Rising with the Second Mission) - Which has left a incredibly sour taste in my mouth.
I have time and time upon again come back to play these games ; but left wondering if not i would have been able to invested hundreds of more hours if it just wasn't for these small annoying facets that at the surface level/Normal difficulty - wouldn't bother anyone really.
But if you really, really do want to beat the game with 5 seals in each category on Primarch ; you're not gonna do it in a diverse way or a varied way. You are going to scum, you are going to abuse certain combinations and you will use a extremely optimized path because the game is tuned in such a way that you CANNOT play it otherwise.
I would guess that this is pet-peeves that come forth after 100+ hours of playing a game that is not supposed to be played that long - But it's there none the less.
WIth all that said ; do i recommend this game?

You awake blinded by colours, shining from the armatures in your space ship. As you emerge from your cryo sleep chamber you realise something is wrong, very wrong. You were on your way to Ganymede, one of Jupiter's moons but you awake in an unknown area of space, far away from the solar system. What's going on?
'Out There' puts you at the edge of the galaxy without help or guidance to find your way back to earth. This however, is a difficult task. Find a way to remain sufficient amounts of oxygen, fuel and steel for hull repairs as you conquer the stars on your long way home.
You can learn to play 'Out There' in three minutes but it will take you many hours to master the game. The game is tough on 'easy' difficulty, leave away 'normal'. But the game is also addictive. You want to continue, moving deeper and deeper into the unknown, continuously revealing pieces of the story that led to your current situation. And every time you die - and you will die - you instantly feel the urge to try again.
Given the fact that 'Out There' is a very simple structured game, it's astonishing how much fun it can be. But be aware, 'Out There' is a strategy game. You need to learn the rules of the game in order to outmanoeuvre it. This is not a simple indie game that you can beat in a couple of hours. It takes patience and learning in order to beat this game.

Some of the platforming sections are extremely difficult (I get flashbacks of the original Rayman) That will require hours of trial and error. I am currently on Level 10.
Logic Missile will test your patience, which is what any good puzzle game should do in my opinion. It\'s honestly refreshing to see a challenging game in an age of overly \"hand-holding\" games that are released. For 99 cents, I think this game is definitely worth taking a crack at if you are a big fan of retro-style platforming puzzle gameplay.

is a point-and-click adventure that is equal parts thrilling and intriquing with a healthy doze of dark humour. It follows the story of the Vanderboom family over generations in a plot that feels mystical, maybe even confusing at first, but rewards you whole heartedly for making sense of it.
The gameplay is what it is. There is not much to praise or criticize as is usual with games that rely very little on mechanics. It's worth noting however that the game was clearly designed with touch screens in mind. The circles that form around your mouse with every click and the way some of the objects in the world are interracted with may be a bit jarring at times, but nothing that would take away from the experience. One thing that I found surprisingly pleasing however was the complete absence of in-inventory item mixing. This may sound like an unnecessary simplification, but in practice it makes a noticeable chunck of the puzzles much smoother experiences as you always have the things that need to be interracted with right in front of you.
With that, almost ironically, given the game's themes, clarity is where the game shines. The infuriating moments where you don't know where or what to do are few and far between. While the artstyle isn't anything spectacular from a purely aesthetic view, it works wonders in telling you what is happening, what to do and what you can work with. A respectable feat once you realize just how bizzare and surreal the scenes and puzzles can get.
The real reason to play this game, and the thriving force that keeps you hooked, is the narrative.
The world of Rusty Lake is a fantastic example of the kind of storytelling that only video games can pull off and still make for a thoroughly compelling story. In the world of Rusty Lake the past is never dead, it's not even the past and we are always here in our past and future lives. Time is not a matter of concern and neither is the order in which you play the games, as they all work to answer questions from other games in the series and asks new ones for the rest to unravel. In this way, the family tree of Rusty Lake: Roots is almost like a microcosm of the series as a whole, with it's splitting branches that all come together in the end to form a story without ever having to do as much but wink at the player from time to time.

This was my first time playing Gothic, so I have no preconceptions of it from the early 2000's.
Foremost, contrary to popular beliefs
It's a corny, epic adventure in a game with an original setting (prison colony surrounded by a one-way magic barrier) with different factions to join and some different ways to play it regardless of how it coalesces down the road in most aspects. There's a lot of rough touches to admire about it, from how weapon animations change as you get better training, to the variety-over-quantity nature of quests, to the ways you get to interact with a game world full of convicts.
However, all while enjoying what the game offered, I tolerated:
• The Access Violation error which makes this game unplayable without third-party fixes.
• The Access Violation errors that can still occur anyway even with third-party fixes. It happened to me twice at the final battle.
• A complete omittance of apostrophes. Probably a format error.
• Horrible pathfinding. Followers and enemies alike get regularly stuck on corners, stairways, and tunnels. It happened a lot, particulaly in the Orc Cemetary with Baal Lukor, the ruined monastery with Gorn, and on the road to the Free Mine with Gorn again where he magically disappeared, probably from falling through the world. Enemies in the
constantly got stuck on pillars and wall corners which made otherwise difficult encounters laughably easy.
• Some ladders being near impossible to climb. When you climb to the top your character won't stand on solid ground, so he simply falls back to the bottom unless you use Acrobatics to quickly somersault forward mid-air. Works sometimes, not always. Fortunately no important ladders are bugged.
• A column in the monastery ruins area which you're supposed to push over a chasm gap but it's set to fall in the wrong direction, so you have to use Acrobatics or a velocity potion to cross the gap.
• Being killed by a follower.
still has his "Guard AI," which means if I attack any of the
that we were there to kill he'd consider that "assault" and attack me. So you have to tell him to wait by the entrance if you want to get anything done.
• Summoned followers attacking each other. Golems refused to play nice with my skeleton army. To be fair, they attack literally everything unprovoked, including neutral npc's.
• Getting locked into dialogue with an npc approaching to talk to me, but their pathfinding preventing them from reaching me so I have to reboot the game. This happened in the Orc Cemetary with Baal Lukor and in the
.. and the list goes on, a menagerie of little bugs and glitches which tested my enjoyment versus the annoyance on a routine frequency. The
question is, do I know anyone who'd put up with all this? Probably not.
I couldn't recommend it to anyone except those who have predispositions toward older games and the prevalent roughness that goes hand-in-hand with them.

"Rusty Lake: Roots" is an entertaining (and cheap!) collection of "locked room" style puzzles that involves not only looking for objects, but also figuring out puzzles and the occasional math equation. The game's imagery (actually, the Rusty Lake series as a whole) might seem a tad weird and convoluted, but in more of an entertaining "Twin Peaks-esque" way than "this is going to give me nightmares". Aside from looks, the only other thing that I think might turn people away from this game is the length; it'll vary depending on one's problem-solving skills, of course, but expect it to be short, with the only 'replayability' once you solve the final puzzle being the new (as of this Review's posting) Achievements. With that said, personally, I thought the experience lasted just as long as it needed to in order to make a good impression on me. I enjoyed this game's atmosphere, and its ability to present a twisted story without heaps of dialogue.  And in the end, not only do I recommend others giving this a try, I also hope that this won't be the last we see of Rusty Lake.

I'll now review this game i started around 18 months ago,
i hesitated for quite a time before giving it a red or green review, i guess to me it'll be a bad one, and i'll try to explain it without hate or anything like that.
First of, lets talk about the game.
It's a TCG (not mmorpg tcg like they are saying, the mmo part doesnt exist yet, and not in a near future)
this game has two part, solo pve or pvp
solo pve (you play vs bot) is kinda a nice experience, a bit less well done than a yu gi oh game, but still nice, and its 100% free.
the pvp is really close to magic the gathering, which this game was based on, kinda well balanced and well done with minor bug. edit 2017, left the pvp, they powercreeped the game so hard even huntard on hearthstone feel slower than the aggro meta currently.
As an improved copy paste of MTG, this game does well, there is tournaments for every kind of player, draft, sealed and constructed. edit : 2017 they lost a lot of players, removed a lot of tournament mode because there isnt enough player, the game isnt going to die, but it wont ever be a big esport game.
Lets talk about some bad point though, this game isnt free to play if you wanna be competitive, sure there will be players screaming you can get some currency from pve and go into pvp after that, but thats mostly being dishonest, ill tell you why.
when you start to farm pve you'll need cards, card that will take weeks or more to farm, only once you have those cards, you'll be able to farm pve effectively, so to be started, you'll need a month playing only vs bot to go somewhere as a f2p player, then consider it might takes around 10 hours of farming pve again to get access to one of the pvp feature : the draft
from now on you'll need to do well in this mode, vs veteran players, while managing to sell what you got to keep going, expecting to keep a bit of the cards you won for yourself.
So yeah you got my point, if you truly want to go free to play u'll need months after months of farming, not counting set should be released every 4 months, so you'll never catch up anyway.
So to play pvp, you need to pay, so the "free" tag here only apply to pve.
a bad point, all the promise they did during the kickstarter campaign, that they didnt do even though they got 10 times what they asked for. (guild, ladder, raid dungeon, stronghold, crafting etc.)
Another lie aswell i have to tell you, this game is supposed to give the card you get some "real values" mean like in every tcg, you could sell and buy the card, then cash out vs real money.
that is only half true, because sure you can sell and buy your card, but once you try to "cash out" from the game, since there is more seller than buyer, u'll barely get 30/40 % of the money you'd need to spend to get the currency in game to buy them.
So dont think this game as a good way to invest, it isnt.

I will leave my initial review in place, below, but I think it would be appropriate to update my review after finishing the game a couple of times.
While I still recommend the game, it gets repetitive much faster than a game like FTL.
A "full win" (of exploring the entire galaxy) can take a solid gaming-day, so you'll get your money's worth, if you intend to pursue all of the possible endings.
But unless you are interested in pursuing a high score via better play, "winning" is easy enough serious players of the Rogue genre won't replay the game much after they finish the Achievements.
[INITIAL REVIEW]
This is a well designed space-themed rogue-like that takes on the opposite concept of FTL.
Where FTL focuses on faster-paced ship management during combat (and crew management, as well), Out There goes for slower-paced exploration and cargo/space management (where you never have enough space to do everything you want to do).
The solar system exploration sometimes feels like a "solo run" of a game like Master of Orion 2 or Ascension. (a good thing)
And the ability to "manage a fleet" of derelict ships is an interesting feature that opens up a range of strategies for winning the game.
A little more forgiving cargo management would have made the game less frustrating.
But it is definitely winnable and balanced, as is.
Definitely worth playing for fans of rogue-likes, or even space-based 4X games.

It'd be nice if steam had a "indifferent" option instead of yes or no, oh well. Out There is an interesting game, it's all about space travel and resource management. There is a lot to see, and I want to see more of it... except, it's kinda hard to do just that.
This game has a tendency to screw you over with random effects. This game is filled with things that are determined based on RNG. It can be fine to do that for certain things in a game, but the more things that are determined by the RNG the more it compounds on itself. For example, early on in the game you're super pressed on space since your starting ship is fairly small in cargo space. So naturally the goal is to find a new ship, except, you need some much later game tech in order to see if there is a ship in a solar system before jumping there. This means that you can fly around for quite some time in the early game with no space to build all the fancy tech you find, nor the space to carry the resources for them.
There are also random events that happen as soon as you arrive at a new solar system. So as a kick in the gutt the game decided take all of my efficent fuel I had in my storage when I arrived at a star..., which had cost most of my fuel reserve to get to. The system in question is empty of any planets, it turns out. So I fly back to the last one which had a spare ship lying around. I get there and have around 0 fuel, that is to say, not enough fuel to orbit it. I try anyway and the game takes me to the screen where I orbit the ship, now at 0.... At this point you'd imagine I could just grab the other ship, right? I mean, that is what would make sense to me. But no, instead the game declears that I have lost since I have no fuel left, despite the fact that there are still valid moves left to do. This is incredibly frustrating, and the game should definitivly be able to do a better job at detecting it's own lose conditions. :/
Another time I lost after my second jump in the game, because the two systems gas giants decided to be the kind that provides you next to no fuel (basically at a loss for orbiting it). That was also quite nice..., not.
Basically, this game could be quite interesting, but the RNG just throws you around in a very non-compelling manner.

A strangely relaxing, throught-provoking but also stress-inducing game.
The written storylets are intriguing (and painful if you choose unfavorably) and set the overall atmosphere of not knowing what to expect. The colorful style and soundtrack help to make you feel curious about what's coming next, either with fear or with joy, depending on your situation.
The current 4 endings range from easy to hard(er) to achieve, all except one requiring a certain (combination of) tech to be used. Unlocking can be pretty hard sometimes, as gained tech is random (alien encounters, landing on rocky planets, events in new system) and for beginners, resource management is pretty harsh on normal mode, which makes it seem quite unforgiving. Also several techs are pretty useless and as such take up space which could be used for fuel, repair or more useful upgrades.
After the second ending though, to shorten my play time, I resorted to quitting the game when unfavorable events happened or I mined/landed on a planet with little resources, which reverted the save state to when you arrived at a new star system (also includes Alt+F4 when getting into bad events after travelling to a new star system, also reverts back to previous star system). I was surprised how often I had to quit to get the most favorable outcome, even more with the alien questions when you have no translated words available yet, making the tech collecting harder than needed.

To put it plain and simple, Xenoverse is a step in the right direction. The video games were stumbling in the Raging Blast era and Ultimate Tenkaichi was basically hand holding you. Xenoverse is the second attempt at an creator your own character and play through their story in this franchise and does it right. The world doesn't feel empty and there is plenty to do(Time Patrol Missions) after the main story and DlC story has been beaten. Ironically, I used to focus on character rosters but I am so focused on my created character that I do not care that it doesn't boast the character amounts the Tenkaichi series did.
Gameplay wise, I do feel like there are some misteps and balancing issues. For example, ki blasts that are post to track do not track all of the time and the Sayian race is overpowered. Once you unlock the super saiyan transformation, you unlock basically easy mode as it gives you infinite uses of your ultimate attacks while activated. This makes playing as other races particulaly hard when Saiyan #2045 is spamming Sphere of Destruction or Emperor's Death Beam.
Another problem is the drop rate on items, clothes, and moves as well as the extra parameters of Time patrol missions. In short they are bad and even if you do the extra stuff in the TPM's they second set of mission parameters won't activate 100% of teh time and even then, any moves or items that need for the secondary missions to activate and be completed are not guranteed drops. This adds in a layer of annoying grind that you find in MMOs and RPGs. They have addressed this issue somewhat with the elder kai method, but getting the elder kai to gurantee your drops is rng as well meaning you are waiting a bit for him to say the right words, aka the golden fruit message.
As it currently stands, there is a sequel to this game and unless you are an completionist like me or want to do the story mode yourself, it maybe best to move on to Xenoverse 2.

If you love Yu-Gi-Oh you'll love this game! I have it on mobile and I immediately fell back into the nostalgia of when I played this as a kid. It has (most? all?) of the OG voice actors and though the voice lines are repetitive at times, they are quite fun and add to the nostalgia (I like Jaden's eggwich line).
Cons:
- The RNG for getting new cards isn't the greatest... at least if you aren't lucky...
First off, booster packs come in "boxes" with about 200-150 packs a box, each one pack costs 50 gems, and you only get 3 cards per pack.
On the plus side, the game is quite generous with giving gems to players and they can be gathered quite quickly, albeit still time consuming.  While it is possible to get ALL the featured/listed cards, you may end up running through the whole box which could be frustrating. They also offer decks that you can buy with gems, so it's a good starting alternative.
- I like my Decks like I like my mecha, BIG.... a max of 30 cards just feels so small, especially with decks that build off numbers and kinda discourages putting in 2-3 of the same card in exchange for more variety
- You really walk a thin line with deck balance as your starting hand in this game can often make or break you. The small LP reserve players have can be a big blow to those who don't draw good hands... Seriously, a good hand can end the duel in 1-2 turns, but so can a bad hand, but you'll just feel bad.
- There is an enemy called the Vagabond and he's kinda hard to fight, at least when you first start out and it kinda makes me feel like I played against him solely for the crazy high XP he offers even when you lose. (Maybe I'm just bad at the game, but I feel like he's way stacked against the player almost everytime)
- I miss having 5 zones for my cards.... In this game you only have 3 zones for Monsters and 3 or Spells and Traps, and while this works well on mobile and the style of playing on-the-go, it just feels... awkward on PC. (But I assume cross-play of PC and mobile so I don't know a workaround other than adding those 2 missing spaces)
Furthermore, some cards/playstyles don't translate well to the 3-zone play style, which does limit how players can duel, if they wish to do so effectively rather than for fun.
Ex. Crystal Beasts, which were introduced recently, are much less effective as they occupy both zone types and it becomes much more of a struggle to balance monsters on the field and in the spell/trap zone.
There's an E-Hero card that allows speical summoning of 2 Lv.4 heroes when one is in play, but more often than not, you'll be unable to use this as the monsters need to be from your hand and you can only special summon 2, not one, which makes this card really useless, unless it were used on the first turn, which is rather unlikely.
Do you guys remember how Ojama King allows the player to block up to 3 Monster zones? (I've never pulled this off, but) If done right, could the opponent be left without any monsters to play at all? Talk about a one-sided battle.
Just food for thought.
TL;DR - 3 monster, spell/trap zones are fine, but it has flaws. You can get used to these flaws, but it is still a flaw.
Pros:
+ If you watched the show, the game is a true nostalgia fest, from the voice acting to the bad censors on cards that make no sense (Ex. Legendary Fisherman's harpoon has been neutered, but hey swords and weapons for other monsters? Cool.)
+ Did I mention the Voice acting? It's so rewarding to have the same voice actors tell my opponent they're a 4th rate duelist with a 3rd rate deck. (It's also cool to hear them say monster attacks or spells/trap activations that are unique to them, it's a fun little easter egg)
+ The 3 space limit and 4000 LP (Ayy, it's like the show!) does help put some pressure on players and makes duels fast, unlike the real TCG with 8000 LP (maybe it's just more nostalgia, like you're in the show?)
+ For real though, duels are fast with the 30 card deck, 4000LP, and 3 spaces, bouts are pretty quick, some only lasting 2 turns, my longest match was ~10 turns and it got real close between me and my PVP opponent! (GG if you're reading this and somehow know who I am!)
+ Players can still play whatever playstyle they choose (Granted they can get the cards they want and can fit them into the small deck sizes) Honestly, playing you're own style and winning is probably more fun because it is harder, but maybe that's just me.
+ I put pros after cons because you have to look past the cons of this game, yes it has flaws, but at its core, it is still the same game that you played as a child and grew up loving. Everything about the game just fits in an unexplicable way.
As everyone else says, get it if you have a sense of nostalgia with the YGO series, following it from the origins and GX (idk if they'll add the others like 5D and etc.)  Yes, this game is fun if you're new or just like the game and not the show or vice versa, but long-time fans will definitely get more from this than others.

I only picked this game up a week or so before it hit Steam, but I figure I've played enough to give my impressions as a newbie to the game. Since I've only been doing single player activities, I'm not going to talk a lot about the PvP aspect of the game (which has very little in common with the single player stuff, save the cards you use). Read this with that in mind.
I tried to type up something long winded, but it felt awfully pretentious and had tons of pointless information. So I'm going to condense it down into the good and the bad for ease of reading. (It's still a bit lengthy though. Sorry.)
The good:
- A good single player experience through the campaign. While hard to do, it can be beaten with your starting out collection, and you can earn gold, cards and equipment for free. It's done RPG style with quests, and there are dungeons that boast some very dangerous boss opponents. Think of it sort of like the Hearthstone adventures, but f2p and with replayability (you get cards and gold every time as opposed to just the first time you win). Having access to 8 different races and currently 3 classes is a nice touch as well, as it gives you lots of options to cater to your preferred style of play.
- The card game can accurately represent what it is like to be caught unprepared by a throng of hungry piranhas. (It's painful, yet mercifully brief, in case you wondered)
- The game has a good level of visual polish. Good artwork, little sound effects to go with every card that's played
- Another good single player experience in the arena. You're using the heroes you'd be using in PvP games here, so it's much harder to win the harder difficulty tiers. But you can grind gold here at a decent clip, and there's enough variety in opponents that it won't feel like the same thing evey time.
- It's a TCG. You can actually buy from/trade with other members of the community for packs and cards, even with the f2p earnable currency. You can also buy the premium currency from other players, again using the f2p currency
- If you can get a deck that performs consistently well in the arena, you can make it a true f2p experience as you'll be able to grind gold efficiently and start to work on the pricier aspects of the game. It will take some time and probably the shameless copying of someone else's deck list to get here, but it can be done.
-If you choose to drop $$$ on the game, you can buy the cards on an individual basis and make a strong, effective deck without spending a fortune on packs (though some cards, naturally, are super expensive anyway. But that's the nature of a TCG)
- The community so far has seemed pretty helpful in-game. It's easy to get some quick advice if you're stuck with something, most of the time.
The bad:
- Entering tournaments asks you to fork over premium money, and sometimes a few card packs as an entry fee. If you do well you'll make your entry fee back and then some, but I find the lack of a f2p, prize-less option a bit dissappointing
- You can't buy packs with the f2p currency from the game's store. You *can* buy them from other players that are selling them on the auction house, but obviously the price won't always be consistent.
- The deck builder doesn't feel incredibly intuitive. There's no way to filter out stuff you already own, and it's not possible to search for cards of a specific costing or shard threshold. This makes it very awkward to try and work out what cards you'd like to work towards getting to go with the cards already in your deck. You can mitigate it somewhat if you're looking for specific keywords, but overall it feels like it could use some improvement.
- The resource system can lead to the good old problem of mana screw/mana flood. I personally don't mind it, but I know it's a big turnoff for some people.
The verdict:
Overall the game is very similar to MTG, but it has enough uniqueness to offset the familiarity. The PvP segment of the game seems difficult to get anywhere with unless you're prepared to grind for it or drop cash on the game, but it seems the developers actually care about providing a good single player experience (which is rare in card games) and I hear an extension to the campaign mode is in the pipeline somewhere.
Give the game a shot, see what you think. If you like card based gameplay, I think this one can easily scratch that itch and at least provide a few hours of gameplay, even if you're unwilling to pay or grind. And who knows, you may find you really like it. I did, and I wasn't really expecting much when I first loaded it up.

First things first:
This is a party-game, meaning it´s supposed to be played with many people on a couch, screaming, laughing. Think Smash Bros, Towerfall, Samurai Gunn, etc. Don´t fret though because the game does have online multiplayer.
The simple goal of Nidhogg is to get into the endzone, that´s it. Too bad your opponent has the exact same goal.
What ensues is a glorious tug of war, because who ever got the last kill is the only one who can proceed. And killing there will be lots of, because besides being a race for the goal, Nidhogg also excells at being a Prince of Persia-style fencing game. Although appearing rather simple, the fighting system is pretty deep and complex with parries, blocks, feints, jumps, rolls, wallmoves, different attack stances, you can even throw your blade at your opponent.
All of this lightning-fast action is presented in a very stylized fashion, reminescent of the good old days of the Commodore 64 and it fits the game perfectly. Animations are fluent (and very gory in a cartoony way), backgrounds are very retro and sometimes deliberately convoluted or hard to see your character in.
Though featuring only 4 Stages on the date of this review, it´s more than enough to get going and further deepens the Retro-Arcady-Feel of this game (yes, leaving things out can actually give a product more character rather than taking it away)
Sound and music are nothing to write home about but they get the job done with little screams and clangs here and there.
Nidhogg is a game it would definetely reccomend if you grew up with titles like Barbarian, International Karate (Karateka) or even the wonderful Moonstone (which NEEDS a remake). It´s fast, deep, satisfying, a definite skill- AND mindgame when it comes to the fencing. People looking for a lot of content and fancy graphics will surely be turned off by this game but tournament-fighters and retro-fans should try it.
One final word about the pricing, I can understand that 11 bucks (or how much that may be in $) is a steep price but devs gotta live too and I´m sure it will be in a sale sooner or later. So consider helping the guys (the guy?) from Messhoff out by getting it right now!

Probably was an outstanding game when it was released in 2005, still fantastic now in Dec 2017. Played the campaign, completed the side objectives, some missions in cadet, some in marksman and some later ones in Sniper Elite.
While the graphics and controls are dated, the gameplay is still fun. A good mix of long range sniper, troop cover, escort, stealth, infiltration and run and gun. None of the missions are particularly like the others, each is somewhat unique and requires a slightly different playstyle.
Here there is significantly less one man army, superhuman reflex, parkour master assassin's creed like BS than modern titles. The game is decently challenging, unlike modern games that spoonfeed you. Nonetheless, the player, Karl Fairburne, is still slightly overpowered, even in Sniper Elite difficulty,  but the game is significantly more challenging and tactical than most modern titles.
If you are looking for something that is tough, tactical and genuinely stealth oriented... this is the game for you.

This initially looks like a low-budget StarCraft ripoff, but after taking a chance on it and playing it for a few hours, it's clear it's much more than that.
It has solid graphics and sound, with easy to identify and well charactered units.  Base building is a charm with the power-node system, and the resource distribution (four types!) forces exploration and additional base-building.  The game borrows some of the best ideas from StarCraft, Generals, Tiberium Sun and Supreme Commander, and balances them out extremely well; it's less macro-y, faster, and less fiddly than Age Of Empires, but less micro-y, speedfreak tournament hotkey nonsense than StarCraft or Dawn Of War.
It really feels like some of the best bits of the C&C Games, (sneaking transports into the back of enemy bases), but with a little more depth, and it just has a really solid, classic RTS feel that's familiar, yet fresh at the same time.
This one is a hidden gem, and has sleeper hit written all over it.  Multiplayer is probably going to be a *blast* with this game.

SunAge is a solid game, not perfect, but solid. The reason I now do not recommend it is because it's lack of staying power. While I am an avid RTS player, both past and present, and I enjoyed certain aspects of SunAge, the game did not captivate me for very long, relative to other strategy games I have played. The game, while interesting, does not carry with it a certain charm needed to entertain for dozens, or even into the triple digits, of hours. The squad system did grow tiresome, and several control options bugged me. The gameplay is fine for a classic style RTS, but it did not fit quite right. I found myself contemplating how the game could be improved, more than simply enjoying the game. Thus, I found the game good for research purposes, but ultimately inferior to other RTS titles.
My original review for the game is below, with what I describe still as good qualities of a game.
Note that this review has only logged 3.4 hours of gameplay, so I have not delved into the depths of every aspect of the game.
Pros:
In the first 3 hours of playing this game, I can definitely say that anybody who enjoys a classic RTS-style game would enjoy SunAge: Battle for Elysium. I've only played a few of the campaign levels, but I already have discovered a fluid squad system, decent tutorials and understandable controls. Every RTS has a learning curve, this game is no exception, but it is intuitive to catch on to. The learning curve, in short, is short. The combat is also very exciting; the varying units make for challenging, but not overly complex gameplay and the multiple resources and base building mechanic make for an interesting management mechanic which is similar to Age of Empires or Starcraft games (with a few differences.)
Major good thing: I have not run into any strange bugs or game-breaking issues since playing the game. (I have not tested this in an online setting though.)
Cons:
The only thing that saddens me is the lack of playability online. This is not due to any problems with the game, but rather a shortage of people playing. I know that, it being almost a brand-new release, this game will grow in its player base, but for now there are not a lot of players online. This makes it difficult to skirmish because via the internet. However (not a con), if you have a group of friends, you can play via LAN or Steam connection privately, so that is a huge bonus.
The campaign levels are a little bit cheesy, with comic book-style cinematics and not-always-compelling dialogue, but that level of cheese is present in a lot of RTS games and not a large problem. (The emphasis is on strategy as it should be.)
The gameplay itself is exciting and fun to partake in; I also imagine actually skirmishing PvP would be equally exciting if not more so. Overall, I would recommend this to any strategy fan! If you like it, spread the word so more people are playing!

If you're a fan of Warhammer, BUY THIS RIGHT NOW.
Dawn of War II is unlike any other strategy game I've ever played. It's go a mix of RTS thinking, small unit tactics, and RPG customization. Your troops are not mindless, faceless, indentical low-poly meat shields. Each squad leader has their unique on-battleifeld skills and off-battlefield personality. You get to know the characters as people and quickly get attached to them. The story is intense and full of twists and turns. But all this cool stuff about plot and character developement wouldn't be worth anything if it didn't have a solid foundation. Fortunately, Dawn of War II DOES have excellent mechanics and gameplay. I never felt like the game was "cheating" or that the battles were unfair. If I failed a mission, it was always because of my own poor decision. I could indentify the moment things started going wrong and what I did to lead myself there. What this means is that no mission is truly "impossible." Even the hardest, most crazy-difficult missions are totally doable if you're smart. The flip side of this is that the game will make you WORK to EARN that victory. The game does not spell things out for you, hold your hand, or do much of anything to point you in the right direction. All it gives you is an objective and a team of heavily armed Space Marines--and really, what more could you ask for?

INTRODUCTION:
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II is the next installment to the critically acclaimed Dawn of War franchise. It was developed by Relic Entertainment who has done a fine job handling the series with respect and care, and giving the Warhammer 40k universe justice.
Dawn of War II is a Real Time Strategy game set "in the grim darkness of the far future" on Games Workshop's popular Warhammer 40k tabletop universe. The player will take on the role of a Blood Raven Force Commander who leads a small task force in a desperate attempt to save one of their last few remaining recruitment worlds from the destructive power of the Aliens who seeks to destroy it.
PROS:
+ Good Visuals: -The game could have used better textures but it still looks nice as it is. Combat animation and movements are great which complements the very well done character and unit models. The game should be 5 years old by the time this review is made, but it has that kind of visuals that ages very well.
+ RPG Type Campaign: -Also a CON (see below). Although the Dawn of War games are known to be a Real Time Strategy Game, this Dawn of War II's Single Player Campaign mixes an RPG element into it (character progression and wargear customization). The original RTS formula is not lost however, because the Multiplayer experience, whether against players or the AI, is still a traditional RTS experience.
+ Wargear and Character Progression (Level Up): -There is an healthy amount of drops and loots in this game which works well on different combinations and situations. This vastly increases the re-playability of the game since the player may experiment with different character builds with different items to attain different results in their missions. This is specially true on the harder difficulties.
+ Variety in Difficulty: -Single player offers a good choice on difficulty by having a fun and satisfying normal mode, and a very brutal higher tier difficulties for players who like to challenge themselves in fighting notoriously hard game modes.
CONS:
- Path-finding Problems: -I noticed that some of the unit's individual AI have a hard time grasping orders. They sometimes run out of cover, charge the enemy even though they are given specific orders for range combat, and even sometimes get delayed response to orders like throw grenades or bombs despite being in range.
-  RPG Type Campaign: -Some fans of the old games might not appreciate the RPG element since what really made the original Dawn of War games fun for them would be the base building, management and troop training rather than squad based tactical combat.
- Recycled Maps: -Map variation in both Multiplayer and specially Single Player is woefully lacking with a majority of maps repeating on missions. Company of Heroes, a game developed by the same studio and using the same RTS principles, had more map variety and originality and it was released 3 years BEFORE Dawn of War II.
CONCLUSION:
With its flaws its still a good addition to the Dawn of War franchise. Although it has deviated from its original formula of a traditional RTS in favor of a more RPG-esque single-player experience, I can still say that I found it fun.
