This game is an enigma. It has some nice aspects to it, mostly that it allows you to experience a watershed moment in naval warfare. Yet it is very limited and certainly not worth the 19.99 dollars that I read was the original price. Lucky for me I paid a trifle for it.
Basically the game is a battle simulator for up to eight warships on both sides and those are limited to two columns. This feature is at the heart of the game and the most developed. However for any experienced naval gamer the lure of options that the game seems to provide does not pay off.  Most do not seem to work. And to top it: the AI is pretty stupid.
These sea battles are tied together by a strategic part of the game. This involves you in conquering ports and blocking or breaking blockades, depending on the side you pick.
The ai gets a big advantage: it goes second after you assigned your forces on a map that shows all commitments. In that way it is sure to get drop on you.
The game is buggy. At some point I was unable to create infantry for totally unknown reason. Luckily quitting the game and reloading solved that. But not so nice was a crash after winning an important sea battle. I had to redo it. More issues cropped up. Be sure to save often.
The stragic game is pretty locked down and historically totally unrealistic. The CSN gets about 2/3 of the USN production, which is nonsense given the strategic advantage of the USN. But this game has to give the Confederates at least a sporting chance and does so by limiting the federal production, giving the confederates an ironclad way before the federals get one and the limiting the federals by the slow production of ironclads. Making a monitor cost about 16 turns in a 48 turns game and you need to get enough money to get it which means about 20 turns from the start you get to your first one. The USN has to hold out against CSN ironclads for like 12 turns. Yeah, Hampton Roads will never occur in this game.
Some ships are totally pointless, like the steam frigate. Immensily expensive(1 million dollars) and with a massive production time, by the time you can field it, the war is almost over.
Game in practice is fought out with a handful of monitors and infantry. Once you know the drill you know the game. Limited, buggy and too expensive: a thumbs down.

9/10 -- Stunning interactive storytelling, ambitious narrative approach, no gameplay challenge (but that's OK), a few technical issues. Many moments from this game will stick with you.
Very brief (2.5 hours) but fantastically inventive,
is a collection of interactive stories about a family that has been burdened for generations with a mysterious curse. About 10 different stories are bound together by the framing device of 17-year-old Edith's visit to the abandoned house to come to grips with her legacy as the last surviving Finch.
To some extent, this is a "walking simulator" like
and the like, so if you're looking for thrilling gameplay challenges, look elsewhere. What's interesting, though, is how this game "simulates" not only walking, but also swinging on a swing, taking photos, flipping through animated flipbooks, playing in the bathtub (as a baby), and even transforming into various animals and monsters in a dream. The most ambitious sequence in the game (Lewis's story-- utterly fascinating) even presents the first-person experience of a mentally-ill teenager slowly retreating into his own interior world as he works a boring shift at the fish cannery. That sequence uses a half-and-half control scheme similar to that of
to represent the growing split in his own mind. As a result of this "breadth over depth" approach, the controls are often a bit clunky, even when you're just walking around as Edith; on several occasions, I had to try four or five times to discover I really could enter that low/narrow doorway, and I lost count of how many times I closed a book or door accidentally because it wasn't clear which way I needed to push/pull. But the game will be patient if you are, and again, it has no fail conditions, so you can take your time and nothing bad will happen. Well, outside of the many bad things that are built into the story itself.
will leave you with plenty to think about, from fascinating imagery (the interactive horror comic, Lewis's hallucinations) to questions about what's really going on behind this story-- what is this curse all about, and what really happened to some of these people (notably Molly and Milton), and what comes after the final cutscene? There's also a subtle but intriguing callback to Giant Sparrow's PlayStation exclusive
that left me with some unanswered questions about the world of
. If you've got a quiet evening free and you're in the mood for a slow-paced but fascinating and moving story about one family's struggle with its own madness, I highly recommend
.

If there was ever a game that deserved the “buy it if you like the genre” rating, this is it. Seriously, you should buy Ironclads if you like the genre, and people who are only slightly interested in the game should probably look elsewhere.
Ironclads is a very realistic approach to naval combat in the middle 19th century, a time period that has gotten almost no coverage. Ironclads definitely does not serve as an introduction to naval combat strategy simulations. Instead, it’s one of the best games of that genre available and intended for veteran players and people who are serious about their naval operations. The realism means that Ironclads doesn’t have the wide appeal like some other games and I can’t recommend it to everyone, but it does fit its niche very well and fans of the genre will not be disappointed.

I've been playing since the alpha. If this is the first time you've seen this game, you're in for a treat. I think one of the most prohibitive things about TCGs is the cost and accessibility of getting to play them in the first place. Perhaps you don't live near a gaming store that hosts things like friday night magic. Perhaps you don't really have the money to drop on expensive booster packs in physical tcgs.
The great thing about HEX is it addresses all those things. Booster packs (bought straight from gameforge, not from steam) are at most 2 dollars each, much cheaper than any physical tcg, with a minimum of 15 cards per pack. Plus, a great bonus of playing online is a bit hidden from view, but the math checks out:
DONT OPEN YOUR BOOSTER PACKS DIRECTLY. Instead, participate in tournaments. Sometimes you'll win some good prizes, other times you'll lose, but that's okay. The entrance fee to a competitive draft tournament in hex, for example, is 3 packs (600 plat) and 100 platinum for a total of 700 platinum (it's a little less than that if you buy packs on the auction house, though). So, we now have 8 people contributing 100 extra plat towards prize money, that's 800 plat total, or 4 packs worth. Well, the prize pool is actually a total of 12 packs, so you'll have a better than 50% chance to walk away with more cards than the plat value you contributed, all in the name of a good tournament!
And who knows, maybe you'll do well enough to pay for your next tournament for free! Good play and good deck design is well rewarded in hex.
So go put away your hearthstone cards, HEX is the digital TCG of champions!
And hey, if pvp isn't your thing, multi-user co-op dungeons and raids are coming!

How Talented Artistic People Shouldn't Make a Game
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
First I should say that I only played "What Remains of Edith Finch" up to just after the comic strip sequence.
At that point I decided the game was "candy coated brain pollution" and uninstalled it  ..... I didn't really care what it had to say,  what meaning it had, or how the devs could tie together what is basically death voyeurism.
Don't get me wrong  .... even as it is, it is far better than the death porn that is 99% of the gaming industry.  If you have the mentality that like fractured fairy tales and slowing down at a collision on the highway to look for a dead body  .... and appreciate good writing ... you will love this game.
So what is so bad about this game IMO?
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
When stupid people write books, movies or computer games  ..... the product is usually an addictive product designed to appeal to human Darwinian desires.  Sad, boring, predictable and not all that relevant  pablum.....  this is 99% of gaming.
When smart artistic people write books, movies or computer games the result is much more chaotic and interesting, but you need to be careful with them as things register with you without you even realizing it.
This is such a game. Pretty much everything is well crafted, but the the whole is candy coated poison.
The first problem is that the game forces the player to collude with characters doing stupid and suicidal actions with no recourse and no way to express how they feel about it.  I spent a good deal of time trying to help the characters involved avoid their fates .... so much so that I got vertigo from the screen panning.  There just was no way and eventually I just gave up and played along.  This is a similar experience to the Stockholm syndrome  (sympathetic hostage syndrome) as you are trapped by your investment in the game and wanting to help the characters and see the end.  This registers on you without you even realizing it.
The second problem is that that writers seem to have a certain glee in crafting the demise of their characters and try to make pointless thoughtless deaths into something more, and glorify psychopathic behavior , both which are just nasty.
Two other games come to mind, both of which involve a child being murdered over and over and over  ...... Little Nightmares and Limbo
Death voyeurism is a very sad human affliction. This game is just that, and it doesn't really matter to me what sugar coated message is at the end regarding family or the freedom to choose even when those choices aren't good.

A stealth title more than 3rd person war time shooter though when you pull out your sniper rifle you're in 1st person. While sniping, you will have to take into account wind, gravity, your heartbeat as well as the air in your lungs, the latter of which you will be unable to exhaust with an elevated heart rate.
The strategic element is important as the AI will investigate noises as well as fallen comrades and quickly gift you a bullet hole too many if you're not mobile enough. The experience of pulling off difficult shots on moving targets is very satisfying. The game employs a bullet cam and provides a stupendously graphic visualization of that soldier's jugular you just punctured complete with blood spurt.
You're scored on your abilities as well and the game recognizes the type of shot in terms of distance, moving targets and parts of the body. The save system is liberal enough so that you can save anytime, though the game will eventually inform you that you have saved too many times and thereby dock your score.
Sniper Elite adds additional realism and tension by allowing you to comprehensively search the dead, many times under threat, for survival necessities as opposed to a brusque pat down which might just yield a couple of bullets, though the ability to move the cadaver to a safer area for inspection is available.
While the visuals are indeed dated, the whole package creates an atmospheric stage consistent with bombed out Dresden and I would like to emphasize this accomplishment given the age of the engine. Once you have created a profile, 1080P is supported. Sniper Elite is the definition of a war time classic.

Completed this nifty little puzzle game just now and wanted to write up a positive review.
This is my first Rusty Lake / Cube Escape game. I found it through my Discovery Queue. I found the overarching story and characters (including the cameos from other games) intriguing enough that I want to play more in the series. The mood and setting is spot-on eerie Victorian with touches of occult, just enough to make you uneasy but not completely revolted while playing.
I found the choice to rely on pictographs, colors and other visual cues over text or dialogue to figure out puzzles a welcome challenge, for the most part. A few times, especially in the later puzzles, it was frustrating enough to figure out what to do next that I went to the Rusty Lake website to look up video tutorials. It's nice the developers make these available (but only look when you're well and truly stuck--otherwise you're ruining the experience for yourself!)
There were several classic puzzles 'reskinned' for the story and theme of the game, and I could also see the 'Escape Room' influence (the first game Rusty Lake made, Cube Escape & its derivatives, is an escape-style game). I've played some Escape Rooms with groups in real life, so I'm curious to see how Cube Escape holds up to that experience.
One last thing, the resolution is kinda small, more suited to tablet than desktop. That didn't bother me, though. I could still easily see and manipulate all parts of the screen.
All in all, even with the small frustrations, I found this game to be well worth its $2.99 price. Go get it if you like puzzle games!

After playing Magic for years, I heard about Hex: Shards of Fate and was intrigued. The notion of playing a tradeable card game without physical constraints offered so many possibilities. Within a game, cards can acquire permanent effects, transform into something completely different, and be created and placed into your deck. You also get to do fun things not possible previously such as steal cards from your opponent's deck or hand, see your opponent's hand without him or her knowing, and placing cards into his or her deck.
The project is very ambitious and the team behind Hex: Shards of Fate has delivered very excellent player versus player and player versus environment gameplay.
The PVP scene offers diverse competition where the rock-paper-scissors battle of aggressive decks vs mid-range vs control is constantly evolving. There never truly is a single "best deck"; weekly competitions feature new, surprising decks constantly.
The PVE portion of the game features an exciting new way for TCG players to explore their creativity. Players can create their own heroes with special abilities that interact with their deck and their opponent's deck. Cards can even be upgraded with special equipment, creating powerful options for cards and combinations.
Finally, enough cannot be said about the community of players supporting Hex: Shards of Fate. Whether through in-game chat or while participating in a streamed event, new players are always welcomed and often given assistance with gameplay, deckbuilding, and even collections.
I'm looking forward to how both the PVP competitive scene evolves and the PVE story is told over time. Hex: Shards of Fate offers hours of gameplay and the freedom to play the game how you want to.

I don't tend to write reviews but play Out There has made me feel like in this case I should. I'm not actually writing this because it's an awful game, but neither am I able to say that it is a good one and due to the very on the fence nature of the thing, I can't help to say that this side more with the negative.
All the more so becuase you really real like there is something sratching away at the surface that could be great but it is never given the opportunity to shine. Ultimately that is the biggest sin of Out There, it feels like a game that was put together but never played through properly by those creative minds. I really like the idea of collecting elemnts that can be used to further your progress and status of your ship, but really all the different ships that you encounter for the most part are simply larger cargo holds to cram in more tat that you may never use. Admittedly there are the occasional different ways to fuel these ships but it isn't something that is really explored in-game, this makes parts of it are frustratingly mundane, but anyone who likes a rogue style game is more than aware that the micro management side of such properties is simply a part of the style of gameplay to one degree or another, but in playing this game you find yourself punished not for the choices you make but just the plodding on of your quest.
There have been several playthroughs in which I have been forced to backtrack almost my entire journey back the way I came, usually just because of an upgrade that is missing or in some cases becuase you just cant go any further. All the more hair-pullingly frustrating becuase you can't zoom out of the starmap to anything other than your own current radius POV, even if you have already visited many places behind your route. lIttle things like this make for a real stalling in the gameplay and it creates that awful feeling of just having had enough of this trudgery, as does the fact that you don't seem to have any quick way of transferring cargo back and fore to your ship, all the more niggling when you are grinding single items at a time to squeeze the most fuel from probing stars and gas giants for your vital costly journies between systems.
If like me you manage to pick the game up cheap then I guess that it can be worth it, the artwork is certainly beautiful and it creates a nice atmosphere but for me this doesn't cover up the real flaws in the game, which frankly don't get any better when you do reach one of the few conclusions to the story and find yourself shrugging at the time wasted on a couple of exploratory dialogues and then promptly ends, asking you to do it all over again following some different, but achingly simlar route to another finale.

I absolutely love games that are often described as "walking simulators" (Dear Esther, The Path, etc.), as what they lack in gameplay they generally make up for in story, dialogue, and visuals. Unfortunately, Rememoried is lacking in almost every aspect.
The art style, while nice and minimalist, sometimes makes it hard to see where you're supposed to be going next. This is especially frustrating during the vertical portions of the game. The dialogue is atrocious, vague, and the sound design leans way too heavy on the reverb. If subtitles weren't present I wouldn't be able to decipher much of what's said. Most importantly, Rememoried is much less a walking simulator than it is a "stepping stones" simulator.
There is so much emphasis placed on platforming in this game when the controls are too sluggish to offer any real precision. I'd often become quite frustrated after having spent so long trying to jump across a seemingly endless amount of rotating cogs or floating boulders, only to fall off near the end, having to start over again several times.
Rememoried is a promising game, I really do enjoy the glitchy visuals and the premise of being trapped in the protagonist's dream but I feel that the developer let its potential go to waste and, rather than focus on a story-driven adventure game, instead opted for yet another platformer type adventure game with a unique art style.
Despite the cringeworthy dialogue, I started out quite impressed and quickly found myself not being able to enjoy Rememoried at all.

As a game though this is a very good one, one that anyone interested in naval warfare should look at.
If you are even remotely interested in naval warfare from the great age of the gun then this is a very good game to check out. The game isn’t perfect, the interface can be frustrating to newbies but the game is fun, and engrossing.
The game is not a fast paced game. Yes, you can speed up the time in the game, in fact, you will have to if you want to play the game at all, but even so this is a slow paced game and the action fulfils itself over time. If you want a quick bang bang style game then this isn’t it. The ships of the time were notoriously inaccurate in their firing and in this game it is evident. In the end I recommend the game.

Rememoried is a first-person adventure game, focused on the ideas of dreams and memories with surrealistic, explorative and puzzle-solving settings.
The way you advance in the game is by looking away from your surroundings, elements in the environment, and other important objects for they’ll constantly change shape and create a new path.
“You count the stars above your head just like the one who pointed a finger at you from the unknown. The closer you get to infinity, the more you get lost in the numbers created to describe the real world, and your eyelids become curtains that hide unexpected discoveries beyond the borders, reached by only the strongest thoughts. This exciting play for one spectator is a reward for everyday gifts of the mind.”
The game is visually stunning, along the sound of flowing water combined with the elegant classical and eerie electronic music.
This combined with a breathtaking environment makes the game incredibly relaxing if you just explore and don’t focus on the objective.
At times the game can be frustrating or difficult to discover what your objective is for a specific level.
All individually difficult to figure out which requires patience to get into its mechanics yet not impossible to beat them.
But overall, I still had a blast playing through this small indie title. A beautiful game with an equally relaxing soundtrack! Definitely worth a try!

My experience with this game was strange. I spent the most time on the first level and the last level. I have no idea exactly how long I played it for, as my actual time lies, I left the game running for a while in between play sessions, thinking I'd only be gone so long. After level one I found the game to be much easier,  and stranger. I think because I spent so much time in level one, I got a little too attached and even scared of the thing that brings you to the next level.
The game itself is like a 2 hourish walk through several strange worlds. I equate it to a dream because most individuals report dreaming  in black and white, however with the few instances of gorgeous color this game fits the description of a dream itself. The game itself is rather fun, there is one blaring issue that comes to mind, which is present in plenty of indie titles and that is the reliance on one major mechanic to tell the story. In fez it was world flipping, in this game it is 'forgetting' you basically look away from the platforms until they move to your liking, when you're looking at them they don't change. To progress through the game you must walk over to a specific point or do something specific in the almost uninteractive environment. Uninteractive doesn't necessarily mean bad for this game as it isn't necessary a puzzle game, more of a goal understanding with you looking for a focal point in a level and then finding your way over.
If I had to improve the game (and probably my review here) I'd do a few things, make it either less or more deep, and probably add more variety in puzzles. I found myself frequently flicking my mouse back and forth to change my stepping stones or to look for something changing by the end of the game.

This is an outstanding visual novel.
Fair warning though, this game is disturbing and if you downloaded it on a whim not knowing what you're getting into then be warned that, despite the cutesy title, this is a straight up horror game which deals with some very dark subject matter in a very unflinching way.
Basically the protagonist is an orphan girl with an abusive past who is befriended by a cheerful piano prodigy and her mysterious and creepy benefactor. As the characters get older, You alternate between the present, where you are mourning the suicide of your best friend and trying to get to the bottom of her death, and flashbacks to your time growing up with her and the history of her troubled relationship with her older benefactor-turned-lover. All the while the protagonist is guided by the voice of her abusive dead mother in her head which you, the player, have to control.
It can be distressing to play at times because you essentially have the choice to influence the character by being either horrible or REALLY horrible and that can feel really uncomfortable at points. I almost gave up quite early on because I found that having to play as the "Mother" character was just too upsetting. I persevered though, and I'm glad I did, although my first play through I felt like I'd done everything I could in my limited power to steer her away from doing something awful and still managed to completely screw her up. There isn't always an obvious "good" option in some scenarios, so you find yourself agonising over your choice of words every single time and wondering if you've just screwed things up or done the right thing.
This game is relentlessly disturbing from the outset but, although there are some gory and unsettling CG scenes, most of the creepiness comes from the writing, which is excellent.
If it sounds bleak, it is, but it's exceptionally well written and all the characters are very well fleshed out. There are no straight up heroes and villains in this, everything is in a moral grey area that's beautifully explored and lets the readers draw their own conclusions and judgments.
For a free game, the amount of content and replay value you get is unreal. The artwork is gorgeous, the writing is excellent and with 4 endings (plus a secret ending) and a ton of bonus content, it's well worth getting. You can tell that the creators of this game really did it as a labour of love - a lot of thought and effort has gone into this game and every single scene and piece of dialogue has been beautifully crafted.
I'd give this a solid 9.5/10. Minus half a point for the fact that I'm pretty sure I'm going to have nightmares tonight.

At first, I would like to applaud the setting, which is unique and interesting. The rise of ironclads is a turning point of naval history and a great background for a naval simulation. And every new naval sim is a good thing. Frankly I'm surprised that the game did not notice the portals and blogs as Wargamer or SimHQ. I found this game by accident. I bought a tablet PC and began looking for games suitable for the technical requirements, and my interests.
In turned-based mode this game is a great introduction to deep strategy games, with a lot of the under-the-hood stuff being cut out to focus on movements and battles. Not very easy to master, but much more detailed than it looks like and, most of all, pretty accurate from historical point of view. The AI will beat you down and exploit every error in your strategy and must have been inspired by an advanced chess program, and if you dont pay close attention when playing youll have your head handed to you in short order. This is the part where the games AI really shines: tactical withdrawals, smart counterattacks, always looking for the gap that can be used to destroy your forces. This part of the game is absolute self-sufficient and I would not be surprised if some people will play the game and do not use manual battles. Even if you're not a fan of naval battles, this game mode will entice you.
The graphical interface of the game is generally clean and simple, well adapted to the skirmish scale of naval battles. I specially appreciate the use of simplified navigating instruments to change the direction or the speed of the boat. Graphically, the game looks pretty good, is functional, and adds to the game. Warships and other units are very detailed, well rendered and look very good.
But for such a game, which appeals to a specific group of fans, I hoped for some more features in real time battle mode. Crew management and such... ships should be allowed to designate how much crew are to work on repairs, put firesout etc. not just random.
In my view, its a little lacks depth in real time mode to be a really great game, but I would recommend it for wargame and naval enthusiasts! Basically if you have any interest what so ever in Civil War naval combat this is the choice of game to place, I highly recommend it!

- Short Review + Personal Ratings Below:
Prototype 2 is a good succesor for the Prototype franchise with a story that continues where the first game stopped. Even though the story takes about 8-10 hours to complete, it feels a little bit bland and rushed towards the end. I was very much into the game just to realize it was time to battle the "big boss", but I guess my confusion was also a result of me checking the percentage of the game being completed not realising that it tracks all the collectables and upgrades of the protagonist.
While the leveling system is totally different than the first game, it is well built and rather easy to  upgrade your powers and get new mutations. The battle mechanics are wonderful but one huge problem I have with the game is the "Target" selection system that fails to work half of the time, especially in locations filled with a lot of targets. Anyway apart from this problem fighting enemies is very satisfying and it always gives you the feeling that you are impossible to kill.
Running, climbing and flying are working good and I am really glad that they actually made a few missions that put these mechanics to work. The climbing mechanic has little issues inside a closed area where it doesn't stick properly to walls or it gets stuck in a corner.
The graphics and animations are good, but the cutscenes while they seem really interesting at the beginning, towards the middle and the end of the game they get tiring and give you the feeling of being repetitive even if they aren't. The problem is the lack of color. Not a single cutscene has any colors other than red and black/white.
The sounds are mainly good, but I personally had moments where the voice of the protagonist would either be very loud out of nowhere or just disappear and see his mouth move without any noise made.
I personally enjoyed my hours spent in this game especially considering that I collected all the little boxes and finished all the side missions, so I recommend this game to anyone who loves killing little digital mutants.

I just got into Magic The Gathering, so I decided to also give this game a shot. I am happy to report my experience so far has been great. The game does have a grind that you do need to get through before you can start to enjoy drafts with other people, but I'm looking forward to trying them when I get the chance. However, here are my pros and cons with the game.
Pros:
- Game does an alright job of teaching you the basics through a single player campaign.
- Community through the in-game chat and on their forums are generally very friendly and helpful.
- You don't need to pay real money to play, but you can if you want to accelerate your progress.
- Deviates from the gameplay of MTG just enough that it isn't an exact copy and actually betters Magic Duels in some aspects.
- Auction House so you can sell your cards to other players to buy others that you may need to build an ideal deck.
- Tournaments running all of the time, so you always have something to do, provided you have the in-game currency for it.
- Cool character system found in the campaign that allows you to give your character different abilities and perks as you level him/her up.
Cons:
- Some server issues, but these can be overlooked, as they are a common side affect of releasing on steam to a brand new audience of people.
- Developer could do a better job of notifying people if there is a problem, such as on the main menu instead of on their forums, it would help the noobs that are lazy find out what is going on.
- HUD could be worked on a tad to make it more user-friendly for people that have not touched a TCG before, or have only touched one such as hearthstone. Don't make it like hearthstone where it's blatently obvious. I don't think the majority of users will like that haha.
All in all, this is a great TCG with a thriving community, and could get even better with a bit more work and care put into it. Also, a note to anyone bashing the game, it's just been released on steam to a new audience. Give it a week or two to be able to iron out any problems related to the servers. It is definitely worth a try as there is no price of admission, and who knows.... you may just find a brand new game to sink time into.

"Contextualization." The process of giving background to a particular mechanic/element. Gothic starts with contextualizing its currency through a fairly novel central premise. It contextualizes abstracted RPG mechanics through trainers, it contextualizes quests through varying camp motives and cultures, and it even contextualizes the arms and armour you find and buy through their faction significance.

Gothic is without a doubt one of the most contextualized and lore-justified RPGs of all time. It rides on it, sustains on it, and manages to be incredibly engaging and involving for it. This is a game that's absolutely committed to its aesthetic, an aesthetic of a magically sealed megaprison where the prisoners have taken over and everyone is looking to either maintain the status quo or find a way out.

On your one-way trip to the colony, you arrive with nothing practical but the clothes on your back and start with what's without a doubt the slowest starting chapter of any aRPG to date. You immediately start running to the three camps situated at opposite ends of the map, grabbing every part time errand you can and getting roughly 90-95% of the game's sidequests in the first couple of hours.



You build your way up slowly, hitting squawking scavenger birds with a pickaxe and coming to grips with the weird controls. Less the controls themselves - it's a hyper-streamlined setup of action+direction, not a billion hotkeys, than the specifics of the combat. And I'm not sure how much of this is incompetence, or Gothic's compatibility with modern software. So we're going to put an incompetence warning here.



I never managed to get the combos to reliably work. The idea being you'd swing right to left, left to right, all that good stuff, it's fundamentally decent. But it seemed to randomly ignore or follow inputs and the only real success I had was from quickly hammering out action+forward/left/right to pretend-combo from neutral. Which worked alright so maybe it's a non-problem outside of the weird refusal to attack from block. But just sometimes refuse. It's odd.





Crowd control is an absolute mess, with limited ways to respond to multiple enemy telegraphs, a limited timed block and the mostly tank controls (you do get a decent strafe), despite having all the tools to theoretically take on any group of enemies at any time, it boiled down to attempting to aggro them one at a time or otherwise hoping you vastly outstat them.

Which you usually do, by the time you have to take them on. It's well paced like that.

One on one it's manageable. You don't take any damage while blocking, but eventually most enemies become invulnerable in most states. Trying to sock those skeletons or such, they just infinitely backstep through your usual sock'em tactics. Thankfully, you can just sock them in the face whenever they telegraph an attack. Or in the case of skeletons, when they strafe. It gets awkward and amounts to kiting in circles and throwing out hits or immediately dying when faced with more than one fire lizard.

You hit hard and get hit hard, combined with enemies not respawning in an open world game and you've got some fast-paced combat. Which is somewhat of a shame, in a weird way, I'd have appreciated more practice at not sucking. I never did figure out how to really hit fire lizards outside of their vicinity roar.



As for the rest of the game's pacing: you eventually get teleport stones to each of the game's main locations, but until then - get walking, prisonboy. This is not a 47 hour game, it's a 30-35 hour one, but roughly 15 hours of that is spent in the first chapter with no armour walking from place to place. If you can survive that, you're basically done with the less than stellar part of the game and it snowballs in speed from there.



There's a handful of minor RPG mechanics; some weird stuff with stealthing and pickpocketing which is great if you hate time and yourself, and the story itself is surprisingly decent - laced with political intrigue and rug-pulls. Factions shift, the storyline takes complete turns while remaining around the center goal of getting out of the superjail, and the dialogue stays exactly as ill-casted, and thus amazing, as you could possibly want.

Final boss sucks, it's a puzzle boss with some mobs followed by a 2-second cutscene, but that's RPGs for you.

Gothic is absolutely worth your time. Despite pretty sizeable technical problems with modern OSs, combat that's very close to playing well and doesn't quite get there, it has the best example of a world that's committed to its aesthetic, pacing that's committed to an adventure and generally a game that's committed to being memorable.

It pays off.

With the English patch (check the discussion forum), this is currently the most easily understood Lunatic Dawn game in the store.  The Legends Pack also has patches for each of its games, but this one is more complete from what I've seen so far.
Passage of the Book is an open-ended, party-based dungeon-crawling RPG.  It begins by having you create a world according to a few simple parameters, and then you're thrown right into it with some basic equipment and money.  You recruit other party members via inns and through talking to other adventurers, and over time improve all your characters by fulfilling requests and plundering dungeons.  There is no overarching narrative; rather, you're left to do as you like and become as famous/infamous as you please.
Creating a character invovles selecting certain criteria from a small window and selecting someone from a list of generated results.  Age and gender can affect one's stats in different ways - a mid-20's character will generally be stronger than a much older one, but an older one may have much more charisma, for example.  There aren't strict classes as much as there are stats which determine what kinds of actions a character is best at performing - a warrior is going to prioritize strength over intelligence, a mage will do the opposite, so on and so forth.  Again, very freeform and the details are largely up to the player. Party members are NOT created by the player - they are recruited once the game starts.
Passage of the Book is tough.  Enemies can be very powerful and there's little indication as to what kinds of enemies will be in different dungeons, but with persistence and a full party you can usually make it out ok.  Equipment is straightforward - bought at shops, can be improved X number of times, and different folks are better with different weapons.  Inns allow you to talk to various individuals, including your own party members, as well as purchase supplies.  Lamps are especially important for dungeons - you can get stuck in the dark without one!  There are also item shops, temples, training areas (where you raise your own skills in exchange for money), and an information broker through whom you can search for info on specific people and places.
Battle is a turn-based affair similar to other Japanese console RPG's, in that you select an action then watch as everyone takes their turns.  The difference, though, is you only have primary control over your own character - your party acts independently, but can be encouraged to focus on particular enemies or utilize certain strategies (this is largely similar to the other Lunatic Dawn games in the Legends Pack).  After battle, loot is divided amongst your party and can be won through a competitive game.  Once divided, loot belongs to each person, not to the player exclusively, and dividing loot is also what helps maintain cohesion within your party (members can become dissatisfied and leave).
Overall, it's a very open, freeform experience that I've never really encountered elsewhere.  I'd almost call Passage of the Book more of a sim than a traditional dungeon crawler.  Either way, it's a unique experience that fans of old-school dungeon crawling will appreciate, as the mechanics are solid and the sense of accomplishment grows very quickly.  Definitely recommend giving this one a go.

This is a game I have trouble reaching a conclusion on. In all honesty I found the game enjoyable and at one point I was looking specifically for band management simulators, a category this game fits.
However there is a fatal error in the game's coding meaning that if you play it on laptop and your laptop runs out battery suddenly so your computer crashes or something like that (I'm not good with technical language), you lose the "load game" option and the "continue game" function stops working, forcing players to start their saved files again. This kind of fragility in the save system is reminiscent of bootleg GameBoy Advance games, not 2017 digital games.
And then there's some of the jokes made in really poor taste. "Triggered" is not funny and trivialising of mental health issues. The game also mocks African American Vernacular English. Making fun of something specifically associated with an ethnic group that has faced systematic discrimination is racist. And we have "jokes" trivialising sexual assault. These are toxic.
Then there's the price tag. At full price the game comes in at $11USD or around $14AUD if you live in Australia like me. This is ridiculous given that I have seen ZX Spectrum title Rockstar Ate My Hamster for as little as $8AUD or less than $6.50USD loose (although admittedly it usually goes for a lot more when in complete condition). Given that the gameplay of Rock God Tycoon is to some extent similar to that of an idle game, this is even further from reason.
The developers claim to be continuing to update the game. I advise that they fix the glitch in the save system and attempt to atone for the alienation they have caused through their low-grade jokes. Until then I do not intend to return to the game, probably only to make a point.
To any potential buyers of Rock God Tycoon: I suggest looking into older band management simulators such as Rockstar Ate My Hamster or Chart Wars (neither of which I've actually played, to be honest) or perhaps looking into strategy games with other themes that appeal.

Incase you can't tell from the title, Dawn of War II is a Warhammer 40,000 game. If you don't know what that is you better look it up before you think about buying something with Warhammer attached to it,
.
It is also a Games for Windows Live Game as well as a Steam game, so if you want a game for its' multiplayer look somewhere else. Now... I'm going to break things down into ratings.
Gameplay 9/10
Very strategic strategy game, tactics will get you a lot more than sheer numbers or unit strength.
Single-Player Campaign 10/10
The Dawn of War II campaign is a mix between Horde Survival, plot and a RTS. And I'll be damned if it doesn't do it well. Dawn of War II is quite different from its predecessors. No longer is their extensive Base Building. Infact, in a Campaign mission you have NO BASE. You may have a location, a base you need to defend for a mission but it isn't yours. You can't build stuff from it. There are strategic locations scattered around the mission maps though. Your 'army' is divided into 4 squads. Throughout the campaign you will end up acquiring more than 4 squads but you can only deploy 4 squads to a mission. Each squad is unique, they have their own strategies and skills. The game has introduced a Experience system. This system is most noticeable in the Campaign. As you kill and kill, as well as complete missions your Squads will gain levels individually (to a maximum of level 20). With each level your squads gain two points to put in a talent tree of your choice. Most squads have certain trees that they can put enormous amounts of points and skill into, while others they can only put a few in because of previously stated differences in each Squads specialization. Also, you may chose the 'wargear' for each of your squads. Some of these wargear provide statistic bonuses and similar to the squad that has that item equiped. Others are weapons that will allow the squad to better fulfill a certain task. At the end of the day though, you can have considerable flexibility with you squads. Invest you points in the right talent tree and a Squad that is intended to fulfill 1 role a certain way can fulfill a different role in a different way. Customization is one of the primary elements that has been introduced in force in Dawn of War II compared to its' predecessors. An added bonus is that the Campaign is two player, so you can play through the Campaign with a friend (who has the game obviously). From experience, doing the Campaign in co-op is loads of fun.
Multiplayer 0/10
The Games for Windows Live was a huge hassal, and it was not a hard decision for almost the entire active Dawn of War II playerbase to switch over to Dawn of War II : Retribution. Retribution's multiplayer is through Steam, not Games for Windows Live (thank god).
Graphics 8/10
There are games just as old with better graphics, but that being said... the graphics are certainly not an eyesore.
Audio 9/10
Outstanding voicework all around. Very realistic sounds to be heard on the battlefield. Be it the sound of the last spent shell falling onto the ground or one of you squads talking to each other on the field. Music is good.
All in all, great game but I would only recommend it for Warhammer 40k fans, particularly ones who have somebody to the play the campaign in Co-Op with.

While it has potential, I feel this game needs some balancing.  There is some depth here - in fact if you really want to push yourself the game can be made incredibly complex.  Write songs, rehearse, record, shoot videos, play show, accumulate fans (IN the cities you want to play shows), find and complete record deals.  If you had the cash flow for it, you could be doing something nearly every day.  It's actually great in many ways.
I have three issues, that really are catastrophic in my opinion:
1) It is WAY to grindy.  After 6 hours of active game play I was still struggling to make ends meet and make any actual progress.  Any time I tried investing in some way - hire a better band mate, buy some better gear etc - to try and improve my situation, it cash starved me to the point where all I could do was busk in hopes of making enough to cover my monthly nut.
2) There's also a balance issue with the music and rehearsals.  I have to basically constantly write songs in order to keep the recording contracts (and therefore money) coming in, but I would have to rehearse a song a good 10-15 times to even get above 50% on it.   By the time I've rehearsed a song enough to play it live with good results, I've made 3 albums since.  Again, it's just not very enjoyable to know that I can't get halfway decent at the songs I've written without an investment in rehearsal time that I just don't have the money for.
3) It's very unforgiving.  You get one chance to run out of money, and if it happens a second time it's game over.  It's the tycoon version of a roguelike.  It's very easy for this to happen, even if you make it for several hours.  Make a couple of bad decisions at the wrong time of the month, and you're done.
Either of these two things in isolation wouldn't be a problem, but combined they make for a very deflating experience.  Based on my game so far I would say it's probably a good 20+ hours to get to a reasonably succesful band that isn't starving for money, but it would take an incredible amount of diligence and careful planning to make it that far without going broke, and at that point it's just not that fun.  I think it needs to be much more engaging to be interesting for that long, and if it's going to be that long it shouldn't be so easy to go under.

I'm sure a lot of people remember that there was a bit of a voxel game craze a few years ago with the release of Minecraft to the Xbox 360. Most of these games were shameless and mediocre rip-offs of Minecraft. Murder Miners, on the other hand, offered something completely different.
First and foremost, this game is the lovechild of Halo and Minecraft which means several things:
-The game has both the addictive creativity of Minecraft and the action-packed fast-paced fun of Halo.
-The game has both the ceaseless griefers of Minecraft and the immature rage-kickers of Halo.
There are a few flaws with this game, with an annoying community that can result in haphazard gameplay being one of them. Another issue is the low fps rate and serious lag in larger servers (someone could join a normal server and it can suddenly become almost unplayable). The controls also can get a bit awkward at times... it was easier to build on the Xbox version and the mining gun can get very tedious.
However, the game is still a great game (and needs more players). It may come across as a novelty but for its $2.00 price tag, it has tons and tons of lasting value. The environment is completely destructible and modifiable, leading to a lot of unique strategies. The gameplay, while not diverse, has a nice variety ranging from capture the flag to zombie survival. Most importantly, it's just a fun game and honestly one of the best indie purchases one could make... it's $2.00 and >200 mb and yet manages to deliver a lot in its simple packaging. Would I recommend it? Yes, definitely.

Tonally, this game is great, the artwork, writing and overall theme all work well, creating a distinctive and engaging atmosphere of loneliness and mystery.
Unfortunately, for me, the experience stopped there.  As a game, this simply does not work.  Options are limited and an impossible slide into defeat can only be turned aside by technological advancement, or stumbling across a new ship.  If you do that in a timely fashion the game changes from impossibly difficult to trivially easy.
A successful roguelike or roguelite can definitely tolerate some of the design decions present in Out There, the reverse difficulty curve of a tough start and easy late game can work well - just look at FTL or XCOM.  A heavy reliance on randomness is also not in-and-of-itself a deal breaker, so long as that random element can be mitigated through player knowledge and a transparent game mechanic.
Unfortunately Out There does not provide this mitigation.  Luck is luck.  If you need fuel and you don't come across a fuel source, you're done.  If you need a ship upgrade and the game doesn't decide to give you one, you're done.  There's no consistent and gradual accrual of resources, no ability to cut your losses when your choices aren't working out, you roll the dice and after 20 minutes you are told you're a winner or loser.
For me, that's not fun.
On top of that the game features a highly opaque resource management system that consists of micro managing whether you spend 1 to 10 fuel for an unspecified risk and unspecified reward when mining for metals or probing for gases.  This system doesn't provide player engagement, or meaningful feedback on how your choices work and how to improve them in the future.  It doesn't even provide basic informantion on the chances of success or failure.  Given the large amount of the gameplay that this mechanic constitutes, I found the complete lack of player engagement baffling.

PLEASE DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME.
Dont get me wrong: This is one of the most gorgeous games I have ever had the chance to see, and it was a real treat for a while that made it absolutely terrific. And then suddenly? It becomes more rage inducing than any game I have ever played in my life.
This game is essentially pretty precision platformer: the game. The main gameplay mechanic is to basically spin around in a circle over and over to make objects magically move positions in a system the game likes to call "forgetting". This ends up being a horrible platformer where you need to spin around in circles to make a platform appear close enough to you so you can land on it, and then spin around some more to make another one get closer to you. Some parts of the game aren't like this, are much more straightforward, and honestly fairly enjoyable. But at one point in the game I just could not take it anymore. The platforms were too small, nearly impossible to see in the dark, and I kept falling off of them because they were literally spheres. It was total baloney.
Once again, do not get this game. Please watch a dedicated and skilled Let's Player play through the game for you so you have the chance to see how pretty the game can really be. Do not buy this game thinking it will be some zen experience worthwhile of your time. The developers wanted it to be zen-like, to be taken slowly, but allow me to tell you that when you're stuck in one area for far too long, it is not worth that "zen-like" feeling.
3/10, pretty graphics and cinematography at least. This was a game designed by a brilliant artist...but not a brilliant game designer.

An incredibly simple premise with astounding execution.
The story centers around a freelance spy named Conway that was almost framed for the murder of a friend and employee of a weapons manufacturing company, basing itself on the whole "Cyberpunk future" idea and possibilities. For instance, Conway owns a pair of high-tech pants that allow him to jump to ludicrous heights and sustain little to no falling damage, as well as a device that allows him to rewire virtually anything connected to a power source to fulfill whatever needs he might have. And let's not forget corrupt companies with their evil tycoons sitting at the CEO chair.
Graphically speaking, it's hit-and-miss. If you like pixel art, you'll like this game's style, but if you don't, well, at least the gameplay and music can make it up to you.
Musically speaking, spectacular. If you're a fan of old noir movies and games, the atmospheric soundtrack to this game will touch your inner detective.
And finally, gameplay. 2D sidescrolling with high jumping and stealth elements, in a nutshell. Every thing is responsive, you definitely feel in control of your environment as Conway peruses the electrical grid of the building he's trying to sneak into and of Conway himself, as he either skillfully jumps into an open window, pummels someone to a temporary coma (or death) or silently crawls on ceilings and walls avoiding the watchful eyes of the guards.
All in all, this game is fantastic. Props to Tom Francis and his development team.

Dont let the game time fool you, I've put a ridiculous amount of time into this game since last september.
Hex got me hooked almost immediately. As a long-time MTG player (started around 1st Mirrodin block) I was able to pick up the basics of the game fairly quickly. But even now I'm still discovering new card interactions and ways to play. Don't get me wrong, I adore Magic, but I've drifted away from the card shop scene, and Magic's digital offerings are completely garbage. Hex, while fairly similar to Magic in many ways (part of the appeal to me imho), has enough uniqueness to both set it apart from Magic and elevate it in many ways.
Hex fully embraces the possibilities of a digital-only card game, and I can't wait to see what Primal Dawn (set 4) will bring to the table.
---
Pros:
-Digital nature allows for some truly bonkers card design. Super fun!
-Collection has real value
-PvP is competitive and fun, even though I still suck at limited :P. Will be even better once ladders are implemented.

I went into Prototype 2 affected by the feedback, expecting an extremely poor game. I'm a pretty spoiled person when it comes to gaming and if a game isn't polished I won't be very forgiving.
Regarding the alleged texture inconsistencies - they're there. I toyed with the settings to no avail, sometimes the game will look great, sometimes it will look ugly because of textures randomly switching to low res. I haven't looked for fixes, but I doubt there are any.
Regarding the poor controls, though, I didn't feel it. Played the game with a steam controller with a custom mapping and the game was really easy to adjust to and very responsive. I can't say about the keyboard setup, but I was already told it's really bad and the game shouldn't be touched without a controller.
When it comes to the gameplay itself, though, I would say Prototype 2 delivers 100%. It's an extremely fun character action game with a really well designed combat system. It really encourages you to change between powers and do cool stuff, unlike games like Devil May Cry, for example. You have a variety of gory finishers for every power, tons of exploding giblets and flying limbs, the game is just hypnotic, I can't really say anything bad about the gameplay except maybe that there were a bit too many vehicle driving sequences for me, especially in the side missions. I still completed them to 100% though, so I guess even they weren't that bad.
Overall I do say - if you don't have a controller I don't recommend the game for you. If you do have one - 100% recommended. In general I recommend the game a lot. I spent over 16 hours on it, barely playing anything else until I finished it.

An underrated RPG gem. Do not be put off by the clunky controls of the game, because this is still one of the most atmospheric and original RPG's ever created.
The story is mysterous and gripping. The pacing is very well done and the characters attitude towards the player through the course of the game makes the world feel very believable. You feel a sense of growth as a protagonist, because in the beginning of the game you are trash, a new kid on the block, and all the "tough guys" give you a hard time. You can't really fight back aswell, cause you are not skilled enough. But in time, as you explore the game world, it's comunities, make friends, and meet characters that can help you to train and advance your skills, you become more and more capable of dealing with situations, that seemed impossible before. The story is also well done in the sense that, the beginning of the game is just about your personal motivations as a player, to escape the colony, work your way up to a more powerful position in the hopes of figuring out how to do that. But in time, you discover, that much more is at stake, and the road to your freedom is filled with magic and acient, long forgotten deities.
Gameplay is very deep. True, the controls are quite bad, but getting used to them is just a matter of few hours. The technical limitations of the time can be felt, but Gothic tries and succeeds at doing things way before it's time. Skills and abilities must be actually learnt from trainers in the world, adding to the realism, sword, bow and crossbow handling animations actually change to more advanced ones after training. Npc's have daily work cycles way before Todd Howard's claims that Morrowind did it first. All npc's are voiced, aswell as the main protagonist. The voiceacting might feel a little dated and campy at times, but the dialogue and it's options ar very high quality. The open world is not that large, compared to modern day open worlds, but it is's very detailed and has no useless empty spaces, to artificially increase it's size. The world feels alive and real despite the aged graphics.
The ending of the game will be the same for all players, because it sets up a sequel, but the way you get to it can be very different for every player. Your choices have consequences and this game gives you a lot of replay value. To experience everything the game has to offer, one would have to beat it 3 times.
In conclusion, I would say It's a must play for everyone that loves a good RPG, and don't hesitate playing because of the age and graphics of the game.

MAIM. MURDER. DESTROY. CUT. DESTROY. MAIM.... Uh.. ANGST. SUCH ANGST.
*Ahem*
So after the first game, which was effectively the Incredible Hulk: Ultimate Destruction with the ability to make everything you come across into a pile of gore, I had high hopes for the sequel.
How does this sequel fare compared to the first one? Well..
***Graphics***
This game (when compared to the first one) is amazing looking, weapon forms are more defined and visceral looking, with pulsating veins running through both your model and your form. The new Blackwatch models are much more menacing now. See, in the last game Blackwatch looked like a generic Umbrella Corp soldier rather than a supposed super powerful sect of the military. Now, the Blackwatch models have a more... discount Warhammer 40K vibe going on, I dig it.
Heller himself looks pretty decent too, the glowing veins on his back certainly help him pop-out.
As for the infected, they look pretty cool. CERTAINLY better than that of the first game. In the first game, the hunters looked kind of silly, almost undefined. Now these "Brawlers" are filled with bone and more Sci-fi anatomy to make them stand out from how they used to look.
The animations are also miles better, everything feels so fluid and real, as though you are actually there this time. On top of this, when Heller holds a gun, he actually looks like a soldier. In the first game, Alex would get really low to the floor and as a result he stuck out so much. Heller looks more like he blends in, adding to the whole "I'm not supposed to be visible to my enemy" vibe.
***Sound***
The music in this game is hit and miss. Certain songs are perfect for mission while other songs are so quiet and mute that they might as well not be there. It uses a lot of the generic Hollywood style instruments, adding to the "meh" vibe it brings.
The sound effects on the other hand..
Cutting people in half sounds so brutal, metal tings off of tanks while the gory gushy sound that is made when cutting into a flesh target sounds so good.
***Gameplay***
While this game is a marked improvement over the first in several regards, this is where they slammed into a wall.
For a start, combat is barebones and powers have no extra moves from what you have been given from the start. This could be contrasted by the weapons evolving but I say nay to this. The Evolution system is cool to see with the weapon form having a different appearence at each stage, but you are not told ANYTHING about what this does aside from making you look cooler.
On top of that, once you get the sword and the tendrils, this game becomes incredibly easy. You become a whirlwind of destruction and while this is very fun during free-roam, it's boring as hell in missions when you have to approach every single mission the same way.
Monsters have the same strategy every time.
Attack.
Dodge.
Attack.
Block.
Attack.
Dodge.
Consume.
Ugh.
This game is also sporting bugs that go beyond the realm of "minor"
For example, in the game's "Lairs," places where the infected have set up shop and you need to kill everything in sight to win. Occasionally however, the target monsters you need to kill will spawn OUTSIDE the damn arena. You know what that means? You can't progress unless you reload the game or die.
The game also has incredibly questionable damage, Heller isn't the most buff protagonist but I swear his skin will randomly become the consistency of glass for no reason. This leads to you dying from nowehere from an attack you swear to god you dodged.
Need more?
The game also has a tendency to lag when you begin running too fast, this isn't bad at first but as you increase your movement speed, it becomes a legitamate problem when the game begins lagging from trying to load as you sprint across the map faster than Sonic on meth.
It's also sad to see the armor power up gone and instead relegated to a skin, A Skin. That costs MONEY.
Okay maybe only on the PS4 version where they seperated these into packs.. But that leads me to my biggest contention with this game.
Radnet.
If you didn't know, Radical Entertainment is dead, they folded awhile back, but Radnet persists. The entire point of Radnet is to give content from Radical but if they are dead, so is the 10$ DLC pack that you pretty much NEED to get longetivity out of this game.
Radnet should not be a thing anymore, knowing Activision though, that'll never happen.
***Conclusion***
The future of Prototype as a series is questionable, this series has a large amount of potential, but with the series not having any potential for a microtransaction laden mess of lootboxes and funbucks, I doubt we'll see Prototype 3 anytime soon.
It's for that reason that I must recommend that if you liked the first game, you could do worse than getting this. If you are new to the franchise, this is a decent starting point as its own game. You don't need to have played the first to enjoy this one, and what is on offer allows for some good entertainment for a 7-10 hour story.
Get it on sale if you can, it isn't worth full-price anymore.. And don't buy Radnet if you seriously don't need it.

I *mildly* recommend this game, and with a caveat that you must have some form of interest or history with the Dragonball series, which is fairly common among people that grew up in the 90's and had basic cable. If you don't care for Dragonball then skip it, since the game is arguably below average.
Xenoverse is a game about Trunks calling forth someone to assist him in fixing tears in time whereby events have been altered from how they were originally supposed to occur. That person is you: you assist Trunks in fixing the timeline by going to various battles in Dragonball history and defeating enemies. I won't ruin the plot but there's a reason why the timeline is being altered; but the main draw here is that you get to see various "what-if" scenarios to past battles in the Dragonball Franchise and have your avatar participate in them. That's certainly part of the draw, and if you know absolutely nothing of the series it means a lot less to you, and a portion of the draw disappears. You don't need to be up to date on Dragonball and know everything there is to know to enjoy this, but remembering the sagas and details on a few of the occurences should sustain you enough to enjoy this.
There's no exploration involved in this game, no traversing a map, and no sidequests that involve anything other than fighting people in large open areas. Even the hubworld is rather empty and just a means to show characters created by other players, which is admittedly interesting. Otherwise I'm a bit let down; the inclusion of more exploratory aspects in the Dragonball universe isn't something that is necessarily *missing* here, as the package works as is. When something is *missing* it's something that is required by the final product and its absence is conspicous-its inclusion would solve issues. There are no issues here with a game mainly focused on arena battles, but its inclusion would certainly 'upgrade' the package and added to the experience.
So what of the battles? Well, the game's fights all occur in large arenas and attacks occur in two formats: close range combat and projectile blasts. You have two buttons for attacks (one weak, one strong) and one button dedicated to energy blasts (hold for continous blasts). Since the game has massive arenas, most battles, just as in the show, are characters flying in the air speeding into one another like car crashes waiting to happen, and attacking each other in quick succession. This has its ups and downs.
For one thing, the look of the game and the battles is fairly faithful to the show itself; everyone is flying around punching each other quickly in the air and bodies are flying far away with each finishing punch, which creates distance between combatants and prompts more flying towards one another for more blows.
But the fight system is fairly simple. A two button melee system means that the combo system is barebones and revolves around, like, 10 different combinations of X and Y in 4 button strings. Additionally, because there is always massive distance between combatants and you're always closing large gaps by flying incredibly fast, you'll often find yourself in situations where youre missing punches (both you and the CPU) and flying slightly past your target and punching the air. It's not a big deal, and it's not as if you'll be stuck doing long animations or anything, but it happens a lot and shows how combat isn't as tight as it can be. When you DO land a punch on an enemy your combo will go off without a hitch, and you can continue it with more attacks, but its worth noting that you might find yourself trying to land that first punch for 7 or so seconds.
Worth noting is how useless the projectile button is. Enemies can simply move out of the way. Ironically these long range attacks are better used in close range. For all intents and purposes this games meant to be played up close to the enemy, which sort of defeats the purpose of huge arenas when its mostly you trying to run up to the enemy-you can cut the middle man and just reduce arena size but that would also take an aspect of the anime away from the game.
This game can be played single player, but you can also play quests and battle with other players. This game has a sort of Borderlands feel in that it can certainly be done single player, but the developers seemed to have multiplayer in mind. You can still "recruit" characters that show up in the hubworld that are created by other players, so you don't even need to necessarily interact with others in order to play with their creations. Other characters certainly help in the game, but it's not a requirement to passing the storymode or optional sidequests.
All in all the game feels like the older beat-em ups. Simple fighting system; multiplayer optional and makes the experience more enjoyable. I still enjoyed going through all these DBZ battles that I somehow remembered (not vividly, mind you) despite having watched the show when I was, like, 9, which kept me from getting bored. Ultimately you have a simple arena fighter/beat em up with a lot of customization, a beautiful engine, a multiplayer and co-op component that makes this ideal for a romp with friends, but a single player experience that still provides a decent amount for people familiar with the series. I'd say it's worth somewhere in the vicinity of 20 dollars.
Lightly recommended, especially to fans of the series that like the idea of being in battles in the series. Otherwise I'd say this game is below average, so 4/10. I'd tell most people to skip it unless they're fans of Dragonball-if you don't care for the series you'll most likely get bored after 6 or so hours. There were sidequests, and I typiucally play games to completion, but I couldn't be bothered with this one, so it should signify that this package is mostly about the Dragonball and the story more than anything else (as the sidequests have no story to them other than a brief sentence).

Recommended, albeit with caveats.
Now, this is not really a shooter where you can just run around and shoot everything. Set in WW2 in and around Berlin during the Russian counterattrack you play as a sniper surrounded by enemies. Keeping it somewhat realistic, you need to stay hidden as much as possible and take out enemy soldiers from afar. Close combat is very dangerous, especially on higher difficulties. But it’s not exactly a stealth game like Dishonored or Deus Ex either. You don’t have some form of «superpower» that renders you nearly invisible. Once you fire your gun, chances are enemies will start homing in on your position, so moving around is often essential to avoid getting pinned down. Adding to this is the enemy AI, which can be both unpredictable and even competent at times! Enemies (usually) take cover when under fire and will occasionally choose surprising routes to get to your position. Trying to keep track of multiple enemies can be quite the challenge.
This game then is no walk in the park, but even at the highest difficulty it didn’t feel unfair or undoable. You will almost certainly die from time to time, either from making a mistake or the (somewhat) arbitrary nature of the AI, but since you can save at any time it’s not really an issue.
Oh, and you can also turn on bullet physics forcing you to take gravity and wind into account when firing at long range.
The campaign is also very well designed. Most of your mission goals feel meaningful and make sense. With large open maps there is also a bit of freedom to do things your own way, which I liked.
There are eight missions, most of them with multiple sub-missions, which adds up to 27 maps + 1 «secret» mission. Each sub-mission plays out as a series of objectives that must be completed. Objectives are quite varied and range from assassinations, providing fire support and blowing up tanks to rescuing and escorting pilots out of Berlin.
Visually it’s showing its age, of course. It’s from 2005, and wasn’t particularly stunning back then either. With almost the entire game set in wartorn ruins, expect lots of drab sepia colored areas.
The sound is fine and does help with the atmosphere. Most of the maps have distant machinegun fire, explosions, screaming and engine sounds like you would expect in a warzone. Russians actually speaking Russian and Germans speaking German is a nice touch. However, the voice acting in general is incredibly flat, especially the main character.
The controls get a lot of criticism, and not without reason. First off, your character moves very oddly, almost as if iceskating. I guess they were going for inertia, but it just feels weird. Secondly, the inventory system is cumbersome to use, so using things like health packs and explosives is more of a hassle than it should be. Grenades are also a bit strange. You see a trajectory path when you throw them, but they seem to be made of rubber as they often bounce far away from where they land. You sort of get used to these things after a while though.
I started out strongly disliking the game, but it actually grew on me. Sneaking around while taking out enemy soldiers can be a lot of fun. That said, anyone looking for a spectacular action game or is unwilling to forgive the slightly clunky controls should probably look elsewhere.

Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War II was pretty good. Unlike its predecessor, Dawn of War 1, the base building concept is thrown out the window with this one. Instead it's squad-based, like Company of Heroes for example, which happens to be a Relic game as well.
It ends up playing more like an Action RPG really, with you using the specific skills of each of your unique squadmates, each with their own personality and class, collecting new armor, weapons, to change up your playstyle as needed, and last but not least, leveling up and boosting your characters. Hell, even the boss fights keep you on your toes, with their own abilities having you to keep moving around in order to take as little damage as possible. I enjoyed that, and I also enjoyed Relic's streamlined approach to ye olde RTS.
And no, streamline does not an easier game make. It very much punished me for getting my priorities wrong when it came to focus fire on the wrong unit. Wasn't a complete cakewalk on Normal difficulty and I'm thankful for that. Though perhaps that could have been because I largely ignored the cover mechanic, which is strongly stressed in these games, yet seldomly did I feel the need to jump into cover.
Now Relic knows how to make good RTSes. Not only that, they also know how to give the amazing Warhammer 40k universe the epicness it rightfully deserves. Now I'm not too familiar with the 40k lore at all, but this game got me curious to want to learn more about it, because it just reeks of awesome. The voice acting's awesome, the music fits right into the mood, and the ambience and atmosphere is spot on.
The campaign mode isn't Starcraft 2's levels of inventiveness and non linearity, but it's not slouch either. You get all kinds of optional missions to do, special persistent buildings that you can capture that maintain passive bonuses for you throughout the game, that you have to keep defending every now and then against invaders. Though honestly, the missions do get a bit repetitive eventually, and by the end I just wanted to go to the ending and get it over with. Again, it's not because I found this a bad game, I liked it a lot, but I played the Campaign mode only, and RTS single player campaigns are hard to get right. While the old school RTSes didn't care at all about their level design, (build base, kill other guy's base, repeat) Dawn of War II at least gets points in effort for trying to mix it up.
As for the story itself, it was admittedly clichéd but again, the epicness of the Warhammer 40k universe is so compelling by itself that I actually want to get Chaos Rising and Retribution eventually just to see how it all unfolds. Dawn of War II was a nice ride, but not one I'd keep coming back to for more over and over again.
