Rock God Tycoon (RGT) is an interesting management style game in it's Early Access phase.  I've played a few hours and surely haven't seen all that the game has to offer, but I feel that I've grasped the basics of what the game is all about.
In a word I'd call it Busking Simulator before I call it RGT.  To scrape by as a fledgling musician, you have to "busk" which means to play your instrument and hope someone throws some quarters your way.  You don't actually participate in this, but your character(s) gain 10+ dollars an hour or so, which helps you make rent for the first few months.  In between this you have your players practice to advance certain skills.  All of this raises tension in the band so you blow half the money you earned busking on a trip to the bar.  You keep doing this over and over.
Every now and then you'll book a show and get♥♥♥♥♥♥on by critics, make a few dollars and shoot your band tension back through the roof.  Off to the bar again!  Don't spend too long there though, you have to busk for the rest of the month to make rent!  Do all of this for a half hour or so on super fast speed and you'll consistently be making rent, a record label will buy one of your first songs for a few thousand dollars and then you can buy a car and move around, busking your way through the northeast United States.  You can get a record deal which requires you to meet a few criteria within a month, pretty simple stuff.  Your record, which will be about as good as your live shows will somehow make you 5k+.  At this point I busked a little more, missed a deadline on my second record deal and went bankrupt.  Oops.  Couldn't really be bothered to spend another hour in Busking Simulator to get back there.
The Pros:
- Niche music creator - you can "make" the songs you write using pre-made riffs (bass, guitar, drums).  Doing this doesn't make the song any better or worse, and in the grand scheme it is a waste of time.
- A fresh take on the management genre, still EA so improvements on the way (maybe?)
The Cons:
- Song writing - the song is always as bad as the lowest skill "song writing" character you include in the song writing process.  Anyone not included in the process starts at 0% ability to play the song.  But get this!  THE PEOPLE THAT WROTE THE SONG ONLY HAVE A 10% ABILITY TO PLAY IT!!!!  If I write a damn song I think I'd know how to play it.  If I write a song and am standing in a garage with my bandmates for months on end, I think I'd be able to show them how to play it.  To improve you have to go to a studio, and you gain at most 3% ability each time (most times it's 1%).  I really have no idea why all the bandmates sit in the garage / apartment....
- Tension - Anything you do creates tension.  You write a song, tension.  You busk (and busk, and busk, and busk), tension.  You rehearse, tension.  You travel, tension.  You play a gig, GUESS WHAT?  TENSION FOR EVERYONE!!!  Go spend $460 at the bar and start all over.  You'd think playing a gig would be a release or something, after all, you are a musician and that's what you love to do?
- Linear Progression - You apply the same tactics over and over and have a linear progression in skills and success.  There isn't any sort of "customization" to your character outside of looks and what you want them to constantly improve.  Your band just gets better a percent at a time, your bandmates get better a percent at a time, you sell more albums, gain more fans, sell more tickets, a percent at a time.
- Playing your songs - To play your "songs" you have to spend the time placing the previously mentioned pre-recorded riffs in a template.  You can make some cool sounding jams (think stripped down Fruity Loops) but again, spending time here doesn't make a difference in the song quality.  However, if you'd like to play the Guitar Hero style mini-game during the shows, you can only do so if you choose songs that you have "made".  I did it twice, had a few note streak things going, but it didn't seem to affect reviews.  Critics still hated me.
In the discussion(s) I saw devs talking with people and some requests seem to have been implemented, so that's nice to see from a dev team.  As it stands now I don't quite know where this game could go (for me).  It's core mechanics are very grindy, unfulfilling, and don't seem to make sense with what most would think of a group of "Rock Gods" in training.
I bought this game on sale.  Not a bad purchase but not really what I was expecting.  I cannot recommend it.

tl;dr: A wonderful game, not just because it is great, but because it is filled with wonder.
Out There is a really good game in the rogue-like genre where most games in the genre are too tough and quite frankly bad. Often times too many games are fail simulators dependent on dice rolls loaded against you. This game, however, is fairer but can be tough at times.
The gameplay involves traveling from star to star and planet to planet picking up vital resources and new technology that improve your capabilities. Eventually you will need another ship and as a result will leave your old ship behind but the base components are pretty much the same. And this continues until you run out of a resource or meet some other untimely demise.
One of the best features of the game is the constant storytelling and worldbuilding. Each log entry, random event, and sentient life encounter enriches the gameplay experience. After 20 or so hours I'm still getting plenty of new stories and notes to be pleasantly entertained.
Other features of note: good soundtrack, great artwork, and fun little choices here and there which can very loosely be called side quests.
I'd say this is a solidly good game with a definite yes recommendation for fans of scifi stories, rogue-like simulators, and survival-type games. I'd rate this a 8.5/10 and I consider myself a pretty tough grader.
Last thought: I really want a sequel, and I want it yesterday.

This is a beautiful, intense and enthralling strategy game by Relic, gameplay is very similar to Company of Heroes but focuses on a single squad of badasses (and some redshirts) getting into all sorts of violent adventures against a plethora of different types of enemies, depending on how deep your pockets are to buy the expansion packs with. This game is truly great but my only complaint is the lack of variety in the maps; here is a game designed to be milked for hours to level your squadmates and get better equipment with which to confront the increasingly difficult battles you have to face (♥♥♥♥ the missions that pit you against Eldar tanks), and you're stuck with the same handful of maps for each planet you visit, same defend the generator missions, same set pieces every time. Some randomization in the map layouts would have given this game some real staying power. I did not care for the multiplayer at all but the single-player is where it's at anyway, and it's glorious despite its flaws. Visceral, personal, condensed tactical strategy done right.

This game hates me is what anyone playing it for a sufficiently long amount of time will think at one point.
However, it is not the case.
Roguelikes are a distinct category of games that are usually unfolding in a fantasy setting. Not over the past year, though. FTL was one of the first ones to become popular and albeit it's usually akin to self torture, the victory is all the sweeter.
I have played Out There on mobile first and when it came out on Steam I was keen on playing it again, this time luxuriously relaxing on my sofa with a Steam controller (or the wireless peripherals of your choice) instead of being hunched over a tablet or a phone.
It has retained the same principles - you're a dude, stranded in space. You need to make do with what you have and then what you harvest from the different planets you encounter. The resources are three - Fuel, Oxygen and Hull, each being replenishable. One of them hits zero. you still have a chance, but that's always a dice roll and I got lucky only once. Says a lot tbh. You can upgrade your ship and you can find and board (or plunder) other ships on your way. You discover technology, but you can also forget how to build stuff. You will meet alien races which have their own language and it's mesmerizing to actually get to discover almost a full language only to end up asphixiated at one point. Or adrift. Or blown up due to sailing too close to the solar winds (literally).
You can mine planets, gas giants, even suns. You can interact with black holes or even create one. You can bring life to planets by terraforming them, only to just chug along nicely to another part of the galaxy.
It is - in the end - a journey. A journey that can end several different ways, however what you feel when you see the credits rolling is that it isn't the end that matters. It's the journey itself.
11/10.

Is Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Links fun? Yes.
Is Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Links for Beginners? Yes.
Is Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Links for Experts? Yes.
Is Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Links really free? Mostly.
Chances are, if you like Yu-Gi-Oh, whether it be as a TCG, a fan of the anime, or looking for something to replace the void that Hearthstone left after you accidentally stopped playing for weeks...you will like this.
The Good:
+ Simplified format makes for quicker games, and easy-to-learn basics
+ Huge selection of cards available for a wide range of strategies
+ Free To Play with Microtransactions that do not generate a "pay-to-win" vibe
+ Nostalgic characters and constant updates (e.g. the new GX update)
+ Online Competitive and Casual PvP modes
+ Lots of missions and goals
The Bad:
- Simplfied format is a little restrictive for experts/TCG fans and takes getting used to
- Short duels (4000LP) mean you can't execute extravagant strategies
- Meta decks are very very apparent and you will struggle to go far without building one
- Steam Trading Cards are earned through microtransactions (ew) as milestones (1 card per 9$)
- Little sense of accomplishment for auto-dueling NPCs for resources
- Some goals feel hard to achieve given the restrictive format and selection of cards being somewhat limited
- As of yet, no synchro summoning, and pendulum and link summoning are just not really possible with the current format of the game, so don't expect any new styles of dueling to be added anytime soon
This review is coming from someone who collects the cards, and loves the anime.

Absolutely stellar game. Best I have had the pleasure to review in a while.
Unlike a couple other recent releases that branded themselves as Tycoons (but were actually more structured games) Rock God Tycoon leaves the majority of choices up to you and gives you the freedom a management sim is supposed to. The goals are simple... Make it big and don't go broke trying. How you go about doing that is left up to you. It is by my definition a game worthy of the "Tycoon" in the title. Those of us old enough to remember Dino Park know what I'm talking about.
Visuals and Sound are great, and the game itself is quite a bit of fun and very addicting. There also seems to be lots of room for growth and I expect nothing but good things given what I've seen so far. If you do what I did and put in 15 hours the first 2 days after purchase, you will notice the music start repeating, but you won't mind. Big fan of the character customization and the little things like the way they all sway in time to the soundtrack.
As for their coding/interface all I can say is wow. I know there are only two devs but this is superhuman. Easy to jump right in and start playing.... Not a single bad thing to say about the way the game runs. No gamebreaking or glaring bugs to speak of. Bit of work to do with some of the place names on the map, but it really is fine as is. (Some have generic names)
Game itself? Depending on your skill level you may think it needs balancing or you may think it's right on the money. I found myself creating challenges for myself like having my first album be only 50%+ rehearsed instead of the lower amounts required by labels. It is very immersive to the point where you'll have fond memories of how hard it was to release your first LP... or how good it felt to fire that ego maniac vocalist. Plus the game cuts out the things that aren't as much fun about a rock band like waiting in line to use a copier to make flyers or expensive rights lawsuits when you lose a bandmember.
Overall I whole-heartedly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys a good Tycoon game and anyone that enjoys rock/metal. I will be keeping an eye on the devs future work and shortlisting it for review... they really know how to make a game. Now I have to look at Project Explore too.

It just isn't fun to me, and I don't think it will be fun to a lot of others. FYI: I received this in a bundle with some other games that I wanted, so I figured I'd try this out,
This is the entire singleplayer game: use the radar in the bottom left to find the enemy, CHASE the enemy around (they never even shoot at you), shoot the enemy a few times, kill the enemy, find the next enemy, chase and kill, get an upgrade, kill the enemy, etc. The just isn't a lot to the game to make it fun, from my view.
The multiplayer, and maybe the entire game, appears to have been made in an attempt to jump on the
popularity, but has unfortunately failed that mainly due to a lack of players. I know developers can't just make more people play the game, but they can do two things:
Add bots that can actually shoot at you! Having actual combat between players and bots would make this 10x better.
Second, improve on the overall gameplay: make it more fun. I don't know if they were going for minimalistic combat, but that's what it is.
Pros: Menu is unique, but needs polishing. Soundstracks/sound effects are good and match the aesthetic. There is a noticable learning curve that helps you get through the game, which I like. I haven't had any performance issues besides a few second freeze when restarting the level.
Multiplayer seems like it will be fun, but I need some other people or bots to actually tell.
Finally, this is definitely overpriced. Maybe if the features I mentioned were fixed/added it could be at the current price, but right now I couldn't see this going for more than $5.
Those are my thoughts on the game. When I have some free time and I don't feel like playing other games, I'll try this one some more. My review could change based on my future gameplay, so I hope the developer won't give up on this game. Thanks for reading.

Out There is a rather interesting Space Journey & Survival Rogue-like that would likely remind one of FTL: Faster Than Light; though without all the combat elements that one would find in FTL and more of a focus on acquiring ship technologies and resource management. It also has a sort of diary occurring between space jumps which helps you understand a bit about your journey.
Unfortunately it is also a game that seems nonsensical at times, and has its fair share of game mechanics that could likely be fleshed out better then what they were. There is also a lack of explanation as to what is going on - both in terms of the Tutorial not covering interaction of ship components, or just and overall lack of understanding of what is happening in the universe. Additionally, the diary elements between jumps begin to get irritating as they repeat.
It is also worth mentioning that some of your runs are just going to fail regardless of what you do - while Rogue-likes can sometimes have bad runs that go nowhere, this one seems revolve around Luck way more then it should. Personally I blame perhaps that amount of fuel that gets guzzled as you travel around for being a major source of trouble.
Anyhow, to delve into some of the cons for this game - why is it you can't talk to aliens once you begin drilling a planet - or why do aliens show up on a planet you just terraformed a moment ago? Why can't you choose to discard a less useful element when you inventory is full and Omega is being offered to you? Why can't I choose to only use some of a stack of an element when my inventory is full?
Perhaps a chief complaint I could levy though would be how the resource gathering mechanic is done - where subsequent attempts will yield reduced returns, but in regards to gathering fuel you tend to always get that 1 Hydrogen (or Carbon as my last ship was sometimes fueled); leading to an annoying situation where you are probing for that 1 Fuel Resource over and over until you get everything.
There is probably something to note about Game Design as well. The developer could have likely done away with orbiting planets that the player could land on - instead opting to have the player just land on planets if they could instead of having to click once to orbit and then once to land. There was an option to skip the jump sequence cutscene between star systems so may as well eliminate the need for having to orbit planets if they can be landed on.
I'm sure more can be said, but it is worth noting that his isn't to say one won't find a little enjoyment from playing this game though. For the first few hours I certainly enjoyed it, and before the flaws of the game annoyed me to the point that I didn't want to play it anymore, I could see myself replaying this game quite a bit. Now though, I don't think it has enough replay value for what is currently being offered - especially if the game is at full price.

Following in the stylistc footsteps of the original Rusty Lake, this wonderfully macabre puzzle game is actually 33 small, compatmentalized puzzles that come together. Each one is a delight to play with a cutout style, dark music, and delightfully dark humor.
Unlike the original Rusty Lake, which had some really gross puzzle solutions, Roots is a bit more toned down. Other reviewers have said that it you're squeamis you should avoid this, but I don't necessarily agree with that. Yes, moments are dark, but a lot of those moments are made lighter simply by the utter absurdity of the situation. Other situation that  seem to be really dark and gloomy end up being ridiculously silly when you get to see the actual results of what happened.
Each section can be completed in a few minutes. In fact, most are relatively straightforward as long as you make sure to check everything and click everywhere. Some of the puzzles require a significant bit of brain power, but the solution is actually quite logical in how it's handled. It's simply a matter of recognizing how to put the pieces together. Fortunately, the folks at Rust Lake have complete walkthrough videos available if you really get stumped.
This game is dark, macabre, funny, challenging, and downright silly all wrapped up into one. If you like dark humor (and, yes, the focus there is on humor even if it's simply absurdity) and you like puzzle games, you need to try this game.

This game showed promise, and with some changes could actually be decent.
First to list some positives; The game features a narrative that, although delivered through text to speech, actually did attempt to set up a backstory and characters.
Physics, while wonky at first due to a lack of momentum, actually do get the job done nicely due to their consistant nature.
Platform hitboxes are usually fine, meaning precision jumping on small platforms isn't as frustrating as it sounds.
However many problems outweigh the good; Render distance, even on a high end machine, is terrible, leading to faraway platforms being invisible in fog, and long distance jumps from bounce pads nearly impossible without trial and error.
Limited sound effects, such as things like jumping or death screams, get repeated so often I actually ended up muting them.
Some levels are a comfortable 45-120 seconds long, while some levels appear to extend well past 3-5 minutes, which is made all the worse because...
Every level features a mandatory time limit. Once the timer hits zero, the game forces you to restart the entire game, with seemingly no way to get back to where you were. However, restarting the current level RESETS the timer with the level, so the timer is pointless, unless you forget to reset in which case it's infuriating.
Your character's torso, while visible unlike some games, can block view of what is directly beneath you, which makes lining up falls onto tiny platforms even harder.
Some levels can be broken by sequence breaking, however difficult it may be. Video of this:

Music is nearly nonexistant. (Music from clip is from Final Fantasy Crisis Core playing in background)
Many of these problems could easily be fixed, but as the game is not in early access and appears to be finished, I cannot in good faith recommend this to many people.
The game was horribly ported, given minimal support, then abandoned. Unless you plan on spending hours pouring through blogs and forums for a chance to fix the many issues, then don't bother with it.

Good. Sometimes even very good, but just not great...
Let's start with the good parts: you roam a (rather believable) city slashing generic militaries and mutants, and it feels great.
It's a shallow fun, to be honest, but the character unlocks and the collectibles keep the fun up, so it's really good time.
I managed to end the game in normal mode, and then finish it again on Hard in Game+ mode straight away, just to get the last missing achievement, and this says something, because I had to play the whole campaign twice in a row.
It's not that complex of a game really: the main missions are relatively varied, but they will not blow you away for ingenuity, and then there are a whole bunch of extra ones that are pretty much always the same. Protect this, kill this target, infiltrate that laboratory, to dome parkour, ecc... The game does what it does well, though, and make you feel like a badass for doing it, so Gameplay is definitely a plus.
The story and characters.... well, those are other matters entirely.
The plot it's forgettable, let's just leave it at that, but it's with the characters, and the protagonist in particular, that Radical really did some numbers...
James Heller (Hell-er. Because he brings hell. Heller. Isn't that subtle?) is a walking racial stereotype. Forget the getto-types of San Andreas, because Carl Johnson and his homies look like reserved wasps near him. It's a caricature, a parody of himself, and controlling him becomes embarrassing mission after mission.
Besides his penchant for curses and profanity (there is no sentence without a f... in it), he's a bit dumb brute smashing things up and murdering pretty much everything that comes in his path, so forget about emphaty.
Despite all this, the game is still fun, so it will not become an all times classic, but if you are in the mood for some open-world destruction, and feel that GTA is too refined, this one will surely please you.

Somewhere at the crossroads of Magic: the Gathering and Hearthstone, you have Hex. Hex is all the pros of an intricate and interactive TCG like Magic with the benefits of a sleek online interface like Hearthstone. Having been on the market for several years already, Hex provides a massive amount of content for new and veteran TCG players alike. The single-player campaign is a singularly unique experience as it seeks to emulate MMO's in storytelling, questing, loot, and more while retaining all the deckbuilding and gameplay challenges you'd expect from a TCG. The PVP content sports a myriad of traditional archetypes with unique twists and sports a low entry cost for the genre. Hex offers numerous formats in which to battle fellow players, whether it's in the Constructed Gauntlet, a traditional Draft, or a competitive tournament. Hex delivers a fresh look at an old genre while retaining everything you've come to love from a TCG.
Quick note for new players: There are usually packs for sale for Gold in the Auction House. You can also go to the trade chat to trade your Gold for Platinum to buy packs or singles.

Incredibly creepy and not for the extremely squeamish.  (I will never look at voodoo dolls the same way again... ditto for "test tube babies.")
If you're already a fan of the series, you'll appreciate the various nods to previous installments; if you've never played any of the games in the series, you won't miss out on much (and may even be interested in trying out the free previous installments).  Either way, this game is worth the low price and is sure to keep you entertained!

EDIT 10/19/17:
After taking a significant break from Hex and recently returning, I must change a few things in this review. Set releases have increased in speed, which is a good thing. The mechanics have been fine tuned and the game runs and looks better than ever and the PS4 release is now live. However, the player base has shrunk significantly and drafts are slower to fire and much less diverse (you'll see a lot of the same players these days) than they used to be. I still enjoy this game as a TCG purist, but I do have to question how they plan to keep it alive going forward with such a small and narrowing player base.
Also of note, much of the value that used to exist in F2P grinding has decreased considerably and building a competitive deck out of pve grinding will take an excessive amount of time. Be prepared to spend anywhere from $60-200 for a competitive deck. With that said, I still recommend that TCG fans take a look at Hex. It is the best digital TCG on the market, without a doubt, but drawing in enough players to keep it going over the long term is going to be a challenge, to say the least.

So I've been playing this for a while before its Steam release. I've invested a little over 100$ in Constructed decks.
This game is not that hard for people who played card games before. It has very good gameplay and offers a lot of replay value, being similar to MTG in almost every aspect. It has some digital-only card game mechanics that are pretty cool (cards that change other cards or put cards somewhere in the deck, for instance). It's not very hard to learn and you can zoom in on the cards to double-check what they do if you forgot. So that's nice.
The game is not pay2win, it's pay2compete just like other competitive card games. Constructed decks cost a little bit of money but not all that much. Most are between 50 and 100 dollars and you can technically go infinite by grinding. You can also sell your won cards in draft in the auction house to facilitate this.
The playerbase is simply too small for a card game right now. There are days where you sit for over 10 minutes in a (paid) constructed queue waiting for an opponent. You can't leave the queues screen while you wait. To make matters worse, you can face the same opponents multiple times in these queues, making for a generally boring experience. The draft (or "Arena" if you come from Hearthstone) is basically the same thing, prepare to face the same people in every single draft. Drafts also takes needlessly long, since there are 17 cards per pack the draft portion alone already takes over half an hour. After that, there is 15 minutes for deckbuilding which is also ridiculous, because you can build your deck while drafting. Prepare to waste at least 3 hours on a single draft, with no option to play multiple games at once or even leave the draft queue window. So while you wait you can't even sell your drafted cards or build decks or whatever, you're just stuck in there.
Back to the playerbase: the playerbase is small for good reason. The game is bugged beyond recognition and should for all purposes not be considered a finished product. The patches are few and far between and have not fixed 90% of the bugs. You're going to restart the client a LOT if you want to play this game. Also, there are some bugs that can simply lose you games you would have otherwise won (naming Brown Fox Scout as an example, there are more though). The developers supposedly refund your queue fee if this happens, but these cards have been in the game for YEARS. There is no reason why they should still not work properly.
Speaking of the developers, there was supposed to be a new set coming out a few weeks ago. Players who happened to stick with the game long enough have been waiting over 9 months for this new set. Any sort of release schedule can not be taken seriously after this joke. 9 months between content updates is not at all acceptable for a card game.
Also, the sets are too big, being over 200 cards. Just play in a draft to see what I mean. Your first 10 cards will be okay-ish, but the last 7 picks are all completely unplayable trash. This does not make an interesting drafting or viewing experience and it honestly makes me question why the packs are so large and if they put any thought in this at all.
Major changes have to happen during set 4 and the developers need to wake up. But I think their time and their window of opportuntiy is long gone.
Small update since set 4 is out now: Set 4 draft is more of the same draft experience as before and has a similar number of completely useless cards in it. I would still recommend anyone to stay away, as there are simply better card games out there.

This game is about being the leader of a rock band in its rags to riches odyssey. So, as such, there’s no tycoon to be found.
As a tycoon you would be supposed to, I guess, scout bands, give them record deals, improve them, send them to rehab,  manage them, deal with agents, balance studio and tour time. This game has nothing tycoon-y about it.
You hire/fire your bandmates, select venue locations, write songs, eventually sign record deals, gain access to bigger venues.
The Cons
-	Gameplay is quite repetitive as you grind your way to the top
-	Flavour events are sparse and quite pointless
-	Band members’ customization is limited to their appearance
-	Talent is meaningless, everyone can become the next Hendrix just by “busking” in the streets for a couple of years
-	No matter how many records you sell, your band will never get out of the bar circuit. At most you can play 1.500 capacity. Forget arenas.
-	Band members have no personality, they are all clones, with, at most, one or two traits and perks each, this leads to zero replay value as there is no RPG component to be found: there is absolutely no interaction between them
-	There’s a clear lack of focus and direction. A simulation? What’s with the Guitar Hero style mini-game? Or the song composition?
The games is missing some key components that would make it more fun and more meaningful:
-	Some kind of interaction between band members
-	Some story element in your rise to fame and success
-	Other elements that play a key role in bands’ success and failure. Label representatives, managers, agents, tour managers, critics, groupies, wives, broken vans, stolen equipment, rival bands, the list could go on for a while
-	Less of the grind. While it is an element of realism, it really detracts from the gameplay: you should be able to go on a tour, select a setlist a go on with that rather than booking each venue day by day and rebuild the setlist at each location.
The Pros
-	The game has its moments and in a way it makes you want your pixel band to succeed
-	From what I understand it’s the work of a team of two very responsive devs
-	It’s right priced
-	The graphics, while minimal, are functional
-	The UI is well laid out
-	No bug breaking issues
Overall one would ask why I recommend the game despite the fact that my list of cons is much longer than the redeem elements? Well, because of its potential. I consider it as an almost empty canvass the devs should build upon. They get the atmosphere right. They get what rock is about.
I suggest them to go check 2001 Rock Manager by DreamCatcher Interactive which is now I believe free to download for some juicy ideas.
Overall: 6 devil horns out 10 and I want to see more of it.

I saw a few glowing reviews of this game online, and it sparked my interest. As someone who loves narrative-driven games, this looked perfect - especially since it was so highly praised. I avoided looking many things about it after that, waiting for the summer sale to hit so I could pick it up. I did, yesterday, and I can say without a doubt that this is likely my GOTY (with Night In The Woods very close behind).
The premise of the game is simple: you are Edith Finch, and for unknown reasons, you left your family home years ago. Now, after inheriting it, you've returned to discover your family history, one riddled with mysteries that you were never told about. You enter the house and start snooping through the bedrooms of long-gone relatives, learning how their lives were, and how they ended.
It's obvious how much love and care was taken to make every Finch their own person - from the bedroom decorations, music choices, and even handwriting style, it was easy to distinguish one from another. And that's important. As you spend the whole game learning about this family, it's necessary that their stories are engaging. Giant Sparrow have succeeded, crafting vividly unique visuals for every person, so that my eyes never felt bored. I was completely immersed in this world where a house was its own character, home to a group of idiosyncratic individuals that each left their unique mark on the world.
Though you follow the many tragedies of the Finch family, the game doesn't focus as much on their deaths as much as their lives. The message of the game is really about celebrating how short and strange life can be, and memorialising all those who have passed on. You start from the very beginning of the family tree and work your way up, and going through that experience was cathartic, even as someone who can't necessarily relate to many of the issues these characters have faced.
Due to the strong connection the game built with me through its careful use of controls (making me actually use my hand to create the motion of unlatching things, or pushing open doors, was
immersive), world building, beautiful narrative, and extremely human message, by the time the end of the game rolled around, I was bawling my eyes out. This game is not very complex in terms of its mechanics - just a linear walking simulator with intuitive controls - but that simplicity helps the twisting narrative of the Finch family shine like a diamond.
I highly recommend this experience for anyone who's a fan of strong narrative and characters. Though relatively short, it was completely worth the money, and I will be replaying this every once in awhile just to enter the lives of the Finches again.
Thanks for letting me explore this story along with Edith, Giant Sparrow. I'm looking forward to what you create next.

Most of the negative reviews for Prototype 2 cover the major flaws in the PC port that make the game unplayable for many users. I was fortunate enough to never encounter any show-stopping bugs in my playthrough, so I'm here to let you know that this game isn't worth playing even if you can. It's not all bad, but as a whole it isn't worth your time.
First, the high point: movement. The protagonist, mad dad James Heller, is given a sci-fi viral infection that lets him leap stories into the air, run around on the sides of skyscrapers, and glide and dash through the air. It's a cool way to move around an open world, and it makes the obligatory checkpoint race activites a blast to play. The Prototype movement system is so fun and fluid that it was also a high point in Saints Row IV, which ripped it off wholesale and dropped it into a much better game.
Aside from the checkpoint races and a handful of chases, your movement powers are mostly used to get you from mission to mission. What you're actually doing in those missions is far less interesting than how you got there. Typically, you're either brawling or sneaking. Brawling is mashy and mindless, and on normal difficulty it's difficult to die. You unlock a handful of combat superpowers that function as weapons, but you'll probably spend most of your time with the same 2 equipped, once you find a pair you're comfortable with. You also have a ludicrously forgiving shield parry move that makes most of the stronger monsters trivial to kill.
Stealth is even sillier. Heller has a stealth consume move that lets him eliminate an enemy and steal his appearance. Stealth consume only works if your target isn't being watched by another enemy, but attempting it will never break stealth. So every sneaking mission in the game goes from the outside in, standing behind one enemy at a time waiting for a chance to stealth consume him, with absolutely no risk of failure.
Prototype 2 is written like a game plot neural net. Evil corporation, bio-weapons, ex-military gruff dude just wants to save his daughter, nothing new and all of it straight-faced and dour.
The final boss reaches for that "mirror match" magic, asking you to take down an nemesis with abilities similar to yours. A classic move that provides some of the most exciting moments in games like Devil May Cry, and it can even work in lesser games like Killer is Dead. Here, though, the fight is too stiff and scripted to give that kind of thrill.
In conclusion, Saints Row IV is good, go play that instead.

I've been playing Hex for nearly 2 years now and there have been an extremely low amount of days where I have not logged in to play a draft or do some PvE or just play around in the game. Yes the basic gameplay is very similar to MtG but that is what drew me to it. It does so many things right and is a much better digital environment to play in then MtGO ever was. If you enjoy trading card games and are looking for one you can play from the comfort of your own home whenever you have the time to play without having to look for a place to play or people to play with then Hex is for you.
Yes the PvE side of the game allows one to play and enjoy aspects of the game for free. Yes you can grind out gold (the PvE currency) to get PvP items from the AH. No, this is not a Pay to win game... it's a TCG. This is how trading card games work, cards have value because they are rare, and because people want them. If they were common and easy to get or useless and never played then they have no value. The value of a card in a trading card game is dependent on what people are willing to pay for it, this does not make a game pay to win it makes the game an investment. If you want to play a card game PvP but don't like that the rarer cards cost money (Which is how TCGs will always work) then this game is not for you, TCGs are not for you so why are you looking into a TCG?
No, Hearthstone is not a TCG, it's a CCG. In a game where you can not trade your cards your money and time disappear into a black hole of nothingness. Hex is a TCG, which means both your money and time is treated like an investment. As long as people want to buy whats in your collection then your collection will have a monetary value. This is the point of a *trading* card game.

What I hate are the hints that won't stop popping up. I played about 20 minutes of the first mission, and every thirty seconds, a hint would pop up on the screen, disrupting the game. At first, I dealt with it, because I thought they would eventually stop. But I got quite a ways into the first mission when I realized that it wasn't going to stop. I'm sure there's a way to disable hints, but I sure as hell can't find it. The game is probably actually decent. But I'll never know, because I can't play the game long enough to find out.
Now, you may think that not recommending a game because of the game's hints is pretty ridiculous. But I'd like to compare them to pop-up ads. Say you're on your computer, minding your own business, when an ad pops up out of nowhere. Big deal, right? It happens. But over time, it wears down on your sanity. You start watching a YouTube video, and suddenly, the video is paused and a pop-up ad covers the screen. You're chatting with friends, and suddenly you see the pop-up again, disrupting your conversation. Until eventually, you can't take it anymore.
I'm not sure why the hints in the game are so obnoxious, but the game is literally unplayable for me because of them. If anyone knows any way to disable the hints, that would be great. But for now, I would not recommend the game.

You fight, yet you do not fight. This is a dance, one of death, and of desperation. It is a series of brief, brutal, yet exceptionally precise fights, which spin out into a tug of war woven over various arenas. You roll, you kick, you throw your sword, you panic, you grab the ledge and haul yourself up, you knock your foe down, you grab your sword. You kill him.
He respawns ten feet away.
This pattern repeats, music constantly shifting with the feet, and on occasion terrain of the landscape upon which you fight. In castles, upon clouds, in dungeons, with lava erupting behind you. A constant barrage of visual information, yet your duellist is kept simple, a monotone duellist with a white sword, and his movements are slick, precise and razor sharp. You move, he twitches, he adjusts his sword with a tap of the key, he lunges, he riposts, he rolls, he grabs his foe and kills him in a bloody manner. He runs forward.
Then he gets eaten by a worm. WINNER.
This is not a game you win. This is a game you play, and you perfect. The art is the fencing, everything else is just icing on the deliciously precise cake. Dark Souls pared down to it's most barest of essentials, fighting games without their glitz, a relentless focus on two things : You. Your sword.
Are you quick enough? No. Be quicker. Be better. Respawn. Try it again. Die. Respawn. Again.
Welcome to Nidhogg.

Hey, ajichuchu-chan here for another review, this time for Gunpoint!
First off, the soundtrack fits the theme really well, didn't feel repetitive throughout my ~4 hours of play time. Imagine your 16 year-old self being late on your first day of high school. The strict, old, cranky lady you have as your English teacher has little tolerance of latecomers. The door is locked. "Jokes on you, woman!" you shout. The door is knocked down, the woman and your fellow students alike stare at you, dominance is immediately asserted the first second you come to class. Your territory? Marked.
I'd like to give a shoutout to Root-chan for providing me this opportunity. Thanks for reading, friends.

Full Review:

Compared to its predecessor, this is a much more tactical game involving heroes who travel from one campaign level to the next, upgrading their stats and equipment as you go. The base-building / massive battles of the original have been replaced with gorgeous close combat and a unique traffic-light cover system. The storyline is much better, with the tyranids finally spewing forth from the hive swarm and taking over lush jungle environments.

It's like other randomly generated "Go from point A to point B" space games.  Most similar to FTL.
The big difference between this and FTL is that the game is not based around combat, but instead resource management.  As other reviews have said, the gathering of fuel and supplies is its own form of tedium, and the game could use some extra type of subsystem/minigame to really make it shine, but since this seems to already be a special edition, I doubt it will happen.
It's still fun.  If you're into these kinds of games, ten bucks is a reasonable amount to pay, and for those people who this game is NOT for, you'll probably recognize it within two hours and be eligible for a refund.
As for complaints about the game being too RNG-dependent, I'm going to actually say it isn't.  Yes, luck plays a big part in things.  But knowing how to make resources stretch, and knowing when to let go of cargo is a key part of playing the game, and can protect you from a lot of the RNG stuff.

I expected a less combat oriented FTL.  Instead I got "probe for fuel simulator 2015".
I really wanted to, and tried to like this game. It starts out promising. You warp around a semi-linear path of stars, exploring planets looking for resources to upgrade your ship and fuel to keep going. It's got text-base events like FTL, limited slots to make you pick and choose what upgrades and cargo you take, a nice soundtrack, and great hand-drawn art style that I really liked.
Unfortunately. The gameplay mostly consists of clicking "probe" on gas giants to scoop up fuel until your ship is too damaged (orbiting a gas giant damages you), then wasting all the fuel you just mined landing on a rocky planet and pressing "drill" to scoop up almost, but not quite, enough iron repair the damage you took from the gas giants. Then you fly to the next system to repeat the process in an endless loop of tedium that eventually ends with you running out of fuel with no gas giant in sight, or crashing into a gas giant in a desperate gamble to mine one more load of fuel so you can mine one more load of iron to repair your hull that was damaged the last time you mined fuel.
Meanwhile, the "game" (such as it is) is also almost 100% pure RNG - significantly worse than FTL. The majority of maps feel like they are completely unwinnable no matter what you do due to bad random layouts, and spending 20 minutes grinding fuel and iron just to die because of something utterly out of your control such 2 bad random events in a row just feels so bad and offputting.
I can't recommend this game, unless you absolutely love tedious grinding and pure RNG combined in one.

I must admit : I approached this game somehow without a deep thought. I picked it up out of boredom, and since it was free, I didn't need to worry about spending money on something I'd never pick up again. The title doesn't promise much : Cupid, being the name of a Roman god of love, suggested I'd get some sweet, standard love story that aren't that hard to come by : protagonist meets love interest, falls for him/her, problems appear but are ultimately dealt with and a happy ending finishes the story, as our heroes live happily ever after.
There's little straightforward happiness in this game, and even less - one that is not covered in a layer of doubt or past pain.
CUPID is hardly a happy game. It's hardly a game in which your choices will be obvious or even remotely predictable.
There's no good or bad choices. There is no real correct way of solving issues you come across, and this is what I adored in this game, more than anything else. You don't choose between good or bad. You don't choose between saving and condemning, helping and scorning. You simply choose. And you will need to deal with whatever happens next.
CUPID tells the tale of Rose - a young orphan, who's life is about to change when she seemingly by a streak of luck becomes a part of a high-class family. People she meets and grows close to will change her life, and show her that there is more to people than just disdain and urge to exploit you. Yet her past and real identity will never stop haunting her and in the end, perhaps, proove to be her only way to survive.
Writing is everything for a visual novel, more than for any other genre. It makes or breaks it, and in this case, it crafts a beautifully disturbing and genuine tale of supressed anger, guilt, sorrow, and perhaps more than anything - confusion and fear.  Depite it's downright poetic approach sometimes (the game is set in an XVIII century setting), it always tells you what you need to know in order to remain on track with the story, which, due to it's jumping from one time period to another, might get slightly confusing if you haven't been paying attention. It sends a simple message : the world is cruel. It will hurt and damage you beyond repair if you allow it, and not putting up your defenses is an invitation to further assault. And yet, sometimes we can't help but willingly make ourselves vulnerable, out of some faint hope that our case is unique.
CUPID has a very simple visual style. It's graphics, while nicely drawn, are simple, quite minimalistic in it's approach. Indeed, coming across it first time, I couldn't help but compare it to something you could achieve in Microsoft Paint. And yet it works, it works so very well. It supports the story perfectly, but it doesn't overcompensate for any lacks it might have. It rather works alongside it, subtly, allowing the narration to lead the way. A big nod must be given towards character design : they do look like human beings, and both male and female models have equal amount of care put into them. Big applause for not overly sexualising the female characters that are present in the story : despite the fact that lust plays a huge role in the story - and, ultimately, in fate of few characters - none of the girls is turned simply into a sex object. And in todays industry, when so many amazing characters are reduced to simply being a boner fodder, thumbs up for this. It's sad that reasonable character design needs an applause, but what can you do...
Alongside visuals, sound design is great again. It has one, hugely important purpose : drawing you in, thickening the atmosphere, and making the whole experience all the more charming. There's plenty of variety to go around : from crowded parties, through gentle, soulful piano music, to darkish, haunting ambient of the later parts. It flows naturally and perfectly, never feeling out of place, and never feeling overwhelming. Its simply perfect.
The game does contain some quite disturbing imaginery and even something I'd call a half-jumpscare (though it's not overdone), but the true feeling of disturbance and creepiness comes from the fantastic writing. The entire experience can be completed in two hours - propably less if you read quicker than I do, and don't go away from keyboard as much. It's worth every minute spent on it. Well, let's get the bad out of the way.
First off, yes, there are still some technical issues with this port that were never patched. The most common seems to be a glitch in one of the early missions that prevents the game from advancing beyond a certain objective. However, there is a fix for this detailed in the game's forums, and it seems to work for most people, so don't let that discourage you. Just try to get to the bugged mission within the "refund" period (easy to do), and if you can't get it to work, refund it. It probably won't be an issue for you, though.
Second, the story is far and away worse than that of the original Prototype. Alex Mercer has been changed from a in intriguing antihero to a mugging villain, Heller is one of the dumbest, most unsympathetic game "heroes" I've encountered in recent memory, and he curses so much that it's actually distracting (and I'm not someone who's put off by profanity), there are almost no likable characters in the whole cast, and the plot is needlessly convoluted to hide the fact that it really makes no sense. If you enjoyed the story of the original game, this one will disappoint you.
And visually, the game is a mixed bag. The lighting is good and the framerate is solid, though hardware V-sync seems to work much better than the game's own V-sync option, the character models are generally good for an open-world title, but the textures range from "decent" to "pixelated mess," and it's really noticeable in the in-engine cutscenes. Even by the standards of a 5-year-old game, this one is kind of underwhelming graphically.
That being said, the gameplay is awesome, having been improved and streamlined from the original Prototype. The incremental upgrades of the original game have been dropped in favor of less numerous but more impactful upgrades to your powers and mutations that grant passive abilities. The awesome traversal mechanics are just as good here, combat has been improved with a new dodge mechanic, and overall it's just great fun to play. So if you're a fan of open-world superhero-type titles and the price is right, Prototype 2 is worth playing.

Gothic feels a little bit unpolished.
[COMBAT MECHANICS]
Developers made a nice approach in combat mechanics, however its underdevelopment make it a controversial experience:
- Attack/Block commands (Ctrl + A/W/D/S) may randomly stop responding, making you helpless in a middle of the fight.
- Autotarget system often stucks on enemy making it difficult to change a target to another opponent.
- No "legal" way to figure out how strong an enemy actually is without save/load. If happened so that you met a stronger hostile NPC, u won't be able to run away.
- No ability to maneuver at the fight.
- Camera adjustment delay!??
There is no fun in fighting an enemy VIA save/load because of unresponsiveness of combat system. That's why player's skill doesn't matter as much as an armor or character's skills.
[ITEMS]
- Ability to take enemy's items makes it so that the character can get the best equipment at very begining of the game (ofc., VIA save/load). So an exploration of the Landmarks, which contains unique swords and their stories is now a worthless as they have lower stats than the ones which you can take from beaten NPC (Lares, Kord, Sylas and so on).
Theretory exploration doesn't feel rewarding in terms of items.
[ATMOSPHERE]
This is a part where the Gothic doesn't lack anything.
- Voice-acted character!
- Well-written dialogues which feels natural, similar to actual conversation.
- Atmospheric music, emphasizing the atmosphere of gothic, magic and mystery. It is probably the only game where loud by default music isn't annoying. There were no situations when the music interrupted dialogs as well.
Overall it is an interesting story which makes me curious how it continues. I would totally recommend this.

(Although my Steam hours have just started, I've been playing HEX since Alpha for many many hours)
There isn't much I can say, which hasn't already been said. So in my review I will focus on a very specific demographic.
Hi there, long time Magic: The Gathering players! The answer to your question is a massive
.
, this is that game you've been waiting for all this time. Frustrated about the fact that Wizards of the Coast is apparently stuck in 2002 (looking at you MTG Online) and you see all these shiny new digital TCG/CCG coming out? You've been looking at your humongous collection of cards neatly stacked away in a closet. And you nostalgically think about the times you used to play MTG for days with your friends. Friends who have since moved far away and don't have time to get together for this anymore. It's 2016 now, surely there could be some way of reliving the joy of MTG digitally?
Well, it's time to rip apart that Chaos Orb! HEX is here and it will give you everything you've been waiting for and so much more! And that, my friend, is a promise. It's MTG, but with all the nice things you can only do in a digital environment.
I've read people complain about the fact that PVP isn't free-to-play. Well, we, as long time MTG players laugh about this. Haha! The amount of money we spend over the years on buying booster packs and single cards will never come close to what HEX costs in a long long time. ;) But I think this is one of the things I really like about HEX. Why?
No, it isn't F2P if you really want to get competitive into the PVP side of things (but PVE is totally free). But that's also why HEX is a
rading Card Game. That
actually makes a huge difference in comparison to other digital cardgames (one with Murlocs for example). You can buy, sell and trade single cards in HEX. Just like you can with MTG. There is an actual auction house and there are third party store websites, which buy and sell singles. So, yeah, you can buy that booster pack for $1.50 and pull out a Vampire King, which is currently valued at $30. You can then sell that Vampire King and buy yourself a stack of boosters or a couple of other singles you want. The money I spend in-game is actually more of an investment. And not a bottomless pit even Harrison Jones wouldn't dare to venture down in...
So, bottom line, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone looking for the best digital TCG currently on the market. Look no further, it's HEX. And if you look at the things these guys have in store for us in the future, this is only going to get better and better. See you in game!

I am the «gameplay first» type of guy so I will be talking more about gameplay as I really liked it. This game is a mix of two genres. The action side will remind you of Megaman games – the aiming system, different guns that suit the situation (I found third weapon to be most useful against air-type enemies, while the default weapon is mostly for situations where the enemy is exposed to you all the time), even the slide is here. Another side of the game has more common with games like They Bleed Pixels or The End is Nigh – the precise platformer with a lot of environmental hazards that will be killing you at a constant rate (the game is really hard if you don’t play on «story» mode). The most beautiful thing in this game is the feel of controlling your character. It’s smooth and it doesn’t have much inertion (so you can overcome precise platforming challenges). So the gameplay consists of intense jumping (including walljump), sliding, and shooting. Another thing I found fascinating is that every encounter is different. There is always a new mixture of different monsters, or the enemies themselves a situated in different way and complimented with some environmental dangers. So there is no filler or dragging. You will always wonder what encounter will happen next. There are also mechanics like wallhopping (and wallsliding) (you can also shoot while sliding) and hand-grabbing. These mechanics are more advanced so they’re used to their maximum by 1/3 of the game. Don’t get me wrong. They’re here from the start, but they become mostly important by 3th or 4th level if I recall correctly. By that time player is comfortable with more obvious and basic mechanics and is ready for the new challenges. The grabbing thing reminds me of Shovel Knight Specter of Torment main mechanics. Your Hand (basically it’s your gun and your companion with big mouth) can grab other hands (it sounds weird when you type it) that are located all over the levels. This mechanic makes you feel really awesome. The whole game is about feeling cool. I recommend you using second weapon as it has another built-in mechanic – i-frame dash that will make you feel like Yasuo from League. Btw every weapon has a secondary use – often times it’s completely unique mechanic – shield that absorbs damage, summon that helps you killing thins, heal, dash, etc. There is also a weird weapon – the last one that is called Vindictiveness – Predator. It’s basically a boomerang but when it’s coming back it also hits you – so you create the enemy yourself. I found it to be a nice touch. It reminds me of all the weird weapons from other games like Nevan from DMC3. There also bosses at each level – half of them is concentrated around bullet-hell, and the other half deals more with platforming.
For those who prefers plot and lore – there are a lot of dialogues between the main protagonist – Yissa - and the Hand. You can even choose the replies. After killing the boss and obtaining his soul the Hand will propose you to give him this soul or to release it (the way I understand it). Choosing different options will lead you to different endings. There also secrets which add up to the plot, but I don’t have any clue how to get half of them so I may have missed something in the plot department.
With all my deaths I beat the game in 6 hours and it was worth it. The game was difficult but manageable like They Bleed Pixels was for me. Every time I died was because of my lack of knowledge or skill. By the end of the game all game mechanics became my second nature and the game itself didn’t lose its grip and met me with new even more difficult challenges (the tenth level was something).
The main thing the game did for me was keeping me in tension. That is what good action games do. You have to move constantly avoiding enemy attacks and feeling like ninja.
Also I like playing as cool beautiful girls so I was bought from the get-go.
Smooth intense experience out of 10.

Nidhogg is absurdly fun.  The combat is similar to Divekick with its simple controls and surprising amount of depth in combat.  Once you kill your opponent you'll only have a few seconds to get as far as you can before you respawn.  Then you must decide if you're gonna take down your opponent again or try to run past him and go for the goal Randy Moss style.
Nidhogg is not without its issues though.  There's nothing for PC specific options aside from volume sliders and the online play has a few issues which could potentially be a dealbreaker.
Creating a lobby at first was an exercise in frustration.  The invite friends list is not alphabatized which isn't a huge deal if you don't have many Steam friends, but I have 200+ and it added extra time to what should be a simple process.  Once you invite someone the other person doesn't get a Steam notification, they have to hit "Join Game" from Steam friends.  There's no indication that you have to do this either.  Once you have this all figured out it works, but come on.  These are basic menu functions in any online game.
In the games I played with my friend the host had a huge advantage because of latency, we had to swap hosting every few rounds to make it fair.  If you can play locally then you won't have to deal with this.  It's a perfect couch game if you are thinking of a Steambox solution.
Despite my complaints about the game I've really enjoyed it so far, though with the issues I've mentioned above it's a little hard to recommend at full price.  Buy it on sale for sure.
TL;DR version:  Buy if you have a friend to play with and can deal with a few online issues.
EDIT
1/14/2014 - The invite system works with Steam properly now, but the friends list in game is still not in alphabetical order.

The basic premise of the game is great - manage a band, book your schedule and try and profit over your salaries/rent/etc. You write songs which you can form into singles, eps, LPs, or sell. You can fully customize your stage presence, gear and outfits for every band member, and book video shoots for your songs. Sign album deals and gain benefits/money from them. You can also play the tracks and customize the riffs of your songs. Beyond that...it's not much.
While I feel like the developers are really onto something here, it seems as though there are just some missing aspects of the game. That being said, they are hard working on updates and this could be a true classic in the near future.
You have all time charts for your albums, but the details of them are lacklustre. You can not really define genres, write lyrics, see release details or long term sales reports, and the general feel of the game is still in a repetetive stage. There is no progression on the random events (in fact, it seems publishers stop asking to buy the rights to songs in the first year), and none of them require any attention after you've made some real cash, as the penalty for an incorrect answer is irrelevant to your growth.
It would be great to see things like letting your bandmates work jobs between album scheduling for some extra cash, so that you aren't forced to pump songs and albums out at a rate that makes them instnatly forgettable, just to remain profitable. I don't know if they do, but it would be great to see your bandmates pick up traits & their negative counterpart as they work for you. It would be nice to make some type of variable combinations within your songs that determine the success of an album.
The asthetic feel of the game is wonderful, the graphics and sound are all perfectly suited for the style.
Overall, I feel like Rock God Tycoon currently sits at at tipping point between "Great Idea" and "Classic Tycoon Staple" a la Rollercoaster, Sim City and more. It's up to the developers and the community support for the game now!

I am really enjoying this game! Management games are my favorite genre and so I tend to scrutinize them more heavily than other games, based on playability, features, enjoyment, etc.
First, let me say that for a new user, the game is quite difficult. I didn't take this as a bad thing, in fact, it made me want to play more to try and find the right mix. My band(s) had difficulty with cohesion and tension early on and it took some experimenting (with many band members leaving/band disbanding) to try and get out of the initial rut. Once you do, however, you'll feel like you put in great work.
There is a "guitar hero" element in the game where you not only have a chance to execute the various instruments (drums, guitar, or base), but you can build songs based on pre-recorded segments. A few users have noted that this process is tedious -- and it can be -- but I built a song that I would actually listen to in real life. Then I got to play it by mistiming every single note on my keyboard. 10/10 would do it again.
Seeing my band improve and deal with the various items that come up has been a gaggle of enjoyment for me. Its a bit disheartening to be so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the beginning, but just stick with it and keep working on your skills/making money. You can do this by a variety of actions, but having a near-perfect mix is important. You don't want your team's tension to reach a boiling point, or else people will quit, ask for more money, etc.
The game is not without its quirks or issues. One thing that annoys me is the gig results. Lets say you wrote 5 excellent songs and you want to play them for your fans. You go to a city and schedule a gig, or multiple gigs. Sounds great! But after playing the same 5 songs even twice, the novelty bar goes down (somewhat exponentially) and the amount of money you make also falls.
Also early on, I would try and schedule multiple gigs or events in multiple cities. This can be tedious because you have to shuffle in and out of the map, and then have to remember to check the schedule, literally click to travel to the next town, and make sure your timing is perfect or else you'll miss gigs, lose money, etc. A neat feature they could add is a "build tour" function where you are able to schedule gigs in multiple towns to actually build a tour across the USA. Early on this is a non-starter -- you have access to only a handful of towns. But as your fan base grows, you could literally travel cross-country and visit fans in every city, but be forewarned -- you'll be doing more clicking than playing.
I could go on for hours about the intricacies in the game -- just purchase and enjoy it. The DEVs are friendly, responsive, and realistic -- clearly this is not their full-time job, but they are dedicated to making the game better. God bless them.

I love roguelikes - they comprise a large portion of my library.  I love science fiction, have a degree in microbio and genetics, and work in IP.
While this game started off with an interesting premise and mechanics, it quickly became apparent that there are deep flaws systemic to the gameplay.  Most of what the other reviews say are right on: namely, that there is no real way to determine if what you do is right or wrong, or how to learn from the experience.  In which case, everything you do ends up feeling wrong.
Beyond this, there are other flaws that show the dev team/writer is out of their league in tackling this genre.  Diminishing returns when harvesting gas or minerals from a gas giant or rocky planet (respectively)?  Are you out of your mind?  IT IS A DAMN PLANET.  You are ONE PERSON.
All the aliens, however different or implausible, apparently speak the same language.  That's not even true of the one species on OUR PLANET.
Many of the "science techno jargon" employed is entirely wrong.  That is not science fiction.  Science Fiction proceeds from known, actual science and posits unattained or impossible results (but in a logical manner).  Using terms incorrectly, contrary to known science, and largely at random is not science fiction.  It shows that the dev team did not do much, if any, research into what should be (but are not) frankly core aspects to a space exploration game.  Star types are tossed about at random (and with no consistency or accuracy), planets are largely arranged in nonsensical order (yes, that gas giant with the rings is right next to the star, precisely where it ought to be).
The end result is something which is not enjoyable to RL players (because of the mechanics) nor to SciFi lovers (because of the experience itself).

You know what you're getting when you sign up for a Telltale game, at least gameplay wise, so it's all about how they tell the story and whether you engage with the characters in enjoying the game. I think this is my favourite Telltale game to date which is all the more impressive (or because of?) as I have nowhere near the same base level of interest as I did in the Walking Dead and Game of Thrones settings and characters. I would say it's actually quite fortunate I hate playing these games episodically because the first episode really didn't grab me in and if I had to wait a month or two after that for the next I quite probably wouldn't have bothered with it.
By the end of the second though I was hooked. The best dialogue in the game is between the two main pairs of people that didn't know each other from the start so once that kicked in I became far more interested in the characters and exploring their stories. The comedy is excellent, I was laughing out loud multiple times per episode which is really rare when I'm playing a game on my own. It's constantly popping up self-deprecating notifications mocking the trope of "X will remember this" in so many ways that it never got old. The general attitude of the game gets used a few times to create a stark contrast for more serious scenes, and vice versa. Several times an incredibly tense situation was ended with such a perfectly timed joke that made them land even better than usual. One of my favourite parts of each episode was the late title screens, always coming with a montage of what each character's up to and accompanied by a perfectly selected soundtrack each time.
The final scene of the game is brilliant and subverts your expectations for Telltale gameplay excellently but I won't spoil how as it's a great moment. The only downside is that you'd have to play through the whole game with different choices to see some of the alternatives and I just wish I could do that end scene over a few times.

Distilled to its bare essence, "What Remains of Edith Finch," is a linear walking simulator with simple mini-games to play. If that doesn't sound like your cup of tea, then just stop right here and walk away. This isn't about a getting an adrenalin rush through fighting monsters or enduring through jump scares (there are none of either). Nor is this about challenging your mind with devious puzzles or having to write down copious amounts of information to remember later. I'm afraid I cannot even say there there are really even any meaningful decisions to make that will impact what happens later in the game.
Simply put, this is interactive fiction, and one of the best presentations of that genre I've experienced. This is akin to a good book and cup of tea on a rainy Sunday afternoon. If you've played the, "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter," and enjoyed it immensely, then I have good news for you: you'll enjoy this one too. It is a story cleverly and compellingly told, full of little mysteries that you piece together as you explore the surreal Finch house and learn of the eclectic - if not supernaturally touched - family that lived there through three generations. This is an almost dreamlike mood piece, full of equal parts whimsy and sadness, that you realize by its very nature is going to be short, yet you can't stop playing because each chapter leaves you wanting more. The first time I played this, I finished it in a single sitting, much to my regret the following morning.
The visuals are outstanding, the narration superb, the accompanying music effective, and the pacing adequate. The mini-games, all of which seamless integrate into the storytelling experience, do not require anything of the user except intuition. The game does not preach at you or deliver a heavy-handed message; rather it just encourages you to think about the human experience, what it means to you, and what we leave behind us when we part from this world.
I am grateful to have played this and saddened I will never experience it with fresh eyes again.

This is by no means a perfect game, and probably not for everyone. I have personally enjoyed playing it a lot - and have sunk 30 hours into the game in under a week after purchasing. Goofy and entertaining, Rock God Tycoon's fun factor makes up for most of its shortcomings.
The premise is clear: get together a bunch of no-hoper high school drop outs with rockstar aspirations, found a band and learn 3 chords. After that, the sky is the limit! Your band consists of 4 members: guitar, bass, drums and vox. Each band member has 4 attributes, musicality, star quality, songwriting ability and skill playing their instrument. You can practice these skills to increase them, and they also increase as you play the game through experience.
You start out in some backwater town and your first tasks will be to write some songs and play some gigs. When starting out, I recommend you spend a lot of your time busking (available for each member from the main screen), which nets you a bit of cash each hour as well as increasing your fans in the city. At the start of the game, this is your only reliable cash source, and you need to increase your fans to unlock additional cities.
As the game goes on, you unlock progressively bigger cities. All cities have a number of locations in them. A gig venue where you can play live, and a variety of other locations like bars, strip clubs, drug dealers, record studios and rehab clinics. Once you have bought a vehicle (a clapped-out car) you can drive from city to city to visit these locations and increase your fan base.
In general, the bigger cities have bigger venues. That means more cash for playing there, which soon provides you with an additional source of income. Once you've got enough songs, you can start thinking about making a record.
When writing a song, you can choose to create a song using a simple song editor. You have a number of riffs for the guitar, bass and drums that you can arrange on a timeline (much like in any DAW or video editor). There's a decent variety of riffs. Unfortunately the riffs are all named things like "Riff1a(2)", which isn't helpful. This can make finding a suitable riff for your song harder than necessary as you end up auditioning each riff time and time again. There's also no copy/paste, so creating longer songs with verses and chorus it a bit tedious. You'll probably end up making most songs 1-2 minutes long and reusing the same template for multiple songs. That said, it still only takes 5-10 minutes to knock together a song.
The length of the songs isn't really a problem though, and you can download songs from the workshop to make sure you have enough variation for your gigs. Half the fun of gigging is the Guitar Hero mini-game where you can play the songs you meticulously crafted in the editor (you can only play gigs if all the songs were created in the editor). The mini game is brutally hard for noobs, especially with 180 BPM songs, so be prepared to suck at it for a while. It's good fun once you've got the basics down, though I doubt you'll want to play every gig this way; you can always choose to simulate gigs.
Other things you need to do are manage your band's tension, as bandmates get annoyed with each other over time. You can do this by drinking beer, eating burgers, ogling strippers and taking drugs. The latter can however land you a nasty addiction with negative side effects. Addictions can be treated at rehab clinics.
All of this is great fun, albeit somewhat repetitive. For me, there's just enough variation to keep me interested and think "I'll just practice and record this song" or "I'll just finish this tour" and then find myself playing another 3 hours.
The background music is also well done and fits the theme perfectly. Loads of classic rock riffs and some nice solos without being too in your face or getting annoying after a few hours.
Downsides? A few. Aside from the potentially grindy nature of the gameplay, the biggest issue for me is the UI. It's functional, but carrying out simple actions requires far too many clicks. Key information isn't displayed where you want it. You might sign a record contract that gives you a discount at a particular recording and film studio, but the game will only tell you the name of the studio, not where it is. You need to manually mouse over all the cities on the map until you find it.
Most of the biggest UI issues should be relatively easy to fix, and the dev has been very responsive on the forums. I'm hoping there will still be some small QOL improvements. At any rate, there have been a few small fixes for things released during the short period of time I have been playing, which is always a good sign.
I got my money's worth already, and will definitely still play this game. Given that it's pretty cheap, if you like the premise, you might as well give it a whirl.

I came across this game while searching for visual novels in the steam store, and since well..it was free, I decided to give it a try. First going into the game I was very confused on who I actually was or what was even going on but as the pieces came together I got further into the story. I in time found it very interesting that the role you get to play, getting to be the person who clouds the judgement and thoughts of someone else, I feel is very unique and something I don't think I've ever seen in a visual novel. I enjoyed each character and getting to see them grow and getting to learn so much unexpected things from each one and seeing them in their darkest times. I found the story to be very emotional and at times had me in tears..(probably because I chose wrong choices xD)..the story line of this story being te 1700's centered in France, it's either one you'll love or you'll hate depending if you like more modernized visual novels or older ones. I for one loved the setting and time period this game presented in and actually have been looking for visual novels of a different time period. I also must say the artwork for this game I absolutely adore, from character designs to their outfits too (I enjoyed actually getting to see the characters design change over periods of time thats another thing you dont see in most visual novels, for me it was nice seeing a character not have to wear the same thing for 10+ years xD). Though at times the art can look a tad cringey because of the such the dark..little bit wobbly looking lines outlining the character fully, and it kind of doesnt fit with the sharpened and perfected backgrounds of the game that appeared to be made with some 3d program probably but its both definitely overshadowed by the beautiful colouring in this game. I wont give anything away story-wise, but I wil say that in my first play through I have received ending 2, and it definitely makes me want to play more to choose differently to see all the the different outcomes. So, do I recommend this game? Yes. It was very enjoyable with lovely characters and a very deep and heart breaking (at times) story. Games like these make me want to make visual novels of my own, so bravo creators, this game was indeed enjoyed. :3
