There isn't much I can say about this game that hasn't already been said, but I thought I'd share my thoughts anyway because I didn't play this game when I was younger, so I would like to think that my opinion isn't altered in any way by nostalgia. I'm in no way discounting the opinions expressed in the review section here by recurring players, I just noticed that there seemed to be a relative lack of reviews from players completely new to the series.
Despite its age, and despite the fact that the first half of my playthrough was a near constant struggle to get it working properly on my modern rig (tips on how to overcome this will follow), Gothic can be a surprisingly immersive, rewarding and refreshing RPG to play. I was genuinely caught off guard by the amount of interactivity the game provides, even compared to many modern titles. As a seasoned RPG player, I am also pleased to say that the game has an engrossing story that kept me engaged and resorted only rarely to typical or cliche fantasy plot elements, and even when these conventions were present, they were heavily downplayed. Overall, I thought the voice acting was pretty excellent, and I found that many of the NPCs were distinct and memorable even without spending an hour telling you their life stories. I won't say that the game isn't fiddly at times even when it's at its most stable, but I found that it works more reliably than one might anticipate at first glance. I would recommend Gothic to pretty much anyone who enjoys a well-crafted RPG IF they have a decent understanding of modding/patching games manually and can deal with a slightly more difficult experience than they might be used to if they're relatively new to the medium.
-Technical and mechnical stuff
If your computer isn't a dinosaur, you will probably need to locate, download and install the System Pack/Player kit in order to get the game running properly. The link can be found on one of the game's most popular reviews or in the community "guides" section on Steam. Once this is done, the only thing you should have to do is locate the game's config.ini file and change the game's resolution to match your preferences.
***Apart from that, my biggest recommendation is to NOT attempt to play the game using the DirectX11 update or any of the enhanced texture packs that you can find out there, but particularly the former. While they do make the game look prettier, they can seriously cripple the game's stability. When I was using these addons, I encountered so many black screens, disappearing assets, memory access violations, corrupted save files and half-broken game mechanics that I almost had to start the game completely over around the twelve hour mark. Maybe try them on a second playthrough if you really want to see the enhanced graphics, but don't give yourself a bad first impression of the game's polish and functionality on your first playthrough when you're most invested like I almost did.
Lastly, you might want to look up the game's controls and do your best to get used to the default keybinding setup because they're honestly pretty strange (in a good way once you are familiarized), and if you have trouble getting up ladders, try spamming the jump button once you reach the top. Good luck!

I bought all the upgrades as I went by, but never used a single one outside the required upgrades like Wirejack, and there really weren't many ways to get to objectives other than the one good route. On top of that, it was almost too easy on some levels to just jack a security camera to activate a door, run past it, jack it to another door, et cetera until all doors you wanted were open instead of, I don't know, more spy-like movement from point A to B progressively.
What I'm most disappointed about is that the game reminded me (outside the jumping part) of Yahtzee Croshaw's "Art of Theft", which is a free game made back in 2007 or so, about the same length but with more depth and you could actually get some mileage out of new upgrades.
I'm just very disappointed and I can't recommend this to anyone. Unfortunately I passed the 2 hour mark so I can't ask for a refund.
Edit.
I'll add that of course for the sale price of less than two euros, if you like this type of game it's worth the value, I'm not petty enough to demean someone's work that much, it just wasn't for me.

The game has been lifted from the curse of Games For Windows Live due to it's death (Hello death of microsoft, you're looking all too close, yet far away) and because of that, I have returned to rewrite my review.
Currently at the time of writing this review, you can access steamworks enabled server support by going into the Beta tab under the game's properties and clicking on the menu to bring down the beta option, and yeah you get it, you're not a stupid, I don't need to tell how to do it since... well it's already rather obvious to begin with.
I currently have not tried to play multiplayer or The LAst Stand or anything save for he campaign on rare occasion, but i do know that those can't have changed, though I did notice easy AI able to win a game on their own, which surprised me in skirmish... since before their AI was just... so passive when coming to base attacks.
At the moment, with steam achievements being able to actually be earned (giving them an actual reason to exist, it would seem Relic saw GFWL's death coming eh?) and without the stupidity of GFWL itself and all the problems it had, the game is much better.
Much like many other games like Dark Souls and Resident evil Operation Racoon City (the last one not being patched, I'm thinking it won't ever be, what a shame that is), the GFWL interface and networking was the game's largest and highest weakness.
Just know that if you wanna play online with anyone... you absolutely need the DLC as I'm very sure nobody is playing The Last Stand on the original game, aka this one.
The game (this version) has the Tyrannids, Eldar, Orks, Space Marines (It wouldn't be Warhammer anything without those last 3) and... actually that's it.
The game dangles Chaos Rising being needed for the Chaos faction in our faces, but not for Retribution (I'm thinking it'll do that for Retribution once you get Chaos Rising, which is actually kinda intelligently done actually).
The game in my opinion doesn't live up to the wonderful, god-like bliss the past few games had and actually doesn't properly deliver the Tyrannid experience. Ironically enough, they were left out of the first Dawn of War game due to how the Tyrannids "Didn't require any of the resources in the game and would work off their own resource" but that sort of thing wasn't supported by the engine.
Guess what the tyrannids use? Requisition and Power, EXACTLY like the past game. Relic... what in the sh.it were you thinking?
Ignoring that utter failure, the game isn't even really in the same sub-genre of strategy and focuses more on unit control with a tactical edge in real time. There's few units in the game, arguably jsut as many as in the last game, though they all build from the HQ.
The game has no base building mechanics and you gain power and requisition form capturing points. You can upgrade power points and your HQ, but that's it, everything's mostly just unit upgrades via previously used wargear systems used in the last game.
Factions other games had, which this game lacks are listed below.
The Necrons.
Sisters of Battle.
Dark Eldar.
The Tau.
Chaos (Gained via the Chaos Rising Expansion).
Imperial Guard (Gained via the Retribution Expansion).
Compared to the last game, this game is a serious 4/10, it's a bit disappointing in comparison, not really even a sequel due to the game focus change shifting from base building and army building to just army building which qualifies it as more of a Spinoff than a Sequel.
On it's own, the game is easily a 7/10, it's pretty decent. The singleplayer is neat and enjoyable, it keeps you on your toes for sure, and the multiplayer is fun if you can find a game or enjoy playing with bots.
The "The Last Stand" mode, otherwise known as Dawn of War 2 Horde Mode is also cool and is only enjoyable if you find a game, otherwise, you can't play it if you can't find a game.
I'd buy this game first and play it for a bit before getting the expansions.

revisits famous battles from the series through the eyes of our custom character! This is the first (Official) Dragon Ball title on PC so there's not much room to complain!
The story is original and introduces some new characters to the series, the battle system is identical to Budokai Tenkaichi (which in my opinion was the best trilogy of the series).
The game disappoints in terms of transformations mostly due to lack of balance (majory of the player base just gets SSJ and spams Ultimate)! The game has a total of 54 (including DLCs) playable characters which is a huge letdown compared to the 127 characters available on Budokai Tenkaichi!
No offense to all the Japanese players out there, but not all of us like to grind and play the same mission over 50 times in order to get one item, meaning this game suffers from awful grind due to it's Japanese origins (which makes the game frustrating). This game has RNG on top of RNG and I'm not surprised most players resort to cheat engine in order to increase the drop rates.
The CO-OP system is extremely fun although the restrictions are another letdown and unnecessary (only the host gets ranks, and story mode is not playable with friends).
The PVP is non existent outside the casual battles, the competitive side of things (tournaments) was totally dropped by the developers years ago, specially now that they're focusing on the sequel (this is why you don't make tournaments that rely on the developers input).
Due to lack of better alternatives (ignoring XENOVERSE 2) if you're fan of the Series you should get this!
SFIV Engine
The game lacks support for any aspect ratio outside 16:9, Anisotropic filtering is also non existent and the options are fairly limited.
Due to its cel shading it hides its age well, looking at XENOVERSE 2 you'll see how a modern title should look like!
The game is well optimized (for a Japanese title) and should run on a toaster, frame drops are expected on low-end PCs.

Generally, this is an excellent visual novel. So much so that they could've, and probably should've, put a price on it.
Pros:
- Nicely fleshed out, original story line. Your first playthrough will be solid and interesting. This to me is the most important part of a visual novel.  And it has a lot to offer: nice character development, humorous dialouge, dark tones, likeable characters, situations that are not too obvious, and yes, a bit of erotica too... It's good. Just really well carved-out.
- The director's bonus material (unlocked upon completing different endings) is as amusing as the novel, and gives you an even better appreciation for the work that goes into making these things.
Neutral:
- You play the voice of Rosa's mother (in her head); the choices you pick influence her actions. It's an interesting concept. I was by no means enamored with this, but it didn't ultimately bother me either.
- Not a dating sim. A lot of VNs are about which lover you choose-- this is not like that at all.
Cons:
- The art isn't anything too special. There are moments when it's really lovely, but it seems kinda like the artist put all their energy into about five things, and then threw everything else together last minute.
- Replay-ablity is weak. The story line doesn't really change ever-- the endings are just  based upon how much information Rosa gathers throughout the story (or fails to gather) and her attitude towards her mother (you). The games' secrets aren't that hard to gather, so in all likelyhood you will get a realitively complete ending. Every playthrough after that feels kinda dull.

It's a cool idea for sure. I've played a similar game called Rock Manager many years ago and that was a far more polished game.  There are lots of cool aspects to this game, but none of them seem to fit together particularly well.  Some of the different parts of gameplay:
You do choose your bandmates, and ostensibly you're supposed to do things to increase or decrease their happiness, but there doesn't seem to be a clear list of things that affect them.  Every so often a random event will occur that will improve or dimish band cohesion and happiness, but there's no guage to show what the current "state" of happiness is and so you can essentially just ignore it.  It's essentially a non-feature since there's no interaction.
Doesn't seem to really affect the gameplay at all, but is a novel feature.  It is kind of annoying to have to arrange every song.  I wish there was an auto-arrange feature so you didn't have to write a song if you don't want to.
There's a calendar, but you have to navigate to it through a map.  You can make some decisions like how to arrange props on the stage or what advertising to do, but it's mostly just scheduling stuff on the calendar.  If you had some long, multi-city tours, this could be cool, but it feels really repetitive scheduling the same rehearsals over and over.
The financial system doesn't seem very well tuned.  One band member can earn more busking for a few hours than an entire gig.  Without busking, you'd almost certainly run out of money.  It kinda feels like they were never able to balance the finances of gigs, and so they just added in a "busking" option that allows you to basically get free money whenever you want, little bits at a time.
Whenever you rehearse or play a gig, you sometimes have the option to play a kind of Guitar Hero mini-game using the keyboard.  The problem is that, unlike Guitar Hero, the first levels are actually pretty difficult, and it's not really clear how much of an advantage a perfect manual score would give over the simulation; you just get a bunch of random numbers the end of the performance and it's not really clear if it was good or bad.
There are probably a handful of other gameplay features hidden in there, but those are the main ones.  At the moment, the game is kind of open-ended, but there isn't really a clear indicator of progress anywhere in the game.  It's not really clear what the strategies should be for improving the band and making money.  I would't recommend this game right now.  Maybe if they streamline the gameplay or give clearer success metrics, but right now it just doesn't feel like you're accomplishing anything.

I've loved every Telltale game I've played, particularly The Walking Dead. I'm a sucker for any game with a great story, and I always get pulled into and invested in them.
I loved Borderlands 2 (still do!) and the world of Pandora that Gearbox had created: the great cast of characters you could play and interact with, the vast landscapes and environments you could explore, and of course...Handsome freakin' Jack!
It felt too good to be true when I first heard about this collaboration way back when, and it absolutely did not disappoint when I played through Tales from the Borderlands. To be able to explore another side of Pandora from the perspectives of new characters and the more story-driven gameplay Telltale prides themselves on felt great.
I instantly came to like the new protagonists, Rhys and Fiora, and loved every minute of their journeys which felt unmistakedly Pandorian: full of dark humour, laugh-out loud jokes and the occasional genuine, emotional moments that make the story so compelling.
Sadly this game seemed to under-perform commercially and so I don't think there will ever be a sequel, as much as I'd love one. But it still tells a brilliant and complete story that I'd recommend anyone to play, particularly fans of Borderlands if they haven't done so already. It is an underrated gem that I will remember for a long while.

I've passed by this game several times and figured since it was on sale , I should go ahead and get the game.  It had so many positive reviews, I was really ready for this awesome story about the Finch family.  The game has beautiful graphics and the voice acting is very well done.  I loved how you moved from room to room, like you were invading some secret fortress through a maze of passageways.  But, I just cannot recommend this game, ESPECIALLY at full price.  Now to explain why I feel this way.  BTW...a bit of spoilage in this review.. just to warn you.
If this game had just been travelling down memory lane about the family members, fine.  However, there was so much mention about this "curse" and how Edith's mother tried to cover up everything.  She even went so far as to seal the rooms off of the house.  Maybe that was the point, but with the way it was built up, I was really expecting to unravel this huge family secret.  I got to the last story.  I opened the book with this anticipation of finally knowing this curse.  And then...I was pulled out right when I got to that page.  It's like the devs had this great story all the way up until the end, and just ran out of gas. I got the impression that it was some kind of disease since a lot of the characters had these strange spots on their skin during their stories.  There was no finality, no climax where everything is suddenly put together and you are surrounded by angels all singing "Hallelujah".  It was more like a slowly deflating tire.
Now I give the game devs credit for some of the most outlandish and wildly creative ways you went through the family member's stories, but this did not make up for the fact that the end of all of them was severely depressing.  I even had the crazy thought that the Finch curse was unusual death, but what kind of curse is that? I sorely wanted to connect with these characters, but it never happened because their outcome was the same.  Sure it was creative as to how they met their demise, but ultimately it is still death (mostly kids too which is even more depressing).
I do not mind if a game is long or short.  What matters is the content within the game, and what I am going to take away from the experience.  While what I say probably won't deter a lot of people from buying the game, let me suggest waiting until Steam has one of their huge sales and this game is a part of that sale.  Hopefully it will be cheaper during other sales, because I can't even recommend it at the sale price of $14.99.   It just had so much potential, so much promise.  The execution of the game was disappointing.  Apologies for the long winded review.

(This is a long review with NO SPOILERS... TL:DR - Sadly, I just can't recommend it.)
What Remains of Edith Finch - A Step to the Side
Truth be told, when I bought 'What Remains of Edith Finch (WROEF)' I didn't read any reviews. I love Giant Sparrow's first game (the Unfinished Swan) and enjoyed everything it was trying to achieve. Enough time had passed so expectations were in-check. If anything, I was hoping to see how the studio had shifted/evolved with their story-telling and I didn't particularly mind if the game lacked varied gameplay. As long as it was a step forwards...
This game can be described as a walking simulator but that isn't always a bad thing. For example games like Gone Home, Firewatch and The Stanley Parable could also be considered walking simulators, and these are all games I would happily recommend to people that are bored of the same shooter/action/rpg/open-world games that we get each year. Unfortunately I can't do the same with WROEF.
To put this into perspective, some of my favourite gaming experiences (I hate the term but oh well) are Shadow of the Colossus, Journey, Ghost Trick, Undertale and Portal. The common theme is that they are all attempting to deliver an interesting narrative in a unique way. There have been other games imitating these (intentionally or not) however I always come back to what made these games special. They are the best at what they are trying to achieve. This might not be the case in a few years or possibly decades, but as of right now I haven't found anything similar AND better.
The sad thing about WROEF is that the story isn't particularly interesting, and unfortunately it is the main focus in these types of games. There are some moments that glimmer, but nothing that really shines through and I get the sense that segments of the game were given to different groups of people who each had their own idea of what this game should be. Again, this isn't a bad thing, but then you could consider this a series of mini-games where only 1 or 2 out of 10 are interesting...
So in the end, WROEF isn't a terrible game, it isn't even a bad one. It's just average. And if you've somehow made it to the end of this review just ask yourself: Am I okay with an average game? If you are, then please support the developers.
If not, then give this a pass. I would have loved to be more specific but I'd hate to spoil anything on the off-chance you decide to purchase this.

Disclaimer: I've been playing this game 18 months.
First off, if you are coming into Hex expecting a 100% free AAA game that gives you everything you could ever want in life and doesn't ask a thing in return... You will be sorely disappointed. F2P, especially in an environment with a living, breathing economy (i.e. TCGs, MMOs), means eventually you will either be spending some time grinding to get the things you desire, or spending money to acquire them. This is not a bad thing. A lot of people put in a lot of work to make this. They have needs (i.e. food, shelter, clothing) which cost money. If they just give away all their things, then they don't get money. No money = no basic necessities = dead developers = dead game.
For people with a realistic view of the world and a rational mind:
There are many aspects to this game. I'll start with the one that drew me in first: PVP. You see, in the early days of Hex, there was no PVE campaign. There wasn't an Arena. There was only PVP. Just to be clear I don't mean, like, the Alpha days (I was not around for that, though I've heard the stories and I admire the brave souls who made it through to Beta). I came across a Beta key just a few months prior to the release of Set 2. I had read a bit about the game some months before, so I had an idea what I was getting myself into. I had played TCG's before (several years of MtG on and off again since the mid 90's, several years of Yu-Gi-Oh more recently) and understood that this game would require some investment. At that time, in fact, there was no way to play without spending money. But I am a draft addict. And I don't mind paying companies for their hard work so long as I am satisfied with the result. And ohhhh.... was I satisfied.
I drafted my way into a fairly decent sized collection of cards when the unthinkable happened - Set 2 released! I now had another 300 cards to collect and mash into random decks. I drafted and drafted some more, and in time I had near complete playsets of both Set 1 and 2. However, things at work had gotten complicated, life did it's lifey things, and I put the game aside for several months.
Coming back 7 months later saw many changes. First, a new set had arrived. A new set, and a new challenge in both drafting and collecting all the cards I could get my grubby average sized hands on. Secondly, and more alarming, the Frost Arena had popped up out of nowhere to tempt me with its F2P design and PvE loot. I tried it a bit (and still do dabble to this day) but for the most part I went full force into draft. And over the last several months managed to collect not only a complete playset of Set 3, but also round out my first to sets for PVP playset completion :D
You might ask: "So what do you do now that you've drafted all the cards?" I might (and will) answer: "I continue to draft." Not at the same 'gotta catch em all' pace as before, but still several times a week I queue up and mash random cards together and try and walk away with more than I put in. Sometimes I win, sometimes I lose. That's not the point. I have fun doing it.
I also found a new love. Constructed. Now that I have all the cards, why not use them? Especially when there are community sponsored FREE tournaments with actual rewards? So, I start playing around with decks, watching others, absorbing all I can. I fail several times, but I learn in the process. I eventually find a deck I like in the $100k tournament and tweak it to my own liking. I enter yet another weekly tournament. Eight rounds later I sit back and wait for the mail to come in with my 10,000 platinum. I, a commited drafter, who for so long ignored the constructed queues, had just gotten first place in a free tournament (single elimination; 140+ contestants). I had just won $100 worth of in-game currency.
Did it require some investment? Yes. Money and time. A fair amount of money, and a TON of time. But, like all good things, that investment payed off. Not just in the form of resources. I've made more friends playing this game than any other in the 5 years since I've built my PC. I've had more fun learning and playing this game than any other in the last 10 years (with the possible exception of Minecraft and CoD: World at War).
The thing is, I'm a gamer. Not just video games, all games. Board, card, pen and paper, dice, whatever. Sometimes I want to shoot things, sometimes I want to sit around a table with my friends for 4 hours claiming I'm not a cylon, sometimes I want to throw cards at people. This game allows me the freedom to scratch that TCG itch whenever I get it, and I don't have to leave the house. I don't have to convince everyone I know to play it. I can just play. And if I take a few months off here and there, that just means there's that much more waiting for me when I return. I will return, always and forever. I <3 this game.
If you're still reading, I suppose I'll get out of story mode and on to a few other points. This game can be F2P, and if you aren't interested in the competitive side it is in fact VERY F2P. No money required whatsoever, and spending money would do you little good anyways. What's good in PvP is not necessarily good in PvE, and some cards that are junk in PvP are actually quite powerful with the addition of equipment. All this and more can be yours from running the Campaign and farming the Arena.
The MMO aspect of this game is still in it's very early stages. It, like all MMO's (and TCG's really) is a WORK IN PROGRESS. If you don't like that (and really, I get bored fairly easily with the PvE content) then set it aside. Allow it some time to properly mature. Do you think WoW was built in a day? It's been through at least 3^14159 updates, patches, and dlc's. This is a very unique experience, and as such they are still working out the kinks and coming up with new ideas. I haven't really played the campaign since the last couple of patches, but when I did I had some serious issues with crashing. I was not the only one, but I know I was one of the worst. I didn't let it kill my love for this game. I understand it is a WIP, and has a lot of potential. For the time I'm generally wrapped up in the PvP portion of the game anyway (especially with Set 4 literally 1 week away). I will come back to campaign, and very much look forward to all the new content they have announced (and the many surprises I'm sure they have in store).
One last thing before I end this rant of a 'review'. This game has the greatest community I've ever had the privilege to be a part of. Within the first couple of hours of being on I had been given a hefty amount of cards (for free) from a couple people in general chat. One of them invited me to check out there guild (guild support is not yet implemented in game, but there are several up and running outside of it). I checked it out, and couldn't have been happier that I did. I mean, as great as the overall community is, the friendliness of the people I have the pleasure of calling guildmates is beyond compare. I highly recommend that, should you find you enjoy the game (even a little), you take the time to talk to people in general chat. Check out the streamers on Twitch. You will not be disappointed.

Rusty Lake: Roots DOES NOT disappoint, and was totally worth the wait and the money. You now don't arrows to click and see another wall in the room, you now have a wide room, which scrolls, and is a lot less confusing and makes the player focus a lot more on the puzzles instead of finding items and clicking everywhere. But the game is still hard, with well made puzzles, (just like any game in the series. These aren't easy, okay?) that will surely make you think. The game is a lot longer than previous games from the franchise, making every penny worth it. Not only that, but when you finish the game you can beat a few levels differently, and find some secrets which lead to a secret level, where... Nah, I'm not going to spoil it. Anyways...

They have a twitter, by the way, and it was really good to see a developer interacting with their fans in such a nice and genuine way! They retweet fanarts, tweets talking about the game, reviews, etc... (I would just like to point out that they also liked every single tweet I sent to them, including something I tweeted on a, I don't know, maybe one or two months old retweet of theirs).
Rusty Lake makes great point and click games, and if you like this kind of game, definitly check out cube escape and both   (premium) rusty lake games, you won't regret it.

As a initial backer of the kickstarter campaign - I have personally logged hundreds of hours into Hex; please don't be offput by my paltry amount of played time.
Hex is a fantastic TCG Hybrid that wonderfully blends RPG and MMO mechanics into a TCG experience that is truly unique.  Many of the concepts delivered by the game truly push the envelope on what a digital TCG is capable of.  While traditional paper TCGs are held back by the logistics of real-world constraints, Hex is constantly innovating on what being a digital game is all about.  A card might secretly show you your opponent's hand without them knowing, a card might constantly generate spirits to fill your deck, or a card could create a random card out of thin-air; all things that are cumbersome or impossible to do in a traditional paper TCG.
The RPG elements of the game manifest themselves in a way that makes playing a joy.  In the beginning of the PvE campaign, players are required to create a new character that contains several RPG tropes.  Characters gain levels, earn talents, unlock abilities, and earn equipment which can be used to boost the power of their cards and deck.  Players progress through a map encountering different characters and challenges that put their skills to the test.  While there is a general storyline to be followed, the map has several opportunities for players to explore "off the beaten path" with many optional challenges and dangers to be conquered.  Defeating encounters rewards the player with Gold (Hex's free to play currency), new PvE cards, and equipment.  Several other collectibles are available as well, such as Stardust for extending the art of your cards or sleeves to swag out your deck.
Veterans to TCGs will find a game with a wonderful amount of strategic depth to scratch the itch of any deck builder.  Cards with sockets allow gems to be socketed into the cards, drastically changing the effect of a card.  A socketed card could spawn a rhino when it deals damage to an opponent, or that same card could deal direct damage to an opponent with a different gem.  This unique take on card customization is a wonderful idea that further emphasizes the fantastic digital nature of the game.  Also as mentioned, there are hundreds of pieces of equipment to collect and use.  Equipment can change the effect of the card from boosting its raw stats to generating some new ability or effect on the card.  Cards that you initially pass up may instead suddenly become relevant as you find a piece of equipment to boost the effectiveness of the card.  This is an interesting addition to the game, as cards that would normally be overlooked in favor of more traditionally "stronger" cards may instead be worth giving a second look.
Although the PvE portion of the game is likely enough to satisfy many folks, many players are more interested in crushing their enemies on the field of battle.  Hex has both good and downsides in this endeavor.  Hex offers several tournament styles and play modes to test your mettle.  Limited players from other games like MTG and Hearthstone will be happy to find that both Draft and Sealed modes are available in Hex.  Even better, with a paltry $2 booster pack cost, drafts can be played with a minimal cost investment.  Other tournaments such as Constructed or Gauntlet (Hex's version of asynchronous tournaments) are available as well.  The wide variety of ways to compete is definitely a plus, ensuring that there is a competitive mode for everyone in the game.
Several community run tournaments are also available - generally free to enter - which enable players to get a taste of competitive play without having to potentially buy-in with real cash.  Hex has also dedicated itself to having higher-stakes tournaments as well.  Earlier this year, the first Hex Invitational Tournament was held with a prize total of $100,000.  With a focus on cultivating the competitive scene, Hex is likely to continue to develop into a game with many high level tournaments for the most hardcore competitive players among us.
Hex bills itself as a free-to-play game.  This is somewhat misleading, as new players to the game may see the free-to-play tag and immediately cry foul when they go up against an established player with a well-tuned deck.  While the PvE portion of the game is indeed free and full of content, players should expect to invest either their time or money if they want to pursue some of the more competitive aspects of the game.  Luckily, Hex makes this relatively easy to do with several avenues to accrue value.  Gold from the PvE portion of the game is often coveted by PvP players for their ability to purchase stardust or spin the Wheels of Fate.  The game does a wonderful job of providing potential value and "feel-good" opportunities within the game.  For example, booster packs purchased in the game also have a small chance to come with a bonus "Primal Pack" - a bonus booster pack that is filled with all rares and legendaries!  Another interesting feature is that each booster pack also includes a treasure chest.  These treasure chests come in a variety of rarities and contain everything from Cards, to Equipment, or in some cases - even another booster pack to start the process over again!  Treasure chests can also be "spun" on the Wheels of Fate; essentially a slot machine paid for with gold earned in the Free to Play portion of the game for a chance to upgrade your treasure chest or get other goodies.  Players can spin into rare cards, powerful PvE cards, or even more booster packs!
The value packed into a single booster pack in the game truly is one of the better features of the game, allowing for maximum amount of enjoyment for a reasonable cost.  While other digital games have no concept of value since cards cannot be traded, Hex's economy ensures that most cards retain some value whether its due to their PvP viability or their potential use in PvE; an interesting duality that helps keep cards relevant.
Hex is a game with a bright future.  A kickstarted game that continues to grow, it has overcome many challenges in its short lifespan.  The PvE portion continues to grow with future updates planned and the continual release of new sets ensures that the game remains fresh.  Hex has struggled to release content in a standardized timeframe, but this is to be expected with a new indie company finding their footing and building their core systems.  Fresh out of the beta stages, Hex is a game that can only continue to become more immense as more features continue to be implemented.  With a fantastic community of helpful players - I urge you to give Hex a try.  Odds are it will draw you into the game with its innovation, beautiful artwork, and depth.

Dawn Of War II is easily one of the best real time strategy games out there. For me personally, it easily beats Starcraft 2, as far as the singleplayer mode is concerned, though. It has a brilliant mix of strategy and light RPG elements that all work together quite nicely. Find some random loot, give it to one of your units and you're all set to kill those damn orcs. It adds a certain layer of personalization. Plus, there's quite some loot to be found so there's always an incentive to explore the levels.
The levels are set up with a cover system. Green means you get the best cover for your squad and yellow is 50/50. You actually have to set up your units carefully and not rush them towards the objectives. They'll only get killed. You *have* to use the cover properly in order to survive some of the tougher levels. Some of these levels even end with a bossfight, which are epic and awesome, even if they're not all that focused on strategy, but more on action.
The graphics are, even to this day, beautiful and colorful. Just don't zoom in too much. The voice acting is also still solid.
Now the story I can't remember so that hasn't made such an impression on me. But I admire this game for trying to bring new stuff to the strategy genre. It was really in need of some new and fresh ideas. Relic has done this beautifully.

I tried to like this game, I really did, but I really can't. When my friend told me about Sniper Elite, I was intrigued; a stealth based game revolving around sniping. It looked like a mix of a shooter and Thief, and when I did enjoy it for the first hour or so... then things started cropping up that really ruined this game for me.
The first problem was when I started dying from enemies shooting through solid objects... I was sneaking around and got jumped from about 20 paces away from an enemy shooting through a solid block!
The second issue is when I had to deal with a T-34 tank by shooting it's fuel cap. Now, I don't know very much about military hardware, but I know a tank would never have such a glaring weakness: the ability to kill a tank with a single bullet is ridiculous. Thats why they have anti-tank munitions. Snipers are NOT tank killers!
Adding to issue 2: later I had to deal with an enemy tank attacking a friendly position. All I had was a stack of TNT... I thought that all I could do is use it to break a track and immobilize that tank. When I used the TNT (on the side of the tank) the enemy tank exploded! Ridiculous! Tanks are NOT that fragile. Again, snipers are NOT tank killers!
The last issue that ended my interest in this game is the cyborg-like vision of the enemies. I heard that this game had a heavy stealth aspect and so I treated it accordingly. I was very careful using cover, obstructions, and crawling as much as needed to be stealthy, even so more often than not the enemy would find me long before I could find them. Even when using my binoculars/sniper scope the enemy is far too difficult to see, whereas the enemy can/will shoot at you even when they're supposedly distracted in a battle.
I wish I could get a refund. As stealth titles go Sniper Elite is no Thief: The Dark Project.

A truly fun game with very smooth gameplay. There's not much singleplayer content other than fighting a line of swordmen with the difficulty increase per time you defeat the next in the row. The multiplayer seems to have a bit delay for now, other than that it's great fun killing your enemy. Your goal is to get to the right of the level and enter the next screen, while your enemy have to get to the left side of the screen. You are only able to move to the next scene when  you have the GO sign in the opposite corner of yourself, It's a tough process and can take a good amount of time if you're playing against a mighty fencer.
There are various ways to kill and disarm your enemy or yourself :3
You have 5 different ways to hold your sword, with different range depending on you're trying to target the enemies feet or head. The higher you aim, the longer range. The lower you aim, the shorter range.
When holding the sword in the upper position, you'll be able to throw it (also when jumping in midair), hopefully killing your enemy or die trying...
When you jump, you're able to strike downward, this is a great ability if you've lost your sword and still want to go offensive on your enemy. You can also roll and kick when approaching the player if his sword is in a high position, else you'll just die horribly by getting stacked in the chest or face.
The sound effects makes it quite enjoyable to stick your sword through the chest of someone else and keeping it inside, making it "bleed"  more and enemy scream even longer is just very satisfying.
The different set of levels gives the player a good amount of space to use his different moves and feature lots of movement to make the scenes more alive, the game does have music but it's quite ambient and might not get noticed because of the  screams coming from either you or your enemy.
.:CONCLUSION:.
It's really good fun and plays great, the price point might be a bit high but there's online multiplayer which makes the price acceptable in my opinion. Nidhogg provides some of the fastest and most enjoyable monochromatic bloodletting one could hope to experience.   The premise is simple.  You are a pixelated swordsman in a territorial conflict with your opponent, most often your best friend sitting right beside you.  Each standoff is lightning fast, and invariably ends in a gratuitous splattering of blood.   Kill your opponent with a well-timed and well-placed lunge, hurl your épée at his head, or just knock him down and rip his heart out.  Savagery is encouraged, and provides a hilarious counterpoint to the civilized image of fencing.  Once you have managed to kill your opponent, you can progress to your goal until just seconds later, he respawns and you must again defeat him to progress. Lose, and he gains ground on you. This ebb and flow continues until one of you reaches the final screen where the winner is given a true hero’s sendup: He is eaten by a flying worm.
Nidhogg is not just a circus of inanity and violence, but is some of the best fun you can have with your friends.  Controls are responsive, animations are fast and smooth, and landing consecutive killing blows provides a jolt of dopamine that keeps you coming back for more.  There are multiple arenas to choose from, each one visually unique and designed to make you rethink your strategy.  Some corridors are too tight for jumping or sword throwing, so both your opponent and the landscape will make you think on your toes.
Visually, Nidhogg exhibits a unique combination of minimalism through pixilation and solid colors.  It highlights the expression of characters through animation rather than textures.  It is aesthetically arresting and securely has its own style.  These visuals are elevated even further when coupled with an exceptional soundtrack by Daedelus.
Nidhogg could have provided only the core one-on-one experience, but if you look deeper there are a lot of extras.  There is a tournament mode supporting up to 8 players. There is a multitude of variants in gameplay to explore. There is a single player experience pitting you against an increasingly difficult array of AI personalities.  Additionally, there is an online multiplayer component, but at the time of this review, I experienced some unfortunate glitches.  In several matches I experienced moments where I killed my opponent, but immediately the game changed states, and my character unexplainably died.  It wasn’t often, but it was often enough to sour the experience.  I’m told that the online component is still a work in progress, so if you don’t have a friend handy to play local multiplayer check the forums for progress.
Nidhogg was first shown in 2010, and since then Messhoff, comprised of Mark Essen and Kristy Norindr, have worked to shine the core game into a full-fledged release.  Nidhogg is available today on Steam for $11.99, and if you have friends, it is well worth your dollars.

OUT THERE is a classic space adventure mixed with resource management.  While it is a port of a mobile game, only the comic sans esque text betrays it.  There is no actual combat in this game;  it's a bit more like a choose your own adventure book mixed with a random number generator and resource management.
The object of the game is to reach one of four points on a fixed star map and meet the conditions required at that point.  The points vary by distance,  which is an indicator as to the quality of ending you get.  Along the way, you have to manage your oxygen, fuel, and hull integrity.   Travel and random events that occur when entering a new system,  many with choices for the player, can help or hinder.  The starting ship is moderately sized but very inefficient; finding derelict ships to swap to is an early game goal.
The language of aliens is one unified language.  You only talk to aliens by triggering an event on any life giving world.  As you interact, the words transform into readable text.  Unfortunately,  these equivalence are random,  so  one play through will not have the same translations as the next.   These aliens are important as they give you the technologies needed to progress.
Running out of fuel or dying means starting over from scratch,  but you will find ships from your failed attempts as derelict vessels that you can loot or swap to.
The biggest issue here is that behind the curtain,  this game is a cross of inventory tetris and random generator results.   This changes a little as you learn the star map,  but not the inventory problem.  Each ship has a fixed number of aquares.  These squares can be a stack of resources mined from planets or they can be a module built from a technology you acquired.  Building one means losing cargo space,  except for one module.  As the game progresses a lot of time is spent recycling parts so you can fit fuel,  then filling your tank from that fuel and putting a drill in its place to get more iron so you can build more fuelling probes and drills and so on. A bad click while doing this can leave you stranded with no engines and no way to make more.
The music is incredible and the game is very relaxing if you can get past the comic sans and the inventory tetris.  I recommend this on sale,  but not for retail price.

While it may seem simplistic in concept as most of the recent wave of indie tycoon games may be (I'm looking at you Game Dev and Mad Games Tycoon) this one has more soul underlying than the rest I have tried.  Perhaps it is the concept behind it, every one at some point in there life wondered what it would be like to start a band and be one of the cool kids. well, I got at least part of the experience ( I have absolutely no musical talent outside of some horrific elementary school violin lessons) so for me, gathering musicians and planning rehearsels and figuring out set lists for shows was like a brave new world.
But for the meat and potatoes of what makes this game fun for me, The song creator, it's simplistic which is great for just jumping in and throwing together tracks without a lengthy tutorial or a lot of outside reading (In the end it has no effect on the outcome of the rating of the track itself, but for me it's a point of pride to make a song that doesnt sound like a jumbled mess of discordant notes being played by drunken monkeys (The ability to now listen to your tracks as the in game soundtrack definitely adds to the appeal)). But yes, its simple to jump in, but the diversity offered is stunning when you think about the team that built this game.  One could ask for more riffs and track pieces to build with, or even better the ability to load your own into the game (maybe at a later date or via workshop, but as it stands now you have a solid ability to make a multitude of aurally pleasing tracks within the game.
As far as the rest of the game, yes, the characters are drawn almost amateurly, without a lot of diversity in the customization of faces, but it's good enough to make your characters stand out, and it gives it a solid indie feel, which I appreciate .. (Put too much time in Epic Battle Fantasy to really be judgy for lackulster artwork). Would love to see an option to slap your band logo on the bands shirts or even better the drumset, just to give it a more "this is mine" feel.  PS you can create your own logo and drop it into the folder,
By the way did I mention this is still being updated and new features being added?  And that community desires and wants are actually being addressed and implemented?  Yah, not bad for a 2 man team.

I have been playing Hex regularly since the start of the closed beta, over 2 years ago. Raptr says I have logged 707 hours in the game prior to Steam Launch. I know not all of my time got properly tracked.
HEX IS AMAZING. I've logged more hours in Hex than any other game.
This is not just a game. It is a hobby. It will own your heart for years. There alre lots of other positive reviews. So, I'll keep mine to a few few things I think you need to understand going into it.
1 - THERE'S A LOT OF DEPTH - We already have hundreds of cards in 3 sets, and the 4th major set comes out next week. Accept that it will take time to understand everything. The community is very good about helping new players out. You're not going to be elite an hour after you finish the tutorial.
2 - UNDERSTAND THE ECONOMY - This is not F2P where everything is handed to you on a silver platter. The PVE campaign and Frost Ring Arena are free to play. These are good places to learn how the game works, and earn some gold to buy more cards from the Auction House (Or sell your cards for the premium currency, Platinum). Hex makes its money selling booster packs and entrance fees to tournaments, like traditional TCGs. These items can be purchased from gold with time, but it isn't quick.
3 - PAY TO COMPETE (Not Pay to Win!!!!!) - It absolutely is possible to trade gold for packs and plat, and turn that around to going infinite with skilled play. That's not realistic for most of us. If you want to play in draft or sealed tournaments regularly, get comfortable with supporting the developers with the purchase of plat. This is a very traditional TCG business model.
Costs are EXTREMELY REASONABLE
For a booster draft (assuming 100 plat = $1):
$2 per booster x 3 packs = $6
+100 plat ($1) entry fee = $7.
If you play Swiss draft, you'll play 3 rounds. That's 3 hours of entertainment for $7, which is a better value than going to a movie - and you can sell some of those cards to finance more drafts. You get a booster for each win, so even at 1-2, you're getting more than the entry cost.
Compare the costs of Hex to Magic: The Gathering, or any other TCG, and I think the value speaks for itself.
The game is not "Pay to Win," because there is a lot of skill involved in Hex. You can have decks full of legendary cards and still get wrecked by smarter players. I know this cause I'm the one with the legendaries who loses in big tournaments =) But I keep coming back for more.
Download the game. Watch Cory's release video. Get ready to enjoy Hex for years to come. Welcome to the party!

If you have ever played a TCG before, you probably have the basics down. This game offers that and so much more.
The community (at the time of this writing) is very friendly, helpful when questioned and overall a good bunch of people.
the game itself though is where things shine.
with the release of the PvE Adventure Zone 1, new ways of obtaining Gold and Cards are available. If you play through as one race and class and get to a point where you are a bit stuck, create a new champion and go through a few of them. Just by playing the storyline you are granted packs which contain very useful items. If they aren't useful to you, the Auction House or the Trade Channel can help you find a way to trade/sell it off and get something which pertains to your deck in question.
Once you get some strength, you can then take on the Arena. A gauntlet match of 20 boss fights, lose 3 times, and you have to start over, but every 5 fights you qualify for prizing.
There are three big reasons to do these events. Cards, Equipment, Gold. Not to mention the fact you get to learn a bit more of the game as you go. Got a dungeon your deck doesn't work for yet? fine tune it with different cards. You may have to change things up to win these encounters.
Plenty of replayability, specially with the different race/class types.
The PvP events are a lot of fun to do as well. If you do want to Draft, start off with the 'Swiss' version, this lets you play all the rounds and you can learn a bit more of the cards. Once you are confident, go on to the Competive modes which are single elimination with a bigger payout.
All in all, this game has been a blast to play since the Alpha, I just wish i could play more.

Hex is taking Magic the Gathering and throwing RPG special sauce all over it. It is a deeper strategy game then Hearthstone. Hex provides a good PVE and PVP experience with mmo style adventure and tournament support.
I have played since Alpha for 100's of hours playing both PVE and PVP.  Players start with 200 cards so you have a lot of options to start playing before having to spend money. As well as earning gold to buy cards on the Auction house. I saw some poor reviews that lambasted HEX as pay to win. I wanted to make sure people understood you get a bunch to start with and play with PVE before you really need to invest any $. Also the claim of PVE harder to force to buy cards shows that people are not using deck builder to update their decks, remember PVE like in hearthstone is more of a puzzle. So you build a deck to solve the puzzle and with the large amount of cards to start you have a lot of choices.
They are still fine tuning the game and releasing their PVE side of the game but the current zone they have released is a taste of building your RPG character and advenuring in their world. character progression as well as gear that boosts specific cards allow players to shift their play style based on their decks and equipment. They also have a taste of their dungeon mechanics that like any MMO will be the key to earning new cards and gear. Their Raid model has not been released yet. Players start with 200 cards so you have a lot of options to start playing before having to spend money. As well as earning gold to buy cards on the Auction house.
PVP as with any MTG store tournament allows players to do anything they could think, as well as thank god supporting draft tourneys.
Their developers are active in listening to the community and have ran their first 100k tourney. On top of that i have yet to not see active team members online going by the NOBLE tags for the game.
Overall for a deeper game then HS I am loving my time with HEX and can't wait for their impromvements.

I've been playing HEX for a little more than a year. It truly is an amazing digital tcg.
I won't go into a long rant about why the game is good, many other reviewers do this - there's plenty of material to read. Instead, I'd like to sum up some of the pros and cons:
Pros
+Real tcg, you do not only collect cards, you can trade them or sell them on auction house.
+PvE content, arena and campaign. Both earns you gold (ingame currency), cards and equipment.
+Campaign the rpg pve will only grow with time.
+Competitive - If you like how MTG plays out in competitive scene, I'm betting you will also like HEX. Being similar is not a bad thing, but do not think HEX a MTG clone, HEX does a lot of things its own way which makes me come to:
+Digital only TCG. This means HEX has mechanics that is only possible through a digital tcg that can keep track of every buff, debuff and whatnot. Example: Arborean Rootfather ability - 2cost, shuffle it back into the deck and give it cost -2, then draw a card. In a physical tcg if you had multiple copies it would not be easily possible to know which of them had the cost -2.
+Free to play IS possible, also in a competitive scene. However, do not expect it to come rushing in. It takes time, effort, some luck and skill. The beginning is the slowest, but once you get into limited and if you are skilled enough AND can play the auction house you can quickly earn more than you spend. Personally half (and probably a little more) of my card collection is through free to play and where I have been paying has been at the beginning to get started up faster and when I did not want to put in the time and effort to earn myself the platinum and/or cards.
+Complicated. HEX has a lot of depth - you will go into mind games vs. your opponent and choosing the right course of action is a lot more difficult than you would think. This also adds a lot of fun to it, since it is not always so straight forward and your action current turn can make you lose the next, or the one after that.
+UI, Graphics and Sound - they are all excellent. UI is smooth, graphics are nice on the eyes - every function is well polished. It is a great experience overall.
+Content in both PvE and PvP will keep getting expanded.
+Support. The hex support team is AMAZING. Are you having a bug during a draft or sealed? Well, you're in luck, because they are very willing to compensate you fully. All you have to do is go to their support site, login and write a ticket and fill in details (it is important to fill in the # of your tournament).
+The community. HEX has absolutely the best community I have ever experienced in any game. They are helpful, generous, mature and generally nice people. Especially those who are part of the twitch community on hex. I can highly recommend the hex streamers on twitch and have a chat. There's also usually giveaways on various streams for cards or drafts. Also a great place to learn - check it out. No seriously, check it out!
Cons
-Waiting time. I love the game, but they can be very slow at releasing new content and fixing bugs. I'm hopeful though, now that they got their core mechanics (with coding) and PvE campaign it's reasonable to believe content will be released in a more steady flow than previously.
-Complicated. Learning all the mechanics will take time and effort. It is difficult. You have to use your head. You need to learn keywords, priority steps, when to do what, what happens when I do this in response, the list goes on. Even after more than a year I learn new tricks - I do find this _fun_, but getting fundamentals at the beginning can be a frustrating experience for some. Do not give up, get into it and ask around for help or look at guides. Help is everywhere!
-Bugs. Being a digital TCG means bugs will be inevitable. Some are worse than others, but sometimes they stick around for longer than I would like. However, this has not made me want to stop the game, as their support team is insanely good.
Give it a swing, it's free to play after all - but do expect to either spend a lot of time or put in some money if you want to join the competitive scene. I do hope the review helped :-)
Edit: Added a few extra Pros that I at the time did not consider.

Definitely an adventure of a lifetime. Oldschool RPGs, while suffering many, many flaws, has a very valuable virtue that is sadly lost on many of the modern ones regardless of how lengthy they are; they reward tenacity and persistence. Gothic is one of the preceptors of the genre as well as a prime example of such a quality.
While future entries in the genre (Thrird game and upwards) suffer from weak stories and characters, the original two titles are quite adept in crafting those. You start of a blank slate and unravel a large and unfamiliar and harsh world full of unique characters and stories that serve to not only flesh it out, but to also entertain you and make you feel like a part of it regardless of how disinterested you are in the grand scheme at large.
You progress slowly, battle after battle, and one quest after another, and feel classically rewarded when you beat early enemies in one fell swoop after gaining a few levels...levels that are to that point quite well earned in blood, sweat, and tears, serving to make a lengthy game even lengthier, without asking you to rush yourself towards the end for any reason.
Sadly, as with Gothic and other similar titles such as Morrowind, Diablo, and Divine Divinity, it is that same quality that should scare you away from the game should you be inclined towards a more speedy playthrough. Such titles have been welcoming to the attitude, and punish such a style of play by running you against a wall of impossible odds and enemies.
Add to that some shoddy combat and interaction elements, modern system running issues, the old graphics, and Gothic becomes a "Diamond in the rough" so to speak. Takes a true oldschool RPG fan to get into it, if you are that, then good luck, soldier, because you will need it. Else, stay well away regardless of the low price it goes for nowadays.
Should you yet find yourself playing this, then take it one step at a time and enjoy the journey. doing so, you might find yourself inclined to listen to the world soundtrack for a while, wiling away time in the prison camps and surrounding hills, or speaking to the many, many, inhabitants of the world to learn of all that is Gothic, and in doing so, preparing yourself for an even better, albeit technically marred as ever, adventure in Gothic 2.

This visual novel contains the following adult subject matter, which could be triggering for some: nudity, incest, physical abuse, mental abuse, verbal abuse, physical assault, r/a/p/e, blood, murder, self-harm, suicide, and general depressing/disturbing scenes.
This story was not quite what I expected. It was a pleasant surprise, but I wasn't quite prepared for such a serious/depressing story. It definitely is worth money, so I'm not sure why it's free. In fact, it is one of the best visual novels I've read on Steam.
There are five different endings, including a secret ending. They range from disturbing to less disturbing. While I suppose there are good and bad endings, there aren't really
endings. I suppose someone could interpret one of them as happy, but it wouldn't be in a conventional sense.
Honestly, trying to give a description of the story is difficult. It's quite abstract. The main theme is love; I guess you could say the dark side of love. The side of love that can drive a person insane over it. While some claim that love is the best feeling in the world, no one can deny that it is also tied to such feelings as pain, loneliness, and obsession.
I wouldn't recommend this visual novel to anyone who has strong feelings about the subjects listed above. It is very dark and disturbing. If you're used to lighthearted VNs, this probably isn't for you.

There are a few games I always wanted to play, but nobody ever made them. A rock band tycoon game/ sim is definitely one of them. Thankfully, someone decided to correct this and make Rock God Tycoon.
Rock God Tycoon is a game about forming a metal band, recording albums, and touring. Having been in a few bands myself, I can tell you that they do get at least most of this experience down as accurately as one could expect from a tycoon game. There are a few issues with that realism, but we'll get to that shortly. The key takeaway for now is that you're a metal band seeking stardom.
I had to specify "metal" there because apart from a few rockabilly riffs and a few other riffs that hint teasingly toward shoeglaze, metal is pretty much the only style of music you can play here. Don't expect to become the next Radiohead, Weezer, or Kaiser Chiefs. If it isn't metal, you're not going to see much of it here. Hopefully this is something they'll correct in the future, though, which brings us to our next point...
Awesome devs!
My internet has been fidgety all week, so I picked this up to kill time while experiencing random outages. Yesterday, I wrote a song and uploaded it to the workshop. Literally within minutes, one of the developers had complimented the song's drums. That's when I came to realize these devs are very active in their community, encouraging to players, and extremely active with cranking out updates. They're also one of the few, rare dev teams that actually listens to player feedback and attempts to implement their suggestions, which is fantastic. I've only had this game for about 48 hours, and in that time there's already been two updates.
Now for some basic pro's and con's:
PROS:
- Very addictive dayslayer tycoon game
- Write your own songs using prefab "intros," "riffs," "breaks," and "outtros" for guitar, bass, and drums
- Active devs are fixing stuff and adding stuff constantly
- Visually and audibly appealing; graphics and sound match the game style and suit it well
- Gameplay has a very low learning curve; any fan of tycoon games will jump right in and get it out of the box
CONS:
- Limited music selection (these prefab music parts are excellent, btw... I just want more of them)
- Bands can't rehearse unless they go to a recording studio, which doesn't make sense
- You'll sign an unrealistic number of record deals; would be better to sign fewer deals with longer/ stronger returns
- Metal theme is quite limiting (unless you like metal, of course)
- Touring could use some work
All told, I think this is a very good game and it looks like it's getting better. I definitely recommend it if you're into tycoon games and you aren't turned off by metal music.
If I could suggest a few things to devs, they'd be:
1. Bands should be rehearsing a set list whenever they have no other tasks assigned to them. That's how real bands work. The band could rehearse whichever song they know least, but this is interrupted whenever one or more bandmates are given a task (writing songs, busking, refining skills, etc). Players could set an option to rehearse specific songs until all bandmates have reached 100% in said songs.
2. Send the band (or specific band members) on vacation to more rapidly lower their tension. This would send those members away for a full weekend (Saturday and Sunday) and would cost money, but they'll return with less tension (variable based on the quality of the vacation you sent them on)
3. Signing a record deal with a label should lock you into a certain number of albums over a certain number of years with said label. You'd be required to produce (n) LP's in that time, with EP's, singles, B-sides, and live LP's being optional (labels may or may not offer those options). Albums are on the market forever, with sales lasting a bit longer than they do now. EP's, singles, etc. have short-term growth and bolster sales of the main album. you can walk into a store right now and buy Houses Of The Holy, an album that came out well before I was born. This idea of records going off the market is a bit bonkers, lol.
4. Touring should be a real thing. While the band is on tour, they can't rehearse. You book tour dates, and each city will require you to pay for gas, food, and hotel accomodations. Scaling food quality and hotel quality will determine how much tension is gained on that leg of the tour. While touring, album sales are improved considerably, but it's exhausting, and touring comes with its own set of random scenarios, too (gear getting stolen, drummer throwing TV's out of windows, groupies robbing you, etc.). I feel like touring is very incomplete, but like I said, these devs are awesome and they'll probably fix it eventually.
4. No Yoko references? Come on guys! Have you ever been in a band? lol

For my first paragraph, I'd like to lay all my cards on the table. This is easily one of the best stories I've experienced in a good while, and definitely my favorite Telltale game.
For my second paragraph, I'd like to go into a little bit more detail. This game has absolutely no business being as good as it is. I'll openly admit to being a fan of the Borderlands series' writing. I willingly forgive the meme BS it constantly tries to throw at you in favor of the genuinely interesting story it hides underneath. This game builds on all of that, and it even ditches the memes two episodes in! Every little bit of story that Borderlands introduces but never works with really shines here. It's a great story about an unbelievably lovable band of Borderlands trademark misfit characters. And, in the least likely outcome, it ties-in the Pre-Sequel's story AND the Hammerlock's Hunt's story in a very meaningful way. Who would have expected that from the worst DLC and an outsourced spinoff?
There's really no good way to describe it. It's an experience that more or less requires you to be up to date on all other Borderlands games, but maybe that's why it works so well. It builds on a universe that you're familiar with in a way that that same universe has never let you see itself before.
It is easily the best Telltale game I've ever played, and it has produced a huge number of characters that I won't be forgetting any time soon. I know this game suffered from poor sales, but I'll still hold out hope that a sequel may happen.
(For the record, Anthony Burch is not the lead writer on this project. Just saying.)

Great f2p game with a fairly fair model, considering it is a card game. It differs from the regular Yu-Gi-Oh! TCG in the fact that it uses Speed Duel Rules, i.e. 3 monster and backrow lanes, 5 extra deck limit and 20-30 card decks.
They are constant events major and minor, and a good level of nostalgia for the original two series. (Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Monsters and Yu-Gi-Oh! GX)
Datamining reveals plans for Synchros, Xyzs, Pendulums, etc. However that is probably a year or two off from now, so keep that in mind if you plan on investing long time into the game. That being said, I can easily see this game, lasting long enough past even those points, the business model is fair, the development is steady and the developers even listen to the players. (Surprising especially considering it's Konami)

After takeing a few days to play this game more and invest a bit more time into it. I stick by my guns saying its fun for the price. But it's more than that. This game really brought me back to the simpler times when developers released top down shooters with simple objectives instead of large FPS style games with arching story lines and Final Fantasy like cutscenes.
This game is a prime example of what a simple idea can achieve. Let this be a lesson to all future game devs out there. A simple idea that has been properly executed is 100X better than a grand massive idea that has been hastily put together.

This game is good, like really good. I bought it at release and played it for a few hours then put it down. The amount of content and polishing that has happened since inital release to this point here is amazing. It's changed so much that this is my second review as I beleive it deserves it
Pros-
It's addicting,
Great tutorial which is fully optional and you only have to look at parts you want. It is text based but no where near as long or wordy as Paradise Lost,
Where's the time gone!
Progression,
Feels epic when you start doing good,
There is a learning curve to a degree but it's easy to pick up and do well on your first play through,
You're not forced to make a song or play it, you can simulate it,
The dev responds fast, like really fast and releases a patch as soon as he can,
New content has been coming out since inital release in November 2016 and then official release in February 2017,
Your suggestions are taken into account and quite a lot have been added.
Cons-
Can easily become a repetitive game but it depends how you play it.
Playtime-
This is purely dependant on how fast you get bored. It's easy to play over 20 hours and for the price that's really good.
I'd definately recommend buying the game.

Let me start with stating that I'm not totally into adventure games in general. Having gotten that out of the way, I can tentatively recommend this game. I've enjoyed my playthrough, but it wasn't a mindblowing experience. I found the story to be okey, same as the humor. Out of the 5 episodes, I only really loved the 4th one. The rest I'd call them decent.
I really like that saying nothing is available as an option on conversations. Cudo's on that. But the timeconstraint to make you choise feels sometimes a bit too narrow. It took time for me to translate what the prompt would say about the character and what of those options felt the most fitting for the situation. Luckily you can pause the game when pondering about the options. Dialog in general, especially the banter between character is well done.
Graphics are in line with the Borderlands series, as with the introduction of characters. Animation quality sometimes fell a bit short though; at times too floaty and too stiff. Audio quality I'd rank as decent.
The plot/story, was not really strong. It didn't realy do much for me. But the interaction between the characters is this game's saving grace if you'd ask me.

You can chose to be cynical, cruel, or stern in dialogue choices that have an effect on the actions of your daughter. The story is set in 18th century France and follows the lives of three individuals who become entwined in a tale of passion, love, lust, loss, and revenge.
Pros:
- Well drawn art, it's manga but it's clearly influenced by the Victorian setting.
- The soundtrack is quite nice featuring a repertoire of piano pieces. You can chose what song plays in the background as well once  you have it unlocked.
- Your actions really do shape the story, dialogue choices aren't just there for the sake of multiple options.
- The story becomes engrossing as you progress.
- Save system/skip system means you can explore all the possible endings with little hassle.
- The choice of vocabulary or diction is easy to follow.
- It's free.
Cons:
- You will have to read, no two ways about it. If you aren't into reading this game may not be for you.
- Some images and sections may contain mature subject matter that may be inapropriate for younger audiences.
Would I recommend this game?
It's a good read with an interesting story and characters that aren't static. I highly recommend it to those who are fans of VNs.

Got this as part of a Humble Bundle. Felt a bit slow at first, but as I liked Prototype, and i'd bought it, I thought i'd complete it.
I found the story to be quite bad, with your PTSD character having almost no signs of the disorder, cracking one-liners mid-fight constantly. Add to that his insistence on causing as much collateral damage as possible when doing almost anything. It seems you play as a bad guy who everyone treats as the good guy. Also, the protagonist from the first game comes back as the major villain, with flimsy motivations.
The powers are introduced haphazardly, often being a sudden one-on-one fight. The flight is also quite clunky, often requiring double-backing and only really being useful towards the end of the upgrade path.
Lots of missions feel repeated, due to the time trials being rolled in to them and there are some long periods of following groups of people to the next encounter, then another and another.
TL;DR It falls far short of the original, in story and gameplay.

The game was very fun and not too difficult as far as rogue-like games go.  I liked the fact that the more times you went through, the more starting money and blueprints (for buying starting gear) you collect.  That way even failure runs can have some benefit. If you are really struggling with the game - there are guides out with a few tips that make the game much easier (how to find the secret areas and how to save townsfolk to get more starting money).
Side Note:  The developers for this game were amazing!  They worked their hardest to address all concerns and even fixed an achievement glitch long after they stopped working on the game.

This is 80% the exact same thing as MtG except digital. Unlike the garbage Mtg video games we got so far limiting how we can or cant build our decks here you will have 100% freedom, this is truly the MtG video game we have all been waiting for.

1. To start you can play campaign or frost arena to earn gold.
2. Gold you can sell to players to get platinum.
3. For platinum you can buy booster packs that you can open to get cards OR
4. Play draft tournaments, to enter you have to give 3 booster packs.
5* If your a GOOD player and win draft tournaments you will get MORE packs, 1st place gains 5 packs. (Each tournament holds 8 players so they go by FAST)
Even if your a BAD PLAYER, every card you pick for yourself in the draft tournament you KEEP. So even if you lose all your games in the tournament you still get the same amount of cards worth 3 booster packs.
In draft EVERYONE is on equal footing, it doesn't matter if some guy spent 1000€ on this game in draft they are ALL EQUAL!
In short, if your a good player you will be rolling in cards very quickly. Very much depends on your skill!

All the things that I heard from this game were extremely positive. Most people consider it one of the best RPGs ever. So one day, my thoughts were "I am not listening to that blabbering anymore !" and so i bought the game. "You've gotta watch what you tell people", so here I am, writing this review.
Since the game released in 2001, "it was obvious there would be trouble ahead", but i trusted Steam nonetheless. As a wise man once said : "Rely on someone and you're in trouble, that's how it goes" and so I was only able to launch the game after installing a mod. In the game, I came to realize that the controlls are pretty hard to get used to, I guess "that was not clever" in that time. But when I got used to it, the game showed me its whole beauty. As a well tought rpg gamer, I went into the very next stoner camp where i snuck into a gurus shed and slept in his bed, while he was working on his desks, cluelessly. As you can see, you can become such a ninja that people won't even notice you sleeping in their bed.
But "let's talk about something else instead". Once you first start your adventure, you are to join one of three guilds. The catch is : You have to impress people in order to join each guild. That means : You have to do quests in order obtain quests that will help you get quests so you can follow up the main quests, aka. joining one of the guilds. That however is one of the game's strongest aspects in my opinion. Everything feels connected. Remember that old lady in Skyrim that told you to save her cat which then turned into a dragon and then gave you a silver plate as a reward and had nothing to do with the main quest ? Well, you won't find that here. Even though the best reward I got so far were some cush, still every single completion of a quest felt so incredibly rewarding, as i progressed in joining the guilds. I've never played an Rpg so addictive as Gothic is, I love everything about it so far ( except for the extremely repetetive monologs Npcs have when walking by, those sentences I used to accomplish a humorous effect in this review ) .
However, do NOT use any sorts of guides for this game because in my opinion, finding out everything yourself is half the fun in this game.
But "hang on. Better not go rushing into anything". If you want to enjoy this game, you have to deal with terrible graphics, controlls and all those quotes I've been using throughout this review, which you will hear every two seconds. Once you get used to those aspects however, you will find yourself in wonderful, mystical world to which you will get addicted exploring.
