You're at the last part of the level and one enemy stands in your way. I had played Murder Miners a lot two years ago (and even managed to clock in 90 hours), and my time on the game was really fun, the game is simple there are a few gamemodes Murdermatch/Team Murdermatch, which is just deathmatch, Murder the Flag, which is just capture the flag (this is the last time they just add in murder) Infection, in which one of the players is a zombie, and has to infect everybody, and finally Zombie Survival, which is quiet self explanatory. The gamemodes were very fun to play but I didn't like the zombie related ones. (but all of my friends liked it so it was just my opinion :P) The weaposn are a machine gun, a pistol, sniper rifle, pulse rifle (mix of machine gum and sniper),a sword, and a minergun, which let you spawn and destroy blocks at your will. There are also a bike, which can carry two passangers, and a helicopter, which can carry four passangers, and even fire missiles. The other mechanics are simple you have a life bar, which replenishes if you took damage after what I recall should be seven seconds, you can sprint for a few seconds and then you lose stamina, and also you can do light parkour by bouncing off of walls, but only once.
I think that all of these mechanics go really well, and make for some really fun games. I remember when me and my friends would play, and have so much fun when we would have either murdermatch games, or play murder the flag with each other. I played for long enough until I was better than most of the people playing, since the game was for free on some site. (I just don't remember which) Eventually I had went onto the Murder Miners forums, and had gotten in contact with some of the 'pro' players, let's keep it short I got destroyed, because the gap between the good casuals like me, and the 'pros' is really big, which leads into my main criticism of the game, which is I hate to say myself, and I don't mean to sound offensive, but the game is dead! Okay I don't actually mean that it's completly dead, but it's really inactive. I tried playing today, and I only found a handful of servers, and even less that didn't kick me immediatly after I joined. I think that this game would be so fun if it had an active playerbase, which I think it cannot get, because nobody has yet realised how fun the game is with lots of people so they are dissuaded from playing the game.
In the end I really like this game, but think that with the state the community is in it's not nearly as fun as it can be, but it is a good price 2$ normally for a 4 pack, and 70 cents when it's on sale, so get some friends to play it like I have (11 not bragging or anything) and have some unfiltered fun.

SUMMARY: An atmospheric space exploration roguelike with multiple endings, involving exo=ploration, finding resources, building technologies, and making choices..  Simple controls make it easy to play, the resource management and many decisions make it a challenge.  Must-buy for space exploration roguelike fans.
Out There: Omega Edition puts you in the position of an astronaut whose normal shuttle flight and cryo-sleep doesn't go as planned, and a simple trip finds him in an unknown part of the galaxy, with a mysterious faster-than-light drive, and a signal calling him to a far star system.  You're in the unknown with limited cargo, and a vague idea of what's going on.
Simple point-and-click navigation lets you travel to various star systems and explore the planets therein.  However every choice costs valuable resources - fuel, oxygen, and hull integrety.  You've got to balance what you choose to do carefully to keep yourself alive.
As you explore, you'll encounter various worlds.  Some will have oxygen and life, letting you restock supplies and perhaps gain some insight or resources from the inhabitants (which also requires you to learn an alien language).  Others may be rich in minerals, providing elements you need to craft new gear.  Yet others are gas giants, providingr fuel for the journey.  Exploring may lead you to mysterious artifacts, ancient ruins, abandoned ships, black holes, random events, and more.  You're never quite sure what's around the corner - though the right equipment may help you avoid (or find) surprises.
Crafting and repairing equipment is a large part of the game.  One broken piece of technology -or one new device - may make the difference between life and death.  Some technologies radically change your ship's capabilities, and some can be paired to enhance their functions.  You might find yourself mining - or scavenging - just to try out something new.
You'll also find different spacecraft if you're fortunate, providing you even more options for exploration.  Some of them are wildly different and highly imaginative - and may or may not be what you're looking for in your travels.
On top of all of this there's an interesting plot with multiple possible endings for you to try and reach depending on your inclinations.  The entire package combines into a fascinating, engaging adventure - each move, each decision, requires some thought and planning.
The game also has excellent art design, though some of the planetary art is recycled or palette-swapped, so it can seem a bit "samey."  Alien design is exceptionally imaginative, and until you're used to all the species, you'll probably go "wow" at some of the creatures you encounter.
The music is quite good, setting the mood without being invasive.
There's few flaws in the game.  Some of the game flow and control options seem odd (can't we just ignore the space-travel filler?).  I've encountered occasional bugs.  Complaints aside, it's an extremely solid game - and quite replayable (you'll probably spend quite some time to get all endings).
This is one of the games I can definitely list as a must-buy for fans of space exploration and roguelikes.  It has the right mix of easy-to-play, compelling and challenging.  It can be enjoyed in short bursts or long sessions..  It's got everything you'd really want in such a game, so give it a try.

I originally found out about the sniper elite games when I saw Jacksepticeye do a video on sniper elite 3. Since I usually play either healer or sniper classes in other third person shooters and FPS and since I like old games as much as I like the new ones I decided to have a go at the first of the franchise. I wasn't too hopeful about it and expected crappy graphics and unrealistic game physics. I have to say this game pleasantly surprised me. It has amazing graphics for a game that came out in 2005 for XP and Vista (btw it can run on windows 7 and 8.1, that's what I have) and it's realistic making the player take into account factors like wind and gravity.
Here is a list on pros and cons:
+Realistic
+Good graphics for it's time
+Can run on some windows 7 and 8 computers
+It is all about the sneakiness but it gives you the ability to have a machine gun to survive firefights
+Has a kind of nostalgic feeling to it even for a guy who hasn't played any sort of sniper elite games like me
+Definite nostalgia for people who have played the other sniper elite games.
+Badass bullet cam shots
+MULTIPLAYER (Game caught me completely off guard with that)
+Good story
Cons:
-May not run on some windows 7 and 8 computers but forget about windows 10.
-The sneaking can be a bit weird sometimes (but only sometimes, don't take it too much into account)
-No knife/strangling. You must only use your silenced pistol on close range (Specifically, when your crosshair turns red) in order to get a guaranteed silenced kill. And if you run out of pistol ammo, forget about it.
-Some machineguns *AHEM* mg42 *AHEM* can sometimes be DEAD ACCURATE.
-Can't pick up traps unless it's TNT (Like, come on)
-Not all tanks have fuel tank caps, as far as I know.
Conclusion: A definite must for all sniper fans out there. 8.5/10

Dawn of War II brings a new perspective to the Warhammer 40k video game playing field, with massively upgraded graphics as compared to the original DoW that don't take too much of a toll on the system, and an innovative battle system that forces players out of their shells and makes them move about a lot, something which may be good or bad depending on player preference.
The Campaign and Multiplayer modes are both as would be expected from any RTS game. The Campaign has a fairly linear storyline that may get monotonous after a while, but is worth pushing through (especially for the cinematics). The Multiplayer, which encompasses both offline and online playing, is a great place to hone your skills. However, perhaps the most outstanding feature of DoW II is the Last Stand mode, which offers a DotA-like experience and allows you to customize your own hero and stand with other online players against increasing hordes/waves of mobs from different race types.
DoW II combines the best of many worlds whilst still retaining some features of the old DoW, and is definitely worth the price. Would give a 9/10.

This review is after about 90 hours of gameplay. I found this game via my explore queue. I am not tight with money but I do not tend to throw it at stuff before I reseach a little and see if I am wasting my cash. It is a casual style biz simulator with a rock theme.
There are a few new mechanisms like song creation and the production flow... but lets just say,,,
IMHO, A gem, a rough gem with some great facets, that still needs some facets revealed and a little polish to be a top ranking  casual indie game. However, it is very playable as is.... just a little weak but still under DEVELOPMENT.  Buy it now.. it's almost done, and I have a feeling the DEVS would really appreciate the love...!
Pros:
Decent Game mechanics like the Song to Album release production flow
Has a little bit of a head banger feel
Pausable/casual gameplay
Survival mechanic inherent with the ability to go broke
Basic trait system (that great guitarist may miss gigs due to habits)
Cons:
Most ingame events seem focused on early game play. Overly redundant with little mid-game impact (click)
Mid game is weak on content
Players band are basically paper dolls... no apparent life. Opportunity for passive animations for visual interest and novelty value (drum stick twirling, hand signs, guitar strumming, nose picking, whatever)
First visted venues seem to have little use for middle-game
No favor/disfavor system for clubs
No age progression leaving it possible to make it big at an unknown age
----------------------------
Mid Game play seems easist and workable if you just camp at a recording studio and crank out as many records you can of decent quality, touring only when required to meet the minimum of a contract. Camping.
At this point, for me, the game becomes quite repetitive with the only real thing breaking that game-flow being the album contract process. (contact/wait/sign/fulfll/wait/create/sales)
At this point I could comfortablly call it "Rock Biz Tycoon" but there really leaves little for me to feel like i am living the dream (or nightmare) beyond that. Early game I felt it. But now I do not feel like an aspiring God. Maybe it time to unlock star-studded rock god glitter outfits, pimp the bus, deal with groupies, due siginings and special shows,.... maybe I am still too early in the game progression but I have a feel that immersion and level of events are lacking... other than the ever present and self supposng ominous "we're watching .. keep in line" message I get alot and forever <click>
Needs:
More middle game events and tasks that interupt or even accelerate game progression.
events that trigger cancellations/loss or gain of a new band member/special condition to be met, etc....
Think: "record sales extended for a period if you do these three gigs... ", Band tries to recruit your drummer, or any number of drama events that affact bands in the process of trying to make it...
With a little time and Love, the Devs couls edd events that add to the feel of a real bands struggles...
"X Band claims copyright infringment haltinfg sales of album for 1 week"
"Groupie found dead of overdose in bus... bus held for investigation-miss gig"
"encore: audience calls for encore perfomance... fans and cash doubled and time at gig extended"
"Weather in North East causes ground vehicles to drive twice as slow and airplane have no access for two days"
Short. Logic puzzles. Sufficient for me.

First and foremost, this game does, to an extent, achieve the mysterious atmosphere of the type of puzzle game it seems to mimic. Also, there was some genuine satisfaction to be found in solving some of the puzzles in this game. There were also some moments where walking to the puzzles was mystifying and genuinely interesting, but I dont know if I can credit a game in which the walk to the puzzle is more visually stimulating and interesting than the puzzle itself.
With that out of the way...
Doors is the type of game that can only be enjoyed for perhaps a few hours. You can see that I have only put about an hour of time into this game myself. To be honest that was all the time I needed to run through this game. I didnt take my time, and could have slowed down to enjoy the scenery, but at some point I felt as though I had seen it all. There is not much substence in this game compared to "similer" games like Antichamber, The Stanley Parable, or Only If to a lesser extent. The game is quick to present itself as a sort of atmospheric puzzle game, but the puzzles stay relatively the same throughout; with little visual changes to stimulate the otherwise less-then-steller puzzles. The game could have used more drastic and visually appealing set peices if nothing else.
I also could complain about the way a story was "teased" at one point, but to be quite honest I only played through this game once, and may not have any legitimate grounds to critique the hidden or symbolic imagery in the game. With that said I  have no desire to replay the game to gain more information, so on that note I can only say there was not enough "meat to grab onto and enjoy."
Also, it should be said that this game has an affinity with the "bacon meme" (where as bacon is apparently the greatest thing in the universe). This is more of a nitpick, but the inclusion of achieving bacon as a goal seems childish, and overall takes me out of the fantasy of the game more than anything.
I can only truely recommend this game to someone who desperately wants to feel anything similer to Portal, The Stanley Parable, or Antichamber, but this is unfortunately not even close to achieveing the same levels of complexity and atmosphere as the aforementioned games. I wish I could enjoy this game more, considering I absolutely adore the atmospheric puzzle / walking simulator games. I love the feeling you get when walking through a surreal environment solving puzzles. It can be a great escape into the world of senselessness, but unfortunately, Doors misses the mark.

If you are familiar with The Binding of Isaac then this game will be familiar to you because it is one of those room by room shoot stuff at enemies while avoiding their attacks games.  This game is decent, with a good variety of weapons and power-ups.  You can obtain blueprints and there is an over world like in Rogue Legacy, where you can purchase weapons and items you have found the blueprints for at the beginning of a new game.  The money comes from rescuing townsfolk, randomly placed within the dungeons, who each add 500 coins to your total to spend on blueprint items and equipment.
I am torn on what to say about this game in regards to Recommend/Not recommended.
The game is fine, it plays well, and some of the features and ideas it lifts from other perma-death games work well in this combination, but I was left feeling like it was too slow.  Not that it ran slow or sluggish, but that your character was too slow to begin with.  There are items you can find that will increase your attack speed and movement speed, but they are largely randomly placed in chests and stores in the dungeon unless you find the blueprint.
So based on the amount of games in this genre, and the number of games I think do it better, specifically the Binding of Isaac, Enter the Gungeon and Nuclear Throne, I think I am going to have to give this game a not recommended.  If however you already own those games, and want another like those, then perhaps this one will still be fun for you, but again compared to those others I think this one moves too slow to stand toe-to-toe with those great games so I’d spend my money on them instead.

非常棒的游戏，解谜要素很多，而且不是最无聊的那种一房间都是差不多的拼图密码锁，每个谜题都不一样（有些非常有本系列特色，比如那个书架和望远镜）俺来讲讲理解和一些分析
【以下涉及剧透注意：3】
剧情和信息量也是相当大，虽然整个游戏都没几句话，但是故事和背景都渗透在各个细节里，稍微观察一下就能明白大概（当然人物太多了不太好记）这个故事的发生时间和Rusty lake hotel差不多（某一关的窗户看出去可以看到rusty lake hotel
里的客人，还有一关可以看到宾馆上的光柱，报纸上也有记载）人物除了乌鸦也都是第一次出场，算是从另外一关角度讲了rusty lake世界观下的故事。从“你”跟Rose的对话可以看出“你”应该是William，屋里也能看到William的画像，其中有一张和另一个人在一起，注明的是炼金术师兄弟，隐藏关结束后可以看到William嗑药（“elixir”）挂了，他的兄弟却变成了乌鸦（我早该发现他兄弟的声音和rusty lake hotel一开始乌鸦的讲述声音一样啊！！），还表示和mr.owl（即猫头鹰先生）认识，又挖了一个坑，估计要下一部填......
至于William是什么人，他是James他叔。叫William的隐藏关在家族树上的位置就在James的下方，树根的位置（这个家族悲剧的根源啊）William把和兄弟搞事造不死药（为什么是不死药我一会解释）的房子留给了James（坑侄子的辣鸡！）目的就是为了复活。William在磕了药之后就变成了活死人（在第一关的玻璃和浴室那一关的镜子上可以看到黑色人形的倒影），所以计划用侄子的整个家族为代价，收集祭品（就是那些身体部分）来重生。在staircase一关可以看到墙上写的药的效果是bring you eternal life or sudden death，William嗑了药，获得了eternal life——变成了活死人，侄子James也想试试，很不幸，他嗝儿屁了。

Not typically the type to review games on Steam, but I felt I needed to with this one. First of all, I too was one of the many who got this game from the Humble Bundle and it instantly ran into technical problems crashing on launch. The way I eventually found from Youtube on how to fix this was by unplugging my keyboard when launching the game. -.- Silly, I know.
I will put my main points about the game here:
POSITIVES____________
-Likeable Protagonist
-Improved Gameplay over the first Prototype
-Decent story
-Collectables are rewarding without being completely necessary
-SOME OF THE FUNNIEST DIALOGUE I'VE EVER HEARD IN A GAME,
don't get me wrong it isn't intentional. Some of it is just so ridiculous
I couldn't help but laugh.
NEGATIVES___________
-Short Story
-Dislikeable characters other than the protagonist and antagonist
-Cliche plot points
-Since this game is a sequel, you'd expect to have more transformations
than the first one, right? Wrong. Half the fun of the first Prototype
game was the excitement of getting your next new power to mess
around with! This game has... ONE new transformation, granted it
is an enjoyable one, but still.
Overall, this is just a more polished Prototype 1, with the main benefit
being that the collectibles are much more enjoyable to collect. The
gameplay is smoother and combat has gotten even more fun. And one
of my favorite improvements is the increase in enemy variety which is
very important to keep the game from getting repetitive. (I actually
never finished the first prototype because the enemies were always the
same, I think I stopped around 80% through)
TLDR: If you're going to play the Prototype series, just play this one. Don't
bother playing both unless you're an absolute completionist.

[This review is based on my many hours pre-Steam release in the alpha and beta versionns of HEX].
HEX is, in my opinion, the best digital TCG out there. That's right, that's a "T", not a "C". This is not like Hearthstone, Duelyst or Magic: Duels. Every card you collect has value as it can be traded with other players or sold on the auction house. This gives an immense sense of satisfaction as your collection grows in both size and value and you can spend as much time battling other players as you can "playing" the auction house market.
Both deckbuilding and actual card battling contain endless depth and strategy. Do not be put off if things seem daunting at first.
(If you're put off by the essential Pass Priority system, make sure you check out the control settings so that a single button press can skip phases for you if you want to.)
More in-depth description below, and some cons at the end.
HEX has two main components, PvP play and PvE play.
In PvP you can battle against other players (durr) in casual games or in a variety of tournament formats. The latter can be constructed (bring your own pre-made deck, complete with reserves to switch in/out in-between best-of rounds) or limited (draft play, where a group of players open packs together in a virtual circle and take turns selecting cards as the packs get passed around, then you build your deck from your picks; or sealed, where you open a bunch of packs at once and then build your deck from a large pool of cards).
There are a few different versions of the above, most notable Constructed/Sealed Gauntlet, which is an asynchronous play mode for those short on time (highly recommend Sealed Gauntlet -- open your pool, seek some advice from players either in-game or outside on the forums, and take as much time building your deck, and tweaking inbetween matches, as you like).
Granted, PvP can be considered to have a buy-in (i.e. you need to bring the packs and an entry fee yourself), but this is no different to real-world TCGs, but remember that once you start getting good at draft/sealed your winnings mean more packs as prizes and thus you can begin to go endless when combined with selling for profit on the auction house.
In PvE, there's currently the first part of the main Campaign. This will be split into many Adventure Zones (AZ), but at the moment there's on AZ1 (still a solid chunk offering many hours of FREE gameplay). PvE is COMPLETELY FREE. There are no exhaustion timers or other F2P crap like that, you can play as much as you like and as you do you'll pick up countless rewards in terms of PvE-specific cards, experience for your RPG-like character (levels up unlocking new abilities etc) and Gold. The latter can be used on the auction house to quickly fill out your collection (players sell common/uncommon cards for such little gold that you'll spend no time amassing a decent basic collection), or traded with other players (many many PvP need gold, myself included, so there's always high demand for it creating a beautiful connection between PvP and PvE-only players).
Other on the PvE side is the Frost Ring Arena, a dungeon of 4 tiers of increasing difficulty that grant you increasing rewards as you progress. A typical "full" arena run nets you about 6000-7000 gold, cards and equipment.
What's equipment, you say? Equipment is another PvE facet that lets you further customise your deck to the nth degree. Your character can wield up to 6 different types of equip (of thousands in the game to find and loot, of varying rarities of course) and each piece can alter cards in unique ways, from basic things like modifying the attack/defense of a card to completely changing the way cards work and almost making them "OP broken" (<<< somewhat of a joke, but there are some insanely powerful pieces of equipment to hunt for).
A few other bits: when you open a booster pack (which of course can be traded just like anything else), you not only get your cards, but it'll also spawn a chest. Chests come in different rarities with different loot tables, but typically contain a piece of equipment or a special alternate art version of cards. At the highest rarities you can find special card sleeves (something you can't trade, so sleeve your cards with pride).
Chests can also be spun (for gold -- that's why PvPers often want gold) on a slot-machine like altar for a chance at unique rewards too.
When you purchase a pack through the in-game store, there's a small chance at proc'ing a Primal Pack -- these contain ONLY rares and legendaries and are highly sought after. Either open them to vastly boost your collection, or sell them for ludicrous profit on the auction house.
And finally, a few cons to round this off:
1) Development of HEX has been much slower than anticipated. We're about to hit the 4th set (a perfect ime to start playing), but this has really taken longer than it should have done. Granted, a lot of systems are now in place that weren't before, so let's hope things speed up from her on out as new content on a timely schedule is critical to a TCG's success.
2) The client still needs some optimisation/settings to run well on lower machines. Expect some FPS drops in the PvE campaign if your system isn't up to spec. Hopefully this will get sorted in the future.
3) Perceived barrier to entry. I would like to see more done to welcome new payers, especially those wanting to only be F2P. The community (at least pre-Steam) is one of the best on the internet, so people are always there to help out, but the new player experience may miss off some key points to help people get into things quickly and easily and understand that this is NOT a pay-to-win game. The PvP aspects are pay-to-play (to a degree) like all the good physical TCGs.

Rating: 7.5/10
Genre: Third Person – Open World.
The Good:
+ Like its predecessor, traversing the world remains the finest aspect of Prototype 2. Running, gliding, jumping, wall running, are all incredibly fluid as you move around.
+ Graphically the game is a huge improvement over the first one and looks fantastic for an open world game. One reason for this is the game is split between 3 separate areas as opposed to one large area.
+ Completing main quests, side quests and collectables all reward you with experience to upgrade your abilities providing a good incentive co complete everything.
+ Cool super powers to wreak havoc on the world,
The Average:
+/- The story is well presented and has some interesting characters, yet every main mission devolves into “go here and kill this person”. The main character is your typical angry persona wanting to destroy everything, it works given the context of the game but also makes for a very forgettable story.
+/- I wish side missions were more varied.
+/- Combat is decent but requires very little skill or effort. I usually just hacked away at the enemy, jumped over them and hacked some more. The targeting system could use some work.
The Bad:
- If you have an AMD video card there is a very good chance you must make changes in your windows registry to get the game to work properly.
- The first prototype had challenges based around your super powers and movement, they were fun and challenging and provided a good incentive to continue playing the game. This game removed all challenges for what I can only assume was to meet a tight deadline. As of writing this I just discovered they packaged all the challenges into DLC.
Conclusion:
Other than the graphics I am not so sure this game really improves upon the first one. Still an enjoyable game and I had fun but didn’t do a whole lot to really add or improve the formula.

I want to like this game. I really do. However, in it's current state, I feel like this game just isn't suited for the market yet.
is a 2D platformer that revolves a protagonist on a quest to destroy a virus causing destruction inside the matrix. Seems simple enough, right?
Unfortunately, this is one of those, "Good idea, bad execution" moments.
I'll get some of the previously mentioned problems out of the way. Yes, the music is repetitive. Yes, Level 3 is
difficult for new players. Yes, fullscreen crashes the game. Yes, the door in Level 3 doesn't work.
Here are my criticisms that haven't been noted by other reviews yet.
Some of my favorite games are 2D plats, and while I appreciate the skill needed to beat some of the later levels, I feel like
just doesn't give the player enough experience to face a level as difficult as Level 3. The two previous levels I beat in two minutes combined, and Level 3 took another 16. The ramp up of difficulty is insane between Levels 2 and 3.
That ushers in a sad reality:
has 50 levels in its arsenal, and yet no one can even get past the first 3. What is interesting is that there are achievements for this game that involve passing milestone numbers of levels (10, 20, 30, etc.), and finding hats for the character. The achievements page for this game is a somber reminder of what this game could be.
Next are the controls. I've found that after starting up the game, the character begins walking to the left as if the player were holding down the A key immediately after the game started up. While this is a minor flaw, it still feels like an easy to fix yet really unprofessional bug in the game. Another thing I noticed is that the spikes in game are almost as tall as the character's jump height. While this wouldn't normally be a big issue, again, this problem really shouldn't follow immediately after two ridiculously easy levels, and Levels 1 and 2 at that.
This game was developed by Hixpix Studio and published by Dagestan Technology, two small time Russian video game companies. I understand that these companies are pretty tiny in terms of resources, but I would highly recommend hiring translators for their games. In
tutorial level, a talking computer explains the backstory of the game to the character. I'm a native English speaker, and while I could understand what was going on and my purpose in the game, the grammar was at times terribly broken and usually just awkwardly worded.
One of the biggest things that I have a problem with this game is even getting it to work. The first time I started it up, the tutorial passed and everything went fine. The second time I started up the game, the tutorial wouldn't start for minutes on end and I was wondering if the game had broken. Eventually it did start up, but I was right; the level select screen greets the player with a terrifyingly corrupted version of the original music. It's pretty unnerving, to say the least. According to a post on the forums for this game, there are several stages to this game's unresponsiveness when it comes to booting up, which seems to have affected reviewers in the past as well.
When it comes to positives, there isn't much to go for. I didn't find the music horribly annoying, but I can understand how it could be, especially considering how it restarts every time the player dies (which happens quite often). I do like the artstyle and the music, and I especially feel like the plot could be advanced and even delved into if the game could progress past the 3rd level.
Until these issues are fixed, I'd avoid buying this game altogether, even if it's 90% off, as that is how much I bought it for. There's simply too little content for this game to be worth buying.

Normal disclaimor about time played - I have been playing Hex since Alpha so many more hours than displayed.
I am a big fan of card based games and like many people, my gateway game was MtG.  I would attend local game stores to play in tournaments and play with friends for game nights.  Time went on and it became harder and harder to attend these kind of events with real life responsiblities.  I tried MtGO and only played about 6 months based on the quality of the client.  Hearthstone is fun as is Infinity Wars.  But no game scratched the itch left by MtG.  I eventually started playing more MMOs (SWTOR, WoW, & ESO).
One day at work I was talking with a fellow gaming friend and he told me about this new digital card game that was coming out that included RPG elements as well  as deep TCG mechanics called Hex.  My ears perked up and I instantly backed the game on Kickstarter.  The game has developed massivley since those early days and is incredibly polished.  The game has kept my interest the whole time due to the wonderful play mechanics (taking advantage of digital space constantly and always pushing the envelope) and the great size of each set that comes out.
Now that the totally free RPG element of the game has been released this is the best digital card game out on the market by far.  If I want a more relaxed play session compared to a draft or sealed deck tournament, I can launch my campaign character and play very enjoyable matches against the AI.  These include quick one on one battles or deep dungeon dives.  You can save your progress in any of these dungeons so if you need to get back to real life you can do so and pop back in when time allows.  It is also fun to start alternate characters and see how differently each race/class combo plays.  There is already hours of game play and the developers have tons of content in store to be released in the future.
You will find no better community in any game (developers and players).  There is always someone willing to help on the forums or on in game chat.  If you get a chance to attend GenCon or some other gaming convention and meet the staff you are in for a true delight.
Everytime I login is an enjoyable experience and I find new interactions with the cards with every game I play.  Do yourself a favor and give this game a try!

Sniper Elite is a fun stealth shooter, which involves some degree of skill and patience to get through its 28 levels (played over 8 missions).
In my opinion the game is worth the full price being asked of us by Rebellion, however the game regularly goes on sale so if you’re interested in it I would personally leave it in you wishlist and pick it up later. The reason why I think that it is worth its full price however, is that I have gotten approximately 20 odd hours of gameplay out of it throughout my time completing the campaign and replaying some of the more enjoyable levels. I expect that I’ll get another 10-20 through future replays.
Rather than presenting you with a wall of text, I’ll go through the main pros and cons of the game that I feel that are worth mentioning.
Pros:
- The levels are well designed. They are large (for a 2005 game), open-ended and promote stealth play.
- The ambiance and constant danger of being discovered and killed adds a thick layer of tension to the game, which is palpable throughout the campaign.
- The assassination missions that ask you to sneak into enemy strongholds and engage your targets from ranged and elevated positions are fun. They also ask you to engage in planning, surveillance and (sometimes) creative thinking to complete them.
- The sniping mechanics are fun and challenging, particularly on the highest difficulty.
- You are provided with a number of traps and explosive devices that are fun to use and necessary for ensuring your survival – you’ve got to cover your rear with traps if you want to survive the assassination missions once you go loud.
- Scrounging around for health and ammo from fallen enemies adds an almost survival game feel to the game that is welcome.
Cons:
- The game’s difficulty is inconsistently paced. Some levels are very easy, while others are very challenging. There is no gradual increase in difficulty throughout the campaign, just a patchwork of easy and hard missions throughout. This can be frustrating and I often found myself completing a few levels at a time and then putting the game down for a day or two.
- The story is a bit weak, but its adequate. It’s very barebones, yet functional – you get a bit of story-telling through the opening and closing videos and tiny snippets in the briefings and cut scenes shown throughout the campaign.
Mixed:
- The graphics are quite dated, but that’s more of a token statement as the game is now over a decade old. They certainly don’t detract from the experience, but there were a few times where I found myself imagining how updated visuals and lighting techniques would really help this old game.
Overall, Sniper Elite is an enjoyable experience with solid minute-to-minute gameplay. It is sometimes frustratingly difficult, but at other times that same difficulty adds a challenge that increases the feeling of achievement you feel at completing a mission. I really enjoyed the (overall) fantastic level design, the fun to use traps and the sniping mechanics. There are some really neat ideas in this game, which I wish would find their way into future instalments of the franchise.
Microsoft and Mojang married together and born this game.

A fun little game that plays just like Halo; it has a regenerating shield system, melee lunging (when you press the melee button while facing an enemy, your character jumps forward to hit them),  normal and sticky grenades, and vehicles. The destructibility of the maps lends a sense of wear and tear, as well as allowing for a bit of tactical burrowing or building if the server has destruction enabled. The weapons seem relatively balanced (except for the shotgun - that weapon is absolute crap), and the battle rifle hearkens back to Halo 2. Murder Miners offers the bare-bones multiplayer modes - Team Murdermatch (TDM), Murdermatch (DM), and Murder the Flag (CTF), as well as a very interesting Infection mode. In this mode, most players start out as normal characters, and they have to kill the randomly-chosen zombies. If killed by a zombie, players then join the zombie team. Zombies do not have any shields, but run faster than normal, have a one-hit-kill melee attack, and have a tentacle weapon that works like a grappling hook, pulling them towards surfaces and pulling players towards them. Whenever a player is killed by a zombie, their corpse remains on the ground for a limited time and can be "devoured" by zombies to gain permanent speed buffs, health buffs, and tentacle / digging upgrades.
Because this game works using a voxel-based building system (think Minecraft with smaller blocks), users are able to create their own maps from scratch, block by block, and host them on their own, personal servers. This feature makes it so that the amount of maps available is limited only by the time and creativity of the user base. Naturally, this also allows certain players to make trolly or just plain bad maps, but these are fortunately thin and far in between.

Murder Miners isn't perfect, of course. There are a few bugs, such as broken spawns on some maps (usually user-made maps, the official maps are pretty well put-together) and occasional glitches through vehicles or walls. In addition, the game can suddenly begin to stutter and lag whenever there is too much destruction or too many effects at one time, even with a good PC; this only lasts a few seconds, though, and although it is very irritating, it isn't extreme enough to cause you to, say, stutter off the map or into somebody's grenade.
TL;DR:
PROS
Plays like a Halo game
Completely destructible maps
Users can build their own maps in the map-editing mode
Infection mode is awesome
You can turn on zombies and infection during normal modes, creating a hybrid gamemode
Pretty balanced
Good community
Active developer
CONS
Some assorted glitches and bugs, including stuttering when too much is going on
Vanilla gamemodes can get old after a while
A lot of servers seem to have an issue with latency
Player population has gone down; there's still enough to get a decent-sized game going, but not enough to provide you with a choice of what server to play on
Overall, a very fun game with a very good price.

You occasionally meet alien life, but not much happens there either.  There is a sort of neat thing where, as the game progresses you learn words from the alien language, but in the end, nothing ever comes of it--you never learn enough words to understand the aliens speech or writting, and even if you ever did, from what I can tell, the only thing the aliens ever really have to say is that they would like an item and they will give you technology if you give it to them.
In short--Fun and relaxing for a couple of hours, but repetitive and dull beyond that.  Would maybe recommend for two bucks as a relaxing ap you play here and there while taking a dump or during commercials.

What can I say about Doors, what is one word that can best describe this game.  Ok, here it is…. RUN! That is it, just run, run away now, put you cash back in your pocket, close the store screen and never ever, ever get this game, even if it is free. Not even if your are paid to play it, just don’t. PUT THE MASTER CARD DOWN, STEP AWAY, AND NOBODY WILL GET HURT!!!!
Game Play
You are dropped into the middle of a dark eerie… somewhere. Follow the path to some doors and you must use you logic skills to choose the correct door to advance to the next level, or pick the wrong one and Die! Your motivation to continue, Bacon! No not Kevin, the other bacon, the juicy, crispy, melt in your mouth one (for the gamer gals, that will still be Kevin).  If you are Jewish, Muslim, Vegan or have a server reaction or fear of Miss Piggy, also walk away now.
Everything Else
The only shining lights for this game is the environment and the movement. The dark, black and white woods area is actually cool and a little creepy and should have been better utilised with some sort or engagement between player and environment, like creepy eyes peeking at you from underbrush or a silhouette stalking you from a distance. This alone could have even enhanced the whole game play. Movement is crisp and clean but is wasted on rails as you can not go more than two feet from the set track.
The puzzle element is down right useless, don’t bother trying to work the questions out at each door, just keep walking through till you get the right one. There is no consequences, you just start back at the beginning of that level and keep trying. There is only music at the menu screen, it’s ok, just. Zip in sound effects, just random tweeting birds here and there.
There is no story, no plot, no player engagement other than BACON!! So for a Logic Puzzler the only logic is, don’t buy it. The puzzle part, why did Calvin Weibel even bother releasing this as it is?
If you want bacon, then go to the shop and by it or, get Netflicks and go for a Kevin Bacon movie-thon (‘Now I gotta cut loose. Footloose, kick off your Sunday shoes!’), your money would be better spent than buying Doors (sing it with me ‘Please, Louise, pull me off of my knees’).

As others have stated, this game is lacking in content. How can you release a game to version 1.0 and still have intended features greyed out. This game is still early access, despite being "fully released".
Tycoon Aspect
-No control over where you live
You just get forced out of the first two places until you get your apartment. Would've liked to be able to pick a place to live and move out on my own earlier, instead of having to wait for the parents to kick me out. Multiple cities to actually live in would be a good feature, which brings me to my next point.
-Poor gig/rehearsal management
Being in a band forces you to manage your time wisely. The game gives you a 1 week timeline to set up gigs and rehearsals, making cashflow too easy as you can just kick it in a town and rehearse  on some days while playing gigs on the other days. I've never known a band to stay in a town for a month, playing at the same businesses. A calendar booking system would be better, as you could plan your tours in advance, trying to make the deadline with your crappy car/van. In addition to that, a penalty should be added if you play at the same venue more than 2 or 3 times in a row, with a cooldown timer of a couple of weeks. After a while, returning home would be a necessity.

Pros:
- Good time waster (while doing something else)

Cons:

A must buy for anyone who enjoys immersive storytelling adventure games.

Fun tycoon-style game where you form a band and try to transform yourselves from a bunch of flat-broke buskers struggling to pay the rent into multi-platinum-selling stadium-filling rock gods \m/
Create your avatar and choose your role within the band (guitar/bass/drums or vocals) - there are already a lot of customization options to choose from!
Along the way you'll have to build up your fan-base to unlock access to ever more lucrative venues, improve your playing / stage presence and song-writing skills, and manage your time & money to slowly climb the ladder to superstardom.
Spend your newfound wealth on stage props, promotional activities, vehicles, studio time, new instruments / clothes / tattoos but remember to keep enough for your rent and band wages!
Create your own songs/arrangements from a variety of preset riffs - steam workshop support planned - and sign record deals to release your creations as EPs/LPs/singles as well as taking your hits on tour.
There is an option to perform those songs by way of a rhythm minigame though thankfully this isn't compulsory as i am rubbish...
Currently there are lots of venues to unlock and play at across the country, with a few studios / record labels dotted around but much more is planned for the map.
On the subject of planned features, it would be well to note that this has just been released in Early Access.  As it stands the game is very playable and a lot of fun - but there is still a lot to be added, tweaked and balanced and the devs seem to be very open and welcome feedback & suggestions.  Their responsiveness and communication on the forums etc is a big credit to them and they deserve every success with what they are trying to achieve...
Possible cons - lack of content (being addressed, really looking forward to seeing this develop!)
- slightly grindy in terms of fanbase growth / skills... (personally i think it's in a good place right now - success shouldn't just appear overnight)
The game basics are fairly intuitive and there are some mouse-over tooltips but there's not much of a tutorial or wiki yet although I hear that work is ongoing.
In my game, which is around 12hrs so far IRL (very casual play with a fair amount of doing nothing), I've played just over a year of game-time, we've released 2 EPs/1 LP/and 2 singles, written about 30 songs the first 10 of which I'd rather be buried unheard, and have got my band up to roughly 50/100 skills.  We had a couple of months early on where we were frantically busking for cash as rent-day approached but now have around $100k tucked away so we don't need to worry about being thrown out of our apartment any more :D  We're still driving a beat-up station wagon around the country and playing to crowds of around 500.  About 25 venues have been unlocked so far with 50+ to go.  Nationwide our fanbase is approaching 20,000 and we're looking forward to releasing a new album soon :)  Drummer's ok, gets a lot of flak on the internet for being useless... My bassist (and main co-songwriter) is awesome, but my vocalist (whilst a decent enough front-man) is a kleptomaniac and if he steals $20 from my wallet again he'll be out!

I thought the puzzle solving was excellent in Rusty Lake: Hotel and I was excited about playing the second Steam release, Rusty Lake: Roots, which chronicles the lives of the Vanderbloom family over 3 generations. I had a feeling Rusty Lake: Roots would offer more in terms of gameplay length, but I didn’t think I would be blown away in terms of storytelling and characterization. I was completely wrong.
While Rusty Lake: Hotel was a strong puzzle game, the characters I encountered were rather lacking in personality for the most part. I didn’t feel for them at all and just moved from one puzzle to the next. Rusty Lake: Roots is a completely different game in this regard. Not only are there are more high-quality puzzles (you can expect 5+ hours of gameplay without using a walkthrough), I felt an emotional connection to some characters as horrible, bizarre stuff happened to them. I had a strong desire to progress the story, not only for the delightful variety of puzzles, but also to see what happened to the characters who over time demonstrated personalities (despite there being barely dialogue). Unlike the first game, the Vanderbloom family members are not props in a scene that experience ghastly deaths with little empathy from the player. I had an emotional investment in the storyline, and that’s a sign of an excellent point and click adventure game (or any video game, rather).
I’m so happy I played Rusty Lake: Roots and it’s become one of my favorite point and click adventure games (and I play a LOT of games in this genre). Beyond the solid storytelling and puzzles, which I’ve ranted enough about, I also thoroughly enjoyed the artwork, music soundtrack, and the ability to solve puzzle rooms in a non-linear fashion (given the multiple branches in the Vanderbloom family tree). EVERYTHING is top-notch, and I will remember the Vanderbloom family for years to come.
Especially Albert.

Another thing which bugged me was the screen resolution. The game's resolution is fixed to a boxed resolution which means that the game is in a sort of a 4:3 resolution whic kind of bugged me
Overall, A Wizard's Lizard is a good rogue-lite game to play in a few short bursts with it's cute visuals and good music

I've been playing Hex since Alpha, and played MTGO for years prior to that. With that frame of reference, I find Hex better in most ways to what MTGO brings to the table and wholeheartedly recommend the game. The great thing is, if you have even a passing interest, the PVE Campaign in Hex is completely free to play, so you can try it out with no investment. Technically you can grind enough to play the PVP side of the game without buying in as well, but it's a very long grind.
There are things MTGO does better:
Variety of formats - Hex is still limited to about four tournament formats that are supported in client and fire with any regularity. MTGO has more formats than I care to count and the player base to support them.
Depth of PVP play - Hex is about to release set 4, so currently has fewer than 1000 cards available for PVP, whereas MTGO draws from the entire history of Magic
Draft Interface - I love the draft interface in the new MTGO client, and the Hex draft interface, while serviceable, pales in comparison.
Everything else I feel is in Hex's favor, and much of these factors are so much better than MTGO that the comparison is laughable:
- Graphics and presentation of gameplay is much more engaging, the music is beautiful and lends itself well to the setting
- The overall UI is much easier to use (the one exception being the "chat" function, which is meh)
- There is meaningful PVE play that awards cards and gold which can be used to buy more cards in the Auction House
- There's an Auction House to easily buy and sell cards and other items
- The game makes fantastic use of the digital space with innovative gameplay that MTGO can never replicate while it is tied to the tabletop game
- The price is roughly half of what MTGO costs for similar events/tournaments/etc.
Note about price: yes, you are most likely going to need to invest to play PVP. This is the same with the direct competition which is MTGO, but the price to buy-in to Hex is roughly half what you pay in MTGO for similar experiences, and you are more likely to get a return on your investment that helps fund further activities. Just don't go in thinking "free to play" means you can easily grind the whole game; it applies mostly to the PVE play.

I simply cannot recommend this game enough. This game is a shining example of what multiplayer games should be. No annoying progression system, no dlc or microtransactions, no 12 year olds ♥♥♥♥ing your mother (usually), just fun in its purest form, and for only $2 as well! I can't say anything about the standard competitive gamemodes in this game, as I've basically never played them, but I can definitely speak for infection. Infection is one of the most craziest, chaotic, and fun gamemodes I've ever played. One person starts out as the infected and their objective is to kill all of the survivors. When a survivor is killed, they also become infected. This keeps going until there is only one person left fending off a horde of infected, and eventually they are killed and the game is over. There are settings you can mess around with as well if you're hosting, such as giving the survivors infinite ammo (I totally recommend doing this, as the grenade spam that ensues is hilarious). This game also comes with an in-game map editor that is extremely easy to use and allows you to publish to the steam workshop as well. The devs are very community-orientated and host community playdates every Wednesday, which are hectic and fun as hell! The main reason I haven't played in a while though is because I'm in college now, but believe if I had more time (and my friends had more time) I would be playing the hell out of this game!
Pros
-----
+ Infection is a god-tier gamemode
+ No progression system, so you can enjoy the full game from the start
+ No DLC or microtransactions (it's sad that this is a pro nowadays)
+ In-game map editor that can be used alone or with friends
+ AMAZING community-made maps
+ Awesome devs who clearly care about the game and the community
+ Other gamemodes such as TDM and CTF (which are still great and use community maps, I just prefer infection)
+ The goddamn hookshot makes the game a lot more fun that it already was
+ It's only 2 ♥♥♥♥ing dollars
Cons
-----
- There are none. It's offensive that you even think there would be.
Overall score: 11/10 (God-tier perfection)
Seriously, do yourself a favor and buy the 4 pack, get 3 of your best friends, and have the time of your life.

This is an interesting little game.
I picked up A Wizard's Lizard because I wanted to try out Binding of Isaac-style gameplay but couldn't stand Isaac's art style at all. Way, way too gross for me. And I think I've gotten my money's worth so far. Full disclosure: I haven't beaten it.
Now, the myriad of reviews telling you that this game is simplistic and not nearly random enough to hold long-term appeal... they aren't wrong. The items don't have as much ridiculous variance as in Isaac, there's not nearly enough item interactivity, and almost none of them have Isaac's insane "what's an upper bound?" appeal. The level design is far less complex than Isaac's and much more predictable. The enemies are perfectly solid, but a lot of them behave very similarly and overall none of them feel standout.
So there's the bad points. That being said, I'd still recommend you try out A Wizard's Lizard, and here's why.
First off, it's ten dollars now. It started at fifteen, which was a touch high, and I don't blame people who paid that much feeling a little shortchanged. But ten is a perfectly tolerable price for the amount of gameplay you've got in this game.
As for that gameplay... I may not have played Isaac, but I like it better purely on the face of it. The game is plenty hard--as said, I still haven't beaten it--but it never feels like it HATES you. It never wants to kick you while you're down, or feels that's necessary. You have more health, the room layouts are more forgiving... It's still not just going to roll over and die, but it's not hateful.
And it IS fun, at least fun enough that I'm still coming back and trying again after ten hours of making it to the Crypt once. It's engaging enough and challenging enough that you feel tested, and I'm STILL unlocking things. If you've been playing Binding of Isaac all these years it may not be nearly as challenging for you, but I couldn't say. And despite the cutsier art style, the story--once you learn it--is actually pretty bloody dark!
So, is this game worth buying? I think so. It's not at the TOP of my list, but if you're looking for Binding of Isaac gameplay without having to deal with updates that make the game less fun and a thematic style that's trying too hard, this might be exactly what you're looking for.

Heroes III is generally known as the most successful title of the series and might be the best turn-based strategy title as well. And why it shouldn't be - everything works like clockworks from rpg -elements to the unit balances. Among campaing there is a couple dozens mini scenarios which can be played with either AI or another player.
For those few who are completly new with Heroes of Might and Magic here is some summary about the formula of the series. You start on some random map with a hero and a castle of your chosen faction. With your hero you go adventuring into world which is filled with artifacts, treasure and resources with which you are able to build structures and hire new units from your castle to fight creatures lurking on the map or another competing factions. Your hero also gathers experience with various ways to upgrade his/her skills and attributes going from being a novice to ultimate master of Might and/or Magic. The scenarios are usually won by defeating other factions, some boss hero or gathering x amount of resources.
All these core elements are flawless in Heroes 3 and this HD version that also gives a slight graphical face lift for it. Excluding a couple very random bugs - everything works without problems on my Windows 10.
However after all this years we could wait some wrapping up of this remastered title, but this is the where it let's people down. It doesn't include expansions The Shadow of Death or Armageddon's Blade which multiplied gameplay time, indroduced new units among brand new elemental-based faction 'Conflux' which is favorated by many players.
I myself could actually turn a blind eye for this neglect but I understand that when there is a steak available the minced meat is going to be hard to swallow. Heroes 3 is available in other cloud stores in a version where expansions are included. They don't have HD on them but I surely would spend my dollar into some significant features instead of graphical details which I usually forget while playing this classic.
In conclusion Heroes 3 HD is solid, mighty and magical turn-based strategy experience and could be recommented even in its normal price if it wouldn't enjoy reputation of missed opportunity. Definitely worth it with a minor price tag though. If Heroes 3 HD should (I've odd feeling it will) have expansions included in the future I hope that for the sake of fairness they could be purchased as free dlc.

- Overall the best online TCG on the market! Play and sacrifice your sleep :)
HEX is maybe best compared to Magic Online. You collect virtual Cards that have real trade Value (in contrast to e.g. Heartstone, were you can't trade your Cards), hence the namen
Card Game. If you never played a TCG and want to find out if it is a Genre you like, stop reading this review and start playing, it's free! After that come back and read the rest of the review ;)
For those of you who already are familiar with TCGs, here are the things that make HEX different from other (online) TCGs:
- It has a fair F2P model (more info later)
- It is purely digital, which means it can use mechanics that are only possible in a digital TCG!
- It has PvE Content!
The F2P Model:
Since this is a "real" TCG you can buy digital boosterpacks to get new cards. One Boosterpack has 15 Cards and costs 2$ (200 Platinum). Compared to real boosterpacks this is a good deal! How can one now earn Boosterpacks for free to play? Playing PvE! When you are playing one of the 2 PvE Modes (Campaign or Arena) you will earn Gold, the F2P Currency.

But how do you get from Gold to Platinum to Boosterpacks? There are huge goldsinks in this game that earn vanity Items like cardsleeves or alternate art cards. So players want to buy your gold to throw it into the sink (literally, the goldsink is a sink :P). The exchange rate at this point is about
. When you are new you can earn about 6500 gold per hour.
---> 55 platin/hour and to reach the magical 700 platin you will need about 13 hours. That is about the time that the PvE content alone would satisfy you, maybe you will spend even more time in PvE alone, when creating different campaign characters (The HEX community is awesome and might give you a little kickstart btw :D).
Why is 700 platin such a magical number? That is the amount you need to play draft! (3 booster packs + 100p)
To explain draft would go into to much detail here, if you are curious, read a guide about drafting. The important point is, from this moment on, you can earn Platinum (if you are good enough). Everyone is keeping the Cards they drafted. 3rd and 4th place earn 2 boosterpacks, 2nd place 3 and 1st place will earn 5 boosterpacks!
Even if you loose your draft, since you hopefully drafted cards that are worth something, you can sell them and only have to earn about 200-300 new platin playing PvE.
Now to some Pro & Cons about Hex:
Cons:
-Kind of slow devolpment of new content (To be fair, they had to finetune the whole game engine ect. first, so there is hope that it will speed up now)
-Some UI Elements feel a bit clunky (chat, auction house, card collection)
Pros:
- Awesome Community!!!
- Super F2P model for a TCG
- PvE content
- Nice carddesigns and fun mechanics!
To sum it up: Give it a try! :D

So, what to say about Hex?
I first learnt about Hex from the Penny Arcade comic linking to the enormously successful Kickstarter campaign. Every part of the promise in the Kickstarter excited me - a Magic the Gathering like game I could play on my computer, designed for online play from the ground up, with robust PvP, drafts, sealed tournaments, constructed - all for a fraction of the price of Magic. Great, sign me up! But wait, there's more! A fully fledged RPG, exploring an open world, levelling up your character, unlocking new traits, working together with friends to take down raid bosses, a full guild system, and tons of cards and equipment to collect. Okay, that sounds amazing. And I won't lie - a big part of what excited me was being a part of such a great game right from the start. I'm sure many people have wished they could have played Magic from the days of Alpha and just had boxes of Moxes and Lotuses. And here was my chance with Hex!
So, has Hex delivered on those promises? Well, partially. The game itself is awesome, and every bit as fun as they made it out to be (I wouldn't have played at least a full draft tournament every week since they were launched back in 2014 if it wasn't!). PvP is great - it's a really fun draft, sealed and costructed format, and everyone is looking forwards to the release of the new set, Primal Dawn, next week.
Now, the PvE side of things has been lagging behind. But this year we're finally starting to be rewarded for our patience, as they added the first major update to campaign. Granted, this is far behind the original release schedule (the very first release date speculation of "hopefully full release by end of the year" given during the 2013 Kickstarter now seems laughable in hindsight). But the promises are now starting to be made good on, and campaign is everything we hoped for - a great single player experience, with fun levelling, dungeons, character creation, equipment and more. THis is a great time to pick Hex up, as it finally starts to become the game it was meant to be - both TCG and RPG.
There is still a lot more to come. The promised multiplayer raids are yet to materialise, in game guild support is still missing, and currently only three of the six final classes have been added, with one more promised with the launch of Adventure Zone 2. Hex isn't yet in its completed state, but what we do have certainly won't disappoint. Campaign is a lot of fun, the Frost Ring Arena is a nice challenge, and, of course there's the PvP side of things, which is basically feature complete. Now is a great time to jump into Hex - you get all the benefits of an amazingly fun TCG on the PvP side, and get to be in at the start of Hex's journey to also being an amazing MMORPG.

Ehhh, I know this trilogy (I'm putting a review here for all 3 games, as you can't really play one and not play the other two, hero project and herofall) are popular titles among the COG community, but for me, I can only give it a 5/10 at best.
One of my biggest pet peeves in COG games, is when it gives what I like to call, "The illusion of choice" where, you're kind of choosing arbitrary thoughts, but overall, you're forced into the same thing no matter what you did really. You'll be asked "What do you think of X" then immediately it'll turn around and say "You're CLEARLY thinking this!" I'm sorry, I forgot when the narrator became of a reader of my mind. I much prefer when the story is written in a way where the world develops around me, and my choices impact the way the story unfolds. Not when the narrator overtly tells me what I am thinking, whilst thrusting plot in my face after saying that. It seems like the narrator has a story to tell, and doesn't want you, the player, steering that of course, which in my opinion, should not be how a CYOA game plays out.
Overall, there are very few choices that actually impact anything. Usually it'll be a thought, you'll answer it, followed by a ominous/scolding/reassuring etc. sentence from the narrator responding to your thought, impacting absolutely nothing.
The story itself goes from upswings, to very low swings, where the story just loses interest for me. Some of the characters are well written, like Prodigal and Victon. Others are just shallow and really really bland, like Black Magic, who gets a interesting plotpoint in this book, then proceeds to just be the least interesting person in the entire world in the next two, only really getting a redeeming scene RIGHT AT THE END of episode 3, when the story is basically finished, and there is no room to expand on it.
For me, this game was really only one I came back to play as I am an avid supporter of COG's, even when some of their games completely bomb, and with this one being a highpoint in some peoples eyes, I thought I should give it a genuine playthrough before casting it off. However, I really can't give it anymore than a 5/10. It has some interesting upswings, some good ideas, it's fun having superpowers of course, but those are equally met with downswings and just lacklustre things. I'd say pick this one up if you really love superheroes, but if you've played titles like Choice of Robots, VERSUS, Samurai of Hyuga, or anything along those lines, you may be slightly dissapointed.

I wanted so badly to dive into the world of Gothic.  I had heard so many good things.  As with most stories, I thought it would be best to start at the beginning.  While I am certain that there is a fantastic journey hidden somewhere within this game, it requires far too much effort to render it accessable.  Please friend, if you have the time, listen to my story and heed its warnings.
Upon first launch I encountered the "Access Violation" error.  Not to worry, this was not my first rodeo.  After a short google search, I was able to bypass this issue on only my third tweaking attempt.  After messing with the default resolution to find a "decent enough for now" setting (there are not really any good, modern options in the game without patching/modding), I was finally ready to play.
Nope, wrong!  The controls are awful, I'd better remap that straightaway.  This took some time, as the UI is not fantastic.  Even after remapping the keys to make things feel more familiar, there was a decent amount of google time to figure out things like: how to pick up items, open a chest, take items from said chest, how to equip a weapon, why does strafing suddenly not work when I am attacking and need it the most--the list is practically endless as (even after remapping keys) the controls to do these actions will be different from what you are used to.
At this point, I am making some progress so I decide to go all in and install the suggested patches to improve the overall experience.  Google redirects me to WoldofGothic, a website that would make Geocities and Angelfire proud.  I bet the homepage looks beautiful in Netscape, but despite the dated website ambiance, it was relatively easy to download the necessary files to patch the game.
Installing them was another matter.  Upon launching the offical patch installer (this patch is required before the installation of the player kit, or other mods/community patches), I was prompted with a question inquiring if I would like to have the installer search for the Gothic.exe file.  Being naive, I selected yes--BIG MISTAKE.  30 minutes later, the search was only 30% completed so I decided to cancel.  Much to my dismay, the computer feigned ignorance of this request, so I tried again--"cancel".  Nope, this patch installer was dedicated and cared little for my human desires, so I was forced to right-click and close application.  This was an annoying waste of time, but no matter, at least I could relaunch the installer and try again.
Now, the installer is saying it does not have adequate permissions to install on my computer.  I restarted the computer, but no dice.  I tried running as admin, but the computer laughed at my meager attempts to outsmart it.  I was lost.
At this point, I knew 2 things.  First, that I could and would eventually get past this step, install the Official Patch, and then be able to install the Player Kit, the System Pack, and subsequently any other mods/patches required to render this game playable.  Second, I knew that being over an hour and a half into troubleshooting at this point with no end in sight, that it was simply not worth it.  While it can be true in life that "with great patience comes great reward", this law of life is best employed in the real world.  The virtual world exists as a realm where these laws should not apply.
Just dont buy it.

Gothic is an average action-RPG from 2001. It has certainly aged in its time and not so well in the parts that most affect the player. I'd like to keep my review here down to earth for expectations, as I feel this game attracted a lot of critics that didn't give it a chance beyond 15 min, and a lot of fans behaving as attack dogs defending it to the letter as the best RPG ever. I'll present my honest story, as I perceived it, without nostalgia glasses. The graphics are what you might expect from the Deus Ex, Tomb Raider, Thief, and Neverwinter Nights time period. They didn't bother me, I've learned to be at peace with old-school. There's not much to speak of for sounds, ambience, or soundtrack. It's rather sparse and you'll get used to, or ignore the same overworld soundtrack playing on repeat. The music in the mines, or underground I liked.
The best feature is probably the storyline, which picks up around chapter 3 (chapter 1 is a tedious trial due to an unrelated reason explained later). Also, there is the characterization of three factions in the game. These factions each have their own cultural behavior, ambitions, and voice acting (protagonist is quite good). Unfortunately, these characteristics are only on the surface as once you've spoken to one generic guy, you've spoken to everyone in the camp. Literally so because they share identical lines and actors. Only the select few "named" NPCs have any dialogue of variation.
Now to the core of what you expect from an RPG (plot and dialogue aside), where it's critics are loudest. The control/combat schema and gameplay. I'll tell you now up front, this game will require grinding. If you have played the Witcher 1, or Mount and Blade, you will find this schema familiar. The controls (keyboard only) are not terrible as many detractors claim. I learned fairly quickly and tolerated them. However, they are still the game's most notable flaw. I'll explain. The character is moved with the keyboard arrow keys. Hold CTRL key activates "action" (interactable or combat direction). Spacebar unsheathes/sheathes your weapon. At combat start, you would need to press spacebar, then CTRL + up, left, or right for an attack swing type. These attacks can later be combo chained. However, if you want to MOVE during combat, you need to release CTRL. Strafing is done by assigning another key such as DEL, PGDN, Q, or E. You cannot move and attack at the same time in this game (because shared by CTRL) which is what most people will not like. If you wish to dodge, or move during combat, you need to release CTRL and keyboard turn, hop a step back, or use strafe keys to circle the opponent at a dangerous range. This applies to if your target moves too. Then you must readjust your char facing direction, as there is no camera lock-on that I found. Any game with a schema like this I prefer to play with a gamepad either way on the PC (
). Resultantly, it is very cumbersome in combat and will require a lot of patience and quick-saving in this arduous journey through Chapter 1. People claim this game is "difficult." I disagree entirely. The only sign of difficulty comes from the cumbersome control schema arbitrarily. As you may expect, combat boils down to individually pulling and "tanking" through chapter 1 and 2. You'll need the opponent to line-up for you, and to get a good pre-emptive strike and combo attack before it does the same to you. Other than stepping backwards, attempting to dodge or any maneuver is a frusterating key combination that all the while you are attacked anyways. I resorted to outright tanking everything the whole game. Each battle is followed by spamming healing consumables afterwards. This is not the Dark Souls or Witcher battle experience i've seen claimed. I digress though, the timespan difference in those games is many years from 2001.
That battle/schema didn't bother me so much. Tanking everything and bypassing all the maneuvers, sidestepping and other means of avoiding being hit I learned to live with. Each attempt to incorporate those just decreased the chance of survival and I found to be less efficient. The true problem of this game rides on the back of all this combat. Once you've fought one, you've fought them ALL. The combat is the same exact approach the entirety of the game for every creature or NPC you encounter, until you're well superior. Pair this with a need to grind at the games start puts this to a level of boredom and busywork. Why the grinding? It's not typically a problem for myself. I expect it in all RPGs. This time though, you may feel compelled to clear the entire overworld of creatures that you can undertake, scouring them all, begging for experience. You'll need all the exp to increase your favored attribute, in my case strength, and your hitpoints upon each level up. This is to offset the lack of gear in Ch1-2. That is because your defensive capability is restricted heavily from obtaining better equipment (discussed below).
The game has an inverse difficulty curve. It will be most taxing at the start. By the time I hit chapter 4, i could pretty much tank everything with reckless disregard and two shot it all thanks to stacking strength and my armor rating. Remember that chapter 1 and 2 will be very trying on your patience as you scour the entire colony for anything to give exp (for an edge up). This includes the introductory quests for 3 factions. In hindsight, you may be better off advancing the plot earlier to CH 2 just to unlock the availability of weapons and armors
Better equipment is issued at the start of each chapter and is bought from few select individuals. In order to afford them, I recommend acquiring the skinning/animal harvesting skills ASAP. Alternatively you can rob entire camps of their currency (another chore thanks to the lockpick schema(QuickSave/QuickLoad... It is nothing but pure guesswork key combination))). Weapons and armors, to include rings or amulets are bought and rarely found.
Expect to always find what you seek at the same couple vendors selling rings, amulets, armor and weapons. The equipment offered will not change until you enter a new chapter. As I said above, this means you'll have a nonexistent defense rating in chapter 1 and you'll feel frusterated that everything including the turkies will have the upper hand on you. By the time chapter 4, or even 3, that equation will reverse with you the king of the mountain. Before the completion of Chapter 2, I had persisted to kill every every creature in the colony to include, the alledged difficult orcs and skeletons. Respawning only occurs at certain chapters like 2 and 4
Something I don't feel mentioned is the capability to break the main questline. There are a few instances items can be vendored, or consumed. In that case, you'd have to hope for a prior GameSave... or restart the game =/
I can "only just" recommend this game. Mostly the game is often boring busywork like the grinding/combat, but I did enjoy the story and found it redeeming. I feel the devs wanted you to stick to the main quest (hinted by the overall course of story sending you everywhere), but the control/combat schema I discussed above delays the player's capacity to acheive those goals. With very little else to do than the main quest, grinding creatures for the sake of character advancement will occupy half your time (~25-30Hrs FinalGameSave). Exploration will reward too often healing consumables, or inferior goods. This is a game you should play after exhausting all other RPGs of renown or to your interest.
I bear in mind the date of release, but review that against my feelings today. After all, we do not live in 2001 now. Yet despite my remarks, I plan to give Gothic 2 and Risen a chance

If you're looking for incredibly zealous outcries to inspire your daily actions, then this is the game for you. Dawn of War II is the sequel to the original Dawn of War and all its expansions and it delivers in spades.
For starters, this game is built on the rich lore and backstory of the Warhammer universe. After their disasterous defeat on Kaurava, the Blood Ravens are down to but a single star sytem from where to recruit their new members to fight in the Holy Emperor's name. One problem; the Tyrannids are coming and they have an appetite for planets and everything that lives on it. You control the Force Commander. A nameless, and voiceless avatar who leads a small taskforce from planet to planet to stop the Hive Fleet before it devours the precious planets of the aurelia system.
Contrary to the original Dawn of War, this game is focussed on tactics rather than strategy and plays out on a much smaller scale. Instead of base building and massing armies you control up to four units, each with their own abilities and weapons. The game also introduces an RPG element that allows you to customise your squads with new armour, weapons and other items to smite the enemies of man.
It is therefore such a shame that there is only one campaign to play. This game offers four different races to play as, but does not allow you to play them in the same narrative context as the space marines. That said, this game's campaign is no slouch. It is a fully realised story with stellar voice acting accross the board. If brawny men with zealous convictions are not your thing, then you better pass on this pack of awesomeness. Unfortunately for you, there are no other reasons to not get it, so what are you waiting for?
