The game itself is fun - a superhero-themed text RPG with choices that shape your hero. You can be a paragon who believes in justice, redemption, and no killing, a renegade who doesn't play by the rules, an attention seeker who always has time for the press, or a combination of any (The game penalizes you if you can't stay true to your ideals, so hopping around from anti-hero to paragon back to anti-hero will have negative effects. This applies to the trilogy as a whole). This game is a decent start to the trilogy, but unfortunately it has it's share of weaknesses.
For example, when infiltrating a club, the three options you are given will always have the same result. Even if you try to run in guns blazing, it will always end with you being hypnotized by a villain. You can play along with her and gain a MacGuffin...that shortens out when you try to use it in the same scene. I haven't attacked her, but I assume it still ends in a failure. Also, for the character "Jury", there isn't really an option to treat him kindly. Punching him in the face is a reoccuring gag and while it's kind of fun (He's a huge♥♥♥♥♥ ) it clashes if you're trying to go for the paragon archetype.
You'll always fail your first case, no matter what. You'll also be viewed as a failure by everyone even if you've proven your skill time after time. Even if you've shown your dedication to upholding the law, the most you'll get out of it is a police buddy who'll help you. The rest of the police view you as a criminal.
But the biggest issue is the forced romance. A character, Black Magic, has an obvious crush on you, and the game doesn't hold back describing how much you want to ♥♥♥♥ them (Their gender is determined by your sexual preference and gender). If you return their feelings, then the romance is sweet and sexy. If you just want to be friends, then the game will still try and force it on you anyway with an awkward scene where Black Magic fakes being in danger so they can ♥♥♥♥ you. Not returning Black Magic's feelings typically destroys any relationship they have with you, so it's either ♥♥♥♥ them and have them obsess over you, keeping your relationship solid, or remain single and have them dislike you. No middle ground here.
Overall, game is fun, but the shoehorning is annoying and so is the linear storyline. Don't worry, the two games that follow are, without a doubt, in my top ten for my favorite pieces of interactive fiction. I recommend it if you really like CYOA games or if you want to get an understanding of the HR universe before hopping into any of the sequels.

As someone who has struggled in recent times to find enjoyment in modern Yu-Gi-Oh! against anyone but close friends, I'm deeply appreciative of Duel Links.
Modern YGO is hardly enjoyable at anything but a casual level, as it's in a sort of coin flip meta right now. Combo memorization, stuns and lockdown are all you pretty much get, and this particular version of the game cuts most of that out. Featuring a 3 zone wide playing field and a cherry picked card pool, Duel Links tidies up the power creep that Konami plagued the game with over the years and reverts it back to a game with very base level strategies and a surprising amount of depth. Staple cards like Mirror Force, Trap Hole, Mystical Space Typhoon, Veiler, and Dark Hole are all absent in favor of more interesting and situational cards such as Enemy Controller, Impenetrable Attack, and Sphere Kuriboh. Many of the game's powerful archetypes are present, though usually without some of their most powerful cards, leading to more interesting deckbuilding. Draw power and searchers are also heavily limited, which makes a lot more decks viable. Turns don't take 10 minutes, games actually last past turn 3 (save for a few OTK's), and there really is beauty in how basic some of the cards are.
Card collection is a bit tricky but tbh enjoyable. I'd recommend getting a deck idea in mind before starting to buy packs. Slowly building up your collection again for the first time feels really good, and knowing there's still work to be done before your deck is finished really helps to keep that TCG feel of things.
In addition to the (imo) improved card pool, there are also different characters to unlock and play as, all with varied and unique traits. Generally, these are unlocked by leveling up the characters through normal gameplay, but you can also obtain ones unavailable through levelups via drops. These traits range from simple effects like starting with a specific field spell active all the way to starting with all 3 elemental gods (Sanga of the Thunder, Kazejin, Suijin), 500 LP and just the mighty Gate Guardian in your hand. Characters and their traits are entirely unlocked through gameplay, which is honestly surprising and welcome in this DLC filled day and age.
If you're interested in ranked, which is personally a big draw of this game, there are a few top tier decks, though the variety there should be enough to keep things interesting.
TL;DR definitely recommended. Has an interesting progression system, packs from the card shop are a bit overpriced when paying with $$$ imo, and there's plenty deckbuilding to be done. Pretty fun.

This game is just about an exercise in futility. Is it impossible to win, no, but the chances are extremely slim and rely on both planning and lots of luck. But something about this extreme difficulty is what really makes this game have charm. You play an astronaut who has been out for who knows how long, as far as we know Earth and humanity may be wiped out and you may be the last of your kind. The ominous fear adds to the basic principal of what ha made humanity humanity. We have always struggled against the impossible when there was no hope, in examples like the ice age, the black plague, and global warfare, even in the bleakest of times we continue on and that is the reason we still exist today. Hmmm.... Tough one to pin down. I paid about a dollar for this when it was on sale, so I feel like I got my money's worth, but  here's the breakdown because I'm a little on the fence:
Pros:
+ Tough but doable logic puzzles, of the truth-table variety. Think of the typical "one person always lies and the other tells the truth" scenarios but with more people and more conditional statements. And the people are doors.
Neutral:
~ It tried to have a story, which made the game have a point, which was cool. Through the first few logic puzzles my thought was "Why on earth did someone make a 3D video game out of a concept that could be a text game?" but then the story kicked in and I was drawn in, waiting for more. But then there's no more story except for a few lines after the credits. I felt a little cheated.
~ Bacon. Don't get me wrong, I love bacon, but to put it in a game as your choices are "bacon or death" gets tired after a while and seems like pandering. "Life or death" is a much more fitting scenario, especially because the iota of story is circling around the idea that people are beginning to suspect that the simulation isn't real. Well, duh, because you're offering bacon or death. That's not what happens in real life.
Cons:
- This was a con for me, but others might not mind so much. As stated before, it was a 3D game despite the fact that all you're doing is reading messages on the ground or above doors and then stepping through. You frequently have to do a bit of walking before you reach the doors, so it's basically a walking simulator on top of a logic puzzle, though for no purpose. You can't go outside the path and, despite being a game where death is a constant threat, you can't actually fall off of any of the areas before/around the doors.
- This relates to above, but you can't see the text on more than one door at a time, which meant walking back and forth between doors whenever you needed to reread or double check your conclusions. I was only playing for a total of 3 hours (including 80% of that time was me making notes on pencil and paper, or making elaborate flow charts or truth tables), but I got a little nauseated from the back and forth (not playing on VR, just normal computer.) This back and forth would have made the final puzzle with 30 doors nearly impossible had I not taken the initiative and WRITTEN DOWN ALL 30 CLUES ON PAPER SO I COULD LOOK AT THEM ALL AT ONCE WITHOUT WALKING. For a game that required me to use about 4 or 5 pieces of paper front and back for all my notes for various puzzles, it's not super well suited to a video game format, at least not without some built-in system so you can make your notes in the actual game.
Overall: I'm right on the fence. 5/10. I got my dollar's worth from this game, but even at a regular price of $3.99, I wouldn't recommend buying at full price. But if you like logic puzzles, and it's on sale...it's probably worth it.

Warning: This review contains spoilers.
This game, which started out as a fairly basic (if awkawrdly-worded) series of logic puzzles, seemd to hit its "something more beneath the surface" stride when you suddenly find yourself in a labyrinthine office building reminiscent of the setting of The Stanley Parable, full of tantalizing hitns about "reeducation" and a mysterious "director." But no sooner had I thought this than I was sucked back into the increasingly time-consuming simulated world of the riddle doors, which took the game through to its bizarrely nonsensical and rushed conclusion.
It really feels as if two or three interesting game premises got into a head-on collision here, and lost their better aspects in the resulting mess. The final product is a game that goes nowhere, is bizarrely paced, and whose humor seems to consist of the concept of bacon, as though this were 2010 and we were all adolescents with ~lol so random~ senses of humor. I think replaying The Stanley Parable would have been a better use of my time.

An amazing game - particularly if you are - or ever have been - a musician. But that is definitely NOT a requirement.
Create your avatar. Hire musicians. Write songs (Either have the game simulate them, or write your own music with the built in music creator). Rehearse, record, get record contracts, play gigs... go broke... (Damn you responsibilities!)
This game offers more content in Early Access than many full releases - and more is added regularly. Bug fixes are applied often in real time. IE: I mention a bug to Seabass (the developer), and he usually makes a hotfix within an hour or two of ready my post. (The conversations that I - and others - have had with him are publically viewably in the forums, btw).
Even when I do something stupid and mess my game up, he tries to help me fix it. But as its in EA, I generally have no problem starting over. Rock God Tycoon is not repeitive (to me, at least). There is no road to follow. No script. Create and treat your band anyway you want. They might not like and they might leave - but screw those guys (and gals).
I have no association with the devs - except for being absolutely head over heels in love with this beautiful game. A game that gets better with every passing week.
Rock God Tycoon represents everything that is good about Greenlight and Early Access. If you're interested but have been burned by EA games before - at least click the follow button. This is something very, very special. I have put in about 35 hours and I cannot see myself getting bored anytime soon.
I have been a musician irl for close to 40 years (yeah, I'm old), and have been on Steam for just over 12 years. This is the single best thing I have purchased on this platform. And its not even done.
Like many "Tycoon" games, RGT starts off slow - and failure is a strong possibility. Then your band hits a level where you are fairly successful, and it is easy to maintain that level of modest success. But trying to get to the NEXT LEVEL is a frantic juggling act of songwriting / rehearsal / record company contracts / recording / gigs. And when things get too hectic, you can always just chill in the garage, busk on the street, or just practice your instrument.
At least keep your eye on this game. If I was capable of making a video game (which I am not) - this would be the one I would make. I cannot wait to see how it turns out.

A Wizards Lizard (AWL) is a top down shooter rogue-lite with RPG elements. For those who are familiar with 'The Binding Of Isaac', AWL is an less hardcore version of it with eye candy visuals! For those who are not familiar with the genre, rogue-lite means that while it fundamentally follows the rules of rogue-likes (permadeath, no save points and randomly generated levels) it adds features that reward you for any progress you may have made in the game. This is achieved by freeing npcs that increase your starting money, finding blueprints for the town shop and finally by freeing other playable characters, each having his own starting skillset!
A great feature of this game and perhaps the reason it's unique, is the after death mechanic, like an extra life with some advantages and disadvantages. Besides that you get a second chance, as ghost or spirit, you will have access to stuff that are literally hidden in plain sight for your mortal counterpart! Be careful though, you total health is reduced and unless you revive, death in this form will result in game over.
To my surprise there are quite many items, and depending on your choices on how you want to do damage, there are the items you will need to support your choice, a quick tip, once you find a good totem try improving it! The basic run of the game consists of 3 zones, each divided into 3 subareas, each zone has its own type of enemies and boss. At the beginning I was a bit disappointed by the maps size but each new area gets bigger! Additionally there are extra areas to be discovered and locks to be unlocked with special keys that you have to find though a chain of boxes, mortal/ghost changing and some careful observation! Seriously an NPC gave me a tip of where to find a weapon relatively early in the game!
I enjoyed it a lot and it got a big bonus for me, when I figured out that there is more than meats the eye! The only negative point is the music that can become annoying. Definitely a great game to introduce the uninitiated to the genre!

A one-dimensional, oversimplified "Binding of Isaac" clone, enjoyable, but only for a couple hours at most.
I had extremely high hopes for this game and was quite disappointed to hear that the developer has already moved on to an early access "sequel" to this game (using this game's assets) rather than properly finishing this game (notably the balance and pacing issues).
PROS:
-Fundamnetal concept is fun
-Progression in town is a good mechanic (allows you to do a "vanilla" run OR to buy whatever gear you want in base once you've unlocked it; the choice is up to the player).
-Clean controls
-Good secrets
NEUTRALS:
-Room variety is somewhat lacking.
CONS:
-Very repetitive gameplay. Floor layouts are randomized, but what is on them is not.
-Poor boss design. There is a boss at the end of each world, but it is always the same boss....the only thing that varies is the attack pattern. Rather than allowing the boss to have a mix of all the available attack patterns, instead you "randomly" get to fight only one of the boss' attack patterns. Design here really makes no sense.
-Different characters (once unlocked) provide little to change the game. They merely start out with different gear/HP, but they don't interact with the game in any unique way.
-Poor documentation. Most game mechanics are never explained (ghost form, pentagram rooms). Some text boxes inexplicably stop (for example, when talking to a shop keeper he will say "Let me explain my items...." then proceed to tell you what his items do, BUT he does not explain healing items. So if he is selling 3 healing items, he will just say "let me explain my items" and then end his sentence there. Very confusing for a new player.)
-Dev released and immediately moved on to a "sequel" using the same game engine/assets/etc. rather than addressing any of the balance or pacing problems of this game.

Hex is a Trading Card Game (TCG), not unlike things we've seen before.
Hex was originally marketed as an MMO/Card game, and while it's not there yet, it is becoming one with each major content drop.
Well, for your PvE experience you will pick a race and a class. You are given a deck containing basic cards, and then you are encouraged to go explore the adventure zone(s) to collect cards and equipment; or you can improve your skills against players and try to be among the best.
Yes, Hex has equipment for your character, equipment that change what cards do, when you can play them, or what they cost.
The equipment is specific to your cards, so you pick and choose what equipment you want for the deck you are currently playing.
Correct, when you get into the game you can choose to run the capmpaign, the arena (PvE) or any of the many variants of PvP available.
The campaign, has dungeons to be beaten, and loot to be found. You level your character, pick your talents, and upgrade your deck.
In the Frostring Arena, you are faced up against a list of 20 opponents with a single deck, and three lives, changing bosses and a hidden random encounter keeps it very fun, and rewarding.
There are several ways of playing against other players:
Sealed deck
Draft
Constructed
Sealed and constructed can both be played as a live tournament, or as a gauntlet tournament where you can play until you have 5 wins, or three losses, and in both then you get rewarded according to how well you did.
Well, the game has two different currencies, platinum and gold.
You can acquire gold from the PvE experience, or by selling cards, chests, packs, mercenaries or equipment on the auction house
With platinum, you can buy packs, starter decks, and entry to tournaments, and is obtained by purchasing it from the store, or by selling your above mentioned items.
Depending on what you want out of the game, it can cost you money, but you can certainly try it and enjoy it at no cost at all.
That's really hard for me to say, but as for time, it is certainly worth mine. Concerning your money, it's not like you need to throw down anything to give it a try, so I would say yes on both accounts.
To sum up, PvE is free, and you are rewarded with cards (both PvE and PvP) as well as equipment, and dust to upgrade the art on the cards to extended art, all of which can be sold to other players for gold or platinum.
You can play against players, and if you are good, and hardcore enough to attempt it, you can try and compete in tournaments for good prizes.
Card packs contain a single rare or legendary card, a few uncommons, and quite a few commons up to a total of 17 cards, when buying or winning packs, there is a chance that it will generate a PRIMAL PACK that will contain 2 legendaries, and 13 rares.
You can construct as many decks as you would like, with as many colours and cards as you want. And you get to pick the champion yourself, there are quite a few, and only more coming.
The game is very promising, the digital-only design space opens up some very interesting mechanics, from as generating new cards, or shuffling cards into your opponents deck, to permanent buffs and cards with sockets.
Content is being released at a rather slow rate at the moment, so if you join early, you have a good chance at catching up.
Tournaments are run weekly, and there are monthly VIP tournaments that reward alternate art cards worth upwards of 15$ each, and the entry fee is much less, but you do need to have the VIP entry tickets.
The game comes with a tutorial, and the community is very helpful.
It may seem overwhelming at first, but start by jumping into the ever expanding campaign, and venture into the world of PvP once you feel like you are ready.
I have played the game since alpha and even now, the special encounters, and race/class rewards in the campaign keeps you coming back for more.

Hex is a deep trading card game that embraces its digital nature, with mechanics not feasible in meatspace.  Whether you're a TCG veteran or a newbie, competetive or not, you'll find something to love in this game.
The PVE campaign combines the depth of a trading card game with traditional RPG elements (classes, levelling, skill trees) to make for a great experience.  The campaign is completely free-to-play, you'll earn cards and gold you can use to improve your deck, as well as any cards you get from playing the PVP side of the game.  There's several hours of content here with much more in the works.
For the competetive types, PVP definitely can stand on its own.  Unlike the campaign, PVP is generally pay-to-play outside of friendly constructed games or player-driven leagues.  Tournaments consist of limited formats such as draft and sealed and competetive constructed where you bring your own deck.  Limited formats are a great place to start if you haven't built up a collection yet, as everyone is limited to the packs they use in the event.

I've been playing HEX for several years, since the beginning of the closed beta.  I've had a lot of fun with it and I'd say it is definitely worth it to download and try it if you like collectible card games.
Hex has a business model similar to Magic where cards are fully tradable and have "value" in that the rare cards are worth real money - but the downside to this is that the game can't really give them out to you for free like other F2P card games and the majority of cards are gained from paid booster packs.  Basically, to win in constructed tournaments you will probably need to pay money to buy the rarest cards from other players (like in Magic).  I think that the HEX in-game auction house works really well to do this.
However, it is definitely possible to go infinite in limited (draft and sealed) if you are good enough, and the rate of grinding real money currency from the PVE content if you are efficient is far superior to that of any other game I've seen.  I am impressed that the free currency, gold, has maintained so much real value over the years.  The economy is entirely player-driven.
The available PVE content is fun and can be completed without spending anything.  I have tested this content without any previous cards or interaction with the auction house and it is definitely beatable.  Depending on what race you choose though, you may have to create several characters and use the free cards collected over all those characters to beat the campaign.  I find the campaign a lot of fun, but it is pretty light on content right now (only chapter 1 is out).  Hopefully more content will be released soon and at a faster rate.
To maintain the value of cards but still be able to give out cards for free, the campaign gives out the common cards as rewards as well as special PVE-only cards.  So for "free" you can pick up the commons that you'd get from booster packs, but to get the uncommons, rares, and legendaries for free you would have to buy them with gold from the auction house or trade your gold for the real-money currency platinum.
I find this game to be more complex (in a good way) in its mechanics than the other F2P card games I have played and though it is very mechanically similar to Magic I think it has some cool digital innovations that Magic doesn't have.  Though it doesn't promise to let you get a full collection for free like other CCG games such as Hearthstone, the fact that you can trade your cards freely and use the auction house actually makes it easier to build the deck you want (rather than relying purely on pack randomness and a grindy crafting system).
In short, I would recommend this game both as a completely free experience with the PVE campaign as well as a paid trading card game that is similar to what you get with Magic but cheaper, more accessible, and more fun.

is an open world RPG created by
, and today it's a classic cult title recommended to everyone who enjoys a role playing game, or an action title for that matter.
The player takes control of our hero, the nameless hero, who just happens to be imprisoned and sent into the colony. For those who don't know, the colony is the king's solution to the war with the orcs. In order to keep extracting the precious ore from the mines, but saving manpower, his highness ordered the magicians to create a dome surrounding the ore mines. Convicts are sent in, and when trying to leave the magical barrier kills anyone who dares to cross it.
Convicts eventually turn againts the guards, and take control of the colony, and since they can't leave, they make an agreement with the king, to keep providing ore, in exchange for goods.
The story follows the player decisions based on his choices, in particular, whatever camp he chooses. Remember that this game was developed in the late 90's, and this sort of action-consequence in video-games were a new thing, and barely explored. The developers not only explorer it, but opened doors to many other video-games inspired by
.
There are three camps available to join, The Old Camp, The New Camp and the Sect Camp. Each camp shares a goal, an objective and a mission. They all intend to leave the colony, in their own way. What they didn't expect was an evil, who lurks in the sleep, and a nameless hero!
For those who are new to the series,
presents some extreme challenges, due to several reasons. The game has over 15 years, therefore, its mechanics are archaic, but playable and even extremely enjoyable if you put enough effort into learning to fight. The controls alone are a challenge, as it uses schematics that are no longer applied in today's age. When
was created, there wasn't many other games alike, therefore the developers had to create their own scheme. I still feel the controls work just fine, and after 10 or 15 hours, they'll feel natural, even for those not used to mouse/keyboard.
The age reflects mostly on graphics, but thanks to the extensive work from community members we now have HD texture packs, and DX11 features available to anyone. Of course textures alone don't make a brand new game, but surely refresh any player's eyes!
Bugs and glitches were also removed and gameplay improved thanks to the community, making
playable, even for the most recent generation of gamers.
is based on an ecosystem trapped inside a bubble. There is a society, groups of people, guilds, monsters, and even flora. Every living thing has their own routine and day/night cycle, it's just not a bunch of NPC's walking around like idiots, there is a sense to everyone acts. I believe this was one of the biggest impacts for the fans, due to its strategic approach, for example; on the beasts, at night, as they sleep, it's just easier to sneak and attack them first under the moonlight. This is just a small but fantastic detail in the
world that gives player the freedom to think and act.
This development mentality was also applied to the merchants. Because the player finds himself trapped, goods from "outside" are valuable. This currency also works accordingly to each camp demands for specific products. Choosing the right person to trade with, will result in a much more profitable deal for you!
The energy "dome" was actually inspired by
, a famous movie directed by
, but in a medieval and magic realm.
It's still a relatively large world, but easy to walk around it. I like to think it's actually bigger than it really is. None the less it's filled with fantastic places for quests and explorers who don't fear the unknown.
The developers didn't hold the player when comes to explore the colony, usually the hero is blocked by a certain enemy. This works to show how much the hero has yet to accomplish, or simply adds a new challenge, in which you're not supposed to do, but you can. This method also regulates the player level, to help him understand if he is underlevel or just appropriate.
The lore in the game is small, but sufficient to give players an idea of the people, the gods, the world, and how big it is, and even how frustrating it is to be stuck in a bubble. Because of this there are no women, at least none slave ones, as well as children. Life in the colony is tough, and the human condition isn't pretty, this also deflects across the different camps, giving each major NPC their goals or preferences. NPC's are repetitive when comes to their dialogues, but important ones are distinct.
wanted the hero to be humble, and that's another thing most new players have trouble understanding. While in most recent games, the hero has everything, but in
, has nothing. The player must conquer everything, with just small steps and simple quests. Eventually, it becomes extremely satisfying to increase strength or dexterity, and finally be successful against an enemy that was previously impossible or hard to defeat. The most dedicated players will be rewarded with god powers if the experience points end up in the right place. It's important to have in mind what you want to be as a character, a warrior, a magician or perhaps a hunter mastering a bow? EXP points are limited, and that's mostly because enemies don't respawn totally per chapter. One enemy per group respawns, and that's barely enough to farm. Weaponry is also an important factor of
, as well their skills to master. One hand or two-handed swords, crossbows, bows, are usually the top choices for warriors. But magic is also well represented in this first chapter of the series, with planty scrolls to use from telekinesis, to transformation and all sorts of attacks.  Summoning allies is also an ability for those following the path of magic.
Skill points will also have to be shared through learning skills such as skinning animals, pickpocket, lock picking, using advanced weaponry and other attributes including magical knowledge. This impulses players to enjoy a second playthrough, and explore different learning paths.

Should be named the "Ways To Randomly Die Horribly In Space Simulator".
With procedural generation, and little story elements interspersed between, it's possible to provide the illusion of story, simply due to the human ability to construct a narrative out of any series of roughly connected events, and many games have hung their hat upon this post. But this does not make it a story game.
Just as it provides the illusion of story, it also provides the illusion of resource management. The semblence of a resource management game is there, with the need to balance limited cargo space with the three essentials (fuel, oxygen and hull repair material) and improved tech (and the necessary parts to build it). However, since it's impossible to  predict the availability of any of these resources or technology there is no possibility of informed play. Learning more about the mechanics of how things work in the universe provides absolutely no advantage, as the available systems to travel to may be lacking in oxygen that you can harvest, or you may run out of fuel because there's nowhere to refuel (despite an earlier playthrough having gas giants on every corner waiting to be sipped from).
If anything, playing this seems to be indistinguishable from randomly choosing from the available possibilities. You might as well have it make the choice for you and then simply progress through by hitting space bar, reading the 'story', until your inevitable horrible death. It's art - but is it a game?
This ain't no place for a hero.

This VN is unique. It's not your typical cute and romantic VN for sure. It has an eerie vibe, almost freaky (good freaky). I can tell it took a big amount of effort and time (2007 really?) to bring out something so different and so good. Major props to (developer).
Storyline: The setting takes place in the old days in Europe (I think). In the VN you play as a mother, who's only real in your daughter's (Rosa) consciousness. As Rosa continues on with her (self-proclaimed) sinful life, she meets Catherine and Guilleme. Ever since she met them, her life has become more complicated. As her mother, you will give her guidance and witness Rosa’s life along with the consequences of her actions. Note: There will be no happy endings. Just sad, scary, evil, and shocking turn of events.
Playtime: Took me ~6 hours for a single play through, and another 2-3 hrs if you want to unlock all the achievements and dialogues.
My personal tags: Romance, Suspense, Thriller, Mystery, Historical Fiction, Family
Pros:
+ Music, art, and storyline are eye-catching
+ Lots of achievements to get, easy too
+ It’s free AND it’s a really good read if you’re into the unusualness
+ Unexpected plot twists; I was hoping for romance but, not that kind of romance
+ Barely any fillers, almost every scene contributed to the major plot
+ Visible character progression
+ It gets interesting every chapter
Cons:
- I still want to know what happened to Rosa's life afterwards or how she got that scar on her eye :( (Maybe a second part?)
- The chronological order of the scenes can be a bit confusing
- Cliff-hanger or not? Hmm not sure...
Overall, I was completely immersed in this VN. I just couldn't stop reading it. It became a memorable and special VN to me. I’m now a fan.  Thanks and keep it up :)
P.S. A cupid who's a playboy, how ironic. Btw, the concept of falling in love with a beast reminds me of Katy Perry's song "E.T." for some reason...

This is definitely on the list of best VNs I've ever played. It's worlds better than some games that I've paid $10+ for and I didn't have to spend a dime on it. Almost enough to make a person feel guilty.
Although love is the overall theme, what really sucked me in initially was the suspense and feeling of slow creeping terror. The atmosphere is wonderful -- writing and art are not perfect but almost always great, and what more can you ask from a free game? They work together to do an excellent job of building tone, creating a sense of gradual mounting tension, and really evoking the feeling of a whole world with a few static images.
I got ending 3 the first time through despite doing my very best to make nice decisions, and once I'd finished reading that I felt like I needed a bath, in the best possible way. There they were, this character doing something unequivocably evil, and yet in a certain sense I couldn't even blame them for it. I was sucked in by the perversity and the mystery of it all and immediately had to dive back in for more.
If I were to voice any criticisms, they would mainly be:
1) From the author's notes bonus I gather that the main writer assumes the meaning of the title "Cupid" would be obvious once you've finished the endings, but I was reading that with four endings under my belt and the idea hadn't even occurred to me in the slightest. I assumed it was supposed to be more of a general reference to love and matchmaking. If this was an idea the team wanted to convey to readers or thought was important, I think they unfortunately did a poor job.
2) The summary blurb for the game in the Steam Store pushes the idea of the player directly stepping into the role of Mother, but this is very misleading. "Mother" is very much a specific character of her own with a specific personality, goals, etc. that you the player do not get to affect very much. One of my big pet peeves in visual novels and text adventures is when you get presented with "false choices" where nothing is available on your list of options that's remotely like what you actually want to say. This game had some fairly egregrious examples of that, particularly being forced to be mean to Rosa and then having the game chide me for my bad attitude in one ending even though, given the option, I would never have said any of those mean things at all. This irritating problem could have been avoided by finding some way to include Mother that didn't require her to be the POV character.
Overall however, these are small issues at the end of the day. This game would be well worth your time at $20 or $30, let alone at the price of totally free. Go check it out.

A Telltale adventure game in the Borderlands world (story-based, cinematic, only watching/dialogue choices/quick time events, not much normal gameplay). Some people won't/don't like the lack of challenging gameplay but I play this type of game for the story and the simple gameplay doesn't interrupt the flow of events with repeated failures/retries.
As a warning, there are a lot of pretty messed up things. Aside from the generic shooting and stealing, there is a variety on how people die/are disfigured/maimed, a few of which you do yourself with QTEs.
Also, most characters (including the ones you play) start out as self-interested/selfish jerks. There are only a few really good people I can think of in the whole game. However, they eventually grew on me (plus facing a bigger bad and having the option of choosing not to be complete jerks helped).
As with most Telltale games I've played before, you have timed dialogue (running out of time automatically chooses silence as the response) and simple QTEs. Luckily, in this game you are free to pause (with the space bar) whenever you want, even during choices. The QTEs are pretty basic (directional arrows/spam a button) and I was able to do it easily enough. Spamming 'Q' was a little annoying because my ring finger isn't quite dextrous enough for that so I had to shift my hand. Someone less coordinated (or not used to games) might find some trouble but at least failures aren't always lethal.
If you like the Borderlands world lore or have played Borderlands 1+2, this serves as a very nice story supplement. It's just a side story and doesn't involve most of the BL cast (other than a select few cameos) but it's an action-packed adventure. That said, it also takes place after BL2 so you see what a few characters are doing.
If you haven't played Borderlands 1+2 it still might be worth a look if you like the setting but you'll miss out on things that tie into the other games (cameos, character/company histories, etc.) You don't need in-depth knowledge to enjoy it but it's nice to have.
The basics you should probably know at minimum:
Pandora is the planet where vault hunters (like Brick, Mordecai, Lilith, Athena) went to search for one of the legendary vaults which are unlocked by a vault key. Marcus (the intro narrator) is the weapon shop vendor and intro narrator of the other games. Scooter is the guy who let you ride vehicles. Huge corporations also were interested in the vault. Originally Atlas was the big player but Hyperion (led by now-deceased Handsome Jack) took over after their fall. Hyperion set up a space station (called Helios) in orbit and have a bad rep for the natives of Pandora (which is a pretty lawless, messed up, bandit-filled type of place).

I've been a long time TCG fan, hacing played pokemon, yu-gi-oh, duel masters, and even harry potter tcgs in my youth, and Magic: The Gathering for much of my high school and college years. This game is what I've been waiting for, a digital TCG that rivals MTG. I have been playing since very early on, having backed it on kickstarter, and probalby have a few hundred hours in on the stand alone client.
The game is well thought out mechanically and introduces several mechanics that would be nigh impossible to acomplish in a physical TCG, however these mechanics are far from mere gimmicks. While you have cards such as Cosmic Transmogrifier which turn their entire board into a chaos of random cards, you also have mechanics such as escalate and prophecy, which buff cards that are still in your deck, and cards which can add new cards to your deck which don't even exist outside the instance of the game. Cards retaining their buffs and debuffs permanantly is a feature that really shakes things up. If you're playing against an opponent who uses cards which can be brought back to life, killing the 1/1 they buffed to a 10/10 might not be enough when he comes back with all the buffs still intact. Indeed, a lot of cards affect eachother before they even hit the field, modifying the cards in your hand and deck adds an interesting layer of strategy to the game.
Another nice addition in Hex is the PvE elements. Currently only the first chapter of the campaign is inplace, but players can choose from 4 races and 3 classes, soon to be expanded to more options, and these race/class compinations have large effects on your decks, from deciding which cards you cna use to buffing certain aspects of cards and your own character. Having the PvE seperate from the PvP also gives Hex the oppretunity to create insane cards that would be considered too unruly or imbalanced for tournament play, many PvE cards have super fun mechanics, such as Holiday which can become a random troop each turn, or are just insanely powerful, such as Wraith of Zaakir which turns you into an almight dragon cabable of incinerating your opponent's troops.
All in all I highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of TCGs. Yes, you have to buy cards if you want to compete, but you have to in any TCG, and with packs only costing 2USD, it's probably one of the cheapest ones out there. Not to mention the regular draft tournaments being played, and the active and involved community. This makes it a no-brainer to any TCG fan who wants to play a game which they don't need to drive to the card shop anad hope someone is playing.

I love roguelikes or more precisely the emerging genre of roguelike-likes.  After the near perfection of Spelunky I had a hard time finding a game that really satisfy my desire for the genre.  A couple games have stuck out and one of them is A Wizard's Lizard.  Clever title aside I have to say this is a really fun game with a couple really clever concepts.
At its core A Wizard's Lizards is a top-down dungeon brawler.  Every time you play you're dropped in maze of randomly laid out rooms.  You're free to explore them all to max out your loot and find better equipment.  Or minimize harm to yourself a go straight to the boss room.  That is the beauty of any great roguelike, the push-your-luck choices you constantly have to make.
The combat system is fairly simple but feels really good.  Find the right weapon and equipment to match your play-style then go to town on the enemies.  Unlimited use of your staff is great just be sure to watch your cool down time.  Your soul orbs give you a nice powerful boost but its number of uses is limited so be careful.
The coolest part of this game and the element that makes it so unique is its light/dark mechanic.  Death is not the end in this game.  When lose all your hit points go from the dark world to one of light.  Many of the enemies you struck down will reemerge as ghosts and ghouls.  Quickly make your way to nearest wicca symbol to give yourself back to the darkest and protect yourself from death once more.  Being able to recover from a near death experience like this is quite exhilarating.
To conclude, this a well thought out roguelike.  It has a very charming, colorful, art style with may funny looking characters.  The combat consist mostly of smart movement and equipment savaging.  All put together a neat little game that doesn't take terribly long to complete but is difficult enough to make you try a handful of times till you make it through.
I liked it, quite pleasant to play, even though I took long at the shutdown. :)

The game fully use it's virtual component to play with cards in ways physical cards cant, such as manipulating core cards in game, decks composition and effects. For instance you can place booby traps inside your enemy deck, increase cost of cards in his hands, lower stats of cards in his deck, etc.
The game offer a solid pvp side, which i am mostly unfamiliar with, but there are such things as drafts and tournaments.
The game also offer a (still in development but the first zone is out) PVE campaign. Some fight feels more like puzzle solving, since you may have to adapt your cards to fit the situation. in others you gotta deal with the situation using your race/class and elements best you can. Deckbuilding is available (similar to mtg), there are already enough cards to see multiple deck types (and heroes) and cards being used in PVP and PVE.

This alone makes it better than games like Hearthstone, Faeria, Duelyst, etc. where you are locked to cards you own. Being able to build assets for the time you invest in the game makes this game one of the best values for your luxury time.

The RPG elements and leveling system offer a lot of variety, and deck building options with PvE exclusive cards and equipment will offer endless replayability! The content release plan is said to have 7 years of content currently planned, with 2-3 anticipated large PvE content and progression patches per year. The experience is extremely unique for a TCG, and will eventually have co-op MMO style modes added.
There is a draft format, sealed format, and constructed format where packs are rewarded as prizes. Including some free community tournaments as well, where packs and plat are rewarded as prizes. Unlike other popular card games now, part of the cost of limited formats, like draft and sealed, is in the packs, which you keep all contents of after the tournament. The constructed format has a rich meta that has evolved with time, and will get better with each set release.
Whether it be Primal Packs(and you will love these babies), Chase cards, Exclusive events, Hitting an amazing chest spin, or trading your gold for plat to remain a free-to-play player, there are a ton of intricate pieces that tie into the Marketing Model for HEX, that really reward you for your understanding. At the end of the day, 1 simple rule applies - Time = Money, but if you put in a little bit of Money to jump-start your experience, it can save you a ton of time grinding early on. If you want to be a virtually free-to-play player, with it comes an understanding to build a strong PvE deck, and having the time to farm gold, and then convert gold and cards on the AH to continue playing all modes for free. F2P is definitely something that can be done, and the better understanding you have, and the more time-invested, the easier it will be for you, as a player, to casually drop 1400 plat in a day to play paid limited tournaments, and convert those rewards.
There are a lot more formats, PvE content, RPG experience, MMO experience, cards, equipment, exclusive events to come. This game is seriously a black-hole of replayability, and for that, I both love it and hate it, as it's hard for me to put the same value into other games, and I find myself spending more and more time playing HEX for both the value and fun experimenting with endless options.

TL/DR: Heroes Rise: The Prodigy is a nice interactive novel for a rainy day. It's entertaining one time through but (like most of its genre) has extremely limited replayability. If it were an actual published story, I imagine I'd find it in the ages 9-12 section of a bookstore.
Details:
Heroes Rise: The Prodigy was entertaining enough to read through once or twice. One particularly enjoyable feature is the final score it calculates based in part on moral decisions made throughout the story. This is soured by the fact that a how-to guide is provided for readers at the end of the first play-through detailing how to improve their scores at specific junctions. Another strength of the game is that it specifically identifies that justice and fame aren't one and the same. Sometimes the reader has to pick one or the other. Unfortunately the main storyline is the same no matter what choices you make, so those decisions only impact the final score. Underscoring that, the same character will always be your love interest -- even if you admit that you aren't interested in anyone during that particular playthrough. This also demonstrates how the characters are one-dimensional, thereby dragging down the quality of the story. If these concerns were effectively addressed, I'd definitely bump up its rating.

Gunpoint: Nuclear Powered Pants
Despite have only put 4 hours into Gunpoint I will start this review by stating, without reservation, that Gunpoint is worth buying. In fact, I will urge you to go buy it right now.
…Did you buy it?
Oh you want more information? Well you’re in luck! I have about  two pages worth of information for you!
Gunpoint is a wonderful little puzzle game. It’s clever, thought provoking, funny, and above all, just plain fun to play. I knew Gunpoint was a great game when I spent something like an hour (or two!) playing the demo level over and over again trying to come up with new ways to complete the puzzle.
Let me give you some context: Gunpoint puts you in the pants of a “freelance spy” who has… well… super powered pants.
These pants, the “Bullfrog Trousers,” allow you to jump forty feet into the air, survive falls from just about any height, jump through plate glass windows, etc. It’s all quite cool. Using the abilities afforded by your trousers and a host of other gadgets, you take on jobs that require you to break into high security buildings, steal information, and get out without being seen.
This is where the fun begins. You’re only told what to steal, not how to do it. Obviously there are specific solutions to the games puzzles. However, how you go about reaching those solutions is up to you. You have the tools are your disposal, and the game lets you go about it your own way.
Along with your super powered pantaloons, you also have a “Crosslink” device that allows you to hack into the various electrical devices in the game such as light switches, card readers, doors, guns… you know, normal everyday stuff. This mechanic allows you to set up glorious chain reactions that always result in something amazing. Whether it works or not.
Beating a man to death with an automatic door programmed to open when someone walks through a metal detector is… Actually pretty hilarious, especially when it results in an infinite loop causing the door to flail open and closed as fast as possible resulting in an unending cacophony of meaty smacking sounds.
What a way to go.
Being beaten to death with a door isn’t the only way to take out the opposition. There are a multitude of ways to dispatch the various guards you encounter throughout the game, some more lethal than others. You can push them out of windows, make them accidentally shoot each other, knock them out with electrical shock, and last but not least beat them to death unconscious with your fists!
Punching dudes in the face is extremely common in this game. And your bare hands are in many ways the most brutal of Gunpoint’s weapons. The only limit to the amount of times you can pummel a man with your fists is the limit of your own depravity (Or rather, how fast you can click the mouse).
One of the first times I beat a guard unconscious, I rapidly clicked the mouse thinking multiple hits were necessary to knock him out. The rapid fire punches created an amusing sound, so I kept hitting him, laughing at the meaty, flat, slapping… until I realized there was a pool of blood under him. Upon completing the level, the game labeled me a psychopath as I had hit the man over one hundred and fifty times without realizing it. I kind of felt bad…
Kind of.
Punch a guard once, and he’s unconscious. One hundred times, and he’s not getting up… ever.
Despite Gunpoint being a rather short game, it is incredibly fun to play. The puzzles are intriguing, require thought and some trial and error, and are set up in such a way to allow for speed running. Once I got really good at a level, I was able to complete it in under 30 seconds. It was fun to continually beat my scores, getting faster and faster. And the unique and varied ways you can come up with to complete a level really add to the game’s replay value.
I will be honest, I completed the whole game in one sitting. But it was well worth the money I spent on it. The art style is fun, and stylish with a little bit of a noir feeling to it. The writing is hilarious, if a bit sweary at times. And the music is absolutely phenomenal. Combined with the fun gameplay and great puzzles, Gunpoint really is a gem of a game.
Plus, there is a level editor that allows players to create and share custom puzzles to play through! I never personally dove into the custom levels, so I can’t speak to the quality of the puzzles out there. But knowing the internet, I’m sure there is some great stuff to be found.
I really have nothing negative to say about Gunpoint other than “I wish it was a little longer.” At the same time after beating it, I felt satisfied. The game didn’t overstay it’s welcome. Not only was the story was resolved, ending on a satisfying note, but the game lets you go back to all of the levels after having completed them so you can play them again!
If you enjoy witty puzzle games, Gunpoint is for you.

tl;dr It's interesting for a couple hours while you're still getting a hang of the game, then it just becomes tedious when you're doing the same thing over and over again (fuel + repair).  6/10
I was really psyched to play this game.  Loved FTL and the description of FTL without the combat sounded great.  Unfortunately, it just doesn't come through with any of the depth that FTL had.  It's got atmosphere, absolutely, but that atmosphere is thin and evaporates quickly.  The only way it's a roguelike is in permadeath.  There's not enough variety for me to really consider it a roguelike.
The biggest downfall is the ships.  You start out with a bucket of crap, which is fine and to be expected.  If you're lucky, you might wander across one other ship before the game gives you the second-best ship for free as an auto-reveal plot point.  There's maybe seven or so other ships in the game, but only two of them are actually better than the bucket of crap you started with...which is completely underwhelming.  The firefly, even though it has zero free space, is fun to tool around and explore in simply because everything is so easy -- it's such a relief after the slow-going of the other ships that it can make the game quite fun for a little while.  Otherwise the only major difference is the amount of cargo space.  Even with the biggest ship (21 spaces), you're still going to be very short on space.  If the ships had been at least minimally interesting, I would've enjoyed the game a lot more.
Synergy - while not explained at all - is very important.  If a tech 'requires' another tech, placing it next to the 'required' tech improves the efficiency (giving a blue outline).  Which means less fuel/o2/mining!
The writing is sometimes interesting, but very much amateur hour sci-fi schlock.  Tons of spelling mistakes and awkward transitions.  Every time you warp to a new star, you get a random blurb/encounter.  After going through almost all the stars, I was still seeing new ones, which is something.  If the writing was a bit better, it would be a reason to keep going.  Unfortunately, it's not.  They don't ever really add to the very minimal story.
Drilling/probing should always be done at 10/10.  Ignore the super mining/super probing tech, they're not worth the space or effort.  Get your tech from the alien encounters as soon as you can.  Certain species will always ask "approve" others will always ask "disapprove."  If you choose correctly you can get tech and new words.
Overall, I really enjoyed the first couple of hours of learning the game.  But it gets old very quickly.  There's not much diversity in things to do.  The tech is shallow, ships are beyond shallow, and the map is far, far too large for how little there is to do.  Get it on sale/bundled.  Do not rush to get it.  Still fun for a bit if you really like the genre.  If you do get it, do yourself a favor and copy your save file before you do one ending so you reload it and complete the others.

Doors is a first person puzzle game. But the first person aspect is limited to you walking over to the next puzzle each time. You walk through bland, uninspired, low resolution black and white landscapes (look at the screenshots). This adds nothing to the game. Halfway through the game, there is a bunker to 'explore' but except for getting some Steam Achievements done there, it's just a colored version of the walking simulator to get you to walk over to the next puzzle.
The puzzles are... weird. They're not easy and they're not hard, but they require you to adapt to the word choice of the creator. An example. The phrase "correct door" doesn't mean the door that you need to walk through to solve the puzzle, but a door with a correct statement written on it. This will get you confused at almost every puzzle. Some people talk about it in the discussion forum but I think it's intended, because once you 'translate' the puzzles on paper and replace it with the real-life words (i.e.
really means
,
really means
and
means
), you'll solve every puzzle with ease. But what's the point of playing a computer game if the actual puzzling is done on a piece of paper, right? I know. So one struggles through it while trying to 'translate' in your head. But when you get to puzzles with, say, six doors and more, it gets hard. Not hard to solve, but hard to resist the urge to take a piece of paper and a biro, and immediately solve the puzzle as if it were a child's riddle.
I see people praise this game because one person made it. Ok. But what does that tell others about the game? We need to judge the game for what it is and especially, if we would recommend the game to other people who have never played it. Well, I can only recommend against spending money and time on this game. The fact that one person made the game doesn't change that recommendation one bit.
One last note about the Steam Achievements, especially for completionists. All achievements are easy to get except for one, which is unattainable. It's not bugged or anything. The person who made the game just thought it would be funny to make an achievement, describe it as "unachievable" (a reference to The Stanley Parable and one of its achievements) and actually make it unachievable. Really, there is no legitimate way to get this achievement. Read the discussions forum if you want confirmation.

+ The music of the game is very nice. It's smooth, jazz(y) and it does an amazing job of setting the mood no matter where you are at in the game.

One of the best RTS of its' gen. It is fast-placed, tactics oriented. If you like micro-management games like Starcraft, this may not be your cup of tea. If you prefer to focus more on your units and battlefield, than worrying about resources, bases building and who will press the X button faster to create workers/ buildings in time: Get this now.
Single-Player: Great campaign, with good story even for non-Warhammer 40K fans. Nothing to do with the original Dawn of War, so it is easy to get into.
Multiplayer: You get three modes. Co-op campaign, co-op PvE and competitive (PvP).
The first is self-explanotary; you can play the campaign with a friend.
Co-op PvE: My favourite mode, it is called "Last Stand". You basically pick a hero and fight waves of enemies, alongside with other people. It is your "arena" mode; something that we used to see in mods and maps in older RTS games -call me Starcraft, Warcraft II & III, LotR: BFME, etc etc. You have a choice of 4 unique heroes (more if you have the expansions), which you can level-up and get gear for individually. This mode is a bit like a "free" extra game that comes with DoWII. My only complain nowadays is the lack of online players.
Competitive MP: Includes FFA and team-matches.
The biggest cons: Not enough people online and that it still uses Game for Windows as a DRM. Due to the later, I lost my saves twice in the past...

Let me start by saying that I am a big fan of these kind of games. I was very early to the "walking-simulator" hype, and while everyone was hating on games like "Gone Home" and "Dear Esther", I loved every second of these games.
And that's why I find it so hard to believe that this game gets such rave reviews.
Let me elaborate: the developers of this game obviously had some insanely creative ideas to show and help us experience their short stories. And I applaud them for this. But a creative way to tackle a story does not make up for the fact that most of these stories just don't feel right.
To me, every story in this game felt like they had started writing it from the ending, or from one basic special element, and then they just worked their way through, filling in all the blanks. This feels so unnatural and therefore I can't begin to even feel the slightest emotion at any of these stories. Or the big overarching story as a whole.
Take away the story and what remains of Edith Finch?
Hardly anything. Gameplay is basic and controls are an absolute pain, but the visuals are stunning and voice talent is OK.
Overall I would not recommend this, and I would say to anyone who is thinking about buying this to try Ether One instead. It has a similar feel and personal setting, but feels much more natural in its delivery.

I am a streamer who has played TCGs for over 10 years including MtG, Hearthstone and HEX since alpha. Here's what you need to know about this game:
PvE is RPG-meets-TCG content that allows you to have fun, learn the game and farm cards and in-game currency at a decent rate. You can also play the auction house, and tournaments will start paying for themselves once you are good enough. A small investment goes a long way to make the grind more enjoyable.
You can enjoy the majority of the game by grinding and trading for what you need. But if you want to compete at the highest level of tournaments, like the $100k invitational, a large collection will be a long-term advantage. It may cost you a lot, but it will gain value over time and can be resold!
HEX has a great online experience, uses its digital nature to innovate, has a growing RPG PvE and is easier/cheaper to get into, but it's not as vast as MtG yet and lacks its face-to-face social interaction.
It's easily among the most helpful and generous I've encountered, and the streamers are fantastic. The official forums and fan-sites are informative and active with guides and great tournaments.
The company is designing their own dream game. That is why this is a AAA quality game, despite coming from a still growing Indie studio. This sustainable perfectionism can lead to longer wait times, but they are worth it in the end.
This is not an instant gratification game that presses your reward center a couple of times and then leaves you wanting. TCGs are one of the most rewarding genres you can get into, allowing you to grow your skill and collection over decades with flexible time and money commitment. You wont regret giving this a try.

Heroes Rise:  The Prodigy is like Skyrim, but good!  It's like the Telltale games (ie. The Walking Dead and Tales from the Borderlands) but without all the annoying quick time events.
In all seriousness, this game is amazing!  Sure, I'd love to see some graphics, great voice acting, music and sound.  Even some type of character creation tool, so you could craft a perfect graphical representation of how your character looks, but this isn't that type of game.  It's essentially a more advanced video game representation of the old "Choose Your Own Adventure" books I grew up with.  Brilliantly built game with an amazingly crafted story!
I've already started the sequel, "Hero Project," where your decisions from this first game carry over seamlessly!  I can't recommend these games enough!
The price these games go for can seem a little steep (Steam pricing ecosystem) for what they are, compared to other indies at the same price point, since they don't have any graphics or sound.  I still say they're worth it.  I got the "Heroes Rise" bundle of games on a sale, but even then, I've never seen them dip more than 40% off.  Overall, I say the amount of fun I've had with Heroes Rise:  The Prodigy, is well worth the price of admission.  Check it out!

(Note:  This review covers the whole trilogy.)
How many of us read comics when we were kids? You know- you'd go on down to the comic shop, drop a few coins or dollars on the latest issues of your favorite caped crusaders, and then proceed to simply lose yourself in the battles and adventures within- and maybe gripe when the blasted thing ended on yet another cliffhanger. Of course, that and a cup full of whatever colored sugar-water they used to call a kids' drink was enough to fuel hours of afternoon playtime as we imagined ourselves to fly like Superman, swing through Gotham like the Batman, or to deflect bullets and fight crime like Wonder Woman. But nowadays, well... video games can only do so much... so why not load up on your favorite sugary drink and see where your imagination takes you? Time to suit up and fight crime in the "Heroes Rise Trilogy".
This is a set of text adventures published by Choice Of Games, the same wonderful people behind another game I reviewed, "Slammed!". I told you this is a company you ought to throw bags of money at and support, and I still stand by that. The options you have are staggering in character creation- you craft up your own hero, with the only caveat that you can't choose your last name. Pick your options (name, superhero name, gender, sexuality- just like the other CoG stuff I've played, you're free to choose among all the options no matter what you pick, which is a plus!), and go to town. There are other options you'll end up choosing, but those are spoilers, and you don't get any from me, especially on these games!
Your role is an up-and-coming superhero, taking your first steps into the heroic life- and trust me when I say that enemies come in all shapes, sizes, and shades of gray. This isn't like the Adam West Batman show, this is more like a damn good season of Justice League Unlimited, the original Teen Titans, or the original X-Men cartoon that used to run on Fox Saturday Mornings. It'll suck you in, and it'll grab your attention to where you want to see what happens next. Every choice you make could influence how you are viewed, how others react to you, and how your powers could develop. It's honestly a great thing, and there are many, many different endings. Characters can live, die, change views, but one thing will always be the same- it's up to you and your decisions alone. How you live, how you talk, how you fight- everything has repercussions.
The story wouldn't be out of place on a comic shelf, drawn by some popular artist. That's what makes this whole game- the story and writing are easily top-notch. There's not a damned error or grammar screwup anywhere. I honestly had a hard time finding anything to knock this game for.
About the only thing I really can knock it for is the lack of the ability to save. If you want to see how choices play out, you've got to restart the whole game- and some of the choices from the first game have far-reaching implications, so sometimes you'll need to replay "The Prodigy" and "The Hero Project" to see new material in "Herofall". Being able to simply save and poke around, even if it's certain points like new chapters. would be welcome.
Other than that, well... there's not anything I can complain about it. You have to think about what some of the characters look like, but... brush off your imagination and use that. If you can draw, do that. But don't just chuck this game out because it doesn't have pretty pictures.
However, it's been confirmed that we are getting a part 4: "The Hero Project: Redemption Season". It launches on April 8th and I almost did the Snoopy dance when I saw that. I'm sure that I'll end up buying this day one when it hits Steam because it is that damned good.
Currently, you can buy these individually on Steam, or you can scoop up the whole trilogy along with DLC for eight Gabendollars. This is the best eight bucks you'll ever spend if you love superhero things or text adventures.
I wish more games like these existed- this is worth every dollar you'll pay for it and every minute you'll put into it.

Gameplay: Dawn of War II greatly deviates from the RTS genre, of which Dawn of War I was the archetype. This game is not really an RTS - instead, it is Squad Command. You control a squad of four Space Marine units. As you progress through the game you unlock different types of units, and in the Chaos Rising DLC a Librarian is added. But the main point of the game is to destroy the enemy and push your way to the objective. For the Emperor!
Controls: Solid. There's key shortcuts for everything in true DoW style, which is great.
Interface: The strange thing in the game is the Squad setup interface. Each squad has four categories which can be increased at every level up - that's another thing, the units gain XP. By increasing the categories to certain points you unlock new abilities that differ per squad, so the Scouts' invisibility energy doesn't deteriorate while standing still, or Tacticals are immune to knockdown while using Tactical Advance. (Best of all is that all units except for the Scouts unlock Terminator armour down the line.) Let me tell you - this system is awesome. The strangeness I mentioned before comes from armour and weapons, which are picked up in the levels. You can sell them for XP (though not a lot, I don't recommend it unless getting rid of old crap), or you can give them to your troops who receive extra protection and bonuses. The problem is the items require a certain level (see above) to use, and the rate at which you get them seems to be out-of-sync, so you're getting Level 8 stuff while at Level 5. It's annoying.
DLC: Dow2 has two excellent DLCs - Chaos Rising, which is an additional campaign, and Retribution (actually a standalone), which introduces Last Stand. Last Stand is a wave-defense played with four human players. It's really fun. There's XP in there too, and you unlock weapons and armour as you go along. All of the other DLCs are extra wargear (weapons and armour), and the ability to play as different races.
Ut Summatim: Overall, the game is great. There aren't any glitches or bugs that I can notice, it runs smoothly. The story is...okay, but the actual gameplay is very fun, if not *that* replayable.

An emotional and unexpected experience
What Remains of Edith Finch is currently available in the Steam Summer Sale so I picked it up as it was in my recommended games. It has beautiful graphic quality and is set on a small island where you explore the abandoned house of your relatives an uncover their stories. The house looks much like the Weasley's house, The Burrow and has a unique way of navigating through a series of passageways and hidden doors. All the rooms are sealed as time capsules / shrines to each of the family members and as you navigate you can learn the story of each room's occupant and their unusual demise which is done via a flashback and small mini games in order to tell the tale.
The game is narrated from the perspective of a young girl named Edith who is the last surviving heir of the Finch family accompanied by atmospheric sounds from the dilapidated house and soothing music.
If you enjoyed games like Gone Home, Firewatch, The Wild Eternal or the Drizzlepath series this is a must have.
Pros
+ Unique story
+ Great atmosphere
+ Strong Narration
+ Music
Flashback mini games are unique and often funny
Cons
- Duration - I completed the game in 2.5 hours
- Game would have benefitted from item interation like Gone Home where examining and moving objects unlocked additional thoughts / memories.

XenoVerse is a great game to play. Even though XenoVerse 2 is already out, if you're looking for an fun-action, new story, and a good combat game, XenoVerse is the game you're looking for! (WARNING: For those who have not played the game yet, the following may contain spoilers.)
I have owned XenoVerse for 2 years and I have to say, this is a very fun game to play. From the new story to the character cutomization, they are tons of opitions in the game that allows you to take the game to it's full potential and do a whole lot more. Not only that, but the story is very new too, which is great because we have seen the same old, traditional Dragon Ball Z story that has been seen in games previously. The new story helps a lot with the depth and allows you to do more as well. This game is about a collapse in history which destroys the timeline and may potentially destroys the world, and you have to help Trunks and others to help save history and keep it safe. The story is very creative and is one that has not been seen before.
The gameplay has also taken some renovations. In previous games, you would usually play as regular characters such as Goku, Gohan, and others, but in this game, you finally get to create your own character, create your moveset, and play the game as YOU. You can even get trainers (Krillin, Piccolo, etc.) and have them take you under their wing. Pretty cool, eh? You can even cutomize the way your character looks, you can get moves, and overall you do anything you want! They are 5 races you can choose from: Majin, Sayians, Earthlings, Namekians, and Friezans. Even though Sayians is more popular, each race has their own weaknesses and strongnesses that can make battles look equal. Overall, the character cutomization is a good feature that I think helped the game a lot.
Even though XenoVerse is fun, however, they are some cons of the game. While the character cutomization is good and it was a great feature to include, the cutomization could've included a lot more opitions and could've been expanded. While the opitions appearance and name and voice helps, I believe Namco should've added a little bit more opitions so that we can really get to cutomize our characters to it's full potential (For example, changing how our attire would look and the way we would be able to fight, even though you can do that in the game, it would've been cool if it allowed us to choose different opitions to wear something else other than the default ones). The combat system could've also used a little bit more renovating. Also, you may get bored of XenoVerse if you play it too much. I played it too much in 2015, and I eventually got very bored of it in September/October, so for anyone who's planning on playing it, try balancing your time on XenoVerse. The missions/parallel quests can also get stale and boring. You can unlock items and stuff, but overall it can get stale fast and that's one of the problems of this game.
Overall, even though XenoVerse has it's flaws and isn't the best game, it is still a very fun game that I would recommend. The unique story, the new character cutomization, newly improved graphics, and more makes this game worth your time and money. They are also missions (even though they can get stale at points), new moves, and a whole lot more that makes this game worthy and even worth more of your time. While XenoVerse 2 is already out, if you're saving up for XenoVerse 2 and you're looking for another fun-paced, beat'em up game to play, XenoVerse should keep you busy for the next few months. So, whatcha waiting for? Go ahead and get yourself XenoVerse!

First I'd like to say that English isn't my native language so a lot of the words in the text were new/unfamiliar to me. However, I understood what the text is about and that's all that matters, right?
I've played the game for about 2-3 hours then I stopped because I had to eat and after that I didn't want to continue. I was hesitating if I should continue reading or not. I don't like leaving things unfinished so I continued reading the day after that and I am glad I did.
The story isn't short but it's not too long either. Took about 10 hours to get all the endings and check the bonus content. Keep in mind that I skipped the text that I'd already read. Yes, you can skip text which you already read. There are several endings (I won't mention how many exactly as I don't want to spoil anything). I enjoyed all of them, some more than others. Overall, I liked the story but I can't say it's one of the best visual novels I read as some people said. Not that I didn't like it, just... maybe because there were so many new words for me that I regretted not knowing English better. I hope that changes one day.
The characters are also nice. They are well-drawn which is a plus because I've played some visual novels where the characters are kinda not-so-well-drawn and some people would lose interest in the game because of that. I wouldn't though, because it's story that matters not how characters look. I liked almost all of the characters. I wanted this review to be spoiler-free but I will have to use a spoiler here. If you haven't played the game I suggest skipping this spoiler.
I liked the other characters. I don't have a favourite character so lets say I like them equally.
The music is great, really. I would like to be able to buy the original soundtrack as I enjoyed listening to one of the songs a lot. It's so peaceful and relaxing. Would be really nice to be able to listen to it not only while playing the game especially now that I finished the game and got all of the achievements...
The art is very good. I enjoyed all CGs (If you've played other visual novels you would know what that is, as I can't really explain it). I can't say a bad thing about the art as it's excellent. In my opinion everything is drawn in a way that pleases the eye.
The bonus content is something you should definitely check after/if you get all the endings. I found some of the stuff there hilarious and I think you will too. Not going to spoil anything more. One spolier is enough.
The achievements are many and unlock after some dialogs or when you reach an ending. Perfect game (no pun intended) if you're an achievement hunter/completionist like myself. It's not hard to 100% it but some people would do so in 1-2 hours by skipping all of the text, which is stupid if you ask me.
To sum up, I enjoyed playing/reading "CUPID" and, I am repeating myself here, but I am looking forward to buying the original soundtrack if it becomes available, which I really hope so. I am not going to give this game a score as I don't think that's necessary.
Also, I supported the dev by sending them money via PayPal. I did that because I think this game shouldn't be free or at least should have artbook/original soundtrack DLC(s). If you want to support them too just look at the community hub. There is a thread where the dev gives their PayPal donation link and one other link.
You know what the sad thing is? That there are flash-games (ltterally) which are free on some online sites but they have a price, here, on Steam. And it's something like 5 euros, which isn't much, but for a game that you can play for free somewhere else is a rip-off if you ask me. What I am basically saying is that there are visual novels on Steam that are worse than "CUPID" and are not free. I mean, this isn't fair. Life is unfair. But you can make it fairer by supporting the dev. I am kidding of course. I can't force you to do that, but if your a kind soul I am sure you will. :)
