Really hard to recommend this at the price, even on sale. Cost me £11.74 for 3 hours or so.
It's no Unfinished Swan. Instead of relying on a single original and fantastic idea it thrashes around with a dozen or so. You never know what's coming next, but when it does it is for the most part disconnected from everything else.
The central theme of mortality was kinda generic for this kind of psychological narrative and didn't really make sense at any level. I could happily have seen some of these scenarios and mechanisms developed further, but as it stands there was zero challenge in any of them, and therefore no feeling of accomplishment or control as I progressed.
If the idea was to bring a book to life then it should have been a better book. The player is a passenger on colourful rails. There is no exploration, no backtracking. It's linear all the way through, with nothing to collect and nothing to do except complete the task the story requires.
If you are a fan of non-game games like the Stanley Parabel or Dear Esther et al then you might love this. Goodness knows the reviews here are ecstatic, but clever graphics do not neccessarily mean value for money.
So, it's an E for effort from me.

Pros:
- Active and helpful community that will help you with any problems related to the game or not.
- Large sets of cards with many unique and fun effects
-  Rich tabletop RPG-like single player with over 10 hours of things to do. Very unique encounters can be seen with a lot of fun mechanics. And more hours of content coming in a future update. No paying required at all.
-Trading with players via mail or the auction house lets you deal with cards you don't want. Your cards have real value with the auction house.
- Tons of new content still on the way. Game is never "finished". New card set coming out in 1 week which will even up the draft playing field.
PvP tournament
Large community tournaments run 2x every weekend. Entirely free to enter and you can earn a lot of packs and platinum (even from just door prizes)
Cons:
- The use of Gold isn't very obvious unless you specifically look for it in the Auction House.

- No ranked ladder. You can play for free against random opponents but there is no incentive other than testing decks. The things that matter cost 100-500 platinum to enter (which is possible to earn in game) where by winning you can earn free packs to open or sell.
- If you lose all your platinum from failing tournaments, you have to grind PvE arena for gold in order to enter another tournament (takes a few hours, but you keep all the packs you open from the tournaments so it can be worth it anyways).

Reality TV shows are everywhere these days, you can't turn on the TV without seeing an advert for a show promising its contestants a shot at fame and fortune.
They all have a similar format too, there's the audition phase where we can laugh at the deluded souls who seem determined to share their lack of talent with the world.
Then there's the "review phase", the glut of contestants have been thinned down to those with some ability and we get to listen to their sob stories about their late dad, dog, hamster etc. It's all very tragic but it's ok, if they get through they'll be fine because they "really, really want it".
Finally we have the live shows featuring a mix of contestants with actual talent and a few novelty acts who make up for their lack of ability with a quirky polarising weirdness which will generate extra publicity and boost the shows ratings.
You also have the opportunity to "get involved" which means spending your own hard earned cash to vote for whichever narcissist tickles your fancy.
It's all good formulaic fun and it didn't do 'One Direction' or 'Kelly Clarkson' any harm.... did it?
Anyway, I sit and watch these shows and idly think to myself, I could do that.
Ok, so I can't sing, I'm not weird enough to be a novelty act... so maybe it's not the best idea but that doesn't stop me from wanting (really, really wanting) the fame and fortune (mostly the fortune) that comes with winning these things.
Then I think a little more about the real winners of these shows, the producers, the judges who "Didn't like the act... they loved it" and the ultimate winner, the manager of which ever vaguely talented narcissist or group of narcissists that managed to "win" the final.
It's the manager that'll pull in a percentage whilst riding the PR wave generated by the show itself.
They're the one that'll be laughing all the way to the bank, they don't have a public shelf life either, they'll be back on the show next year to exploit, sorry promote, the next batch fresh faced wannabees.
So I've come to the conclusion that being in a commercially successful group would be cool for my fifteen minutes of fame, but managing a band would be better for my bank account.
Now I've played plenty of tycoon games in my time, I've managed football teams, software companies, prisons and theme parks.
I'm a pretty good armchair tycoon so I'm sure I'd be brilliant at managing a band, but just to make sure I've started playing Rock God Tycoon, a rock group management simulation title by Emberwulf.
The first thing you should know is that Rock God Tycoon is, at the time of writing, still in early access but thankfully there's already plenty of game there for you to enjoy.
This isn't one of those "buy now, play later" titles, you'll be good to go as its finished downloading.
​And when it has finished downloading and you click the play button you're going to find yourself in a character creation screen, that's right, RGT not only lets you manage the band, you're a part of it too!
There are plenty of body bits to pick from to create your perfect rock look.
You'll have to make difficult decisions like which hairstyle rocks, which nose has the X-Factor and which mouth screams talent.
So after spending too long agonising over which set of eyes to choose for your rock star avatar (which you'll probably end up hiding beneath a pair of shades anyway) you'll throw on a leather jacket and some cargo pants, pick which role you'll play in your new band, vocalist, drummer etc. and then it's time to make the most important decision any group ever has to make, you need to come up with a name.
It's sounds like such a simple thing, but I spent longer than I'd care to admit trying to come up with something cool...  then I gave up and called the group "Rockwell".
Only it wasn't a group yet was it? it was still just a solo rock star wannabee wearing his shades and posing in his moms garage, but our leather clad, x-factor nosed hopeful is going to make it big one day (because he really, really wants it).
All he needs are some band mates to make up for his lack of musical talent and luckily he has a little money saved up to buy himself some new musical friends.
It's time to put your hand in your pocket, allocate a recruitment budget and see what the auditions bring in.
In Rock God Tycoon groups consist of 4 members, vocalist, lead guitar, drummer and bass guitar.
There's no flexibility here, it's a four piece or nothing, so if you'd got ideas about forming a sprawling rock choir or an a cappella indie-punk duo you can push those from your mind right now (and rightly so, they're both terrible ideas).
Anyway, after throwing some money at the audition process you'll be presented with a list of hopefuls each with a small bio (flavour text only) and a set of stats so you can judge their musical prowess and star quality.
You'll also get to see if they have any traits which might impact your choice, a substance abuser for instance might be too wasted to show up for rehearsals, still if they're cheap you might consider them, there's nothing stopping you from firing them later if it becomes a problem.
Once you've chosen your group of misfits it's time to decide what to do next.
You could (and probably should) work on writing a few songs, it'd be a good idea to have something to play when you show up to gigs.
The quality of the songs will depend the writing ability of which ever member (or members) you get to pen the melody.
Of course song writing takes time and just like in real life, there a bills to pay and most of your money will have already been spent on paying your fellow narcissists to hang out with you in the garage.
You can make money in a few ways, you can book paying gigs, although initially the venues that'll risk putting you on stage is limited, or you can go out busking, it might not be glamorous but it does bring in money (it might even get you a fan or two too!)
So you've written a few songs (which you get to name) and still have a little cash left in the bank.
It might be worth investing in some rehearsal time at a studio, you'll need to choose which songs you want to rehearse and which members you're going to take (it all costs money) but it'll be worth it in the long run, going to a gig unrehearsed isn't going to go down well with the critics.
When you feel ready, you'll pick your venue (there's only one that'll let you play when you first start out, but that'll soon change), you'll pick the date you want to perform and any PR you want to go along with the event, then you'll wait... maybe try to refine your musical skills or get in some more practice before the big day.
For the moment the gigs themselves are simulated, meaning that you don't get to see anything.
The gig will happen behind the scenes, you just get to read the critics reviews of the event which will likely tell you why your band sucks and which person or song sucked the most.
On the bright side, you're group will have gained experience (and fans) from the performance and might even perform a little bit better the next time around.

This is not a good rogue-like. Or a good rogue-like-like.
A rogue-like, in my mind, is defined by high - but not unfair - difficulty. As you progress through a rogue-like, you should become skilled in avoiding enemies, avoiding damage. A rogue-like should force you to become skilled, and you should enjoy yourself by conquering challenges as your skill increases.
A Wizard's Lizard has gotten that wrong.
You never need to become more skilled. You don't need to learn anything, in fact. I beat the game on my second attempt. Took less than two hours. Well, maybe the additional characters you unlock change things up?
No.
Unlockable characters are IDENTICAL to the base class; all that changes is starting equipment, which you'll trash within minutes of playing anyway.
Well, what else could keep you playing? Increased difficulty? Doesn't exist. Speedruns? Yawn. Achievements? Nothing challenging. Seriously. The achievements for WizLiz are nearly all achievable without significant changes in play or thought.
It's just...not a fun game.
Don't buy it.

It's Magic: The Gathering for the 21st centuy.
MTG players will be at home with its mechanics and be delighted by the new ones made possible only in a digital medium. I'm a big fan of the works that the Portal community has provided This, in my opinion, is certainly one of, if not, the best example of a fan made mod made for Portal 2. Here is a breakdown of my impressions:
GAMEPLAY: A
The game is effecitvely Portal, yes, but with a very unique twist. The Portal gun has been replaced with a Paint gun which creates the Mobility and Repulsion gels instead of the orange and blue portals. It's not a completely "out of the blue" idea considering the colour scheme remains intact, and effectively flips the ways the game works into an inverse example of itself. Instead of working out how to get gels from point A to point B using portals, you are instead attempting to work out how to use Portals A and B using your gels. This also opens the way for a more dynamic use of gels.
Several instances involve gels being constantly used in a running gauntlet, quickly changing from blue to orange in order to fling yourself across the room and while this creates an element of much needed mobility that Portal 2 lacked, this is also where things fell short at times. Too often I'd be caught out by some awkward bounces to the far left for seemingly no reason, or massive dramatic jumps just wouldn't quite work out until the third or fourth try - the novelty wore off at points, but not to an ultimate detriment.
I would have liked to see more elements working in conjunction rather than separating tests into "ones where you go fast" and "ones were you use portals." The best puzzle games combine everything you've learnt so far, and at times I felt like a lot of things I had just learnt weren't actually going to be used in the end. That said, the option for community based maps may rememdy this depending on who's clever enough to make something even more mind-bending. And as we've seen, I doubt there will be much issue finding someone eager enough to develop these ideas.
STORY: B+
As we're dealing with a puzzle game based off of a pre-existing puzzle game there is not a whole much to discuss. The mod is first and foremost about the new puzzles but does have the semblance of a subtextual story presented through "Nigel's" quips. He talks through a lot of the regulations necessary in testing subjects as it is his first time processing Aperture Science Test Subjects. It starts off a little stilted and awkward, but nothing felt forced or attempted to ham itself up in an attempt to combat the original. What I thought was particualrly clever was the way it gently started creating a theme of commercialisation and corporatisation through an increased amount of product placement. Nothing terribly profound, but a very nice and subtle hint at something more.
PRESENTATION: A
Using a lot of the original game's resources, it would be ridiculous to say that the game is anything other than great to look at. That said, there becomes a shift two thirds into the mod that creates biomes of its own, and without spoiling anything, is incredibly clever, visually stimulating, and just an overall fantastic touch. I would be more than satisfied remaining within the confines of Aperture Science as I know it, but the team behind Tag have gone above and beyond what it necessary to create a visual identity of its own. And it shows.
My primary gripe is with the voice acting. It's not bad by any stretch. The character of Nigel is endearing and awkward without being an idiot like Wheatley, and at times passive-aggressive without being malicious like GLaDOS, but the presentation of the lines falters when there are faults in clarity and diction. I really wanted to hear and understand what the character at to say. I liked him, but sometimes it wasn't very easy to make out exactly what he's saying which left me more disappointed than bothered.
OVERALL: A
Whether you're looking for something new, fresh, and exciting without 'breaking' what you know and love about Portal, or just looking for the absolutely astonishing talent the Portal fan community has on offer, this is the mod for you. It's fast, stimulating, and just all around fun.

I liked the presentation of this game when I first started it: a WW2 game all about sniping and stealth! I appreciate games that embrace a more niche appeal as opposed to mass appeal where everybody wins easily because the mechanics are streamlined to the point that the gameplay lacks depth. Such mass appeal games tend to lack personality in my opinion: you could substitute one for any of a dozen others and be forgiven for forgetting which one you were playing. Sniper Elite has personality and some depth to its mechanics, but the execution of the whole package didn't satisfy me.
The most important deal-maker/breaker for this game with most people is going to be the controls. They're weird. When prone and crawling, your character (Karl) is slow but he responds to your keyboard commands readily. When crouching or walking, though, Karl has a startup time before he moves or turns. He moves the way a semi truck drives: slow to accelerate and slow to stop once moving, with turning being pretty limited and clunky without extra room. Another analogy: Karl doesn't walk, he ice skates. I'm guessing the developers were trying to capture how human beings build up momentum before reaching top speed, but in gameplay it feels awkward. I took the time to learn and adapt to the controls, but they're not comfortable overall.
The missions are very long when I compare them against most FPS games nowadays. Some missions span up to five different wide-open levels, and your saves are limited. I actually like the idea of limiting saves, but overall the difficulty wasn't quite tough enough to pressure me into improving my skills enough to avoid spending my save files. Sniper Elite is a dynamic difficulty game, so it changes itself to suit the player's skill as you play. I chose hard difficulty (Sharpshooter, I think it's called) from the beginning because that allowed me to turn on all of the game mechanics like bullet drop and wind, etc. and I wanted to experience the game as I imagined the developers intended.
The game permanently stuck me on max difficulty ("Sniper Elite" difficulty) after the first level of the very first mission, but I didn't realize this until I was a ways into the second mission. I didn't notice because the game didn't seem any harder. Even with bullet drop, wind, max difficulty A.I., etc. sniping is very forgiving in this game. You can mess up your shot multiple times and the enemies might run and hide, which means you mostly lose time trying to draw a new bead on them, or they might try to shoot back at you. But even at max difficulty, one or two enemies at a medium to long distance won't take you out very quickly, and you can just fire at will until you hit them and they're dead. So much for needing to flee and find a new vantage point once you've been discovered.
For as much lip service as the tutorial's narrator pays to how the player must “think like a sniper,” I've solved numerous situations by just grabbing a machine gun and mowing down enemies. I don't even use stealth half the time anymore because the enemies can't stop me consistently unless an entire platoon is firing at me. Or, more likely, the objective for my current mission will fail automatically if I don't use stealth. Otherwise, I play as G.I. Karl, All-American badass. Karl doesn't need to line up the perfect shot because Nazis and NKVD soldiers are rendered impotent shots by the burning flame of democracy in Karl's chest. I've been chucking grenades and even wasted a valuable rocket launcher shot on some dawdling enemies for fun at one point because there wasn't enough reprisal from the game to dissuade me.
I almost feel like I've been rewarded for my blatant aggression instead of punished for not using more stealth.
In fact, at certain scripted points in the game (there are many) enemies will not pop out of an area you need to progress through unless you get so close that stealth is nearly compromised without immediately running away after triggering the event flag. I would think that I should be able to take advantage of the level design and pick off any inconvenient enemies from afar while moving around the perimeter of the area, but some enemies don't spawn until you actually try to move deeper into the level. I assume the developers did this to keep players on their toes, but it feels antithetical to a sniping game. Example: If two Nazis are going to come sprinting, guns blazing, through an alleyway just as I'm halfway down it after I killed everybody in the area and carefully belly crawled for 50 yards to said alleyway just for extra precaution, what's a sniper like me to do? I whip out my MP-44 and become G.I. Karl, All-American badass, instead. Die, Nazi scum.
Should you buy this game? Sure, if you're a fan of WW2 games and open to something more slow-paced and less Call of Duty. I did have fun with the game when it took its stealth seriously and punished me for breaking cover, and when it rewarded me for taking down enemies in single, well-placed shots from afar. On the other hand, don't buy this game if you're intolerant of odd control schemes or looking for a really challenging sniping game. There's some reward for getting a hang of bullet drop, but you're not punished much for being a scrub either so you may feel cheated for trying to master the mechanics when goofing off as G.I. Karl works just as well much of the time.
Overall, I don't think the game lives up to its potential, but it's alright for what it is.

If you're interested in purchasing this game, chances are you've probably seen someone play it and use the "create your own superstar" feature. The truth is... this feature is amazing. WWE 2k17 was my first foray into a wrestling game since the SNES, as I had stopped watching wresting in the late 90s. You can completely customize your character from their looks, costume, and customize everyone one of their wrestling moves from a list with hundreds of moves.
The most fun part of it is making your own wrestlers, shows, arenas, etc, using the feature to upload your own art.
But this is where an otherwise pretty fun game gets ruined.
2K's servers are apparently monitored by an automated system which decides what is offensive and what isn't. So even if you NEVER play online and everything you upload is for your personal use at home, you can be permanently banned from the image upload feature and every other online feature. The thing is, you can be banned if whatever you upload is completely unoffensive and meets their ruleset, as this automated system can easily interpret something offensive and is not fool-proof. This is what happened to me. After enjoying this game for a year and putting over 200 hours in it (yes, I know some people have much more), I was banned without warning for something a bot interpreted as offensive. Initially I thought it was a bug as there was no notice or warning, so I reached out to 2K's abysmal tech support, only to find out after 2 days of troubleshooting that I was banned indefinitely for this, with no help at all. I then searched Google, only to find out that enough other players had experienced this that there had been stories written about it on some gaming sites a year ago. Sadly, I never knew about this, and I'm sure if you're considering purchasing this game you haven't either. People have been banned for uploading a normal, "safe for work" portrait of two women, for example.
So I know what you're thinking. WWE 2K18 is out now, but it's too expensive and you're considering getting 2K17 because it's a bit cheaper. Well don't. Because it could be you who puts 200 hours into this game and then all of a sudden you're randomly banned in the middle of making characters for no reason. So then you're thinking, well I'll just get this and not worry about all the customization and play with the regular WWE wrestlers. Well guess what, customization and making the game truly your own is the only reason to buy this, because lets face it, the AI in this game is pretty mediocre, and the wrestlers of today are pretty bland. The rankings in my career are pretty garbage, you can kick in the #1 contender's face in 10 different matches and you'll be lucky to move from 6 to 5 in the contenders rankings. There's only so many times you can destroy *insert bland wrestler here* before you yern to make your own league with interesting wrestlers and shows in My Universe. Also, with every new update the game becomes more unstable. It rarely crashed when I first purchased it a year ago, now I can't even do a full 30 person Royal Rumble without the game dying 3 wrestlers (or less) into it.
So yeah. Save your money and hope someday that the WWE license will pass to a better company. One that at least lets you upload images to your own game for home use, and not rely on their overly complicated and ban happy website way of doing it. Oh, and by the way, from the looks of it 2K18 is the exact same game, right down to the same hair styles available to you in the customization mode, but with a little bit of polish.

I've decided to start the Sniper Elite Franchise as well, as it was on heavy sale. I've missed the WWII settings, it's been a while since I've played a game set in those times.
Sniper Elite is a Third Person Shooter, with sniping sessions obviously in First person. You can approach your missions any way you like but the action-assault approach is very heavily penalized, if not almost prohibited sometimes. Stealth approach is often the most advisable, you can get behind enemies, distract them with diversive noises, hide in shadows or ruins, or even shooting while there are some bombings to prevent enemies soldiers from spotting you. Soldiers have a really good sight and an incredible hearing... Maybe excessive. Still more realistic than the classic metal gears view cones... XD
Your arsenal includes your main weapon, the sniper rifle, a silenced gun and various rifles or machine guns. In your inventory you can count on some dynamite, time bombs, wire traps and a rock... A simple stone to create a diversion and distract enemies. XD
Your missions vary from assaults, taking contacts, rescuing prisoners, ambushes and so on, and the settings are quite nice, ranging from bombed cities, trenched parks, factories and so on, and the single playr campaign is quite long, so it will keep you busy for a while.
The soundtrack is not exactly outstanding but is a pleasant background, with some dynamic interactions when approaching an enemy or when approaching more enemies, or when you're being spotted.
The game is quite old but the graphics is not that bad considering its release date. What I don't like are the characters movements, they're quite rigid and kind of... confused, I can't tell when he's crouched or standing, nor it doesn't crawl naturally as he keeps on turning when you move the mouse. Still it's a clever system, where you can increase or decrease its movement speed to also reduce the noise produced while moving.
There is also a difficulty system which allows you to set your games in many details, beside the AI such as gravity (for long distance sniping), explosion radius and so on.
Even considering the campaign and the story behind the missions, Sniper Elite isn't an outstanding title as there's no particular innovation, no involvement in the story nor any outstanding visual or musical parts. BUT it still is a nice title as, besides some very minor graphic glitches, there's nothing really wrong about it.

BugZy's Review: Doors - Bacon is wonderful
The following is my opinion.
Mmm, bacon.
Doors is a superb atmospheric logic puzzler with a simplistic art style developed and published by Calvin Weibel, fueled by bacon. You have to use the power of deduction and true or false facts given to choose which portal - or 'door' - to go through. One or more doors leads to bacon, the others death and sometimes, a door leads to an office.
If you have played before and know most of the correct doors it'll be a breeze, but it makes up for that by making your first time very difficult, especially if - like me - you weren't expecting something quite so challenging. Get your brain working, because you'll need it!
It plays very smoothly, a few frame rate hiccups every so often but nothing so bad as to be game-breaking. There is also no HUD but in all honesty, Doors has no reason to have it.
Despite being simplistic, the game is visually brilliant with the audial ambience just as great. One moment you're staring into the void of black and grey, trying to figure out which door takes you one step closer to your delicious victory and never-ending supply of bacon, the next, you're wandering through an office as though you own the place. The sound effects add to the mysterious atmosphere as well, sounding somewhat like you have entered the stomach of a dinosaur.
Overall, the game is a great concept brought to the world using an almost perfect balance of atmosphere and gameplay for a puzzler like this and if you enjoy games of the puzzle genre, I highly recommend you buy it.
I give it 9 out of 10 juicy rashers of bacon.

As someone who enjoys rogue-likes and FTL I thought this game would be quite fun.  I love story driven games, and I love super difficult games.  This game though is horribly flawed.  The most infuriating thing about this game is running out of a resource, finding a planet that has it, and then getting less from it then it took to even reach the planet.  If I go to a gas giant, I expect ♥♥♥♥ing gas, not levels of hydrogen so low that I was actually better off never going in the first place.  Sure rogue-likes are supposted to be random and luck based, but when this happens 2 or even 3 times in a row and end your play through, its no longer about difficulty as much as it is straight up stupid.
The fact that everything also requires its own special element and you will almost never find said element when you need it nor ever have the cargo space to carry 1/5th of them for future use makes the game incredibly grindy while also being too luck based to grind in the first place.  This is also my experience on Easy mode, f$%k if id ever try the harder modes if easy alone is not enjoyable to me.
The second problem I have with this game is the story.  The aliens you meet are boring and their dialog is always the same, with very slight differences.  The hundreds of events you run into when jumping to a new sun could have easily been incorporated into the alien life meetings, but they wern't which was a huge mistake.  After you get whatever technology you need for your "mission ending" there is no longer a point to talk to aliens, which devaluates what should be a very important aspect of a game that pits you as being very alone.  I should be alone because everything is foreign to me, not because the backwater hillbillies on every planet speak gibberish and toss me useless Omega or space wasting technologies I give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about.
Lastly this game has very few endings for a rogue-like that needs to boast replayability, and most of the endings are poorly designed and give you a very poor taste and bad memories of the game afterwards.  A game like this should have endings that are memorable, and few of them are with the others feeling like they robbed you of your playthrough.  With 0 bonuses for completing a playthrough and a lack of diversity in the game making multiple playthroughs feel more like a chore then an enjoyable experience you feel like you are better off just youtubing the rest of the endings instead of forcing yourself to grind them out (which I did for the endings I didnt recieve yet).
This game saddly feels like something that would play great on a phone, but is ill suited for the PC in its current stage.  It has a lot of promiss, but it feels horribly unfinished.  I get this bad feeling that this game needs to be put right back onto early access, not have a "new edition" title added to it.  Go play FTL or Darkest Dungeon if you want a fun rogue-like experience, this game has a lot of growth left to it.

I've been a fan of the Warhammer 40,000 Universe for many years now (even playing the tabletop games for a number of years). The Dawn of War Franchise has been without a doubt on of the most fun RTS series I've played, I'd fully recommend the first Dawn of War for the storyline alone, and though the subsequent games in the first series on the whole did away with such a strong narrative, the gameplay they gave was well worth the money. I'd also say to most people looking at DoW II to get the first Dawn of War just for the background which while not important at all in the second series, is just nice to have there.
Now, for those who have played the first series, be prepared for a difference in game styles in relation to this. During the campaign thee is NO base building, you can't bring in new squads/vehicles throughout the game as you only have a maximum of 4 units deployed (though you can replenish loses easily enough or revive them if the squad is wiped out so that is not an issue). Even in skirmish/multiplayer the armies do not get as huge as the first game, because for example a tactical squad is only 4 men or a devastor/assualt squad only 3. However, this does not detract from the fun of the game. The maps are the perfect size, combined with the more tactical playstyle of needing to use cover and abilities well to make this downgrade in size of armies workable without issue. There is more customazation involved in this, especially during the campaign where you can upgrade your squads and specialize them, making an assault squad for example less mellee orientated but a more mobile tactical squad, and upgrade their armour and weapons through drops during missions.
I'd honestly recommend any War40k fan who enjoyed DoW1 to get DoW2 if you're not sure. Even if you dont get the expansions it would be worth your time and effort. Only wait for it to be on sale as £20 for a game a few years old now is too steep and £15 at most should be its cost.

What would be a simple and promising puzzle game tries too hard to make itself interesting outside of the puzzles that it weighs down the entire experience.
I bought this game because it reminded me of a riddle I really enjoy, but was ultimately disappointed in the product. The puzzles themselves are not always bad, but the game as a whole is poorly constructed and feels like it tries too hard in too many areas that don't add anything to the experience people are here to enjoy - puzzle solving.
The puzzles are simple. You're presented with a group of doors, each door has a sign above it with some text above it, and you have to use the text to figure out with door to go through. In addition, before each set of doors there is some text on the ground that gives further information you need to solve the puzzle (usually telling you how many of the doors are lying to you). This is a fine idea and can lead to some satisfying puzzles, but the way it's presented has some things to complain about.
Firstly the wording. The door you want to go through is described as "leading to bacon" (a poor, meme-like attempt at humor I wish I could say only appears in this once) and the doors you don't want to go through "lead to death". The doors where the text above them is telling the truth is described as "correct" while the doors that lie to you are "incorrect". This wording is confusing, and they never explain exactly how all the wording works. They tell you bacon is good and death is bad, but they don't explain that correct and incorrect refers to the text above the door being true or false, rather than the correct or incorrect doors to walk through. Knowing exactly how this wording works is absolutely essential to solving almost every puzzle, which makes it the puzzles seem frustrating, unfair and somewhat random until you figure out their unintuitive wording scheme on your word. All to include a joke about bacon. Clearly the designers had their priorities straight on this one.
This all could have been solved if they did away with the bacon/death thing and used correct and incorrect to indicate which door you wanted to go through, then true and false to describe which doors are lying to you. This makes sense, and probably doesn't even need explaining to most people. Just establish that to progress you go through the correct door, and the rest explains itself. If a blue door says "The blue door is incorrect" you know that's not the door you want to go through. But then if another door says "The blue door is false" you know the blue door is lying to you. And so the puzzles begin, with no need for explanations and minimal confusion. It would also help with the text on the ground before each set of doors. They might say something like "One door leads to bacon, all other doors lead to death." But with bacon being substituted for correct, it could simple read "One door is correct." There's no need to explain that the rest are incorrect because correct and incorrect are opposites, and people can intuitively figure out for themselves that "all other doors are incorrect."
Now, with that simple poor use of words aside, the puzzles aren't bad. My only other gripe is that the game's idea of difficulty is the number of doors a puzzle uses, so as you go, the puzzles begin having more and more doors. This isn't entirely a bad thing, but there are two things about this I do't like.
Firstly, since this game is played from a first person perspective, keeping track of what all the doors say means walking around constantly and looking at each one individually. This works just fine at first, but as the game progresses and the number of doors goes up, it's honestly more challenging just to keep track of everything than it is to actually solve the puzzle.
Secondly, Some of the most interesting and thought provoking puzzles are the simplest ones with the fewest. They certainly seem easier, since you don't have to keep track of what 10-20 doors say at a time, but they're interesting and more rewarding. it would have been nice to see them break up the string of huge multi-door puzzles with a really interesting smaller puzzle every so often.
(It is worth mentioning I didn't finish this game, so it's possible they actually do some of this later in the game. If they do, good on them, but I honestly doubt it.)
Now, if that's all I had to complain about, I'd probably have enjoyed this game a bit more. But no. There's visuals and atmosphere to consider as well, and here's where this game really falls short.
Most of the time, the game takes place in a black and white environment with a minimalist art style. These places actually look quite nice. It's atmospheric without being distracting, which is perfect for a puzzle game like this. It also helps the colored doors to stand out, which helps you find the next puzzle once you're teleported to the next area. Of course, this wouldn't even matter if they didn't make you walk so far after each puzzle for seemingly no reason, but whatever.
However much I like this art style, it really clashes with other parts of the game, most notably the "bacon" gag. For a game that isn't above using a cheap meme of a joke in the core of the puzzle solving, the serious-toned and mysterious vibe the environments gives off seems like an odd choice to compliment that (and really, if one of the two has to go, it should definitely be the bacon).
Worse than this is the portions of the game that attempt to... You know, I'm not even sure what the intent was. Was it trying to have a story? Make things more mysterious? Add to the atmosphere? Whatever they tried to do, it failed.
There are parts of the game where weird trippy stuff happens for no discernible reason. My first encounter with this was when some random text appeared in the sky but disappeared before I could read it, and shortly after the whole screen "glitched out" as if I was inside a computer, and suddenly I'm walking down a long white hallway. Then I somehow end up in an office building? The hallways of the office building have no sense of direction and are littered with posters that try to be funny with little success. It feels like I'm playing The Stanley Parable, except there's no narrator and it's written by a Facebook account that does nothing but repost relatable jokes. Some of the posters are kind of amusing, but most of them just seem to think random equals funny. (HaPpY PlAtYpUs DaY!!! . . . No, one of the signs actually said. I wish I was making it up.) But even the jokes that stand up on their own (A.K.A. don't make you cringe) are not clever or witty, or even relevant. After wandering the hallway of bad jokes and unnecessary turns, I stumbled across a room with some sort of sci-fi test tube looking container. It was open, so I walked in. It closed, lowered me into darkness, and the I appeared at the next puzzle.
Can... Can somebody explain to me what the point of any of that was? What does that add to the game? What does it add to the experience? Why is it in the game? It is really hard to resist the urge to use caps lock right now in order to better convey my sheer bewilderment and confusion at the inclusion of the sequences in the game. If the rest of what I talked about doesn't ruin the game for me, this absolutely does. It takes me right out of the experience and leaves me more confused and annoyed than at all interested in the game.
In the end, this was a simple idea that tried too hard in too many unnecessary places and ruined what could be a fun puzzle experience. If you can get past this, you might have a good time, but I personally find it unenjoyable overall.

Although love is the overall theme, what really sucked me in initially was the suspense and feeling of slow creeping terror.  The atmosphere is wonderful -- writing and art are not perfect but almost always great, and what more can you ask from a free game?  They work together to do an excellent job of building tone, creating a sense of gradual mounting tension, and really evoking the feeling of a whole world with a few static images.
I got ending 3 the first time through despite doing my very best to make nice decisions, and once I'd finished reading that I felt like I needed a bath, in the best possible way.  There they were, this character doing something unequivocably evil, and yet in a certain sense I couldn't even blame them for it.  I was sucked in by the perversity and the mystery of it all and immediately had to dive back in for more.
If I were to voice any criticisms, they would mainly be:
1) From the author's notes bonus I gather that the main writer assumes the meaning of the title "Cupid" would be obvious once you've finished the endings, but I was reading that with four endings under my belt and the idea hadn't even occurred to me in the slightest.  I assumed it was supposed to be more of a general reference to love and matchmaking.  If this was an idea the team wanted to convey to readers or thought was important, I think they unfortunately did a poor job.
2) The summary blurb for the game in the Steam Store pushes the idea of the player directly stepping into the role of Mother, but this is very misleading.  "Mother" is very much a specific character of her own with a specific personality, goals, etc. that you the player do not get to affect very much.  One of my big pet peeves in visual novels and text adventures is when you get presented with "false choices" where nothing is available on your list of options that's remotely like what you actually want to say.  This game had some fairly egregrious examples of that, particularly being forced to be mean to Rosa and then having the game chide me for my bad attitude in one ending even though, given the option, I would never have said any of those mean things at all.  This irritating problem could have been avoided by finding some way to include Mother that didn't require her to be the POV character.
Overall however, these are small issues at the end of the day.  This game would be well worth your time at $20 or $30, let alone at the price of totally free.  Go check it out.

HEX is unfinished. It's fun. It's playable. It's even compelling. But it's unfinished.
The Kickstarter promised dungeons galore, PvE adventures, guilds, set bonuses, raids, double backs, and more. All of that is missing, despite it's now "launched" status. If you know the rules for Magic, and enjoy it, then you can hop right into HEXand feel at home. The drafting is a blast, the tournament scene is killer.

I look forward to what this game could become in the future.

I really wouldn't recommend this game. I'm a huge advocate and connoisseur (as pretentious as it can sound sometimes) of games based around story and character aka my bread and butter, but the narrative here I just feel isn't up to par with its competition, nor does it give us a reason to care about the characters. I'll try to break this down into an easy to follow format so bare with me. The gameplay is creative, and the interactive narrative bits are actually fun and interesting to see, that's no my issue here, and for narrative driven games I hope this becomes more of a standard. What I do have great issue with is how the game sets you up to try and solve, or figure out the mystery behind the family's deaths (spoilers to follow) but you quickly learn that their deaths are mundane, and in fact it's their own faults that each of them die, not an unusual or supernatural force, or anything remotley similiar which the game sets you up to think is the cause, stated by Edith herself that the house felt "weird" and she had always been afraid of it, and how the family talk about some "creature" or "manifestation" that plagues them. If anything, the family does little to help and support each other throughout their history (aside say Edie and Sven) and most of the issues could be solved if they'd come together instead of continually drifting apart. Some characters are more relatable than others, but I assume this relies on whomever you yourself can relate or find something in common with them, for me that was Walter, but I won't go into that. It also feels rushed in some places, as where certain characters have full on sequences where you have them to interact with, others are wiped away quickly before you ever get to known more about them, aside how their room is designed. The story, at its core, is essentially a self fullfilling prophecy, if you think your family is cursed, then something cursed will happen to you, and the curse is blamed rather than the family or your own actions, as a person who came from a disfunctional household with many issues, I find offense to this and I'm sure those who do come from such environments will feel the same as to how simplistically they portray this. Now I'll go ahead and close with some of the more positive aspects of the game itself, as I mentioned before the gameplay (for a walking sim/narrative) is interesting and fun to go at, the voice acting is really well done and truley helps to flesh out the characters in a meaningful way that the story just doesn't. I'd also commet on the price, but I recieved this as a gift, but in short I think it needs to be cheaper than what it is. Overall I'd rate the game a decent 5.5/10, it's not a "bad" game per say, it just falls really short in many areas, and is a mundane experience overall.

Basically this is Magic the Gathering Online done right with an added free PVE campaign.
I've been playing MtG for a long time, and have fond memories of the Shandalar PC game
. So when the Kickstarter talked about dungeons and a PVE campaign, I was in.
Hex does a lot of things right: accessible PVE campaign with an easy way to grind (PVE) cards, a well-done game UI, crazy-fun cards (its digital nature allows Hex to go for more wacky things than MtG which has to work as a paper game), a working free player / paying player economy and excellent cheap (compared to MtGO) drafts.
The community is awesome, check out the Hex Twitch streams if you haven't, I regret following them way too late. Who doesn't like giveaways?
Don't play this if you expect to compete in high level PVP and don't plan to spend money. You will most likely have to invest some $$$ to start playing competitive PVP unless you really like grinding.
There are still some Kickstarter promises that haven't been delivered on. But Hex has steadily released new features and content. I expect them to keep doing so; and hope for an increased pace.

Day of Defeat: Source is a fun, straightfoward, WWII themed, team-based FPS.
And there isn't that much more to it, to be honest.
There's six different classes to play as, each with their own unique weaponry.
Matches can range from short to absurdly long depending on the teams, and overall the gameplay is a bit slower paced than the rest of Valve's games, so a lot of teamwork is required, especially when friendly fire is enabled.
It might take a while to get used to the stamina bar and each weapon's accuracy, but I think that's just part of the experience.
The community can also be a bit toxic, but most of the people I've met are actually pretty cool.
If you're looking for a simple and fun FPS game, then you should probably give Day of Defeat: Source a try when it's on sale.
It's a surprisingly good time waster.

Should you buy this: Yes.
Should you buy it on sale: even more so yes.
Do you remember "Rock Star Ate My Hamster"(1988) by Codemasters? If answer is still yes, you have already bought this.
There's a caveat thou;
Its not quite there yet. Its early access, its missing features, it has bugs, its a work in progress. But it really doesn't matter. A beautifully coded framework is already in there, and developers are listening keenly to feedback. Nearly in real time! I'm lovin' it!
I feel this is the best chance you are ever gonna get replaying that sweet nostalgia from the early 90s. Playing this for 7 hours my initial evening I was for the first time in almost 10 years so enthralled by the potential of a game it was hard to turn it off without visiting just one more venue. Just one more city... Game has that "one more turn"-feeling.
For the uninitiated; the gameplay consists of being a manager for a group of 4 budding starlets. You pick the lineup, you chose their daily activities and you send them out on the road for that sweet sweet glory of rock'n'roll hall of fame. Without ever actually gettin' to write "rock'n'roll" or "gettin'" in the game anywhere. But I digress;
Exactly how much depth will be added by the developers until the game is done is too early to say. Something tells me the more of you buying the game; the greater the chance of this game surpassing "Rock Star Ate My Hamster" in depth and features.
Game is my pick for management/tycoon indie game 2016. Being November, I think it won't be surpassed at this point.
Bonus: the music is awesome! The loop is short at the moment, but I wouldn't mind it being 24 hours of pure instrumental metal joy. I was listening to Dark Tranquillity when I loaded up the game, I didn't even notice initially that I had turned them off and the game audio on. Devs! Get jamming with more tunes! (oh, and I notice on almost every song where the inspiration is derived from. I'm lovin' that too!)

This game is like a piece of ore - it's very crude and hard, but if you can process it, you will have something valuable. In this case - experience of having played the game. Which is not easy to do. You probably won't be able to play this game without some patches and mods. Good thing the community surrounding this game has got you covered. Nevermind the obsolete software and hardware that is required to play this old gem, with a bit of tinkering i bet you'll run this. But the game itself is not really easy to play. It has probably the weirdest controls i've seen in my life. But they can be got used to, although the control scheme had stopped me from playing in the past. Some things are cryptic, some things are counter-intuitive and some are downright broken. The bugs are big parts of the game. And you need to save very frequently not only because the game is hard and unforgiving, but because some glitch can wreck your playing real hard. Overall feeling of the game is charmingly unpolished. Personally i love this intimate feeling of unrefinedness. You might not. For it's time it's really impressive what the creators were able to achieve.  But it can be obvious sometimes they were too ambitious. For example - the whole game's dialogue is voiced. But there were only a few people for hundred of characters, so the main hero were delegated to sound like a goof. I played with the guidance of my DEAR friend, so i did not fall for many of the game's traps and i finished it in about 26 hours. So it may be true that you can get the 100 hours of gameplay listed in the description, if you play thorough enough.

Really good RPG game - the big difference is that monsters do not spawn. It feels FAR from the other RPG where you just have a click-fest of 100000 buffs and farming the same monsters 1000000 times. The combat system is really simplistic and offers large room for the skilled players to show their skill, and still is very friendly with players who are not good with games. No respawn, once you die you have to load a saved game, but you can save anytime. You can kill almost any NPC, however I strongly suggest you don't, as you may find yourself unable to continue the storyline! It also gives you room to explore almost any area including near-end game areas, without affecting the main storyline much.

The steam page accurately refers to it as "interactive fiction" with some heavy resource juggling. Instead of any sort of combat (none of the ships you can use have weapons of any sort) you'll be presented with a dialog box with two, maybe three or rarely more choices, usually each choice affecting your resources in some way. That's where the similarities to FTL start and end really, if you mess up and run out of any one of your resources, you're screwed, and this being screwed can happen at random even if you're careful in some cases.
Interestingly there are multiple ways to end the game, with wildly different outcomes; its very much a choose-your-own-adventure type game with lots of text and some nice comicbook-esque visuals. It was originally conceived as a mobile game and it shows, but (much like another mobile game I liked a lot, Plague Inc) its kept patched with the occasional new feature, he's actually adding an "easy mode" apparently, since death or failure in this game really can be sort of arbitrary.
For the people on my friendlist who played and liked stuff such as Sunless Sea or Long Live The Queen, this is the sort of thing you'd likely enjoy.

The game sets you up to fail.  I've played about seventy-one minutes and I've given up.  The small cargo hold in combination with the constant self-defeating need to refuel and repair drag me down every playthrough.  To be clear, you need to repair everytime you go to a gas giant, where you go to refuel.  And getting the components for repair requires you to land on a planet, and both taking off and landing require fuel.  Why can't I get hydrogen and helium anywhere but gas giants?  Isn't hydrogen the single most common element in the universe?  To top it off, installing technology and upgrades onto your ship to make the game easier requires cargo space: but you have very little of that.  Each unit of space can hold either one upgrade, or up to twenty units of a single element.  You need a variety of elements in order to get different upgrades, you need a steady supply of iron and helium/hydrogen for the refuel/repair grind (or should I say...  timesink), and you need certain techs in your hold just to stay afloat.  Some will say that you're supposed to recycle upgrades you don't immediately need, but that just means you need to retain a wider variety of elemental components in order to constantly manufacture the different upgrades necessary for each situation.  A variety of components which are unlikely to all fit in your hold if you mean to keep a decent supply of fuel.
It's clear that the game is designed to kill you so that you have to keep starting over before making any progress.  Which means you play more.  But why would I play something that's just frustrating?  No thanks.

This Rogue-Like game is not about fighting, it is about resource management, planning and priorities. This makes it unique and great in this sea of Rogue-Likes. Even though there is no completionist bonus, if you get that one perfect run, going all the way to New Earth, undaunted by resource shortages, you know you have done it.
I would say if you like strategy games - or puzzles - and Rogue-Likes, this game is for you. See it through to all four ends and complete it!
That being said, the one achievement that I miss, is the one based on luck "Junkfood". This is my main critic here, a luck achievement should never be so rare, that it forces you to play a game without a goal until it sours. That is bad design.

TL;DR: The game is dark and the player is used in an original way with lots of varied endings but the story is linear and there's not enough depth to some of the main characters.
God, I was so torn about this game and I'm truly starting to dislike the whole yes/no only system.
I finally decided on no because of the overwhelmingly positive rating the game has. To clarify: the game is not gonna suffer from this review, especially since it's free.
I really believe that this game deserves a chance from most VN fans and if you have a few hours to kill, I can easily suggest that you give it a try, your money won't be wasted, trust me! Your time, however...well, that depends.
I'll mention the issues first so we can end on a positive note.
Cons:
- The game is linear. When not considering the endings, the rest of the game has a very straight path, I would have liked a little more branching during the story line,  nothing major just that some events were a little more varied.
- Some characters are not sympathetic. You're given little reason to like them or care what happens to them, outside of some rather cliché attributes. If anything you almost cheer if someone dies. *cough*
*cough*.
- The ending is not a natural conclusion. This ties in with the linearity, there is not enough of a change throughout the story to justify the final 'snap' in the protagonist's personality one way or the other, it's just too sudden.
- The game's text/choice ratio is off. There are huge parts of nothing but reading then huge parts with a lot of choices and that throws off the balance as if they suddenly remembered, 'oh, right, the player!'.
- The endings. This is a personal gripe with 'hidden', 'true', 'secret', etc. It bugs me when an ending can only be reached if you play the game so and so many times, with no in-game reason for WHY.
- The genre. This is nitpicking, I know, but this kind of game is just not an RPG, there's too little agency. I know that technically EVERY game is an RPG but for people who assign a certain meaning to that genre, this just doesn't cut it.
Pros:
- The story. In itself it's interesting, it's dark and psychological and I wanted to know what happened next.
- The naughty bits. They are very well written and despite what some say I found that they fit in the context.
- The endings. Extremely varied and take a lot of choices into consideration and it's interesting to try out the extremes.
- Dark theme, The dark parts are well explored and the overall setting never strays from its ominous and mysterious path.
- Rosa. You do care about her plight and how hard she's trying and there is a certain feeling of 'poor girl' while playing.
- Originality. Playing mother's voice who tries to influence her daughter is a very intriguing prospect, and even though there isn't always a satisfying response, that sometimes really works in the game's favor as you find that your influence isn't as rooted as you thought.
In conclusion: The game is definitely worth the price tag and if you have an afternoon with nothing else to do, it's at the very least interesting pass time. It won't be good to everyone but if you're a VN fan, you're no worse off for giving it a try.

I have played this game for a few hours when i first saw it, and, despite having recently started another walkthrough, i find myself incapable of finishing this game. It`s not that there are some exceptionally difficult fights or bugs impedeing me - i just can`t summon the effort to see any more of what Prototype has become.
The first blow to my expectatons was dealt by the graphics. Yes, it is arguable that the original game had that distinct a visual style - mostly it was stock concrete jungle, accompanied by similarly mundane spec-ops military and a slightly more custom transformative mass of twisting flesh in the shoes of a protagonist; all followed by the holy game design trinity of brown, gray, and red. Such visuals, however, worked in conjunction with the general atmosphere of despair and futlility, as well as a grotesquely powerful antihero protagonist, to create an impression of an everyday reality falling victim to something completely out of place, turning into Hell on Earth. It had to be generic army men fighting a blade-nailed doom jockey to achieve this effect.
Meanwhile, Prototype 2 starts off by taking the generic spec-ops people from the original game and stuffing them with irresponsible detail. A standard trooper now looks like Bane from DC universe tore some clothes off an Assasin`s Creed character and then plunged headfirst into an LED shop; when sticking out the top of an APC, one is easily mistaken for an unreasonably intricate flasher. The whole concept was dumbed down, too. In the first game, despite a clear image of unprincipled murderers who stop at nothing to fulfill their goal, the Blackwatch had ambiguity to spare - yes, a lot of them were in some way responsible for the outbreak of infection in the first place, but so did Mercer, and unlike him, the ops were actively working to contain and ultimately suppress the epidemic, being fully aware that such danger leaves no place for  negotiations and palliatives. In Prototype 2 they all go "Hurr, got atroshuss xpermunts ta do, durr", becoming so unoffencively evil they might as well be dressing in SS uniform. The story was hardly a selling point for the original Prototype, but at least it had the courtesy to make basic sense and go somewhere; the grateful heir, however, has chosen to effectively reset the plot and build a significantly less consistent one. Meet James Heller, a very determined American marine, who, after hearing that the city of New York, where his wife and daughter lives, has caught another case of that zombifying deathplague that wiped it almost clean last time (also no explaination how it got repopulated so fast), decides and insists that his family stays in the increasingly infected city waiting for him to pull his descision-making buttocks out of a tour. I mean, what could possibly go wrong with such marvellous plan, right? So, after seeing his family dead (OH SNAP), determined Heller decides to kill Mercer. About five minutes of cutscene footage later he meets Mercer (yeah, it`s a small city) and quite predictably fails to kill him, becoming infected in the process and ending up a test subject for Blackwatch. About ten minutes of gameplay later he escapes, meets Mercer again, and, instead of trying to kill him, decides to listen about Blackwatch cruelties. I could go on about how he systematically mistreats his ally, then fails to kill a major enemy commander literally because of a "Martha motive" and excercises in being a generally illogical and unrelatable character, but i hope it`s been established.
The final nail to the coffin of the prospect of me having any fun was composed of the "improvements" to gameplay. Stealth consumption controls are made a little less intuitive (pressing a special stealth menu key and then pressing 'e' to consume at a convenient moment back then versus pressing a grab button and then QUICK PRESS CONSUME RIGHT NOW OR ALERT now), movement feels a bit more clunky, despite Heller starting with some traversal abilities that Mercer had to unlock, and then there`s that overly restrictive level-up system instead of a good old buy-what-you-want mutation menu from P1...
So, yeah, my suggestion is that you play the first game, and then, if you`re really itchy to find out how dull it can get, you go to YouTube and watch an all-cutscenes of Prototype 2. It really does make sense that Radical got disbanded the same year this game came out.

Having already played PROTOTYPE 1 some years ago, I could immediately see the sequel was the step in the right direction in terms of playability, replayability, side quests and the story itself. The protagonist received some new and cool abilities, allowing him to do things like turning humanoid NPCs into living bio-bombs, performing gruesome devastator attacks and even commanding some of the infected creatures. The "Radnet Edition" of the game included an online hub with a whole array of new challenges and rewards, like new mutations and skins for the main character and exclusive items such as behind-the-scenes videos.
The one flaw that I have to mention here is that the first time I played it, I did it on a fairly decent rig, but still, the game stuttered like hell, due to poor optimization (the testing was done literally on 3 different PCs with roughly the same results). Only recently, after purchasing a PC with an i7 CPU on board, were I able to finally enjoy silky smooth gameplay with no stutters that so many players experienced. It is also worth noting that any further development of the game, including possible optimization fixes were rendered impossible since, shotly after the game's release, Radical Entertainment has been closed down by the parent company, Activision.
All in all, I consider PROTOTYPE 2 one of the most enjoyable games I have played in the recent years and I am sure you would enjoy it too...as long as you are able to play it comfortably ;)

Been playing MTG since 1993, Hex since alpha (2012 ish).
Played a ton of other TCGs/CCGs in between.
Have approximately 800-1000 USD invested in Hex.
The Good:
1. Mechanics. Largely based on MTG. Anybody who tells you differently is wrong. I mean, WoTC - the maker of Magic - actually sued Hex for being too similar. There were straight up carbon copies of cards from MTG to Hex (see: Murder, now "Kill" based on the outcome of the lawsuit). But the mechanics are fun so overall it's a plus.
2. Some good innovative features on top of the MTG base that are made possible by the purely digital format.
3. Overall in vision the game is promising; however, the following Bad/Ugly categories make me hesitant to recommend pouring large amounts of money into the game until things start to turn around
The Bad:
1. Slow release schedule
2. Questionable leadership
3. Expensive barrier to entry
4. Limited F2P content - you have to pay eventually
5. Poor transparency - no one ever has any idea what is going on
6. Small community with a few favored members
The Ugly:
1. Broken promises: these guys cannot hit a release date to save their lives. It has been 9 months from the release of set 3 to now, which is allegedly on the precipice of set 4. Their original promise of PVE has largely fallen to the wayside with the revenue chase and as of now, 3 years since the kickstarter was funded, we have a reasonably fun adventure zone 1 and a frost ring arena which is just a sequence of matches.
2. Questionable integrity: original kickstarter promised 30+ dungeons and said the game was almost finished and just needed 300k to polish it up - fast forward 3 years and less than half of what was promised is in game. The forum is filled with apologists that will downvote and troll you if you have anything negative to say about the game (likely what will happen to this review).
3. Hitching their wagon to the MTG star - see lawsuit details.
Overall: Currently not recommending until/if things turn around.

TL;DR: I have hundreds of hours on the Magic Duels series and Hearthstone - I uninstalled both shortly after discovering HEX and haven't looked back.  It's free - try it!
HEX is a digital trading card game done right, embracing digital mechanics and having robust tournament support.  PvE modes are fun, rewarding, and accessible, but expect a significant grind to play PvP as a F2Player.
Highs:
- Magic the Gathering (MTG) players already know the rules
- Unlike MTG's digital offerings, HEX embraces mechanics that are only possible with digital cards
- Unlike Hearthstone, HEX is a complex game with considerable interaction between players
- Robust tournament support, including synchronous Limited that fires regularly (<hourly) and asynchronous Sealed
- The RPG campaign is unlike anything I've played before (working on my 6th clear atm...)
- Best community I've ever seen!
- Devs clearly love the game and have a number of awesome features in the works
- All cards (and other items/currency) are easily tradable to other players
Lows:
- Auction house is tedious to use - I tend to stick to "trade chat" transactions
- Takes about 10h to grind a draft entry fee as a beginner - I'd recommend spending $10 on drafts to jump-start your collection and speed up the grind

Let me start this off by saying that it's been ages since I've played the first installment of the trilogy, specifically. I only just finished the third part of the trilogy, which probably says enough about what I think of this one in particular.
Also, please note that this review will contain mild spoilers, as this game is an RPG that focuses most heavily on story.
Heroes Rise: The Prodigy is an interactive novel in which you delve into this world of super heroes. What will strike you as different off the bat will be how widely accepted Powered people are. Despite protests from people, those with Powers are more accepted than how other franchises depict them (such as X-Men).
This story is very well-written. I love the option to have my character be a different sexual orientation than what is considered the norm at this time. The absolute amount of in-game customization is actually very well-done and in-depth, given the type of game this is.
Characters are written as human. They have their strengths and weaknesses, like every human does. You can relate to these characters in some way or another, and hell, pretty much every character can be liked or disliked with valid reason. (Bear in mind I might be wrong about this, having not played this installment specifically.)
However, I feel that a few aspects of the story can be seen as rushed. Of course, they seem to prove a point later in storytelling, so this can be seen as either a plus or a minus. Some of the characters may also seem to act a bit... out there, which may not be to your taste.
I found the stats system most interesting, and how your ending score is dependent on how you played to your stats.
Overall, I recommend this game and the rest of the series. To me, it is an adventure that will definitely last a long time, despite its somewhat-simple appearance.

The Heroes Rise trilogy has an awkward obstacle keeping it from being great. The word is that the third installment is supposedly the best of the series, and that the second one, "The Hero Project" isn't half-bad either. The problem is that you have to suffer through the first one before you can get to better character customisations in the later games. And the customisation of "The Prodigy", unfortunately, just isn't that great.
For starters, you don't get to choose your powers. That's understandable, but my problem is... you don't even get to choose from a set of powers. Having to choose from at least five powers would have gave the game a better sense of variety, but unfortunately, you only have the option of being 'defensive' or 'offensive', which would affect your 'defensive' and 'offensive' stat. And that's really kinda boring, really. What's the point of playing a superhero if you don't get that many options of choosing your powers?
From that, it's clear that the game suffers from the same rigidity every game with choices (like Mass Effect) suffers from, which is sacrificing the player's freedom of choice to force him onto an enforced storyline. While the game does offer a number of ways your character operates (either being a solo hero with a sense of justice, or a lawless badass who's on a team), the ending to this first game will largely be the same. Basically, kinda like the Mass Effect 1 and 3 ending but with a wider variety of colors.
The variations the game offers comes in the form of three sets of 'percentage calculations':
Set 1
- Fame/Justice
- Lawless/Lawful
- Offensive/Defensive
- Soloist/Team Player
Set 2
- Power Level
- Health Level
- Money
- Legend
Excluding 'Legend', the stats on Set 2 won't affect the story too much. Then there's also Set 3, composing of 'relationship stats' that will affect the kind of character interactions you'd have. Set 1 and Set 3 are the stats which will vary the storyline. Although the main story you're on will begin the same way and end the same way, the few flavors in between your choices are enough to give you the kind of illusion of choice you'd see in the first Mass Effect game (this game unfortunately won't reach the level of nonlinearity ME2 and ME3 did, with their multitude of relationship sub-stories).
To be clear - this isn't really so much a flaw as it is an impractical element of gaming. An enforced storyline with a few variations is an obstacle no game developer has found a practical way of working around yet. Games with choices will always have one enforced storyline with some variations to the things that affect your character. You won't have three or five different kinds of adventures with different settings or genres to choose from, just one, because it otherwise costs too much time and money. Bioware has done this more successfully though with ME2 and ME3, where the variations are numerous enough to give you a sense of individuality - The Prodigy does not have that. Furthermore, this obstacle brings out the real flaw of the game - the writing of the one story you're forced onto.
Telltale games (minus The Wolf Among Us and Game of Thrones) have a similar structure: one storyline with variations that are a lot more subtle than Heroes Rise: The Prodigy. This isn't a bad thing when the story is well-done (The Walking Dead). Choices and nonlinearity don't matter when the story isn't well-done (Life is Strange). Heroes Rise falls somewhere between professional comic book storylines and amateur ones (the poorly-written kind game developers shoe-horn into cheap superhero games like Marvel Heroes Online). It does deconstruct the superhero genre a little bit, offering a few twists that are kinda clever, but don't expect Grant Morrison or Neil Gailman material. It's not terrible, but it could have been better.
That being said, The Prodigy's story should be well-written enough to keep you distracted before you get to the meatier, more dramatic stuff in the second and third game. The sense of individuality still doesn't reach a great level in the sequel, "The Hero Project" (which I just started playing), and the whole "Reality TV" storyline seems trite and uninspired (not to mention tasteless for some people), but I heard that the third and final game, "Herofall", is supposed to be really great for some reason. Furthermore, the variation in flavors does increase to a little extent in the second game. So it's essentially "play the first rigid game to get to the less rigid second game so that you could get to the reputable third game".
In a time when CYOA superhero stories are rare and few, this is unfortunately the best you can get if you're interested in superheroes like myself. For non-superhero fans though, I can't really recommend spending money on this amateur work. You can find much better CYOA games out there, like The Wolf Among Us and maybe even Choice of Robots (Choice of Games' most popular work, it seems).

And so, lets go with this other Minecraft Styled FPS game.
Now what does this add to the mix, what makes this game unique: this is a halo style + mincraft styled first person shooter.
The gameplay mechanics are similar to that of halo, and the game looks very similar to Minecraft/Halo, the guns the everything is similar to Halo. - Halo theme/style/guns look
-Character customization (you can customize your character, your halo type suit many different colours to choose from and there are many helmets too)
-On top of the normal game modes this game also has infection and other zombies type game modes included

- Will run on any type of PC, I have a crap PC and am getting 60 FPS.
-Low size requirements (260 MB)
-Variety of weapons to choose from (but still very simple)
What I Hate:
- Not too many servers with lots of people (infact CTF cannot be played cuz no one plays it)
-High Ping users
-No level progression system or points to unlock anything (doesnt have an incentive to keep me playing the game , nor it stores your stats, this heavily effects the longitivity of this game)
Thats pretty much it:

I felt that there was such a huge disconnect between the dark and mysterious delivery of the world and the simple logic puzzles that it was actually off-putting. To me, it would make more sense if the darkness theme was somehow integrated into the puzzle-solving mechanic, or didn't exist at all. As it stands, I think that the world is an obstacle between the player and gratification, not something that positively contributes to the experience. The middle part in the office felt entirely unnecessary and out of place because it added nothing useful to the game. The penalty for going through the wrong door is far too small and could be easily improved by randomizing the puzzle on death. Overall, this felt like a proof of concept written to meet weird specifications on a sophomore CS assignment than a finished, marketable product. 2/10; would not recommend.

Contrary to what a lot might be saying about this game, I'd at least recommend this if you can buy it during a sale - with DLC, of course. Thing is, this game (and series as a whole) fills a niche that very few games I've come around actually fills - and that is the ability to create your own universe of custom characters, all made by you, or even downloaded from the community. If creating and pitting characters against each other is something you enjoy, this is your game.
Now of course, the game doesn't come without flaws. The battle system, while not exactly as repetitive as you might think, is quite strange. You've got a health bar that barely makes sense, a 'momentum' counter which builds up as you dish out pain, a finisher bar, and a stamina bar. At some point during the game I could also see the amount of reversals I had, but I haven't found out how to turn that back on. The game crashes occasionally but I haven't had it happen in any customization yet, so I haven't lost any real progress. It handles the crashes fairly nicely, but they shouldn't happen in the first place, so...
Anyway.
The sheer stat system and everything behind it is... well. There's quite a few cheesy strategies you can pull off and barely anything is restricted from you outside of MyCareer. Even against hard opponents, they don't exactly come off as hard. So the difficulty is out the window.
Is the system itself any good? Well- it reminds me of other fighting games, like one I used to play, Naruto Shippuuden's Ultimate Ninja Storm, this because of the system with reversals being limited yet replenishing. It turns into a game of who has the most reversals, and if you manage that, all is fine.
I haven't tried the PVP
The mechanics on their own are solid, but nothing refreshing or new. All in all, the game really serves that one niche, and the actual gameplay in it is fairly lackluster - yet not disappointing. In fact, it *can* be quite fun if you really get into it, but I'll stick around here making my custom wrestlers.
In short; A meme and custom wrestler paradise. Not the best in the series from what I've heard, but really polished for what you get. Worth about $30-40 maybe. Not full price.
