Out There is a game I was really excited about when I stumbled on it a few days ago.  I was expecting a game like FTL, but with its own unique style.  It
have a unique style, but the gameplay is severely lacking.  Resource management is much more complicated than it needs to be.  You constantly run out of everything.  Running out of any one of the games three resources--fuel, hull, and oxygen--leads to an immediate game over.  Space on your starting ship is very limited, and you will constantly find yourself destroying and rebuilding modules to make more space for resources.  Game overs are frequent because you can run out of resources at any time if you hit several systems that lack planets to resupply at.  Game overs are far too frequent.
The game itself is unrewarding.  Unlike FTL, there are no unlockable ships.  You can find ships randomly during your adventure, but there is no way to start the game with a different ship.  Different ships require different materials to repair and maintain, which means you can stumble upon great ships that need materials you don't have because you never have enough space to carry them.  Not being able to unlock different starting ships makes the game stale as it limits your options.
Technology gains are also completely random, and whole sections of the map later become inaccessible later in the game if you haven't stumbled upon certain required technologies.  Even after you acquire the design for a technology (which can be lost in random events), you still must build it, often out of resources you can't keep on hand because of space limitations.  And for every technology you add to your ship, you have less space to gather materials.
The map of stars is fixed, but the planets and events are randomized.  This may sound like enough variation to keep the game fresh, but the lack of choice made the game stale for me after a few dozen attempts.  There are four different endings, but nothing that any of them offer could compel me to play further.  There is too little strategy, too little choice, and too much chance.
There are makings of a good game here.  The art and music are both excellent, and the production values are high, and it does have some interesting ideas.  It's just poorly balanced and unrewarding.  Making ships unlockable (so that you could choose to focus on different materials and have more freedom) would be a welcome change.  If a sequel is made that addresses my complaints, I will be the first in line to buy it.  But I cannot in any way recommend this game in its current state.

When a friend of mine posted her screenshots of this visual novel, I was both intrigued and slightly disturbed at the same time. I would walk away from my computer, but those images would stay in my mind. I never thought I would play something like this, but you know what they say...
So once the kiddos were safely put to bed, I played it, prepared for a really sordid, disturbing, gratuitous time....and actually got something quite different.
Nothing in this visual novel is gratuitous. This visual novel really is a dark fairy tale at heart, taking its inspiration from Greek/Roman mythology, which can also be pretty twisted if you read it. The story itself (I really don't want to spoil too much, since you get enough of a hint from the store page.) is dark, sensual, and passionate. However it can also be endearing, touching, and lighthearted. The tricky thing is that this visual novel can change tones in a heart beat, so when it goes from light to dark or disturbing, it can be really startling. I know I jumped a few times, because there is no warning. There are many many achievements because there are so many ways that this story can be played. The game is only as twisted as you want it to be. The first time I played, my character had a good motivation, and the mother was not as abusive as she could be, but understanding and ultimately fueled by a parent's love. As a mother, I couldn't help but insert myself in the mother's role and try to pick the best responses. When you go down that path, you reach the happiest and least sordid of endings. But then I got curious...and I discovered that the more dark you want the game to be, the story will match how far you want to go....and it can go a LONG way downhill. Far worse than the sexual content of this game (since most of it is read anyway) are the themes of child abuse and verbal abuse.
Now the look of the game is beautiful. I love the Victorian time period, and the colors are just gorgeous. I loved the fashion and the beautiful places you get to go to. The game features some disturbing visuals as well, but they are done in a way that you can't really look away. I've never played any other visual novels except The 39 Steps, so for a Free to Play, I would say this is very very good work.
The soundtrack is gorgeous. It fits the time period perfectly, and also includes classical music when appropriate to the story. The sound effects build tension in the game when necessary, whether its fear, anxiety, insanity, or sexual tension.
Now some cool extras. I've already mentioned the many achievements and the multiple endings, but there is more! There are extras that tell you about the inspiration of the story, how the game was made, and the road that was taken to make the game a reality. The more achievements you get, the more you unlock, rewarding you with entertaining and hilarious extras! I really enjoyed learning about the creative process since it helps you appreciate the story more.
So in the end, I am really glad that I played/read it. I would hope that my review would answer questions or relieve any doubts for other players who are kind of on the fence about titles like this. This visual novel poses interesting questions on the nature of love, and its many faces and disguises. It also takes an interesting look at the question of loving someone and acting out of fear. For a Free to Play, this has a whole lot to offer.

In short, Sniper Elite is a third-person-view PS2-era shooter about American covert operative in Berlin in May of 1945, sniping Soviets and occasional Germans with that famous "bullet cam" effect, "borrowed" from Max Payne games. I can recommend it only to people who want to kill Ruskies in bulk. There you'll be mowing hundreds of those stupids. Which is good, if you're, say, some right-winged Nazie-lover, still wishing for re-count with USSR. I repeat - for the most of the game, you'll be running in Wehrmacht uniform, assisting Germans in killing Soviets and hiding some "war secrets". Great deeds for every karma, don't ya think?
As of shooter rules, obviously, this game is focused on using the sniper rifles. Using those boomsticks was somewhat elaborative for the year 2005, as those rifles are using basic ballistic rules, so the rifle bullets are flying on some parabolic arc and not just direct line. Which means that you need to aim higher on bigger distances. You can use some other weapons, like a silenced pistol, or guns picked from your enemies (machine guns like DP-27 or PPSh), but their ballistics were nerfed alot, to make player use his main rifle more than other weapons. Alas, the situations where you're supposed to perform really long shots is quite numbered. Damn, there are only 5 maps for the whole game! And only 2 of them are of some use for sniper work.
As of "stealth" there... Just forget the word. You can't be stealthy. Your silenced pistol can't work, your enemies will always be knowing where you are, no matter how good you're with hiding in dark pixels.
Now, WW2 tag. It's fake. The history details were not simple altered. The whole game setting is a pure phantasy! Where diesel tanks can be blown up with normal bullets, where war veterans waltz in the war zone without cover, and don't hide in front of enemy. Where... everything is not simple not based on reality, but twisted with good amount of absurd and ignorance.
What I have against that game other than siding with Nazies in their fight against good guys? As I am sure that Russkies in the 1945 were certainly good guys killing the dragon with the sword, whereas USA was dropping A-bombs and performing all other usual stuff like turning into dust by carpet bombing cities like Tokio, Dresden, Würzburg, Swinemünde and so on... And yes, the story of covert support of Nazies retreat and revival is one which (some people in) USA is quietly proud of, and I strongly despise.
Read some books about it before critizing me there, folks.
Okay, again - why Sniper is a bad game, in my opinion?
First is the setting, where you have 5 maps on 28 "missions", with huge backtracking part, always. The structure of levels leave to player a light possibility to make some maneuvers, but in practice it is even more strained, than in the Crysis 2. If you count the possibility to turn left or right from rails as "non linear game play", I'm sorry for you. In the end, Sniper Elite turns out just as beeline as any typical shooter, very far from the defintion of "non linear"-something.
Second, the AI. It is horrendous. The meanest soldiers of the Europe of year 1945 never use any real combat tactics. They just standing in the middle of a street, shooting at you, or rushing forward on your position. On the other hand, they will be always knowing where would you go, no matter how silent you are, how many hours you spend crouching and proning in the shadows. Dead stealth experience.
Third, the weapons aren't any good, even with addition of ballstic rules. I know dozens of other games, where you can hone your sniper skills much better.

A great point and click game, possibly the best game in the entire Cube Escape/Rusty Lake series except for maybe "Cube Escape: Seasons".
Pros:
- Over 30 levels (!), including some secret levels.
- Rich, creepy atmosphere, which is par for the course for this game series.
- Nice artwork and music.
- Adds a ton of new lore to the series, and background stories for some of the recurring characters, without losing the obscure, esoteric appeal of the series.
- Reasonably priced - for 3$, you get a lot of bang for your buck.
- Decent length: my first playthrough took me 7 hours (although I was taking my time).
Cons:
- Despite the large number of levels, each level is rather short and the puzzles are simpler than in other games.
- Levels are self-contained, meaning that puzzles don't encompass several levels (except for one bonus puzzle after you beat the game). If you liked the gigantic puzzle in "Seasons" that took 2 hours to complete, you might be disappointed here.
- Many of the puzzle types are recycled from previous games in the series (and from other games in the Point & Click genre).
- Little replay value.
All in all I greatly enjoyed the game, and would definitely recommend it to fans of the Cube Escape series. For those who aren't familiar with the Cube Escape universe, I would recommend playing the previous games first (they're available for free online, and great fun).
Final Verdict: 8.3 out of 10

Gothic is a hard game. not hard in meaning the game is hard, no. Let me begin with some simple things:
Image you are new to a "ghetto city" and youre the total loser there, the "new one". Thats what Gothic is. As i said, the progress you make in Gothic is pretty slow but still not that slow that you stop playing. the Storyline and Quests keep you playing next to this, everyone jumps on you, threaten you and kicks your♥♥♥♥♥that you somehow build this deep feeling that you just want to, mildy said, "kick their balls" and want to show them whos "the boss". Doors is a relatively brisk logic puzzle game that has some great ideas that it executes well but, ultimately, suffers from a need to expand upon those ideas.
At a launch price of $5, Doors managed a cost of about $1 an hour for completing and getting all the achievements but the unachievable achievement (someone let me know if "unachievable" is a lie but I suspect it isn't). I'd say it's worth the money, and arguments that there's not enough gameplay here suffer from poor cost/benefit analysis. I'd recommend the game for it's cool high-contrast graphics and fun puzzles at full price in a heartbeat. That said, it's hard not to be a bit sad that this game isn't what it could have been.
There's definitely a neat underlying storyline here that remains all but unexplored. I won't spoil anything (because it really is genuinely fun to discover what little there is), but the whole thing is contained almost entirely in a 5-10 minute area about halfway through the game. There's a tease after the credits that's cool as well. However, it seems like the entire game should have been the prologue to the real game, due a lot to the way that it's set up. If there's a 20-hour follow up to this game, great. If not, real opportunity missed.
Still, despite its flaws, it has cool puzzles with a good difficulty curve that gets to the daunting by the end, and is well worth exploring. I wouldn't not recommend this game simply because of what it could have been, but I do hope that we eventually get what this world really deserves: a full title.

This was the first game I ever played (if it wasn't, that's how I remember it anyway) and it shaped my understanding and love for RPGs enormously. It has a very special place in my heart and I will always be nostalgic about it, so it is probably impossible to provide you with an unbiased opinion.
But if you are currently looking at this review because you're thinking about buying it in 2017 (or later, I guess) I want to give you an idea as to why you should.
The main reason why this game still feels great to play is because of its world and atmosphere. The premise of the story is a very clever trick to excuse a small game-world and a unique as well as rough society within it in a believable way. The different camps feel distinct and thinking about which to join while you progress through chapter 1 is a real challange, since you likely made friends in all of them. This of course, because of the quirky and witty dialogues. They feel real, even when uttered by a pixilated same-head, and even talking to a random npc can pull you a bit deeper into the world. The friends you make along the way have often interesting backstories and I found myself coming back to Gorn or Diego repeadetly just to see how they are doing, even if I didn't have a quest with them at the time, and even 13 years after finishing the game for the first time. The game feels like it has a real society with its own rules and mannerisms.
The story itself is a little bit cheap, you could say, but it serves as an excuse to have a game and a goal within it, and once you immerse yourself into the diegesis it won't bother you at all.
The music is really great and moody and does its part well to immerse you further into the world. Even the background chatter, although very repetetive, illustrates the character and feel of the world. I obviously played the game in German, so I don't know how the translation holds up in these regards.
Progressing through the game is a bast. You can feel every new skill and every new level greatly, and every time that happens you immeadiatley know what to do. Wasn't there this guy who beat me up a week ago? Well, let's see how he holds up now. Isn't there this huge♥♥♥♥♥creature int he forest that I couldn't even damage last time? Well, let's see whats in this cave behind it.
To aquire new skills you always have to go to a trainer once you leveled up. It makes progression more believable and gives trainers a role in the world. Often they are great characters anyway, so you don't mind coming back and maybe asking what's new.
The quests in this game are simply amazing. Far from the copy-paste fetch-this-fetc-that Bethesda questing. More akin to how questing feels in The Witcher series. They often are linked and complex, require you to actually listen to people (not just the quest giver) and think for yourself (only one of the reasons being no quest markers) and refusing a quest - or doing it deliberately wrong - has meaning to it instead of just representing lost eperience. Every quest you finish will make you feel relieved and/or like you achieved something.
The combat-gameplay might be a little rusty and it takes some getting used to for sure, but it manages to always feel challanging and rewarding and once you mastered the controls you will never feel like fighting the controles instead of the enemy. What's more it's quite an interesting take on swordplay and the such.
Of course this game doesn't come without flaws. The still prevailant bugs being a part of them. Cluncy animations and dated controles being another. But honestly I struggle to see them through my rose-tainted glasses.
And of course you will sit there for a few hours (if you are lucky just a few minutes) to install the right patches and mods to actually be able to run this game. But I assure you: It will be worth it.
(A lot of negative reviews on here are about the developers being to lazy to update a game this old, but the deleopers actually sold the rights for gothic to the publisher, that's why they worked on the risen series after gothic 3 instead of the newer gothic titles, which are a pile of garbage by the way)
If you enjoy RPGs like Morrowind and Witcher 1 and maybe a bit of TwoWorlds and don't mind a 16-years old blocky graphic (there are mods, but not a lot and they can't sweep away 16 years), you should give this one a try, it's not expensive anyway.

I'm giving this game a negative review, although it's mostly about the content to price ratio. It's got alot of good points, but it's too simple to be worth $10. It was made to run on a phone, and it shows. Very little content. Excellent writing, but very little story. The artwork is great, but the game is just not what you'd expect at this price point.
This is a Roguelike set in space, so of course it gets compared to FTL. So imagine FTL without combat, crew management, shops, system upgrades (although you can keep the augments), alien races (you can keep the occasional space-monster), and the rebel fleet. What's left? Jump, read event text, harvest system, jump again, and try not to run out of fuel.
The biggest complaint I have is that the game claims to be more than it is. The game is 90% resource/inventory management (which was pretty simple/uninteresting), 9% flavor text (which I thought was very good), and 1% "meeting intelligent species that won’t care about you, but also dealing with ancient powers linked to your destiny and the fate of mankind itself." In my humble opinion, a 100 word dialog in the end scene about earth does not make the game about the fate of mankind. Also, the game purports to be story driven, but the story is just a series of unrelated microevents that occur when you warp into a system.
Also, I'm not saying this as a negative point, but this game is unforgiving. All roguelikes will kill and frustrate you at first, but I thought this one had more to do with luck than skill. The games are quick enough that it's not like you've got a huge amount of time invested, but there will be games that simply cannot be won.
Honestly, the game is kinda dull and repetative, but the artwork and writing really are great. I just was expecting a little more.

Doors is certainly a slightly off-beat game, and one which put paid to my long-held suspicion that I'm just sheer and utter crap-house at puzzles requiring "logic".  A word of warning: If you're no good at even the simplest of "riddles", be fully prepared for this game to make you feel like the dumbest♥♥♥♥♥who ever walked the Earth.
Essentially it's just a series of "choose the correct door or die" conundrums, in which you select the correct portal by way of a process of elimination...a process which I still managed to get wrong at least half of the time (so yes...dumb +♥♥♥♥♥= me)!  But it's a smidgen more than that...it also sets itself up as a bit of an atmospheric mind-♥♥♥♥, emulating not just a logic-based video game, but indeed a kind of corporate or governmental logic-testing simulator, complete with minor electronic "glitches" and so forth.  At first the slightly spooky landscapes you briefly traverse to get to the next puzzle seem like little more than an opportunity for some nice sound design and some snazzy screenshots, but as the game progresses, it does succeed in making you feel like you've just been a part of a short-but-sinister psychological experiment, the end result of which may very well be your own extermination (for the aforementioned crime of being such a chronic and incurable dumb-♥♥♥♥).  It's a minor touch, but a welcome one, just the same.

Oh, and on the subject of "shortness"...yeah, it's short, but don't let my brief playing time or all the boastful reviews fool you.  Sure, all bar one of the puzzles involves so few doors that you could just zip through them methodically 'til you find the right one, but anyone seeking to solve all the riddles fair-and-square is bound to take a little longer, unless they have an extraordinary natural talent for this kind of thinking.  Oh, and good ♥♥♥♥ing luck to anyone believing that they can solve the second-last puzzle in under two minutes without cheating (which I most assuredly did, by looking up a walkthrough...'cause in less than two minutes I knew it had me beat, plain-and-simple)!  There's also quite a few wacky little Achievements to pursue, for those so inclined, so earnest players could easily get more than a couple of hours out of this game if they don't give in to the ever-present and most assuredly evil allure of the walkthrough.

If all this talk of logic and puzzles has done your head in already, you may want to skip this one.  For anyone else, the price being asked is more than fair for the product being offered, though the sitting-square-on-the-fence people might at least want to wait on a sale.  Recommended, but only heartily to those mental masochists out there who enjoy a good head-pummelling.  Me, I could probably go a few rounds of Killing Floor or Borderlands right now.  And I by-and-largely DETEST Killing Floor and Borderlands for being so ♥♥♥♥ing mindless.  But right now...a bit of mindlessness is sounding mighty ♥♥♥♥ing tempting...

I purchased this game on a whim (steam sale 50% off) and it was one ofthe better decisions I have made as far as purchases go recently. I would gladly pay full price for this game knowing what I know now: this game is fantastic. It is very simple, yet extremely complex. You have a ship which needs fuel, air, and metal to survive. (Fuel to move, air to breath, metal to repair the ship). You collect these resources from different planets you encounter. Planets are in various solar systems you travel to. Gas planets have fuel; oxygenated planets have air and life and metals and one form of fuel (carbon); rocky planets have metals and carbon. You discover technologies as you jump from solar system to solar system through random events. (You can also lose tech through random events: ex. space bugs chewing through part of you computer causes it to lose the info on how to build a certain tech. If that tech is destroyed you won't be able to rebuild it if you don't re-discover the tech). This is what makes the game so addicting. The randomness of the gift of tech and space ships and life forms that all have their own advantages and disadvantages. Life forms give you gifts randomly or by saying and giving them all the right things. They have a randomly generated language (every time the game is restarted). Learned words are always the same every time you restart. So, whatever languages you learned with this current space explorer's life, you will have for his duration. Once you die, everything beins anew. I just beat the game- finally- and I plan on replaying it much more. Why? Because I only got one of the endings! There is so much more I have left out, but I think this is adequate enough to pique some of your interests. Note: the game is very tough due to the randomness. If you can have things fall your way until you find a bigger ship and gather some useful tech then you will increase your chance of survival exponentially. (I went from lasting maybe 20 or so solar systems explored to over 100 in my last playthrough).

Dawn of War 2 [DOW2] is many things, but it is not your original Dawn of War [DOW], nor its expansions. The logistics, so heavily featured in the campaign, and multiplayer [MP], of DOW, and its expansions, have been all but erased from existence in this iteration into the DOW franchise, and have been replaced with an extreme emphasis on tactical placement of but a few squads, both in the campaign and in MP. In fact, one of the only comparrisons I can make between the campaign and MP portions of the game, thsu I will discuss the campaign portion of DOW2, then dive headlong into the MP aspect.
In DOW2, you are the a newly appointed Force Commander for the Blood Ravens, the faction of the Space Marines that were the primary protagonist in DOW. Assigned to Calderis to aid Captain Thule, you take command of the Force Commander and a squad of Tactical Marines, lead by Sargeant Tarkus, to crush an Ork uprising. During the Calderis missions you are introduced to other squads (Assault Marines, Scouts, and Devastator Marines) that you can bring with you, and use, during the campaign. Each squad has a designated 'hero' in its ranks, and for the Tactical Marines it is Sargeant Tarkus. The squad can lose members in battle, and have its number replenished at waypoint beacons. However, if the 'hero' takes too much damage, he will be incapacitated (all units in the squad will die), and will need to be revived by another squad. You can tell if the 'hero' is taking damage by looking to their icon at the side of the screen, which will display the 'hero's' health as well as how many marines are alive (blank person icons incidate that the squad is down men).
During the campaign, you can only deploy four squads at one time. You must make your selection, and choose carefully as you cannot switch out squads in-mission. The Force Commander must always be deployed with your team, however you can switch out the others, depending on the tactics you wish to employ during your mission, with ease. And, with the removal of logistics in this game, tactics are very important in order to keep your squads alive.
In DOW2, you will encounter something very familiar to you, if you have played Company of Heroes [COH]: color-graded cover. Muck akin to COH, when you position your squads, your cursor will show you how good the cover is, by displaying yellow, or green, colored circles. During the campaign, it is quintessential to place your units in cover, as on higher difficulties, your squads can be eliminated in seconds if they are in open terrain. This also applies to enemy units that find themselves without cover.
Each killed unit will garner your squads experience [EXP] during the mission, while undeployed squads will only receive a partial EXP boost. Your squads will gain levels and be granted two points, each level-up, to spend on 4 different trees: Stamina, Range, Melee, and Energy. For every 5 points in a tree, the squad will be gain a new ability, ranging from using a melee power, of having the passive power enabling the use of Terminator Armor. Depending on where the points are placed, this will dictate how you are wanting to use this squad in combat. You can make each squad different each time you play, depending on where you allocate their points.
However, it must be said that if you are inexperienced with micromanaging units, you could struggle, and be overwhelmed, with all the powers, abilities, and items that each squad can use, not to mention trying to tactically place 4 squads before an engagement begins, or has already begun.
And, during missions, you will also receive loot, such as weapons and armor, that can be equipped to your squads. Some items can only be used by certain squads, however, and some items will require you to wait until you are a high enough level to use them.
After you complete each mission, you are graded by three things: Fury [amount of enemies killed] Speed [completion time] Resilience [how many squads were incapactitated]. You are then awarded between 1-5 stars for each category, which is then talied into your rank. This rank is meaningless essentially, save for achievements on Games for Windows Live, a service that will thankfully be no more next year.
The story in DOW2. though, is your standard affair with the DOW series. The Blood Ravens must rise to the challange and overcome their enemies. The story requires little thought, as you are ordered to go several different planets to stop enemy uprisings and to ultimately stop the biggest threat to the sector:
.
The real challenge in this game's campaign is to keep your squads alive, and that's what keeps me coming back to this series. I embrace the challenge of finding my sqauds overwhelmed, yet are able to hold off the hordes of xenos and not lose a single squad in the fight. If the challenge of keeping soldiers alive in XCOM: Enemy Unknown was what kept you going, then this game is definitely for you.
One final thought about the campaign, though: You can Co-op the story. And Co-op is where the story's gameplay shines.
No longer tasked with commanding four squads, you and your partner will comand two squads each, though the host must always keep the Force Commander with them, if I recall correctly. Only needing to command two units each, the squad management is much easier to grasp and learn, which can also act as a learning tool if you wish to play the story by yourself again. Both players can assign points to, and equip, each squad, even ones they are not actually in control of. But, keep in mind that Player 2 does not save any progress for the Co-op campaign, as it is saved only for the host. Player 2 will have to start the campaign fresh, if they have not played the game at all before playing Co-op.
While that is a small misstep for the Co-op portion of the campaign, the rest is truly fantastic and nothing beats the feeling of you and your partner working together, taking out squad after squad of enemies without taking a scratch.
DOW2 also features a new, MP, Co-op horde-mode style gametype known as Last Stand. Last Stand is a three-player game mode in which you each pick one hero to do battle with against waves of enemies. You hero will receive EXP and level up during your playthrough. However, instead of gaining points to level your hero up with, you are given items for each level up that can be used to make a supremely deadly build. Each hero has to be leveled individually. Expect to fail in this game mode often.
In DOW2's MP, you can expect to see a game very reminiscent to COH. You are required to capture Requisition and Power points in order to train units, and to level up your Tech Level, at your HQ, as to create higher-teir units. You have no buildings you need to create in order to build units. Cover is essential, just like in the campaign, as is the unit's positioning. Devastator Marines can be easily overcome if they are flanked. The rest is your standard affair with COH. Expect few units early, and many often.
With that said, the MP portion of this game is quite boring, in my experience, and I have found little entertainment in it. But, other, who have spent far more time in this game, may disagree with me.
But if you want a single-player and Co-op experience in the DOW universe, that abandons logistics for a tactical, real-time, action RPG than look no further than this, as it sates those needs perfectly.

and it's two expansion packs,
and
. Simply put, I believe this to be the best strategy video game adaptation of the Warhammer 40,000 universe to date.

Out There is a game that sounds decent. Music's fitting, SFX are nice and in time, if a bit scarce. Tad generic, but everything works pretty well.
Out There is a game that looks decent. The occasional stunning view or the very nice intro are counterbalanced by the general hand-drawnness of the game (nothing against that style, I just think it doesn't work very well in this particular game). The text boxes and the fonts also look wrong, maybe overly clean, maybe too much spacing to the sides, maybe it's the artificial feel of the fonts. At any rate the game is kinda irregular throughout but when it works it works, I just think it falls short of the style they were obviously aiming for.
Out There is a game that reads pretty nicely, the random tidbits on arriving to a new system tend to be pretty entertaining to read. Although it doesn't get too boring you'd think they would have way less walls of text
, buut I guess if that's gonna allow for more variety I guess that's fine. Most times those text messages are just elaborate ways to tell you you've lost something, so pretty soon you'll be skipping over them and get the non-verbose "here's what you lost this time" message. Other times you won't understand whoever you're talking with, and through trial and error you'll finally be able to understand what they're telling you. I think it's a neat mechanic on paper but that alienates the newer players and gives an advantage to veterans. I tend to have problems with mechanics that work like this.
Out There is a game that
sounds great: you start on a ship with hull, oxygen and fuel. Traveling costs fuel and oxygen. Approaching certain bodies will cost you hull. Different ships take different elements for each of those, and you can get the elements strewn across the 3 main kinds of planet: rocky (metals), gas giant (fuel) and breathable, where you can also interact with other races. You can build modules with those elements as well, and there's also a variety of random events, including derelict ships you can take for yourself, peppered across most of the systems you'll go to.
Out There is a game that manages to kill all of the previous due to what I think are really sloppy late-cycle decisions that constantly remind you how much more fun you'd be having with the game if the main source of difficulty weren't incredibly obvious arbitrary restrictions aimed squarely to kill you faster. Now, when I say "arbitrary restrictions" I don't mean the ones that come along with the systems the game chooses to base itself off, such as the tile based inventory. If anything, a tile based inventory feels more at home with this game than many others: after all, you can tell me you have 16 universal, fixed compartments on your ship that can only be occupied by one resource and I'd be cool with it without even asking why there doesn't seem to be barrels in space. I can sorta roll with it. If the game played fair.
You see, through the game you'll constantly catch yourself thinking "wait, I can't do this now?": have you just looted a lot of fuel but your cargo hold is full? Tough luck, buddy! No, you can't transfer the fuel directly to your reservoir. You can't transfer the fuel that's in your cargo hold either, despite being totally fine anywhere else outside of the loot screen. No, you can't just exit the loot screen and go back to it after arranging your cargo. Do you have the one single unit of silicon to craft a module? You need to free up another entire compartment to build it first, despite the fact that there'll be one or more empty compartments after you craft it. Want to mine a breathable planet before talking to the natives? No siree! The option to talk to the natives will be gone by the time you come back from the loot screen. Do you want to transfer this module between ships? Christ, no! Even though just a while ago your dude went out on EVA to get into a transparent station to shoot a negative energy ray to a sun. You can only dismantle them, AND THEN get the elements back to your ship.
Now, here's what I think happened with Out There: They planned the game, they prototyped it, they coded it, and when it came time to testing it they realized that some testers were beating the game too easily, or that the existing system was too prone to exploits. But either because of an exceedingly rigid development plan, because of deadlines or because the game was  way too far developed to redesign it into something that solved the issue they were having, they instead made a list of the strategies the testers were using to beat the game and just simply took the common elements in these strategies out of the game. It is the equivalent of having a game where you have control over your stuff but with the developer sitting next to you and slamming on the keyboard every now and then screaming "NO YOU CAN'T DO THIS IT'S NOT FAIR." Not only will that feeling come to you when you'd need those things (and, again, you'll constantly think about these things since they're commonplace), but you'll also be constantly penalized by an entropy that honestly seems wildly exagerated and out of whack: flying to a gas giant will take you 10 fuel, and mining it between 5-10, and the probe that's designed to scoop fuel from a gas giant and return it to your ship will come back with barely enough to cover ITS fuel cost, let alone your ship or the jump to the next system. While wasting oxygen and hull at the same time for good measure. This can happen up to three times in a row (and I couldn't keep counting because my hull disintegrated trying to get to the fourth), showing that the game wants to kill you way more than have you presented by a series of decisions in an environment where you are in control. I tend to bash on tower defense games calling them "antigames" because there's only one ideal solution and maybe a couple sub-optimal ones to each level, but in Out There there isn't even that. In most cases you will find youself dying without any chance of control over it and no satisfaction for that playthrough. And yes, space is merciless and life sucks. That doesn't mean my experience with a game has to suck just because those two things are true.
So in closing, Out There is a game that although majorly pleasing to the senses and a solid concept comes apart because of a series of very obvious, very arbitrary design decisions that will constantly remind you that this is not a game made to be challenging and fun, it is designed to make you fail unless you are very lucky a lot of times. The entropy is stupid and the arbitrary restriction of player control is inexcusable for a game that calls itself "a genre bending roguelike". Roguelikes should be hard, but fair. And this game doesn't play fair.
I honestly can't bring myself to give it a bad score because of the solid core, but I can't honestly recommend this game because of the very big and very evident flaws on its execution.

I can't really recommend this game unless you get it for 1$ or bundled. I remember this one back in 2005 when it was regularly featured on Gamer.tv which used to air on an obscure channel called Now (how I miss that show). The game was built for the PS2 which explains the outdated graphic engine. And I say outdated because this was a year after Farcry, Doom 3, Painkiller and Halflife 2 (2004-That was the best year for PC shooters). But anyway the graphics are decent...neat skyboxes, great depressing atmosphere without being overly gritty.
Used to give a F**k about this game as I was around 18 when it released and upgraded my PC to play the then top of the line games as mentioned above. Man! it's a decade later and I decided to buy this along with the other two sequels. As a man almost in his 30's now, You would think I would really go crazy with this game in a pseudo intellectual way...World War, History etc.
Turns out it's an action-stealth game with the sniping simulator as a pretext. Well all that's fine, it plays out more or less like a Dishonoured where you can stick by a rule or just go around on a murderous rampage. Control-wise there is a lot of Splinter Cell influence. In terms of realism it's in between arcade and simulation leaning more towards arcade. Just don't expect an early Ghost Recon or Rainbox Six(1998).
Sniper Elite can get pretty repitative, with very little to shake things up. The game is lengthy which in this case, doesn't do any good. It faces the same problem as many Modern games, too many ideas thrown in...few good, few excecuted properly.
Rather than be a sniper centric game, it tries hard to be alot more, hence rather than getting one thing right, ends up being sup-par in every aspect. Lets take a look a great idea- Tripwire traps, Awesome!
Excecution? They had to create a situation for you to use them or you just forget about them.
I guess the biggest drawback here is age, see this game was crafted to be a Modern game, and unlike retro games and classic games...this one won't age well. It was meant to be played and disposed , There was another game that released in this year for the same platform and that was Shadow of The Colossus, I still think about that game till this day. That's what made it a classic. And this? not even a bargain bin classic.
Back in 2005 I would give this a 6/10. Today I would highly recommend getting it bundled and giving it 4 hours of gameplay to see if you like it. I had a bit of fun with this one and it's way more entertaining and ambitious than a modern day Call of Duty.

This game is deeply frustrating. The storytelling is simply superb, as are many of the small episodes contained within, each with their own unique mechanical and presentation styles. Unfortunately the actual story being told is lacklustre. It intrigues by presenting itself as a mystery, and although many of the best mysteries remain unsolved, this one goes out of it's way to leave you with so little resolution that you may resent it. The magical realism of some of the self-contained stories can be easy to dismis, or even enjoy, as narrative devices, but the unadressed implausabilites and lack of any real explanation of the framing world that is supposedly real is a real failure. The final sentiment of the story, that stories are important, seems especially ironic in this regard.
I still reccomend it, though only grudgingly, as a collection of small set-pieces that are a joy to experience.
Ultimately this is a story about nothing, beautifully told.

It's free, has lots of achievements, overall a good read. One of the better VNs that isn't a Dating Sim. If those are good to begin with is a different story... they can be but often they are not.
But since I am guessing that whoever is reading this is looking for opinions, here's mine:
I won't be the first one to point this out (at least I would think so) but this VN reminded me a lot of "Interview with a Vampire" and that's not just because of the Renaissance setting. I like that one and after completing CUPID it comes with little surprise that I'm thinking positive about it.
The plot jumps back and forth in its timeline which I didn't like at first because it is confusing and little makes sense but the picture comes together as the chapters pass. Now I think it is fine. I also like how the player doesn't decide what the main character is going to do/say - at least not directly.
Most of the CGs are beautiful, like the ones shown but not all of the game is looking that nice, so the Store page is a bit lying about that. I can tell though the devs put effort into facial expressions as they change with almost every line of text, this is "compensated" with a serious lack of poses. The soundtrack, a mixture of ambient, technospheric (I just made that one up) and classical stuff, has some good tunes.
Story itself is written extensively at times and detailed whenever critical events happen, with a sophisticated word thrown in every now and then, as one would hope to see when looking for something exciting and new. Reading the whole thing once without skipping anything takes about 5 hours.
The grande finale, once it unfolds and the decisions to be made, when the secrets are reveiled, is where the story has its peak, and I admit: I did not see the "outings" coming and they turned the plot into a whole different direction, so don't think you've already figured it out, once you got an idea, I was on my toes when coming up with theories of what might have happened to the characters since there's tragedy involded. The fact that the plot jumps, as mentioned earlier, didn't help since you get to see the results before "it" even happens.

“Heroes Rise” reminds me of one of those really bad tabletop RPG sessions, where the DM doesn’t understand what the point of a roleplaying game is and railroads the players into a very specific plotline, where the illusion of choice is sometimes presented but ultimately all “choices” lead to the same destination, and there’s no real input from the players.
I can forgive the game for not giving the player a choice in powers. That’s not too huge of a problem to me, as long as there’s still enough variation in how we can utilize that specific power. The game definitely
to give you this, although I’ll admit that I didn’t really explore a lot of the different options in combat, so I don’t know if selecting the “wrong” choice railroads the player into the path that the game wants you to go down, like it does during non-combat choices.
And that’s this game’s fatal flaw. There are many moments where you are presented with a choice, but picking anything besides the “right” option will result in the game saying “well, that didn’t work, so you end up doing THIS instead.” That’s not how interactive fiction works. The name of the publisher is “Choice of Games,” right? As in, we get to choose how we proceed through the story? Not so in “Heroes Rise.”
Let’s talk about one particular example of railroading in this story: the forced love interest, Black Magic. Early in the game, you (the player, not the character) are asked to name your first celebrity crush. Turns out that Black Magic looks JUST like that person, and is rumored to be their direct descendent. This is lazy writing. It’s the game’s way of saying “Hey, you should be pursuing this character!” without having to actually give them any depth or redeemable qualities, or any real in-character reason to pursue them (beyond the fact, as the game CONSTANTLY reminds you in any scene featuring Black Magic, that this character is just OOZING with sex appeal). It relies on basing their physical appearance on someone that the player (not even the character, but the player themselves) has (or had, once) a crush on, and hopes that that will be enough to justify railroading the player character into a romance.
The last straw for me was when (without trying to give too much away) Black Magic creates the illusion of terrible danger for the sole purpose of getting the player in bed. There’s a few options on how to respond to this. I went with completely rejecting her, because holy hell I am not interested in pursuing a character so terribly selfish and manipulative. And after selecting that option, the game literally told me that rejecting her was not a real option, and suddenly my character is sleeping with her anyway.
Is there anything redeeming about “Heroes Rise”? I suppose the writing itself is decent. Maybe it should’ve just been written as a story, instead of disguised as interactive fiction. Not giving the player any real choice in how to pursue the story goes completely against what interactive fiction is all about, and thus I cannot recommend "Heroes Rise."

This has to be one of my favorite mods/subsequel/fanmade game simply because it has enough nostalgia to remind you of why we love the Portal series so much. The game maintains the humor from Portal and Portal 2, has very unique tests, nostalgic easter eggs and references, similar approaches to chambers, and a KICKASS soundtrack! I already completed this game twice (one time off-record and one on-record), and I have two things to say:
- Most reviewers online insist that this game is long, and that it should've ended sooner. This is fundamentally wrong because for one, it's quite short, as proof by my time in the game and other players testimonies. And two, if it's taking them long, they're probably not that smart :)
- Other reviews are giving negative reviews because the game is not what they want and they're judging it by what it could've been instead of what it has to offer. I love this game, I remember back when I played it on ps3 I thought it was fantastic, but I could never get the hang around to it in order to finish the actual thing, not really sure why, I guess some personal problems or something.
Either way, there's much to love here, the game oozes character even in it's upgrade menu, which have plenty of different upgrades that turn you into an overpowered killing machine, the game it's also absurdly violent and "gory" with blood, dismemberment, and pieces of enemies flying all around, consuming enemies which serves as an ability to also absorb their physical appearance it's among one of the coolest abilities in recent videogames in my book.
They also added a new "stealth" sort of mechanism this time around, it's fairly simple, you get the ability to steal someone's appearance, say a soldier or a doctor, and then repeatedly keep doing the same, it never gets repetitive tho, and really all you have to be concerned about it's finding the one character that isn't being "watched" by other enemies, you do this by activating some sort of view it's called "mutation view" or something like that, essentially highlighting the one enemies that you can't consume in red, while the ones you can in yellow.
It's incredibly simple but also immensely satisfying to use.
Then there's the overall combat and the powers, which feel amazing, I don't think I had this much fun in destroying things in a videogame since Hulk: Ultimate Destruction way back for the Ps2, and GameCube, it's enjoyable to jump on top of a tank to shred a rocket launcher and then use it against other vehicles, it's fun to slice your enemies into pieces while you watch the floor getting covered in absurdly vast amount of blood, it's liberating to traverse the map gliding through it like some sort of monstrous squirrel.
It's hilarious to jump in front of a chopper miles away from you only to then use one of your powers to "tie it up" with a series of mutated tentacles that then proceed to "pull" everything around it and smash it against it, making it explode in hundreds of pieces.
Then there's the story, which is incredibly "cheesy" but I love it for it, I think if you understand what the story is, and you take it for what it is, then everything will be fine for you and you'll almost certainly enjoy everything about it, but if you're expecting something sincere, personal, deep, and emotive, then you're simply going to end up feeling disappointed.
The main character in the game James Heller might as well be one of the funniest characters in any game, every sentence that comes out of his mouth needs to be shared with curses, and an incredibly deep tone of voice.
It's hilarious.

A pitchfork is an agricultural tool with a long handle and long, thick, widely separated pointed tines (also called prongs) used to lift and pitch (throw) loose material, such as hay, straw or leaves. Pitchforks typically have only two, three or four tines while dung forks have four or five, other types of fork even up to ten tines with different lengths and spacing depending on purpose. They are usually made of steel with a long wooden handle, but may also be made from wood, wrought iron, bamboo, alloy, etc. In some parts of England a pitchfork is known as a prong[1] and, in parts of Ireland, a sprong refers to a 4-pronged pitchfork.[2] The pitchfork is similar to the shorter and sturdier garden fork. Pitchforks and scythes have frequently been used as weapons by those who couldn't afford or didn't have access to more expensive weapons such as swords, or, later, guns.[3] As a result, pitchforks and scythes are stereotypically carried by angry mobs or gangs of enraged peasants. In Europe, the pitchfork was first used in the early Middle Ages[clarification needed], at about the same time as the harrow. The pitchfork was originally made entirely of wood; today, the tines are usually made of hard metal. A notable American artistic display of a three-pronged pitchfork is in American Gothic, the painting by Grant Wood. In this painting it symbolizes hand labor. There are other paintings by various artists which depict a wide variety of pitchforks and other tools in use and at rest. Political usage[edit] Because of its association with peasantry, the pitchfork is often a populist symbol and part of the nickname of populist leaders, thus: "Pitchfork Ben" (Benjamin Tillman) "Pitchfork Pat" (Pat Buchanan) The Gangster Disciples, a street gang in the midwestern United States, use a three-pointed pitchfork as one of their symbols.[citation needed] Religious symbolism[edit] The pitchfork is often used in satire of Christian demonology in popular media, especially in early humorous cartoons where a popular joke was a caricature of an angel and a pitchfork-wielding devil sitting on the shoulders of the protagonist.[citation needed] The Hellenistic deity Pluto wields a bident, a two-pronged weapon strikingly similar in form to a pitchfork.

Most people seem to compare this game to Binding of Isaac, and that's a fair comparison. A Wizard's Lizard is a topdown twinstick Rogue-like shooter in which you explore the floors of the different dungeons, gradually earning new equipment, weapons and powers to help you along the way.
As far as a "clone" of Binding of Isaac goes, this one is actually pretty solid. It feels and plays the part, has great music, and is presented in a graphical aesthetic that feels all it's own.
One of the game's innovations is the hub village area you start in before you set out for your run attempt. At first, the village is barren and lacking in population. With each run you will occasionally find villagers who have been kidnapped by monsters. Rescue them and they return to the village, each villager rewarding you with a permanent 500 Gold boost for future runs. In each run you will also occasionally find purchasable Blueprints, which when bought will add one random item to the village store for purchase. Eventually, you will earn enough starting Gold to buy some starting equipment that fits your play style, or experiment and try different things. It's a really well thought out idea that encourages replaying and rewards players that stick with it long enough so that they can influence their run's start and not leave upgrades entirely up to luck.
What really helps distinguish this game from Binding of Isaac is the life/death mechanic. Traditionally, you'll be playing most of your runs alive, but if you lose all your health, you die, and come back as an afterlife spirit, giving you a second chance. The flipside to this is that there are far more enemies in each room in death, so you have to be even more careful when in this state. If you lose your health while a spirit, you die for good, and it's Game Over. Certain points in the game will allow you to bring yourself back to life, and there are some sections which require you to be either dead or alive to access or pass through, so it's a pretty nice idea to keep things interesting.
Newcomers to this who play Binding of Isaac frequently with the Xbox 360 controller, a small warning. This game has native controller support, but your shots will be aimed in any direction you point the control stick, not just N/S/E/W. If you're like me, you could be aiming in the slightly incorrect direction due to the placement of your thumb on the controller. With just four directions, there's plenty room for error in Binding of Isaac. Here, you have put in a bit more effort to make sure your shots are going in just the right direction. You'll eventually adapt, it just takes getting used to at first.
It's no Binding of Isaac, but if you're looking for a cute, gore-free alternative that's pretty enjoyable in it's own right, you could do worse than A Wizard's Lizard. Highly recommended when it's on sale.

The Heroes Rise trilogy was suggested to me by a friend, because 1. she loves superhero comics and the like and 2. she thought the game's inclusiveness was great. I'll admit, I was initially hesitant to play what essentially seemed to be a text adventure. Thankfully I was wrong.
This game is pretty well written. In addition to being suspenseful and dramatic, the writers managed to handle some of the social issues in the plot a LOT (no spoilers but I'm thinking of one thing in particular) better than I would have expected. The characters are pretty likable (except when they're not supposed to be... ♥♥♥♥ off Jury) and overall I thought the writing was pretty consistent. They also managed to explain the mechanics of the game pretty well without it being super overbearing.
It does have its faults, however. This first game in the series is fairly linear and while there are choices to be made, most of them have little to no effect on the plot overall. While I understand that this is the first game in a series and the devs don't want the player to do anything that might cause plotholes later, a little bit more leeway would have been nice. Thankfully the sequels don't do this, so don't let this turn you off from playing the other two games.
Overall, a pretty solid game you can get through in about an hour and a half for not too much money. If you're willing to use your imagination a little, I'd recommend getting the trilogy.

It's easy to read the reviews for this game and assume that this game is boring or pointless, and that is true if you are not a fan of logic. I personally enjoy mapping out every variable of a situation and coming to the one and only logical and optimal conclusion to a problem.
Let me tell you, if you are walking through each door until you are finding the correct one, you are cheating yourself out of any potential enjoyment you could be getting out of this game and refusing the opportunity to improve yourself even a tiny bit.
I have two complaints about the game though. The first one involves a level that breaks up the monotony of choosing doors by sending you to a completely different environment. At least two acheivements and much of the enjoyment of the game can be found in this new environment, but it is way too easy to accidentally leave this level and never have a chance to return. The only option left to the player is to finish the game and restart from the beginning until you reach that level again.
My second complaint about the game involves the puzzles. Almost all of them follow an obvious pattern that looks like this:
There are X correct doors.
Assume a set of X doors are correct.
You will either see that assumption leads to a conflict or that an additional door becomes true from that assumption.
Exhaust all possible combination of doors being true until you find the one that does not lead to more or less doors than X being correct.
What I appreciated about this game the most was the final puzzle. I don't want to spoil it for anyone but I thought the contrast between the second to last puzzle and the last puzzle to bring up an interesting question in the player's head, and I believe bringing this question to mind is artistic in the way that only video games can be.
Overall, steam says it took me around 7 hours to complete. I think this must have involved a lot of idle time where I left the game unattended. However, if you are playing this game correctly, it should take you several hours to complete.

I wish steam had scales between thumbs up and down as I want to like this game, this game has the DNA of everything I love, so even giving it the benefit of the doubt, in the end, I cannot give this game a completely good review.
Even without living in the shadow of FTL, after several playthroughs, what hurts this game is that it touts resource management -which literally suggests that if you "manage" your resources wisely that you'll have a chance to survive.
This is hardly the case as you are constantly up against no win scenarios. I know this game is suppose to have an element of chance to simulate the harshness of space; but when 9 times out of 10, you either run out of fuel or hull material, or just wind up stuck someway because you encountered a chance scenario that breaks your space folder and drill and you have no material to fix it and you can't drill for any (this happens surprisingly often). There is a problem with the game that doesn't allow your choices to ultimate determine how far you get.
There is no strategy because in order to even survive, you must drill or probe very conservatively, meaning you must only use as little fuel as possible while mining for as much resource, fuel and hull repair specifically. I've gotten farther on some attempts vs others but when 5 out of 6 sides of your dice ends the same way, it becomes tedious and I no longer want to  play. In other words, when your game isn't allowing me to have fun, when every turn ends the same way despite the choices I make, there is a problem. I have encountered so many no win / stuck scenarios - and this happens the further you progress. Everything depends on chance in a way that is unfair and unfun rather than being unexpected and challenging.
I've beaten FTL several times, don't get me wrong, I've died 10 times more than I've survived, but NEVER did I feel like my choices didn't impact my result - sure chance situations occur, but my cumulative choices in those situations still allowed or disallowed progression.
I still think this game can be fixed with an update where they allow changes in difficulty and altering gameplay mechanics in the options menu. Also allow for the ability to create fuel and hull material using other materials (this may be currently allowable but after 10 playthroughts I still haven't experienced it). OH and please add a Move all resources to cargo button when probing or drilling. and/or keyboard hotkeys for pc. Thanks
But until then, your game might as well be telling me to simulate space by putting a plastic bag over my head.

I don't even know where to begin with this gem of a game.
Maybe the absurd amount of polish? Maybe the well implemented mechanics? Maybe the simple yet stunning visuals?
Cublast HD took me by surprise for sure, but boy am I glad I ran into it while rummaging online. At first glance I saw it as just another indie platformer, but after giving it an hour of playtime I can tell you for sure that this is one of those games that you could play for a long time while being completely immersed.
Let me walk you through my thoughts when I first booted the game up. First thing's first, as I mentioned earlier, the polish. Right off the bat, the menus impressed me. Which isn't exactly something I usually pay attention to, but my gosh the menus are nice. The little animations, the minimalistic style which reinforced the whole game's theme, and how simply they're organized made me actually like using them. And let me just say how surprised I was to see CO-OP and VS modes as well level building (resulting in community made levels, of course) and even cutomizing the color theme of the game. Can you tell I like the game yet? I mean, I did just make a paragraph about the menus.
Moving onto the mechanics, it is indeed a platformer. However, with the certain platformer elements handpicked for this game, tactile and smooth controls, and the polish already apparent; this game is darn fun. Jump pads, chaging gravity, pushing boxes on buttons, a great feeling of momentum for the sphere you play as. All good stuff.
I'll stop here since I'm basically just rambling. I will say I don't often post reviews, so I'm sorry if you didn't gain from this what you wanted.
TL;DR:
Good game. Get it.

TL;DR Great theme and art spoiled by monotony and a heavy reliance on RNG. Always drill and probe 10/10. Focus is more on resource management than space exploration -- what could be a whismical journey is instead just looking for the next fill up station.
This game... this game would be awesome, if you weren't constantly concerned about finding the next gas giant to fill your tank or hoping you find a garden planet for oxygen. When you do, prepare for some inventory managment so you can stock up!
In the screenshots, the game seems like your main focus would be exploring strange new worlds, encountering life. And at some point in the game, maybe this does happen. But in my 2 hours of playtime, I couldn't manage to get past the first 10 or so galaxy hops. All this game was, in my experience, is drilling planets for materials, probing gas planets for fuel and hoping to the Random Number God that the game would bestow a planet with oxygen at some point so I didn't asphyxiate. Too many of my playthroughs ended simply because the game didn't randomly give me a planet with fuel, or a planet with oxygen. Reading the forums and guides, I do not see how I could have played differently; the game just didn't spawn what I needed, so it was a lost game no matter my choices. DYING TO RNG IS NOT FUN.
The game also has another false choice -- in the beginning, when drilling or probing for materials, the game presents a prompt for how deep you want to go, out of a scale of 10, where the higher number gives more of a chance of your tools breaking. Unless you knew ahead of time, you will waste you time until you find out that you ALWAYS, no matter what, go 10 out of 10. Repairing the tools is less than trivial, so 10/10 is always optimal. If you don't, you simply just waste more fuel and get less materials.
Once you find this truth, the beginning game is monotonous -- you simply hop galaxy to galaxy, consuming planets like Galactus, waiting until the game starts to throw some random event so you can actually start making any sort of decisions. By this point, I was too bored. You still have to hope that the game spawns what you need and doesn't just not give you oxygen until you die. I'd rather have more agency determining the outcome of my run.

If they wanted it to seem like it was closer to the reality of space travel by making it harsh and unforgiving, then I don't understand why they included fantasy things like warp drives. They could've just made a game where you start flying to another star in a conventional spacecraft and die of old age 0.000001% of the way there.  Or why did they even include starting again when you die. That's not real. If it were realistic you'd game over once and then the game would delete itself. None of this endlessly repeating early stages of a journey, you'd just see the early stages once and that'd be it.
What's the point of this design mentality really? What does it achieve? A game I can't actually play, is all I see here. A game where a player unexpectedly loses all progress due to circumstance beyond their control - you can frame it as "game over" but it's an effect identical to a game with bugs that cause it to crash randomly.

Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Links is a great game. You start off the game either as the "Pharaoh of Egypt" and "King of Games" Yami Yugi, or the "I'm so much better than you" and "I'm definitely richer than you" Seto Kaiba. From there on outwards you battle other duelists like Mai Valentine or Joey Wheeler, who are all by the way, voice acted (a sweet plus!) While taking on other AI duelists, they will drop cards so that you can begin upgrading you deck.
How would you upgrade your deck you ask. Well, there is a card store for you to buy card packs with premium currency called gems. Now hold on, before you take a pass on this game because of premium currency. Though you can pay grabbing card packs and extra gems, it doesn't cost once cent if you truely wish to stay free-to-play. It is possible to play throughout the entire game without paying once. Sure there are stuff people can buy but even if you don't pay once, it's still possible to play and have a good time without. Heck, the game literally gives you free gems from reaching certain milestones, completeing tutorials and even sometimes just for logging on!
Now comes the competitive part of the game, PvP. You can either play casually or take on others in a tier based match that's better than CS:GO's ranking system (which isn't saying much I guess...) It should pit you against same level players (and decks [the meta.]) However, after a while, everyone gets thrown back into the silver league so be wary around the time everyone resets!
They recently added Yu-Gi-Oh! GX into it so if you guys remember and love them too, now is a great time to hop on in to Duel Links.
Overall, I think Yu-Gi-Oh! DUel Links is fantastic with so much stuff piled in this game and completely free too! You should definitely pick it up if you enjoyed the series or even if you just want a card game that isn't completely P2W like some other card games. If it's free, what's there to lose?
I think the number of hours I've spent on this game show how great it is!!

Here is the biggest problem with the game.
None of the mechanics that the game advertises actually work!
The game bills itself as a stealth game where you sneak around from cover to cover, completing your objectives, while occasionally taking a stealth shot at an enemy.
In reality, your camoflage system is worthless.  In the first mission you are decked out in a German forest commando pattern. Unfortunately the mission takes place in a generic war-torn eastern european city. Essentially you are a giant green tree in a sea of brown. Good luck getting your "hidden" over 50%.
The game tutorial gos on and on about using your binoculars to scout for enemies before moving out of cover and advancing. Seems good in theory, but in practive all the enemies stay hidden around corners until they are scripted to pop out of their hiding places once you get within spitting distance. And when they do so they come out guns blazing like a wall-hacker in an FPS! What is the point of playing a sniper who has to scout out the enemy and take them out from a distance when the game mechanics actively make that impossible?
The game  even acknowledges that it failed at it's objective when during the later part of the first mission it litteraly tells you to pick up a sub-machine gun and start blasting waves of enemies about to come at you. Yep, that's exactly what I want out of my SNIPING GAME!
The only good thing I can say is the actual sniping mechanics of wind and gravity affecting the shot work pretty well! Now if only you were given a chance to properly use them.
If you want a stealth game with a decent sniping mecahnic you would be bettter off playing and of the first 4 Hitman games or even their middle-market counterparts Death to Spies.

From the makers of the Cube Escape games and Rusty Lake Hotel comes Roots, the newest dark, quirky addition to the family. A full, blind playthrough of the game takes around 5 hours, split up into 33 snapshot-like levels that focus on one specific person or event lining the family tree. While the content is new and fresh and the story continues the saga of figuring out just what is happening at Rusty Lake the puzzles are more familiar. They can still be tricky and there are several new types, but expect to see the beloved water pipe puzzle and the weight/scale puzzle.
The game is fun, frustrating, twisted, and occasionally gruesome, and an exciting new addition to the Rusty Lake family tree.

Though "What Remains of Edith Finch" might not be an awfully long game, its imaginative storytelling overshadows its length with rich emotion. Each tale has its own characterization, accentuated beautifully through artwork and gameplay, which leads you through an absolutely stunning home. A game that requires a specific mindset and a few hours of quiet, but in my opinion that would be time well-spent.

Despite the small playing area and the lack of plot, the sheer Christmas spirit, coupled with incredible hidden object scenes, result in a bit gaudy, but fun game.
If we would somehow form the essence of the corniest Christmas decorations into a hidden object game, we would get Christmas Adventure: Candy Storm, where every pixel emanates enough garish holiday scenery to drive any Grinch clinically insane.
Both the gameplay and the levels are textbook definitions of short but intense. There are four screens in total, so packed with hotspots that it takes excellent memory or the spam of the hint button to find our way among them.
The eventual reward is a plethora of great (and repeated) hidden object screens, where the items are numerous, yet easily distinguishable. They are the only noteworthy part of Christmas Adventure though, because there is next to no actual story, and the conventional puzzles are more like ways to increase playtime than actual challenges.

If you enjoy exploring and getting immersed in a story, this may be right up your alley. In WROEF you're not likely to get stuck and/or miss things. The narrative points you in the right direction quite well. The game
very detail-rich, so idle exploring is fulfilling and the little details do help you understand the story and the characters. You might also get some extra "Ohh, so
what [object you saw in another area] was about!" moments. Those were little highlights for me.
Pros:
+ Great soundtrack (I can easily recommend the Soundtrack DLC, it's very relaxing!)
+ Detailed and immersive environment to explore
+ Relative freedom to leave the story for a few minutes and just roam around or enjoy the atmosphere
+ Voice acting
+
story rich for its length
Cons:
- It's short. Took me a little over 2 hours to finish, even when I spent some extra time looking around.
- The game simply starts. There isn't a main menu you go through, you're immidiately in the game when you start, which can be confusing.
,
- If you take things very literally, some moments may leave you scratching your head or just make you cringe.
Important side note: I switched from mouse & keyboard to a controller after a few minutes, and I absolutely recommend doing the same. Using M&K won't ruin the experience, but a controller does give a much more fluid and intuitive control over movement and actions.

When I first read the mixed recepetion of this game, mostly about it being a bad "PC port", I was curious, were the others right?
Or did we have a Saints Row 2 Situation here, where if you can fix the main glitches, you have a great game?
Well after fixing the glitches I've been having, I can easily say I find Prototype 2 a fantastic game, and a massive improvement over the orignal.
Also this will contain
for the game and last game.
You play as SGT James Heller, who is in pursuit for Alex Mercer from the last game, who is enraged at Mercer for causing the 2nd Outbreak of a virus, killing James's family and most importantly his Daughter, after chasing Alex through the Red Zone, Alex decides to infect him with his version of the Blacklight virus.
James is found later with new found powers, he then escapes a lab, finds Alex and asks why he gave him the powers, Alex tells James that the humans are his enemy, after stopping Blacklight with the help with Father Luis Guerra, James finds out that both sides need to be stopped, as Blacklight wants to wipe out New York Zero and ruin the lives of millions of people by making them sterile, while Alex wants to infect the world and rule it with an ironfist.
The story this time was a lot more intresting then last game, while it is simlar to the last game, the humans weren't as twisted like they're in this game, while they wanted to make the virus into a Bio Weapon, they never attempted to wipe out an entire city and ruin the lives of millions. This game's stakes were much higher and it kept me intrested.
As for James himself, while he acts tough and edgy like Alex in the first game which I didn't like, as the game progressed, James slowly become more angry, violent, and even more edgier then Alex was in the orignal, when he lost Father Luis Guerra, he was cyring, and then rushing to leave after finding important infomation, but before leaving, he takes one last look at Father upset, then left, James has a massive range of emotions that Alex lacked in the last game, meanwhile in the orignal Alex always acted edgy from the start and pretty much stayed the same.
Also Alex turning evil isn't explained well, which is the only downside I can think off.
My biggest issue in the first game was the city, it lacked colour, the structure was boring, everything looked the same, no memorable landmarks, and the peds did nothing except walk and drive. Honestly New York in the orignal was the worst city I've ever played in any game ever.
However this game improves the map IN EVERY SINGLE WAY POSSIBLE!
We have 3 Zones, the Yellow Zone which you start in is an area filled with refugee camps, slums, old apartment buildings, very little amount of vehicles, people wearing masks coughing and being in pain, people hanging out on roofs and around fires in barrels, people in line to escape the yellow zone while being tested for infection, people in Hazmats treating them and others testing them.
Then we have the Green Zone which is the safest zone, full of cars, your average Joe walking around, bums and drunks sleeping against walls, Blackwatch Propaganda on the walls and with tons of electric lights all over.
Then we have the Red Zone, we have giant infected fleshy towers latching onto crumbling buildings, with Zombies below running around, suffering and eating the flesh of the dead, smoke filling the air, with the fires of the Dead Zone in the distance, with Survivors on roofs in the south, with some being on the ground level with hungry Zombies.
I LOVE THIS MAP! It's full of life, detail and colour, a massive imrprovement from the orignal with some memorable zones like the Church, security checkzones, the leftover bridges from bomb attacks, and the infected covered towers in the red zone.
Prototype 2 has some new toys for you to play with and beat up! But I won't spoil them!
The first game had stealth, but it was never used except for once, now this game does stealth a lot more and it's a welcome change of pace.
The best bit about the orignal was how fun it was, this sequel keeps that tradition and is very addicting!
This is the biggest reason why this game has a mixed rating, it has some nasty bugs, which can be fixed, the most infamous one is with the mission Flytrap where you can't finish it, however it can be fixed, I fixed it myself by changing how the game used my CPUs in task master during the mission, then changed it back to normal when I finished the mission.
There are other glitches like game crashes, but they were few and far between (Well to me anyways)
2nd biggest reason why this game has a mixed review, Alex was likeable in the orignal and was the hero, now he is the villain for this game for no real reason, and you do end up killing him... however funny thing is, in this game, HE IS EVEN EDGIER THEN IN THE ORIGNAL... HOW DID THEY DO THAT?
If you can fix the major bugs yourself like I did, you got yourself a fantastic sequel that trumps the orignal in every single way... well except for optimisation and bug fixes... but Prototype 2 is the better game overall, it fixes so much what the orignal struggled with and made it awesome!

Very roughly put, you have to lick the a  ss of the admin for a nice time on his server.

I can really expand this list of, unfair kick motives, but this review will get the size of a book and nobody wants to read a book in a review. I already feel it's too much written.
