Most of the players nowadays in DoDs are mature to very mature (that's a plus, really not many kids here), but the thing is...these players come in the game to blow some steam, or better said, to chat a lot and have "fun", but in my book, that is equal to troll a lot (like playing only bazookas and camp in a certain point all the round just to get a flashy 2 kills and then laugh after in microphone). They just camp, camp and camp, and talk on mic, and if somebody gets in their way, well they score a kill and again, back to talking and laughing, but they don't bother to win the game, to actual give a f  uck, you know ? Now, considering all the points I have made above :

While my experience with text-based Choose Your Adventure games is fairly limited, I thoroughly enjoyed being engaged in the awesome story of Heroes Rise: The Prodigy. The story is basically a "Zero to Hero" type of tale in which you as the protagonist (you can choose name, codename, gender, sexual orientation, etc) go through all kinds of hurdles as you try to be a legendary superhero showered by fame or (in my case) worthy to represent justice.
Overall, the story is decently written. Sure, it's nothing profoundly deep, but it offers a plethora of characters you can engage in conversation with and several of those interactions feel somewhat real, as if I'm right there experiencing the hilarity, the intrigue, the frustration or the sadness. Heck, the game even has story parts that are quite unexpected and interesting to read. However, the game come across as if it wants me to sympathize with Black Magic after their dark secret is revealed considering the choices you get presented (more positive choices than negative ones) -- which feels kinda off-putting, but it's nothing too bad.
All in all, it was a lovely superhero story that I got the opportunity to play and become the hero I always wanted to be, a   pro-teamwork warrior of justice that doesn't care about the law and does what he thinks is right.

is an extremely basic Hidden Objects Game (HOG). No story, no puzzles and no aspiration make up a game that's better skipped, even if you're looking for some Christmas atmosphere.
Your car is turned into candy near a house that's inhabited by three sisters. The sisters help you gather the necessary items to make a potion to turn your car back to normal. That's it. That's all the story there is to
.
The setting is extremely limited, too: the house consists of three scenes and the outside scene where your car is stranded makes four. That's it. Four scenes is all you get.
Gameplay consists of ten or so very easy Hidden Objects Puzzles (HOP). The rest of the game is spent gathering items to use on certain objects in the house. This is classic HOG gameplay but
doesn't even try to be creative with that basic premise. One example: you need sugar but the sugar bowl is locked. To open it, you need two strawberries. Not strawberry-shaped keys but actual strawberries. Put two strawberries on the sugar bowl and it opens and allows you to take the sugar inside.
A good HOG contains a fair chunk of classic but interesting or challenging puzzles to solve.
does not. The whole game contains only three puzzles. The first is a puzzle of chance: just click around a bit until the puzzle is solved. The second puzzle is bugged and has been for at least a year according to the forum where the developer promises to "fix it in a next few days" in January 2017. Fortunately, you can skip all of the puzzles anyway without penalty. The third and final puzzle is ridiculously easy.
The whole time playing
, you'll have to put up with very bad English. I'm not talking about some language errors only purists can spot but I'm talking about near-gibberish. One striking example: "I need inserting all the stars to open the jar". I chose this example because it also illustrates my earlier point: you see a glass jar and need its contents but instead of just throwing it on the floor or hit it with an item from your inventory (like a hammer!), you actually need to stick 4 star-shaped items to the side of the jar to be able to open it.
On two occasions,
managed to do to me what I hate the most in point & click games: I used item X on object Y and nothing happens. Later on, after doing some other stuff and being stuck, I find out I have to use the very same item X on the very same object Y. It didn't work before so I struck it from my list of options, only to find out the very same action is actually required a bit later on.
I got the feeling even the developer couldn't be bothered with this game near the end as in the last of the four scenes, several tooltips are missing. The mouse pointer changes to gears, which means a mouse-click should tell you something about the object and what to do with it, but absolutely nothing happens instead.
The graphics are standard HOG quality, meaning static but not too bad-looking. It's just that the amateurism shines through in this aspect, too. For example, at one point one of the sisters tells you to go find 12 apples in the garden. When you get outside it's hard not to laugh when you see 12 identical 'sprites' of an apple placed in the scene, with no regard to perspective. So an apple on the foreground of the scene is the same size as an apple on the background, which looks absolutely massive in comparison.
The music sounds cheap. For quite a while you'll hear a basic classical piece that screams royalty-free and gets very bombastic at one point. It has nothing to do with the Christmas atmosphere you'd expect this game to try and spread. The rest of the musical score isn't christmassy at all, either.
You'll hear some standard sound effects but nothing special. There is no voice acting at all.

I was thoroughly enjoying this game right up until the point I ran into opponents with super armour.
The combat was simple but enjoyable, racking up 20+ combos and landing Kamehamehas was satisfying; things did tend to get a bit silly when there were too many allies or too many enemies as things turned into a hit-stun-fest but it wasn't entirely a dealbreaker.
But you see, attacks cause a hit-stun which enables combos, and combos are the foundation of this game; some opponents are immune to hit-stuns unless you hit them a dozen times in short succession -and only for a short time, making you start all over again.
So you have to land a dozen hits, during which they can punch you at their leisure which hit-stuns you, and then they start their own combo on you, and when you can finally combo them, you knock a few pixels off their health bar and have to start the process ALL over again.
Buy Xenoverse 2 instead, there's no super armour.

My main issues with A Wizard's Lizard are: the game is too
; there is not enough
; and everything becomes
(enemies, rooms, equipment).
A Wizard's Lizard is
similar to The Binding of Isaac, but has an upgrade system similar to Rogue Legacy. During your crawl in the dungeon you can rescue an infinite number of villagers (3 max per crawl) who each give you 500 Gold to start each of your runs with. You spend your money before you enter the dungeon (or choose to save some or all of it for in-dungeon purchases). You spend your money on weapons / other equipment of which you purchase blueprints for in the dungeon. Dying will leave you in ghost form, but you can return to normal on the second part of each area.
There are 3 main areas (
) each with 3 parts to them (e.g. Sewer 1, Sewer 2, Sewer 3) and 2 sub-areas with 1 part each respectively. That's it. All crawls feel the same because everything is set in stone. Blueprints, shopkeepers (and the kinds of items they sell), secret enemies and paths will always be in the same areas (e.g. Cemetery 2 will always have a blueprint for purchase, and Crypt 1 will always have a villager to rescue in the area). You always fight Death at the end. There are no surprises. Someone even wrote a guide on what you can find exactly in each level:
Many of the weapons feel the same and I think a lot of them should not even be in the game. There's even a weapon called the Owl Slayer that is very effective against Owl enemies. The problem with bringing such a weapon is that Owl enemies are only in the first area (Cemetery). Owls are not even difficult enough to warrant bringing a weapon for the sole purpose of making it easier to kill them. As stated before, there are 3 main areas with 2 sub-areas. One of the sub-areas does not have a Boss at the end, so that's 3 main Bosses and 1 sub-boss. There are also a couple special enemies you can fight if you want to, but you usually do not want to. Unlocking shortcuts to the Crypt and Sewers are laughably easy. You just have to kill one of those special enemies in each area once, which is not hard at all. You will also encounter the same enemies over and over with the exception of a few rare enemies. The game has 72 blueprints to collect (those 72 blueprints do not even include every piece of equipment in the game). The game has a Museum that lets you know which weapons / equipment you have completed the game with. I have completed the game with every weapon and piece of equipment and I can say it was not worth it.
: There is so much BS in a lot of the rooms that you have to be overly careful. Every room becomes a tedious nightmare making the game difficult for all the wrong reasons. There are so many non-enemy structures that when destroyed will send projectiles flying out and are very annoying. The Crypt is littered with arrow wall traps and the Sewers have wall traps that spew green liquid on you that slows you down and is more of a nuisance than anything. Rooms freeze with all activated / deactivated traps as they were when you leave a room. So if there is a sliding spike trap located near a door and it barely misses you as you get through the door, you will have to take damage on the way back for not paying attention. Another instance of this happening is when you die and become a ghost; all ghost enemies in previously completed rooms will be unfrozen like the spike trap. I died on a crawl one time after I was backtracking to get revived when I went through a room I had cleared before when I was alive, but now it had a skull ghost in the doorway which killed me instantly upon entering the room. Another annoying part of the rooms is that they can have annoying traps like webs on the floor that slow you down, fans that push or pull you, spike traps that spring up from under the floor, and spike traps that slide across the floor when you get in range. They are all annoying and everywhere.
: Damage upgrades are necessary if you want to have a fun time in your crawls, but they are somewhat rare (for one thing you cannot purchase any of them at the town before a crawl) and all of the damage upgrades except for the charms come with a downgrade. The downgrade is that with each piece of spiked equipment you put on, your fire rate will go down.
: Once you enter a room with enemies you cannot leave until every enemy is dead (except for the 2 crystal enemies). This becomes especially annoying when you go into a room on accident. Some of the enemies can be fun to fight like the two types of Owls who attack you depending on which Owl type you attack which have some great strategic scenarios. And then there are all of the other enemies who all feel the same. Some enemies can freeze or slow you, but the majority of them just charge at you. The later stages feel like there are too many enemies / traps and the enemies have too much health. Some enemies can even kill you in one hit with an explosion against a wall.
If you're a completionist, you may find some entertainment from collecting every available blueprint (which was a pain to do by the way) or completing the game with every weapon and piece of equipment (which also was not very fun). The Museum also tracks how many times you've killed an enemy and will make the trophy of that monster Golden when you've "Mastered" killing them. This can mean a low number of kills like 25 or upwards of 500+. I'm not even going to try that because a lot of the enemies are rare or take a long time to get to.

Murder Miners is a multiplayer first person shooter with the average goal of
the opposing players on the opposite team. The game features different weapons, tools and vehicles that are used in certain situations such as the grappling hook. The Zombie Survival and Infection gamemodes are highly built around this game for the variety of the goal type and gameplay.

After giving this game more play time to reconsider this review, I now find it overall enjoyable and I find myself coming back to this game quite often. Although I do tend to find myself in a powerless situation at times where the host can do whatever they wish since I can be booted for being too good against them or they could become invulnerable which decresses the level of fairness, I would highly recommend hosting your own server or play with a friend if you're experiencing the same issue. Other than that, the game is very decent and can be really fun at times, especially with friends.
I would highly suggest on adding a matchmaking system where no hosts are required and to add a vote system, it should be up to all of the players in the match to decide what's right and wrong. It's the dictatorship and abusive privileges of the host's that can easily kill this game's fair and fun factor.

A Wizard’s Lizard is a rogue-like that resembles Link to the Past in its design. In it you play as Raga, a wizard’s pet lizard. Your master tries to cheat death and Death comes to take him personally. It’s up to you to go and rescue him.

The town of Amberfall is all but deserted when you start, but you can find villagers as you traverse the dungeons in search of your master. Each villager you find will increase your starting gold by five hundred. So, if you save ten people, you’ll start each run with 5000 gold to spend. You also find blueprints, which eventually make every item in the game accessible. With enough patience and enough townsfolk rescued, you can unlock almost every item in the game and have enough money to outfit yourself before you even step into the dungeon itself.

Like most rogue-likes, A Wizard’s Lizard is randomly-generated in almost every aspect. Random dungeon layouts with random monsters with random loot and random rewards. All of which goes down the tubes when you die. There’s no reward for skill or progress beyond saving townsfolk and recovering blueprints so you have access to more items. There are shortcuts, which can be unlocked by destroying giant killer crystals, multiple times. But other than that, it’s just running the same random rooms over, and over, and over again. I’m just not impressed.

There are nine levels in all, spanning a Graveyard, a Sewer, and a Crypt. There are others but darn if I couldn’t find them but once in a blue moon. I only ever got as far as the first area of the crypt. The random nature of the game along with the dwindling chance for health items as you go makes for a nearly impossible path from start to finish. The best you can hope to do is just open all the short cuts so that you start out further along than normal. This game suffers from a lot of strange issues. Let me count them out:
-Occasionally the controls will lock up and have you running upward forever.
-The aiming retical here is NOT on top of everything like it should be, you can lose it in a crowd.
-There are a rather large number of enemies that can’t be harmed when they’re sitting still.
-There are weapons in the game that can kill you if used improperly.
-There are zero enemies in the game that can be killed in one hit, even with top weapons and armor.
-The game keeps track of all the enemies you’ve killed and items found when this could’ve just been done on a menu screen to track progress. Instead it’s a weird museum-statue area.

The unique mechanic that comes with this game is dying. When Raga dies he becomes a ghost and suddenly you must fight both the living and the dead enemies in every room. Handfuls of living enemies turn into spirits, skeletons, and flaming skulls. So, if you wander into a room and you’re already dead chances are you’ll have to kill most everything twice. This isn’t fun, it’s tedious.
Thankfully there are rare resurrection circles. I had to google what they did since the game doesn’t tell you— but if you stand in one while in ghost form you’ll be brought back to life with some of your health. But, if you die as a ghost the game’s over. You lose all your items, money, and progress. Like nothing mattered.

I can go ahead and say I couldn’t beat this game, it’s just not for me. I made it seven levels in and it wasn’t from lack of trying. I didn’t get a single one of the game’s difficult achievements. I didn’t save the wizard, and I never even made it to the final boss. The increasing difficulty and the decreasing of health-items makes the game harder than it should be. Combine this with bad weapon-balancing, mobile obstacles, and the random nature of the beast and you’ve got a recipe for frustration more than you do for fun. Avoid this one.

I generally do enjoy the game, but the inventory system is a problem, as it's a problem in every game that tries to bodge a clumsily restrictive tile inventory together. Music's perfect, atmosphere's evocative, art is simple while suiting the game well, but the design isn't
there for me to recommend this game without reservation. Still largely worth a buy, I'd say. And if you don't like it, get a refund - easy.
Edit: I'm going to change this to a no simply because there are too many design shortcomings that negatively impact the experience. The inventory is a major factor in the way it paints you into a corner or creates arbitrary crises simply through bad design. I don't mind losing in a difficult but fair game, but the game wasting my time because it's poorly designed is inexcusable.
I'll give an example: in the course of the game you need to gather and stock various rare elements (like gold, thorium, platinum, etc.) in order to build and repair some of the more exotic ship modules. Good so far. The problem is that the ships you're flying will generally tend to be between 14-16 tiles, with a good 2/3 of those taken up by essential ship hardware, leaving maybe 6-7 to store cargo in. You want to be stocking full 20-stacks of essentials like iron, hydrogen, oxygen, or helium if you can get your hands on it, but rare elements you only use for repairs, or the omega element that's essentially a wild card, all MUST take up an entire cargo hold even if you only have 1. So if you have 1 omega, 3 hafnium, 3 gold, 8 thorium, and 5 platinum, that's FIVE of your 6 cargo holds used for storing crumbs of rare elements that you need to mitigate RNG with. In a sane world these crumbs (that incidentally total up to 20) would only take up one tile of space. Where's the iron, helium, hydrogen, and oxygen going to fit? Nowhere. Something needs to go overboard, and sure enough, as soon as you dump it, you'll get a random event that requires the element you threw away. It's like the developers, or all the people giving this game awards, never bothered to play it.
This is 3/4 of a good game, with the last quarter being lazily programmed and amateurishly designed garbage, as is distressingly common with a lot of these games that rely on their music, writing, or art direction to draw people in, like Don't Starve, Sunless Sea, and several other overrated culprits. It's like going to a restaurant with attractive ambiance, a great band, and being served a perfectly arranged meal that tastes like cat vomit.
Developers, fix your ♥♥♥♥in' game; it isn't too late. This game is already highly modular and begging to be expanded on (orbiting derelicts, trade posts, maybe a little space combat hazard to use the Resistance stat, stealth - emission sinks, etc.). An inventory fix, and fixes for a few other imperfections, would be just the thing to throw in there.

Well, there are no two ways about it – it’s either you reach the bacon (nice and crispy) by choosing the correct door, or you DIE!!
Doors is a walking simulator / puzzle games. You will be walking through this dark atmospheric world and the end of each short walk you will be presented with doors. A comment will be on the top of each door. Essentially it is a riddle; understand it and choose the right one and you will be closer to the bacon. At the start you will have a couple of doors, then a few, then several with different shapes which will make your neurones sparkle more than once. The riddles become progressively more challenging as you go alone.
I really enjoy the dark atmosphere in Doors - the slow, short walk to the door really makes you wonder what the next riddle is?
Well suited to those who enjoy riddle / puzzle games, although I encourage everybody to give it a go, even if you are not familiar with the genre.

Negatives:

A Wizard's Lizard is a pleasant, vaguely Zelda-like procedurally generated action game. You play the familiar of a wizard who has been abducted by Death, and you must find your way through a series of dungeons to face down the monster and rescue him.
Naturally, this isn't something you're going to be able to do on a single life. For most of your attempts at the game you're going to be gathering money, paying to upgrade the village store, rescuing villagers who will then assist you the next time you play, and learning how best to handle the various traps, monsters, and bosses you face. Expect to die, die, die, die, DIE, each time starting your next game with a few more options than last time.
Additional note: If you wanted to play The Binding of Isaac but that game's blood-soaked graphics and child abuse theme turned you off, A Wizard's Lizard has similar mechanics (if not as much variety in power-ups) and, for me, scratches the same itch.

The difficulty is absolutely ridiculous in this game. It starts out alright, but the second set of introductory levels (the "Easy" difficulty set) get absolutely stupid. The controls are incredibly floatly and difficult to handle. There are spikes everywhere that instantly kill you if they touch you, and they will touch you a lot. One of the most annoying elements of the game is that there are all sorts of mechanics that require you to know where everything is off-screen, but the default camera position is zoomed in super close. You can press the down arrow to zoom out slightly, but you'll still have to jump off screen to your death constantly just to see where you have to go next.
I mostly enjoyed the first set of levels ("Beginner" difficulty) and the first few from the second set. Controlling the ball feels super bad, but the basic mechanics of the game are fun. The fun wore off very quickly when the difficulty got stupid, though.
The menu designs are also annoying. They're designed to work with a keyboard, but are very clunky. They can also be used with a mouse, but are even clunkier that way. Levels slide into position and replace the previous level on the screen when you select them on the menu. When you mouse over the next level to select it, it slides to the center, which means you're now mousing over the level after that, which slides into the center, and so on. There's no delay or anything, making selecting anything with a mouse an exercise in frustation. The game badly needs an interface rework.
Also, the reviews of the game at the point I'm reviewing it are sketchy as hell. They look like the reviews you'd expect a friend to post or people to give in exchange for a key. They're all positive, but I don't think a single one of them is an honest review from someone who legitmately played and enjoyed the game. Stay skeptical when reading them. They all look fake. Unfortunately, this review won't count for Steam's rating since I got the game in a bundle.

A contemplative, atmospheric Roguelike, "Out There" has gorgeous art and interesting challenges. Sure, eventually you'll solve most of the encounters and events - making the game's replay value limited to a few tens of hours, I suppose - but it's well worth the cost.
This is not the game for everyone - it requires patience and reading to fully enjoy, and the desire to learn and remember the "right" outcome of various events - but it's a game I can appreciate, a game that stirs the imagination the way most games these days just can't do. A game that has a story which you can get invested in, paradoxically because you know just how likely it is that the story will end with the phrase "This is the end of my journey."
One word of advice: If you have a large tablet or touchscreen laptop, I'd get this game for the tablet instead. The mouse is not the ideal control scheme for this game.

I love the game because, personally, I find it well balanced.
Maps are good.
Weapons are balanced (a lot of people would say they aren't but they are).

Items are not overpowered (armour is the main cause of rage here but you can often get lucky with or without it).
People claim it's pay to win but again, it just isn't. Every weapon can be used effectively with a little practice including the starter ones.
Community is not bad really considering it's an FPS.
The best part is the variation involved in game modes. There are plenty to suit everyone's tastes, including some good co-op with good rewards if you succeed.
They are always adding more content and more weapons which is always a bonus.
Despite the calls of "hacker" every time you kill someone, the game is not full of hackers. There are just a select bunch of players who seem to understand the game better than everyone else.
Graphics etc are a little dated now but the general game mechanics are great.
Recent changes back to the original way of being able to buy weapons permanently without spending any real money is a serious show that the developers do care despite being slated for everything they do.
All in all, a great game in my opinion.

As much as I enjoy this game and typically turn to this game when I just want to unwind and relax, this game has some glaring flaws.
The gameplay itself usually is very good but that's only if you can ignore major issues that arise here and there. Irish whip your target into the turnbuckle and there's a possibility that when you use your running strike that you will just bounce off your opponent like you missed. Outside of table matches, tables will not break if you try to drive your opponent through them due to a patch that broke how tables work. Not only that, but you won't even be able to pick the table back up. The announce tables work perfectly but not the regular tables. Then there's the issues with frame drops and, when using created wrestlers and arenas, the loading times can get very long. This is coming from someone using an i6700k CPU, 16GB of RAM, and a GTX1070. It is a locked 60 frames per second and, on my rig, it is pretty stable in terms of frame rate outside of when someone interrupts your entrance. At that point, it drops down to 30-40.
Graphically, the game is tolerable. It's far from realistic-looking but it's not bad in terms of how it looks during gameplay and entrances. The problem is that it's got a lot of low-resolution textures and images for things like tattoos and logos. There are graphical glitches where you get a colored line (like a black line stretching from black fingernails, for example) on created characters at times. They're not too common but they do exist. The hair also does not act like hair; it's basically early PS3-level hair physics.
The creation suit is very basic, though. I love creating new characters and entrances; it's very hard in this game to create anyone who is unique that would also be someone that could be a real character. You can create some weird♥♥♥♥♥♥ gorillas,  and stupid things like that but unless you're really good with uploading images, making face-scans, and things like that then you will have one hell of a time creating anyone unique without a mask or a ton of makeup caked on. Creating an entrance can sometimes be fun if you're into that, though my two biggest gripes is you can't use your custom entrance if you're holding a championship belt and the fact that you can't make custom lighting or choose camera angles. The camera angles make it very jarring because the number of hard cuts makes it obvious when the entrance doesn't match up (entering ring from left side, suddenly on ringside on the right in the next scene, for example).
Simply put, if you can get this with the Season Pass for $25 or less and you can't wait until 2k18 releases for your platform of choice then definitely get this one. At full price at this point, I'd recommend against it. However, I have to give this a "Recommended" as I put hundreds of hours on the PS4 version and decided to rebuy it on PC. Between the bugs, how minimal the improvements from 2k16 are, and the very stripped-down/barebones creation suite? This is definitely a 6/10, maybe a 7/10 if you wanted to be generous. Hopefully 2k18 will be a significant improvement now that the PS3 and XBox 360 will no longer be supported.

While for whatever reason the tutorial video may mislead you into thinking this is some sort of realistic war simulator such as Arma, this is a pretty standard action game for its time.
The game has you going around the ruins of Berlin completing objectives, which can vary from getting from Point A to Point B, sabotage, and assassination mainly. Some missions require stealthing with your silenced pistol, some may recommend stealth, but can end up being exponentially easier if you decide to go guns ablaze. In general, the stealth element is more or less half-baked.
As for difficulty, it is very forgiving. I played through the game once on Sniper Elite and hardly found any troubles. Actually, I lied. I really began the game on Marksman difficulty, yet by the next level the game automatically increased my difficulty to Sniper Elite due to my high score. This difficulty adjustment component is a cool, subtle feature that encourages players to take on a greater challenge when showing capability to do so; however, since the game is hardly challenging at all, it didn’t really matter.
This lack of challenge comes from the previously mentioned ability to just blast through certain stealth sections, along with the surplus of ammunition that your current sniper rifle is constantly stocked with. It is also very easy to replenish health, as medkits are common and can instantly heal you to max health. Though there is a heart-rate feature that kicks in after strenuous activity on the protagonist (i.e. running for long periods), making it harder to aim when scoped, yet it can be sidestepped with some skill. You are simply too powerful. And because of this low difficulty, the game is quite a bit less memorable, but that doesn’t necessarily make it completely boring.
The star of the show here is the well-known bullet-cam feature that was popular at the time in games and film. It is still quite satisfying to activate it when getting a long range head shot on an enemy sniper. One great thing is that it does not trigger too often, and still requires a decent shot to activate. This prevents the feature from growing stale, which if it did, I may have dropped the game altogether.
One attempt to mediate a lack of replayability is a scoring system, as mentioned previously. At the end of each level, you are given a score based off of your kills, headshots, difficulty, etc. However, since there were no leaderboards or an additional medal/reward system, I had no idea how high of a score should be considered “good” or why I should care.
The game is also marketed with supposed “Non-linear game play”, which is referencing the open-ish design of the maps, which are fairly large, considering its release date. Some missions may have alternative routes or methods of completion, though I found these to be a bit few and far between in my playthrough. This also means that you must constantly stop to check your map to make sure you won’t run into a dead end. I cannot say that the maps are worth a retread because of this element.
There is also a multiplayer component, though I can’t comment on it due it being dead as a doornail.
For the time, the graphics are adequate. The models and textures are generally decent, and some of the skyboxes look rather nice. The animation quality when characters are talking is somewhat laughable, but the animation on the player character’s movement and enemies are passable. A problem I found is that I could hardly tell the difference between my allies and the enemies, as well as the enemy Germans and Russians. Luckily I never killed one of my allies because of this, though it was just annoying to have to wait a few moments to see if the soldiers would take a shot at me or not.
One issue I have is that in some of the daytime city environments are drenched in this urine-colored hue, as you can probably see by the screenshots. Now I myself was never around to see war-torn Berlin to debunk their historical representation of it, however I can’t see much reason to depict it in this relatively unpleasant manner. Though not all maps have this yellow-ish filter place on them, some take place outside of the city and at different times of day, which somewhat helps the immersion factor.
A few other aspects of the presentation I generally liked, particularly the war film-esque introductory video that really got me psyched to play the game. Yet while the tutorial video carried this aesthetic, it was arguably very misleading of how the game should be optimally played.
A strange issue I ran into is that when you launch the game, for your previously selected graphics settings to take effect, you must load your profile first. I don’t really understand why graphics settings were decided to be tied to the save file, but it never really hindered the experience.
The game features a standard, forgettable orchestral soundtrack that fits the WWII-Cold War era quite well. When the missions are stealth focused, the music complements it with a quieter, tenser track. When you’re placed in the middle of the action, the music complements it was a fast-paced, booming tune. Standard stuff. I found that that only marginally stand-out track was the main theme.
The game also features a standard, forgettable war-hero storyline that centers on an American OSS Sniper, Karl Fairburne, in his mission to uncover nuclear secrets and eliminate German/Russian resistance during the post-WWII and pre-Cold War era. Nothing of the story really stood out to me, besides the mediocre voice acting, and the jarringly high-pitched voice of Karl, which was not particularly distracting, but just an odd choice of casting for the role. You would think a graduate of West Point Military Academy would have a deeper voice than a high school male who just hit puberty.
While I purchased the game for only one dollar and got roughly nine hours of gameplay, I can safely say it was worth the money. However, whether the game is worth your time or not is subjective to you. I found the game to be overall pretty forgettable, besides those fun moments where the bullet-cam kicked in. This is a budget action game and it shows. I can see why Rebellion decided to develop a remake/sequel to this title, because there is potential in this game to become something greater. The problem is that the developer was just not as steady with their aim as they could’ve been.

Winning or losing is entirely determined by your connection error, or rather the server's connection which is so flimsy it could go either way. The game lags and has a lot of talking npcs and unncessary click steps yet has a timer. Which means they must've intended the game not to be played as Yugioh, but as a completely arbitrary gamble and the Yugioh cards are there for aesthetic and to trick idiots into buying gems.
Overall it is more balanced than real Yugioh, but that's because real Yugioh is everything you should not do in a card game. With so much dependent on first hand cards, spells/traps only existing as complimentary utility, and a lot of power creep from set to set, it wasn't hard to make this game at all more competitive by just tightening the board and changing set rotation down to hand selected cards that aren't all that good in the real format. What this is, is Yugioh where they only correct their own bad game design by limiting cards that broke the real game as either extraordinarily rare (again, to trick idiots) and leaving the meta complete hogwash because of consistency constraints and tight board management making a lot of archetypes obsolete.
Yugioh as a game is all about the rareity and power creep of a card, so in essence this "fixes" that by making♥♥♥♥♥♥servers that run on a Atari 500 and insuring most players never even see the really broken stuff they've made over the years. But if you're expecting to duel hardcore, make friends, do really anything besides wait around for the server to crash and get a loss for it... you'll need to play another card game. Which I can't even recommend to you one because the industry is just so unconcerned with improvement and actually in-depth gameplay they're all just as bad. If I could give it a rating instead of just a recommendation I'd rate it two stars because it's like some evil genie wish of technically fixing Yugioh, but in the most contrived way possible. It's like these programmers work harder to aggravate and troll than they do making a game.

I suck at this game. Not suck like the inescapable event horizon of a black hole, but more suck like a animal hair clogged vaccum cleaner that hasn't been turned on for several years. That said...
I love the Dragon Ball series, but honestly haven't played any Dragon Ball titled games other than Xenoverse. I guess I've always found the general feel of the games from what I've seen to be just... off. Then again, most are either very old and almost all of them to my knowledge are (duh) fighting games in the similar vein of stuff like Mortal Combat or Guilty Gear or one of those side by side type deals. But for once I gave it a go and I've had some fun. Though the difficulty curve here is atrocious and using a keyboard/mouse setup just doesn't feel good at all. After a few hours of using keyboard/mouse setup I switched over to my Xbox360 controller and the game felt much better. Though I suspect this game was designed with a controller in mind.
The game looks great though and performs like silky smooth butter on lightly toasted bread. Delicous and just right all around, save for feeling very difficult. It almost seems like your meant to replay earlier missions to farm experience, as some of the enemies you face, especially when you reach cell, are absolutely ridiculous to fight. Though I feel this is something I've experienced several times in Japanese games. Replaying levels and constantly refining and grinding to beat the next best thing. Not that this is bad, but if this is the intention to be difficult, save for pros at this type of thing, then that has pushed me away from being able to finish the single player in this game.
I will note, I do like the subtle triggers in battles to make different enemies appear or change certain circumstances in order to attain a higher rank and in turn much more experience. This does keep replaying levels from becoming boring and gives the player something to strive for, that said, I'm slightly conflicting with my earlier statement about forcefully replaying levels. But I've had my fun and these difficulties didn't sway that factor to much.
As said before, in terms of performance, this game runs great. Not a single fps issue to speak of and it feels very responsive to controls. On that whole, this is a pretty well done game, though I do feel it caters to a certain niche audience beyond the already niche anime crowd. Once again, not necessarily a bad thing, but I do feel this explains it's difficulty curve when catering to an audience already familiar with how these games function.
Overall, I've had my fun and I'm sure any fan of a good old brawler game or Dragon Ball Z in general will have plenty of fun to. Is it worth a $39.99(USD) price tag though? I really can't say for sure, I still feel a bit divided, as I should go back and put some more time into the game. Do I recommend it? With a soft yes. I suppose that's a very subjective matter. But if you like DBZ and you see it on sale, I'm sure you'll have a good time and won't feel your money is wasted. But if you have some extra money to spare and think this looks good, I'd still say wait for a sale.

What Remains of Edith Finch is a game I went into with low expectations. I went into it expecting an average indie game filled with bugs and a lousy story. I can tell you now that everything that I just said, is NOT present in this game. This game took me on an adventure that I was very sad to complete. You play as a woman named Edith Finch who returns to her childhood home to uncover the mysteries of her family from the last 100 years. Her mother was very secretive about the history of their family, as it was very tragic and did not like to remember the past. Upon her death, Edith's mother leaves her a mysterious key and tells her to return to the house to learn the truth about her family. You go through the lives of each family member, both the enlightening and tragic moments, as you uncover what really happened to your family. With a very compelling story, amazingly detailed characters, beautiful graphics and fantastic sound design, What Remains of Edith Finch is a game unlike any game I have ever played. Although it is a rather short game (It took me roughly 2 and a half hours to complete it), it was most certainly worth the 20 bucks I spent on it. This game is not an action packed game, this is not a game you will likely play through more than once, but the amazing attention to detail and the stories located within every corner of the game is enough to let you know that this very well may be one of the best story driven games of all time. Definitely worth playing through at LEAST once. I'd have to give this game a 10/10 because, well, I really didn't find anything that I did not like about the game. One of the best games I've played in a very, VERY long time.

I bought the Heroes Rise trilogy while it was on sale after greatly enjoying the Choice of the Deathless demo (which I still plan to buy). Most of my childhood was spent in the 1990s, so I was able to experience the actual "choose your own adventure" novels that were popular back when bookstores still actually existed. At the time, I actually didn't care for them. Nearly every one I read would have ridiculous consequences for choices that seemed logical; your character could die because of a sound choice you made, just because the author wanted to trick you out of a decision. That was my one concern going into the Choice of Games library of games. That, and whether the story would actually suck me in.
It did. Let me just say I'm not a huge superhero fan. Sometimes I watch the movies, and most of the time I'll play the games associated with various Marvel and DC characters. But I tend to find heroism too black and white to be practical, and tend to be far more interested in the villains of such stories, so I was a little worried this story wouldn't keep my attention. I read this interactive novel from start to finish in one three hour sitting, however, because it didn't shy away from keeping you actively involved in the outcome of certain events. You even get to make small decisions about what your character looks like that I did catch repeated later, helping you stay immersed (i.e. you get to choose what color your "energy" is, and I noticed the game would describe this later on in fights).
Is it written well? For the most part, yes. I noticed some misspellings that could be attributed mostly to typos, and for some reason, the author here has a significant bias against using commas before the conjunction "but" that I noticed popped up multiple times throughout my playthrough. Are the mistakes noticeable? Yes. Are they game or immersion breaking? No. All in all, I noticed about ten errors over the course of a three hour interactive novel, which isn't too bad of a balance.
Is the story any good? Yes. It's mostly a story about going from a nobody to a superhero in a futuristic, arguably dystopian society. The world is just as corrupt as its criminals, with a justice system that crosses the boundaries of reason, technology that is far too incorporated into human life than is safe, and laws that are questionable. You are able to choose where your beliefs lie in this mix, and I was pleased to see I was able to choose a path that wasn't just righteously heroic or immorally anti-heroic. You can also decide what your beliefs are early on and divert from them later, if you so choose, but the game will punish you for this diversion. Throughout the story you are able to choose what sexual orientation you have and you are also able to choose to romance one (or more) of a few characters. Even though I chose relatively early on to romance one character (and had a teen-rated romance scene with said character), I was still given the choice to profess feelings for another later on, so choices hadn't been taken away from me just because I'd already chosen someone else.
With that said, there were some choices that didn't quite make sense or that I made that in the end, didn't really matter. (I'll keep this spoiler-free.) It was revealed to me that a character I cared about had a pretty shocking secret, and I had to choose whether to be okay with this new information and accept the character with their flaws or not. I chose to say that I understood and was okay with it--and despite this, my character decided on her own to stop talking to this person and ignore all attempts of communication from them. In the end, it did end up that this could work out the way I had wanted it to begin with, but the story ended up deciding for me how my character felt despite me telling her to feel otherwise, which broke the immersion a bit. There's also a clear trust violation committed against you by a main character, and even though they explain it was done for your benefit (and you have the choice to refute that), you still end up giving into their whims and doing what they've wanted you to do all along, which really irked me. The story ended up telling me that my character just knew "it was right", and I honestly didn't agree. Because I had created this character to mimic my beliefs, to see her going against them angered me a bit and made me question the influence of some of my decisions.
Overall, this was a well-written game that gave me more choices than I anticipated, and most of them made sense. Quite a few of them mattered quite a bit (for example, characters in this CAN die). I admired the author for steering clear of the goofy superhero format and sticking with the gritty, more realistic superhero formula that won't shy away from killing characters or having true consequences to actions. Although I was a bit disappointed in the mostly uninteresting villains this game had to offer, the heroes themselves had enough downfalls in their personalities to keep me intrigued in their character development. Because I got three hours out of one playthrough, I think the game is worth its full price even if you'll only go through it once (though, of course, there is massive replay value here). If I had to give it a rating, I would give Heroes Rise: The Prodigy an 8/10. This is a great game at a great price that will grab your attention and hold onto it until it concludes in an epilogue, and it should not be missed.

First let me preface this by saying that I like the genre of IF and text adventures and that i enjoy reading traditional books in my spare time.
But exactly because I'm a fan of the genre I was rather disappointed with Heroes Rise: The Prodigy, mostly because it has a stark lack of actual choices that have consequences. For the most part you only can expect a short flavor blurb. And while I understand that the amount of story forks and side stories need to be limited even in a purely text-based game there isn't even a SINGLE meaningful choice in the entire adventure or any substantial side story.
Another problem is the writing itself, for the most it's serviceable enough but in some aspects it's decidedly less than stellar, mostly when it comes to the villain. While I do not expect them to produce a villain worthy of Shakespeare the main villain and also other villainous characters are just very cheesy and ham-fisted but the author tries to play them straight. As a result I couldn’t help but roll my eyes at many supposedly serious but unintentionally silly scenes.
TL;DR: I can’t recommend Heroes Rise: The Prodigy to anyone who likes to have even minor consequential choices or side stories.

Damn I love Gothic. One of the core games of my youth.
It is not a perfect game. Not even close. It has some weaker plot points, a couple of useless mechanics (bow combat is underpowered, skills like pickpocketing are a beginner's trap) and the game is buggy as hell - it likes to crashe out especially in the second half.
But beside of that Gothic tries (and succeeds) to do something unique for a computer RPG - it puts it's fictional society in the center of the game and focuses not on quantity, but on quality (unlike, for example, Gothic 3).
You can easily point out two very different parts of the game: the first act, during which the player explores and learns about the world and fighting (in almost open-world fashion) while trying to find the place for his character in divided, brutal society; and the second part (acts 2-6), when the plot becomes very specific and linear, mostly replacing exploration with complex story, small group of characters and so on.
Because of that you have to remember: the game is neither sandbox nor a well orchiestrated action packed story, but something in between. Surprisingly it helps the game to stay fresh for quite a long time.
Also the game doesn't tell you a lot about its setting. After beating the game you know almost nothing about other parts of the realm and the main focus of in-game exposition is the background related to the NPCs, some legends or rummors. Very often you may find a useless character which serves nothing more than just sharing with you some foreshadowing thought or a casual joke, an empty cave or a small island, some human bones beneath the tree or a short letter made by some unlucky dude.
Because of that the game becomes twice as fun if you'll try to invest yourself and use your imagination to fill this areas and characters with your own ideas. The game uses many tricks to make you feel like a part of this world - and if you will allow it to do so, you won't be dissapointed.

Although more restricted than titles such as Choice of Robots, Heroes Rise is still enjoyable in its own right. I'd have to say it is more of an interactive novel than a choose your own adventure, if you can understand my distinction between the two. Some choices seem 'not to matter' but actually affect your stats which in turn can affect your Legend score at the end of the game.
Some people will be disappointed that they can't decide what powers they get or what their background is, but that is what I meant by an interactive novel. This is part of a series with a plot which can seem a bit more rigid than some of the other Choice of Games. I don't feel this should stop you if you enjoy the idea of superheroes and a setting with a decent enough background.
Another complaint I have seen is somebody saying it was too 'dark' for them and they wanted something 'silly'. I don't think that part of their review warranted the downvote. In fact, if you can get past feeling led here and there, the story can be quite moving.
In the end, this is not as good as some of the other games from the same company. Maybe wait for it to go on sale if you aren't sure, though honestly it doesn't cost much.

The gameplay is however very deeply flawed and heavily reliant on luck (each game you play the universe and it's inhabitants are randomly generated) and acts as a barrier to enjoyment rather than a source.
If this game could either improve the frustrating and flawed gameplay or just remove it so I could enjoy the story it would be an instant recomend.
As it stands, I can not recomend this game and have refunded it (thank you steam for finally implimenting a refund system)
For people who just want to know what the gameplay is like, i'll give you a run-down of my various failed playthroughs.
You start the game in one corner of the galaxy map and your objective is to reach the opposite corner, you jump short distances from star-to-star just like in FTL, but unlike FTL there is no combat.
Instead the "challenge" comes in the fact that each jump consumes rediculous portions of your fuel and you can only obtain very small ammounts of it by "probing" gas giant planets.
How do you find a gas giant planets? you jump to a star system and hope one of the 0-3 planets it will randomly generate is a gas giant.
In the 4 seperate attempts I made to play through the game less than 30% of the star systems I encountered had any gas giants at all.
Once you DO find a gas giant, you probe it for gas resources, you are only allowed to extract a small ammount before you are told "there is nothing else here" as though your very tiny vessel had absorbed the entierty of a jupiter-sized planet.
If, and I stress IF, you are lucky enough to find one of the 2 gasses that count as fuel instead of one of the many that don't you find just barely more fuel than you spent obtaining it.
Unfortunately you also damaged your ship orbiting the planet (this happens on every planet no matter what, aparently your ship is made out of balsa wood) so you will need metal to repair the damage, which means spending tons of fuel finding, landing on, and drilling a planet with metalic resources.
Doing THAT, consumes more fuel than you could replace by visiting a dozen gas giants, oh and landing on this planet ALSO damages your hull, and when you drill into the planet to get the also dumbfoundingly-limited metalic resources you flip a coin and either damage or destroy the drill you used to do so.
There's a less risky way to drill but it consumes much more fuel.
So I tried, I really really REALLY tried to like this game, the alien encounters seemed neat, the music and art was interesting, but you end up spending each game sucking d**k for gass, and STILL end up dying around your 5th planet no matter WHAT because you either run out of gas or metal.
Even THIS could be solved by carefully designing the planets you will reach and the order in which you will reach them, to ensure that a crafty player will always be able to squeak by if he manages his resources correctly and takes the right risks at the right time.
But designing a galaxy map takes time and effort, and writing a script to randomly generate the galaxy adds "replayability" and "challenge" to the game via rendering 9 out of 10 generated maps impossible to complete, and like corporations and stuff and like man it's an like an experience man, and you're entitled and stuff.

It's regrettably but I did not enjoy this game. The game is similar to Our Darker Purpose and Binding of Isaac, and has some interesting mechanics that make it not just-a-clone. The real downfall IMHO is repetitive playthroughs feel quite similar and deaths feel cheap. Allow me to clarify the positives and detriments that befall this game in case you already played the previous two games I mentioned and want more.
Unlike BoI and ODP, most items have 'slots' and can be freely picked up and replaced, and most of the items have trade-offs. You have access to a variety of weapons, as well as a secondary weapon with a cooldown called a totem, and then a limited use generally-more-powerful spell; all of which can be modified to different degrees by your equipment. Also unlike BoI and ODP you can fire at any angle using either a mouse or analog stick. Another interesting mechanic is the land of the dead vs land of the living. When you die as a living body your spirit continues to fight until you die a second time, however the dead spirits of enemies also will be able to attack you, providing a harder experience but also more charges for your spells. All in all, this is great news and I love the design.
So why do I not recommend this game? Without a lot of items that boost your HP there are some enemies and passive explosive barrels that will one shot you. Sounds simple though right? Avoid bombs and explosive barrels which are immobile and you're golden! However one slip up, especially upon entering a very busy room, and you die, even at full hp. My first half dozen play throughs I would have fun learning patterns of enemies and killing them, but my timer of entering the vicinity of 2 explosive objects would be up and I would be forced to restart from the beginning. Once you master the art of prioritizing identifying the instant-kill barrels, the last area in the game has wall-traps that will kill you in around 6 hits from full, have 0 to 8ish per room, and require you to juke them (unless you have a fair amount of speed items). Additionally with how the lighting works, if you're alive you will have trouble seeing them in some rooms unless you walk along the walls. Again, like the explosive objects once you learn what to look for it's not hard to avoid them... but requires a lot of attention and I found it a huge detriment to my enjoyment.
And I hear what you're saying, if you don't want to be forced to start over from punishing traps then don't play a roguelike. To clarify, my issue is not having to restart from punishing enemies/environments, but all the enemies and environments are what I want to experience and then I get instant-gibbed by a barrel that I didn't spot. This means you have to pay a lot of attention in a game genre that I feel is most fun running through zoning out/multi-tasking.
I did put 10 hours into this game, and it is a good game, but honestly it just made me want to play BoI or ODP. I would not recommend this game unless you're a fan of the genre and want to try some variety.

Running out of fuel: The game.
This is a mixed review.
The game is solid at what it focuses on: environment and isolation. The scenery and soundtrack are both enjoyable and engrossing, while the challenge of surviving alone in an indifferent universe will engage you for many hours.
Where the game fails however is in the execution of the resource management and randomized systems. Limited cargo space makes stockpiling difficult, while the sparsity of gas giants for fuel makes it all but impossible to actually net fuel in the long run. I've had games where I had 3 stacks of stockpiled fuel and a full tank and I lose anyway because the next series of systems I visited had no sources of fuel. Games. Plural.
In 30+ games I've yet to get more than halfway to the target systems at the far end of the map and that was only because an event teleported me much closer (only to leave me stranded because I didn't have the jump distance systems to get out of the cluster). I can understand some difficulty, but the journal entries, encounters, and events start feeling stale and repetitive after seeing them the second or third time in a playthrough because you've not gotten that golden game where everything goes right.
This is compounded by some UI oddities that stem from the game's mobile origin. Lack of many simple shortcuts makes for tedious management of things. To get more fuel you send out the Hydrogen Probe and it returns with whatever it found. Rather than being able to put it directly into your tank from this screen, you have to switch over to the ship view and drop it into the fuel tank there before switching back over to the planet screen to probe for more fuel. Rather than a button to empty everything from a probe or drill or double clicking to transfer to cargo, everything is drag and drop or rightclick to select transfer to cargo (then watch the game drag and drop it for you, meanwhile you can do nothing but wait for it). Normally these wouldn't be an issue in a game, but when you're doing this a dozen times at every gas giant you go exploring for fuel, it gets massively tedious.
Abandoned ships you encounter are often side-grades from the shuttle you start in. The few ships that are larger have oddties or are in need of serious repairs before you can use the extra space they afford; the few ships that are smaller only amplify the resource storage problem.
The technologies you find are interesting to find but don't help much and are an uncommon find if you don't get lucky with finding the right tech and the resources for it. The new modules save a small portion of your resources by taking up space where you could have stored them in the first place. I imagine finding three or four would actually make for a much more efficient ship, but again the problem is luck in finding them.
I will likely continue to play to try to find some closure for the plot, but as it stands for me I don't hold much hope of ever finding it. Such is the drawback of random generation and encounters: Some players don't get lucky.
Despite these flaws it is a solid game of exploration and resource management. I encountered no bugs or glaring issues while playing. If you enjoy exploration and atmospheric games, grab a touchscreen and this will be an enjoyable experience for many hours.

Pros:
Beautiful graphics/illustrations. It's like FTL, but prettier.
Lots of interesting story elements.
Cons:
The game gets repetitive too quickly. While the story has constanly new and different elements, even that loses its flavor after awhile, because unlike FTL, which had more immediacy to it... there is very little driving force to push you forward. Your focus is to keep your ship going... but you are severely limited in how you can do that,
The new technologies you can discover seem neat at first, until you realize they don't tend to do all that much differently or improve the gameplay all that much. Your ship is extremely limited. You can actually discover new ships, apparently, which does improve things, but there is no garuntee of this and the existing ship has very little space in it. It seems like poor design decisions led to combining your cargo with the slots to install your new tech in. I don't recall you ever being limited in cargo in FTL and that is one of my big gripes here. Plus, in FTL, you could easily expand various capabilities of your ship beyond just new tech you can install. The tech seems more varied in Out There, but also far more limited.
Having to micromanage your cargo space is annoying, because while all the elements you can find have info on them, most of these elements are pretty much useless unless you stumble across the right technology that requires these elements to build.
Also, if you go to a breathable atmosphere planet and immediately fill up your O levels, why can you not also fill up as much inventory of O as possible? I would have to drill for it, and still too often get too little. The balance of elements to drill or probe for seems out of whack. Also, more often than not, it seemed like a waste to drill or probe a second time, as it produced little to nothing in addition. I would think drilling 2-3 times could still yield some good resources, at least more often than not. Otherwise, why is there an option to drill or probe a second time other than to waste your resources? Just make it only doable once and be done with it.
I played through three times, and got better each time, but mainly, I stuck very strictly to doing very specific things, because otherwise, it is way too easy to run out of resources in this game.
FINAL SUM UP:
I think if I didn't have such limited cargo space and the elements were not quite so out of whack when drilling... the game would play better for me. It is in many ways a more laid back kind of game compared to FTL, which has combat and the risk of being attacked if you explore too much... and I want to like this game for the graphics and story, but it seems like there isn't enough of a game to really make it worth more than a few playthroughs. Maybe if there was more story that a player can actively get involved with, but it is all so passive, almost like a visual novel you can die in and have to do a little bit of work in, but mostly, just... yeah.
So I cannot really recommend it... very lightly, very mixed. .

A solid spin-off of the traditinal RTS, DoW II takes the premise of a stong first showing with DoW and Winter Assault and takes the game to a whole new level. The single player campaign allows for some solid action and adventuring against a new host of enemies while the new levelling and item equip system establishes some continuity and a more goal-oriented approach than the traditional "Build up and tear down" RTS campaign can offer.
Rich voice acting and solid graphics couple with the telltale chaotic pumping of bolters, plasma guns and chain swords to provide a great visceral experience with great ambiance and enough versatility to allow you to customize your style of play / strategize from mission to mission using different units to suit different approaches.
Best of all, a "Drop in, Drop out" mission by mission co-op feature to the campaign makes gaming with friends easy and effective. A great buy if you can get Chaos Rising and Retribution in an package for $10 - $20.

Sniper Elite taught me something about Sniper Games: that I don't like them.
I
I liked sniper-type gameplay. The sniper rifle is my best friend in Borderlands, or Deus Ex, or L4D or any other game that will give me the option.  But what I really like, it seems, is taking advantage of game AIs that don't contend well with a sniping approach.  I love taking out foes that have "taken cover" but left part of their heads sticking out.  I adore taking the time to line up the perfect headshot as an enemy runs directly towards me, across open ground, in a straight line.  I giggle when my shot from the rooftops drops an enemy in the middle of the street, which causes all buddies to rush out and cluster right in my sights.
Sniper Elite, first of all, is a strong adherent to the reality-is-brown school of graphical design.  Which doesn't do any favours to the graphics, as they're already rather poor, even for 2005, relying too much on textures to save polygons.  So you trudge through a bland, unimmersive environment in order to accomplish your mission, only to find that the usual AI-abusing sniper tactics don't work here.  Unless you've played a level already and memorized the locations of the enemy NPCs, you have to sneak (slowly) everywhere, because NPC snipers are ready to do to you what you'd normally do to them if you go running around in the streets.  So you have to be patient.  Very, very patient.  Which is boring.  When the game
get exciting, it likes to do so by throwing a tank at you, or spawning a couple of guys at short range, so that you don't get to play with the sniper rifle anyway.
Between all the sneaking, and crawling, and waiting, and waiting some more, and crawling a bit, and waiting again, I've never had a less fun time with a simulated sniper rifle in my hands.  On the plus side, the game did manage to capture the feeling of being a very vulnerable, mortal soldier, alone in a dangerous environment.  I just prefer the feeling of being a cunning, dangerous predator, methodically eliminating hapless prey, and Sniper Elite was not going to give me that.

The easiest dessert:
Apple Crisp (serves two)
Heat oven to 350 degrees.
Butter a shallow 8 inch square pan. (A pie pan is okay too.)
Peel, core, and slice 8 sweet tart apples (about 2 lb.) and heap into pan.
In bowl, crumble together 3/4 cup flour, 1/2 cup (1 stick) of cold butter, 1/2 cup white sugar, 1/2 cup brown sugar, 1/2 teaspoon cinnamon, 1/4 teaspoon salt. Don't mix to long, keep it crumbly.
Spread crumble mixture in a thick layer over the apples in pan.
Bake 45 minutes, until apples are soft and crumbles are bubbling hot.
Allow to cool slightly, serve hot or cold.
Can be served with whipped cream, sour cream, or vanilla ice cream.

After a decades long hiatus, I've only recently returned to gaming. Looking back now, I realize I'd vastly underestimated how much the technology of today has changed the expertience of gaming from what I remember in my youth. This paradigm shift was incredibly intimidating, and had it not been for the advent of VR, I might have just stayed away all together. Luckily, VR's novelty leveled the playing field for me, and feeling more confident in my abilities, I decided to branch out and try some non-VR games. After buying and playing many of the most popular FPS shooter, survival horror, RPG, and MMO titles, I was left a little disappointed in what I found. There was no connection for me, no magic, and no sense of discovery. Then I found "What Remains of Edith Finch" and everything changed.
WREF is the kind of game/experience I'd hoped I'd find when I came back to gaming; rich with narrative and innovative storytelling techniques that grab you and don't let you walk away until the journey is complete; an experience that elevates the player and the industry, regardless of age or any other demographic. "What Remains of Edith Finch" is a masterful example of gaming's ability to revolutionize the art of storytelling into something nothing short of transcendent.

Some of the choices in this story don't feel fully flesh out, which results in some choices to feel completely ignored, no matter what choice you make. The story sure takes its time to ramp up, and all the video game-ish mechanics being explained in a fictional world comes across weird. Instead of feeling "warn out", you have a chip in your wrist that tells you that you are "low on mana". I feel like that could be kept within the story's boundaries and explained with just a few sentences.
I think I'm almost done with this book, but depending on the ending I may not start the second in the series. My character is kind of a push over hero, and a little too attached to her fame status. The Legend level thing also feels a little to RPG-ish for a fictional book world. Just let my Hero walk down the street and have someone want to take a selfie with her. Keep me in the story, don't pull me out to explain how games work.

"Underrated Masterpiece"-This game is the definition of the RPG genre.I own a hard copy of this game for more than ten years,since then i play this game every 1-2 years,so you can only imagine how much replayability it has^^.I even bought it on steam as well because i couldn't activate it from my CD.
Here are a few things that you'll definitely like and some that you will not:
+Very well designed world,with three main camps  that you can join,each one being very different to the other two.
+Solid and unique story,brilliantly imagined,with 0 predictability from a chapter to another.You play as a convict who's sent in a prison colony that's surrounded by a magical barrier.There,you have to do whatever possible to survive,join a camp,make friends,do missions,get better gear,learn new abilities and solve the mysteries surrounding the area.
+For it's time being,this game allows you to do alot more things than most modern RPG,thus making it more realistic.Your character can cook and eat food,play the lute,blow a horn,light a campfire,sit,sleep,smoke,drink,craft weapons and many more.Also,all the characters have a fixated schedule,when they eat,sleep,sit,patrol,talk with each other and so on.
+The dialogue with the other characters is very funny engaging as well.For example,you can be disrespectful towards those that try to mock you.As a matter of fact,every characters has it's own personality,you'll barely encounter two characters that are similar.Even more than this,they all react towards the hero's actions.If you walk inside someone's house,you'll be asked to leave,if you draw your sword they will draw their swords as well and if you steal or pickpocket from them they'll attack if they catch you.
+There's a very large range of creatures that react and fight differently.
+A very wide range of weapons:swords,warhammers,axes,bows,staffs and crossbows.There are also many types of unique armors,some of which you can only get from a certain Camp or Guild.If you choose to become a magician you'll be granted acces to many types of magic,including fire,ice,lightning and eventually dark arts magic,which you acquire progressively by learning the circles of magic.
+Realistic nature sounds,as well as relaxing music that's very different from a place to another.
-There are some technical issues which might crash or freeze the game unless you apply some patches that you can find in the Steam Guides section.
-Controls feel bad and hard in the beginning,but you'll eventually get used to them.
-Minor bugs and graphical glitches,none of them are gamebreaking...at least they weren't for me.
*The game has a hack and slash combat system,with parry and dodge,which you might like,or you might not like,depending on your preference.I have personally enjoyed it alot,as it was more challenging.

I really wasn't sure what to make of this game, when I played through the first chapter. It starts slow with your wannabe super hero or villain taking on his/her first case. Regarding your background, you're stuck living with your grandmother (which I personally wasn't a big fan of) and have this know-it-all best friend I tried very hard to get rid of. On top of that, you can't choose your powers and have very limited customization options. In the beginning it felt like I was playing a bad superhero cliché written for teenagers...
As I stumbled through my first mission, however, my opinion of the game changed quite a bit. Some of the choices you can make are hilarious. The more miserably my fledging hero failed, the more I became invested in her story. Also, there were some twists and turns I really didn't see coming.
In sum, the game is a lot more complex than I initially gave it credit for. Choices you make in the first game have an effect on what happens in the finale. And yes, you can get key characters killed by accident.
It's also worth mentioning, that the writer created a world that is fully LGBTQA inclusive, which I appreciate.

A rogue-like game similar to The Binding of Isaac, and definitely worth checking out. The gameplay is fun, unique, and interesting enough to keep me coming back for a round every now and then. For example, you can find citizens of the game's main town lost throughout the dungeons. Each one you rescue adds money to your starting stockpile of cash. That means for every person you save, the more money you start with each playthrough. This allows you to buy items from the shop to give you an edge over the earlier parts of the game, and perhaps beyond, rewarding you for playing further. Another unique factor that I enjoy is the blueprint system. The shop in town starts with only a few basic weapons, but you can buy blueprints from shopkeepers inside of the dungeons. These blueprints unlock additional items in the shop available to purchase, expanding the variety that the starting shop offers. Overall, this game is definitely worth the price and I'd highly recommend it.

I really like this game, and you might also if you liked 'Binding of Isaac' or 'Rogue Legacy'. Its an action roguelite. The play style is overhead rooms like Legend of Zelda, although they don't fit entirely on the screen at once, sometimes being as large as about 2x3 screens to fit the entire room.
You get two lives, one as a normal character and a second as a ghost, but then you start completely over. As a ghost you have to fight the regular enemies and also sometimes their spirits or floating heads. Its a great mechanic. It affects puzzles in the game and makes you dread either death.
The items are fun. There are different pieces of armor, totems, spells and weapons. The weapons have decent variety. Anything from swords (all are thrown/ranged) to spears, bouncing axes to buzzing bees, dual split daggers to explosives. Spells and totems are equally varied.

Although "What Remains of Edith Finch" is truly, an amazing and spectacular story: one which has left a heavy impression on me, I would not qualify it as an experience or "game". Don't get me wrong, I loved the use of creative art approaches and the diverse ways Giant Sparrow used in order to convey these stories in a way that isn't monotonous. It made me laugh, and gasp in awe each time a new "secret" was revealed. It's a work of art. However, aside from this: I still felt as if there was a discontinuity within the story itself which stopped me from enjoying it fully. If you're just here for the tl;dr: I don't think this "game" is worth $20, maybe just $10. You could've easily gotten the same experience  by just watching a lets play or gameplay of it on YouTube (and even better in my opinion because I enjoyed watching the first story more than playing it). Actually playing the game doesn't offer much more than watching someone go through it because it's very passive throughout most of the stories/mysteries. The only up side to buying it would be you can spend your time and gawk at the pretty aesthetics of the game.
It felt as if someone began the story, and someone else had picked it up afterwards. When I finished the first few stories, and was led to the cemetery: it felt as if the game was ending, and made me feel conflicted. There were still many stories to be told, yet in the middle of the adventure: it felt like it was climaxing. Aditionally, the first few stories before going to the cemetery had a more elusive and supernatural feel to it; whereas the last stories felt more grounded. Personally, I also felt that the first few stories lacked the creativity put into the "after cemetery" part of the game. Maybe it's personal preference, but I enjoyed the last half much more. There was a more cohesive story line instead of it just being elusive. Yes, I know this is a mystery story: but you still need to have SOME form of cohesion.
Spoiler ahead so, yeah.
The second half of the game was better than the first half, and had the most creative uses in my opinion. It didn't feel passive like the first few stories were. You could see the world through their eyes: their lenses. You weren't just along for the ride, but you WERE them. Instead of hearing the characters themselves talk about what happened, you actually experienced it for yourself. It went from being a "story" into a "game" especially in Lewis' and Gregory's stories. However, with these two stories being the only ones really worth "playing through" yourself: it's not worth the $20.
Yes, the graphics are beautiful, and the music is fantastic. However, as a game: it fails to give me that same "experience" you feel in a Legend of Zelda or Professor Layton game. Yes, these games are vastly different, but they're both story driven and gave me the "experience" you can't get from just watching it on youtube. If it's on sale for half the price, I think it'd be worth it for the two hours it kills.
