On the whole, I am happy to be able to recommend this game. I am personally a huge Dragon Ball fan.  However, this is not a perfect game.  It has, in my opinion, 4 flaws.
Flaw #1
Not a huge deal, and not at all a deal breaker, but, as a Cell fan, I am kind of dissapointed that there isn't a Bio-Android race.  I don't know how you could work it in, as each playable race has it's own unique perks and abilities, and I certainly wouldn't want them to force it in and make it sucky, but I find it unfair that Cell, my personal favorite villain, get's zero representation while Frieza and Buu get their own races.  Again, this isn't a huge flaw, but more a minor dissapointment for me personally.
Flaw #2
Saiyans are so ridiculously overpowered!!!  This is coming from someone who plays almost exclusively as a Saiyan.  As soon as you get Super Saiyan, you are unbeatable.  It makes all your attacks more powerful, and none of your ki based attacks cost any ki.  This is "balanced" by the slow drain it takes on your ki until it runs out and you return to your original state.  But once you transform, you can just spam Final Flash or whatever your personal favorite ultimate is until everyone is dead.  It won't take long and it certainly won't take as long as it takes for your ki to run out.  This has led the online battles and such to be completely dominated by Saiyans.  If you don't play online much, like me, this won't really matter to you, so you can ignore this.  But for those who want to play online, but not as a Saiyan, you'd best get good fast or you won't last long.
Flaw #3
Earthlings are pointless in my opinion.  While most of the show's protagonists are at least half human, the species is utterly pointless in this game.  Saiyans can use all the same equipment, moves, etc. as Earthlings, while also getting better racial perks and, of course, Super Saiyan.  Unless you just really wanna know what it's like to be Krillin, I don't really get why you would play as an Earthling.
And, finally, Flaw #4
This is unfortunately, a fairly complex flaw in the game and also it's most glaring.  The story.  First,
.  Second, they spend far too much time in the Frieza saga and almost no time on the Cell and Buu sagas.  You basically go through every major battle during the Frieza arc (Zarbon, Dodoria, every member of the Ginyu Force,
, Captain Ginyu in Goku's body, and Frieza himself,
) leading to this being the bulk of the storyline.  Cell and Buu, however, get less than that combined.  Frieza's a good villain, don't get me wrong, but he's not the entire show.  Finally, the story just isn't that strong.  At it's best, it's on par with a half decent filler arc, and about the same length.
I realize that this is a fairly long review, especially for a recommendation, but the point is, if you can look past these flaws, it is a solid game.  I thouroughly enjoy it in spite of these, but I felt that they should be considered before deciding to spend forty dollars on any game.

So would I recommend this game? Absolutly. Is this a game for everyone? Maybe, maybe not. Let me explain why.
First the premise of the game. You are a lizard-buddy from a wizard (hence the title) whose master gets taken away by some evil guys. Now it is up to you, to rescue him. And to do so you cross various dungeons and defeat a lot of baddies along the way. You get various equipment and skills and it's up to you to combine them and make the best of it.
Sounds like fun, doesn't it? Oh wait, but that isn't everything. We all have seen these type of games before. I mean Legend of Zelda or Binding of Isaac. But A Wizard's Lizard adds a little twist to it. In the dungeons you can save townspeople. Townspeople, you say? Yes, because you have access to a little townarea that serves as your main hub. Some townspeople just give hints (in the beginning that is) but the rescued ones actually give you a reward. They'll put in a small amount of cash in a treasure box in the town. With this cash you are able to buy weapons, upgrades, armor etc before entering a dungeon. A big plus since having for example a lance is beter then your starting sword.
But it doesn't stop there. Mostly when you die, that's it. Game over, start over. But not in this game. You resurrect as a sort of 'angel' lizard which gives you a second chance to finish the game. Combine this with the ability of certain rooms to turn you back to normal and you have a pretty much bag full of content to keep you entertained for a long time.
Are there any cons? Yeah, perhaps. The floors, although randomized, can get a bit repetitive. For example the 1st floor of the first dungeon has the exit on on side of the path and a little graveyard on the other side. What's inbetween them or where you spawn is random. But these two are a certain give. Good side about this is, you want to get to both sides for the cash and the exploration. Also sometimes the music can get a bit repetitive as well.
One last 'bad' thing is the enemies. Although most of the enemies are relativily fair some are a bit of a screwover. For example you have owl-enemies. But hitting one means all of the owls in that room starting flying around like a bunch of wild dogs and sometimes chase you. If you're stuck in a corner running for them, it can very easily screw you over.
So just to summarize the game with the pro's and con's:
Pro's:
+ Main hub-area is a nice new twist to the genre
+ Rescueing townsfolks adds a bit more exploration-iniviative for the players
+ Upgrade your character before going into the dungeons
+ Controls are smooth
+ 'Resurrect'-mode adds a lot more gameplay-time
Con's:
- Floor's & certain rooms can get a bit repetitive
- Same goes for the music
- Some enemies can really cheapshot you

Who could have thought that a portal game would work without making portals? I sure didn't. I was attached to everything i had learned and enjoyed in the official games and initially, it bothered me how different it felt without a portal gun in my hands. That is until i began to realise how much potential and how many ideas they had for thier paint gun concept.
Be warned though, early stages feel a little dull and clunky because they are effectively a tutorial, so the game is takign it slow and you are learnign new concepts throguh trial and error. Once you know what you are doing and the game takes the training wheels off, it really starts to feel like a brand new experience. Puzzles are challenging and kinetic, but true to the original games, no less cerebral.
In terms of difficulty, it starts simple and eases you into more complex puzzles. As things go on, you will experience increasingly brutal puzzles, but nothing that will cause serious frustration like the extreme difficulty seen throughout Mels Story.
For story, you're being walked through things by a brand new core. And yes, he is very good. He manages to be funny, though mostly through his core-like shortcomings. Similarly, he can be unintentionally cruel for the same reasons. Without spoiling it, he sees no problem with completely messing with your head with his attempts to expose you to artificial stimuli for the sake of science with no regards for your characters emotional wellbeing. There's something deeply fascinating about his unintentional cruelty that keeps you in a place where you can't dislike him because you pity him.
The music is absolutely fantastic. Great sounding tracks all the way through, particuarly "Trials" in the late game, which is deeply immersive and in touch with the aesthetic of that chamber in particular. You wont get tired of the music, because there's alot of different tracks and they are all enjoyable.
In conclusion, an unexpectedly great game. You wont regret it for such a cheap price.

This VN will definitely not be everyone's cup of tea simply because of the darker and more mature storyline that it explores. The story and somewhat uncomfortable topics are handled very well though and I never wanted to stop in the middle of a playthrough because it felt...dirty or whatever. Yes, I did find myself pulling faces at some points but it did not detach from the VN itself. At it's core Cupid uses it's story to explore the different, and sometimes darker, sides of love, the sides that we maybe don't always see or don't even know exist.
The characters are all lovely and you can see so many different sides to their personalities in the short time you go on the journey with them. There is also the very interesting character of the Mother, who is essentially the player basically talking to Rosa throughout the game. Instead of directly making any choice, you play as the voice of Rosa's beloved mother guiding her.
If you have interest in the game at all, I highly recommend giving it a chance, it is free after all. And aftering playing a while and potentially finishing one route you will know for sure whether you want to keep playing or not.

I kickstarted this game, and this is the type of game kickstarter was made for. A game with a weird premise that would never get published in a million years.
In Sethian, you are a researcher dropped on an a planet, trying to find out what happened to the Sethians who lived there. All you have, and this is the whole game, is a Sethian computer. Unfortunately, this computer's inputs and output are all in Sethian, an alien language. Fortunately, you know a couple languages that are related to it, so you're not completely lost. Also fortunately, the computer is an AI that will answer your questions, should you be able input them in so it understands. Right clicking will bring up your notebooks, which automatically updates and details your thoughts on what the computer says, the words you've learned, and what questions are waiting to be asked.
Your learned words are in a different section of the notebook, so they're easy to look up, and once you reach a certain point, you'll be able to right click on a symbol (input button or response) and get the definition for it so you don't have to remember every symbol, though you'll no doubt pick some up naturally as you go through the game.
I've taken a couple courses on Japanese, so I know a little about translating from one language into the next. Sethian has the same feeling from learning a new language. You look up all the words in your dictionary, hoping you got the meaning right, and then you struggle to put the sentence together and understand what it means. And then, after reading it over a couple times, it clicks! Ah ha! THIS is what they're saying! That moment of understanding, Sethian replicates it perfectly.
If you have no clue what the computer is saying, don't worry, the notebook will be updated with what your character thinks it says, so I had lots of fun translating the reply myself and comparing it to the official translation.
The graphics are very basic, but this is not a game you play for the graphics. It's just you and the computer, struggling to ask questions and struggling to read the answers, piecing together what happened.
It took me about 2 hours to get my first ending, but I'm excited to get the others, which I think will go a little quicker.  The story is interesting and the fact that you have to uncover it yourself adds to the satisfaction.
This game definitely won't be for everyone, but if you enjoy puzzles and languages, and something a little more complicated than "translating" Al Bed, then definitely give this game a try!

You awaken from cryogenic sleep on your journey from the moon to Jupiter only to discover that you're not in our solar system anymore. You've traveled "Out There." Its now up to you to explore a new galaxy and find your way back home. Out There: Omega Edition boils down to a combatless, inventory management game in a beautiful space setting with randomized solar systems and events. For your survival, you need to manage your cargo while maintaining fuel, oxygen and hull to stay alive. Its an easy and relaxing game to play, relying on mostly button presses with your mouse or touch pad. Death is permanent, but since the game is randomized, you'll have a personal story to tell each time you play.
While exploring this strange new galaxy, you'll find abandon space ships that you can take as your own. You'll be required to take a look at your ship in order to manage your inventory with ship components and your cargo. To refuel, repair and oxygenate your spaceship you'll need to click and drag minerals from your cargo and drag them to the maintenance. Its just that simple. Each ship has different requirements for its hull and fuel. Most require helium or hydrogen for the fuel and iron for the hull. Helium will refuel the ship faster. The inventory is a grid and you can click an empty square on the grid to craft additional components from schematics that you'll find scattered throughout the galaxy. Components can also be dismantled for their minerals which is helpful when you abandon your ship for another one.
Minerals stack up to twenty per square. Its odd in a way that twenty hydrogen takes up the same space as twenty platinum or iron. You have no weight limit either. Just a grid limit. Different ships have different grids. Smaller ships have less of a grid, but consume less fuel. I found smaller ships to survive far longer than larger ones strictly for their fuel consumption.
On your way, you'll encounter anomalies that will send you on quests, none of which I've seen through to the end, even after six hours of playing. They're always at the furthest reaches of the galaxy, like your ultimate goal. You'll also meet aliens in picture form and learn words to their unique language.
While the solar systems get randomized or "rogue-like," the map of the galaxy isn't. Its the same galaxy time and time again. You'll encounter the same blue giants, red, yellow and white dwarves, black holes and super novas every time you play. Your ship has a radius that it can travel and if a system is in the radius you can travel there at the cost of fuel and oxygen.
Each solar system can consist of random rock planets, gas giants, anomalies, garden planets and a star (or black hole). Even when you're in these solar systems you need to spend a set amount of fuel and oxygen to orbit and visit the locations. Everything amounts to a beautiful background scene with your ship over it. Again, its nothing fancy, but it does do a good job of a space ambiance.You'll never know what's in a solar system until you visit. Nor will your ship remember what was in a solar system. There is of course a ship component to analyze solar systems.
Gas giants are the most important, they're how you'll get precious fuel. Even visiting them will damage your hull. To get the fuel, you send out a probe and you're given a choice how big of a probe. The larger the probe, the more fuel you'll get. Always spend the maximum amount of fuel on a probe. Otherwise it will never return with enough fuel. Ever. The larger the probe, the easier it is to return damaged or get destroyed. You can easily repair anything broken with iron that you have on board. Even if a probe gets destroyed, you can recover its components and use iron to make a new one. Its a small price to pay to have more than enough fuel on board. Its a constant struggle in the game. You can probe over and over, but the yield will be half of your last attempt, making it ineffective.
Rock planets are how you obtain iron and other resources, but nothing feels as important as iron. To get the minerals you'll have to orbit the planet, then land. When you're done you'll have to take off and all  these procedures cost fuel and oxygen. Again, this is an inventory management game. When you're on the planet, you need to drill much like probing. Always use the largest drill to get the most yield.
Garden planets are the most interesting. You can land on them to instantly replenish your oxygen, drill for different types of minerals, but more importantly, there's life here. You can speak with inhabitants and while they don't speak your language, you'll learn a word or two from them; even give them things or receive schematics or the Omega from them. This Omega is special and can be used to repair things amongst other interesting things further in the game. The garden planets have different minerals that are used for components most of the time.
In terms of components, some of them feel useless, but there are others like shield generators and wormhole generators that feel more useful. You can improve fuel efficiency and other things all through components. The only down side is some components require others, so that's two slots from your cargo used.
When drilling or probing, you're forced to take or abandon things without having the ability to use my maintenance to fuel or repair your ship. It seems only logical that I deliver hydrogen straight from the probe to my maintenance, but instead I need to jettison something from a full cargo hold.
In terms of anomalies, those are abandon ships, quests or cubes. The cubes will replenish one specific thing whether its fuel, oxygen or your hull. They're very helpful and give you a reason to always live dangerously with low fuel, oxygen or hull hoping to find a cube. Visiting stars themselves will heavily damage your ship and it doesn't seem like there's a use for them unless you get a ship component that lets you fly through a black hole or harvest the power of a white dwarf or something. Other anomalies will wormhole your ship to a different solar system.
When you get to each solar system, sometimes there's a random event will play out through text. Sometimes you're given a choice. Things like you're being attacked, do you hide or flee. Again, there is no combat, so your choice determines does your hull get damaged or do you expend extra fuel escaping? The game recaps what you've gained or lost. With everything playing out via text and the fact that you travel from one star to the next, Out There can feel like a single player board.
The game is beautiful, vivid, colorful backdrops of space, planets and other celestial bodies. It feels spacy with great ambient music and that's all you really need for any space game. Just give a feeling of isolation and gorgeous backdrops. Its a place you can sink a lot of time into.
Depending how far you get, the game will shake things up a bit with hostile aliens that will conquer planets. You won't be able to visit these planets, making a tough game even harder with no difficulty settings.
Now for the major problem that I had, your ship has a radius that you can only jump so far in. About 30 minutes into each play through, I'd come across dead end after dead end. The galactic map never changes, so you can remember your route and where not to go. You need to start relying on random luck to find schematics for worm hole generators or anomalies that will randomly teleport you to places. This makes the game feel unbeatable unless you have luck. Back tracking seems like a brutal death sentence.
For anyone that can get into the game, its a good, relaxing time sink that will keep you playing again and again. There's so much here, but unless you can find a new ship or efficiently manage your fuel, you'll be doomed. That still won't stop you from continuing to explore the outermost galaxies of Out There. I'd like to thank Delphine and Plug In Digital for my copy of the game.

Wow. How could I have never heard of this game when it was first released? I was probably still playing some Medal of Honor games on the console at the time and I don't recall seeing any advertisements for this game during that time either. Whether it be PS2, Xbox or PC. Just like Sniper Elite V2, I got this game because it's a WWII shooter.
Unlike Sniper Elite V2 and 3, this game follows a different incarnation of Karl Fairburne: he's younger than the other Karl and he's got a pretty cool Wehrmacht Heer disguise (which stops working on the German soldiers just after a few levels for some reason). The opening cutscene also explains that the reason why he was chosen for the mission was because he lived in Germany for a while and knew how to speak the language. From this we can see that the Karl from this game has a slightly more developed character than the one from V2 and 3.
The story is similar to V2 also. You're going around assassinating those who want to defect to the Soviets and sparing those who want to defect to the U.S.
This game is also slightly more difficult than V2, even on Sniper Elite difficulty. I guess that might make it more enjoyable for those that played V2. Personally, I still like V2 better.
I also noticed that some music and levels in this game were later remade into V2. I thought that was pretty cool.
If you're interested in playing multiplayer, you'll need a program called GameRanger. Trust me. You won't be able to play multiplayer without it.
But yeah, this game's great. I'd reccomend playing this before Sniper Elite V2.

Borderlands is a FPS/RPG hybrid game set on a lawless planet called Pandora and promises great co-op gameplay, lots and lots of guns and insane fun. But how does it fare? This is what I think of Borderlands.
This game is one of my favourite games of all time. I've had a blast playing it on multiple platforms over the years and I can honestly say there is no game quite like it. Despite being a little light on story, the crazy characters you meet along the way, the hilarious humour of the game and the fantastic gameplay make this an unforgettable experience. And there's the guns of course. Mountains and mountains of guns. Borderlands also has a very unique art style. I remember when I saw an early preview and they were going for generic realism. I'm so glad they changed it to cel-shaded graphics. Not only is it unique, but it makes it stand out even after all this time. It has been done since, but not quite as well.
The story begins with you entering the small town of Fyrestone via bus, as one of four mercenaries. Each have different skill trees and active skills and are each unique. You have Roland, the soldier who can deploy a turret to fight with him. Lilith is a siren, a sexy magic wielding maniac. You have Mordecai, who has his own pet bird that helps him in fights. Last but not least is Brick, a huge slab of meat who can punch things really hard. Probably plays bingo on a Tuesday. Each starts with a different weapon type but each character can use what they like. You start getting visions from a mysterious woman who guides you on your quest to find the Vault, an alien treasure trove said to contain untold riches, powers and other earthly wonders. Who wouldn't want to to find that, eh? The story essentially is a journey across Pandora, meeting the eccentric locals and shooting most people in the face in search of the Vault. Good times.
The gameplay is fantastic in this game. With several types of weapon to choose from, you shoot and loot your way across Pandora, picking up all kinds of great weaponry with many different effects. Some are elemental, shocking, burning and melting foes, others include things like a shotgun that fires rockets. It's crazy, it's bonkers and it's brilliant. You can play solo or with up to three buddies, both are a very good time indeed. Each character has their own skill trees, as said above, and you can mix and match depending on your playstyle. It's well worth a playthrough with each one to experience what each character offers.
It's the humour in this game that makes it stand out. It doesn't take itself too seriously and is a hilarious time. Pop culture references galore await within and rare is the time in game when you don't have a smile on your face. Few games are ever this funny, and it knows it. The characters are weird and memorable, especially Scooter and Tannis. Fantastic stuff. Pandora itself is a great setting, providing you with the danger of a lawless planet with bandits around every corner and the wildlife trying to eat you when your back is turned.
The game also has some terrific DLC. The first, the Zombie island of Dr Ned, tasks you with traveling to a secluded island overrun with zombies. Back when zombies were still relatively fresh before being in pretty much every game ever for about two years, it's a great time. Mad Moxxi's Underground Riot is a bit of dud, but the other two, The Secret Armory of General Knoxx and Claptrap's New Robot Revolution, add hours of fun to the base game and are fantastic additions.
There aren't many negatives to point out, other than the slightly under-baked story and the quests rarely evolve past simple "go here and shoot this" variety but you'll be having so much fun with the gameplay you probably won't notice it too much. It's a lot more fun playing with friends but as a lone wolf myself, it is more than good enough solo. It doesn't have the longevity of the sequel though, as you can't reset challenges in order to continue having things to do and increasing Badass Rank. Why they didn't remaster this with the other two and put the Badass system in I don't know.
Overall, like I said before, this game is one of a kind and one of my favourite games ever. Eclipsed by the sequel, this is nevertheless a fantastic game and is a ride you won't want to miss out on. If you still haven't picked up this bonkers game yet, you owe it to yourself to play it. Strap yourself in for a wild ride, and embrace the madness.

The game basically goes like this :
1. Walk for a bit.
2. Stumble upon some doors. Read the writing above them and on the floor, choose which one you think is the "right" one. Two possibilities :
- Wrong door. You die. Reload and try another one until you find the right one.
- Right door. You can continue playing.
Rinse and repeat until done. Some exceptions here and here that spice up the boring linearity of the game a bit, but it's so rare and insignificant that you won't even remember it. The main problem is that the game lacks substance and could be summarized by a series of multiple choice logic questions written on a piece of paper. And even if it tries to compare itself to The Stanley Parable, there just isn't enough stuff other than these questions to keep the player interested.
My advice : don't wait for a promotion to buy Doors. Just don't buy it if you want anything more than logic questions.

The famous looter shooter. Looks good for its age, but behind a cute and playful cel-shaded veneer hides a genuinely poor PC port. Some of the problems(like low FOV and general lack of options) can be fixed via third party tools. But being a single-threaded UE3 game, Borderlands doesn't run too well in some places, no matter how powerful your PC is. This problem is exaggerated for those who don't own an Intel CPU, for the engine is clearly optimised for the blue team.
But it doesn't mean that it can't bring dozens of hours of joy. Fully beating the SP campaign and all DLC could easily take up to 50 hours, not to mention the new game+ for those who really enjoy the core gameplay loop. As an FPS it is unremarkable - gunplay is meh at best, only remedied by the gun variety. But the constant progression and acquisition of a of better loot are what ultimately makes the experience. Definitely worth trying to determine whether or not you'd want to dive in the franchise further - there's a lot more if you like this one.

The game begins really simply, and you start to think that all it is is a mindless puzzle game (which actually would have been fine). The fact that I can try over and over on the same puzzle, being helpfully loaded right back in front of it, leaves me with no motivation to truly solve it.
The influence of The Stanley Parable is evident here, but it feels cheap. The office section of the game just screams it, but almost nothing is interactable, and the signs don't make any real sense to the "narrative" we find ourselves in. If it's satire, it's not working. I also would have liked to see more varied humor on the doors. The main joke with the bacon falls very flat. We get it, bacon is so great. Instead the word is shoved down your throat so much that when the actual bacon does show up you don't want it at all.

While the game has a cute asthetic and interesting gameplay aspects (like diagonal shooting and a ghost system that gives you an extra life in exchange for facing more enemies) it ultimately fails at what it is trying to do. A wizard's lizard is ostensibly a rogue-like with randomly generated floors and rooms, but unlike a game like the Binding of Isaac, the rooms are not prefab. In other words, any combination of enemies and traps can be in almost any room. This seems like a cool feature, until you realize that it often leads to unavoidable damage. I've even had spike traps spawn right on top of a door, making it literally impossible to enter the room without taking damage. This wouldn't be a big deal if health was reasonably easy to come by, but it isn't. Health is either randomly dropped by enemies (with a very low chance of doing so) or purchased in stores for a huge amount of money. Money that you need to buy weapons and upgrades that will stop you from taking damage. I'm sure you can see the problem here. Your success in the game is nearly completely predicated on your ability to not take damage, and often times damage is unavoidable. Your hitbox is unclear, so even in the rooms where it is possible to avoid damage you'll still take damage that is not your fault.
There is a sort of Rogue Legacy-esque permenant progression in the game, allowing you to gain more starting money and purchase items before entering the game's dungeons. Which brings me to my greatest complaint. The items are almost all worthless in any situation where you would want an advantage. Say you have an enemy that annoys you, owls for instance. And you want to kill them faster. Surely an attack upgrade is what you need? Actually, all the items that i've seen upgrade stats by 1 which is utterly insignificant. Owls (the brown ones at least) have twenty health and your normal attacks deal 10 damage. the most damage upgrades I've been able to stack (filling every single item slot available to me with attack upgrading items) was 6. So no matter how much attack you stack up you will never be able to kill the owl with one attack from a normal weapon.
You can get better weapons, but they all have silly drawbacks and often their gimicks will get you killed. While it is fun to find all these different items and see what they do, and this game actually does a better job than Isaac and similar rogue-likes explaining what effects items have, it ultimately falls flat because the only items that make any difference at all are weapons. Almost all your abilities put you too much in harms way and healing is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ the permanent progression turns the early levels into a grind, and the game's difficulty stems far too much from a lack of HP being available and rooms having nearly or completely unavoidable damage on them. I honestly can't recommend this game at all.

I've spent roughly 8 hours of this game and while I don't think it's bad per say there is a lot lacking when stacked up to existing Roguelikes and ones coming out on Steam in the near future through Early Access and Kickstarter. Not going to criticize the art or the music, those things are subjective and you can like them or dislike them as you see fit. There are also bigger and more frustrating issues with A Wizard's Lizard to address. For starters, the Gold for saving Villagers. While in theory it is rewarding to give the player an extra mission on top of "Beat the Game" but in execution all it does is makes the game grind-y. Progression in a Roguelike is nothing new, nor is giving players abilities but none of it seems to matter in A Wizard's Lizard and that combined with the Grinding makes the entire experience feel like a slough. The progression is also staggered, items are locked behind their "location" not just cash which means you'll have to spend hours dumping time into each location to unlock everything if you so desire. To make matters worse, weapons do miserable damage but we'll touch on that later. This is helped along by unlocking "Short Cuts" however in a Roguelike intentionally cutting your playing time so you can grind is not a good thing. And that's the biggest issue with A Wizard's Lizard. It's grindy. It's grindy to the extreme. Which makes the second issue all the more problematic.
The Grind isn't fun. The gameplay is uninteresting. Unlike The Binding of Isaac which gives you a unique run each time you boot up the game both in level layout and item generation or even Magicite which varies both the level layout and the tools you can use while throwing interesting traps and obstacles at you, A Wizard's Lizard does not. The rooms are plain square or rectangle in shape, filled with enemies and the standard sliding spike traps along with stationary floor spikes that deal quite a bit of damage to you. There are secret levels but they are not extra levels however they're a single level long and instead of being "extra" to your run they instead overlaps with the stage you'd otherwise go to. This makes the additional threat of these levels is thus not adequately paid for as you are just as strong for doing them than not. The only reason to go to them is to unlock special or unique items to their location thus making them simply another spot to grind.
The enemies also seem to suffer from a bit of Rogue Legacy's palate-swapped enemies. While I grant that creating enemies is both time consuming and cost prohibitive especially of Indie Companies, the variety gets stale after four or five runs. A Wizard's Lizard also suffers from a failing many Roguelikes have started to make and that is swamping players with enemies in an attempt to make the game more difficult. More enemies does not a hard game make, and cramming them in only causes the game to feel even more grindy and unfair to beginners who lack the skill to crowd control. On top of their numbers, enemies have a great deal of health and deal a good deal of health when they hit. As mentioned above with the player's damage, enemies take forever to take down even with the "best of weapons". I won't even bring up the Mimics and other "Hiding" enemies, who you know are there but have to bait out and risk damage or just adds to the time needed to progress through the game. All of these complaints are amplified for the bosses, requiring you to grind for the best of items to even hope to deal significant damage against them. This of course means you have to grind past them time and time again to get the gear needed to smooth the process out. The boss fights other than them being damage sponges that are boring just as the rest of the game. The bosses are your stock standard Zelda-esque fights that, if they were more balanced, would be just plain standard. Instead they're boring fights we've seen a dozen times in more interesting games and in more interesting formats with the health meter cranked to 11. And that's my over all take of A Wizard's Lizard. Is it terrible? No. Would I recommend it? Not really. There are better, cheaper, and more interesting Roguelikes on the market or coming to market. Look into those.

First off, if you don't like Dragon ball, walk away right now. Like seriously, this game will not interest you one bit.
Moving on, Dragon Ball Xenoverse is a fun romp through the Dragon ball universe with your own character and everything. You can equip your character with various skills and outfits to defeat various Dragon ball characters.
THE GOOD
This game is absolutely a blast for Dragon ball Z fans. Seeing your character go through all that is fun and they made a half-decent story.
Every special and ultimate has impact and feel pretty good, and while there are some that are exponentially better then others, there are few that are entirely useless.
This game does have a half-decent run time and while the end game can peeter off very quickly, the campaign is pretty fun, although hard.
THE BAD
THE MOST ANNOYING THING ABOUT THIS GAME IS ITS ABSOLUTE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T RNG. You wanna get that move? Well too bad, you gotta grind for hours. Heres an example, To get Super Vegeta, the super sayian for blast users, you have to do a mission which requires you to kill a few easy minnions, then bring Krillin from another area to the original area, let Freeza kill him, have Goku show up, fight until Freeza has reached full power. The Vegeta shows up and once you defeat Freeza you have to hope to good that the ultimate finish goes off. THEN you have to defeat a Super Sayian Vegeta, and HOPE TO F'ING GOD HE DROPS THE SKILL. This is absolutely the most absurd part of this game and really kills the enjoyement, until you learn that trick with Elder kai that gives you basically 100% RNG, but thats still DLC and Time spent running in doing  a quick mission talking to him, doing it over and over and i've made my point.
This game is not hard. It just decides to give everyone ubscene amounts of health and super armor. You want to combo late into the campaign, to bad that sucker shrugs your attacks off like nothing.
The online play is apparently really bad, and although I personally don't really play online that's still a point against it.
All that said, i had a lot of fun with this game and appreciate this game for what it is. It's a new look into the Dragon Ball saga through games that hasn't really been done the same way before. Am I gonna buy Xenoverse 2 eventually? Yes. Am I gonna play it online? Probably not.
TD:LR If you want a pretty good Dragon Ball Z ARPG with lots of grinding then this is for you, If you want a good Dragon Ball Z ARPG with trash online play but with way less RNG play Xenoverse too.

I don’t normally write reviews but I felt I had to contribute due to the increase of negative responses, which does not justify this visual novel.
Cupid follows a nameless female orphan set in the 18th century of France, guided by her mother’s voice who you will play the role of (by selecting choices that pops up once in awhile). She becomes entangled into the affairs of her best friend, Catherine, and her betrothed, Guilleme.
The main theme in this story is love - the good and the bad kind.
It is an extremely well-written visual novel, the pace is just about right, with beautiful artwork and sound-effects to accompany this. It is not your typical visual novel, it has very dark mature content (think psychological horror), so it can become quite complex and disturbing, but I LOVE that!
As this is a free visual novel and it delves into controversial topics, I can see people trying this out and well… not liking it. So I would not recommend this if you do not like dark disturbing content, or reading visual novels, neither would I recommend this
a first visual novel.
However I highly recommend this if you like psychological horror, the twisted kind.

Procedurally generated space roguelikes are few and far between, this game is actually quite unique in what it does. In FTL what will kill you is a missile or sweeping laser hitting you at a bad time, where as in 'Out There' what will get you killed is a decision you made ten turns ago. Like say thinking that you will be good without keeping that common-as-dirt iron cluttering your ship's hold  or thinking you have plenty of fuel to make another jump.
'Out There' is like slow moving chess, with quiet dreamy music and little vignettes. It is the first game I've played in a long while that emphasized the exploration part of game play and it is a refreshing change. Even talking to aliens is a neat little mystery as you have to guess what they are trying to say and as you go along learning little snippets of language and the backstory as it unfolds.
There are fun little jabs of humor and it would be relaxing if you weren't on the knife edge of survival at every instant. You can see gameplay elements in managing your ship's resources. You'll be thinking about fuel, oxygen and whatever rare metal dugup and trying to make sophie's choice on which to abandon and which to carry on the chance you might get a technology to use it. Make no mistake this is a rogue like, a pretty, quiet, sedate one but still a roguelike and you will die many many many times.
It is an interesting reversal of the normal formula. The game is at its most random in the start when you have nothing and a bad roll of the dice can doom you on turn two. But if you can just last long enough to find a good technology, or a new ship, or a lucky streak of events you start to get a lot more options and agency. It is thrilling to get to that point, to get into a good routine.. then it becomes your own damn fault if you got greedy and risky.
The game is a port from on the phone but the visuals are a nice moving comic motif and the sound score does much to set the mood. For what it is it doesn't feel cheap and runs well. Even though the UI can have a bit finicky things but they are minor.
Anyone who is a fan of exploration and roguelikes will enjoy this title. I know I have. I even bought it on my phone

Sniper Elite is your basic intro into a sniper's gunnery world. I've found very little deflection in windage affecting cross-drift of the round - enabling me to make 200 Meter or so headshots without a significant problem.
Bear in mind that this is an old game and one of the first 'proper' sniping games... dont bash this game after playing more modern sniper games. Enjoy the 'retro' feel of this early title... and remember it for what it is...RETRO.
Its a shame that I got this after the multi-player on-line servers had shutdown, but that doesn't stop you playing via LAN I should think... worth an afternoon to realize how far the genre has developed... a must have for your war library at a couple of bucks.
Missions are fairly linear and the AI is not challenging, though it does get a tad ridiculous when enemy soldiers show eagle-eyed propensity to detect you from dozens of meters away.
Oftentimes a whizz of a close-passing round will make me hit the dirt and spend some time reallocating to find out the shooters location... unlike other reviews who claim that this game has limited ammo... I always find myself clearing levels with supplied ammo untouched...this is a SNIPER game after all...not DOOM II!
If you are an all-guns blazing type...move on. if you like to think over your shot, watch your target patrol/do his thing before committing to the trigger... come on in.
Bullet time is decidedly retro. Its like finding gamp's rusty old musket and cleaning it out to fire a few rounds to take you back to yesteryear... cant wait to clear this and move on to the other two successors I also bought. Hopefully, like wine, this series gets better with time...

A fantastic puzzle game built around the infiltration of secure facilities. The 'puzzles' involve the main character (Richard Conway, Freelance Spy) having the ability to remotely rewire vulnerable electronic systems to allow him to open doors or incapacitate patrolling guards. There are usually multiple solutions to any given situation beyond the initial 'tutorial' puzzles, and you can choose how much of a jerk you want the main character to be - whether you will avoid lethal force on hapless guards, or just kill everyone you come across.
The mechanic of rewiring is simple - find an input, route it to an output, when input is triggered, output is activated - but allows for increasingly complex event chains during later maps, for example, wiring a motion sensing camera to trigger an elevator call button, which will activate a sound sensor when the elevator arrives with a 'ding!' which is wired to a door, behind which is a guard whose pistol's electronic controller has been wired to trigger something else entirely so that when the door opens and he sees you and tries to shoot...
Combined with a snarky script, a very 'cyberpunk noir' atmosphere, and very generous checkpointing, the game is fun throughout. And there's even a level editor in case the stock missions just weren't enough for you.

This game is a complete pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Where to begin...?

I suppose I could start with the compatibility issues. My God. Having to install several patches to get rid of crashing, texture ♥♥♥♥ups, and crappy performance is one thing, but when some of these issues persist even after the fixes, all I can do is shrug and bear it.
The combat is just a mess. It's one of those games that tries to convince me that I'm fighting on the same terms as my opponents, though it quickly becomes apparent that it's designed to be simply unfair. The combat mechanics seem to favor one-on-one fighting, which is just brilliant, considering 99% of the game's enemies attack in groups, leading to the old tried-and♥♥♥♥♥♥tactic of luring these noisy sacks of♥♥♥♥♥away from their comrades one at a time. When the game does decide to spring a "fair" mano a mano battle on me, a new set of problems show. Thought that attack hit? Nah, it missed, even though I clearly heard the hit sound and the enemy dodged a full second too late. If that's the game's idea of a successful dodge, then I wish it applied to me. Then the controls get stuck for no reason and blocking or dodging becomes impossible. Raising skills and getting stronger weapons does help a bit, but for the most part, enemies can clean house in quick combos that are unfeasible for the player to perform and react to.
The quests are confusing. When clear instructions are given, it's fine, but occasionally there will be one that's a total ♥♥♥♥ing mystery, requiring the player to wander around until the objective is stumbled upon. The world isn't annoyingly big or small, but with a lack of options for getting to specific places quickly, getting from point A to point B gets old fast. Even starting a quest can be a ♥♥♥♥♥. They usually require exhausting most of the dialogue options for specific NPCs for the purposes of obtaining some object or allowing discussion of a certain topic with a different character, because usually the most obvious dialogue suggesting quest progression might not actually advance the quest, but the offhand, marginally related dialogue will. Several times, characters would tell me to go clear to the other side of the map, and I would, only to discover that my trip was pointless because the quest hadn't actually started, as I had not selected an additional piece of dialogue in the conversation I had 15 ♥♥♥♥ing minutes ago. Beyond that there is only one correct way to finish most quests, due to the constant scripted sequences, which are mandatory for the player to sit through, and even the slightest deviation from the intended path will screw up the game, from simply rendering the quest incompletable to crashing the application. If I'm going to crash a game, I prefer it to be not so easy to do.
The strangeness of the quests is affected by the faction/guild system. Apart from my allies and comrades being hostile toward me for no reason, the actual effect of the guilds is limited to a few parts of the game. Several chapters in, the guilds might as well not even exist. Because of how closely intertwined the guilds are with the rather linear main story, the player is inevitably forced down the same path every new game regardless of guild choice, and the satisfaction of picking a side is short-lived.
Despite all of its shortcomings, there is one redeeming factor; One shining variable that not only saves its offerings from being buried under a tide of technical oversights, but catapults the game to an almost godly position amongst RPGs: You can deal weed in this game.

Neat, breezy, text game.  And it's ALL text.  No graphics, no music, just you and the words on the page.  It's basically a front-end for an old-fashioned "Fighting Fantasy"-style RPG gamebook.  You have hit points and superpower points, and you have to choose which powers to use, which actions to take, etc.
There are points where the game is essentially on rails - it stops short of "but thou MUST!"-levels of forcing you down one path, but it knows where it wants you to go.  There are side paths you can take, but the fundamental throughline is very straightforward.
It's worth a buck or two just to support this oddly archaic playstyle, ESPECIALLY if you have fond memories of marking the pages of a Choose Your Own Adventure to pick the best outcome...  (you can't do that here - it keeps track of all your choices.)

A roguelike dungeon-crawler with randomly generated room layouts, A Wizard's Lizard has you playing as Raga, a lizard whose wizard got kidnapped by Death for trying to cheat death with a potion of life. Having had some of the potion of life spill on him before the wizard got spirited away, Raga gains the ability to die twice before it's game over. Upon dying, you may find yourself having to kill the ghosts of the enemies you just killed, and in some areas, you can step into a magic circle to come back to life! Hanging between life and death, can Raga traverse the dungeon, defeat Death, and save the wizard?
No two gameplay sessions are alike. You only get stronger by finding better equipment or learning not to get hit. Normal gameplay has dark dungeons with little visibility which can work against you, Dying once lights the entire dungeon up, but forces you to take on unique ghost versions of some enemies. If you play enough, rescue trapped villagers in the dungeons, and buy item blueprints in dungeon shops, you can start out with more gold and unlock more items to buy at the shop before you enter the dungeon, making it easier to start the game out. It's a very neat sense of progression and makes dying less disappointing when you can actually gain something from your attempts at a crypt run.
With a charming art style, a cute lizard, a tough-as-nails dungeon labyrinth, the ability to cheat death, and a system where you can gain progress from dying each playthrough, A Wizard's Lizard is a challenging but enjoyable roguelike game.

9/10 it's the Dark Souls of Rogue-lites -IGN
All sarcasm aside, I find this game to be so addicting. While I personally lack the discriminating tastes necessary to judge graphics, I can say several things about the gameplay.
The dynamic of the life/death system seems to have quite a lot of potential, but instead it is relegated to somewhat pointless difficulty spikes and a requirement for advancing certain secrets. We could see updates that add more use to this mechanic, however.
The item variety is far from that of it's next nearest cousin, The Binding of Isaac, and the item synergies are practically nonexistant. The fact that there are 9 kinds of items in which two of the same kind are mutually exclusive (as opposed to 1/2 in Isaac), the game feels restrictive with regards to how you will built your character, practically demanding that you min-max.
I've been rather harsh on this game, but that doesn't mean I dislike it. There are several factors that actually make this game fun for me. For instance, the controls are very solid. When playing with keyboard and mouse, I know that any mistakes I made were a result of poor reflexes in all but a few cases, in which you aren't exactly given an opportunity to react fast enough.
The progression system also adds a sense of worth to even your worst runs, assuming you can get at least one blueprint and/or save one villager, which gets easier as you become better. This system makes the game even more addictive than it already is; my quote about this game being the Dark Souls of rogue-lites is actually quite accurate, since the game is punishing until learned, and still difficult once learned.
A Wizard's Lizard is a solid title despite it's somewhat restrictive nature. If it weren't for the fact that The Binding of Isaac serves as a baseline for games like this, it would be even greater in my eyes. I can't recommend this to everyone, but if you're a rogue-lite fan who feels burnt out on The Binding of Isaac, or just wants a fresh look on the sub-genre, I'd say that you should consider picking this game up.
I'm also going to add that the protagonist, Raga, is cute as a button.

I am a massive fan of Binding of Issac and have played a lot of rogue-likes since then which have all tried to emulate the same style of gameplay but either end up feeling too similar or too different to really scratch that itch.
A Wizard's Lizard is a perfect mash-up of BOI and Rogue Legacy, while bringing some of it's own very creative ideas to the table. The Rogue Legacy trend of persistent improvement has often fallen into the trap of making your character too powerful or over-ruling the skill aspect. With A Wizard's Lizard it feels like the equipment that you unlock and the gold that you build up is all about building the character you'd like to play as, while being very balanced. If you want a lot of offense, you'll need to sacrifice attack rate and you won't have much money left over to increase your other stats. It also saves the frustration that can occur with random generation and not getting the items that you most enjoy playing with.
Highly recommend AWL, it has gamepad, keyboard and Mouse & keyboard support - the latter has surprised me as my favourite, but having an aiming reticle has gotten me out of the BOI trap of only shooting in 4 directions. There's also a really interesting second life mechanic which is used in some creative ways - yet to figure it out!
Love it, I know I'll sink a lot of time into it.

Dawn of War II is a strategy game set in the Warhammer 40000 universe.
Although the game is a sequel and directly references the original Dawn of War series, it plays significantly differently as it focuses on squad combat as opposed to controlling an entire army and bases. It means that gameplay is much more intense, fast paced and forces you to think strategically because you will always be outnumbered and cannot use the "defend, build and overwhelm" tactics that are commonly used in strategy games.
The single player mode focuses on the Space Marine race with a very strong focus on storyline. There are several difficulty levels to appeal to both those who just want to play for the storyline and those who want a real gaming challenge. There is a pseudo-RPG element to the game with units being able to gain passive and active abilities on levelling up and can be given equipment that will change their appearance, stats and combat
There are also different online modes including both pvp and co-op. My favourite would be "The Last Stand" where you choose to play one of several hero units (each from a different race and with unique gameplay styles), teamed up with 2 other players and thrown into an arena with ever increasing waves of enemies. Again, the pseudo-RPG element applies with your heroes gaining new abilities and equipment on levelling up. However, it can get dull as there are only 2 maps with the same enemies.
There are also 2 expansions which further build on these: "Chaos Rising" and "Retribution".
Chaos Rising essentially continues the Space Marine story after the events in Dawn of War II. The strong storyline is maintained and you still play in the same locations, but with a different storyline, a few new locations, one new unit and new equipment and enemies. You can transfer your finished Dawn of War II campaign save file to Chaos Rising. As an expansion, it does feel a little shorter overall when compared to the original Dawn of War II. There are also new units for the Last Stand mode.
(The original Dawn of War II and Chaos Rising require Windows Live logins)
Retribution is a stand-alone expansion. It continues the story from the end of Chaos Rising, but you now have the choice to play through the story of 6 different races (Space Marines, Chaos, Eldar, Imperial Guard, Orks and Tyranids), each with their own unique units. Whilst being great that you now have access to 6 races, the storyline feels a lot less intense as a result since all races play through the exact same maps in the same order. The maps themselves are also similar (if not the same) as those in the previous 2 games, but this since Retribution is an expansion, this can be excused. Again, there are new units for the Last Stand game mode.
Overall it is a worthwhile strategy game to consider playing if you love squad-based combat, Warhammer 40000 or both.

This game and it's expansion packs offer something very different from its prior title. The original was a tactical game yes, but this is somewhat more heavily focused on making use of your brain than your brawn. You will be outgunned & outmatched on every mission, however clever usage of cover & managing your hero character/squads abilities can turn the tide against almost anything. The game also has a lot of voice acting between the hero units which make you empathize with the characters and draw you deeper into the games storyline.
The lack of base building means you do not produce units, you have a starting force and occasionally will gain control of another unit/squad. This means you have to be very careful and balance your force based upon your missions introductory intel. For example, you may click on a mission on the starmap which will reveal that you will be up against enemy tanks. In this case you will pick a force loaded with anti-armour weapons and big guns. The game is never this linear though and will often make you sacrifice firepower for agility, utilizing surprise attacks, jetpacks, ambushes and snipers instead of an all out force. My only greivance is I couldn't seem to find a quick save button (meaning a failed mission meant I would have to start the whole mission from the loadout screen. Frustrating, when playing such a tactical game which can take up to 20 minutes or more for one mission.)
Overall though, I love this game. More so than the original, it took a lot of getting used to but I just love the focus on tactics. Things like sneaking into position as a sniper and laying down remote mines, then sending in jetpack marines to draw the enemies back, watching them give chase towards my bombs and then detonating once clear. Tactics like this actually work in this game and reward you for it by giving you more advanced wargear (items you can upgrade & equip on your hero units) for completing missions with certain parameters such as under 15 minutes, killing 100% of enemies on the map, all squads staying concious etc.

I would recommend this game (ON SALE) most to fans of 'giant monster loose in the city' type of situations, who don't mind or even enjoy some visceral violence.
I bought this game and played through it on 360 without knowing anything about the franchise and was pleasantly surprised. This game conveys the scene of a 'disaster' / 'outbreak' / 'giant monster in a big city' setting better than most any other game I have played. The game ratchets up the tension exponentially as the campaign continues, leading to some pretty epic battles between you and the pursuing forces and monsters trying to eradicate you.
The game is also very violent, with a nefarious overseer / big brother type feeling to a lot of its cutscenes, with security forces unleashing biohazard weapons and mutant creatures on the general populace.

Although the traversal options / parkour / gliding / flying your character uses have been seen in many titles since this game's initial release (i.e. Saint's Row 4 / Gat Out of Hell, Just Cause, Infamous, etc...) what is here is still animated well and presented in its own unique way. The game's violent setting, and the sneaking / hunting / infiltrating / sabotaging (before being caught and having to smash everything) vibe of a lot of its missions are what I dug the most.

tl;dr: Entirely pointess - get the original and download the free HD mod.
+ things look pretty and are large even at high resolutions
+ that's ... pretty much it
- doesn't include anything from the expansions. It's especially missing convenient mechanics like pressing space to re-enter a building. It's hard to go back to after playing Heroes 3 complete.
- Doesn't add any kind of mechanical improvements over the original. No Steam cloud, no improved menus (e.g. No load/return to menu during battles which would REALLY have been a great addition). It's just lazy.
But the main thing really is that the HoMM3 HD mod lets you play the game with both expansions, adds many great shortcuts (e.g. if you're moving the last stack off a hero, it will automatically leave 1 creature on that hero). Having played with the HD mod for so long, I REALLY miss those conveniences and it's hard to go back to this.
The only situation where this version might be preferable is if you have a small, yet very high-resolution screen, in which case this game will look better. But even then, I wouldn't say it's worth it.

The characters are laced with feelings of guilt, shame, inadequacy/unworthiness, abandonment fear & fear of intimacy, volatility, as well as obsessive & insatiable desire!
In a way it's very sick & deranged, but also very alluring & rather hot! Cupid is not your typical erotic thriller. It is bizarre & otherworldy (and quite the mind****).
This VN swings from one extreme to the other - in an instant! - like a wiiiild pendulum. Uff!
It sure as heck had me stuck to my chair, all tense and absorbed by the story (which I thought was really well delivered - bit, by bit).
Even though some parts felt a bit drab & long-winded, there was always enough suspense & batsh*t crazy content right around the corner to keep me going for sure!
It is definitely different from what I've seen so far in the VN-genre, and I consider it a definite must-have both for lovers & newbies (or if you're curious, but unsure - go ahead and try it). You might be pleasantly surprised!
I got ending number 3 (= potentially incestuous) when I finished the story (there's a total of 4 + bonus content to unlock).
I'm so grateful the developers chose to offer this VN for free - I enjoyed it so much I wouldn't mind donating or paying for (optional!) downloadable content (like artwork or soundtracks).
Which brings me to the endearing & enticing visual aspect & the eerie (but very effective) sound effects which grabbed & held my attention at the right time :)!
I found the music very touching as well. It evoked all sorts of emotions in me (which I appreciated).
Animation-wise, Cupid is pretty basic (i.e. limited expressions, but good enough!). It does the job.
I loved the addition of animated, flashing stills during gameplay. I found that very captivating & titillating. Most definitely tickled my senses & imagination (in a good way).
On a final note, I found the story interesting, with more than sufficient content delivered (i.e. characters, text & scenery).
I especially appreciated how the content was delivered in an elegant way and was in no way vulgar (i.e. both artwork & script).
I wouldn't mind more of this!

You're driving with gifts in your car and suddenly, candy, gifts and other Christmas stuff are being dropped on you and you can't ride anymore! This is a short adventure game. The story is just "help the sisters for tasks like finding what to make clothes for birds and you'll be on the road again". There is no evil plot, no hidden secret, nothing. In other words, Christmas Adventure's story is just inexistent.
The gameplay isn't innovative as all, as it's find items, use them, clear hidden objects scenes and solve some puzzles. But there is a little problem with the gameplay. Actions to make aren't always making sense, some new areas are appearing out of the blue and I often existed the hidden objects scenes because while trying to click on an object, I was in reality in the exit area. Besides, you have just 4 locations: the three rooms where the sisters are and outside. You don't visit anything else.
The graphics are acceptable, they're fitting to the Christmas ambiance. The soundtrack is also reflecting this.
I should have known that for the price, I wasn't getting a great hidden object game. True, it's well polished. But when you're used to play longer games, you're kinda deceived. However, I would have probably given a thumb up if actions were making sense and if I was seeing more than four locations. However, I was disappointed in the end. I didn't really enjoy the game - and trust me, it's pretty rare when I'm thumbing down a casual game.
EDIT: Since the review, achievements have been added, which is a nice feature, however, I was victim of some bugs: one with the puzzle for the kitchen door and one with a missing window (though by going back to the main menu, it was solved). So, apparently, bugs that weren't there before are now present... I'm still not recommending the game. Didn't change my mind from May 2016.

The winter holiday season can be one of the most joyous times of the year for many, and it goes without saying that Christmas is a big part of that joy. If you celebrate Christmas or are just familiar with the usual festivities then you’ll understand this game right away. It has all the things the holiday has; snow, candy, gifts, cooking and baking, helping out others and of course adorable little old ladies.
If you’re a scrooge then bah humbug to you, try
anyway!
The story is very simple, you’re dashing through the snow  in your red pickup truck loaded with presents when all of a sudden you’re hit with a magical wave of energy. Your car has been turned into candy and you’ve landed in what seems to be a festive holiday land!
but your character seeks help in restoring it to its metal form. It seems these three nice old ladies that live in a gingerbread house made a mistake with their spell and now need your help to reverse it, while they also need help with other mundane tasks. At one point I was getting suspicious that they actually stopped me on purpose to have someone help do things they couldn’t do since they’re old. However, they are very nice and they help you get back on the road again. The game’s store front page says you’re playing as Santa’s Granddaughter, Lisa, but this is never mentioned in-game, which was a missed opportunity on the part of the developers.
You use your mouse to play the game, clicking on things and people to interact with them. You also collect useful items that will need to progress through certain obstacles along the way.
You’re given a list of items to find and a chaotic scene of Christmas fun to sift through, in the end finding the one actual item that you needed. There are also puzzles as well but there are not many and most are rather easy. You will mainly be helping the old ladies out and doing quite a few hidden-item scenes in this game which I really liked.
The graphics are straight out of a Christmas card. Everything Christmasy can be found here, trees and candy canes, angels and bells, so it’s over-the-top festive. The game is very beautiful and full of color, the visuals put an instant smile on my face when I opened up the program. There are beautiful holiday lights, garland, twinkling stars and so much more everywhere. To go with the theme, the music is also holiday inspired some tunes even being old classics you may recognize.
I played this game in April but it felt like mid-December the whole time. This is a bare bones hidden object game, the plot is simple with no twists or turns and the gameplay is traditional.

is a fun treat any time of the year and I fully recommend it.

Before I start, it should be noted that this game does not currently support 21:9 resolutions. Though developers have replied in Steam forum threads saying they are working on it, just beware that this game has some issues if you are running an ultrawide. For whatever reason, running the game in 1920x1080 on an ultrawide makes everything very blurry, and it seems everything is being rendered at something like 800x600. To get the "actual" 1080p display on my monitor, the game was running at 2560x1440. I have no idea either. It also introduces some graphical errors, where sometimes the game would zoom in very far and text would get cut off, but it would only be for a few seconds at a time. It's not game-breaking, but I hope devs work to fix this soon. There is also no FOV slider. It's definitely a little tight, but even though games should be shipping on PC with FOV sliders in this day and age, I woulnd't recommend skipping over this release just because it doesn't (unless you suffer from motion sickness or migraines from low FOV of course).
Now onto the important part..
This game is genuinely one of the best, most unique storytelling experiences I've ever played. I love the world of walking sims, and I think this will now be the game I recommend to newcomers that want to test the waters with the somewhat controversial genre. There are a ton of great walking sim games, but this one might be my favorite of them all. It's definitely a strong contender to Firewatch.
This game managed to hit a lot of different points for me. Each part of the game brings back different memories of childhood and growing up, all rooting from different specific emotions. I think no matter how you've grown up throughout your life, there will be something in this game that will connect with you.
I've never quite seen a game use it's environment to tell a story as well as this game did. Without spoiling anything, there are some sections of the game that are just pure fun to interact with, and put a huge smile on my face, while also being just absolutely clever in the way they were presented. The cat section near the beginning of the game was just great. It really caught me off guard, in a good way. Some parts, like the "photography section", combined the music and gameplay together to envoke emotions that the developers intended, and it worked so well. It was melancholic at times, nostalgic at others. I personally think Lewis' section may have been the most prominent of all. I feel a lot of people playing this game will relate to the way he felt in some way - we've all felt like he did at times.
You can tell a lot of time went into choosing the right songs for each section of this game, and I think that time spent paid off massively. Music is largely important in games, and in the walking sim genre it's something a lot of devs are putting time and thought into. This game took that effort and doubled it. Everything just fits.
The world design is beautiful. It's unrealistic in parts, but it's somehow exactly how the world felt when you were a child. Things were exaggerated, but not to the point where it took you out of the experience - it just added to it. This game instilled a sense of being so calm, it was really a nice experience to just be in the game for the few hours it took to complete. The voice acting was great all round, and even though the pacing of dialogue was sometimes interrupted by character movement being slow, it still flowed together nicely. It was like reading a book and you don't want to put it down because it's just that good; you have to know what's coming next.
Overall I think this game is a standout among others in the genre. It truly holds up as one of the best of its kind, and was a pleasure to play from start to finish. Gaming in the modern world can often feel saturated and almost as if there's no heart or soul being put into some of the titles that get pumped out yearly, and it's games like this that remind you that there are developers who care about their product and aren't just doing the bare minimum of what needs to be done to be passable. Genuine thought and passion goes into games like What Remains of Edith Finch - and it pays off.
This is one that I definitely wouldn't miss if I were you.
