First off - I played  and finished Gothic 1 on a non-steambound copy, so my amount of played hours is inaccurate.
As you can see by the pictures on the store page, Gothic is a pretty old game with old graphics so if you can't stand playing without more up-to-date graphics but still want to have a simular experience you should check out Risen - the spiritual successor to the Gothic series. Combat in Gothic is kind of clunky and you'll have to invest in teachers (with gold AND xp) to make it more viable - making every skill decision even more important since the spent gold wont come back to you unless you kill your teacher - which is a pretty stupid idea since there aren't many people around who can teach you and most of 'em require you to do 1 or 2 quests to gain their trust!
Despite having outdated graphics the soundtrack and voice acting of Gothic good (at least the german voice acting - sadly I haven't heard the english one yet). The map is large and littered with monsters, trinkets and many rememberable locations - such as the old camp in the mine colony or the sect in the swamp.
Another downer about Gothic are the bugs - but most of them can be fixed using the debugging console - so if you're willing to (maybe) go to the trouble of bugfixing once or twice you'll still have a great time – given the game runs on your computer (It has various issues with Windows 10 and 8, mainly random game crashes!)
Now that those points are clearified: Let's talk about the RPG-legend that is Gothic! Gothic is the first installment of Piranha Bytes "Gothic" series. It's story begins with the nameless hero being thrown into the "barrier", a magical border around a colony of mines in the Gothic universe. This setup can be compared to Stephen Kings novel "The Arena" – making the whole approach very unique. A bunch of criminals, mainly male, is imprisoned in a large, rough and unforgiving area full of dangers and new social structures have established. Gothic manages to make the game feel extremely "alive" by clever chracter relations, item placement, location-setting and the overall development while progressing through Gothics story.
Gothic will treat you like filth in the beginning - most of the combat will be extremely tough and you wont just stumble upon a viable weapon after 2 minutes of playtime. You'll long for new sets of equipment and will be happy for any piece of loot you can aquire! The game will not hold your hand and you'll have to figure out how you can reach your goals - making it even more rewarding if you solved a complicated quest or tricked a strong enemy into being killed by NPCs.
After playing a while you'll be able to join one of three fraction - the old camp, the new camp or the sect of the sleeper. Each fraction has a unique realtion to the people of Gothic and you'll be treated in a different ways by NPCs depending on which fraction you chose. The questlines and sidequests of these paths differ a lot and are all genuinly well implemented - even in the late game, giving you a solid reason for replaying.
Overall Gothic is (in my opinion) an extremely detailed game with plenty of hours of fun and immersive playtime to keep you busy - and if you don't mind the old graphics and genuinly enjoy RPGs you should grab it on sale and give it a try!

I recieved a free, early copy from the developer. Keep that in mind.
If you’d prefer a video review, have a look here:
The whole gameplay loop is that you’re presented with doors and some instructions, and all but one leads to death, and the one that doesn’t, apparently, leads to bacon.
I was a little torn with the presentation. On one hand it’s simple and clean, on the other I think you could argue it’s a bit boring. I tend to lean to the former rather than the latter, but I do think there’s a small subset of people who would be put off by it; if you’re not a fan of the bleakness of a game like Limbo, say, in terms of colour and style, then you’re not going to be stopping to take in the world. All that said, I think it serves the purpose well; I much prefer a simpler approach like this as opposed to an ugly attempt at something more complicated. It also fits in quite well with the story, and there is a story, and a theme, and an atmosphere, but i’ll talk about that in a sec.
The mechanics, well, there aren’t really any gameplay mechanics. This is where the game is going to lose most people. It’s not a walking simulator, like dear Esther, but it’s hard for me to class it completely as [PAUSE] a puzzle game. I’d say approach it more as a short brainteaser book that, doesn’t have too many puzzles and they're all really the same puzzle at varying difficulties but, there’s also a narrative there that you need to read between the lines to discover as you continue on in the book. I’m not saying it’s not a game, it is a game, but it has that quality where it’s for a very specific kind of person. Not necessarily for the person that loved Gone Home, but maybe a fan of The Witness would enjoy it, or any other puzzle game that asks a lot of the player. And the mechanics have their own intrinsic issues; you can brute force the game by guessing the answers and, I’ll admit, I ended up guessing a lot of the final puzzle in impulsive frustration. The fact that it’s possible to do so I think should be put down as a negative mark for the game, because I’d argue that, unless you have the will of a black hole, the minute most people get frustrated they’ll begin to just guess in order to beat the puzzle.I do think that’s a design flaw, but at the same time it’s slightly difficult to criticise a game for giving you more options you know?
So there is a story to the game. In particular before I say anything specific I'd like to talk about the atmosphere, and I think it’s pretty much as good you can get for a game like this. It’s a really interesting mix of horror and humour, and I think it works. Ambient, ominous noises chirp away at your ears, if you’re wearing headphones, but at the same time your final goal always seems to be.. bacon, which is so tongue and cheek -- I think there’s people who would argue that’s almost a little too much in the other direction. In terms of the actual story itself, and underlying narrative, I thought it was super interesting. If you want to know nothing going in, which I’d recommend, I’d say you should hit that annotation on the top right that will take you directly to the score, or hit the temporary one in the top left to take you to the overall verdict section. The fact is, the story is so minimal, that to say anything about it might be a major spoiler for some people. I’ll still try and keep it as vague as possible. I do wish there was a little more to the story than there was, but it was good enough to give an otherwise empty, soulless, game, a breath of life. It gives it some heart and context; I could imagine what the scenario was, and it managed to make the mix of the two H’s: Horror and Humour, actually make sense. There’s a reason why some things are scary, and there’s a reason why some things are ridiculous. It all makes sense within the context of the story and, I’ll harp on about it, story is a huge part of a lot of games because it’s the glue that brings all of the pieces together to work as a cohesive whole, and even if the mechanics didn’t satisfy me much, I still felt like I had a complete experience because of the story.
In the end I got a couple hours out of the game, and it was a fairly interesting experience. Personally I’d say that the $5 is not necessarily too expensive, but I do think it could be lower. There is a discount for the game on launch which I believe will bring the price down another dollar, but, ultimately, I’ve gotten way more out of some games that even cheaper. Blitz Breaker is a recent game I reviewed; I got 15 hours out of the game and it’s $3 on Steam. I also think that was a much prettier game with a lot more visual polish; what i’m saying, is that the pricing of Doors could be a lot better, or the game could have more to offer. I’d say, if you like games such as The Witness in terms of the style of gameplay, and you like minimal suggestive storytelling, and you don’t mind if there isn’t much eye candy; maybe you want an experience kinda like The Witness but in a bite-size portion -- I think in that case it’s probably a must buy. I just don’t know how many people that actually is; it’s really a unique game directed at a unique audience.
SCORE:
PRESENTATION: 7
MECHANICS: 6
STORY: 8
PRICE/QUALITY: 6
PERSONAL ENJOYMENT: 4
FINAL: 6.2/10
Doors get an above average, 6.2 out of 10. It’s a full point above average. The presentation was ok but a little boring; what pushed it up to 7 rather than 5 or 6, was the quite striking contrast between the doors and the rest of the environment, which I liked, and the thematic relevance of the presentation as a whole, including spoilerific parts of the game.
I do think the mechanics are above average, they show a level of creativity beyond what tends to turn up in the Steam store, but I also have a hard time imagining someone loving the game, or even really enjoying it. And I think that comes down to the fact that there really isn’t a mechanical reason for this to be a game, if that makes sense. It’s just logic puzzles that anyone could look up online, but the thing that makes this different from an online blog, is of course the story which I rate quite highly. It’s handled pretty well, and gets the point across, I just wish there was a little bit more of it, and a bit more fleshed out. admittedly I didn’t look into the details of the story, but I’m just talking about a few more story beats for the casual player. The story also didn’t blow me away, it’s not the next Portal 2 in terms of originality.
The price is good. It’s pretty fitting. $5 for two or three hours is, like, really really acceptable. I’d maybe even lean towards cheap, which is why it gets a 6. But it could have been more for the price, or cheaper still.
If we’re talking personally though? I just found myself frustrated at the puzzles a lot. I didn’t really feel good solving them either. My brain isn’t really built for logic puzzles. I would have rated it lower for enjoyment if the story hadn’t intrigued me as much as it did, though. It’s one of those things where I can recognise a pretty good game, but I didn’t really like it myself.

I was conflicted about whether to recommend this game or not. First off, to anybody looking at this review, know that I
recommend it if you can get it for $1 or less, but my review is written for the $5 price point. There's basically an equal amount of good parts and bad parts in the game, so I'll categorize them.
- Gameplay: okay
The main problem with the gameplay was just the paint gun. I think the developers should've made it spray paint so that the shots would be more accurate. If you're painting far away, the gel will fall down and curve, annoyingly. You get used to it, but it would be nice if you could paint exactly where you wanted. The other problem with the paint gun is the lack of cleaning gel. In Tag, you can use water with right-click, so it would be nice if this game had a similar system. However, I do get that it might be hard to implement a system with scrolling to change gel colors for primary click. Everything else with the gameplay is fine, physics are the same as Portal 2.
- Puzzles: great
The puzzles in the game are pretty good. I liked the addition of the paint fizzler that you could use to your advantage or disadvantage. The difficulty curve is weird, because one of the later puzzles can be easy and one of the first ones can be mind-wracking. In general, though, I felt that they were well-designed.
- Modeling: good for the most part
There were some custom models found in the game, most notably the paint gun. It's well designed and makes sense. Almost everything else is great, and the paint fizzlers are cool-looking. However, Nigel's model is a bit too small and the animations are very rigid. I think the developers should've either expanded his facial expressions like Wheatley or simply kept him offscreen. He looks like a statue that can blink on the monitors, and in person he's just... underwhelming. The main character is basically a remake of Chell, which is fine, since you can only see her about once during the game unless you turn on thirdperson.
- Voice acting: bad
Nigel's voice actor is really annoying. I can't turn off his voice to just read the captions without also turning off the really good music, so I sacrificed a good voice for good music. He's too nasal and generally just grating. His voice also doesn't really fit well with the attempted theme of the game. There should've been an actual antagonist like GLaDOS or AEGIS (from Portal Stories: Mel). The closed captions also had typos, which felt unprofessional considering that you have to pay to play this game.
- Writing: bad
By writing, I mean both the dialogue and the story. The game seems like it's trying to be funny, but it rarely actually hits. I only actually laughed once, and then Nigel overexplained the joke and ruined it. I chuckled/snorted a few times, but it was nowhere near as funny as Portal 2. The plot is basically nonexistent until the end where Nigel
If they had included an antagonist like I suggested, it would be much easier to make a story. Heck, Valve made a plot out of literally only one talking character in Portal 1.
- Music: amazing
The music is definitely the best part of the game. Harry Callaghan is an amazing composer, and he also did work on Portal Stories: Mel (which, by the way, I recommend playing if you like the Portal series). His music isn't quite as memorable here as in PS:M, but it's still nice to listen to. I liked how the music played from speakers in this game, it helped with the immersion.
- Whole game: meh
I feel like charging for this when it's so unpolished is a bit of a slap in the face to developers of free mods like Rexaura (for P1), TWTM, and Portal Stories: Mel, not to mention the creators of thousands of test chambers in the workshop. The fact that you can make your own test chambers for this is a nice feature, one that PS:M lacked. I can tell that a lot of work was put into it, but it came out seeming a bit lackluster. Overall: buy it if it's $1 or less, like I did, but don't pay full price. I would be much more lenient with my rating if it was free, since I don't expect as much quality from a free game, but it isn't. However, it does have some pretty good aspects like music and the custom test elements, so it would be a decent free or cheaper game.

I've never played a text adventure prior to Heroes Rise, for the obvious reason of being before my time. Heroes Rise has kind of sold me on the idea though.
What you get (for crazy cheap), is essentially a knock-off Telltale Games adventure (in the best possible way). The story is fairly simple in the Prodigal, but manages a few really good moments. It manages to sustain "the illusion of choice" throughout the whole story with only a few hiccups. There are a few decent twists, though the main twist was clear to me even before they started giving clues which the protagonist fails to put together.
Heroes Rise also has a fair bit of comedy, both the intentionally written and when you screw with the ability to write in your own name. An example of the latter would be my heroic codename: Grimdark. It was hilarious imagining serious people and heroes referring to my hero as Grimdark. As for intentional writing, my favourite moment was blackmailing two superheroes having a homosexual affair, because it was the most heroic thing to do clearly.
The 'combat' is mostly a veneer. You'll have text options to choose a series of attacks that will generally cost a differing number of 'power points'. However despite the games numerous warnings of the need to conserve you're strength and to use appropriate levels of force, I rarely came close to running low and never ran out. Same thing with health, so the risk of hitting zero (and death) is virtually nil.
So I do recommend it. Buy the bundle while its at a discount or even after that. What this game is, is a fairly fun romp for a decent number of hours (depending on how fast you read).

Altogether.. Pretty fun!
Except for one major gripe: Lag. The trend of HTML5 and other such similar mediums for newer games is swell, it's great to see accessiblity and flexibility, but a lot of them seem to give up performance. As soon as you get a few levels in and start having a decent number of enemies and projectiles on screen, you'll start seeing some serious performance hits. In a run-n-gun kind've game that revolves around dodging and avoiding being hit, it's a big sticking point.
Besides that? The game could use a touch more exposition. They present you at first with a cute tidbit of story, and an opening town; save the villagers, save the wizard, be a great lizard, etc. It isn't really made clear right off the bat that there is no save point, the only 'persistence' comes through saving villagers and, as such, unlocking more starting gold, which you can use to buy more/better items to begin with (some of which are also unlocked via dungeon-ing.) So it's a little confusing with your first foray into the Cemetary wondering how to get back to town to spend your saved-up cash. The long and short of it, though, is simple: gather loot, kill stuff, rinse/repeat. You'll see a lot of .. inspiration.. And I hesitate to even use that word when inspiration is sometimes as much 'copied' as 'inspired.' Face-huggers, "lurkers" (aka zoras from Zelda), and other such things make an appearance.
All in all, it's a relatively simplistic game that is part roguelike part shooter. Minus the lag and I'd give it an altogether positive review, but with the lag it's really just beyond frustrating given the level of graphics and such; the loss of performance when things get hairy is just a really big hangup.

A few problems I have with the game (Spoilers)
I had originally played this from the Choice of Games (CoG) and bought it as a chrome App. I like the "game" (putting it like that as a few people don't like calling it a game). It does suffer from a few problems though and here a few major one I have:
1. Grammar and errors - Don't get me wrong this is a well written story and it is compelling but it has quite a few grammar errors and even a few words spelt incorrectly, some probably from a slip up. Its not a huge glaring thing at first but after playing through it a while you start to notice a lot of them dotted around, which can cause you to be pulled out of the story. And since it has been out since 2012 on CoG I would have thought many of them would have been fixed or corrected but to my surprise many of them are still there.
2. Biast choices - This game is about being a hero, YOU being a hero. Not the writer. But it seems as though the writer had a little trouble trying give pro responses for other choices. For example when you get nominated for the HoT award and you have to choose between saving your Sidekick or a reporter. It paints that saving the sidekick is the "Right/Justice" choice and saving the reporter is the "wrong/Fame" choice, it even reflects this in a stat update once you make your decision. For me this is one of the problems with the Stats and the way the game part is done, it could even be not the creators fault in the end. Its done in a very "Stereotypical" mindset and doesn't try to go outside the box too much. Why is saving the sidekick the Justice choice? Sure they help during missions but does that mean you should sacrifice a civilian just to save your sidekick? Maybe saving the reporter is a good bump for your "Fame" stat but why has it got to be seen that way? Why isn't saving the reporter also seen as a Justice choice? You are saving an innocent person, who isn't even a hero. Why can't I choose to save the reporter as I think its the right thing to do? Rather than just for fame? Its even more annoying when you reach an extreme in one stat it will grey out other choices! Why take away my control?! Maybe I am blowing this out of proportion but it just grinds me the wrong way. Maybe a CYOA game is very restrictive in how you do things. But still at least the wording could've been done a little better. And I don't even think its as annoying as it is in the sequel, where it really starts to irritate me but we'll get to that in their review.
3. Lack of Graphics - Now I know its a Text game but a little graphic content would be nice. Like font colours for special text. Maybe an image for the cover screen? Or maybe showing off shots of various areas around Millenium City? I would like to see what the Fringes look like :D Even if its just an arial view. Seeing as this game is making its debute here it would've been nice to add a few extra features here and there.
4. Graphic Content - Talking of "Graphic content" why are there hardly any swear words? They've all been mostly replaced with the word "Slugger". Whilst amusing at first it got really annoying when an tense scene happens and all you character says is "Slugger" it kind of dampens the mood of the scene. I could understand if this game was aimed at pre-teens but it describes bloody scenes and people dying in, sometimes, gruesome ways. And yet the writer shy's away from swear words. If your going to use serious scenes go all out, not half-way.
5. Lack of Customisation - Now this is the lowest major problem I have with the game. I can understand why there is little customisation in the game other than the big 5 - What gender are you? What Sexual Orientation are you? What colour is your power? What is your costume? What is you name/Codename? Personally I would've like to choose other stuff, like build or something, but I'm not hankering for it. Its just a little n.iggle.
But still even with the problems listed above I still like the game. It shows promise and the sequel will hopefully live up to it (I've played it and know it does and moreso. It does suffer from bigger issues, however, but again that will be in that review).
Thanks for reading and good luck out there heroes!

Someone recomended me this game because it was supposedly similar to "Binding of Isaac", but had native controller support and other roguelike elements and I decided to try.
The game was interesting on the first run, but once I realized how little the items added to the gameplay and the repetitive nature of the levels it got boring pretty quick.
In my opinion, what makes "Binding of Isaac" shine as a great game are the unique items and the carefully balanced challenge. You keep trying to do one run after another, motivated by the thrill of what new item combination you will obtain, how will it affect your gameplay and how far can you get with it. I felt no such thing in AWL, none at all. After 10 runs or so the SAME items would keep popping over and over, and I could barely tell the difference between any of them. The weapons were the most interesting part, but even so they had all the same damage and it didn't fell much different from using any of them.
The "level design" was OK at best, switching quickly from empty rooms with a zombie to a large room with 5 enemies at close range, while a goblin throws daggers at you and a werewolf comes charging from off-screen.  Then an empty room with explosive barrels and a switch that opens the door. I get it is "randomly generated", but the generation mechanics and base rooms should be more interesting or ballanced. The player should be given the opportunity to gear a bit or meeting new enemies before being thrown in a room with 10 of it charing at him.
The totem mechanic interested me a lot, but then I got an abbacus and checked the totem damage, which was basically the same as my own weapon and got disappointed. I tried to make a full-totem build by obtaining the totem book and shaman items, but in the end using it was so clunky, having to put it on the ground and kite enemies to it while waiting for it to poof and hope that the hitbox didn't cheat me. Most of the times it was simply easier to backtrack and throw hits at the enemy one at a time than wait for them to get hit by the totem.
Now don't get me wrong, I love "roguelikes" and the difficulty associated with them, but what makes them fun is the possibility to test your limits and play the game everytime with a different set of cards. This feels to me more like I am playing an old NES game like Ghosts and Goblins where I have to keep repeating the same stuff and the difficulty is centered around perfect timing, patience and execution of it.
I personally do not recommend the game, and if you feel that the things I cited are important for you, if you enjoyed "Binding of Isaac" for the items and hate doing the same stuff again, maybe this is not the game for you.

From a nostalgic point of view this game gets a 10 out of 10 from a contemporary review it gets a 5/10 at best because it's outdated, yet i still give it a thumbs up because the atmosphere in Gothic is awesome.
You're thrown into the barrier, somebody, a stranger, a loner, nobody cares about you, nobody wants to even know your name and you don't even know that the ♥♥♥♥ is going on when we get punched in the face and left in the dirt. Here tstarts the adventure of the nameless hero. That part really reminds me of Akira Kurosawas Yojimbo or the Western remake For a handful of Dollars by Sergio Leono, a nameless guy comes into a gritty world, only were Eastwood was quick to take advantage you start as a nobody with no skills and no knoledge about the land. Trapped under a magic barrier 3 camps want you to win you over while you have to deliver a message to a group of magicians who are trapped here.
Gothic is a very old-school RPG, the makers constantly said that classics like Ultima 7 were influences when they started to make this game and you can tell it on evey corner. Quests are like "Go there....somewhere....get me something" and not how modern RPG works were an arrow leads you exactly to the point of interest as well as the game making sure that you never feel as a Hero. You're not the knight in shining armor, you're not the saviour of the world. In the beginning even 2 Scavengers can kill you, a group of Blood flies  kill you faster than you can say "i wish i had a proper sword", you're a nobody who has to learn everything, has to level up and find a role to play, wether it's a Swordfighter, a Archer or a Magician with specifications in between: 1 hand or 2 hand Sword? Bow or Crossbow? Magician of various arcance ways? Of course also the question which of the three camps you follow or if you play them all against each other like Eastwood did in the first Dollar movie. You can even do that though ultimately there's one way to Freedom.
I'm old enough to remember when the game was previewed in german gaming magazines and the hype was build, though even back then there was bit of negativity toward the controls and while Piranha  Bytes went from Keyboard only to a more comfortable Keyboard + Mouse system it's still a far cry from todays fluid controls. Picking up items and fighting is uncomfortable and will take a while to get used to it.
Also since this is a old-school RPG the difficult is considerably higher than what gamers today may know from the likes of the Bethesda games. A single enemy can kill you, you need to be more strategic in your fighting early on and use your learn points wisely to level up in the fields you desire (as mentioned: melee 1 hand, 2 hand, bow, crossbow, magic) you can't be a master eof everything like you can be in Skyrim.
If you fight through, learn some skills and get used to the gritty world you will find a very atmospheric world that takes cues from medieval europe as well as being influenced from Lord of the Rings, A Song of Ice and Fire and german Fantasy works like Das schwarze Auge (The Dark Eye) with a dark realistic world and a great soundtrack with atmospheric music.
I recommend it with a warning about the controls but if you can get over them as well as the outdated graphics you will find a really good RPG. Altough i guess the english voice acting and translation is a far cry from the german original. If you know some german play it in it's original form!

I've thought about making reviews before, but this is the only game I've ever felt like I actually have to review.
It took me two hours to get one ending. I was glued to the screen the entire time in a trance, there's just... wow. And this is FREE. I actually wouldn't have minded at all to pay for this. This game is now sitting in my own top list of favorite visual novels, and it really deserves to be played by anyone else who likes them.
I'm going to keep playing this for all the endings, I just have to.
Also, the sprites and cgs? They aren't bad at all. The art style is a lot more on the realistic side than the anime side. I thought some of them were absolutely gorgeous, and others were absolutely terrifying. It's not joking with the M rating. The sound effects and music overall, especially where there is no music, is just perfect!
Besides the overall story, my favorite thing is that you are Mother. You'll read in first person at some points, but you are always influencing Rosa as Mother. She doesn't have to listen to you either, and the more I got into the story the more I picked answers I thought would make Rosa listen to herself more. Mother does love her, but... y'know, the whole "mother knows best" isn't always right.
So, play it. It's free. There's no reason not to try it if you're even just a little bit interested.
Edit: After putting in more hours, I've thought a lot more about what I'd like to say about this game.
It is not for everyone. The game even has a mature filter, which only works on the CGs to my understanding. I'd compare it to a VN that has a mature filter for sex scenes, but keeps in the details for the plot. (also, there is one sex scene in the game. I don't think it's skippable.)

is easily one of the best visual novels I've ever played. It also happens to be an OELVN, so it proves that occidental visual novels have nothing to envy to Japanese ones. The attention to details and work put into it are not what you would expect from a non commercial one.
The peculiarity in this visual novel is that the player has to play as a third person point of view character — that of Mother. Whether you'll find yourself trying to manipulate or consoling, know that your choices only end up affecting the main character's actions and not completely controlling them.
As the plot takes form, you start to notice that the story is all centered around the theme of
, but not in the traditional 'romance' sense. All its good and bad qualities are present. Be they an obsessive, abusive, twisted love, or storge, love between friends, carnal love.
The story has a nonlinear narrative, events are portrayed out of chronological order. It also sometimes changes perspective from one character to the other, so that the player gets to see other sides to the story.
The artwork is well done, the character sprites have several expressions. Some CGs have a variant for who enables the mature filter content. I wished that the menu had a larger and more visible font.
I loved the music. There are famous pieces (Bach, Rachmaninoff, etc.) next to original ones that I found haunting and difficult to forget (in a good way!).
I found myself surprised in front of details such as the sound effects that were so spot-on with the scenes.
There are four endings and one secret bonus ending that you can get when you unlock all the previous ones.
I'd like to state that maybe you should step back from this game if you think that its dark themes might be too much for you. List of trigger warnings under spoiler:

If you are new to Heroes of Might and Magic III, then the first thing to note is this game is well over 15 years old and as such it doesn't have a lot of the niceties that you'll find in games made in the last 10 years. This edition is solely one designed to make the game play nicer with modern operating systems, and increase the visual fidelity of the assets.
If you are an old hand at HOMM games, then HOMM III HD Edition is just how you remember it, but with a nice lick of paint. The lack of the expansion packs does hurt a little, but for a walk down memory lane it serves the purpose excellently.
It's hard to recommend this game to people who have played newer turn based strategy games before this, there is a lot more manual calculations for determining how much damage you'll do a troop and the subsquent counter attacks, and the information you'll want takes a lot more effort to track down. If I was playing HOMM III in any kind of serious way I'd definitely have a pen and paper ready for notes. The best example of this is when you mouse over units, you need to right click to get a static screen of statistics when many modern games will calculate win/loss ratios for you by simply mousing over an enemy unit.
I do recommend this game, to people who have fond memories of playing the original and to the new folks who get to see a game which paved the way for so many others, without all the hassles this normally entails with getting older programs to work on newer hardware/OS'es. But be warned, the years have not been kind as far as the interface is concerned.

Last of the truly good WWII games, Sniper Elite is more dedicated towards engaging your targets from a distance with a collection of different famous and accurately modeled sniper rifles from the era. You can adjust and customize your difficulty and all factors that affect the challenge of the game as you wish.
It works without any problems on highest settings on Windows 7 64-bit. The graphics and voice acting are the weakest links in this otherwise fun game and it has great longevity as well as replay value. Unlike the later Sniper Elite games there's actual challenge here which feels exciting and authentic rather than purely scripted.
There is barely any story to the game and the intro video is probably the as deep as you'll get to know anything about the setting of the game and its main character. The main point here is the gameplay which is tight and exciting. Of course, more so than its sequels, Sniper Elite is absolutely NOT purely an action game. You will die instantly if you run around trying to kill everybody. You need to act like a sniper and wait for the perfect shots and this is the main attraction for this game. The hunt for the perfect spot to snipe unsuspecting enemies from a mile away. There is at least 12 hours worth of single-player gameplay here plus multiplayer modes which I'm not personally familiar with.
Remember the game can get highly challenging on higher difficulties and also READ THE GAME MANUAL BEFORE YOU START. There are quite some keys used in the game which you may need to write down in order to remember. No steam achievements.
All in all, like good wine, this game has aged considerably well. If you look past the terrible voice acting and the old, repetitive graphics then you're in for a lengthy, exciting game full of sweat-inducing anticipation. Definitely worth picking up on a sale.

I like this game because I am 100% biased toward any thing and all things Portal related. However, I have to recommend that you don't buy this game as there are far better mods out there available for free. I've listed the positives and negatives below.
I must also note that workshop support for this game seems rather pointless now that the paint gun from this game is now available in Portal 2 via BEEmod 2.0+. If you want to limit chambers down to ONLY paint gun and no portal gun, then by all means boot up this game and then head into the workshop, as you'll find more puzzles for the paint gun here than in Portal 2.
-This game was CLEARLY not sufficiently playtested, as many of the puzzles allow you to get stuck, or are VERY EASILY cheated. There are several bugs with mechanics and audio at several points throughout the game.
-The voice acting isn't fantastic. It's servicable, and the actor certainly is enthusiastic enough, but the actor doesn't speak as if he is in the situation he is acting. Often times, the voice actor is actually very annoying. (example: "CHOP CHOP, You should be able to reach the exit quickly!")
-The Paint Gun mechanic isn't properly introduced and the puzzles don't increase in difficulty throughout the game. Puzzle difficulty spikes and dips throughout the game.
-The Paint Gun doesn't even fire directly at the crosshair, but instead seems to fire from the player-character's waist. It feels clunky and slow. This is not helped by the fact that the paint is fired at a slower speed than the player can fling themselves, so flying through the air as the game intends sometimes renders the paint gun entirely useless.
-The music is pretty good, but it often consists of only a 6-second loop that repeats over and over at different keys and octaves.
-Early in the game, several modern elements such as light bridges and tractor beams are used in classic cave-johnson style tests and the game never explains this mixup of testing elements. It seems that no attention was payed to themes other than the new original theme later in the game. (See below)
-There are FAR TOO MANY vacuum tube rides early in the game, then about half way through the game, they disappear entirely as if the developer got lazy.
-The audio mixing is good, but the sound design leaves a lot to be desired and often the wrong sound effects are used, such as explosions when metal doors slam shut.
-The game breaks when you quicksave during a timed mission, such as the escape before the reveal. The game will always load the quicksaved point, so if you saved with insufficient time to complete the mission, you are stuck unless you restart the chapter.
-The game will nearly crash and send the player back to the title screen if you attempt to quickload during a cutscene.
-The store description boasts a "full campaign," though there isn't much story at all. The narrator who directs you through chambers occasionally hints at other workings and events happen which makes the player assume "this will all be explained later in the game," just as 'Portal 2' and 'Portal Stories: Mel' do, but these events are never brought up again and nothing is ever explained. The full story is basically this:
-The game does not use the interactions between portals and paint very often. There is a lot of unused potential here, and the game suffers without it.
-It seems the game is trying pass off unused 'F-Stop' assets as original assets, though this section is insignificant to the story anyway. They're used for a gag, but it's poorly delivered.
-Inconsistent with canon Aperture lore and history, but is alright if you think of this game as its own entity.
-Cool new themes, such as the "outdoors" which is basically four walls painted to look like the outdoors or even outer-space, and several panels are missing which makes the entire scene look rather comical.
-Special music-synced tracks play from several "Audio by Aperture" speakers in most tests. "Audio by Aperture" is a clear play on "Beats by Dre," and I chuckled a bit when I first discovered it.
-Easter eggs are in fairly hidden places, though the loud music that plays from them after they are found does not stop playing.

I have had many mixed feelings about this game so take this review for what it is, not for the recommmendation of the game.
This mod to the original Portal games is something that I would not recommend to to get while its not on sale, however I would recommend getting it if it is on sale. I understand that hard work went into the game, but at the same time, if you plan to add a price tag then you need to have some pretty fun gameplay. This was only sort of executed upon.
Pros:
-  this game has a very interesting concept of using a non-portal gun in the facility that made portal use a norm. While the gel gun may not be as fun to use as the portal gun (in my opinion) Its still something to have fun with.
- The ability to make and upload community made levels on the steam workshop is something that I personally appreciated with this game. This is really the reason I left my review with a "recommended" rating.  Since the story is rather short.... it makes it nice to be able to make and share levels with other people.
Cons:
- The single player game is a mess. To be honest, I was quite interested in the story mode at the beginning because it was introducing new concepts and attempting to develop the game as its own thing: something that's part of the universe of Portal, but something new added by the developers. One of the two major problems with the single player that I had is that the level design becomes less and less about solving the puzzle and more about trying to stick a lucky jump or run. This is pretty frustrating since the game has a very small number of autosaves in quick-time based parts of the game.
- The other problem with the game is the story is very disappointing. Not only is the voice acting not super great, but the story is too short and has a terrible ending. What made this even worse for me was that I played this right after playing through Portal Stories: Mel (Which is a fantastic mod that I VERY strongly recommend), A game where the story is not only well developed, but is just more entertaining as a whole.
Closing thoughts:

I've played a good few Text-Based games before. I remember the days of my boyhood where I would go to Funcoland (Something that existed before Gamestop younglings) and would buy PC text-game with my hard earned 5$ allowance. Back then I barely understood what I was doing half the time and just tried to get the the "official" end of the game and could by this point claim satisfaction as a kid playing his windows game.
When I saw Heroes Rise on Steam Sale, I looked and thought "Here comes some poorly animated, poorly done, badly written mess with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story and terribly graphic'd final-fantasy fights. Safe to say I was shocked to hear that this was a text-based game and of all things the Choose-Your-Own-Adventure kind. It made me curious and I bought the game only to load it and start playing with the intent that the game would be something of a time-passer at best when I was sitting in my classes or pretending to listen to my friends over the phone.
----------------------------------------------------
Firstly I will say this about Heroes Rise. If you bought this game expecting to play a variety of characters, then you will be sorely disappointed. Your story is summarily pre-written with you only to change certain things to fit your mood or tone. Sadly you cannot be a vigilante with no special powers, an alien who crashed on earth, or any of the other overused and overdone origins we see in most superhero stories. The explanation for "Powered Heroes" however makes up for this and if thought about considering the setting, does fit the bill enough if you suspend your disbelief the amount NEEDED to play a game like this.
However it should be noted that your characters name, gender, alias/codename as a hero, costume, morals, and their sidekick are yours to decide from several options that make the game in my opinion more than worth playing over again some few times after you've beaten it, just not excessively because let's face it...You wouldn't crack open a book you just finished a week ago to read it again, would you? For replayability value, the same ideal applies to this game. Though in all of the decisions that you could make that I listed, you're likely realizing that I didn't list what often is wanted in a Superhero for wanted variety. Powers.
Sadly, your character comes with predetermined set of powers and that is sadly what drags the game down from being better in my honest opinon. With a bit of extra writting and coding I'm sure they could've given more lovable variety to this game by letting you choose a bit of variation to your powers such as elements or origin. However again, when you consider the story they are telling, it can be forgiven and glanced over. Especially given the twist concerning your powers and your potential should you press the subject during gameplay. Which brings me to make clear that the game has it's moments of deep immersion and well-written storytelling (aside from some typos you can spot) throughout your playthrough.
It both caters to and even manages to stray away from some of the tropes and stereotypes a fan of comic-books or superheroes would be familiar with. Some things that I myself as a reader of comics had assumed would happen, ended up proceeding -completely- differently than I expected them to. Though I'll admit there are several inconsistencies I believe to have spotted...however again this game is based off of your imagination and suspense of disbelief so such things can be forgiven easily so long as you don't dwell on them as critically as I have.
In the end I can say that this game is worth the money you pay for it. It's fun, stimulating, makes you think of how you want your character to act, and really the only thing about it that saddens me is that the game doesn't have actual graphics to it. However it wouldn't be TEXT-BASED then, now would it? With this being the first installment and my already buying the sequel as well as awaiting the third installment to complete the trilogy I'm sure things will be revised as time goes on. All in all the game is worth the few dollars it cost when I purchased it and so long as you aren't expecting a priceless gem, and can settle for something that just shines on it's own...I reccommend buying it despite my critical review of it.

QUICK REVIEW -
If you enjoy randomly generated dungeons with only one life, similar to spelunky, then there's a good chance that you'll enjoy this game and should definitely pick it up.
LONG REVIEW -
You find yourself playing as Raga, a wizard's familiar, who has to save his master after his kidnapping by death. Each level of the dungeon is randomly generated and you always have to keep an eye out for any chance to improve your future dungeon runs and think about how best to spend your gold. For example there are blueprints for weapons you can buy in town before a run and lost villagers who will contribute to your starting amount of gold. Even though you only have one life per dungeon, death isn't the end. You keep going through levels as a ghost which can be both to your advantage and disadvantage. As a ghost you can get items you can't obtain while alive (keys, etc.), though you will face more enemies in the form of ghosts of enemies you've slain. To revive yourself you merely have to find a revival sigil in one of the floors of the dungeon. This presents an interesting choice, kill yourself to get special items and try to revive yourself, or play it safe and keep as much health as possible for the boss. This game reminds me a lot of playing spelunky with its random item merchants, one life per dungeon and addictive gameplay. The only features of the game that I didn't like where that you can't see what an item is before you buy it, you have to memorize what item has what perks, and that there is no way to bring up the map without having to pause the game. Overlooking these points, I really enjoyed this game and have found it quite addictive to play. I definitely recommend picking it up.

Possibly the best £2 I've ever spent.
This game captures the spirit of the old "Choose Your Own Destiny" adventure books, which I used to love as a kid.
There is no graphics and no sounds: just plain text, formatted similiar to a book with decisions that will greatly affect your character's story, reputation, relationships and abilities.
Most importantly, the game will require you to make tough decisions and...there is no turning back.
You cannot revert to an earlier savegame, as the game will allow you to manually save only at the end of your adventure in order to carry over your story when playing the sequels (the game will be saved automatically each time you advance to another page, so you can close the game safely anytime).
I really enjoyed the game and its sequel: great story, tension and drama, and for that price it's really worth a try if you're unsure.
Highly recommended.

This game is a game that says it rewards the ideas of choice. It is a choose your own adventure after all, and many of your decision points have three or more sets of choices. The problem is that the game does not reward choices unless you go down very specific paths. Some of those paths are even pre-chosen for you. Note, that the full review will have major spoilers.
1: The entire plot is linear. You always fail your first mission, you always join the big group, you always fall in love with the one superhero who looks like your childhood crush. I understand this is a text based game, but I felt like some of my decisions were simply choosing my method of going into the next wall of text rather than actually changing what would happen.
2: The choices you get completely free will on are purely aesthetic. You choose your first and last name for free, you get to choose your superhero name for free. You get to choose the name of your parents' "Song" which is engraved on their wedding ring. Most importantly, you get to choose what your character's childhood crush is because there is a sexy superhero who looks just like them! They give you a ton of predetermined choices on those BTW.
3: Your character's moral alignment has to be pure one way or the other to get a perfect score. Most of your choices purely affect your four moral alignments: Fame/Justice, Solo/Team, Offensive/Defensive, and Lawless/Lawful. You can only get a perfect score if you stick to your guns ENTIRELY TO ONE SIDE. Do you want to be in it for the fame, but work with a team and the police? Or do you want to be a soloist hero who breaks the law, but does it for justice? These complex characters are not rewarded, but are in fact penalized with getting the "bad ending" of the game in which 314 people die because your character was too slow.
4: The "bad" alignments are sometimes bad for no reason. I want to work on my own, but I'm not a♥♥♥♥♥♥ There is a scene I got where I found two of the members of the not!Justice League making out in the bathroom. My choices were "Blackmail them?" or "I saw nothing, don't worry." I wanted to be a soloist, but doing the latter raised my team player points because I worked with the team. Why does working alone mean you have to be a♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you just had a Mass Effect "Paragon/Renegade" slider that would have been better.

: As of update 2.0.12, all game-breaking bugs have been fixed. Recommendation changed. This is a fun, tough little action-roguelike. There are still a few small issues like slowdown when there are too many mobs on the screen, but nothing that makes the game impossible. It seems like the devs are still working on balancing bosses as I've noticed huge swings in their difficulty between this update and the last one. Progress is VERY incremental, as you slowly save villagers and buy blueprints to give yourself a better run. Some of the items look really similar, and the names are not displayed before you purchase them, so it can be frustrating thinking you were buying a Helmet of somethingorother when it turns out to be a Helmet of someotherthing.
If you liked Binding of Isaac or classic LoZ, try this one.
I am including my original review below. Most of the issues are no longer applicable, but they still existed in a $15 game:
I'm surprised this isn't labelled Early Access (I wouldn't have purchased it if it were).
In the 70 minutes I played, there were no less than 3 game breaking bugs I experienced multiple times each.
1. On Win7, game must be run in XP compatibility mode or you get only a black screen on launching.
2. Sometimes when hitting an exploding barrel the game crashes to desktop
3. Sometimes (for no discernable reason) the game's visuals will freeze. You can hear the menu options and run into things, but the screen is frozen.
These kind of bugs are totally unacceptable in a roguelite, or any game with permadeath. Hopefully the devs will be able to get it patched fairly soon, but it's pretty frustrating that this is for sale on Steam as is without a "beta" or "early access" tag, considering how buggy it is.
All that said, the bits of the game I got to play are pretty fun. The controls are very similar to The Binding of Isaac, though movement is a bit less slippery and shooting a bit more precise (due to the controller support adding 4 more aiming directions, and the projectiles not taking on any of your own character's momentum.) It's a shame the bugs make it unplayable. Once it gets patched up I think it'll be a fun little action RL.

How is it that Konami, of all people, does free to play RIGHT?
Duel Links is a speedier version of the original set of YGO rules. Duels take a couple of minutes at a time, which is great for drop in, drop out play, but at the same time you can play as much as you want, unlike other F2P games. You have a standard set of AI duelists that respawn every few hours, which you can refresh with an uncommon duel reward, a set of Legendary Duelists (based on the show's characters, with voice acting!) that can be fought with rewards from those standard duelists, and ranked play against other players, which is ALWAYS free, at any time, and gives rewards to fight the Legendary Duelists too along with its own set of rewards, so it's entirely possible to do a four hour run of the ranked ladder and come out of it with a good amount of rewards for the time you spent.
Card packs are fair in every way imaginable - the game is constantly giving you gems at you for packs, there's always an event going on for more gems. You never end up in a position where you don't want to think about what you want to buy, but you aren't being nickled and dimed either - saving up rewards can result in something like enough gems for 50 packs before you know it. There's also a Card Trader who doesn't have a ridiculous range, but can pop up some really powerful cards for when your old collection needs recycling.
They even have fairness on the rarities - you WILL get the rarest cards in a set if you keep buying the packs...eventually. I pulled a Dark Magician of Chaos (an Ultra Rare, only one copy inside the 240 cards in the pack) the second pack into a set, and an extremely powerful Tribute monster and his spell to bring him out inside the same pack about 10 packs into a box, while aiming for another, extremely common card had me 40 packs in without getting it, but I'll get it if I keep trying. You can even refresh boxes whenever you want for another chance at the rarer cards once you've opened them.
The game always has some way to reward you - at the time of this review I had two sets of challenges for leveling up two different worlds, some challenges for unlocking characters, a meter to fill up with duels for rewards as part of an event, a unique duelist popping up who I could fight for even more rewards, every individual character's reward track that has cards, gems, coins and new abilities, and a track for the PVP that gives me rewards for my wins. You'll never NOT have something to work towards.
The best part is that, all of these things together - infinite duels if I want them, fair amounts of packs to try my luck with, with the knowledge that I WILL come across that Ultra Rare as long as I keep at it, and always having something to DO, with a reasonable reward behind it, makes it feel like I never have to spend money. And yet despite that, I DID. This is the first F2P game I've actually given money to, and just because the game is this fair, I'm thoroughly tempted to give them more. Money in this game doesn't give you an unfair advantage - everyone has the same set of boxes to buy, there's no power increase paid people have that free players can't catch up with, whether by persistence or luck.
The actual game remains as excellent and enjoyable as it was back in the day. The slimmed down gameplay and return to the basic set of rules, combined with a new, unique set of cards with their own boxes keeps things way more interesting than just throwing every card from the old game in, and it has me constantly looking at my deck, wondering what card can be safely cut out, what needs to be kept, what cards I need to hunt down next, and the duels, oh god the duels. While getting run over by Cyber Angels or Naturia decks isn't particularly great, getting into an even fight can be some of the best games of Yu-Gi-Oh I've ever had, like this video here:
Since the game more or less accelerates "meta" players up the ladder and keeps people around their own skill otherwise, hopefully you won't run into them too often.
The fanservice is also fantastic - the actors do a great job of sounding like themselves, and Kaiba bullying schoolchildren is something I never knew I wanted in my life. Even the unique lines between a set of competitors (Yugi and Kaiba being the obvious combo, but pretty much every fight in the anime happens to have a line or two here as well) is a really nice touch. The 3D models are slightly more distracting (obviously a mobile-restricted thing) but thankfully all of that can be turned off (even the voices, which results in an accelerated game if you find it all too distracting).
The PC port, while an obvious port from the mobile version (which I wasn't able to play for very long due to the only compatible device I had being an old tablet that almost audibly groaned under the strain) runs really, really well (although I do overshoot the minimum requirements by a massive margin). A bit of Alt+Enter for fullscreen and it doesn't skip a beat; farming AI duels is super fast, controlling the port using the mouse is natural enough once you realise it's more like a touchscreen than a proper mouse-controlled interface, although some keyboard commands for menu things might be nice, and it looks great in motion. It's not even two gigabytes all up, which is great for someone who needs his hard drive space.
I played over 20 hours of this game within four days of the PC port coming out, at complete and utter surprise to myself. I used to love the game back in the day but as it fell out of favor with the end of the original series and the newer rules, I never really got to play it again. Feels like the old days. And with a new, free to play, incredibly fair version of it available right in front of me whenever I should be doing something else, I'll keep playing Duel Links, and with the ten million downloads on Android alone I hope I'll always have someone to duel against. If you have any interest in old school Yu-Gi-Oh, CCGs, or any kind of neat strategy game, you need to give this a shot. It's absolutely worth your time.

You'll sacrifice, for example, fuel and hull for the chance to pick up some oxygen at the rocky planets you come across as you travel along the line of stars between you and your ultimate destination.  You'll keep finding rare elements like tungsten and platinum that you can't use for anything until you discover relevant technologies, but they leave you annoyed at the lack of space in your cargo hold.
You'll meet an alien who gives you the mysterious omega element and decide to throw away your highly common silicon to make room for it, and immediately afterwards you'll chance upon a random event in which robotic termites eat your space folder, leaving you stranded.  If you only had some silicon, you could have repaired it.
There's clearly a story simmering in the background.  You encounter all kinds of zany alien life forms, and a lot of them try to communicate with you.  You gradually pick up some language that might help you to make decisions during these interactions if you actually have a run that lasts long enough, and they're all worried about judges or architects or something.  The writing is the sort that makes you feel like it
it's good, like it's really got something to say, but it's actually cringe-worthy much of the time—and badly in need of proofreading, as well.  Here's an example:
That's terrible, right?  Come on.  It's hard to care when the writing is that bad.
So there's really nothing compelling me to continue playing this.  I guess I'm curious to see what it's like to have a nice ship decked out with a bunch of tech that makes life easier, collecting rare elements and building interesting new devices, but getting there is a matter of pure luck.  There's no progress between runs that helps your goal to seem more plausible, either.
Everything that I manage to discover before inevitably running out of fuel after desperately traveling to the nearest fuel-rich gas giant that the game tells me on arrival has nothing left to probe—all of the technologies and new ship types (with their ample, blessed cargo space) that I've found along the way are gone.  I haven't unlocked anything that makes the crapshoot of space travel more manageable next time.
One of the game's selling points is that it has no combat; it's just you against the environment.  Well, maybe if it did have combat I'd actually feel like I have some control over what happens.  The idea of a game without combat appeals to me!  But it needs to be better designed than this.
Out There is no FTL.  There's no real strategy that you can employ as you play to have a greater chance of success.  In the moment-to-moment gameplay, it's just dull, while in the grand scheme of a full session it's frustrating.  Pass on this.

I went into this game optimistically, since community made Portal games such as Portal Stories: Mel left me with a sense of satisfaction, and I thoroughly enjoyed them. With Aperture Tag, though, this was not the case at all. The paint gun mechanic, while a very interesting idea, was not successfully delivered. Unlike the gradual introduction to new mechanics in the original Portal games, the introduction to the capabilities of the paint gun was rushed, and often left a feeling of confusion.
The level designs were sloppy, especially in the lower Old Aperture style levels where I was immediately met with elements that did not belong in that era such as lazers and light bridges, and I often found myself stuck using routes that seemed like they were not intended to be used at all. I even found myself moving across pipes right at the bottom of the chamber, or along the very edge of panelled walls, which would not be possible if the level had been composed correctly. Some puzzle elements were barely needed, and cluttered the tests. Honestly, I'm glad I got this game when it was on sale. It should have been free. The only fun thing I can find about this game is the increased mobility that portals could not provide. I adore momentum based tests, so that was a plus.

Out There: Ω Edition is a resource management rogue-like game which recently released on Steam after huge success on mobile platforms. In Out There: Ω Edition you play as an astronaut who has just woken up from cryogenic stasis on a journey from Earth to Ganymede, you quickly realise you've gone horribly off course and you're nowhere near your destination, you're out there. You must carefully manage your fuel, oxygen and hull in order to stay alive in an unexplored galaxy, along the way you will not only find remnants of the human race who have mysteriously vanished but you will also find alien races and alien artifacts never before seen by man. Out There: Ω Edition is a story about the survival of one man who is way out of his depth on a journey that shouldn't have taken place.
This game has a fair few similarities to FTL: Faster Than Light, in fact it's these similarities that made me buy the game, so you'll see me compare the two games a couple of times over the course of the review. I'm a huge fan of anything Space related and this title did not disappoint
+Gorgeous art style
+Everything in the game is well designed, in particular the ships and the alien life forms
+There are several different ships, each coming with pros and cons meaning each ship has a unique play style
+Usually when you jump to a new star system you get a journal entry/mini text adventure which all have great stories but they're let down by the writer's knowledge of English (I'll come back to that later)
+The galaxy is procedurally generated each time you play so you'll never see the same galaxy twice
+Interesting storyline with an interesting yet mysterious protagonist
+Outstanding (even outstanding doesn't do it justice) soundtrack that even rivals that of FTL
+Great gameplay based around resource management, kind of like FTL with more resources and no combat
+The game has no combat, a bold move that work fantastically, fighting to survive against the environment is much more interesting than fighting to survive against hostile life forms
+As you get further into a run you begin unlocking more advanced technologies to help you get further
+Abandoned ships always seem to turn up just as your ship becomes obsolete which is perfect
+When you encounter alien life forms you often learn parts of their language
+You frequently come across mysterious alien materials and artifacts which often provide ways of improving your ship
+It's impossible to see everything this game has to offer in one run so you're definitely going to come back for more
+/-When something goes wrong, such as your Hydrogen probe being destroyed, it's incredibly unlikely that you're gonna make it since when something goes wrong in this game EVERYTHING goes wrong
-The game is riddled with poor grammar and spelling mistakes which really takes away from the fantastic story in this game, in all fairness the Dev is foreign and English is probably his/her second language but I still don't see why they couldn't have had someone proof read the game
Verdict:
9
Despite the game's numerous spelling errors and grammatical errors this is a fantastic resource management game with a gorgeous art style and fantastic design.

is a very simple game that puts a modern-indie-game spin on the classic logic puzzle of
. There isn’t much innovation to the gameplay, but there is a good atmospheric presentation and an alluring simplicity to it all. I enjoyed it, but I can confidently say that not everyone will. I really enjoy solving the style of logic puzzles used in the game; I even sometimes look up riddles similar to these for entertainment when I’m bored at work. If you like this kind of thinking game too, then you should consider trying this game; but also be aware it is very short, and will be beaten in one sitting.
So, yes,
is very short. If you approach the game with a comfortable pace, and actually solve the riddles, it will probably last about the same amount of time as a modern Hollywood movie. I like short games a lot, because I like variety and won’t live forever, but I will say that I would have been more content with more content. Yes. Mostly because I was enjoying it and I wasn’t ready for it to be over. It definitely could benefit from another hour or so of gameplay.
The riddles start off pretty easy, and slowly get more complicated as you go on. Some of them towards the end are quite tricky and the final puzzle is definitely hardcore. If you get stuck you may be tempted to just bulldoze the puzzles with good ol’ trial and error, but you would only be eliminating the purpose of the game (which is to solve the riddles by understanding them).
The atmosphere is easily the most alluring aspect of the game. There is a persistently mystifying ambiance which is juxtaposed with suggestions of an unknown actual reality.  It feels like you’re down the rabbit hole. There are clear and strong influences from games like
,
, and
.
It won’t appeal to everyone. It is/was clearly a very small project that is intentionally compact and quaint. But if you are like me and like these types of riddles, then you probably will enjoy this entertaining, but quite brief, game. Consider it for a price you are comfortable with and give it a whirl.

In Doors, you solve brain-teaser-like puzzles in a simulation. That's pretty much it.
Is Doors groundbreaking? Heck no, it's essentially a book of "The blue man lives in the green house, and the green man is next to the red man's house, so who lives in the purple house?" style puzzles put into a game. Despite that, I enjoyed myself thoroughly. Doors' is a match made in heaven between Limbo's sharp visual splendor and The Stanley Parable's wit and charm. The gameplay is really well done, and it keeps introducing new concepts. Storywise, Doors falls a little flat. I won't spoil anything, but the ending could've been handled better, and it just felt lackluster.
Doors is not a game for everyone. It's very short (we're talking 30 minutes to an hour) and is definitely more logical than Limbo or The Stanley Parable. Doors has little replayability due to the nature of its' design. There are a few easter eggs here and there, but Doors is ultimately a really great concept with great design, subverted by the lack of content. I recommend it, but only if there's a sale going on, or if you like logic games.

This game fails on a puzzle design level.  Two basic quality standards I expect out of a puzzle game of this nature are that there are no superfluous parts of a puzzle (provided that misdirection is not the point) and that the requirement for a rank such as three stars is the optimal solution for at least a large percentage of the puzzles if not all of them.  This game fails repeatedly on both.  A sample puzzle could have 20 dots and claim that three stars is ten moves or less.  I just completed it in three moves without even touching three quarters of the grid.  This alone tells me that no quality control went into the puzzles themselves.
To add insult to injury, twice within the first 15 levels I completed one below the three star rank only to be given two stars, at which point I replayed the puzzle with the same exact solution and was given three stars, so there's a serious bug.  Further, the difficulty is schizophrenic even if I limit myself to the three-star guidelines; the game takes three levels to start throwing seemingly random collections of dots at you and then every puzzle looks the same.
Finally, the navigation interface is cumbersome.  The escape key pulls you completely out of a puzzle back to the level select screen.  There is no restart button so the above is the only real way to restart - except that there is a restart button when you complete the level.
I do not recommend this game even on sale until these issues have been properly addressed.

Bought at 90% off this is about acceptable, but at full price its quite poor.
The game involves leap frogging dots around a grid to get one particular dot to a finishing point. The puzzle idea itself is pretty solid and I could see some interesting things come from it, but this implementation has numerous problems.
-The music is repetative and loops after a minute or two, so you get the same song doing the same things over and over to a maddening degree even within the short time it took to complete the game.
-Early levels are bugged in that you can finish them in the move limit and not get your three stars.
-There is a lack of mechanics, basically dots you can flip over, cant flip over, or that disappear after one flip. You get those mechanics near the start and thats all you get, it seems like this kind of game could have had a lot of other creative mechanics and its a wasted opportunity.
-Perhaps one of the reasons for the lack of mechanics is that the level design appears to be almost non-existant, as if the dots were just randomly placed in most cases.
-That all plays in to the fact that after a few levels where you have to be careful to get the move limit the limits become almost nonsensically large, again like the design just picked them so no testing would be required. Id take blatently awful paths moving dots around in the shortest jumps possible and still be literally dozens of moves under the 3 star limit.
The whole thing feels like a game that the developer got bored of half way through, threw together random levels and pushed it out for whatever money they could get for it. Its a shame, because it had some promise.

I was a bit unsure about dropping money on a text based superhero adventure game, mostly because there are a lot of potential pitfalls in combining the genres, but I think steam has chosen it's first text based game well. It doesn't overcome the limitations of the genres, such as the sometimes constricting linearity of text adventures, and the cheesiness and melodrama of superheroes, but instead embraces them and works within these constraints to craft a satisfyingly complex narrative that lives up to the best standards of the genres. The choices you make are convincing in how they drive the story, and it's nice to have a meaningful stats screen that actually helps, rather than hinders, you to enjoy the game. For those who already like the genres: you'll enjoy this; for don't like these genres: look elsewhere; to the majority just looking for an entertaining game: keep an open mind and I promise you'll get your money's worth. This is a smart, well written adventure, and that's something anyone should be able to get behind.

Where to start with this one? I don't think there has been a video game series that I've enjoyed more than Gothic. Steam will lie to you and it will say I played 0.3 hours of this fine game, but know that is complete bollox. I've played and finished this game at least 10 times, and another 20 where I stopped somewhere along the way for role-play reasons. It has good world building, albeit a lack of your or an NPCs personal backstory. Good enemy variety and, if you are playing it for the first time, a very good game difficulty. Not to mention the best progression system I have ever come across in an action RPG. Let's dive in deeper to see what this gem has to offer.
As I mentioned before the world this game is set in is amazing. It takes place in a prison that serves as a mining colony for King Robhar. All the criminals of his realm are sent there, regradless their crime. Naturally, you will find all type of people in it. Those who haven't payed their taxes, thieves, some of the worst murderers in the kingdom and many, many more. Now to ensure that the prisoners do not try and escape, Robhar sent out his best mages to erect a magical barrier around the valley that welcomes all, but lets nobody out. The mages cocked it up and the barrier became a lot bigger than it should. While all the guards were looking at the pretty magic lights prisoners killed them and took control of the colony. Some stuff happens, ba da bing ba da boom, you show up. A convicted criminal ready to be chucked in there with the rest of the scum. This is the game's starting point.
Now for what reason you are sent in there God only knows. You are terrible at literally everything. The game makes up for this by offering its amazing progression system. Every time you level up you gain learning points, or LPs. You use these LPs not magically in your character screen or a level up screen, but at a trainer who will demand LPs and possibly some gold for his services. It is not just that your stats will improve, but your animation will get better, at least for weapons training. At first you hold a one-handed weapon with both hands and are extremely incompetent. When you train your skills you will begin to hold it with one hand, offering faster animation and more critical chance. That makes character advancement in this game very rewarding, at least that is how I felt. Also if you get quite skilled at this game, you will notice you can do stuff you couldn't before. Like beat an Orc warrior at level 1 if you want. While stats matter, the most important thing is your ability.
The world has a full day and night cycle that matters for both monsters and humans. Most monsters hunt during the day and are asleep during the night, which makes it prime time for hunting if you are not comfortable at fighting them off fair and square. Humans also behave according to the DnN cycle. They will gather at night near a campfire to drink, sing and eat, or they will go to sleep. At day they will be at their posts, trading, training or doing whatever. This is a thing games that came after Gothic touted about. In some respects like this, Gothic was ahead of its time.
Its not all sunshine and rainbows in Gothic land. The game visually has not aged well. It sill has great visual features, like an amazing view distance. But the texture quality is outdated and it shows. Sound overall is great. Nice music, decent and recognizable sound effects, however to say that the English voice acting is lacking is like saying Pepsi is better than Coke. Don't lie to me, I know you like Coke better you hipster. To be fair, the German voice acting is, from what I've heard, great. Also the controls are weird, but you get used to them pretty quick.
To put it bluntly. If you like action RPGs get this game. Do not be put off by outdated graphics and controls. Don't be that guy. Nobody likes that guy. If you spend and hour understanding this game, you could enjoy it for years to come.
