Heroes Rise: The Prodigy is much better than I expected it to be.
Visually, it stands proudly in the Interactive Fiction camp: a verdant land where graphical resolution is limited only by the imagination, and GPUs never melt. Mechanically though, it is much more similar to Visual Novels, as the player navigates using a series of multiple choice prompts to branch the story instead of a clunky text parser to repeatedly fail at picking up ye flask. What really makes the game shine, however, are the small mad-lib sprinkles. At several points the reader/player/whatever is given the choice between several descriptions for characters/things/whatever. In addition to the default options, there is a magical, wonderful text box.
This text box is what allows you to reject all of the suggested options, and have the sexy female hero/love interest (depending on the gender/orientation options you chose, presumably) look like Gary Busey.
The IF truly is stronger than the FPS.

When I was still in high school, I was a regular customer for internet cafes and computer shops. Then one day, I encountered a game titled "Prototype" in one of the computers I played with during the time. Out of curiosity, I played it to know what exactly it was and after a few hours in, I was hooked. "Prototype" was a big hit for me. Enjoyed every second of it. Eventually, I finished the game. That was 2010, I think. 2 years later, I was informed that a "Prototype 2" was going to be released and of course, I wanted to play it. I borrowed my dad's laptop to play it and damn I still enjoyed it as much as the first one.
NOTE that back at that time, I had very low standards for games. Lag didn't bother me at all. Graphical settings were nothing to me back then. I know, I was pretty stupid. But hey.
Years later, college came. I had my own laptop. It was a Samsung rocking a i7-3537U 2.00GHz processor, AMD Radeon 8750M 2GB GPU and 8GB RAM. Pretty decent specs. Of course, in the time I had that laptop, the idea of playing Prototype series never left me and so I played them. Again. Prototype ran fine. Easy 60 FPS. Then, Prototype 2 came. It was a huge frustration to me. I am not sure if the game was really demanding or my specs was just low but when I verified the spec requirements, I was more than capable of running it. But somehow, the game ran bad. Like REALLY bad. Never achieved 30 FPS on that. I didn't understand what was wrong. That laptop was able to run DmC: Devil May Cry at Ultra and still at 60 FPS. So I gave up. I left Prototype 2 for a long time. Time jump again 4 years later, I got a new laptop. An Acer Aspire VX rocking a i7-7700HQ 2.8GHz processor, NVIDIA GEFORCE GTX 1050 Ti 4GB GPU and 8GB DDR4 RAM. That skyrocket in specs shook me. Once again, with the game still not left my mind, I ran it again. I was expecting things would turn out great for me and the game. My specs were not like what they were. I was worlds apart from my old laptop. But for some reason. For some reason I myself cannot fathom. The game runs at a stupidly low stuttering FPS of 35-47. In addition to that, the game still runs bad even at a 1366x768 with everything at low. My graphical settings didn't matter. Whether the lowest or the highest, it all runs bad. The frustration is much worse knowing that this is all coming from a game that came out 5 years ago. With all that said, you have now know my journey and frustrations with the game. Prototype 2 is a great game. Might be a little beginner friendly compared to the first one but the mechanics are more refined. Story won't stick to you too much. It's your typical edgy storyline where a villain is fed up with the world and wishes to change them by evolution. The gore is still there. And what made me happy was that they added an ability to drop down a person you picked up. I was looking for that with Alex Mercer. I know it's a small thing to notice but the fact that it was a small thing and it was noticed, made me pretty happy. My happiness is pretty shallow, I know. But you know. Games makes me happy. But this port does not. I have tried what most people have tried and nothing. The game is good. The port is bad. Thanks for reading. Have a great day!

***IMPORTANT NOTE: THIS REVIEW HAS BEEN UPDATED TO ACCOUNT FOR THE CURRENT 2.0.10 BETA VERSION. TO USE THIS VERSION, RIGHT-CLICK THE GAME IN THE LIBRARY, GO TO PROPERTIES, THE BETA TAB, THEN SELECT BETA IN THE PULLDOWN MENU.***
A Wizard's Lizard is not so much a Roguelike as a "Binding of Isaac-like." When I first saw gameplay of this game, I was instantly charmed by it. Being a Binding of Isaac fan, I've really wanted something to sink my teeth into while patiently awaiting BoI: Rebirth.
Right out of the gate, this game has a lot working in its favor - an adorable protagonist, a creative premise (which informs its dual-natured gameplay), a great degree of challenge, a decent soundtrack, and a style and humor all its own, with references to Final Fantasy, Zelda, and even The Wicker Man.
The challenge is something that comes on strong right from the start, as you are left with very few resources at your disposal to counter the massive hordes of enemies with their sights on you. To counteract this, the game rewards you for multiple playthroughs by allowing you to find blueprints and rescue villagers. If you are able to find an item blueprint, that item will be available for you to purchase back at the beginning hub town. In addition, each villager you rescue will allow you to begin the game with an additional 500 gold. At first I felt this slightly cheapened the experience by taking a random element out of the gameplay, but I quickly found that it allowed for a more customized approach while still keeping the game's random elements intact. In addition, these elements are completely optional, and playing through "naked" is a completely viable tactic to those who are brave and skilled enough.
There is a great variety of weapon and armor styles in the game, with even the starter weapons ranging from a spear that travels further and more quickly, to double daggers that are weaker against single enemies but are better suited for dealing with larger groups. The weapon variety isn't as vast as that of Binding of Isaac, but it is still early on in the game's life and new content has been added and rebalanced at an incredible rate already.
The game sports some other options for battling, however. Raga - the titular lizard in A Wizard's Lizard - is capable of two forms of magical attack. The first is a soul-based magical attack, which attacks surrounding enemies, dealing incredible damage. Each usage of this attack will use up a collected soul that you have stored. It can, however, turn the tide of a seemingly hopeless battle in a hurry, making it a spectacular desperation attack.
The other alternative is Totemic magic. Raga will place a totem on the ground and that totem will attack with a magical effect a number of times before disappearing. The default totem is a little underwhelming, shooting a four-way, low damage fireball. However, there are many totem upgrades you can find, such as one that fires long-range boulders, one that performs its own version of your soul attack, or one that freezes enemies in place, allowing you to attack them or make a quick escape. The advantages to totems are a: the attack comes from them and not you, allowing you to focus on other things, and b: you have unlimited usages of totems, unlike soul-based magic. the disadvantage is that totems have a significantly longer cooldown time, and you might often find yourself sighing in frustration early on as a poorly-placed totem hits nothing, causing you to wait several seconds before you can place another.
The soul magic also enters into another mechanic of this game - death. In A Wizard's Lizard, if you die once, it is NOT game over. Instead, you become a spirit and now are fighting on another plane, in which formerly harmless ghosts are now substantial and dangerous. The upside to this is that you will find significantly more souls to fuel your magic attacks than in the physical world, and can also find treasures normally not accessible to you. I do feel that this idea could lend itself to more dual-layered gameplay than it does, but it is nevertheless a creative and unique concept for a Roguelike. I have no doubt that as levels and content are added, this will be addressed admirably.
And ultimately, this one of the strongest points I can recommend this game on. I've been paying very close attention to this title, and the developers at Lost Decade Games have shown an incredible amount of effort and passion in adding to and rebalancing the game. It's a sign of a company that takes gaming seriously and wants to offers the player the most enjoyable experience possible.
What it really all comes down to is this. If you are a fan of classic-styled adventure games and/or Binding of Isaac, and you are looking for something new to sink your teeth into, this is definitely your choice. It is an incredibly challenging game with with, style, and charm to spare.

This is more a mixed review than a negative one.
I bought Out There because it looked similar to FTL, but without the tedium of combat, and in that respect it did not disappoint. Like the starship Voyager, you jump from system to system trying to replenish limited resources, and along the way you meet alien lifeforms and learn new technologies that increase your chances of reaching home. I think the game aptly portrays the feeling of isolation in space, from the ambient soundtrack to the uneasy log entries of the protagonist, a lone astronaut who wakes from cryo-sleep to find himself far across the galaxy.
However, in going from FTL to Out There, I seem to have traded one form of monotony for another. Drilling rocky planets yields iron to repair your hull, but landing on and leaving those planets costs additional fuel. Probing gas giants yields fuel necessary to travel from system to system, but orbiting those planets damages your ship's hull. If either resource (or oxygen) reaches zero, your session ends. Drill, probe, drill, probe. From my experience so far- about three hours- I'd say this routine forms the bulk of each session, which I personally find uninteresting.
There never seems to be enough space to really exploit the technologies you learn on most ship types. Each technology takes up one slot, and most of the ships I've seen so far have no more than a dozen total. Not to mention, around five of those slots will always be taken up by your most essential ship systems. In addition, each unique element / resource takes up its own slot regardless of how little you have of each, and some technologies require multiple elements for construction.  Keep in mind the technologies you learn each session are randomized, so you won't know which metals you'll need at the outset, either. Often I just didn't bother with technology so I could stockpile the three basic necessities, since each slot only stacks up to twenty, and you often need more.
When you meet alien lifeforms, you're usually presented with a choice of Approve or Disapprove, but because you don't know the languages spoken, and because translated words don't carry over from session to session, you may as well flip a coin unless you're writing down all the words you learn on the side. The other events with choices feel equally arbitrary, though I acknowledge this was also built into the design of FTL and may not faze everyone.
In short, if the premise and feeling of the game are what interest you, and the above issues don't bother you, there's a good chance you'll enjoy Out There. If what you're looking for is mechanical depth and varied gameplay, I'd caution you to take a closer look before buying.

Star Date: Wrote this on Patch 1.1.2 - April 2, 2015
------------------------------------------------------------------
Where am I?: Time for the journey of a lifetime! You have just been thrown into some random star system and your only task is to get to this other, equally random star system in your laughable spaceship. On the way there, pick up upgrades, mine more resources, and meet the locals but try to not get eaten by them. Avoid being stranded in space as you run out of fuel or suffocate in the endless expanses. That's the premise of the game. It's a combination of FTL's spaceship customization but with a much heavier focus on the storyline which serves to be the centerpiece for this game.
------------------------------------------------------------------
Silence is Golden....
(+) Storyline - The storyline is beautifully written. Each time you play and fail and trust me you'll fail a lot, the events you get will be different. What choices you pick will determine what happens to your poor vessel. Exercise some common sense or not because finding out all the ways to die is part of the fun.
(+) The Aliens - Each habitable population that you meet has a vocabulary that changes each iteration but fear not, as you progress in a campaign you'll slowly learn what they are saying. 'No don't give those worms hydrogen fool! Ok let's get out of this planet while we can. Let's look at the bright side, we learned what thb\e word death is in their language and all it cost was these subsystems and hull sections!'
(+) Ship Customization - There's a plethora of ship upgrades to stick on your ship from improving fuel efficiency to shielding during atmospheric landings. Stick the upgrades to the basic modules for an adjacency bonus. The tutorial didn't explain that but I later found out so I'll share it with you guys for reading this far. :)
(+) Resource Management - Gone all the days you can stick 64 stacks of ships, food, tonnages of metals, people, livestock, etc into your pocket. There's a very limited amount of space on each ship that you get. You'll need some space for backup resources to repair your modules and to fuel your ship. That same space gets occupied by cool new techs you'll want to make your ship better. It's a fine balancing act and the game honestly does force you to make tough choices there.
(+) Visuals - The backgrounds to each planet look gorgeous, especially for the volcanic planet.
(+) Price - I can't even buy a large sandwich where I live for $9. For the amount of narrative and gameplay you get, it's definitely worth it.
------------------------------------------------------------------
...but it's maddening as well...
(-) Lack of 'Action' - Ok this one isn't a bit fair but it's more of a warning. Incase you didn't read the game's description, i'll state it one more time - THERE'S NO COMBAT. It's not FTL so don't expect FTL. If you like reading and playing through old-school adventures then this is the game for you. If you're studying for the future starfleet command then you're playing the wrong game.
(-) Tooltips - I tried googling too but some things such as a ship's power, ecosystem,  and resistance. What do they mean? Oh there's an adjacency bonus? I wish the game told me. Some ship upgrades give you a qualitative description of their boost but I want to know the exact numbers please.
------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall, it's a gem for those who like an adventure game that has rogue-like survival elements. The game might get a bit repetitive once you've figured out how much in backup supplies you should carry to reasonably get to the next fueling point but there or once you've read through all the possible ingame events. Nonetheless, it'll be a while before you get to the latter part and for $9, you could do a lot worse. Have fun insulting aliens who you can't understand!
I give it a resounding 7.5 Babbalas out of 10 Rytssalas

This is a really weird game, in a good way.
Pros:
_Beautiful: The game looks really great. The art style is bold and nice to look at. The planets art are imaginative and appropriately alien.
_Great music: Subtle and ambient, the music is really nice here.
_Rogue-like: Every run is different.
_Interesting and Immersive: The game world is very strange, yet somehow kind of makes sense. You'll want to explore all the weird wonders this game has.
_Good writing: Can be a bit pretentious, but nice and well-written otherwise.
_Great resource management: There's always a compromise at every turn. Everything that goes on is a trade in this game. You're trading space for material, trading materials and space for usable ship parts, as well as fuel and oxigens; and, worst case posible, you're trading in parts of your ship for materials to use during emergency. It's managed to be very intense and thought provoking.
Cons:
_Techno-Babble: Sometimes the game will use terms that you won't understand. Sometimes the game will have an entire paragraph that you won't understand.
_Can be slow: As with any game that is more focus on discovery, the game can go on long stretch without much happening.
Pros/Cons:
_Has no combat: Your ship doesn't have any guns on it, at all. This doesn't matter, because the resource management is the crux of the game's tension and conflict. Whether this is good or bad, depends solely on how you feel about that.
Is it worth 10 bucks? Yes. It's very intriguing and strange and weird. You'll want to experience it, even just for a little bit, just to see what they mean by "FTL with no combat"

This is my first game review so bear with me. Also keep in mind that I have not played every mode in the game.
In terms of gameplay options, this game is pretty bare. The graphics are not the best and the only real option3 you have for playing are Player vs Player, Player vs Zombies, or map building.
Player Vs Player:
- Very straightforward first-to-the-point-limit wins
- Optional game timer
- maximum of eight players
- Capture-the-flag mode available
- A few gameplay options
- Teams
- Player Options
- Infinite Ammo (This does not have realoads, instead it just makes your clip bottomless)
- Turbo Fire (All weapons excluding the building tool fire as fast as you can click)
[Sidenote that I found fun: With Infinite Ammo and Turbo fire on, it is possible to use the shotgun's kick to fly.]
- Fast Movement (You, other players, and all zombies are Usain Bolt)
- Some other ones but these are the ones I used most
Zombies
- The zombies are both underwhelming and ridiculously overpowered based on the map and settings you choose
- Zombies  normally have waze-based spawning mechanics (these can be "overwritten" in a way by turning on the setting "Max Zombie AI". When the setting is enabled, the game seems to continuously spawn zombies up to a maximum amount)
- The zombie AI is horible and the poor creatures frequently have a hard time navigating the simplest of obstacles. On top of their horrible ability to pathfind around obstacles, the zombies seem to have a hard time understanding gravity and will readily walk off of any cliff edge between them and their target.
- The one credit I have to give the AI, however, is that the zombies are not afraid to try and jump at their target if they are close enough (and wow, can they jump. I'm fairly certain all the zombies are ex-NBA players with the heights they reach).
Build mode:
Ah, build mode. I spent about five minutes in this mode before noticing just how poor it is. You CAN use the mode to build but there are a few key issues with it.
- The build tool is clunky and difficult to use at times
- Limited options for building
- Place one block
- place a beam of five or so blocks
- Replace an area of blocks with another type
- Remove a 3 x 3 of blocks
- There are many blocks you can use but some have non-togglable functions
- (Eg a block that would be awesome in a space-based map but always throws the player)
Multiplayer:
- With friends, this game is fairly fun for a bit but can get old fairly fast
- There is no such thing as a private game. For friend to join, it MUST be public
- There is a "closed" game option that seems like it would allow for friend-only games but it's just singleplayer
- Host advantage is not THAT noticeable as the game does not really need to move much data around
Options (Not many):
- Character appearance (colors and type of helmet only)
- Resolution
- VSync (on/off) (does not matter much as game will not go above 60 FPS)
- "Fog Distance" (normal/far/infinite)
- Blood Particles (on/off/green)
- Super Sampling (on/off)
- Rebindable controls (controls cannot share keys)
- Volume (0 - 100 in increments of 10)
- Music (on/off)
- Debug options (menu - fps and a few other things)
- Credits (I guess it's an option)
Maps:
- There are TONS of maps
- You can make your own
- You can grab more off of the workshop if you want
Sidenotes:
- All of the game options are available so you can do 4 v 4 CTF w/ zombies if you want
- None of the menus offer any notes are what the options do so you just have to try them to find out
- Controls did not seem very intuitive so you may have to rebind them
- Not many servers available (from what I've experienced)
- The game seems to have occasional lag spikes (these are rare but do happen)
- Not many maps have proper spawns so you tend to get spawn killed sometimes
- The game is bad at choosing spawns and will drop you right in the middle of a horde of zombies if it so chooses
- The multikill effect (from killing enemies in rapid succession) gets to be obnoxious (spinning flashing number in the middle of your screen)

First and foremost, I can only recommend this game if you have someone else to play it with, otherwise it's just a boring game that leaves me feeling unsatisfied.
Borderlands is a first-person shooter with RPG elements, including a leveling system and, "multiple guns," with varying stats.
The main appeal of the game is to, "shoot and loot." Which brings the question; why play the game? The story makes an effort, but at the end of the day, it doesn't have a big enough hook to make me want to play. The (stolen) cell-shaded art style is (not really) unique, but every area looks the same with all of the colors blending into a lot of brown, yellow, and red. Just look at the logo of the game and that's basically all you're gonna see. The best looking area in the game is the last level, which finally gives your eyes a break with a change of scenery.
The leveling system keeps the game interesting for the most part, as it really does feel like your level makes a difference; although, there isn't much of a challenge in this entire game. Everything flows really smoothly, with no huge difficulty spikes or even tough enemies. This adds to the reason I feel the game is boring; enemies are too easy. To have any sense of challenge in this game, you have to purposefully fight something multiple levels above you, which goes against all sense of logic in a RPG.
I put, "multiple guns," in quotes earlier because they're really just copy and pasted guns with slightly different stats or a elemental effect added to it. The reality is there's only about ten different guns in the game, but thousands of those guns are in the world with a different color scheme. Not really sure why they tried so hard to make that a selling point.
The problem is that nothing in Borderlands feels ambitious. It seems like they wanted to make a cooperative game without having to put too much thought into it, and while there are fun moments, the game is just too repetitive to keep me satiated.

Now, don't get me wrong; this game does play pretty damn nicely. The concept and gameplay (when you don't have to look up solutions) are great and the amount of work & love that went into it is seemingly gigantic. However, I have a few concerns about the game that just spoil it for me:
1) The voice acting. It's way too distracting from the actual game itself, and for me it feels like the game was using it as the main source of comedy. This is largely due to the facts that the rest of the game is almost brooding, and the voice sounds too much like Dom Fera from 'The lazer collection'. Which is VERY distracting.
2) The menu. When I go into options, I am not sure whether I am being blind or if there is no way back out without closing the game. This fustrates me, as it is LITERALLY something hard to overlook.
3) The plot. It's too much like Portal 1's first half: start to like the overseer, then get greeted with a fiery death at the end. Fairly self-explanatory as to why this bugs me, but if you can't tell: I feel the plot was just copied.
4) The actual paint-shooting. I can't have been the only one who has noticed, but the paint blobs fire UNDER the crosshair.  RRRRG! This fustrates me because perfectionism. It's a nice idea, using the fire paint blobs command found in the developer console, but mabye tweak it to be a little higher in future.

Multimirror is a 50 level long grid-based puzzle game that tasks you with "mirroring" a circle around other circles, in order to hit an end gate. Though the concept itself is interesting enough, the execution is so poor that I can't bring myself to recommend this game to anyone.
Multimirror suffers from a laundry list of problems which include:
- Generic instrumental music which loops endlessly (you only get one track per set of 10 levels).
- An inconsistent level of challenge ("hardest" levels are easiest to 3-star in some cases).
- A lack of depth (you're presented with two new concepts early on and that's it).
- Far too short (I completed the game in just over an hour and I'm notoriously slow at puzzle games).
- BUG: Text would occasionally disappear completely or be totally out of place.
- BUG: Clicking the red circle would sometimes reset the level.
- BUG: Sometimes I only got 2 stars for a level when I met the requirements for 3.
- BuG: The game would occasionally give me 3 star completion of a level I hadn't even attempted, or I had quit out of.
In all honesty, I don't believe that this game is worth any amount of money, especially in the state that it is in. It looks and plays like a free browser-based game.
It's fun and challenging. Grinding might be a good idea but YOLO is the best way the do missions!!

I really can't recommend this. Even for a 5 bucks game, this game feels unpolished and unfinished. The mechanic is passable, but the execution...sad to say, but I've seen free android apps that work better. :-(
The levels all look the same, and to most extend also play that way. Of course the abstract level design doesn't help in that aspect, but there's no shift in tone, background or even basic layout. There's no progression in difficulty or overall theme in levels. It all comes across as if the developer just threw a bunch of dots on a grid and said "here...go fetch". There are no screen tips or even a mentioning that escape quits the game (heh...I read in a patch note that 'R' to restart was added later...it's mentioned nowhere within the game).
While there's no sound in the game, the music is passable. And while I personally found it dull and uninteresting, it does have challenge. Perhaps even too much...from the start you're mostly given all dots that can jump over another in a peg solitaire kind of way (with one you've got to guide to the finish). It would've been better to start out with just the immovable (black) dots and only introduce the blue ones gradually (and the green ones much later). Oh, and even though I don't recommend the game as a whole, I can't deny that a level editor is a plus.
But all in all, I feel this is a missed opportunity. As if this game was rushed and never got proper beta testing or thorough thinking on how to properly design levels. It probably would've been a great early access or public beta...but as a finished game? Sorry...I'll always advice other games over this one, even at this price point.

It looks like the majority of glowing reviews for this game come from those who played it back in the early 2000's when it was released. Prepare for another review from someone with nostalgia-tinted glasses on. I'll keep it as spoiler-free as possible, but I make no promises.
Back in 2003 Gothic was an obscure game adapted into English and sold in NA by the now defunct publisher Xicat Interactive. A friend happened to pick it up at random and it quickly became a favorite of my entire circle of friends. Truly a hidden gem.
The intro video (which hasn't displayed properly since upgrading from Windows XP) introduces us to a fairly run of the mill medieval fantasy setting with orcs vs. humans. Nothing too original here, but as soon as the Nameless Hero is introduced and the magical prison of the mining colony is established it's hard not to get hooked. The story takes off immediately with the aid of the iconic ally Diego, who gives the player a crash course on the colony and an invitation to join one of the three factions of the world within "the barrier".
One element I was always fond of is how the designers figured out a way to make the "invisible wall" mechanic work into the storyline so well. The barrier, and the lands visible outside of your reach, contribute to a genuine feeling of imprisonment and fill you with a desire to know what sort of world extends beyond the confines of the colony. We know there is a king, a desperately needed supply of magic ore, and a war with the orcs, but all of that is put on hold as we are made perfectly aware that there is no escape for the Nameless Hero and the only way to survive in this hostile territory is to make it to the first town alive. This proves harder than you'd think...
The most frustrating part of the Gothic experience is adjusting to the wacky controls. Re-configuring the defaults is pretty much mandatory and figuring out how to pick something up is arguably more challenging than any of the trials you face in the progression of the story. But, once you understand the "action key" function things get a little easier; at least until you're killed by the first scavenger.
There are some other perplexing situations where the controls could have been a bit more intuitive; one being the trading system. Once again the action key is needed here. Also unexplained is the fact that you control not only your inventory but that of the merchant as well. It took me quite a while to figure out that you can press shift to move in stacks of 100 and the "turn" keys to move in increments of 1. Another confounding issue comes up way later, when you use a transformation scroll for the first time and cant figure out how the hell to turn human again.
None of the RPG's I've played have had particularly remarkable combat mechanics. Fights tend to become repetitive and secondary to the main appeal of exploration and plot progression. In this area Gothic has not aged well. The target focus is very awkward, and keeping track of and keeping yourself facing an enemy can be frustrating. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that you cannot effectively fight while moving. Thus, following a strafing target can be a hassle and makes handling multiple enemies very awkward. You cant "skill" yourself through this game like you can in others. There's a pretty finite line drawn between what you can and cannot kill at your current level. The noticeable lack of shields further simplifies the combat, but does make you rely heavily on the block mechanic.
While weapon upgrades are critical to being able to take on tougher enemies, armor plays an ever greater role in the character's growth - both as a status symbol and in terms of survivability. Due to the combat being as rudimentary as it is, being able to take more hits proves more useful than being able to dish out more damage a lot of the time.
The magic system is decent. There are several tiers, each unlocking more powerful spells. Most of these are your typical elemental spells, but there are a few in there that are pretty unique. Unfortunately, not all of them are all that useful and some are plain useless (I.e. pyrokenesis).
Bugs are common occurrences in Gothic. Some are typical visual errors and others can cause frustrating movement or combat glitches. There's a bug that occasionally makes your lock-on targeting stick to a target, leaving you unable to shift focus onto another or disengage. This can be fixed by pressing ESC or putting away your weapon. A few bugs can only be fixed with cheats. Anyone who has been permanently locked out of the Old Mine knows this. There have also been runs when zoning out of an area would cause the game to crash every time. As far as I know those glitches are unfixable and a previous save game will need to be loaded. So yeah, make backup saves. Playing around with Marvin Mode can be fun as well as useful, as some of these bugs can be solved with the game's version of "no-clip".
The story told in Gothic is highly immersive and the progression gripping. We are given the most freedom in the first act, when we are encouraged to explore all the camps and venture as far into the wilds as we dare. Things become a bit more linear in the following acts, but the writers do a good job of weaving the story together in a way that brings all the camps and the key players together in interesting and surprising ways. Side quests aren't very plentiful, but they are all fun to do.
The only complaint I have about Gothic's story is the ending. The "final boss" isn't much of a challenge, and the encounter doesn't give you an opportunity to take full advantage of your arsenal. The ending offers a satisfying conclusion to the story, but not a satisfying test of your abilities.
The quality of the script is pretty solid and can be quite amusing. The English voice acting is comically overdone, but that contributes a bit of charm in its own right. Some of the voices, especially that of Xardas, are quite good.
Lastly, Gothic's musical score is great. From the gentle, ambling melody of the overworld to the lively theme of the Old Camp to the dark and mysterious temple ambiance, this game has a very memorable soundtrack. The title theme is especially good.
Overall, Gothic is an amazingly impressive first production from an indie game studio. The limits in budget and game development in its time are all the more noticeable now, but it still manages to impress with its well thought-out storyline and immersive world. It's sad that anyone jumping into the Gothic series this late in the game will not have as remarkable an experience as those of us who did around its release, but I still think this is a game any RPG fan can fall in love with if they take the time to get used to the admittedly weird controls and tolerate the bugs that might pop up.

Music: 10/10
Enjoyment: 9/10

For me, all Heroes of Might and Magic games have 4 things in common:
1 - they are serious time burners (the actual hour meter here is heavily misleading, during the years I have spent hundreds of hours with II III and IV, each)
2 - despite the countless hours I've never finished all the main missions
3 - I re-started playing from the beginning, either because of epic HDD failures, outdated systems or fancy new releases.
4 - I have box sets of the initial releases (for all the old Windows) as well as digital downloads @ Steam and uPlay that work on contemporary machines
In my opinion, HoMM is the definite turn-based fantasy game*. The actual part III is probably the nicest of all of them with its fine cartoon-esque GFX, atmosphere, the balance and game mechanics, still without going too deep into it (the following part IV did it). It follows the well-designed path of the first two games while seriously expanding / refining them on all sides. It was a little gem of a game back in 1999 when it came out and it's most probably one of the best balanced turn-based strategies ever created, in any genre.
You can find an ample of fantasy creatures and magic and rather flat good vs evil (or evil vs good) storyline but story is not really important here: the way of creating it, is. Surely you're not new to turn-based strategy games if you reached here. Heroes III is great for one, a solid and stylistic game that stood the test of time without change.
Among the series, IV is my fav as it is the deepest of all of them but III is really close behind. If you're a fan of fantasy and turn-based strategies you can't really go wrong with it. Absolutely recommended.
*King's Bounty is a serious runner-up

This is one of the best WWII shooters I've played. It may be old yes but you will still find plenty of servers. Unlike the original DoD, it only has multiplayer although you can make a server yourself and I believe with a bit of tinkering adding bots is possible. Unlike BF1 or CoD, its fairly historically accurate, especially the weapons (EDIT: Did Germany even fight the USA in WW2??). The Germans have guns like the MP40, STG44 and the Karabiner 98 Kurz. The Americans have the M1 Garand, a Tommy gun and a Browning Automatic Rifle (BAR). As it is  WW2, the maps are cities or towns and games can be fast-paced due to rushes and machine-guns. The game isn't much for bolt-action rifles, as the only ones are the Kar98k and the M1 Garand which is semi automatic. And for the playerbase? Well there are heaps of servers, but the key is finding the right time so that the servers are almost full.
TL;DR, this game is an oldie but a goodie, definitely up there in the best WW2 FPS. Unfortunately, due to its age and the fact it's a Valve game, the graphics aren't very good. That can be a good thing for people who don't have very good gaming rigs, and a bad thing because it's 2017.
My rating: 9.5/10. Get it if you love FPS and WW2 games.

The question really comes into play is if the Omega edition does enough to stand out from it's mobile counterpart. It's got upgraded resolutions and more possibilities, and the base of the gameplay is still a bunch of fun. It's no level of FTL, as it's definitely a lot more simple. I do wish a tiny bit more of variety in the first couple of moves, but in the end, there is a lot of variety when the game opens up, and you learn little by little how to take advantage of things.
+:
-Addictive nature, one more run kind of gameplay.
-Lots of variety and opens up as you get further and further into galaxies.
-Upgrades all really serve different gameplay styles and there's reason to choose different upgrades depending  on your situation.
-Visuals do the job well.
-Like the language options as you find more races, you learn more and maybe can answer their questions better.
-New ships always feel like a relief and are mixed in reasonably well.
-:
-When things go wrong, things go wrong. You have to be prepared, but sometimes it really does feel like the game will screw you over for no good reason.
-There's a lot of information to process, and at times it can be overwhelming. It's simple on the surface, but if you want to be successful, you got to learn all the trends.
-Full screen on multiple screens did not bound to the game's boundaries.
-Sometimes, you have to reboot the game as you can't seem to click through. This was noticed in conjuction with recording software.

I have over a thousand hours logged on the android version, and have sunk a couple of hundred bucks into the game; so let me be frank.
This is one of the only thing Konami has done in the past 5 years that wasn't an utter disaster.
Duel links is a truly good iteration of the original Yu-gi-oh series; The format has been compressed and stream lined, such as a 30 card deck limi, three spaces for monster and trap cards, the removal of phases; but it works, and it works really well.  Most of your favorite cards are there, with more being added monthly to bi-monthly, and you can use all of your old strategies to really unleash a serious beat down on your opponents.
Even though it's Konami, the game isn't money hungry either. Gems are used to buy card packs, but they come in an ABUNDANCE. Free events, all the time; give aways that require you to do nothing, log in bonuses, rank up bonuses. You don't have to spend a cent to get ahead.
Likely though, you will. I don't know what sort of devil magic Konami used to polish this as much as it is, but it worked. I wanted to drop money to support the game, to open new card packs and get excited when I pulled Ultra and super rares. I wanted to drop "Just five more dollars" on the promotinal 5 for 10 + SR Packs.
The last thing I want to talk about is Ranked- It works really, really well. You will find matches near instantly, with little down time. Unless the opponent tries to stall, turns move quickly, too- and with the inclusion of the stall busting timer, they can't indefinately lock you in until you quit, otherwise they'll take an automatic loss. It's never a problem for players who take a little extra time to think of a strategy though, so worry not.
All in all, this might be a better title than some of the console iterations- They've recently added a GX section- though it's completely seperate from the original world, which means going forward, even if they add new series to the game, it isn't going to impact the series you enjoy playing. You won't have to contest with Synchro monsters when they're introduced using your OG yugioh cards. In this sense, it makes every battle feel equal, you dont feel like your cards are going to become obsolete.
It's a must try if you're a Yu-gi-oh fan. Even if you're not, but you have a casual interest in the card game via nostalgia or curiosity, it's worth your time to check out, most definately.

You are an astronaut awaking from cryonics not in the solar system, but... out there... in a far and unknown place of the galaxy. In Out There, you will have to survive, tinkering your ship with what you can gather drifting in the void, and spot garden planets to refill your oxygen supply.
Space is an hostile place ; dangerous and mysterious adventures will mark each step of your travel. You will not only meet intelligent species that won’t care about you, but also deal with ancient powers linked to your destiny and the fate of mankind itself.
Survival and understanding of what is really at stake in the galaxy is the core of what Out There has to offer.
FEATURES
• A dark adventure in deep space
• 50+ achievements, leaderboard
• Explore a freshly procedurally-generated galaxy every time
• 350+ unique text adventures with multiple choices
• Epic main storyline leading to 4 different endings
• 10 spaceships with different specs to discover
• Crafting system with 20 alien technologies built from 15 materials
• Engage with alien life forms and learn their language
• No combat! it’s you against the environment
• Eerie score by award-winning composer Siddhartha Barnhoorn (Antichamber, The Stanley Parable), featuring vocals by Lara Ausensi (Forest Kingdom II, Shevannai - The Voice of Elves)
• Fantastic pulp comics graphics
• High replay value

A nice idea but the game too often seems to focus on unintuitive solutions and speed.
I lost track of the number of times I had to look up guides on how to get through chambers because the solutions were nothing that I would have thought of. A number of times you're expected to know exctly how and where to ricochet yourself off a certain wall to get to the exit or make jumps that absolutely have to be perfect.
There's a sequence later on involving a race to the end before the area you're in blows up but you have to have to have the entire course memorized and go through it perfectly in a single go, there's no room for stopping to see where to go, how to make your way there. It involves a lot of perfectly timed accurate placings of the correct paint in the correct location without a second of hesitation and the only way to know that is to have the entire run memorizedby pure trial and error.
These are all major faults of the gameplay and I admit I gave up trying after 30 failed attempts to get through because I have trouble memorizing things at speed however this game is also lacking in a lot of things that made Portal and Portal 2 so good. There's a major lack of dark humor from what I heard, the game seems to focus more on presenting odly designed puzzles that don't even remain consistent with the established world building of the Portal Series. The biggest example of this that I can cite is that connections between buttons you place boxes on and the doors that are opened often have to traverse massive gaps and the only thing illustrating their connection is just a beam of light instead of showing an unbroken power connection. Such a thing felt and out of place.
One thing I can praise is the music of the game, there is a fantastic soundtrack to this game that I honestly loved.
But not even a great soundtrack can make me reccomend this game to others. Save your money, save your time, and save yourself a lot of hair pulling stress.

I recently just got this game yesterday and I believe that a proper review was in order.
THE STORY:
The story was kind of non existant. I didn't know what was really happening and I think that this game is mainly just a puzzle sort of deal. No real plot twists and no real connection.
THE CHARACTERS:
Nigel isn't that good of a character. I can tell what they were going for: A fun but untrustworth core who would chat with you throughout the tests. I often muted the game due to his voice work and the fact that I couldn't enjoy him like Wheatley or, his much better counterpart, Virgel.
THE PUZZLES:
The puzzles themselves are a lot of fun. The new testing element, the paint gun, often had me smiling as I quickly dashed through curves and figured out solutions after a couple of minutes of staring at the test from different angles. Although that is the case, some of the puzzles have some pretty awful bugs. Sometimes, the blue jel would not respond to the spacebar or by running over it. This caused many early deaths for me and could make me so frustrated I'd consider quiting the game entirely. But when it works, it works.
CONCLUSION:
So all in all, I think this game is alright. It definetly needs some work but I did enjoy the play through. But I doubt it'll be pulling me back in to replay it ever again.

This is a first-person shooter role-playing game, marketed as a "role-playing shooter" back when it was released. While not the first of its kind, it started the huge FPS-RPG trend we have today.
The game begins with your arrival on Pandora, a forsaken mining planet. When the local wildlife emerged from years of hibernation, the planet became unmanageable, and the corporations cut their losses and left. Now it's a wasteland of ghost towns, bandits, and monsters. A legend about The Vault, a lost treasure trove of alien technology, draws adventurers called "Vault Hunters" in search of fortune and glory. A mysterious message and a funny little robot soon point you in the right direction...
Mordecai, Lilith, Roland, and Brick are the playable Vault Hunters you can choose from. Each has 21 skills available in a skill tree system, plus a special Action Skill unique to their class. Other than that, they can all use the same gear except for Class Mods, which give bonuses to skills and other abilities. Mordy is a hunter with a pet bird named Bloodwing. Lilith is a "siren" with alien powers, who can Phasewalk in an invulnerable spirit form in short bursts. Roland is a soldier with a robotic Scorpio Turret he can deploy to provide cover and support. Brick is a berserker, who can use a Berserk rage to deliver powerful punches and heal rapidly. Each skill tree has three branches, allowing you to customize your play style, and you can fully "respec" (recover all your skill points from the skill tree and invest them differently) at any New-U save point.
A central feature of the game is the loot system, which mimics dungeon crawler games like Diablo and Torchlight. Items like weapons, equipment, etc. are "procedurally generated" by randomly combining properties from internal charts and tables. This generates a wide variety of possible items with different abilities each time. The game is said to have millions of possible guns, and other items and enemies are also varied in this way to some extent. Not only can you find this stuff in chests and buy it from vending machines (yes, this world has gun vending machines) but enemies can carry it as well, and enemies that use items can use it against you.
Controls are pretty standard for an FPS game, mouse/keyboard is WASD by default but everything is easily rebound in the options menus. Press left mouse button to fire your current gun, hold right mouse button to aim down the sights (or use a scope if your gun has one) which improves your accuracy but limits you to walking speed. Mouse wheel cycles weapons. I ended up binding melee, grenades, and Action Skill to mouse buttons since I use these a lot. Reload isn't something you should worry about rebinding as long as Activate is bound to something convenient, as you can Reload with your Activate key whenever you're not facing a usable item. Holding the Activate key when picking up ammo, money, and health vials will vacuum up all of them within a few feet, holding it when picking up a gun or shield will equip it on you instantly. Your target reticle shows where your shots will go, based on weapon accuracy and recoil.
You have little Health in the beginning of the game, but the tutorial missions in the first town let you buy a Shield belt which can absorb damage, and will begin to recharge after a few seconds of not getting hit. Better types of Shield become available later, and some Shields and Class Mods can buff or regenerate Health as well. You can have two weapons, a Shield, a Class Mod, and a Grenade Mod equipped, and have 12 backpack slots in your Storage Deck for loot. Two more weapon slots unlock much later, and 30 extra backpack slots can be gotten from Claptrap robots you rescue along the way.
Losing all your Health doesn't kill you immediately. Instead you fall down and enter "Fight For Your Life" where you can only turn and attack, while your view sways drunkenly and a timer runs down. If you kill an enemy you get a "Second Wind" which gives you a little Health and full Shield, and returns you to the fight. Failing to get a Second Wind in time (or getting hit by a vehicle or falling off the map) respawns you at the nearest New-U checkpoint instead. This costs you a small percentage of your money and (in singleplayer) returns your enemies to full health, but that's about it. This encourages run-and-gun over playing the game like a cover shooter, since it's hard to hit anything in FFYL beyond close range, making it more useful in close quarters battle.
You soon get "elemental" weapons that can inflict Explosive, Fire, Shock, or Corrosive damage. Higher tech weapons have higher chances to inflict more damage over time. There are also Grenade Mods, which give your hand grenades elemental damage types and/or new features: From cluster bombs and proximity mines, to transfusion grenades that release a swarm of homing darts to steal health from your enemies.
You get the ability to summon vehicles from any Catch-A-Ride station early in the game, and these are useful for exploring the huge outdoor maps. Vehicle weapons are awkward, but running things over is fun. Each vehicle can seat two, and you can have two vehicles at once, so the whole team can ride together in multiplayer. There's an auto-aim system for the turret if you don't have a partner to operate it. If they get blown up or stuck somewhere, you can spawn more for free. Vehicles are relatively easy to flip over with your hands or melee attacks if you find your car upside down. The driving controls and physics are not great, but it's OK for something that isn't a driving game.
This game is more for co-op play than solo. Up to four players can work together, and some types of Class Mod give bonuses that help the entire team. You can also revive a downed teammate by holding Activate on them for a few seconds, giving them a Second Wind without them having to score a kill in FFYL. You can drop guns and gear for them from your backpack, and any cash picked up is added to everybody's balance, but guns and other loot must be shared. There are a few class skills that help other characters in various ways, but you don't really need perfect teamwork. In the context of a shooter game, I see this as an advantage: Since most of the ways you can help your team are passive, you can better focus on the action.
You only get rewards for completing missions if you're at about the same point in the main quest as the host or beyond them, but still find money and loot normally. However, because of the way difficulty and loot are scaled, a player too far behind will be useless and get loot they can't equip yet, and a player too far ahead will overpower everything but will get junk loot. If you're serious about co-op, it's best to play with a regular group, so that you advance at about the same rate and experience the missions together.
The cel-shaded comic book art style has aged pretty well, and the Road Runner cartoon desert environment is charming and works way better than it should. The twangy music does a good job of setting the mood, and the sound effects are of satisfying quality. There's some great voice work, and bizarre supporting characters who appear as questgivers, although the player characters mostly just have witty combat banter and such. The "space western" setting and cynical humor work together nicely. There are a few dramatic moments, but the story doesn't take itself too seriously.
Minor gripes: The loot system has a bit of a "+1% Pointlessness" problem, where it often creates items with attributes that make a barely noticeable difference in practice. A glitch related to deleted missions can break multiplayer matchmaking. There are a few unique weapons with gimmicks that make them awkward to use, a few bullet sponge bosses, and other game-isms.
Overall, I had lots of fun with this, in singleplayer and multiplayer, and I recommend it to FPS fans and RPG fans alike.

Did you like Choose Your Own Adventure stories when you were a kid?  How about playing one with a well-written, smart, gripping storyline?  One where the characters are interesting and hold secrets- if you care to delve deeply enough?
Not the traditional Steam offering, but I'm glad they chose to take a chance with this one.  It kept me playing for almost 4 hours straight, because I had to know what happened next- what the consequences of my actions would bring me.
Don't listen to any review that says you end up in the same place no matter what- it's not true.  It's true that are certain events in the game that will begin to unfold, no matter what your choice- that happens in real life all the time, too.  And like in real life, it's the choices you make AFTER that that have the most impact, and will define who you truly are.  You can end this game a hero or a villain- it's up to you, and it's impressive that the story is well crafted enough that all paths seem viable.
Give this game a chance if any of this appeals to you- you won't be sorry.

If you're looking for a new game to play with a simple storyline, decent graphics and a casual nature, this is the game for you. If you're a hardcore Prototype fan, you might be left with a sour taste in your mouth. While it does provide closure to the first game, I find the game lacking in difficulty and the storyline of the first game. The game is very straightforward and simple, providing help and explaining abilities and powers quite well. It has an open atmosphere with more freedom to roam than it's predecessor. It's not a demanding game, even weaker and outdated PC-s can manage 60 fps with high graphics. Main missions are quite dull and repetitive while the side quests and collectables provide more depth than most of the main game. The good thing about the simplicity of the story is the fact that someone who hasn't played the first game can quickly pick up with even a short clip explaining the main parts of the first game (can be found in the main menu). The artistic styles are interesting and vivid, the biggest contrast being shown in the cutscenes. Overall, it's a solid game, I recommend you at least give it a try.

Multimirror is a low effort puzzler that feels like it was coded in powerpoint by someone who was entirely too proud of the fact that they passed algebra 2 with a C.  The basic gameplay has you using dots on a board as pivots to move other dots to other parts of the board in an effort to get the one dot that's colored red to a specfied point on the board.  It's boring and pointless, but if you dig deeper, you'll realize how sinister this game really is.
The red dot to a certain spot mechanic is a metaphor for the white man moving Native Americans onto reservations, and the game celebrates and rewards this behavior.  Worse, the game introduces green dots, which disappear when you use them once.  Again, clearly these dots are meant to represent the unreliable Irish.  I quit after 6 minutes in outrage, but I'm sure the game has many, many more subtle racist messages embedded in it.
Worst of all, the game costs five bucks.  There are better built, more entertaining flash games that I can play for free, and they don't come with racist baggage.  Viruses yes, but no racism (for the most part).

I found this interactive novel to be quite enjoyable. I was a big fan of pick-your-adventure books when I was young, and interactive novels I have always enjoyed. Fate/Stay Night was a particularly good one from Japan, but there are a lot of graphics since they like to make their novels into anime.
Here, instead we have no graphics, no sound effects. Just the power of words well written. I like how you could choose how certain characters reacted to you with different personas. The MeChip butler, diva or caretaker all gave a different feel for the game, for example.
For those looking for 27 endings of different plots, you'll have no fun with this novel. It's not really a game, more like a novel that you can immerse yourself in more deeply than a regular book because you get to add a bit of your own personality to the characters. I really became attached to the character in this story, and I've since bought the sequel, Heroes Rise: The Hero Project, and read that one through multiple times as well, I am looking forward to the final installment of the trilogy.
I've stated before in my reviews, that I base a lot of it on how much a product costs me to play for the time I invest in it. At under $5.00 I've easily gotten my money's worth, and with it on special til June 24th at $1.99 it's hard to go wrong for something that you'll spend a few hours at a minimum reading. It's hard to find a paperback in a used bookstore for that price.
Anyways, for what it claims to be, an interactive novel with memorable characters, it was a great investment for me. I hope you purchase the novel and agree.

A text based game in a superhero setting.
Not something I would have expected to find on steam. As I do enjoy books and love customization options in games, including roleplaying and writing little short stories of my own I thought I'd give it a try. If nothing else perhaps it would give me some good memories of playing City of Heroes.
Sadly the game couldn't live up to the things the description says it would offer.
I was outright shocked that I couldn't pick the hero I wanted to play. I didn't expect to be able to adapt my main protagonist down to every single ability, but I couldn't even pick a powerset, a background or anything like it. I was thrown a bone of a pre-designed character that I could pick gender, name, sexual orientation and favourite color for and that was the full customization available.
For a moment I thought about just closing and forgetting about this "game", but I decided to see it through. Maybe the story or the other parts of it would be better. The game starts you off in a pre-defined setting, with all predefined characters. I played around with the choices they give you, but the differences are barely noticeable. No matter what you pick the outcome for the story is the same. You always end up in the very same spot, no matter what you pick and not just once at the very end, but all the time at nearly every part of the story.
Choice to me always is to influence something, not just to have meaningless statistics go up and down. If the world around my character doesn't react to my interactions in any way, what reason is there to give a choice in the first place?
You can do your worst to treat romance characters poorly yet they still end up wanting to be together with you, quite the same applies to other aspects. Theres a lawful statistic, yet you can never really work together with the bad side.
No serious customization. no choices that matter. So what remains of this game? It's a railroaded story, like a book and on top of that not even a very long or good one in my opinion.
Characters are without depth without motivations that make any sense and cliche is dripping from every corner. Antagonists in the story jump on you without real reason just for the sake that you have some bad guys to work against, but no one ever explains why they even dislike you in the first place. The only real motivation that gets obvious is for the main antagonist and even that one feels very forced, not very well thought through and just there for the sake of having something to make the story work, not because the character feels like they would really do anything like it on their own.
Overall the game felt very lacking to me, and not just because it has no fancy graphical options or cool interface. It lacks meaningful choices, good character design and a world that reacts to you as a player. While the price isn't that high for it and I don't really worry about the money, I might have spent my time better by picking up some visual novel or a book instead, or  some other game if I seriously wanted a lot of choices.
I cannot really recommend this game as it is. There are many better text based games out there that offer real choices, better writing and on top of that are free.

Alright, after many more hours with this game I am amending my previous review.
I previously said that the equipment you get makes such a small difference it's unnoticable.  I take that back.  The equipment that raises your attack speed and your overall speed definitely make a noticable difference.  The equipment I have a problem with is the spiked set.  Raising your damage by 1 really doesn't do anything to help you, and it's much more worthwhile to wear, say, the Ranger set to increase your mobility or the lead set to increase your HP.  Spiked set should add more offense.
I also said that the never-changing layout was dull.  I fully retract that comment.  The more I play the game, the more I'm thankful that the layout (i.e., blueprints always on the same floor, pentagram always on the same floor, townsperson always on the same floor) stays the same, so I know what I should be looking for each floor.
Now that I'm at the point where I'm nearing the crypt, my only real problem other than the spiked set is the slow down.  In the sewers, the slowdown (which I believe is caused by the poison traps in the walls) makes things very difficult, borderline unplayable.  After fighting the boss of the sewers five times in a row and each time having my run end unfortunately with a massive slowdown, it begins to get frustrating.
Other than that, this game has grown on me quite a bit, I find it a blast, and I would recommend it to anyone.  Hopefully there are tweaks to come.

I've always said that if Konami really wanted to make money, they'd make Yu-Gi-Oh a free-to-play counterpart to the physical games wherein you could play against online opponents and collect cards by paying real money (which wouldn't be reaching at all; after all, that's how you do it in real life).
This is kind of that, almost.  Rather than the traditional format, Duel Links uses the semi-recent Speed Dueling format which is more limited than traditional.  This put me off at first, but time's moving on, more cards are being added, and more combos are being introduced.  The speed of DL gets faster by the day, as well as the satisfaction that comes with being able to set up a deck that just works and the amount of leeway that comes with that.
I generally go pretty long-form with my reviews but there isn't really much to say.  Konami did good for once, and their Free-to-Play model restricting the number of NPCs one can face pushes players to move on to PvP, which is where the game really shines.  That said, the restriction in question is praiseworthy on its own as it's the type of fatigue system that only barely has a penalty, as later I only found myself dueling against Legendary Duelist NPCs (since they have better rewards), the Vagabond (since he's a legiitimate challenge) and, mostly, other players in Ranked or events.
During all of this I never felt held back or wished that the game had just been a regular retail game without microtransactions, a sentiment that I feel towards quite a few Free-to-Plays.  If you like YGO and especially if you can't play it in real life for whatever reason, give this a go, it's the best move Konami's made in decades (something I honestly never thought I'd say again).

TL;DR:
Don’t expect this to be some Portal 3 quality experience. Just sit back, relax, let yourself sink into the old Portal 2 vibe, find different ways of solving the rooms and have a simple good ol’ time :)
Longer review:
For the experienced Portal player, the first half of the levels don’t form a challenge. The second half of the game, the levels do get tougher and they do require some different angles and a different way of thinking. In general, it doesn’t exactly match the original Portal 2 game, but what would you expect from a mod. That being said, it is well crafted. You can tell the creators of this game loved the original game and tried to stay true to that, while also adding new features.
Pro’s:
- Generally good Portal 2 vibe with familiar surroundings and controls.
- Gives you, say, 4 hours of gameplay. You as a reader can determine whether or not that’s worth the money.
- Little homages to some of the original Portal 2 maps, including hidden areas.
- Soundtrack that taps into the original soundtrack but adds a new atmosphere as well.
- There are custom maps (though I haven’t played these myself).
Cons:
- Whenever you shoot gel, the actual firing is delayed a bit and deviates from where you are aiming, which forms a handicap in the fast paced parts of the game.
- I found myself able to solve a couple of puzzles in a
fashion.
- Not as much humor as Portal 2, which is a missed opportunity.

Though I scored it low, I can't say that Turnover is "bad." In fact, I found myself applauding when the game covered private military contractors in Iraq and the disastrous Citizens United case during the intro. The premise of the game is pretty cool. The game also appears to be bug free.
However, playing the game devolves into tedium quite quickly. The game, in some ways, pulls from Hotline Miami. Pixelated graphics, a top down view, the ability to pan your view out in each direction, and the absurdly quick death animations. However, the gameplay itself is quite exciting in Hotline Miami, being very fast-paced, and the thumping soundtrack almost makes the player feel as though they're in a trance.
Turnover is also difficult, like Hotline Miami, and players should expect to die quite a bit. However, the slow, quiet, unexciting pace of the gameplay coupled with the brutal difficulty lends to quite a bit of frustration. I think this game could absolutely use checkpoints. With Hotline Miami, I was excited to hop right back into the action. In Turnover, I let out a hearty groan.
Additionally, I think it would be better if the sound made by the player was visible in the game itself rather than down on the mini-map. The necessity of dividing your attention between the main screen and the mini-map grows tiresome.

tl;dr: Uninteresting and linear story that doesn't warrant to be presented in form of a game.
**Contains spoilers**
'What Remains of Edith Finch' is a short story about a family's dying members that is experienced by walking through the weird family home and exploring rooms to uncover the stories of each individual person.
I am going to come straight to the point. This story has little to no redeeming qualities that would justify it to be presented in form of a game. The experience is driven forward by walking on a set path and occasionally clicking on things when told to. Doing anything other than following the instructions will make you waste your time. You can not go back and revisit areas or try to find things that you may have missed because the game won't let you. There is no decision making or any meaningful input from the player required which makes me believe that this story would have been a more enjoyable experience if they had chosen to tell it through a short film.
No doubt it would have been a good short film either in terms of the artwork. If the game has one thing going for it, it's the aesthetics. The 3D work in this game is great! In addition to the overall great and stylized look, the layout, modeling and texturing is very detailed and makes for realistic and believable enviroments and the lighting in combination with atmospheric effects set the mood quite nicely.
One thing I am on the fence about are the controls. Your character moves quite slowly which is okay for nagivating inside the house (although I know no one that moves through their house at a crawl speed) but in more open spaces it can get annoying very quickly because it feels like you are not getting anywhere. Luckily these spaces are few and far between and you spend the majority of your time inside the house. The objects you interact with throughout the game often times have to be manipulated by moving your mouse or pressing the directional keys, be it opening a book and flipping through the pages, opening a door or playing with a flip book. It's supposed to give you the feeling of you actually interacting with the object, which seems like a nice idea at first but gets old really quick. Only once I felt like this mechanic actually added something to the experience but this moment didn't feel impactful enough to the point that I think it was a necessary story telling element (which means I think it would have worked better as a short film still).
But what about the story, Is it any good? You play as Edith Finch who goes back to her former family home to learn about the deaths of the other family members who all died of unnatural causes. The game is a visual representation of a letter she wrote for her at the time unborn son, so Ediths point of view is narrated by herself. The various deaths are shown by small, playable flashbacks that last a couple of minutes each, some are longer than others. The causes of the deaths are quite unspectacular. The baby drowns in the bathtub, someone falls off a swing, the next guy falls off a cliff, the girl ate something bad, another one commits suicide because he was unhappy with his life and two people just vanish without further explanation. You only learn the bare minimum about each person to make you understand their death and nothing more. This makes it impossible to get emotionally attached to any of the characters in the game or feel for them. The only thing you know about them is that they once existed and how they died. The story doesn't give me any reason why I should care about anyone. At the end you learn, unsurprisingly, that Edith is dead as well, which was quite obvious by the games title and the way the narration was presented. After not even two hours of play time you see her son standing over her grave and that's the end of the story.
You go through a house to briefly learn about the unspectacular deaths of people you know nothing about because you wanted to sum it up for your yet to be born son before dying yourself. There was no twist, no climax, no mystery or anything that would make this story remotely interesting.
Okay, but this is still all my preference. What if you like these kind of stories and don't mind the gameplay? Is it worth the price? In my opinion, no. For the 20€ (or your equivalent) you get content that maxes out at about two and a half hours of play time if you really look at every object for multiple minutes. You are much better off by going to the cinema a couple of times or buy a few books if all you want is a good story. If you really need to play this game you should wait for an at least 50% discount in a future sale.

Aperture Tag is a fan-made Portal 2 mod, but with a catch. Your Portal gun is replaced with a paint gun - as you may have deducted from the title. The puzzles revolve around the blue and orange gels from Portal 2, of which you shoot from your gun. Portals are mixed in occasionally, however for the most part the game consists of originally made puzzles.
Aperture Tag's charm comes from the fact that it isn't like other mods; it does something different. Aperture Tag isn't just a Portal mod with a new story and some new chambers. It completely refreshes the Portal concept with all new mechanics.  Of course, I have some personal problems with the game of which I shall address, but in general Aperture Tag is a great mod. My first problem with this game is the difficulty. Some chambers are stupidly easy, while others are painfully hard - and not in a good way. For example, there is a level in which you need to escape from Aperture Science. You have 50 seconds, meaning you need to go non-stop through the course. It's mainly made up of surfing with a few parts in which you need to strategically place gel. Fun, right? Well, it has a few problems. Not only is it 100% trial and error, but the level wasn't even well made and there were multiple times in which the level glitched and I had to restart. The level is
beatable by trying over and over and learning exactly where to go. You also need to hope you don't get stuck, and hope that the map functions correctly. In the end I had to use the skip button they luckily provide, because I could not be bothered to spend hours learning the map. And then there are polar opposite levels to this, where everything is so much easier. The entire game changes out of nowhere in difficulty and it makes it hard to even want to carry on playing. Don't get me wrong, however, I did enjoy Aperture Tag's puzzles. Quite a few are exceptional in excecution and I enjoyed figuring out what to do with the new paint gun. To improve, however, the levels could have a better balance when it comes to difficulty, making the easy puzzles slightly harder and the hard puzzles slighty easier.
Aperture Tag's campaign isn't just a cluster of levels; some levels have a little puzzle to get to them, others throw you in straight away. But each has commentary from a Wheatley-like character, named Nigel. The voice acting is a little... Lacking. The original personality cores had character in their voices, I feel Nigel was a little too boring. The actual character himself along with his lines isn't actually that bad, and the game's story is actually decently gripping.
Aperture Tag's story delivers 2 - 3 hours of content depending on your play style and how quickly you'll solve the puzzles. But is this not enough? Do you want to play some more levels with the paint gun? Then fear not, as the game also includes an edited version of Portal 2's chamber editor. You can not only create your own paint gun levels, but play everybody else's, making theoretically endless hours of paint gun fun. Of course, some may argue that £3.99 ($5) is a little steep for 3 hours of game play, but with the aformentioned Steam Workshop chambers, I disagree. Aperture Tag has virtually infinite play time with all the maps created and uploaded.
PROs -
CONs -
I feel as if I've been very critical on Aperture Tag in this review. In reality, I really did enjoy the game. I don't see any reason why I won't go and play it again, whether it is playing through the campaign or playing some user made levels. I would recommend Aperture Tag - if 2 - 3 hours of gameplay puts you off the price, you can play the Workshop levels for more gameplay. Aperture Tag: The Paint Gun Testing Initiative
