You have to either be looking at this game through rose tinted nostalgia, or be autistic to enjoy Gothic 1.
The game's controls are archiac and awkward.  A lot of people say "you get used to them" and sure, you do, but I could also get used to my uncle fingering my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ every night as a child.  That doesn't mean it's pleasant.  And it's not just the controls, it's the combat gameplay and design of the game.
Gothic 1 is difficult for all the wrong reasons; the AI cheats.  As soon as your attack animation triggers, like, the milisecond it triggers, enemies will dodge your attacks.  Every creature from molerats to wolves seem to have gone through a lot of combat training because they all dodge in perfect synchronization.  Blocking rarely works, for example, when I tried to block a lizard my animation would instantly stop working as the lizard charged for no apparent reason.
There is no key to switch the target you are locked on to, you can only look at what you want to attack with your mouse camera, which means you have to pray you can some how keep the enemy you want to fight locked onto.  Praying wont save you if you fight multiple opponents though, which as fun to play as it is to watch as a bunch of creatures dance awkwardly around each other.  And you better bet every living creature in this game travels in huge packs.
But the AI isn't "smart", you can just jump on a piece of terrain and glitch all of them out as they try to grind the boulder you are standing on to dust by rapidly smearing their face against it.  Cheesing this way got me through some difficult encounters, but it's boring and the fact that I have to abuse glitchy AI should tell you a little bit about how much fun the combat is.
Quests are locked behind a level gate, and while you get some XP off of quests you will need to grind your experience off of monsters.  As a low level character, this is stupidly difficult for several reasons.  First of all nothing ever tells you what combat skills are good, or the fact that you need to heavily invest in one combat skill and nothing else (there are even things to bait noobs like learning how to skin an animal, which costs the same skill points you'd use to train your combat skills).
This game came out in a day and age where you had to actually read the game manual to know how to do anything, because the game literally tells you NOTHING about essential controls.  Not even checking the settings menu will show you essential key combinations you need to know.  This isn't "challenging", or an "RPG that doesn't hold your hand!", this is forcing me to google♥♥♥♥♥♥because the designers made an unintuitive control scheme and didn't include any indications in game.
The english voice acting is totally misplaced for most characters, it sounds like they just got random people to do the voices.  It's a german game so it's forgivable, but when the leader of a religious cult sounds like a backwater american hick I can't help but laugh.
The game crashes often.  I applied the community patch and the player patch and whatever, but the game still crashes often on Windows 7.
There is no quick save/quick load button.  A minor quip, but all of these little things add up.  You can't walk backwards, you just skip backwards like an idiot.  There is a LOT of going back and forth and back and forth and backtracking between the same areas, with no fast travel, for really tedious quests that have you talking to an NPC, running all the way back, talking to another NPC, running back... a lot of your time will be spent just bunny hopping all over the map.
All of this is a shame, because underneath all the grime is a gem of a classic RPG that could've been so much more.  There are some cool ideas here that show that, in some certain aspects at least, Gothic was ahead of the game when it came out. As it stands, I can see why this game is only really popular with a few people who are fond of it because they experienced it long ago or grew up with it or whatever; it's too rough around the edges and there are too many nuisances to justify the experience.  It felt like a chore trying to grind my way through chapters.  I made it to Chapter 3 and got sick of it.

Gunpoint is like a mix of Hotline Miami, Mark of the Ninja, and Arkham Asylum. You're a corporate spy in a 2-D world trying to solve a murder that you unwittingly pin on yourself. Each mission involves avoiding or knocking out guards, re-wiring electrical systems, smashing through windows, and hanging off the walls like Batman. You can jump ultra-high too without hurting yourself. Late in the game you can pull out your gun, but I don't recommend it.
You gain abilities by purchasing them in the store, and take missions for a variety of (competing) clients. You communicate with them via text message, and the conversations are often hilarious. They may have a variety of requests - complete the mission without hurting anyone, or kill everyone, or be completely silent.
Manipulating the various buildings is simple but extremely fun, and doesn't get old for the three hours it takes to beat the game. Given the length it might be a stretch to recommend this one at full price, but at $5 or less it's a no-brainer.
Some performance notes: it's more demanding than a 2-d pixel art game warrants. My 2010 Macbook couldn't play it, despite meeting the minimum Mac requirements. I have 4.6 hours of playtime because the first 1.6 hours were spent struggling to try to play it on the Macbook before I gave up and played it on my main rig.
The realism may turn off some run and gun gamers, but even those fans will have a hard time not appreciating what Sniper Elite brings to the table in terms of great and entertaining game play. 7/10

This review is brought to you by someone who had not played an RPGMaker title in full prior to this one.
The Book of Legends doesn't reinvent the wheel, rewrite the history books (I'm here all week) in terms of gameplay, plot or art direction...but they're all decent enough to be inoffensive, and I found the content to be enjoyable. For one, you can tell that a lot of effort was put into the characters and dialogue options by Aldorlea - I can only imagine it must've taken forever and a day to write it all. There are around 30 characters you can recruit, and they all have unique dialogue, loads of lines with each other and are constantly commenting on even the most minor sidequest discovery. I was pleasantly surprised and eventually impressed by the depths that the dev went to in making you care about such a large roster of characters. It's no Suikoden-style ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic character buffet, but kudos are in order.
Battles seem to proceed in a fairly standard RPGMaker manner, although playing as a main character who is ostensibly overpowered in both story and gameplay terms is a nice change these days. The story is troped up to the max, but also quite self-aware and pokes a lot of fun; it got a few laughs out of me, which I didn't expect given that I'm a mirthless, senile old grouch. It took me a good 25 hours to get through the story and polish off most of the postgame content, but the game encourages multiple playthroughs due to the aforementioned character roster, with two major paths (Jasmine or Melusine) being notable. I plumped for Jasmine and enjoyed the relentless ♥♥♥♥♥ing and banter, for what it's worth.
The sidequests are actually pretty interesting, and give a good feeling of immersion with each of the individual towns and villages out there. Some of them are outrageously obscure and certainly require a guide, but if you're the type to salivate over secrets hidden all over the map, then this is one for you. That includes items found in random pots and such, too. There were some drawbacks; the backtracking was a little excessive at points, and some level progressions were questionable, and the typical RPGMaker palette isn't exactly going to light up the Tate anytime soon...but on the whole, I was quite taken with the charm of the game.
I don't have a Skyborn to compare The Book of Legends to, but it held up surprisingly well for this fresh-faced greenhorn. Worth looking at as a competent and lengthy game in the genre, but definitely wait for a sale.

Yugi-oh, a long lasting trading card game from the 90's. The objective is to whittle down your opponent's life points to 0 before they do it to you. You can design a deck of 20 cards or more and deck it out with your friends or the online AI. The game starts you off with very simple AI starting with Levels like 1-5, 6-10, etc. All these AI can be easily beaten with a quick buy at the shop and getting 3-4 star cards with high attack stats (1700-2200). Once you get these cards, you can simply auto-duel and you will win. The lower level AI will just be crushed under the weight of power creep. This sadly proves one weakness of the game where power creep and rarity creep rule Yugi-Oh.
Gameplay-wise, you need a 20 card deck (minimum), understand that there are only 3 summon slots and 3 spell/trap slots and start with 4000 life points. You will also need to use a character that will come with a list of hero powers. Every turn you are limited to just 1 Normal Summon. If you go first, you don't get to draw and creatures you summon don't get to attack. If you go second, you get to draw and attack as per normal rules. There are also 2 phases, the Main phase and the Battle Phase. In the Main Phase, you Normal Summon cards. In the Battle Phase, you assign creatures to attack opponent creatures or the opponent's face.
There are tons of nitty gritty rules for beginners to remember. Learn to differentiate between Normal, Tribute, Special and Ritual Summons. Polymerisation is also another special card to note. When to activate your Quick-play Spells, Traps and creature abilities are all nitty gritty that you must note.
Conclusion, I would not recommend this game beyond the single player campaign. The single player campaign will let you play the anime series again but the business model is a disaster. Generally, if your experience is like mine, you will notice a simple formula of getting overpowered cards and smashing your AI opponent's face in. To really play Yugi-Oh, you must grind out suitable decks. Pay To Win is something that I am greatly against.
1. Interesting Franchise
Based on Yugi-oh and Yugi-oh GX, there are 2 storylines in the game. They follow the anime series so you will get to fight all the characters in the anime in sequential order. That is the greatest plus point for this game, in my opinion.
2. Intuitive Commands
If you slide your mouse pointer upwards in the same way as a creature attack, the game gives you a prompt asking you if you wish to change to Battle Phase. This is a great GUI idea.
3. Has A Decent Player Base
As of November 2017, 13,000+ players make for a decent player base. It will crash later but while there are people still playing. It's time to join in.
4. Level 2 to 3 Quizzes
I love solving the quizzes. It's difficult and complex and I scratch my head while I think about the order of casting spells. It's like a great puzzle to solve. However, you will find that it feels like learning nitty gritty rules. E.g. 3 Way Fusion Puzzle. Learning about Trap Space is interesting. Since you have only 3 slots to cast Spells/Traps, if you have no slots, you can't cast spells. Oddly, I almost never came across this scenario in the past. E.g. Jack Queen King Knights with the Instant Polymerisation and ridiculous damage.
5. Hero Powers
I love it. You can create variations of decks just by using Hero Powers. However, it is possible to be too situational and for certain heroes to gain superior optimization.
1. Pay To Win
You want to get the best cards in the game? Remember to pony up the cash or grind the gems to pay for cards. In the game you pay 5 gems for 1 pack or $1.48 for 1 pack with no guarantees of rares.
2. Extremely Situational Cards
Many of the cards have specific combos that will match with only named cards. This forces you to find the matching named cards and put them in your deck, else the combo won't work. It's highly restrictive. E.g. Warrior Elimination : Destroy all face up Warrior Type Monsters on the field. If you or your opponent don't have warriors, it's a wasted card. E.g. Y Dragon Head, specifically calls out to X Dragon Head only. If you don't have X Dragon Head, it's a wasted card.
3. Power Creep
If you look at the normal monsters, power creep is fairly obvious. There are cards that are just stronger than others stat-wise.
4. Rarity Creep
Want that Man-eater Bug or Ankh of Resurrection? It's a powerful card but it's rare.
5. Keys
Black, blue, red, white. All the colours of the rainbow. If you want to progress in the game, remember that you have to farm for keys.
6. Card Trader
Oh what a convoluted scheme of things! You need SR levels (which can be grinded), gold and special elemental orbs just to trade for the card.
7. Auto-Dueling
Once you get rare and powerful cards with super stats, you can simply press auto-duel to run an AI match. While this saves time, it destroys the game. Why do you even play Yugi-Oh at all? Also, if it's already simulated, why do you even need to watch the cards playing out? Just simulate the numbers and give EXP, gold and gems.
8. Glossy Cards
Seriously, glossy cards actually give you extra EXP if you play them during a game. E.g. 100 EXP for playing a glossy card.
9. Sub-Optimal Decks
It is very easy to create a sub-optimal deck in this game. Due to this gameplay design, billions of strategic combinations are discarded down the drain. You are basically railroaded into net-decking and finding the most optimal build of cards online to win.
1. In Game Replays/Streams
While it's good to know that top-level plays have decks filled with special cards and fancy effects, it is sad to also realise that you need those super rare cards to play competitively and that those cards are out of reach due to a gambling system. If you don't have that card, good luck on playing that competitve game. Everyone does not start fair in Yugi-Oh. An overpowered deck will crush a sub-optimal deck 999 times out of 1000 games.

As you can see on the hrs ticker, Ive put in my fair share of time in this game and even played outside of the Steam tracker, so definately more than ~630 hrs recorded here. On its own, its a great game with great depth, part of why I put in so many hours into it. The depth from taking part in combat, either PvP or PvE, and then taking part in a galactic economy from mining ores to constructing ships is really unmatched from any game I know. To the newbie, it can be VERY overwhelming and take a few months and lots of time to get just the basics down. Joining a corp is a plus to help with that, just make sure you select one with more than 20+ active members, or you'll end up in a dead/dying corp. Lots of resources online such as tools and references to help.
Now to the meat of my recommendation, the playerbase is the most toxic I have ever encountered (a quick google search confirms this), and are empowered by exploiting technical loopholes which are used to harass newbie/loner players in highsec, loopholes which CCP doesnt seem to care about fixing. Obviously not everyone who plays Eve falls into this toxic group, and I have encountered pleasant people from time to time. But certain alliances dedicate themselves to using these loopholes in harassing newbies or people who just want to PvE. For whatever reason, this game seems to attract a small group of people with antisocial/psychotic issues who enjoy using these exploits and ruin the experience for the rest of us, and I dont care to reward such people, hence why myself as well as a few others I know gave up and stopped playing.
I would say, play to get the experience, especially since its free, and the recent update opens up a lot more potential for free players. Do a month or three of Omega to get the full experience. Join a corp.
Then re-evaluate if its worth investing your time long-term. If you find yourself frustrated because you are being bullied for trying to get the basics of the game down or trying to work up to get that cruiser, quit. Its not worth the frustration, as I have learned.

At the time of this review, I've played this game for about a month. Here is where my review currently stands.
Pros:
The game is great, offering a fair amount of customization for your created characters which will actually affect your style of play in the game. The combat system, though simple, is wonderful and easy to pick up. Finding players that play in a style akin to your own is great as it allows for some pretty insane combos and damage. The story, although predictable (rince and repeat of the same story albiet with some changes) is a fun one as you can see your own character grow in power along with the cast of Dragon Ball.
Cons:
The game has a sort of peer-to-peer connection system when it comes to playing online. This wouldn't be a problem except for the fact that much of the player base consist of children who have no control of their internet providers, thus resulting in some shoddy connectivity on some instances. On the subject of the young player base, 90% of this player base consist of the Saiyan race. The issue with this is that Saiyans can transform into Super Saiyans, which is a form that allows them to cast skills back-to-back at no cost at all, resulting in spam. This is infuriating in two ways. The first being that it ruins combos when playing alongside these spammers. The second issue is that PvP is stagnant, as these skills are easy to dodge and counter, so playing against another player that actually uses skills to fight is a 1/10 chance. Another issue would be the DLC quests. Although they are fun, the quests themselves are high level and have no restrictions on who can play them (granted that you've bought the DLC). Normally, you can't play certain quests unless you've gotten further enough in the story or beaten prerequisited quests. A.K.A: It boils down to you being a high enough level to even play them. With the DLC quests, all you need to do is buy them, so this results in people who just began the game fighting off enemies who are level 80+, so a lot of 1-shots to beginners. The sad part is that unless you view someone's profile yourself, you have no idea what level anyone is when in quest lobby, so you wont be able to tell if that stranger that joined is new or experienced enough for these quests.
All-in-all, a good game, but it's left in such a way that you'll dislike much of the community when playing, so keep your eyes out for the few hidden gems that play well and add them.

Gunpoint is a a solid little stealth platformer puzzle game. You control a spy-for-hire who sneaks into various buildings to steal items or hack information. The game eases you into the systems at a steady pace, with the complexity ramping up nicely. There's also an interesting assortment of upgrades that give you various advantages like increased stealth or stronger abilities.
The music is pretty perfect for the gameply, sorta jazzy but with a Mission Impossible/Oceans Eleven feel to it. The graphics are retro but plenty serviceable, with everything important to gameplay easy to discern. And it also has a pretty good sense of humor in the between mission dialogue and achievements.
Only downfall is the whole game can be completed in about four hours, but there's some replayability, as it's pretty clear there are at least two endings, and plenty of different achievements for doing missions perfectly and using all the abilities to their maximum potential. I'd had this one in my library for quite a while and finally got around to playing it, and I'm glad I did. If you're considering it but on the fence, let this be your endorsement from a fellow former fence-sitter.

What happens when you cross Inspector Gadget with Max Payne?
Welcome to Gunpoint.
After playing through the entire game, I have to say that I was a bit disappointed with how short it was. With only ten levels, it's easy enough to beat the entire game in just a few hours. However, it's a fairly inexpensive game even at full price, and easy enough to come by via trades, and the gameplay is so much fun that it keeps me coming back even after playing all the way through.
The premise is simple: you control a detective with an awesome pair of pants who gets framed for murder. No really, those pants are great. You can jump super high, and fall from the top of tall buildings without getting hurt, all thanks to those damn pants. I'd like to see Old Navy try to top that.
As you progress through the game, you'll earn money which can be used to buy new gadgets that let you rewire the electronics of a building, kick down doors, sneak like a ninja, and sometimes even shoot people in the face. And who doesn't love getting to shoot people in the face?
The main appeal of Gunpoint is the amazingly brilliant yet simple implementation of the rewiring gadget. You can rewire a security camera to open a door, then wire that door to a guard's gun so he shoots another guard in the face. Or you could rewire a light switch to turn off the lights on another floor so the guards up there get confused. Or you could wire every single door in the level to the same light switch, then turn off the lights on that floor and watch the guard open the doors for you. Or really anything else you can imagine. The possibilities are nearly endless, and that's what makes it so much fun.
Gunpoint doesn't have spectacular graphics. It's not Skyrim, or The Witcher 3. Instead, is has beautiful pixel art to accompany its "noir detective movie" atmosphere, and it works perfectly. The pixel art gives the game a slightly "vintage" feel, which is just fine for a story that's more at home in the 1950's than the 2010's.
There's also a level creator which is a ton of fun to play around with. You can place anything from the game in a custom level and share it on Steam Workshop so all your buddies can see how sadistic you are when you place five guards in front of the main objective and don't allow them to carry a gun for that level. Or you can create a level with electronic devices everywhere and just run wild with rewiring everything to everything else. The only problem I had with the level creator is that it's difficult to recolor the electronics, but I worked around that by just putting about a hundred recolor commands all over the circuits in hopes that one of them might miraculously be in the right place.
Overall, Gunpoint is not without its shortcomings, but it's still a spectacular game. If you like puzzle games, 2D platformers, or stealth adventures, you shouldn't even be reading this review anymore. You should be playing Gunpoint.

Prototype 2 is a game developed by Radical Entertainment and published by Activision and is the sequel to Prototype
Traversing in the open world city of Protoype 2 is amazing, probably one of the best in any open world game. You can easily run up buildings, jump off to great heights and then glide very seamlessly
The side activities are very fun ranging from running obstacle courses hitting checkpoints, killing a certain number of enemies using certain powers and using helicopters/tanks to kill enemies. Every activity has a bronze, silver and gold medal depending on how well you complete it
The gameplay mechanics work well, you are given several different powers/abilities to kill enemies and completing main mission, side activities reward you with experience to upgrade your character.
However, Prototype 2 does suffer with bland graphics even for an open world game. Granted, the number of pedestrians, vehicles, enemies, explosions etc. on screen is very impressive so have bland graphics is easier to accept
The game does have a decent story that is told both through cutscenes and consuming enemies/people. After consuming a person, you are treated to a short video of their memory. A cool way to tell the story and mix it with the gameplay. The game is all about getting you in the action as fast as possible so the story takes a back seat to everything else
The main missions are fun and are somewhat varied but most of them feel like you are either killing tons of enemies or running around chasing somebody.
Sadly, Prototype 2 is a technical mess to put it mildly with a very limited resolution and given the vast number of objects on screen at any given time the targeting system seems to target everything except for the one thing you want it to target and the boss battles can create a frustrating difficulty spike
However, Prototype 2 is a very fun if not flawed game. If you feel like running around and killing things with crazy powers and watching a lot of things explode, then this may just scratch that itch

At one point you're faced with a dilemma - how do you gain entrance to a club being run by a villain, so that you can search for clues?  You have three options:  Go in powers blazing, infiltrate the place posing as a customer, or sneak in through the back entrance.
No matter which choice you make, you'll end up hypnotized by the villain running the place.  It's a false dilemma where all paths lead to the same destination.
The game is full of these, where all your decisions really do is inform the window dressing.  For a text-based game, where a narrative should be able to be expanded into multiple branching paths very cheaply, this is quite disappointing.  If you've made a text-based game whose central mechanic is simply player choice has less respect for that choice than a AAA game like Fallout: New Vegas, then you've dropped the ball.
Embarrassingly, I found a couple of typos as well.  The writing is interesting enough at first, but it gets frustrating later on as you'll probably figure out the big "twist" long before any of the characters do, but are powerless to do anything about it.
It's amusing for a while on a single playthrough, but that's about it.

It's not very often that a story has made me so drawn to characters that I was unable to see, but that's exactly what Heroes Rise: The Prodigy has done. This is one of those hidden gems, tucked in the corner of the closet, just waiting to be opened up. If you're put off by the imageless narrative and text-based gameplay, don't be. It doesn't take away from anything and I personally think it makes it more powerful.
Scenes are fleshed out and described with detail and precision. Characters have reason and motives behind them, making them feel a lot more alive than their 2D or 3D counterparts.
There are a lot of decisions to be made in this game and it's very refreshing and comforting to see that they do affect the story. Choices matter, even down to how powerful you make your attacks. Do you want to rip apart an enemy boss with a whirlwind or just incapacitate them with a punch? This game is fleshed out by your decisions and by your imagination. It's brought to life by your realizations and the amount of effort you put into it.
Graphics are not everything. In this generation with our never-ending quest for true-to-life graphics, sometimes we forget what really matters: the story and the experience.
Those things being said, my only gripe is that there is no 'undo' button. There were times when I accidentally skipped over an option because I'd press on my screen twice, making me restart the whole game again.
Pick this up, though. You will not regret it.

Heroes Rise: The Prodigy is the first of hopefully many games released under the Choice Of Games brand.  These games were typically released for the mobile and web browser markets, and so you can imagine my surprise when I suddenly discovered one of the Choice Of...games suddenly show up on Steam.
Now you might be looking at the screenshots, and seeing the minimalist approach to the game.  It's pretty barebones right? White screen, text.  And...well for the most part that's it.  That's how the games are intended, and the engine is actually available to make your own games.
Okay great...enough background. So what is this game?  It's a Choose Your Own Adventure.  You remember those from when you were a kid?  "Want to see the glorious death you'll receive for making bad life choices? Turn to page 24!"  Well it turns out that they translate very well with text games like this one.   However don't be fooled in thinking that the game is this simple.  Choice of Games has a simple engine that allows for a lot of interesting ways to script events and allows the game to remember what your choices were.
For you it basically means that you'll have a Super Hero RPG that you can have multiple playthroughs.  You will have romance options and NPCs to interact and build relationships with in the same way you do in a Bioware game.  The difference? Less pretty graphics.
Here's the thing...if you hate reading? Don't buy this.  It's all about reading.  The game itself is relatively dark in its portrayal of super heroes.  It sort of gets increasingly darker as the game continues in the sequel.   I found the characters interesting, and the options for designing my character throughout the game gave me the feeling that I really was making a bit of an impact.
The nature of the beast is that the game is kind of linear. Your choices, and you have many of them,  still eventually follow the same road, despite how you might take different paths to get there.   However if you like super heroes, love text adventures, enjoy choices and moral dilemas in your games then I suggest you try this.  You'll pretty much have a couple play throughs at least and considering how inexpensive the games are...I think it'll be worth it to you.
I think it'll take you around an hour or two hours to play through it.  Obviously that's assuming you are reading the story.  Typically after the first playthrough you're probably gonna skip through things until you make a different choice and see what happens. Huzzah.  Have fun.

Westerado: Double Barreled is an open world set in western times, released in April 2015. You take on the role of a gunslinger who is tasked with hunting down his families killer.
The way in which you complete this task differs from other games in my view; you have to find clues about the identity of the culprit by completing missions and objectives for locals around the towns. This really adds to the mystery behind the killer. Even the options menu has a screen dedicated to showing you all the clues you have found along with a model of a character showing the clues on, such as a "fat, blue shirt, medium sized hat" figure for example. These clues are all randomly generated each playthrough as well.
Another really new feature in Westerado is the that you can draw your gun at anytime, even during a conversion with any NPC, this can sometimes trigger a different set of dialogue, initiate a new quest, or just go completely wrong and end up in a gun fight. This also means you can kill anyone in the story too, no matter how important they are to the plot, anyone can die.
The main gameplay is a top down action game, in good old western style, you have your gun which you have to manually reload every six shots, or you can upgrade it to a big ol shotgun. The gunfights can sometimes feel a little bit clunky, but once you get used to the controls and how the game responds to them, it soon becomes clear and easily executed. Another one of my favorite parts of the game would be the buffalo scenes; riding horse back defending carriages from bandits on a buffalo's, although simple, it is really compelling to play.
Westerado has a very clever story, and has all the main plot points that any good western film will have in it. Although you can make the story different each time you play, for instance just killing one of the main quest givers, I am not sure it actually changes the whole outcome of the game, I think all that will happen is you'll just miss out on those quests rather it have an effect on the grand scheme of things.
The world in which you play in is huge, it's set out like a very Zelda style map, each tile on the map has four entry points, north, west, south and east. This makes navigating across the map very easy and you can always make your way to where you need to be very quickly. Each of the zones look amazing too; lots of detail has gone into adding plenty of objects, background items and scenery to add to the western feel. Although the graphics are the ever growing popular, pixelated style, it still has a really nice look to it.
Length wise, Westerado can be over and done with in less than an hour if you just do the main story, which is actually what I did on my first playthrough. However it is highly recommended that you don't just do that, as you are missing out on tons of content in the side missions, along with loads of story too. There is so much to see in Westerado if you just take the time to explore.

A spaghetti western. The aesthetics are immersive. The landscape is appeasing to behold, and the soundtrack is enjoyable. The mechanics are simple and convenient. Just a handful of keys on the keyboard, and they can be remapped. Death is a setback, not a game-ender, so you're encouraged to explore choices and consequences. Want to pull your gun on someone in a conversation? You can! \o/ Want to anger an entire town by getting into a saloon fight? You can! \o/ How about rob a bank? Yep. Kill an oil tycoon and create a new franchise? Uh huh. Hurl dozens of tomahawks at hostile folk whose only defense is a hat? You got it! There's a sandbox quality to exploring the land, but the way to end the game is by completing your Quest for Vengeance. Who is your target? Well, that's randomly generated, and you've got to find clues. Or, I reckon you could gun down everyone. If you can't have nice things, then neither should they.

So, worryingly, I've looked my game timer and I've spent (wasted) 59hours of my life on this game. Visually, it's a nice game. The scenes are good. OK, maybe if you're used the old grind of MMOs (I don't normally play them) you'll enjoy this. But I do not. Waiting 3 days to learn one skill is not fun (and there's hundreds to learn). Or sitting by a rock for 25minutes, mining ore to sell for 700K of in game currency (which will buy you some low end ammo or gun, but to buy real stuff like high end guns, high end ships, upgrades etc. you need tens of millions), is not my idea of fun. Then you have the fact that some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ groups of mining guys will wipe out any resources in an entire system in an hour, and you have to spend 20minutes jumping from one system to the next to find an asteroid field that actually has some ore to mine in it. (only the very basic mining stuff is available at Alpha, Omega get strip miners) Then that system probably has a really low sell price, so really you need to jump to another system to get more money for that ore. Also, the free Alpha account is not really viable in the game. You need Omega (and ♥♥♥♥ it if I'm paying £120 a year to play a half-arsed version of a space sim). A good game costs £30-40 to buy, not paying £100 a year to play this snooze fest.
I'm done. It takes too long to get anywhere (and i was given 100mil in game by another player, and it's still boring as F). The combat interface is cumbersome and basic. Unless you waste literally years of your life. And the amount of stuff to learn is ridiculous. Each thing has a thousand variations and factors determining it's effect. Yeah it's clearly had a lot of time and thought into it, and if this was the only thing you did for the next 10 years, it might be cool. One of the best RPGs I've ever played.
Its hard to convince people to jump back on old games like this but this game definitely stands up, even though its old, has dated graphics and clunky controls.
It set some benchmarks, it really did. For people who are younger than 20, you dont understand what its like to first experience a true day/night cycle, and to experience actualy A-Life. A game that lives and breaths with or without you. NPCs who go around and do their daily things and live their lives and remember you and your actions.
This was one of the first games to ever feature this.
You probably played Skyrim right? Well the settlements in Gothic are just like that, the people live their lives, they do their daily things, they go to bed at night, they might pick fights with out, and they remember your actions.
This was BIG back in 01 because no one else was doing it. NPCs around that time just stood there waiting to be talked to, or they may wander around in a room, thats about it, you would never see a NPC from one camp randomly decide to walk to another or patrol around the landscape or hunt.
Another thing that made this game so great was how gritty and mature it was. This isnt a childs game. This is a game in a world full of Convicts. Everyone hates you, and you have to survive tooth and nail. You start out as a true weakling with no training, and really have to work your way up. You cant even take on the weakest of NPCs at the beginning of the game, you may have to resort to stealing and attacking them at night just go scrape your living. You have no idea how to fight, you can barely hold up a sword, and one swing and you're on your♥♥♥♥♥ and guess what... they dont kill you, they loot all your money (ore) and take your weapon, and tell you to ♥♥♥♥ off. Yeah YOU yourself get LOOTED if you lose fights.
And maybe you'll come back a few hours later when you're stronger, and take your revenge for that crude sword you worked so hard to get. It might not be very useful now, but its the principal of the thing, it was the best piece of equipment you could have ever owned at the time, and that ♥♥♥♥ stole it from you.
Seriously, ground breaking game.

This game is an outstanding one to play. It is a long game with plenty of replay value. The artwork is beautiful. It's settings and characters are very oriental depicted. There are 2 levels of choice to play. No secret rooms as such but plenty of hidden items in all areas. The characters have many facets to themselves and there is a lot of humour throughout the game. Levelling up is a must as they aqcquire better magical skills and a lot of these skills are required. With 28 side quests as well as the main storyline gives this game it's most appeal and length. There are 18 humans - some only available on re-plays, 12 animals plus 1 demon to have in your party list so making the game rather interesting. There are multiple endings depending on your choices throughout the game. A "go-through" is availble after you have finished some areas. The story line centres on finding and stopping demons arising to take over the country and Jordan ( the main character and very egoistic) is given the task to stop the 1st one arising but things do not go as planned and so the real task begins.  The Book of Legends depicts when and where these events will occur. Battle scenes are the usual rpg type and are random encounters. An auto-save  is available and Jordan  also has a save spell. Turorial books are in most areas for help. Party splits are also used in the game. The sprites depicting each character are very artistic and beautiful. Overall it is a very interesting and colourful game to play and I would much recommend it to players.

İlk oyununda Alex Mercer'i kontrol ediyorduk, bu oyunda ise Alex Mercer başka birine de kendi mutasyonundan veriyor. Ama ne hikmetse, bu ikisi düşman oluyor. Yani demem o ki, bu oyunda Alex Mercer'i yönetmiyoruz, hatta onunla düşmanız.
Bu oyunun kapasitesi çok yüksek, kapasite derken oyun boyutu değil. Ancak 2011 yılında yapıldığı için kabul edilebilir. Eğer Prototype 3 çıksaydı -ki çıkmayacağından eminim çünkü oyunun sorunları olmasına rağmen yapımcılar bir güncelleme dahi getirmedi- GTA gibi daha açık bir evren, daha güzel bir hikaye, daha güzel grafikler görebilirdik.
Oyunda biz özel bir mutasyonuz. Vücudumuz geliştirilmiş, süper insan haline gelmişiz. Kollarımızı Red Tentacles (Kırmızı dokunaçlar) ile birlikte keskin bir kılıca, kalkana, çekice dönüştürebiliyoruz. Binaların tepesine çıkarken pencerelerden koşabiliyoruz, örümcek adam gibi normalde tırmanabiliyoruz. Patlamalara ve mermilere karşı dayanıklıyız. Havada özel gücümüz sayesinde biraz süzülebiliyoruz. İnsanlara bürünebiliyoruz, yani ben, sen olabiliyorum. Böylece üslere sızmak daha kolay oluyor.
Sadece insanlar yok, diğer yaratıklar da var. İkisiyle de savaş içerisindeyiz. Böyle bir oyun oldukça güzel, havalı ve tam istediğim şekilde. Ancak dünyası çok karanlık, bunu oynayınca göreceksiniz. Canlı bir dünyası olsaydı daha iyi olurdu. Hikayesi malesef yeterince iyi değil. İlk oyunda direk olayın içine giriyorduk zaten, oyun hikaye üzerinde değil de dövüş sistemi özellikli, yaratık katletme üzerine kurulmuş.
Birçok kişi aratıyor, ancak Türkçe yaması yok. Ben Türkçe yama çalışmalarına başlayacaktım. Dil dosyası sistemi RCF ve P3D uzantısından oluşuyor. Bunlar eski de kaldı ve gerekli tool'lar yeterince iyi değil. Örneğin dil dosyasını çıkartabiliyorum, ancak düzenlemek için program yok. Misal düzenledim diyelim, tekrar RCF'nin içine sokmak için programda "Import" seçeneği yok. Program yapımcısı "Export" koymayı akıl edebilmiş ancak bir "Import" butonu koyamamış. Kısaca dil dosyasını çevirsem bile oyunun içine gömmemi sağlayacak program yok. Yani doğal olarak çeviri iptal. Başlayamadık bile.

The Book of Legends is a classic-style JRPG created with the RPGmaker engine. The game begins with Jordan, a man on a delivery of utmost importance, who is promptly robbed on the first night of his journey. He teams up with some unlikely allies (including a chicken…) and goes in search of his lost item. Presumably other hijinks ensue, but I didn’t make it far enough to find out.
I honestly thought this game sounded cool, and it definitely has its good points, but ultimately I ended up giving up on it in pretty short order. I generally like the silliness of the game: being able to recruit a chicken is rather novel, and I found having a protagonist as evil-looking as Jordan to be pretty amusing. I also like the snappiness of a lot of the dialogue, but unfortunately its implementation (phrasing, I guess?) feels very unpolished, which detracts from its overall appeal. The story hook was pretty mediocre; not super interesting, but not a deal-breaker in and of itself. What really killed it for me was Jordan himself: I found his character to be unsympathetic and generally unlikeable.
In another genre, an annoying protagonist is surmountable, but in a JRPG, where the gameplay is usually the weakest part, there has to be some combination of character- and storyline-investment to incentivize grinding onwards, and I just couldn’t get invested in this game.
This game definitely has some good points, and I think that other JRPG fans who find Jordan less grating might enjoy it. Personally, though, I have enough other unplayed games of this genre in my library that I can’t imagine ever coming back to it.

PROTOTYPE 2 is the sequel to 2009's open world action-adventure video game [PROTOTYPE], it pretty much keeps what made it's original game great, the over-the-top action, gore and combat. It's what really makes PROTOTYPE 2 a successful sequel and an overall superb game. Though it also has (just like [PROTOTYPE]) a really mediocre story, it's not exactly memorable, with the main character being forgettable alongside every other character excluding Alex Mercer, who was already slightly memorable from the original game.
Now to expand on the story it's pretty much you start off as James Heller, a soldier who comes across Alex Mercer and tries to kill him, he doesn't succeed and gets infected by Mercer and hence the story of PROTOTYPE 2 begins from there really. And really after that point the story is forgettable, I care for none of the characters, sure the way the cinematics are made to look is nice but that doesn't I will be intrigued by what's going on in the cutscene, because it's just not entertaining to learn about. Now saying that I myself found the ending to be actually ok, it doesn't really elaborate on the after events, but the boss battle is really good at the end, even if it does seems to be the same as the others except with more health...
And that leads me to the gameplay of this game.... my ♥♥♥♥ing god the gameplay is superb, this game alongside it's predecessor has superb gameplay, it's ♥♥♥♥ing great, just going around killing everyone with abilities you gain throughout the game, causing chaos towards the city of New York is just so satisfying. The fluidity of what you are doing is there, it's just so fun, you can go around in the Green and Yellow zones completely destroying bases full of Blackwatch soldiers or go into the Red zone fighting against all kinds of monsters created from "Blacklight virus". It's just so fun just going around destroying everything, and I could honestly say that it is as fun to do as in Just Cause 2 and 3, which PROTOTYPE has in some ways a similarity to.
The graphics are ok, it's not brilliant but looks very much like a game from 2012, if you want a game which is graphically pleasing this isn't really anything special which is sadly to be expected as the engine was more so a improvement of the original [PROTOTYPE] engine for the gore and chaos instead of the graphics.
The controls in this game are something to debate on, it's not bad but it's far from perfect, the controls are correct and it's all what it should be for a typical game on PC, but it feels at times that the mouse sensitivity is broke and that there is a mouse accerelation in the game that you can't turn off, it doesn't feel right and can get really annoying, but if you have a controller it won't be an issue as it seems to be extremely well there.... and that's a problem, because it also shows how this game was really not focused to be on PC, for christ sake the PC port took 2 extra months to release and just like everyone else is saying, it's a bad port, my PC build is a GTX 980, i7-4790k, 16GB DDR3 RAM, Windows 10, and I have seen on High settings an average of about 60-80FPS, sure it's not bad but this is a game from 2012, and worse of all if you have an AMD GPU/CPU you may not even be able to get the game running at all, and heck I consider myself lucky as Windows 10 users with NVidia GPU's have reported the same issue. And if you think this will be solved, well it won't as the developers pretty much shut down before the game was even released on PC! And it's a shame because if these issues were to be resolved then this game would be a solid buy.

What happens when you cross Inspector Gadget with Max Payne?
Welcome to Gunpoint.
After playing through the entire game, I have to say that I was a bit disappointed with how short it was. With only ten levels, it's easy enough to beat the entire game in just a few hours. However, it's a fairly inexpensive game even at full price, and easy enough to come by via trades, and the gameplay is so much fun that it keeps me coming back even after playing all the way through.
The premise is simple: you control a detective with an awesome pair of pants who gets framed for murder. No really, those pants are great. You can jump super high, and fall from the top of tall buildings without getting hurt, all thanks to those damn pants. I'd like to see Old Navy try to top that.
As you progress through the game, you'll earn money which can be used to buy new gadgets that let you rewire the electronics of a building, kick down doors, sneak like a ninja, and sometimes even shoot people in the face. And who doesn't love getting to shoot people in the face?
The main appeal of Gunpoint is the amazingly brilliant yet simple implementation of the rewiring gadget. You can rewire a security camera to open a door, then wire that door to a guard's gun so he shoots another guard in the face. Or you could rewire a light switch to turn off the lights on another floor so the guards up there get confused. Or you could wire every single door in the level to the same light switch, then turn off the lights on that floor and watch the guard open the doors for you. Or really anything else you can imagine. The possibilities are nearly endless, and that's what makes it so much fun.
Gunpoint doesn't have spectacular graphics. It's not Skyrim, or The Witcher 3. Instead, is has beautiful pixel art to accompany its "noir detective movie" atmosphere, and it works perfectly. The pixel art gives the game a slightly "vintage" feel, which is just fine for a story that's more at home in the 1950's than the 2010's.
There's also a level creator which is a ton of fun to play around with. You can place anything from the game in a custom level and share it on Steam Workshop so all your buddies can see how sadistic you are when you place five guards in front of the main objective and don't allow them to carry a gun for that level. Or you can create a level with electronic devices everywhere and just run wild with rewiring everything to everything else. The only problem I had with the level creator is that it's difficult to recolor the electronics, but I worked around that by just putting about a hundred recolor commands all over the circuits in hopes that one of them might miraculously be in the right place.
Overall, Gunpoint is not without its shortcomings, but it's still a spectacular game. If you like puzzle games, 2D platformers, or stealth adventures, you shouldn't even be reading this review anymore. You should be playing Gunpoint.

Having played the Duel Links app for a long while I was curious to see what they would do with the steam version. My main beef has always been that it’s a condensed version of the original trading card game (OTCG). So, I was hoping that with the additional real estate (the computer screen) they would expand it to the full version. Alas they did not, but I am sure that was so they could keep the mobile users integrated with the new pc users.
If you are now joining us on steam, good on ya and here is what you can expect. Duel links is a concise, condensed, and uncomplicated version of the OTCG. So, if you wanted to play “real” Yu-gi-oh this is not the place to do it. However, it still offers a fun experience with quite a nostalgia trip. They pull the voice audio of all the characters from the anime which adds to the fun. Also, the visuals are pretty good and gets us one step closer to that, “what if we could do 3D duels in real life?” What makes this game unique is the inclusion of specific and nonspecific character abilities to use during duels to give you an edge. And while you can duel the AI’s until the sun burns out, you can jump right into pvp as well. Unfortunately, there is no full screen option which is weird.
For people like me who are hoping over from the app, there isn’t much new but a few note worthy things. It’s bigger! (no really) Also there is a higher graphical fidelity which is nice. The main thing is the duels themselves are much improved. During any duel it gives you detailed information about what’s going on and what things are much easier. Also its lot easier to do stuff with a mouse than with a finger lol. Just please remember that if you are porting over from your mobile device you to set up your data transfer account with Konami if you don’t want to lose all of your progress!
Pros:

Nostalgia trip

Gunpoint is a true masterpiece. It's so ♥♥♥♥ing good. As advertised, gunpoint is a 2-D stealth game in which you are able to rewire objects in order to complete the levels. The gameplay itself is really solid, and I haven't found any bugs to date.( Playing on Windows 8 ) But the things that make this game amazing are the dialouge, the choices you make, and the story that unfolds.
Although a single playthrough of this game is about 1:30-2:00 hours, this game has great replayability. Each dialouge choice you make or in some cases what missions you take affect how the overall story goes. Sometimes, you might find yourself saying, "Did I make the right choice?" or "I wonder what would have happened if I picked the other route?". This game also has a couple hard-hitting moments, ( In my opinion ) that can make you feel a little guilty. I found myself resenting one character in the game, or becoming worried about another. As stupid as that sounds, This is really awesome to have in this game.
Let's talk about the dialouge itself. When you find yourself in a conversation with someone, you will have multiple choices to choose from. These dialouge options can be very humorous, or you can take a more serious option, giving the main character the personality YOU want to give him. I found this fairly interesting, as I hadn't played a game that had this feature before. Even the other characters have their own personalities and witty dialouge! The setting and story are also great, but I won't spoil them in this review. ( This may not be everyone's opinions ) Also, if you are into achievements, this game has plenty of them, including hidden ones.
Workshop support has also been added to the game, and you can now share and create your own levels. I'm also pretty sure crashing on the mac ports has been fixed, but seriously don't take my word for it.
If you are a fan of stealth or dialouge driven games, BUY THIS GAME. Even at a full price of 10 dollars, this game is fully worth it. Also, I forgot to mention the soundtrack is amazing.
EDIT: Going back and looking at my review, I realised I needed to talk about gameplay, so I will. Before, when I said Gunpoint's gameplay was solid I meant really ♥♥♥♥ing good, just like the rest of the game. At its core, it is a 2-D stealth game that consists of smashing through windows, avoiding or knocking out guards, and hacking stuff. The game is segmented into different missions given by your client. Your client might also give you an objective like: No violence, No living witnesses, Hack all laptops, make no noise, that sort stuff. But aside from this, you can buy many gadgets that change the way you play and solve puzzles. Two of the required gadgets are the Crosslink, which allows you to rewire electronics to solve missions and is a key feature of the game, and the wirejack, an accompanament to the crosslink. Optional gadgets include gadgets that allow you to rewire guns, fall from heights silently, kick down doors, a gun, and other stuff. This is all perfectly meshed together with a smooth and excellent stealth system.

Gunpoint is an indie puzzle game with loose ties to “stealth” and “technology”, Gunpoint was developed by Suspicious Developments and released 2013.
The story is all in written format, somedays I feel like reading all that is writen in a video game, other times I see a chunk of text and think “I don't really care” and skip right into the mission.
Gunpoint lets you skip dialogue and jump right into the puzzle solving action if you feel so inclined, however the story is quite well written. You're a detective and have multiple choices for interaction with your clients. (Naturally I was as condescending and insulting as possible – the reactions were very much worth it!)
The game controls start out very simple, jump, and movement. You jump with the mouse button, and you use ASDW to move right or left, and climb up or down. As you complete various missions you earn skill points that you can spend to improve your skills, and money to unlock upgrades. Some missions require certain upgrades to progress, but generally the game is very doable with minimum upgrades.
Generally there are two elements to the various puzzles you face while playing Gunpoint. Firstly, you need to keep out of the site of guards. This is where the “stealth” tag gets placed on the game. The guards line of site is pretty standard for most games of this genre... Secondly, there is “wiring” you do some very rudimentary “wiring”, for example you can wire a switch to turn off a light, call an elevator, ...and when the elevator arrives it makes a noise and that triggers a sound sensor to open the door in front of you.
There are two types of Achievements in this game: Hidden, and visible.
I personally find “hidden” achievements annoying because you can find them by looking at global statistics anyway.
After your first play through you will probably have roughly 40% of the achievements, a second play through will earn you another 40% (as long as you do things differently). After my second time through I simply replayed the levels required.
As a side note, you don't need to reset your game and start from scratch like I did, you could just replay old levels. Since the game is such a fast play through anyway, it hardly maters if you reset or not.
One final note, for achievement hunters, this game is an easy 100% completion with relatively less commitment for achievement work.
Gunpoint is priced at $9.99. I personally spent 8.6 hours playing the game. I played through twice, and earned all the achievements. As far as I'm concerned the game value comes out nearly perfectly at 1 dollar an hour.
If you're tight on money you could certainly wait for a sale, however... the developers are indie, so supporting them is good!
The game itself was fun, the humor in Gunpoint was hilarious, the story was well written, the gameplay was fun and easy to learn, the achievements were all relatively easy to get but more importantly funny to get
, the price is as fair as you can expect.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys 2D games, indie titles, puzzle games, or “stealth” types of games.
...Maybe all that matters is that I now have the ability to kick down doors. Thanks for reading my review!

For a simple title with not much meat to the gameplay (walk around to line up with the enemy, click, bang) Westerado compensates by making the dialogue system amusingly interactive (in the ammended words of Todd Howard:
) and features a number of branching quests that'll culminate in different sub-endings while pointing you in the direction for your final showdown against the killer. Each time the journey can greatly differ, as does the appearance of the varmint that gunned your family down, but the destination ulimately remains the same.
A playthrough of Westerado can last anywhere from a mere 5 minutes (when you've been through vengenace limbo more than a few times) to a fistful of magical hours discovering everything during your first run in this whodunnit 'em up, plenty of replayability exists on top of this to chalk up a few hours more finding everything you've missed or irreparably accidentally'd (which WILL likely happen sooner or later).
A definite reccomendation for those looking for a charming little 2D western oozing freedom and can tolerate something a bit more basic, some words of caution over how repetitive it can get after the magic fades (just like Todd Howard's game, all of 'em).

The Far West is closer than ever before.
Objectively speaking, Westerado: Double Barreled is not the most realistic western game out there; yet it somehow manages to convey the sense of lawlessness and romanticism of the Old West better than any other. Sure, Red Dead Redemption or Call of Juarez show vibrant 3D worlds packed with action, but I did not miss any of it while playing the game of Ostrich Bandidos.
The first thing that struck me was how easy and immediate is to simply draw the gun and kill an NPC; the second was to realize that this often leads to an irreversible loss of an optional quest. It may bother some, but this is freedom in its purest form: you can do virtually anything withing the constraints of the gameplay, as long as you accept that those actions will have consequences. And these are not necessarily bad, since it is always possible to reach the end of the game -- only completionists will have to be extra careful not to skip any secondary quest.
And the rest... you should see for yourself. Don´t be put off by the retro graphics, which look surprisingly ok after the first half hour, or by the limited range of options. Instead, play this game for the unique feelings that it conveys in its modest visual style.

If you're a fan of the show, odds are you've already bought the game.  If you haven't, wait for a decent sale, 30 bucks with the DLC, tops.  I was never particularly amazed by DBZ games since they always featured reliving the battles for whatever inane reasons they could come up with (if we were given any).  This time around, there is a framework and overarching plotline that provides an actual reason to do so.  It's not a great plotline, no more or less so than any of the DBZ cashgrab movies, but I give them credit for doing something different and finally letting us build our own characters in the DBZ universe.  There is a severe lack of interaction with that universe's characters outside of any you may have to battle, and so you always get the feeling that although you've finally broken into the universe in a personal way, it's still going to be at arms-length, but at least your foot is in the door.
If you're not a fan of the show, there is no reason to buy it.  If you're a casual fighting game enthusiast, you will only enjoy yourself as long as you accept the fact that you will never know what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on.  If you're a fighting game aficionado, then definitely skip this title as the mechanics are too basic for you to get any enjoyment out of it.
The game itself has many treats alongside typical DBZ-game flaws.  I don't like the fact that if you're playing solo, you still have to connect to a server.  That tells me that someday when this game's servers go down, that's it.  No more.  You can customize your move-set completely, apart from basic attacks, but energy moves far outstrip the damage of conventional striking and strike-supers.  Personally I wouldn't mind this but the energy moves almost always have horrible tracking.  Although you can pick other races (and many do), they're not balanced that well, and for some godawfully stupid reason you cannot make multiple characters until you beat the game.  Every race has tendencies towards one of the six stats, which means that no matter how many points you dump into a bad stat for that particular gender/race/build, it will NEVER be as good as one with tendencies towards that stat.
As an example, I built a beefy saiyan male, wanting him to be balanced. That particular combination of traits (male, muscular, saiyan) is pretty bad at energy blasts.  I got him up to level 70.  My thin, tiny female saiyan does the exact same damage as him with the same moves, point dumps, and equipment --- at level 30.  Equipment, items, skills, and money are thankfully shared between all characters.
The game's set up like an instanced-mmo with a small pool of RNG drops for every mission.  Side missions, of which there are many, can be done with a team, though the game is tricky about adding your friends to one.  Story missions must be done alone, with or without AI companions.  For whatever weird ♥♥♥♥ing reason, you cannot have a team of both one other person AND an AI companion, even though solo you would have two AI companions.
When you're not bashing and blasting your way through the somewhat short story, you'll probably be doing pvp matches or PQ's, parallel quests. PQ's are oddly where most of the game's content is, alongside being able to adopt specific characters as masters that are unlocked through the story in order to learn their special moves.  Each PQ has a page telling you what the potential rewards are, but not always how to get them.  Some of the unlocks have incredibly specific requirements, and even if you do everything right, RNG kicks in.  You might get lucky, or you might be repeating the same mission for HOURS.
The game can be very "challenging."  AI characters eventually will have stats your character could never, ever have, and missions will start dumping you against ridiculous odds (as in versus multiple fighters at one time, by yourself).  Enemies have a tendency to spam ultimates one after another to juggle you as you're getting up.  Transformed characters that theoretically should run out of energy and return to their original forms never do.  Time and again I've seen enemies be completely surrounded by AI companions only to dash out of the circle, wayyyy over to where you're trying to build energy so they can spit tiny unblockable ki blasts at you to interrupt whatever you're doing.
Combat isn't terrifically balanced, either for or against you.  Energy moves miss a LOT.  There is a definite hierarchy in both moves and builds, and outside of roleplay, these are hedged into very narrow combinations if you want maximum efficiency.
You cannot hit characters that are knocked down.  I assume this was done for pvp reasons.  If you send an enemy flying, then begin an energy move, it WILL be absorbed into the ether as they regain their footing just fine, undamaged.  You can use this trick yourself, avoiding the quick-recovery in order to buy yourself more time to recover stamina while you enjoy your inexplicable invincibility frames.
Supers (either the strike version or an energy blast), as far as I've been able to tell, cannot be interrupted, save by special moves that take skill slots.  That character will take all the damage to their stamina instead.  There is a TINY window warning when you are being targeted, and assuming you can get over to them before the blast is finished, you would have to hit them enough to consume ALL of their stamina to knock them down, during which of course they have invincibility anyway.  Even the computer itself has only managed to do this to me twice in 50 hours.  Yeah, good luck with that.
In spite of occasionally cheap battles, merely functional AI, and what can be extremely tedious farming for mission rewards, the game will still pull you into its universe, for quite awhile if you let it, and with Xenoverse 2 apparently being a hot mess of bugs right now, this is the best we've got to work with.

This is a dragon-centric game obviously made by dragon-fans and for dragon-fans. I really liked how the dragon looked, as in his colors, paws, tail, wings, sounds he produces and his funny british-accent voice. In terms of story the game doesn't contain anything groundbreaking, it takes itself lightly and the humans are presented in the game as pests bothering this here draon while he sleeps. He doesn't know much about humans so it's rather funny to read his first thoughts about them.
If you do love dragons you'll have nice time playing this currently simplistic game, in other cases the game currently doesn't have too much to offer but for a game in early access made by only one person it plays quite nicely - you have full 3D levels where you can fly (the height of your flight is limited by your jumps, basically it's more like hovering in original Spyro games, withoit losing height though), you can jump, claw and bite your enemies as well as eat certain prey (peasants and sheep). The mechanics work well, the only exception is when there are many enemies the dragon turns the other way around when you wanna bite this enemy in front of you, it happened to me several times. There isn't a lot of games where you can feel yourself as a powerful dragon having fun killing off stupid human vermin and this one surely can fill the void for dragon-enthusiastic people like me.
What the game currently lacks is more cool abilities for the dragon like magic or specials that could result in massive area-damage, some better targeting when you're flying - your fire-breath looks rather weak and it's quite hard to flame lots of enemies when you're flying. What I wanted to do is quickly fly around to avoid acrcher's arrows and set them all on fire, and it was hard to do as the fire is quite weak, this probably needs to be tuned.
Another cool thing would be adding RPG elements - learning new abilities for your dragon, improving its stats and HP etc.
Also the health bar could be more creative than just a simple green line, something like a dragon's tail/wing or heart, or his snout. Example of cool-looking healthbar is the game Drak on (search it on newgrounds).

So this is the first DBZ game I have played in a while. I had been dissapointed with some of the past games and had taken some time away from the game series though I am a huge fan of DBZ in general. That being said I am glad I returned to the series for this game, even though it was long after DBXV's release.

The only two issues I have with the game are that the combat system is pretty simple and could use more complexity, mainly the melee combo system, and because of the roster of older games the roster leaves something to be desired. Neither of these issues, however, are unforgiving.

As the demon Azutura threatens to reawaken, Jordan has been chosen to take up the task of keeping him asleep. However, things go unfortunately wrong and ends up plunging you into a quest to try and take out all of the other demons. To finish this quest, you'll need to recruit numerous allies to aid you. Thankfully, the game provides 31 potential allies for you to recruit. These allies range from being a chicken to a celebrity, and there's even a dragon you can recruit in!
It's a good thing the game provides so many characters though, even if some are quite well hidden. The Book of Legends has a major love for giving you party splitting sections, ranging from just a few battles to entire dungeons. I really disliked these sections as I've never really been a fan of things that force you to have split parties. Thankfully the game does give experience to those characters who aren't in your active party (though the experience doesn't spread out to those in a split party, at least I never noticed it doing so).
While I heavily disliked the party splitting, I did enjoy The Book of Legends overall. There's a lot to do, especially for folks who are completionists, and the story is fairly enjoyable.

Sniper Elite, the original sniping game, was a console game port set in WW2, and it is an interesting "sandbox" type game where you are given an objective and how you approach the mission is up to you. You work for the OSS, predecessor of the CIA, and your job to prevent the high-tech German scientists were working on from falling into Soviet hands. This means you will be fighting both Germans and Russians, usually behind enemy lines. You will crawl, sneak, walk, and run around the level, set traps to cover your back, make a silent kill or two, use sound of artillery to cover your shots, and so on. The levels are quite open, and enemies have patrol routes but will react to you and other factors. Actual approach is up to you. Ambush with bombs, shoot with gun, or other approaches? The interface is clunky due to console port laziness, but the "bullet cam" where the viewpoint tracks the bullet and the kill lead to a lot of imitations since. All in all, this is a game that started the genre, and it can be extremely hard, but extremely rewarding. If you find this too hard, try its sucessor, Snipe Elite V2, a thoroughly modernized remake.

Having played the Duel Links app for a long while I was curious to see what they would do with the steam version. My main beef has always been that it’s a condensed version of the original trading card game (OTCG). So, I was hoping that with the additional real estate (the computer screen) they would expand it to the full version. Alas they did not, but I am sure that was so they could keep the mobile users integrated with the new pc users.
If you are now joining us on steam, good on ya and here is what you can expect. Duel links is a concise, condensed, and uncomplicated version of the OTCG. So, if you wanted to play “real” Yu-gi-oh this is not the place to do it. However, it still offers a fun experience with quite a nostalgia trip. They pull the voice audio of all the characters from the anime which adds to the fun. Also, the visuals are pretty good and gets us one step closer to that, “what if we could do 3D duels in real life?” What makes this game unique is the inclusion of specific and nonspecific character abilities to use during duels to give you an edge. And while you can duel the AI’s until the sun burns out, you can jump right into pvp as well. Unfortunately, there is no full screen option which is weird.
For people like me who are hoping over from the app, there isn’t much new but a few note worthy things. It’s bigger! (no really) Also there is a higher graphical fidelity which is nice. The main thing is the duels themselves are much improved. During any duel it gives you detailed information about what’s going on and what things are much easier. Also its lot easier to do stuff with a mouse than with a finger lol. Just please remember that if you are porting over from your mobile device you to set up your data transfer account with Konami if you don’t want to lose all of your progress!
Pros:
Good graphics
Generally fun
Nostalgia trip
Cons:
Not the full OTCG
No full screen
Kind of grindy

Westerado is an old spahgetti western game with a robust world that has plenty in it to keep you entertained. Simple gameplay and giving the player the power to go through the game leisurely make for a fun time. I went in not expecting much and the game got hooked for the entire playthrough.
Soundtrack
When it comes to sound design all I ask of games like this, is to go with what's happening on screen and set an appropriate tone. Westerado does this and then goes further. Making enjoyable sounding music to accompany the game throughout. Although all talk is text they do get the sound effects on point to balance it out. Thanks to the sounds shootin' yer guns feels satisfying as ever.
Gameplay
The gameplay as stated before is quite simple and yet it is so effective at inducing fun. You have a large 'open' world with plenty of places to visit and even tasks that you must complete to get to some of them. Or you can choose to ignore it all and follow you're main objective which is not related to any of it. Your main objective is figuring out who murdered your family and burned down your ranch. The game leaves that person up to RNG. It's a guess who approach. The murderser's appearance is randomized and you must complete quests or speak with certain people to gain small clues as to who it was. It can be done quickly or it can be done as you please. Either way after a short tutorial what you decide to do before you find your man can result in very different endings. The variation is surprising here and well done. Combat is a highlight. You can move, run, draw your gun, and shoot. The shooting requires you to line up your gun horizontally with an enemy onscreen. And it can be hectic at times but once you get the hang of it you'll likely have no troubles. One of the best parts is you can walk up to anyone and perform any of these actions on them as well. It's funny you have the power to interrupt anyones dialog by drawing your gun. I really enjoyed this freedom. More games need this kind of approach.
Story
The story is about revenge, love, greed, and guns. That is if you're counting the sidequests. Becasue the main story is as simple as previously described. You can engage with all of it or none of it. Someone take away your home and family from you and you seek revenge. There really isn't much more to say.
Graphics
The pixel art is fantastic and it was a great choice for this game. Made for some really great moods in certain locations and fits with the rest of the game's simplicity.
I would recommend this easily. I thought it was just one of those games to play when you're up for wasting time but I was pleasently surprised by what this game had to offer. Pick it up, it's a fair price and delivers lots of fun and variation.

I've never written a review for any game before, but I feel like I have to say something about Westerado. It's one of the best indie games I've played in a while, and even though I got it in a bundle, I'd say it's worth it at full price. From the moment I started Westerado up, I was hooked.
The story deals with you figuring out who murdered your family and burned down your ranch. The murderer's appearance is randomized every time, and each game, you complete quests to get clues as to his appearance. You can do this fairly quickly; it only took me a couple hours to beat my first playthrough.
What really sets the game apart, though, is how replayable this simple premise is. The complexity is in how the world reacts to you. It's got a quasi-open world map, in which you can go anywhere on the map and talk to and shoot anyone at any time. This can actually lock off certain endings and quests, and doing certain questlines also locks off other questlines, making it impossible to see everything the game has in one playthrough.
The gameplay is simple but extremely satisfying. You can move, run, draw your gun, and shoot. The shooting is fairly simple; it only requires you to line up your gun horizontally with an enemy onscreen. However, the gunplay is immensely satisfying, due to the simple controls and the outstanding sound effects. I really can't stress enough how good it feels to play this game. I've only playing using a keyboard, but a controller should work just fine as well, since there's only a few buttons needed aside from movement.
Westerado also really nails the western movie aesthetic; the world they've created, the interactions you have with it, and the characters within it feel lifted out of a movie, and there are actually a few fourth-wall breaking moments that allude to this fact.
If you're looking for something unique to play, don't pass Westerado up. It may seem simple on the surface, but it won't leave you disappointed.
