Great game but you can complete it in about 1-3 hours so wait for a sale.  This game is a retro-style isometric-2d game where you play as a gunslinger in the west looking for your family's killer.  It has some pretty cool mechanics such as pulling out your gun first, cocking it, then being able to fire  which allows you to sometimes bluff someone into not fighting or giving you info and you can do this in dialogue options as well.  So, you run around helping people to find out clues about the killer and you will find out tidbits about what he is wearing (pants, hat, shirt, etc).  Once you have all of your information, you can look for him in the towns and train stations to find him, chase him, and kill him.  There are a lot of side quests, the combat is simple but fun, and there is a good amount of humor referencing hats and the western/southern accent (I is always pronounced "Ah" with the main character, as in "Ah'll see what Ah can do.")  The game is also fun to rivisit from time to time since it is such a short playthrough, but depending on how you play different things can happen plus the killer is always randomized.
Great game, very short, feel free to get it on a sale.  Heck, with Steams refund policy, you have a good chance of playing, beating it, and refunding it...although I would encourage you to keep it since it is a good game.

One of the most beautiful and emotionally-moving games I've played.  Very similar to games like "Gone Home."  It's short (~ 2 hours to play) but the gameplay is as diverse as the stories you experience.  As you explore the house, you live the last moments of a dozen family members with unique gameplay mechanics for each one.  In one story, I was a child imagining myself as a cat, owl, shark, and them something "else."  In another, I read through a chillingly-narrated comic book and controlled the character's POV actions in several frames.  All in all, I would have paid more than $20 for an experience half as good as this game. I imagine I won't forget this experience anytime soon.

I really enjoyed a lot playing Portal and Portal 2. Unfortunately, I didn't really get interested in this mod. This is due to 2 facts :
- You don't really want to see the end of the game, because there's no tension, no suspense, you don't feel stressed, you don't fear anything. Also, nothing suggests a "surprise" which would make you wish to complete the game. As a result, Aperture Tag is one of these games, staying in your library, forgotten while not even completed...
- The gameplay itself isn't really fun, as you'll have to stop to prepare your paint before you can move forward in the map. This was not a problem in Portal, since you had to think and reflect about where to place your portals. Here, there's no difficulty, everything is obvious... Well, you can try to speedrun and to shoot the paint while running on it, but then it goes very, very much harder and you don't want to tryhard a game which doesn't reward you for performing well (it could have been with Steam Successes for example)
To conclude, developers made a good work on this mod, but it wasn't enough to make it interesting.

To call it a game is somewhat understating what Eve is. Eve is brutal, you will be blown away just because someone had a muder-boner for killing people that day. People will set out to destroy everything you have made.
But it's more than just that. Eve will test your logical thinking skills and fine-tune your ability to analyse a situation and make tactical changes on the fly. This is less a game and more an anarchy simulator in space. There will be great times where you feel like you can take anything on, there are hard times where days, weeks, or months of hard work you have put in is lost in a single bad choice. You will make enemies, that much is guaranteed. You will also make some of the best friends of any gaming community online.
There game will make you work hard for everything you attain and leave you under no illusions that if you might not lose it all. Whole empires have been crushed in single battles. And it's worth every moment.
Life isn't fair and neither is Eve Online. But if you put a bit of work in, you can have more fun in this game than any other game on the market.
If you've got the drive to play it and balls big enough to handle it.

Also the steam version of the game WILL NOT LAUNCH with Windows 10 (and prior releases if the reviews are to be trusted) and that is why I cannot in good conscience recommend this version of the game. Here's how to launch it correctly :
First, start the game like you would do normally. Nothing will happen but Steam will say that the game is running. you'll have to go to the Task Manager (ctrl+alt+del, or to open it directly, ctrl+l.shift+escape), then go to details, then right click on GOTHIC.EXE, then click on "analyze wait chain", then close whatever program's interfering.
Then you'll have to download the 1.08k patch, then the player kit for Gothic 1, then the system pack. Once you've done all this, install them all, IN THIS ORDER : if you don't, the system pack won't be able to install.
AND THEN you'll have to go to the root directory of Gothic 1, go in the System folder, right click on gothic.exe, select "properties", select the "compatibility" tab, and tick the "run this program as an administrator" box.
If you're patient enough to do all this, then congrats, one of the best series of role-playing games of the early 00's awaits you, adventurer.
If not, you're forgiven. just get the GoG release, I hear there aren't any bugs.
FIX YOUR DAMN GAME, STEAM !
PS : Don't trust the numbers you're seeing here, I put waaaaay more than enough hours into this game to be able to have an opinion on it. The system pack comes with a launcher that bypasses steam I believe, that's why I seem to have played only an hour when I really have played dozens.
PPS : Also, beware of exploring TOO much. This can lead to bugs that can potentially break your game. For instance, in my first walkthrough, I explored the monastery north of the swamp waaaayyyy before the story tells me to go there. When I did, the game bugged and broke. I couldn't progress into the story anymore, no matter what I did, because I was supposed to open the gate leading to that place when AND ONLY WHEN a certain NPC was there. So yeah, be careful. Don't go to any remote place until the game specifically tells you to do so, or if you're willing to play through hours of content you've already done, back your main save file up by saving in a separate file AND THEN do it.

TL;DR - Game is well worth buying, but there's a chance it won't launch for you.
The game itself is amazing, it follows on from 1 in terms of hype and gameplay really well, unfortunately like many of the other negative reviews you'll read on here it doesn't launch for me. It stalls for a little bit on a black screen and then exits.
Oddly enough, a while after purchasing I saw something which reminded me of prototype 2 and I figured I'd try launching it, fresh with the desire to play the game again, only this time it randomly worked. I mean I hadn't touched the thing since I bought it and tried to fix the black screen issue, but now it just ran. I completed it in around a week while it was still launching alright, then I forgot about it for a while, and when I tried to return to 100% it, it's back to the same old issue.
Mainly treat this review as a "buyer-beware" - If the game will run for you it's fantastic and well worth playing especially if you're a fan of prototype 1. If it doesn't, there's no fix that I've found that's worked - there are dozens of online forums detailing the same issue and I have yet to see a cure-all solution - so you'll have just wasted your money.
I want to recommend this game, but morally I can't knowing that for a good portion of people there's the possibly that it might not even run.

I know that somebody put a lot of effort into this game and I really tried to get into it, but eventually the game got just so horribly unbalanced that I couldn't force myself to try to grind and try any further.
The story isn't very innovative and the main character is quite unlikeable. The fact that every time one of the characters makes a 'joke' the author had to add 'ahaha' at the end of the line really gets to you after a while. The dialog is lengthy and not well written. It's also quite repetitive and after some time you really have to force yourself to still pay attention to it.
It's a typical RPGMaker game in presentation, but I have to admit that the graphics and music are well chosen, The locations are again lengthy and exploring them grants you a lot of usable items, but sadly not enough equipment. Which brings me to my main complain about this RPG.
The game is unbalanced. Heavily unbalanced on multiple levels. The first 'dungeon' is far too easy and your character way overpowered. You continue and gather other characters and the game is still way too easy and that's not because I gained too many level early on. A level up in this RPG basically has no effect on your combat performance except when you get a new skill. The increase in HP and attack power are so minimal that it's hardly worth to grind at all. In terms that means that you have to rely on equipment to give you the needed boost to get better in combat. For a good amount of the game that doesn't matter much as the 'mob' fights are ridiculously underpowered and you won't have a problem at all, but in boss fights it shows that something isn't exactly working out. You can still push through those with a bit of tactic and luck, but it's starting to get really frustrating.
At some point the game forces you to play as a group of characters that are completely underpowered. Only one of them has magical abilities and they aren't very powerful. This is when the game grinds to a halt. You can't make them stronger by leveling up nor can you get better equipment. So every tougher fight is a pure gamble if you'll get through.

So far that's not too bad, but add to that one enemy that always attacks first, has a quite strong AOE spell that costs you about 50% of your HP and is nearly not hittable because it dodges every attack. I'm not kidding. In random encounters those enemies flee after a couple of rounds, but then you run into a forced encounter with three of them and they don't flee. I tried it five times, each time grinding a level for each character more and there's no way to get past them except for getting extremely lucky and hitting them with every attack.
I don't like not finishing a RPG, but this one is just so annoying to play that I won't try to push through. Don't waste 14 hours on this one like I did and get a better RPGMaker game instead.

"Battle Crust", like it says on the description, adheres to the 80's/90's style “traditional” shooter design in aesthetic and gameplay, which are less commonly seen nowadays compared to the more modern “bull hell” design of shooters. I've expressed my preference for the former in previous reviews here on Steam, so I'm always delighted when new ones show up that are well crafted. "Battle Crust" delivers on that front. “Vertical R-Type” has been the common description for it, which pretty apt. The controls are pretty simple, one button for regular shooting and one button for charge shots. In order to use the charge shot, you need to have collected at least one power up. It's straightforward enough where someone can pick up and play it very easily. In addition, adhering to the classic style shmup formula, there are multicolored powerups to collect that transform your standard pea shooter into an assortment of different weapons with strengths and weakness. The game does a good job of placing these accordingly, tailored to whatever is going on while you are playing. It's easy to recover you charge shot upon death, and you never feel like you have to rely on your weak default weapon for too long. You can also select from three different charge shots upon starting (and continuing), which have different properties, and change the flow of the game accordingly.
The game is pretty well designed and telegraphed, so you never feel like your deaths are unfair. Skilled shump players, however, who habitually single credit Cave shooters and the like would likely find the challenge lacking except on hard maybe, and consider it a sour point. For others, it will be challenging enough (I'm just now getting to last stage on Easy on a credit, to give you an ideal of my skill level), and thus best suited for more casual players, beginners, or people nostalgic for classic shooters. The presentation is enough of a draw for groups outside of this to at least check it out though.
And then there's the music, done by my personal favorite VGM composer Hyakutaro Tsukumo. Previously known for his works with the defunct company Technosoft ("Thunder Force V" chief among them), and more recently for his soundtracks to indie dev Dracue Software's run and gun mech games, such as "Gunhound EX" (also on Steam). Instead of employing his usual over-the-top modular synth rocking that defines lots of his works, he opted to compose the soundtrack with old school FM synthesis to match the classic theme of the game. Despite the retro, chiptune sound, the music still has a lot of the rock and roll grooves and melodic, bombastic highs common in Tsukumo's style. On the whole, it is very well done, and a soundtrack release is the only thing I'd like to see from this down the road, because I think it deserves one.

First I want to say that the game is a solid shoot'em up. It feels like a vertical R-Type with a late 8-bit/early 16-bit feel to it. The gameplay feels like a good starting point for players who are just getting into the genre and don't want to have a wall of bullets thrown at their face. It also offers just enough difficulty in the later stages in normal mode to keep things interesting for novice players like myself. The hard difficulty is where players with a little more skill than myself will find their fun since normal mode is pretty much 1CC'able first time around for expert players.
The music is also pretty darn good and really gives an older play like myself a warm and fuzzy sense of nostalgia when playing. The sound effects also sound like something straight from a classic shooter from the yester-years. Overall I think the sound and music for the game are spot on and go great with the aesthetics.
Weapon variety in this game feels great and weapons don't feel thrown in just for the sake of choice. The play gets to choose from 3 charge attacks in the beginning. Each attack comes with pros. The Megashot, for example, stops your ship upon fire rather due to kickback, but grants you a huge damage boost. The weapon upgrades feel great and all have different damage levels along with utility that make certain situations more tolerable.
The game is pretty bare when it comes to configurations. To put the game into TATE you have to set your monitor to landscape. This isn't a big issue, but people will find this annoying. The game also automatically scales to your current monitor resolution instead of allowing you to select it. The game itself runs fantastic. These are issues to be expected from a game made by a ridiculously small team with a micro budget.
Overall this is a solid purchase for those looking to scratch that shmup itch.

Having played the Duel Links app for a long while I was curious to see what they would do with the steam version. My main beef has always been that it’s a condensed version of the original trading card game (OTCG). So, I was hoping that with the additional real estate (the computer screen) they would expand it to the full version. Alas they did not, but I am sure that was so they could keep the mobile users integrated with the new pc users.
If you are now joining us on steam, good on ya and here is what you can expect. Duel links is a concise, condensed, and uncomplicated version of the OTCG. So, if you wanted to play “real” Yu-gi-oh this is not the place to do it. However, it still offers a fun experience with quite a nostalgia trip. They pull the voice audio of all the characters from the anime which adds to the fun. Also, the visuals are pretty good and gets us one step closer to that, “what if we could do 3D duels in real life?” What makes this game unique is the inclusion of specific and nonspecific character abilities to use during duels to give you an edge. And while you can duel the AI’s until the sun burns out, you can jump right into pvp as well. Unfortunately, there is no full screen option which is weird.
For people like me who are hoping over from the app, there isn’t much new but a few note worthy things. It’s bigger! (no really) Also there is a higher graphical fidelity which is nice. The main thing is the duels themselves are much improved. During any duel it gives you detailed information about what’s going on and what things are much easier. Also its lot easier to do stuff with a mouse than with a finger lol. Just please remember that if you are porting over from your mobile device you to set up your data transfer account with Konami if you don’t want to lose all of your progress!
Pros:
Good graphics
Generally fun
Nostalgia trip
Cons:
Not the full OTCG
No full screen
Kind of grindy

Yes, I'm aware that the expansions are not included (that's not really their fault). Yes, I know there's an HD mod for the original version (in fact, I love it). Then why did I essentially buy Heroes III for the third time, giving Ubisoft, who has otherwise not treated this magnificent video game series with the respect it deserves, my not-so-hard-earned money? I've probably sunk more time into HoMM3 than any other game, and experiencing this brilliant game with high-resolution graphics is quite refreshing after playing it for well over a decade with sprites made for 800×600 screens. Unlike some other reviewers, I think DotEmu has actually done an excellent job upgrading the graphics (with a few minor exceptions). The gameplay is of course still there, as captivating and enjoyable as ever. The third instalment is the pinnacle of the series, and with the way games are made these days, there will probably never be anything quite like it again. I think this HD edition is the closest you'll ever get to a true 21st-century Heroes of Might and Magic game (not that Heroes IV is bad – it's just different), and that's worth getting, if you ask me.

This is a hesitant recommendation. 15$ is perhaps a little steep for what the game offers - with a little over five hours I've beaten it twice and seen most of what it has to offer. That's all I can really think of. It's likely because I don't look too far into games beyond gameplay, because I'm a simple dude, but in any case, the two cons listed really can get to you if you're not of the temperament to handle them. But all in all, Xenoverse is a good, fun game that I definitely recommend picking up. Of course, the sequel's out too, and I've heard it made some pretty good changes, so I also look forward to getting that. But I digress. It's a good game for those who enjoy Dragon Ball fighting games, and I do, even if I'm not really a fan of the show itself (It has some interesting things about it, though, and don't get me wrong, I don't really hate it).
In any case, I'm glad to have this game back, and I'm glad I'm getting out of it what I'm getting.

EVE Online is a massively multiplayer online space game that has a long and storied history. Its playerbase predominantly consists of long term players who I found to be extremely newbie friendly and supportive in many ways. This is a game that is less user friendly than any game I have ever played, and has a much steeper learning curve, so that support that the long term players provide is essential.
The game revolves around the skill point system, which consists of accumulating points over time as long as you continue to pay the subscription fee. They continue to build regardless of your online status, which is nice. Its a definite pro, but its offset by the fact that any player who has subscribed longer than you will always be better in terms of those skill points. These skill points are spent on gathering evermore skills, which in turn open better ship types, weapons, and defensive options to you. Ships, weapons, and defences (sheilds, armor, etc) all cost alot of money (ISK), and so you spend most of your time trying to acquire more and more ISK so you can buy fitted ships to use in Player vs. Player combat. In fact, losing ships is more fun than actually acquiring them in this game.
That brings me to the pvp. Player combat in this game is very different from any other pvp game. Losing a fight means losing millions of ISK in ships. Since acquring ISK is difficult and time consuming, you actually feel like you have lost a lot more than just a ship. You lose time. Given this fact, every battle you engage in has that "oh crap!" factor. The, "I cant afford to lose this ship!" element that puts you on the edge of your seat in every battle. Since there is no "safe" areas in EVE, every time you undock your ship, you potentially enter a battlefield. Its both exciting and terrifying at once.
I will close by saying that this ~IS~ the best pvp game I have played, and I have played in nearly all of them - both space and fantasy based. So, if you crave pvp combat of a gut wrenching nature, this game was made just for you. If you prefer the option of fighting battles when you feel you are ready, then may not be the best place for you to spend your time and subscription money.

TLDR; - I was working up the justification to actually recommend this game... Really. It has a charm to some of its dialogue that is rare and on the strength of that, combined with its semi-open world approach to plot, I was actually going to recommend this. That is, until I moved on, away from the main land the game starts on. Suddenly, the game went from LOLERSKATE city difficulty (even on HARD) to MELT FACE!!! Difficulty, without so much as a 'by the way, YOU"RE GONNA DIE OUT THERE!!', beforehand.
IOW: The first 2 or so hours are actually worth playing. That is until it becomes IMPOSSIBLE to play.
...
Full Review Points:
Pro:
- Charming Banter:
This is the first RPGMaker game I've played that gets the banter on point, and in character, most of the time. Combined with meeting some really ODD people in the world, I had to list this as a pro.
- Exploration Encouraged:
This is a mixed bag, as you may find yourself obsessed with checking every possible object in the game for potential loot... OR you can do what I did, and simply check the ones on your route and ignore the rest. I still managed to find 2 extra party members and several equipment upgrades this way, so I figure it’s a bonus worth a pro.
- Open World Questing:
This is the FIRST RPGMaker game I've played that allowed for side quests to be completed BEFORE you know about them. At least two of them, I didn't even know I had completed until I met the NPC that gave them. The banter even included the surprise that the player accepted a quest they knew they had already completed, and how wrong it felt... This is something more games should do.
Con:
- The intro forest is WAY TO LONG, WAY TO BIG, and WAY TO EASY:
It sets up the player to expect a cake walk, only to be insulted and smacked in the face for their trouble, by the time the actual difficulty curve sets in.
- Overpowered until Underpowered:
The main character is WAY overpowered until suddenly he isn't, and it occurs without ANY warning. And good luck keeping your optional party members alive... It’s a practice in frustration, and futility.
- No Fast Travel or Sprinting:
Back tracking is a problem... There are no easy exits to ANY area. And at least one quest had you re-enter an area you already cleared AGAIN to find a new hidden object. It is lame... LAME. But forgivable. It wouldn't be so bad if the back tracking was for a GOOD REASON and had worth wile rewards. But it doesn't.
- Grinding Required:
Equipment upgrades are few and far between. Optional party members join your party at extremely LOW level, requiring a ton of grinding if you hope to keep them alive longer than ONE hit, and that is BEFORE the difficulty spike from hell.
- The intro, is BADDLY translated... Or filled with lazy typo's. Both possibilities are terrible.

Warhammer 40K Dawn of War 2 is the first pure example of THQ's new take on the real time strategy genre. The resource gathering is all but gone and there are no structures to build, production or defensive. Instead you get to control small squads of soldiers with a variety of abilities in a micro battle against either the single-player hordes or an equally micro intensive multi-player opponent.
Dawn of War 2 stands a bit a part from other RTS's by having the single-player campaign and the multi-player battles play rather differently. In single-player you control individual soldiers, heroes if you will, through various maps filled with entrenched enemies and a boss at the end in a very RPG-like fashion. Your heroes gain experience, unlock new abilities and collect wargear to improve themselves along the way.
The story is great and captures the WH40K feel quite nicely and the story missions are mostly of a fairly high quality, unfortunately all the mission in between the story ones are just repeats of the same maps, the same enemies and the same bosses and it gets tiresome rather quickly. The highest difficulty actually succeeds in making the game a challenge although that dissipates somewhat once you start to max out gear and levels around midway through the campaign.
In the multi-player you take control of squads instead but the same RPG elements persist even if they are just included within the map and their effects doesn't persist beyond that. This produces some heavily micromanagement intensive battles which will be interesting for some, dreadful for others. I found myself missing the classic strategy base building quite often and as such the multi-player never really grew on me.
The developers also added in a second style of multi-player that quickly found itself far more popular than the standard match-ups called "Last Stand". In this mode you play together with up to three friends each controlling a persistent hero character that earns experience and unlocks equipment after each battle.
Last Stand plays out in an area, you and your 3 companions must survive increasingly tougher waves of enemies being thrown at you while earning score the better you play. That score is at the end of the round turned into experience for your characters.
While Last Stand is essentially a form of action RPG it feels more truer to the style THQ seems to have been aiming for in Dawn of War 2 and as such playing it comes much more naturally to those that do the single-player campaign first. I had a lot of fun in although the matchmaking system and the prevalent lag issues did annoy me quite a bit.
Graphically Dawn of War is a pretty enough looking game and the WH40K art-style works wonders as always. The sounds are as satisfying as ever and the voice-acting is sufficiently competent to keep you in the mood.
It is also worth noting that this is a Games For Windows Live game with all the problems that goes along with it. Don't even bother if you have an unreliable internet connection.
All in all Dawn of War 2 was a game I enjoyed despite it's flaws, the single-player was fun albeit a bit grindy at times. The regular multi-player was quite dull but the Last Stand mode made up for it, when it worked. It's a good game and a good buy, if you can stand owning a game with GFWL.

Gunpoint is a game that takes a  variety of genres-puzzle, platformer, and stealth-and fuses them effectively. The result is a majestic experience. Almost everything clicks-you have to deal with at times fairly complicated puzzles with the Crosslink, but they're never extremely difficult, and you also face plain old tests of speed almost as often. A forgiving autosave system and an extremely capable main character makes you feel vulnerable but never weak.
The level design is also extraordinary, almost always featuring multiple ways of accomplishing the same goal. This design, as well as an effective custom level editor, add replay value to what is otherwise a short game. The jewel in the game's crown is its jazzy soundtrack that fits the theme perfectly.
As a standout game, I highly recommend Gunpoint.

These issues are more prominent with custom made belts which brings me to the next glaring issue: The audio.
As pointed out by several other people the annoying repeating sound at a show start is just a glaring oversight which indicates that this game was either rushed, had no Q&A or the Q&A failed miserably or was overlooked.
There are numerous more issues like the recent Jerry Lawler fauxpas in the Hall of Fame DLC where a botched recording was actually left in the game.

I love this game, but it has its flaws. Online is a terrible, laggy mess. The character customization is much better this year with improved load times, but 2K really cut down on the ability to edit your character's body type. It forces a somewhat realistic body type on your custom superstar, so no characters where their hips are so thin it's almost invisible. Career mode is also very lackluster. It seems like the game is just rehashing last year's career mode and just adding features that really don't do much, such as selling T-Shirts. The promo engine is also pretty uninspiring.
The gameplay and fighting mechanics are pretty much the same as 2K16. It's good, and I've grown familiar with it. I do appreciate how all matches are rated on a five-star scale now though, as it encourages me to have a good match with different moves and spots instead of just trying to get the win as fast as possible,
The saving grace (for me, not sure about others) is the universe mode. I never played universe on the other games (I have WWE '12, WWE 2K14, WWE 2K16, and WWE 2K17) but this year I actually got to sink my teeth into having a full fledged Universe. I found it a lot more fun when I use my own custom characters and characters that my friends made, as opposed to just using the in-game superstars. I had my very own brand split, and I've had a blast playing it. The rivalries and cutscenes can become subpar and repetitive in its execution, but if you have a good imagination you can get over that.
Overall, get this game if you like to fool around and create your own stories. Get something else if you are looking for a serious fighting game/simulator.

Eve is a painfully addictive game. And not in a fun way.
First of all, this game is NOT free-to-play, that is false advertisement. It's a trial, even with the new Alpha skill set you are still limited to 5mil skill points (not a lot). After that you either sub for 15 a month or buy skill injectors for real money, otherwise no further progression. Daily Alpha injectors? Real money or many many hours grinding, forget getting one a day in game as an alpha clone (not subbed).
Skill progression is done on/offline at same rate, does not matter if you are playing or not. And without high skill points you will get nothing done. So you log in and set skills and log back out untill your character is skilled enough to do anything. Gaining funds/items/ships is either a VERY time consuming and grindy process or you spend real money to buy game money, VERY much pay-to-win.
Many will say this is not so, because you still lack real skill in the game, I call bs. Combat in this game is a rock-paper-scissor affair, there is very little skill involved. What it does take is massive amounts of patience to even find a fight, or you join a blob of others roaming about to gang up on 1 or 2 guys. Industry/mining is a point and click affair which takes many hours to days to get real payoff. Actual skill isn't involved.

Gothic was a pretty awesome experience. Had been hearing about it here and there from RPG fans, and I can see why it is considered a classic. After finally getting it to work (look up and download the Gothic 1/2 System Pack), the learning curve for the weird controls really messed me up for awhile, but while frustrated, I was at the same time intrigued with the atmosphere and other stuff being presented to ever think about quitting. Summing things up...
Pros:
+ Open world with a strong explorative element
+ No hand holding (learn as you go, and save a lot!)
+ Cool dark fantasy feel
+ Creative terrain and environment design with what resources the company made use of
+ High level of freedom, although the lack of direction may end up confusing some
+ The feeling of steadily growing from a scrawny weakling to the baddest dude around is great! Just make sure you commit to a certain stat path to avoid mediocrity
Neutrals:
Voice acting was... okay. Not the worst I've ever heard, and occasionally "bad" in a way that was more funny than annoying. Music was limited with atmospheric tracks, which is fine, but would have personally appreciated more background emphasis at important parts
Cons:
- Because it's so old, it was kind of a pain getting things running to start
- Controls are archaic to match the setting!
- Most characters were generic and flat, with few as memorable as the protagonist (being fully voiced), Diego, Xardas, and whatever crew you spend the most time with
- Would've been nice to see more of an ending resolution to when that freaking barrier came down. Also more consequences to having joined a certain camp
- Final confrontations with key antagonists were kind of anticlimactic, and could be easily cheesed using the environment and summon scrolls. Nitpicking? Probably.
Overall:
8.5 out of 10
Despite the oldness, frustrating combat, and occasionally flickering textures requiring a reboot to get rid of, Gothic is definitely worth at least one play through. Looking forward to playing the sequels (once I get them to work!)

Storyline is a little... melodramatic, which would've been funny if it were better written. Vocabulary is maybe fifth grade level? Use some bigger words.
Dialogues are poorly written. Characters are immature. Kids act like kids. Adults act like kids, which in some cases are acceptable but if it's all the time, it just becomes annoying. It's ok to have one annoying character in the party but not all of them.
Character actions shouldn't go into the dialogue box. It's like reading a play and the character is only acting out half the actions in the parentheses. There should be an additional animation, sound, or thought bubble.
Cultural themes are inconsistent. Everything looks mostly Asian. Then suddenly there's a cross. Then someone quotes from the Bible. I understand that this is technically a completely different world but it's still very confusing.
Dungeons are way too big for not having a map. It gets incredibly frustrating to go through them.
Battles are unbalanced amongst both characters and enemies. Characters are either way too strong or die too easily. Enemies from one dungeon to the next have too big a gap in level. Most people will not want to grind 20 levels before entering the next area.
Abilities and the battle system are poorly explained. For anyone who plays enough turn-based rpg's, it's no big deal. We can figure it out. For anyone else who's playing this type of game for the first time, the introduction is horrendous. No tutorials whatsoever.
Artwork is good, although I'm not particularly picky about 2D graphics as long as everything else is good.
Part of me wants to keep playing because I do like exploring all the areas but I think I'd have better use of my time doing something else. People often complain about "RPG Maker games" but I think the game engine is actually pretty good. It's all about how you use it.

Note: This review includes the entire DoW II collection including the original, Chaos Rising and Retribution with exception of Retribution's singleplayer campaign which entails the same campaign told from each faction's perspective with minor variations.
The simple description
+
It's Warhammer 40k.
Good squad-based tactical combat.
The graphics don't look outdated.
Excellent campaign.
Your character carries over from the first game to Chaos Rising's campaign if you so choose.
Excellent multiplayer.
Diverse factions.
Multirole commander mechanics for multiplayer.
Khorneflakes.
-
There aren't any particularly large maps available.
Basebuilding is almost none-existant
First intallment has Windows Live incorporated.
Like the first Dawn of War game, battles cannot reach truly epic proportions due to the unit cap.
Why? (verbose description)
I missed the idea of proper based building being dropped for a more mobile approach and the fact that the unit caps are somewhat small and contrictive. If you've played the first DoW games then this one will come as a different experience in a number of ways. Combat is more tactical and ability focused (ie a Marine squad can equip grenades to lob over a wall or obtain a squad leader that boosts performance in a variety of ways). Use of cover is important and cover is also destructable making firefights more dynamic. Vehicle combat is similar to that of Company of Heroes (also developed by Relic) in which vehicles will take more damage if shot in the rear and the positioning of the vehicle is important and can be directed. Vehicles also have abilities (ie the Baneblade most be told where to fire it's main gun and mortar) and add-ons (ie Imperial guard vehicles can equip additional armour and Space/ Chaos Space Marine Predator tanks can equip Lascannons).  As far as basebuilding goes, the most you can do is contruct turrets and that's about it, you start out with a command center + two basic turrets and this is where all your 'built' units will come from. Overall the mechanics work and the gameplay is well executed. There are however some issues that may bug some people. The lack of basebuilding, for instance, is a bit dissapointing and the unit cap is rather constrictive preventing you from having truly massive battles. This is in part due to the map playing field which is noticeably smaller than the original Dawn of War. Even the 6 player maps aren't really large enough and while the diversity in the map design is not bad the first Dawn of War definitely had better diversity in the maps.
All in all, DoW II is a fun and enjoyable game that represents the Warhammer 40k universe well if only a fragment. As for which of the 3 you should buy, get all of them. The first two are best for the campaign and Retribution has the best multiplayer experience of the 3.

What Remains of Edith Finch is an amazing story and the greatest "walking simulator" I've had the pleasure to experience, this sets a new bar as to what these types of games should aim for.
The game begins with a brief walk to the family house that you have just inherited and learning, via memories and memoirs about the people that once were family. The house is large and built like a puzzle box with several hidden passageways you have to "find" and traverse. The house, and game is easy to navigate and getting from A to B is easy and it's almost impossible to get stuck due to the game's linear structure. Puzzle elements are incredibly light and usually involve opening or interacting with something you just saw or experience in a memory. This keeps the pacing perfect, and with the almost frequent narration from Edith herself there's no "low" moments of wandering around aimlessly. It's incredible.
The art and sound design are absolutely perfect, while you're the only one in the house it feels alive and lived in; with a history it's dying to share. The game also has a very surrealistic element when it comes to the stories, as you hear the stories from several children who let their imaginations run wild. One of the stories, and my favorite, is told via comic book narrated by it's own Crypt Keeper type character.
The best part of the game is the writing, the history of the Finch family and it's members are tragic but it's not over the top and all very poignant. Several of the stories will tug at your heartstrings and really make you appreciate the family you have now. It's touching and wonderful.
If you're big on "walking sims" then get this, because it's the best of the bunch, if you don't care for walking simulators play it anyway or enjoy a let's play of it.

Gunpoint is a short and sweet stealth puzzler. If you enjoy puzzlers, then don't let the stealth aspect turn you away. All of the games "stealth" consists of not standing directly in front of an enemy so he shoots you. The steath is enjoyable, and minimal. The game's story is an spy thriller that you've probably heard somewhere before. It's setting and characters are all original, but what really shines is the game's writting.
There is no voice acting in Gunpoint, which some people may not like, and all character interactions are done via messageing between Conway (you) and the client (other character). You have a choice of what to say, but it's mostly cosmetic. The same things will happen no matter what you say, but the dialogue is HILARIOUS. I'm serious, I found myself chuckling and laughing out loud multiple times while playing Gunpoint. I don't want to spoil it, but trust me, it is GOOD humor.
The gameplay is rather simple but extremely unique. Some puzzles will wrack your brain as you try to figure them out. Solving puzzles using Gunpoint's Wirejack and Bullfrog Trousers is very fun and I have not encountered anything like it before. The Wirejack allows you to rewire electronics, so that lightswitch opens a door instead.
The Bullfrong Trousers are the best, though. They allow you to jump. High. Very high. You can also upgrade them to go even higher. It's fun when you launch yourself at an enemy and push them down. You can then punch them to knock them unconsious. You can also punch as fast as you can click. Keep punching that poor nightwatchmen, and you can and will turn him into mashed potatoes.
My real and only issue with this game is it's length. You may have noticed I only have two hours in this game. That's because I just beat it. And I'm not even any good at puzzle games. You live a week in the life of Richard Conway, freelance spy for hire. You solve one, rather intense, case and then the game is over. The pacing and storytelling is spot on, but it is short. There is Steam Workshop support to keep you solving puzzles, but I just wish there were more cases to solve. You will too.
So, final verdict? I don't really rate games, but for review's sake I will. Gunpoint, in my opinion, get's a solid 8,5/10. It would be a 9, but it is short. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes a good puzzle game, anyone who enjoys a stealth game, anyone who enjoys both, and anyone who wants to be a freelance spy with an amazing trenchcoat and fedora. "For your own safety, don't insult the hat." - Richard Conway, in regards to a rude comment.

I liked WWE 2k16 a lot, you can check out my review on that version, it wasn't perfect, but it was the best wrestling game in the last several years. Fast-forward to 2k17 and not a lot has changed, which is good, but I'll explain why this version is even better for me.
First off, I highly recommend the game if you like wrestling games. It's one of my favorites of all time, but if you didn't like 2k16 for whatever reason, you probably won't like 2k17, but it depends. CAW, which is my favorite feature in any wrestling game, is better in most ways in 2k17 than it has ever been.
I 've created about 30 wrestlers so far, so I've used it extensively. They've added a lot to every catagory (hair styles, clothes, teeth, etc...) but one HUGE disappoint for me is that you still cannot create little people. I would love to create a much shorter wrestler, but the shortest you can go is only 5'6", which continues to bum me out year after year. How hard would it be to extend the range of heights to under 5 foot??? I want to make a dwarf dammit!
Aside from that, you pick from body types and pre-made parts (arms, legs, chest, etc...) instead of using a body slider. This is a step back as it doesn't let me have the customization we once had. Gone are the days of making an incredibly huge breasted thin woman. Not that I create that type of CAW or anything...other than that, the CAW has improved in every possible way=more of everything!
It still irratates me that Yukes always does this year after year. Adds something, takes away. No create-a-finisher either, in this version, but next year they'll tout it as a "brand new never before seen feature!!!" Love/hate relationship when it comes to Yukes.
The graphics are a bit better, but some wrestlers actually look like♥♥♥♥♥♥compared to others. Not a big deal to me because I usually just use my CAWs, but you can tell some wrestlers got a little more tlc than others. Audio is pretty much poop as  Diddy's song selection is downright "weird" for a wrestling video game, but again, no issue, as I turn on most every wrestler's entrace as my menu music (jukebox). The commentary has been recycled for the last 5 years but it doesn't really bother me much, I'm more in this game for the actual gameplay.
The gameplay is about the same as 2k16, but with slight improvments! A 2nd opportunity to reverse on certain moves, the option to change the god-awful submission system to more of a classic button mashing submission system, and the "Break Out" feature after the match, which allows you to further pummel a wrestler you have already beaten. I LOVE these new features. ! The game pace is still more geared towards simulation, so expect slower pacing, not blazing fast arcade pacing. Although you can change some options, and that gets us to my final point...
If you don't like the game and you think it's utter ****, for the love of all that is holy and sacred in this world, CHANGE THE SETTINGS!!!! and change the balancing!!!!! I cannot emphasize this enough!!! I really did not enjoy this game that much until I changed some settings. The pacing was too slow and the time the wrestlers were stunned was way too long, which made for a very boring match! After tweaking the balance, I'm good to go, and now have a bit faster paced matches. That may not be your cup of tea, but there is plenty of settings you can change to make the match more fun for you, whatever that may be. Guys/gals, seriously, I've been playing wrestling games since NES, the settings in these Yukes titles can make a big difference.
In closing wwe 2k17 is the best we have yet on PC just don't go in expecting a No Mercy as everyone seems to do, every friggin year...ugh...in ways it's better than No Mercy,, the CAW feature alone will keep you entertained. As far as issues with crashes, rare, in my playtime only 3 times so far and it was during load, not during the middle of anything, so I never lost any data. Runs smooth maxed 60fps 24/7 on my system.
***I do not play any wrestling games online mode after atrocious matches I tried to have in a much earlier version, I believe it was wwe 10 or something, spamming the same move was the name of the game. Know going in that online in any wrestling game is a low priority and it should never be bought for that, it usually does not work well at all with many people picking a wrestler who is fast and can pull off the same exact fast move, over and over, so I could care less about MP in a wrestling game

Before I begin, I just want to say that I tried to like this game and complete it. Lord knows the blood and sweat I invested in the grueling 21 hours I put into this game. With that out of the way, let us commence:
I hate this game. I heard many a person say it was great, it was one of the best RPGs ever and that it rivaled Baldur's Gate, Morrowind and similar products. I decided to try it.
First off, the controls are clunky and take some getting used to, due to the fact that this game was made with a "Mouses aren't needed!" mindset, so the intended way of play is with the keyboard only. Seems somewhat puzzling, but remember that the game is "old" and it isn't that hard to become accostumed with the keybinds (plus, you can use a control scheme that includes the mouse if you so desire). However, I was able to adjust and proceed.
I won't speak of the graphics, because as I've said it's old so I won't judge that aspect. As far as the music goes, it's average. A mild soundtrack that didn't produce any awe inspiring moments in me or has any memorable tracks. It's just there.
And now for the gameplay... Oh dear God, the gameplay, and more specifically the combat. Never have I experienced such a rage inducing, badly made, awkward combat. In case you're wondering, picture Morrowind's combat (or any modern TES game for that matter), but the weapon movements are handled in a horrendous rhythm game type move set. You have the left and right swings, the up command for combos and down command for blocking. Sounds simple, except that in practice, it's so poorly implemented and executed that it makes even one on one fights a daunting task (and don't even attempt to picture how fighting a group is done).
As for the story, I won't speak of it due to spoilers and the fact that I didn't finish the game (I reached about half of chapter 4, when you
). From what I played, it was a slow crawl that remained uninteresting, albeit with a few good moments. However, as I've stated before, I didn't finish the game so I can't discuss the whole experience or evaluate any denouements.
I'll say it again: I tried to like this game. I seriously did. But in end, it was too much for me, I had to uninstall and move on. If you still wish to play the game, go ahead as you may enjoy it and find it entertaining. I just wanted to provide people with a warning, lest the same occur to them.

Response to Ato (since Steam won't let me post it in the comments due to it being over 1,000 characters in length.)
There are many issues with the game, such as lack of an FOV slider and lack of being able to change resolution in windowed mode and you promised split screen, which is on Xbox, but not PC. The problem I have is that you're expecting us to buy MMX for the fixes. I understand that MMX will have a lot more content, but it's frustrating that in order to have features that should have been in the game from the beginning you have to buy the sequel.
Also note that continuing to update the game will help draw in more fan and keep current fans. Look at games like Warcraft 3 TFT. They've updated it so that you can play it in modern resolutions despite it being 12 years old. Another example is Terraria. It's four years old and got a massive update with at least 800 new items, new events, and new features to make the UI more easy and quick to use. I'm not saying that you should add more content to MM1, just that the issues should be fixed.
I've also realized that this game is impossible for me to play on on a larger resolution monitor due to simulation sickness. I'm fine on my 1440x900 monitor, but on my 1920x1080 monitor the game makes me feel nauseous unless I play windowed, which makes it so I can't focus on the game. An FOV slider that goes up to 90 or higher FOV would fix this (MM1 has approximately 75 FOV which goes up to 90 FOV due to the aspect ratio; which isn't enough for me on a 1920x1080 monitor due to the size of it. I know you've said that TF2 has the same FOV before, which it doesn't. By default the game has 75 FOV on a 4:3 monitor, and 90 FOV on 16:9 monitor. You can increase it to 90 FOV on a 4:3 monitor and up to 110-120 on a 16:9 monitor.) Here's an example of what I mean
Yes, I had played many hours and had fun playing competitively, but now that I can't really play on one of my computers and the developers are expecting me to buy MMX for these to be fixed, I've lost faith in JForce.

I've played this game for a month (apparently), but I played on Android and Memu. The new Steam version is the same and performs better than on an emulator, with added screen for card info and duel log. But the game? In a nutshell, it's pay2win gamblebox hell. Let me explain...
Cards in this game are Common (C), Rare (R), Super Rare (SR), or Ultra Rare (UR). Gems are the free currency, but they're hard to come by. 50 gems (or $1) gets you 1 pack containing 3 cards (2 C's + R or better). The packs are bought from account-based boxes that can be reset*. Each box contains 200 (or ~85**) packs which contain 1 copy of every UR for that set, 1-2 SR, and a lot of R's and C's. C's and R's are virtually worthless in competitive play, SR's are good (some godly), but UR's are the real cards that make your deck WORK. Your deck only contains 20 cards so the game is based around tight strategies that usually revolve around key UR cards.
Now lets do some math... If you grind 50+ duels per day for a YEAR (19,000+ total) and complete all the limited time events, you'll be able to get all the characters to level 40 and buy around 1,000 packs. At worst, it takes 600 packs to get 3 copies of any UR you want. This means that you'll be able to bulid 1 half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥competitive deck OR snatch a variety of useful/splashable/tech cards (like Sphere Kuriboh) and build more PvE based decks. Either way, you just spent a year of your life on this crap and are still missing majority of the cards, decks, and fun. Also, a new box is released roughly every month, bringing new p2w meta decks and tech cards with the same power creep as the original card game. There are now 8 full boxes and 7 mini-boxes. In ADDITION to this demon of a grind, you'd need to spend about $1000+ to get the rest of the cards, or $5000+ if you want 3 copies of everything. AND you still don't have them all, now you have to grind Legendary duelists for the rest.
To make matters worse, this grind is BORING. You mostly just auto-duel and tap on your screen every few minutes, and have to recharge standard duelists (hourly energy system). They don't even give you more XP when they level up, but they'll use multiple copies of strong cards that aren't even available in the game! The dev's must love salt.
The game also suffers from simple technical issues (crashes etc.) and slow pace. Obvious decisions aren't automated, so you have to keep tapping buttons even when there's only one possible outcome***. It requires an always online connection too, and uses a lot of resources.
Duel Links had a lot of potential but Konami ♥♥♥♥ed it up as usual. Stay away if you value your wallet. If you want a free card game, play Chess Evolved Online instead.
*If you get lucky and pull all the UR's you want you can reset the box, because otherwise you won't pull any more.
**Every other box is a mini-box.
***"I see you're using Polymerization to summon Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon, and there are no other possible combos. But please, slowly select all 3 Blue-Eyes White Dragons in your hand and confirm that you are indeed doing what you've already set out to do." This engine is bad!

In defense of FourChords...
Firstly: Everyone is comparing this with Rocksmith and in all honesty that's somewhat unfair when you consider the fact that a multi-million (Billion?) dollar company (Ubisoft) produced that game. The reason I say it's unfair is because this game has something that the other one hasn't and that's charm.
Rocksmith is like the trainer who says, "Do 60 push ups and you'll eventually be an athlete".
FourChords is like the friend who says, "Do 20 push ups and I'll pay for the pizza".
Secondly: After a long day or a tough workout, I don't want to see a complicated layout showing the exact pattern of how to play a song. No, I just want to strum along with the chords I already know and this game does that. Sometimes you have to "Downgrade" your skills to experience the magic in music and this is what FourChords does.
My point is, Rocksmith can be intimidating with all its features and that affects the passion you have for something. FourChords doesn't ask anything, play a song and switch chords until you strum something that sounds somewhat like the song you want to play.
Cons
*The same background image of the girl holding the guitar, maybe add some creativity/animations to motivate the player.
*It doesn't have a feature where it can detect your chords, it has a strange point system which says, "I don't even know how you played but I'll pling your points anyway"...PLING!..."You're a Level 2 Amateur Club Rocker!".
*Computer generated music, it's not the original songs that you strum to so it might turn you off when it comes to sound quality. (Note: This is a pro also)
Pros
*The computer generated tones helps with strumming, playing along with skilled guitarists will mask your own faults and cause sloppy muscle memory.
*The straightforwardness makes you play songs without much effort, which is the reason we start playing guitar in the first place. Counter this with Rocksmith and you practice more than you play.
*Its charm makes me want to strum along with the guitar, giving it this organic feel with a variety of strumming patterns. (Which leads to the most important aspect)
*When it comes to learning rhythm then it beats Rocksmith by a landslide because you don't play to rack up points, hoping it will detect the sound. You listen to your strumming so that your beat is on point.
In conclusion, if you just want to become the guy who can strum a guitar around the fireplace then you don't have to know how to play 'Thunderstruck'. There's no need for that when it comes to the average Joe, you're still just as charming with a few basic chords and proper rhythm.
P.S. Don't use it to play charaoke with your family, the cringe caused by such an event will lead to the forming an awkward black hole implosion, possibly causing the death of humanity as we know it.
Other then it being an RTS, it is pretty authentic to the real game, lore wise.

I'm going to quickly compare this to Rocksmith Remastered,  because if you're looking at this you probably already own that. FourChords is an intersting counterpoint to Rocksmith. Rocksmith has an interesting difficulty approach... It waits until you get better, then gives you more to do so it can inform you that you stink again. I really like that game, but found its difficulty progression so whacked that I actually just set all the songs to 100% and skipped the silliness of partial chords.
Here's the main difference between FourChords and Rocksmith.... After I started with Rocksmith, I learned that it was often nice to sit and learn something from a book where you could progress as slowly as you wanted. Even the Rocksmith games, which are supposed to be solidifying your skills to play the songs force you to hurry or fail. FourChords doesn't care if you mess up. Perhaps that makes it a bit less ambitious than Rocksmith, but I also disovered it's a lot more relaxing to play. The somewhat stripped down versions of the songs are also an interesting take if you are simply wanting to learn to play the campfire versions of a ton of popular songs. This is much less complex than Rocksmith Remastered, but for a beginner is is just as good if not better as a way to practice open chord changes and get a lot of basic playing under your belt.
This is much more like an interactive book than a game. It focuses on delivering the information to you, and doesn't judge or care if or how you use it. I find it relaxing and fun and consider it totally worth the $30 I've spent on the core game and DLC.

You play the son of a rancher, who upon returning to your family ranch find it burned to the ground and both your parents murdered by an unknown assailant.
And that is the objective of the game. To find the killer and bring him to justice. You go around an open world completeing little jobs or missions for people in exchange for items or sometimes clues. The game is not linear and it is up to you how you want to go about completing the game.
The game is published by Adult Swim, but don't let that put you off. I'm sure many other people who are older (30+) see Adult Swim and automatically think obnoxious and immature game, like their shows, but that is not the case here. The game doesn't take itself TOO seriously, but the little humor it does have isn't over the top stupid like you'd expect from Adult Swim.
The controls themselves are good, and the interface works well. The only down side, and I guess this is a big one, is the combat. All shooting is done left and right. Don't get me wrong, this doesn't ruin the game, it just makes fire fights feel a little less meaningful.
One of the cool parts of the game, aside from the fact you can talk to every single NPC in the game, is that during conversations you can literally point yout gun at the person your talking to's face. Sometimes that will make them stop talking to you. Sometimes it will make them run. Sometimes it will make them attack. Sometimes it will make them give you their money because they think you're robbing them. And sometimes they will give you a clue about the killer.
The game itself isn't very long, about 4 hours. However, there is infinite replayability in the sense that every time you start a new game, it's a brand new killer. So if you bought the game and enjoyed it, you shouldn't feel dread whern you complete the storyline, because you can just do it all over again and huint a new killer.
Plus the fact you can shoot and kill anyone in the game is always nice when you're craving some "GTA like" blood lust.
Overall, I would recommend this game. I do think the $14.99 is a little high considering the length of the game and the fact that not everyone will want to replay it. I think 9.99 is a more appropriate price. But for ME, I do not regret spending the 15, and therefore I can recommend it to tohers.

What Remains of Edith Finch is a game I had been watching for a while. It seemed to have a lot of promise, and my trip to PAX South only served to further cement my interest in this game. So, I was pretty stoked when Annapurna Interactive, the publisher for What Remains of Edith Finch was courteous enough to extend a couple review copies for our site.
What Remains of Edith Finch typifies what is requisite in a good walking simulator/exploration game: an excellent story. However, Giant Sparrow, the developer (whom you all might remember from their previous game, The Unfinished Swan (which was excellent as well in point of fact)), wasn't content to simply offer an excellent story. They just had to go and craft what might be one of the most interesting and well thought out stories I have ever had the pleasure of playing through. It also defied classic tropes and stereotypes, preferring instead to take a lot of risks in presentation and topic matter, and I must say, the results were nothing short of brilliant.
You play as the narrator and protagonist, Edith, named after your grandmother, matriarch of the Finch family after its fateful migration to America and the path that journey set for the Finch family from that point forward. It seems the Finch family was destined to sorrow, with so many premature deaths, both accidental and mysterious, that the only constant with the Finch family was the certainty of a premature demise (with the sole exception of the elder Finch, who seemed to outlive all her descendants (excluding the protagonist of course)).
You, Edith, have returned to your family estate after the death of your mother as the only living member of the Finch family, to revisit your memories growing up here and solve the mysteries surrounding the deaths of everybody else in your family, or simply reconnect with them via memories and memoirs. This provides the core basis for everything you do in What Remains of Edith Finch and provides and incredible journey as you live through the last moments of all your relatives lives. After all that, you are provided with a shocking resolution that will have you thinking about this game for a long time after you complete it.
I will say there were a couple parts that were so evocative that I almost started to tear up. That, in my opinion, is a testimony to how connected you become to each Finch family member and how amazing the writing was that it could reach deep within both you and the game, create a symbiosis, and draw forth a wide array of emotions as you experience the individual stories within balanced against the overarching story being narrated by Edith Finch herself.
On a comical note, the Finch family was apparently filled with foodies, as the majority of books in the house that weren't historical in context were actually cookbooks....and the house is literally filled with books.
I found the story to be as refreshing and compelling as it was somber and introspective. It's been a while since I have encountered storytelling of this caliber in a video game. The story in What Remains of Edith Finch is an easy 10 out of 10
The gameplay in What Remains of Edith Finch is also quite innovative and unique in its approach. With most walking simulator/exploration games, you really have limited opportunities to interact with your world, instead simply observing the world as it is or was. However, in Edith Finch, you absolutely take an active hand in the events that shape the story. This innovative approach is actually just as relevant as the story telling itself in conveying the full weight of the events portrayed in the game.
You still have the classic elements of a walking simulator, but the bar was raised by adding new gameplay elements to capture each Finch family members last moments. For example, one section is set up as a cel shaded, comic book adventure with full interaction and even weapons to be used. Another section features a certain Finch family member transforming into a variety of animals with the gameplay reflecting the actual movements of each unique animal as it consumes everything in its path. Another involves kite flying, yet another a bathtub orchestra and dance. My favorite was the isometric dungeon crawler sequence mixed with a block and chop mechanic.
The actual variety of gameplay from one family member to the next, each specific to the individual family member and their hobbies or interests was incredibly impressive. Each was unique and provided excellent context to the story being told as well. A nice feature included is the ability to go back after finishing the game and replay any individual section independent of the others. This will be particularly relevant for achievement hunters, but I actually found myself simply wanting to experience certain aspects of the game again regardless.
The actual game itself, outside of the variations of gameplay, handled immaculately. I was running at a constant 60FPS with no drop off and no real strain on my computer as well. I think the average physical memory usage was about 6% throughout and it did not burden my rig in any way. I also experience no bug, crashes, or anything untoward while playing. This was a seamlessly crafted game through and through.
Another resounding 10 out of 10
The graphics in What Remains of Edith Finch were as amazing as they were quirky. Initially, you get the beautiful and yet standard forest walk setting typical of a large percentage of walking simulators. However, once you see the Finch estate, everything changes. What you get then are detailed graphics that are both entrancing and thought provoking all at once. Additionally, because there are so many mini games within What Remains of Edith Finch, you actually get a vast array of programming styles as it pertains to the graphics. The cel shading I mentioned in the gameplay section is only one example of the variety you will experience. I don't think the graphics work was groundbreaking in any way, but this is simply a gorgeous game regardless, and everything has a real purpose in adding to the visual experience as it relates to the story and gameplay as a whole.
9 out of 10
The audio in What Remains of Edith Finch is top tier.
First, I want to talk about Valerie Rose Lohman, who voices Edith and is the primary voice actor for this game. Hers was one of the finest examples of voice acting I have heard. She really captured the true essence of the character and was able to not only convey a sense of adventure and mystery, but also whimsy, humor, and thoughtfulness. What she really did was completely humanize Edith and not only make her a person you could completely connect and empathize with, but was also able, through her reading of passages written by or about her Finch family members, to truly bring them to life as well. I really can't overstate how amazing a job she did with this story and script. You can really tell when an actor connects with her character and that was definitely the case here.
While the voice acting was the shining light, the sound design was the icing on the cake. From the orchestrated music to the simple ambient noises in the house itself, everything made sense, sounded great, and was truly on point.
The audio in What Remains of Edith Finch was for me another easy 10 out of 10.
What Remains of Edith Finch might simply be the single best walking simulator/exploration game I have ever had the pleasure of playing. I think all told it took me about 2 hours to complete, and you could easily spend another hour wrapping up achievements and taking screenshots. This is a must own must play game that definitely shined on PC.

It feels a bit sparse, and in my eyes it doesn't quite compare to some of the earlier games in the series. It's as though more effort went into the earlier games. I haven't played many of the WWE games in years, in fact the last one I actually owned was WWE SvR 2009. Therefore with an 8 year gap between games, the difference in quality is striking, whether this is due to the series being taken over by 2K or just a general lack of creativity among the creators. It feels very uninspired and unfinished. I understand that these guys are expected to put out a new game every year, but still.
The graphics are better than 2009 etc, but that's to be expected and not something that I focus on much. It does make my PC lag pretty badly, but with a crappy little box like mine, that's more my fault than theirs.
The MyCareer mode feels outright repetitive with the illusion of challenges thrown in to try and spice up the repetitive slog of match after match after match. It also bugs me that you go straight from the training facility to WWE RAW. In my second week I was put up against Brock Lesnar. There's no sense of build-up, aside from the paper-thin Championship rankings, etc. I get that this is how it's been for years now, but in previous years the Career mode had actual storylines with rivalries and choice-based branching paths. This version doesn't even have voice acting besides the commentators, the ringside announcers, and A-Train near the start. This is how it was in WWE 2005, 12 years ago! And even then, WWE 2005 had actual storylines. It feels like 2K decided to focus more on implementing larger rosters and "sharp, fluid gameplay" rather than making things actually entertaining.
It's very jarring to have your match interrupted with an Instant Replay whenever you do something big. It's a great example of putting realism before player enjoyment. I just did the move! I know how it works! I don't need to have the pace of the match brought to a screeching halt to see it 3 more times. Save it for the post-match highlights if you need to put it somewhere. I know I can skip it, but it still throws me off, because *it doesn't happen every time you do your finisher*. You can't be prepared for it! At least you can choose to turn settings like these off.
The AI is choppy at times. Every now and again you'll get thrown to the floor and your opponent will instead step out onto the apron and throw punches at thin air. Or else your teammates/opponents will get out of te ring and not try to climb back in before the 10-count. I won't mention the glitches though. Those have been around for ages and they're not getting fixed any time soon.
One thing though - and I'm not sure if I messed up or if something's actually wrong, but in MyCareer mode, my created superstar's entrance music doesn't play despite me making 110% sure that it does. The post-match music works perfectly though. What gives?
Also - and this is something I've seen tons of other people complain about - the game keeps crashing! I have to constantly hold thumbs that the game won't conk out when I'm in the middle of doing something important. Yesterday I spent 20+ minutes tweaking my created superstar's moveset when the game crashed out of nowhere and I lost all my progress. Seriously, there's like a 50% chance that if I try to edit my character it'll crash. And then I need to wait 5 minutes for the damn thing to boot up again (if I don't give up and play something else for a while) and run the risk of it just crashing again. The PC version has been out for nearly two months! Surely this is something that could (and should) have been fixed early on? I'd be so much happier if I could just play the damn thing. Please just fix the crashing issue and I can deal with the rest. Are we just on our own from now on? This stuff is game-breaking. People are spending serious money on a game that only works when it feels like it.
It also bugs me that I can't skip cutscenes. I'm so sick of watching the RAW and SmackDown intro sequences.
I do like how they can read out my full name though :P "From Cape Town, South Africa... Adam McKay!" I never get tired of that. I also like the roster, with the potential to buy a ton of bonus superstars (and for in-game currency too, thank god!)
As I mentioned before, this game feels unfinished, making me wonder if I should have bought one of the earlier games instead. Considering that you don't really get your money's worth, I probably wouldn't recommend it to a friend. There's just so much missing from previous years that were awesome! Finisher creators, Storyline creators, Career storylines, actual voice acting! I get that the game is already 40+ GB as it is, but making it seem less sparse would definitely make people enjoy it more. As it is, I feel silly for paying so much for something with not very much to offer. I feel as though I'm lumbered with it, rather than being the proud owner of my first WWE game in 8 years.
It's not fun.

The deepest, most complex, sandbox oriented MMO I've ever played. Some will argue this is detrimental to the game, and it would be if the learning process wasn't as fun as it is. You have to take your time in this game. You will not learn it overnight, or even in months, take it one step at a time and slowly learn things as you go along. Try different activities like Exploring (great for new players), PvP, Industry. Lose some ships doing them. But most importantly; have fun. Don't min/max ISK per hour as a new player. Go at your own pace and learn things at your own pace. Try to take the mindset of enjoying losing your ship to a player that has been playing longer than you, because you learnt from that experience and can use it the next time you are in that situation. When you start applying some of the things that you learn, EVE will be one of the most rewarding experiences you can have in gaming.
Should you play it? I don't know. Try it. It's free.
P.S Join a good good Newbie Corp with good people. It helps a lot.

A great new idea that means you have to think differently to Portal 2. I enjoyed playing with the gels in Portal 2 and so I enjoyed using them in Aperture Tag.
Overall the story felt rather short and left me wanting more puzzles. I was able to finish the main campaign in about 2hr 30m. I picked this game up for about 80p and so it wasn't a big deal however I feel that if I were to pay £4 for this mod with compartively short gameplay compared to some other Portal 2 mods I would feel rather disappointed. I would recommend waiting for the product to come on sale before purchasing.
Another thing to be aware is that although the game has community maps avaliable, the game does not have an official co-op campign.
Some of the levels are recycled from the original game and you have to to a new approach to figure out how to solve them using gels rather than portals. There are a bunch of new levels and the environments are really well made. Towards the end of the game the levels have a theme to them, such as a forest theme with tree and wallpaper on the walls of the test chamber. That made a very nice change from seeing room after room made of the aperture science panels.
The narrator orb, Nigel, is the only character in the game you will meet. He's a fun, quirky character and the voice actor is rather good. You encounter him in person later on in the game and he follows you around on a track, which I found a rather neat concept.
Being able to utilise the level creator from Portal 2 and being integrated with the Steam Workshop means that there are a bunch of levels available to play besides the base game, which helps keep you amused for longer. I did not try the co-op community levels, but by the sounds of it they are a little buggy.
All in all a great mod, and I encountered very few bugs and no crashes, though I'd wait for it to come on sale before purchasing. 7/10

Playing in UAVA has some sort of play style to make up for it, you have something called "peek advantage", camping is generally not as good thing compare to other FPS because it is always the one that peeks other have advantage. If you understand the concept of matters does not travels instantly, you will understand what I'm talking about. Whatever you saw, has already happened. Let's say a 1 pinger vs a 200 pinger, and let's say the 1 pinger and 200 pinger guy rush into each other, then the 1 pinger guy land a shot on the 200 pinger guy on his screen, but the 200 pinger guy also land a shot on the 1 pinger guy. On the 200 pinger guy screen, he will not experience death until the end of the 200 milli-seconds latency, he will experience something called "no reg" it means you see successfully landed the shot and see blood spewing out but the target is not dead, because the server took the 1 pinger shot prior to the 200 pinger. Basically, having a low ping does not mean you have the peek advantage all the time, it's all about the engagement moment whether if you are the one that peeks or get peeked. A 1 pinger peeks a 200 pinger, the 1 pinger will have advantage. A 1 pinger remains stationary and gets peeked by the 200 pinger, the 200 pinger will have advantage. A 1 pinger and a 200 pinger run into each other, the 1 pinger guy will have advantage.
